The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.

p.seg: Not believing that spirits can transform,
a whirlwind blows down a living lamp-wick flower.
It is said that during the Kāiyuán era of the Great Táng,
in the region of Zhènzé,
there was an official named Liú Zhíqīng,
who had served as a Jiànyì Dàfū.
Because his memorial impeaching the Prime Minister Lǐ Línfǔ was unsuccessful,
he resigned and lived at home.
His wife had once advised her husband not to be so talkative,
so at this point, she could not help but reprimand him with a few sharp words.
That official was an upright man,
so how could he be willing to swallow his anger?
Because of this exchange of words,
the wife was unhappy in her heart
and fell ill.
They called a doctor for treatment,
but her condition fluctuated between better and worse,
and she could not fully recover.
Suddenly one night,
the lady was sitting on her bed
and ate a few mouthfuls of congee,
then called the maid to take away the bowl.
Seeing the silver lamp grow dim,
the maid said:
"Madam,
what luck to have such a large lamp-wick flower!"
The lady said:
"What joy do I have?
Just trim it off for me
so that things are bright before my eyes
and my heart feels refreshed."
The maid went forward,
used two fingers to pick up the lamp-rod and gave it a flick,
flicking off the red flame.
Suddenly the lamp light brightened,
and the spark fell onto the table.
From behind the lamp, a gust of cold wind arose,
blowing the lamp-wick flower until it spun left and right,
resembling a bead of fire.
The maid laughed and said:
"Madam, what fun,
the lamp-wick flower has come to life!"
Before she had finished speaking,
the lamp-wick flower spun three or four times,
spinning until it was as large as a bowl;
the ball rolled down to the floor
with a loud crack
like the sound of a firecracker.
The lamp-wick flower burst open,
scattering sparks all over the floor,
and instantly vanished.
In its place appeared an old woman about three feet tall,
who greeted the lady with a bow:
"This old woman heard of your illness, Madam,
and I have a dose of immortal medicine here for you to take."
At first, the lady was frightened,
but hearing her speak such words,
she took her for a manifestation of an immortal
and instead felt joyful.
Truly, medicine heals the illness that is not fatal,
and the Buddha delivers those with a karmic affinity.
She took the medicine then,
and although the illness was cured,
later this old woman actually pestered the lady,
insisting on visiting like a relative.
She would ride in a sedan chair carried by four men,
with attendants shouting in front and crowding behind,
often coming to the house to make a disturbance.
She could not be sent away,
nor could she be slighted.
If anyone contradicted her with a single word,
she would wave her hand,
and that person would fall flat on the ground.
By some unknown magic,
a heart and liver dripping with blood
would already be held in her hand.
Only after everyone begged piteously
would she throw the heart and liver into the air,
and they would naturally slip back into the dead person's mouth,
so that the person revived.
Because of this terrifying thing,
Jiànyì Liú’s entire family was distressed
and secretly sent someone to track her to her dwelling.
They saw her dive under the water of Yīngdòuhú.
Consider, what kind of water is Yīngdòuhú?
How could a home be established underwater?
It must be a demon!
They repeatedly invited ritual masters to write talismans and chant spells,
but none could restrain her,
and they instead suffered for it.
Finally, an old monk from Nánlín’àn invited a Jīedì deity,
who cast a net of heaven and earth,
and sent divine generals to capture her.
When her original form was revealed,
she was a three-foot-long macaque that had been a demon for many years.
That Jīedì was named Lóngshùwáng Púsà.
Jiànyì Liú had usually made offerings to this deity
with extreme sincerity,
so today he came specifically to rescue them
and eliminate the disaster by slaying the demon.
A poem says:
In life, one must never keep a macaque,
for their wild nature runs rampant and cannot be restrained;
do not speak of lamp-wick flowers becoming strange anomalies,
for even normally, they are prone to lewdness and theft.
That macaque resembles a human form,
and its nature is most clever,
even in common acts like climbing windows and tables,
opening trays and overturning jars,
tugging sleeves and pulling clothes,
scratching for lice,
or fiddling with its private parts,
its temperament is most uncouth.
Moreover, after many years,
how could it not become a monster?
There is also a larger kind,
named the Yuán,
which is even more agile.
Among those apes, there is a "through-arm" variety
whose two arms are connected;
as it extends one arm on that side,
the one on this side retracts,
forming one long arm stretching out.
Thus they are skilled at scaling cliffs and climbing trees.
If someone shoots an arrow at it,
it catches it if it comes from the right,
catches it if it comes from the left,
catches it if it is near,
and catches it if it is far,
completely without fear.
There are also those who have attained the Way over long years,
well-versed in Yīn and Yáng,
capable of using talismans and spells,
with vast divine powers
that cannot be fully described.
How is this seen?
One observes:
Born in the position of Shēn,
descendants from Bāshān;
born in the position of Shēn,
the descendants of the Shēnyáng official gather;
descendants from Bāshān,
the clan of the Marquis of Bāxī flourishes.
Tender hearts are easily broken
while howling at the bright moon;
who does not feel sorrow?
Long arms can connect to reach the treetops;
why fear a skilled archer?
Mathematics passed down from Fēnghòu,
who knew it was a calendar master of previous generations?
Blade techniques taught to Yúncháng,
mistaken for a swordsman of the mortal world.
Its divine power is that of the Dragon-Subduing Ancestor,
and its transformations easily outmatch the Bìmǎwēn.
It is said that during the time of Zhōu Jìng Wáng in the Spring and Autumn period,
Wú and Yuè were at war.
Wú Wáng Fū Chāi
besieged Yuè Wáng Gōu Jiàn on Kuài Jī Shān.
Fortunately, the lower Grand Master Wén Zhǒng
went with humble words and generous gifts to request a peace settlement.
Wú Wáng agreed,
stripped Yuè Wáng and his wife of their royal caps and robes,
and imprisoned them in a stone chamber
to raise horses for the state of Wú for three years
before finally releasing them to return home.
Yuè Wáng was determined to avenge this grievance,
but thinking that the state of Wú had three thousand "Fish Intestine" swords,
it would be difficult to withstand them.
The senior Grand Master Fàn Lǐ offered a plan:
select six thousand "Gentlemen Soldiers"
and train them day and night.
He heard that there was a maiden in Nán Shān
who was proficient in swordsmanship,
and by the order of Yuè Wáng,
invited her to be the national instructor.
The maiden packed her things and descended the mountain.
Halfway through her journey,
she encountered a white-haired old man
who called himself Yuán Gōng.
He said to the maiden:
"I have heard that you, young lady, are proficient in swordsmanship;
I, an old man, know a little bit of it myself,
and would like to request a trial."
The maiden said:
"I dare not hide my skills;
I leave it to the old man's trial."
Yuán Gōng looked toward the treetops,
where a stalk of withered bamboo extended out.
With a sudden leap,
he had already pulled it out
and threw it into the air to fall down.
That bamboo caught the wind
and snapped into two pieces with a crack.
The maiden caught the bamboo tip,
and Yuán Gōng caught the bamboo root.
Yuán Gōng followed the momentum to thrust at the maiden;
the maiden, calm and unhurried,
parried with the bamboo tip
and turned to strike Yuán Gōng.
Yuán Gōng flew up to the treetops,
transformed into a white ape, and departed.
It turned out the maiden was no ordinary person,
but rather the incarnation of Jiǔ Tiān Xuán Nǚ.
Because Wú Wáng was lawless,
Yù Dì sent Xuán Nǚ to the mortal world
to assist Yuè in destroying Wú.
That Yuán Gōng was a long-armed white ape from Chǔ Guó who had practiced Taoism for many years.
When Chǔ Gòng Wáng held a hunt at Jīng Shān,
he caught eighteen of Gòng Wáng's royal arrows in succession.
Gòng Wáng was furious
and summoned Chǔ Guó's foremost archer, famous for piercing a willow leaf from a hundred paces,
called Yǎng Yóu Jī,
to come and shoot him.
The white ape knew that Yǎng Yóu Jī was a divine archer,
and being unable to dodge in time,
he fled like a puff of smoke.
Gòng Wáng ordered the three armies, large and small, to surround the mountain peak
and search, but finding no trace,
they set fire to all the trees on the mountain and burned them.
To this day, the legend that Chǔ Guó's lost ape
brought disaster to the forest
is because of this.
From then on, the white ape hid in Bái Yún Dòng on Yún Mèng Shān
and concentrated on practicing Taoism.
Today, knowing well that Xuán Nǚ had descended,
he intentionally transformed into Yuán Gōng
to test her swordsmanship.
Later, the maiden met Yuè Wáng
and trained the six thousand Gentlemen Soldiers.
She neither reported back to Fàn Lǐ
nor bade farewell to Yuè Wáng,
but simply drifted away on her own.
There is a poem to testify:
How could Xuán Nǚ's divine strategy be bestowed in vain?
The six thousand gentlemen are but ordinary men.
If one wishes to know the slight wonders of Heaven,
they are already the foremost of the mortal realm.
It is said that the Chǔnǚ descended from Nánshān
and came to Yuèguó.
At that time, there were people sent by the King of Yuè to welcome her,
with fragrant carriages and precious horses,
it goes without saying.
Today she left without bidding farewell,
and could not help being alone,
amidst half-clouds and half-mist,
traveling to the old road.
She only heard a cry from within the dense forest calling "Xuánnǚ Niángniang,"
and another calling "Master."
The Chǔnǚ stayed her cloud
and looked with her wisdom-eye.
It turned out to be Yuán Gōng kneeling on both knees,
holding a stone tray with both hands.
On the tray were arranged four types of long-life fruits,
and his mouth only called out:
"Master,
have pity on your disciple's sincere heart
and take me in to instruct me."
Now, those four types of long-life fruit products
were hazelnuts,
pine nuts,
fěizǐ nuts,
and walnuts.
For example, the oranges,
pomelos,
and bayberries of the southeast,
or the línqín,
pears,
and dates of the northwest,
these are all fine items,
but in short they are only considered seasonal
and cannot last long.
Only those four types are hidden within shells;
the wind cannot dry them,
the rain cannot dampen them,
and after a long time they remain as if new.
Therefore they are called long-life fruits
and forever serve as the stored provisions of mountain dwellers.
Later, among painters, there was the "White Ape Offering Fruit Painting,"
which refers to this story.
At that moment, Yuán Gōng set down the stone tray
and kowtowed repeatedly,
calling out again:
"Master, you must take in your disciple here."
The Chǔnǚ, having been seen through by him as the incarnation of Jiǔtiān Xuánnǚ Niángniang,
said:
"I did not expect this old fellow to be so formidable."
Seeing that he was very sincere,
she then took from the four types of fruit products he offered,
taking one of each.
This was to accept his sentiment.
The rest she gave as an act of merit to the servants sent by the King of Yuè.
Thereupon, in the dense forest, Yuán Gōng
formally and correctly
knelt and bowed.
Xuánnǚ accepted it,
and from her sleeve she took out two pellets the size of longans
and gave them to Yuán Gōng.
Yuán Gōng received them with both hands
and placed them in his palms.
Seeing these pellets looking just like cast iron
and not very lustrous,
Yuán Gōng, though he said nothing,
was suspicious in his heart,
thinking:
"If they were two dumplings made of flour,
they would be good for satisfying hunger.
Even if they were made of silver,
they wouldn't weigh more than two liǎng,
which wouldn't be of much use.
If they are just two lead pellets,
I, old Yuán, do not practice using a slingshot;
what would I want them for?"
While he was hesitating here,
over there Xuánnǚ already knew.
She then blew a breath onto the pellets
and shouted "Haste!"
At once they emitted light.
In an instant,
jumping to the left
and leaping to the right,
like two golden snakes coiling and circling,
they darted back and forth around his head and neck,
bursting with ten thousand rays of cold light,
piercingly cold and hard to withstand.
His ears heard what sounded like the clashing and stabbing of a thousand knives and ten thousand blades.
Yuán Gōng was so frightened that he tightly closed his eyes,
and his mouth only cried:
"Good Master!
Your disciple already knows your divine power;
please forgive me!"
As it turned out, these two pellets
were the male and female twin swords refined by the immortals.
They could extend and contract
with infinite transformations.
If their light was withdrawn,
they were just like two lead pellets.
Should they leap up,
they could, amidst a million-strong army,
rampage and collide,
coming like an arrow
and going like the wind.
Therefore, when the immortals fly out these lead pellets,
they hit the mark a hundred times out of a hundred.
Today Xuánnǚ was merely using a small bit of her divine power to frighten Yuán Gōng.
Although it was fierce,
it only shaved off some hair from his head and eyelashes;
there was no other damage.
If his heart were not sincere,
ten thousand heads would have been taken off.
Xuánnǚ then flicked her sleeve
and withdrew the sword-light.
They were again two lead pellets,
and she took them into her sleeve.
Only then did Yuán Gōng dare to open his eyes.
He broke out in a cold sweat
and for a long while could not open his mouth.
From then on, he followed Xuánnǚ wholeheartedly back to Nánshān,
picking flowers and offering fruit in service all day long.
Xuánnǚ pitied his carefulness and prudence
and taught him all of the sword techniques.
Yuán Gōng followed the model to refine his own male and female twin swords,
which he kept in his sleeves.
They also could transform,
and he was endlessly delighted.
At this time, the King of Yuè had already led six thousand of his "Gentlemen's Army"
straight into Wúguó,
defeated Fūchāi,
and established hegemony over Jiāngdōng.
Thinking back on Xuánnǚ's previous merits,
he again sent people to Nánshān to search for her,
but there was no trace.
He immediately ordered the construction of the Xiānnǚ Temple atop Nánshān,
where sacrifices continued throughout the years.
Do you know why they could not find her?
While Yuèguó succeeded here,
over there Xuánnǚ had already gone up to Heaven to report back to Yùdì.
Moreover, with the marvelous powers of immortals,
if they want to appear they appear,
and if they want to hide they hide;
it is not something ordinary people can fathom.
Now it is said that Xuánnǚ took Yuán Gōng to Heaven
and had an audience with Yùdì.
Seeing that Yuán Gōng loved the Dào,
Yùdì enfeoffed him as the Báiyún Dòngjūn
and instructed him to take charge of the Secret Books of the Nine Heavens.
What are the Secret Books?
All the books that exist in the human world,
regardless of the Three Teachings and Nine Schools,
are all present in Heaven.
But among these books in Heaven,
those that human ears have not heard and eyes have not seen
are also countless.
Therefore they are collectively called Secret Books
and are stored in golden chests and jade boxes.
Every year on the Duānwǔ Festival in the fifth month,
the Xiūwén Shèrén comes to perform an inspection.
This is a subordinate official of the Xiūwén Yuàn.
Although Yuán Gōng was in charge,
he was bound by the prohibitions of the Heavenly Laws,
and in ordinary times he did not dare to open them privately.
Suddenly one day,
it happened to be the Great Peach Feast of the Xītiān Jīnmǔ.
Yùdì led a group of immortal officials, generals, and officers
to Kūnlún Shān's Yáochí to attend the banquet.
How can it be seen?
There is a poem in the ancient style as evidence:
Kūnlún lies on the sunny side of the Chìshuǐ,
anciently called the head of the earth and the center of heaven.
The stars and constellations hang their brilliance on the Heavenly Pillars,
and the sun and moon give way as they travel by its side.
Jade chambers and piled stones open into the Xuánpǔ,
precious trees and fine flowers have colors of antiquity.
Within, there are flat peaches ten thousand zhàng high;
they hold their buds for a thousand years before they bloom once.
A thousand years to bear fruit, a thousand years to ripen,
moist cinnabar-colored and as large as a dǒu, like red jade.
At this time, the Wángmǔ opens the birthday feast,
and a hundred thousand immortal transcendents join in joyful celebration.
The birthday banquet is grandly opened in the Bìlín Táng,
with phoenixes singing and luán birds dancing, soaring in confusion.
Jade youths lead the way holding feathered canopies,
divine consorts follow in line blowing mouth organs.
After drinking the jade nectar, their countenances are graceful,
as jade trays bring out the fruits of the immortals.
Eating them makes one's life as long as Heaven and Earth;
how could one manage to steal and taste one or two?
Although Yuán Gōng was said to practice the Way,
he had not yet attained the right fruit of enlightenment,
and since he was an official with duties in the Tiāngōng,
he could not follow along.
He was originally one who loved eating fruit most of all,
and hearing that the Pántáo were as large as bushels,
and that they only flowered and bore fruit once every three thousand years,
and that those who ate these peaches would have a lifespan equal to heaven,
how could he not salivate?
Feeling depressed,
he took out two pellets from his sleeve,
blew a breath of air,
and shouted, "Quickly!"
They transformed into male and female swords.
Jumping to the left
and leaping to the right,
he danced and played for a while,
then flicked his sleeve,
gathered the sword light,
and stored them back in his sleeve as before.
In the midst of this boredom,
he suddenly remembered
that he himself was in charge of many secret books
which he had never opened to enjoy.
Why not take a peek today for a while?
While speaking,
he glanced around with both eyes
and saw those golden cabinets and jade caskets,
all labeled with categories of the Three Teachings and Nine Schools.
Yuán Gōng looked at many marked with the Confucian label
and muttered to himself,
"That scholar business,
don't bother with it."
Pointing to those marked with the Buddhist label,
he said again,
"That yellow-faced old fellow
is also not easy to get along with."
Seeing the ones marked with the Taoist label,
he said,
"This is my old Yuán’s own profession."
In the middle was a small jade casket
with numerous seals laid across its surface.
It turned out that every year when the Xiūwén Shèrén came to inspect it,
an imperial seal was added.
One only saw seals being added, never being opened.
Yuán Gōng thought to himself,
"These layers of seals
must contain something wonderful."
He tore off the imperial seals,
and when he used both hands to lift the casket lid,
it was as if it were a single solid piece, completely unmoving.
Yuán Gōng repeatedly called it strange, saying,
"If it were an iron casket,
I would fear it had rusted shut over many years,
but this is carved from fine jade.
For it to be so tight,
I do not know which jade-smith made this;
if he had consulted with old Yuán
and polished off another thin layer,
it would be easy to open and close."
Having spoken,
he summoned all his lifelong strength
and gave it another hard lift.
That jade casket seemed as if it had been reinforced with nails
and then sealed with molten gold;
do not even think of moving it a hair.
Listeners,
if an ordinary monkey failed to open it twice,
he would inevitably grow frustrated,
using his hands to pound,
feet to stomp,
and head to butt it;
all these things are possible.
But Yuán Gōng, after all, had practiced the Way for many years,
and his fiery temper had subsided,
so how could he be willing to act rashly?
Right then, in a fluster, he held the jade casket with both hands,
bent his two old legs,
and called out,
"My teacher, Niángniáng Jiǔtiān Xuánnǚ,
please bless your disciple to have a fated connection with the Taoist arts
and open the casket lid.
I will forever be a protector of the Dharma
and dare not do wrong."
He kowtowed three or four times,
climbed up,
and lifted the jade casket again.
The lid rose easily with his hand.
Inside was a bundle wrapped in a flame-like embroidered cloth.
Opening it to look,
it was three inches long
and three inches thick,
a tiny little volume.
On the cover were three characters
called the Rúyì Cè.
Inside were detailed one hundred and eight methods of Taoist transformation:
thirty-six great transformations,
corresponding to the number of the Tiāngāng,
and seventy-two small transformations,
corresponding to the number of the Dìshà.
Truly, it contained marvelous methods for shifting the heavens and changing the stars
and wonderful uses for commanding ghosts and driving spirits.
Yuán Gōng was overjoyed in his heart
and said,
"Just this one book
is enough for old Yuán to enjoy for a lifetime!
All my life I have followed a master to receive the Way,
and today when it comes to hand,
I still picked it out myself.
It is truly 'knowing early on that the lamp is fire,
how long ago the rice was cooked'."
Yuán Gōng held the Rúyì Cè in his hand,
gave a long whistle,
flew down from the clouds,
and went straight into the Báiyún Dòng on Yúnmèng Shān.
There, the apes,
the grand-apes, and all sorts of monkeys, large and small,
danced with joy
and all came forward to pay their respects.
Yuán Gōng said,
"Now that I have obtained this book,
I shall be the founding teacher who transmits the law;
on the day I attain the Way,
every one of you will be well off.
You must take the cliffs on both sides of the cave
and plane them smooth for me;
I have a use for them."
When the monkeys heard this,
they all joined him;
which of them did not leap forward eagerly?
Some chiseled,
some polished,
and in an instant, the cliffs on both sides
were made to look like the surface of a mirror.
Yuán Gōng took out a brush and ink,
placed them on a table,
ground the ink until it was rich,
soaked the brush fully,
and on the western wall he wrote the Thirty-Six Tiāngāng Great Transformation Methods,
and on the eastern wall he wrote the Seventy-Two Dìshà Small Transformation Methods.
Then he ordered the beasts to use hammers and chisels
to carve the characters three-tenths of an inch deep.
Yuán Gōng laughed and said,
"People say there are no private favors in heaven,
so how can there be a private book?
You act as the Great Emperor of the Thirty-Three Heavens,
yet you keep such private carvings.
I, old Yuán, shall do good for others;
you, my disciples and children,
whoever wants to learn the magic, go ahead and learn."
The beasts said,
"How bitter!
How can we understand this?
We rely entirely on your guidance, Old Grandfather."
Yuán Gōng said,
"Like a maid acting as a matchmaker,
I can hardly save myself.
I, old Yuán, can only memorize it;
I haven't mastered it yet.
Just wait;
stay calm for half a month or ten days,
and wait for the time when the old Yùhuáng is silent.
I, old Yuán, will take a break
and come to this cave
to practice with you section by section."
Before he had finished speaking,
a series of booming sounds was heard.
The beasts said,
"Thunder is crashing;
it must be a change in the weather!"
Yuán Gōng said,
"This is not thunder,
but the sounding of the Announcement Drum at the Heavenly Gate.
Whenever there is a legal case to be judged in the Tiāngōng,
the Announcement Drum is beaten;
it is what the Confucian books call 'beating the drum to attack.'
You all guard the cave closely;
I, old Yuán, will go up to report for duty
and find out some news."
After speaking,
he gave a leap,
left the cave mouth,
and drifted toward the Heavenly Gate.
With this one departure,
it is destined that
Yuán Gōng will violate an unpardonable Heavenly Law
and make a heavy vow of Dharma.
Truly it is:
Though one may use infinite schemes in the heavens,
it is hard to avoid the disaster at hand today.
After all, what happened?
Please listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
Who can understand and obtain the Precious Book?
When carved, one transcends and ascends to Yíngzhōu.
It is said that the Yù Dì returned from a banquet at Yáo Chí,
and the attendants guarding the Heavenly Palace all came to receive him.
Only Yuán Gōng was missing.
An official of the Xiū Wén Yuàn, Mí Héng, courtesy name Zhèng Píng, came forward and memorialized:
"The Lord of Bái Yún Dòng has privately distributed secret books;
he stole the Rú Yì Cè and has been in the mortal realm for seven days already!"
The Yù Dì was greatly shocked and said:
"This Rú Yì Cè contains the secret methods of the Jiǔ Tiān
and must not be leaked to the human world.
Because the hearts of people in the world are not upright,
if they obtain this book, they will surely cause trouble and harm the people.
That beast's animal heart has not changed;
he has violated the laws of Heaven
and cannot be forgiven!
Immediately, the report drums of the Heavenly Gate were sounded,
and the hundred gods all arrived.
The Yù Dì issued an imperial decree,
ordering the Thunder God Fēng Lóng to dispatch the Léi Gōng and Diàn Mǔ of his department
to descend to the lower world with all haste,
capture Yuán Gōng and bring him to the Xiū Wén Yuàn,
and instructed the officials of that office to join with the Běi Dǒu Zhēn Jūn
to interrogate him and execute the law.
Now, Yuán Gōng had just arrived at the Heavenly Gate to scout for news.
When he heard this news,
he muttered to himself:
"Which talkative gossip
wasn't busy taking a nap over there,
but instead went to report the news
and stir up such trouble?
I should pack the Rú Yì Cè properly
and put it back inside the jade casket;
then I'll just deny everything when the time comes.
As he walked,
he reached out to feel his sleeve,
but it was an empty sleeve.
He was startled,
realizing it was still on the stone bed
and he hadn't brought it with him.
He hurriedly turned his cloud around and returned to Bái Yún Dòng.
The crowd of young apes and monkeys,
seeing Yuán Gōng return so quickly,
swarmed forward to ask for news.
At this moment, how could Yuán Gōng have the heart to say a single word to them?
He stretched out both arms to push them aside,
rushed straight to the stone bed,
took the Rú Yì Cè,
and turned around to ascend to the Heavenly Gate again.
He happened to run right into the group of holy beings including Léi Gōng and Diàn Mǔ,
riding on thunder chariots
and rushing forward.
Diàn Mǔ then brandished her lightning bolts wildly,
her fiery whips danced in the air,
like golden snakes leaping and darting.
Yuán Gōng was greatly shocked and said:
"This old woman is quite formidable!
She actually knows a fair bit of sword arts!"
Just as he was about to reach for his male and female pellets to fight her,
he saw Xiè Xiān and the others from the Department of Thunder beating the continuous drums,
with a sound like mountains crumbling and the earth collapsing.
Thunderous flames blazed all around,
clearly trapping Yuán Gōng within a city of fire.
He almost had his fur scorched off,
so frightened that Yuán Gōng covered his ears,
closed his eyes,
and shouted:
"Everyone, let's talk this out;
don't be so rough!"
Léi Gōng said:
"By the divine decree of the High Sovereign,
we are here to retrieve the Rú Yì Cè from you.
Whether you have it or not, come to the Xiū Wén Yuàn to answer."
Yuán Gōng replied repeatedly:
"I have it,
have it,
have it."
He thought to himself:
"Since the Sovereign has an order to seize me,
why am I being taken to the Xiū Wén Yuàn?
It must be that they want me to retrieve the original book.
This Xiū Wén Yuàn is like my own home to old Yuán;
I only need to take it out from my sleeve and that will be that."
By now, his terror had already subsided by most part;
besides, seeing the divine powers of the Thunder Department, how would he dare to resist?
Immediately, Xiè Xiān took an iron chain and placed it around Yuán Gōng's neck.
Riding on the thunder chariot,
they entered the Heavenly Gate in an instant
and headed straight for the Xiū Wén Yuàn.
It was truly a case of the Azure Dragon and the White Tiger walking together;
whether it would be auspicious or disastrous was entirely uncertain.
Now, as for that official of Xiū Wén, Mí Héng,
he had already taken his seat.
What was his character like?
There is a "Xī Jiāng Yuè" stanza
as evidence:
His compositions surpassed the eminent scholars of his time;
possessing talent, he dared to look down upon kings and nobles.
The visiting card in his pocket was worn but not lightly presented;
only Kǒng and Yáng were his good friends.
A tragic dream before the Yīng Wǔ Zhōu;
sorrowful sounds within the Yú Yáng drums.
His whole life of integrity marked him as a pure soul;
he received a post at the Xiū Wén of the Heavenly Palace.
Before long,
banners and precious canopies were seen,
surrounding the Běi Dǒu Xīng Jūn as he arrived.
How was this seen?
There is also a "Xī Jiāng Yuè" stanza
as evidence:
The mechanisms of the Seven Governors are precise;
the root of Yīn and Yáng lies in the humble gateway.
Shè Tí follows the handle to point at the stars;
the four of the Dipper and the three of the Handle are fixed.
The Way of Heaven arises in the south and moves to the north;
the Seven Lords manage the judicial proceedings clearly.
Zhāo Yáo and Xuán Wǔ surround the forward banners,
and do not allow human laws to interfere.
At that moment, the Xiū Wén Shè Rén descended the steps to receive him and perform rites,
asking the Xīng Jūn to sit in the seat of honor.
Meanwhile, Léi Gōng and Diàn Mǔ escorted Yuán Gōng into the Xiū Wén Yuàn for the transfer;
once they had returned the imperial decree,
they went back to their own departments.
As for Yuán Gōng, having been troubled and agitated by the thunder and lightning,
by the time he reached the academy,
he was as if in a daze or a dream.
The attendants and soldiers on both sides
forced him to kneel below the steps
and reported in a loud voice:
“The book-stealing thief has been captured and brought before you!”
Yuán Gōng raised his head to look,
seeing two rows of banners and pennants neatly arranged
and staves set out in a solemn display.
Looking upward,
there sat two presiding officials in an upright manner.
On the right was the Xiū Wén Shè Rén,
who held authority over this academy,
and Yuán Gōng did not pay him much mind;
on the left, in black robes and holding a jade tablet,
he clearly recognized Běi Dǒu Xīng Jūn!
This shock was no small matter,
for it is said that Nán Dǒu governs life,
and Běi Dǒu governs death!
Regardless of whether one's lifespan is as short as that of Yán Huí or Yáng Wū,
if one could beg Nán Dǒu Xīng Jūn to add a few strokes to the record,
one could live to a hundred and ninety,
and even Yán Luó Tiān Zǐ would not dare to think of meeting him;
but if one provoked the temper of Běi Dǒu Xīng Jūn
and he moved the tip of his brush even slightly,
one’s life would be ended instantly,
and even if the Yù Dì issued a thousand imperial pardons,
there would be no hope of returning to life!
In such a perilous situation today, how could he not be terrified?
At that moment, Yuán Gōng did not wait for those above to speak,
but held up the Rú Yì Bǎo Cè with both hands to offer it up,
kowtowing repeatedly
and only crying out that he had committed a capital offense.
Běi Dǒu Xīng Jūn shouted:
“Vile creature!
You dared to open the heavenly seal without permission
and secretly stole the hidden methods.
This is even worse than a guardian stealing from the trust,
and you deserve to be sentenced to decapitation!”
Yuán Gōng could only beg for his life,
kowtowing without end.
Nǐ Héng Shè Rén asked:
“Have you leaked the secrets of heaven?
Speak the truth!”
Yuán Gōng said:
“I, old Yuán, have never told a lie in my life.
The various methods of transformation within that Rú Yì Cè
have already been neatly engraved on the stone walls on both sides of Bái Yún Dòng.
As for leaking it,
I truly have not met with any living person.”
The Xīng Jūn thought to himself:
This creature is actually quite honest.
He shouted again:
“You engraved the secret volume onto the stone walls—
what was your intent?”
Yuán Gōng said:
“I have often heard it said that the High Emperor is selfless,
and yet I do not believe there should be the word 'secret'.
If one speaks of a 'secret',
then there would be no need to leave behind a written record.
Since a written record was left,
then it must be meant to be passed down through ten thousand ages.
The Yù Dì keeps it in a chest,
and I, old Yuán, carve it in stone—
the intention is one and the same.”
The Shè Rén shouted:
“Creature, stop using such specious arguments!”
Yuán Gōng hurriedly kowtowed,
repeatedly crying that he had committed a capital offense,
saying:
“I, old Yuán, have been foolishly honest all my life,
and I am merely stating my case based on logic;
how would I dare to argue stubbornly?”
The Shè Rén said:
“I have heard that this jade chest is a magical treasure of the Heavenly Court
and has three conditions under which it will not open:
it will not open without the decree of Hùn Yuán Lǎo Zǔ,
it will not open without the decree of Jiǔ Tiān Xuán Nǚ Niáng Niáng,
and it will not open without the decree of Yù Dì.
You hairy creature,
how were you able to open it?”
Yuán Gōng said:
“At first,
I truly could not open it despite trying two or three times.
Afterward, I focused my mind and took refuge in my master, Jiǔ Tiān Xuán Nǚ Niáng Niáng,
praying for her to bless her disciple as one destined for the Daoist arts
to serve as a Dharma protector forever
and never dare to do wrong.
Only then did the lid of the chest instantly lift.
If it had remained unliftable to the end,
I, old Yuán, would have given up;
surely I would not have called a jade-carver to grind it open to see.
Had I known the laws of heaven were so strict,
Xuán Nǚ Niáng Niáng should not have allowed this crime to be pinned on me.
In the past, I often lamented that the paths of the world are narrow,
where often over a single invitation card
or a single piece of writing,
crimes are laid upon people.
I did not expect that even in the vastness of the Heavenly Court,
for the sake of looking at a tiny book only three inches long,
they would not recognize my heart that loves the Dao,
but instead convict me as a book-stealing thief.
My regret is beyond reach,
and I cannot die content.”
When Nǐ Héng Shè Rén heard those few lines about the paths of the world being narrow,
his expression changed with sadness,
thinking of how he himself had offended Liú Biǎo,
also because of a single letter from Sūn Cè.
Furthermore, being upright by nature
and seeing Yuán Gōng's passionate words
and the flow of his tears,
his heart felt great pity.
He said to Běi Dǒu Xīng Jūn:
“What this hairy creature says
is quite reasonable.
When considering the transmission of Daoist arts,
there is also fate involved.
Moreover, he is a distinguished disciple of Jiǔ Tiān Xuán Nǚ Niáng Niáng.
I must trouble you, Zhēn Jūn, to join me in petitioning before the Yù Dì
to allow him to turn over a new leaf.
I wonder what is the Zhēn Jūn's opinion?”
The Xīng Jūn said:
“He was originally personnel under your jurisdiction, sir.
I leave the decision to you.
However, since this interrogation
is known to all the gods,
a formal confession must be prepared
so that we may report back.”
The Shè Rén said:
“The Zhēn Jūn's words are very appropriate.”
He then ordered the attendants to give paper, ink, brush, and inkstone to Yuán Gōng.
By this time, Yuán Gōng knew that the Shè Rén intended to help him escape his crime
and was overjoyed.
He hurriedly took the brush and wrote:
Confession:
Yuán Gōng, age unknown,
has long resided in Bái Yún Dòng on Yún Mèng Shān to practice the Dao.
Due to the recommendation of my master, Jiǔ Tiān Xuán Nǚ Niáng Niáng,
I received the Emperor's grace and was enfeoffed as Bái Yún Dòng Jūn,
to manage the secret books of the Nine Heavens.
Attached to the Xiū Wén Yuàn,
I served as a guardian for many years
without any fault.
Recently, because the immortals of the Nine Heavens all went to the Pán Táo birthday banquet,
I considered my own humble Dao and thin virtue, being unable to accompany them.
I wrongly opened the heavenly seal privately,
desiring to glimpse the secret volume.
Twice I failed to lift the lid of the chest.
Only after praying with a focused heart for the protection of my master, Jiǔ Tiān Xuán Nǚ Niáng Niáng,
did I finally open the chest and see the book.
Recklessly thinking that the heavens are selfless
and wishing to make it immortal in the human world,
I then engraved the text of the volume onto the walls of Bái Yún Dòng.
I believed in the predestined nature of the Law,
yet my unauthorized actions are indefensible.
However, all this stemmed from a heart that loves the Dao
and was without selfish thoughts or wicked schemes.
If I am granted a pardon,
I am willing to focus my mind on protecting the Law
and dare not recklessly leak it to mortals.
If I go against my word,
may Heaven strike me and Earth destroy me.
The above confession is the truth.
Běidǒu Xīngjūn finished reading the deposition,
laughed, and said:
"You have certainly described yourself as perfectly clean."
Yuán Gōng jumped up and said:
"I, Old Yuán, am not only clean in body,
but also clean in heart.
When I say 'one,' it is 'one';
when I say 'two,' it is 'two.'
I am not like others who gossip and double-talk."
The Shèrén and those around all burst out laughing.
Immediately, Xīngjūn and the Shèrén rose
and led Yuán Gōng directly to the Língxiāo Bǎodiàn,
reporting back to the Yùdì:
"Although Yuán Gōng's crime is deep,
his circumstances and words are pitiable.
Moreover, the Hùnyuán Lǎozǔ once left behind four lines:
'When the jade casket opens,
Yuán shall come;
When the jade casket closes,
Yuán shall go.'
The word for predestined 'Yuán' is the same as the name 'Yuán.'
Perhaps Yuán Gōng has this predestined affinity,
which is why the jade casket opened by itself.
Since he has no wicked heart,
it is appropriate, for the sake of Jiǔtiān Xuánnǚ,
to release him with leniency."
The Yùdì granted the request,
spared him the death penalty,
stripped him of the title Lord of Báiyún Dòng,
changed it to Bǎiyuán Shén,
and ordered him to guard the stone wall of Báiyún Dòng.
He also first issued a celestial decree
ordering the local Chénghuáng and Tǔdì
to drive away all the ape offspring
and all their kind.
Within ten lǐ,
none were permitted to stay;
only Yuán Gōng alone was allowed to reside there.
If he should recklessly pass teachings to mortals
or cause disasters and trouble,
he would be punished accordingly.
After Yuán Gōng finished expressing his gratitude,
the Yùdì passed an edict
bestowing the white jade treasure censer from before the imperial presence upon Yuán Gōng.
This censer was named the Zìzài Lú.
When Yuán Gōng practiced cultivation in the grotto,
the curling incense smoke from the censer
would naturally be continuous
and rise straight to the Tiānmén.
If Yuán Gōng left the grotto entrance,
the incense smoke would then be extinguished.
This clearly used the bit of true fire in the censer
to subdue Yuán Gōng's wild ambitions
and prevent him from becoming distracted.
Yuán Gōng thanked him again
and petitioned:
"The Báiyún Dòng on Yúnmèng Shān where I reside,
though dangerous and remote,
is not entirely cut off from the mortal world.
I have heard that the celestial official Zhāng Kǎi can create a five-lǐ mist.
I beg for the celestial grace to borrow it
to conceal the grotto entrance,
so as to avoid prying eyes from outside."
The Yùdì granted the request, saying:
"If you want mist, there is no need to trouble the celestial official."
He then called for the keeper of the Tiānkù
to bring out a rare and priceless treasure.
This treasure was named Wùmǔ.
It turns out the upper realm has Four Mothers,
all of which are the supreme treasures of heaven:
The first is Qìmǔ,
which encompasses the Primordial Qi.
The vast universe
revolves within it.
This is the very cloth bag held in the hand of the Chán Master Mílè.
There is a poem to testify:
The monk's belly is like an urn,
his eyes smile until they are but slits.
He carries the cloth bag from morning to night,
knowing not its weight in his hand.
Ask him what is in the bag:
the wondrous use of the Primordial Qi of Yin and Yang.
Laughing at the sentient beings of the world,
like fleas and lice moving about in a pocket.
The second is Fēngmǔ,
which stores the winds of the eight directions.
How is this seen?
The Tāofēng of the East,
the Xūnfēng of the South,
the Biāofēng of the West,
the Hánfēng of the North,
the Zhángfēng of the Southeast,
the Róngfēng of the Northeast,
the Jùfēng of the Southwest,
and the Lìfēng of the Northwest.
These eight winds wax and wane within the wind bag,
and the Wind God Fēilián governs them.
There is also a poem to testify:
In the human world there is still a history of governing winds,
how much more so in the Heavenly Court—could there be no master?
With a deer's body and a snake's tail, he is called Fēilián,
the Wind God's merit has always matched the rain.
The maiden goes before as Mèngmǔ goes wild,
Zhédān points the way as Fēngyí is busy.
Even if it has the power to soar a thousand lǐ,
it never leaves the breathing of a single wind bag.
The third is Yúnmǔ,
formed when Chaos first divided
from the condensed vapors of mountains and rivers.
It is round like a flowery canopy,
and its clouds are of various five colors.
If the year is one of abundance,
the cloud color is yellow;
if there are soldiers and bandits,
the cloud color is blue-green;
if there is death and mourning,
the cloud color is white.
Black clouds govern floods,
and red clouds govern drought.
If the five colors are clear and azure,
this is a sign of auspiciousness.
The Cloud Master Píngyì governs it.
There is also a poem to testify:
Though "white clothes and gray dogs" are unintentional,
red stamens and golden feathers also have their signs.
If the Cloud Master had no official duties,
how could the Bǎozhāng identify the causes of cloud phenomena?
The fourth is Wùmǔ,
shaped like a cloth curtain about eight or nine feet long,
also called the Wùmù.
As soon as it is slightly unrolled,
it is clearly like a steam basket just being opened,
with thick steam spraying out.
If it is fully unrolled,
it spreads for a hundred lǐ,
shrouding the entire universe in darkness.
When it is rolled up,
it is like a suction tube in water,
and the mist is immediately stored away.
Back when Xuānyuán Huángdì was on the throne,
there was a feudal lord who was most lawless,
named Chīyóu.
He obtained this Wùmù
and could call forth a great mist.
He also created swords and halberds
and great crossbows,
and thus relied on his own strength, believing himself matchless in the world,
stirring up the masses to rebel
to seize Huángdì's realm.
Huángdì fought a great battle with Chīyóu on the plains of Zhuōlù,
and the whole army was confused by the mist,
unable to distinguish east from west.
For three days and three nights,
they could not achieve victory.
Thankfully, Jiǔtiān Xuánnǚ descended
and granted Huángdì the secret strategies of the Yīnfú,
and constructed a chariot
named the Zhǐnánchē.
On the chariot stood a wooden figure;
the wooden figure extended one hand,
and the hand extended one finger.
Regardless of how the chariot turned left or right,
this wooden figure's hand and finger
pointed accurately toward the south.
He immediately defeated Chīyóu,
pursued him, and beheaded him.
His blood flowed upon the ground
and turned into salt.
The Salt Lake north of Qìngyáng Fǔ in Shǎnxī today is that very place.
Because he created weapons,
his transgressions were deep and heavy;
therefore, the common people of all generations
eat his blood.
This Wùmù was retrieved by Jiǔtiān Xuánnǚ,
presented to the Yùdì,
and stored in the Tiānkù.
There is also a poem to testify:
The divine manifestation of Huángdì was a sage ruler,
the wild evil of Chīyóu was also a baneful star.
If the Wùmù had not been returned to the Tiānkù,
how could the sky have cleared for the sun and moon to shine?
Later people also had a poem saying:
The wonders of the Four Mothers were unheard of in antiquity,
who knows what is false and what is true in the Heavenly Realm?
The gathering and dispersal of wind and clouds follow the principles of Yin and Yang,
do not say that each take shape and has its own god.
This poem refutes the four rare treasures—the Qìmǔ,
the Wind Bag,
the Cloud Canopy,
and the Wùmù—
claiming they are absurd stories.
They do not know that this is the view of someone looking at the sky from the bottom of a well,
those of shallow vision and limited knowledge.
If a mirror can draw fire,
a clam can produce water,
a fierce tiger can create wind,
and a lizard can cause hail,
there are many strange and wondrous things in the world
that are inconceivable,
how much more so the affairs of the Heavenly Realm.
Now, let us set aside this idle talk.
It is said that Yù Dì saw that Yuán Gōng was wholeheartedly protecting the Law,
with no deceit,
and furthermore, since he was a disciple of Jiǔ Tiān Xuán Nǚ,
He took this Mist Curtain and gave it to Yuán Gōng,
to serve as a treasure for the eternal protection of the cave entrance.
He instructed him:
“This curtain should only be unfolded a little more than a foot,
then there will be ten lǐ of mist;
it must not be fully unfolded,
for fear that it would be inconvenient for the people of the world.”
He further said:
“From this day forward, if you reform your ways and turn toward the good,
and focus your mind on cultivating the Way,
there will still be a day for you to ascend.
Otherwise,
heavenly execution shall not be pardoned,
and you will fall forever into the Wú Jiàn Dì Yù.”
Yuán Gōng continuously uttered his assent
and bowed in farewell to Yù Dì.
At that moment, the Xiū Wén Shè Rén bowed again
and requested the imperial seal
to reseal the jade casket,
which was then kept in the Xiū Wén Yuàn.
Běi Dǒu Xīng Jūn also bowed in farewell and departed.
Yuán Gōng went again to the Xiū Wén Yuàn to thank the Shè Rén,
and went to the Běi Dǒu Sī to thank the Xīng Jūn.
Holding the white jade incense burner in his right hand
and tucking the Mist Curtain under his left arm,
he then left the Heavenly Realm
and headed toward Bái Yún Dòng on Yún Mèng Shān.
That troop of monkeys and apes,
and others of their kind,
had already been entirely driven away by the local Chéng Huáng, Shān Shén, and Tǔ Dì acting upon a heavenly decree;
Yuán Gōng was all alone,
which was incredibly pitiful,
but he was glad to have his life
and to have obtained two supreme treasures,
which is truly a case of 'one part sorrow and one part joy.'
He then placed the precious incense burner in front of the stone chamber,
and immediately a dense fragrance wafted about,
rising straight beyond the nine heavens.
He also unfolded the Mist Curtain by a little over a foot
and hung it at the cave entrance;
as expected, white vapor rose into the air,
and in an instant,
it dispersed into ten lǐ of thick fog,
wrapping the mountain cave as if in white flour,
so that nothing outside the cave could be seen,
and presumably, it was the same for those outside looking into the cave.
Yuán Gōng said with great joy:
“Most things in the world are famous in name but lacking in reality;
even the name of this cave has always been a hollow reputation,
but today it finally does not bear the name of Bái Yún Dòng in vain.”
Having spoken,
he bowed before the precious incense burner
and kowtowed four times
to thank the Heavenly Grace.
From then on, he did this every day,
not daring to be negligent.
Every year, on the hour of Wǔ Shí of the Duān Wǔ Rì in the fifth month,
he would roll up the Mist Curtain,
go to the Tiān Tíng,
and have an audience with Yù Dì once to repent for his sins;
once the Wǔ Shí had passed,
he would return to the cave,
and again unfold and hang the Mist Curtain,
cutting off the inside from the outside,
as if it were another world.
The inside of the cave was quite spacious,
with various famous flowers and exotic fruits
available in all four seasons,
which was sufficient for Yuán Gōng to enjoy.
From then on, Yuán Gōng only cultivated his reality and nourished his nature within the cave;
in his leisure, he would take out the male and female pellets
to play and dance for amusement.
Although the two walls were engraved with one hundred and eight methods of transformation,
upon careful investigation,
they were all tricks of 'stealing the sky and changing the sun'
or of 'chasing and seizing souls,'
among which were the various harmful arts of bean-men and paper-horses,
and ghost-blades and spirit-swords.
Yuán Gōng said:
“No wonder Yù Dì was so secretive and protective of them,
not allowing them to be leaked to the human world.
These kinds of techniques
are clearly the heterodox paths of Jīn Gāng Chán,
and have nothing to do with one's own nature.
Had I known this earlier,
it would have been better not to have opened the jade casket.”
His heart was filled with irremediable regret,
and he took a brush to add several lines of characters after those on the stone wall, saying:
“These are the secret methods of the Jiǔ Tiān,
cherished by Shàng Dì.
If anyone in the future is destined to obtain them,
they should only act on behalf of Heaven,
protecting the state and blessing the people.
Every year, at the Zǐ Shí of the night of the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month,
with a knife in the mouth and hair disheveled,
climb onto the roof and straddle the ridge,
and make an oath to the Běi Dǒu:
‘I, your disciple [Name], have practiced these arts of the Way
for so many years now,
and have committed no errors;
if I cause trouble or harm the people,
may the Léi Shén strike me down.’”
There were seventy-six characters in total,
engraved according to the previous style.
Dear reader,
what was the meaning of this?
It was because Yuán Gōng had made a confession and a vow at the Xiū Wén Yuàn,
and he feared that if someone obtained the arts in the future
with an improper mind,
the consequences would be no small matter.
He himself had been captured by the Léi Shén
and interrogated by the Běi Dǒu Xīng Jūn,
so he said that the practitioners should report to the Běi Dǒu,
and those who cause trouble would receive retribution from the Léi Shén.
The twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month is the time when Yù Dì descends;
only now is it seen that Yuán Gōng’s heart truly loved the Way
and had no selfish thoughts.
Nevertheless,
as I see it,
by still engraving them on the stone wall,
he invited this further trouble.
I suppose it was fated to be so,
which is why the Tiān Tíng did not order him to destroy them.
Because of this,
there is a story to tell:
Within the Cliff of White Mist,
he would again encounter a thief of the book;
in the world of red dust,
the calamity of meddling with the law would suddenly arise.
Truly it is said:
It is better to have no trouble than to have it,
how can the human heart compare to the leisure of the heart of the Way?
After all, who would later steal the arts,
and what troubles would arise?
Please listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
Transformations arise in many ways,
but no illusion ever surpasses the fox.
Feigning a Buddha or posing as a god, they are unrecognized;
why doubt the Shèng Gū Gū of today?
It is said that among all insects and beasts,
many have the power of transformation,
such as the black-fish man,
the white-conch beauty,
tigers becoming monks or old women,
bulls calling themselves kings,
leopards calling themselves generals,
dogs acting as masters,
deer as Daoist priests,
and wolves as small children;
these are seen in stories and other books,
too numerous to count.
Among them, only the two types, apes and monkeys,
are the most spiritual.
Yet they are ultimately not as adept as foxes at becoming demons and causing mischief,
with their many varied deeds.
The fox is born with a sharp mouth and a pointed nose,
a small head and a large tail,
and yellow fur;
as for the Xuán Hú and the white foxes,
they have lived long lives and their colors have changed.
According to the Xuán Zhōng Jì:
“A fox can transform into a human at the age of fifty;
at a hundred, it can know things a thousand lǐ away;
at a thousand, it can communicate with Heaven;
humans cannot control it,
and it is called a Tiān Hú.”
They are naturally good at bewitching
and their transformations are infinite.
Thus, from ancient times to the present,
foxes have often been compared to humans.
For instance, if someone's appearance is seductive,
it is called hú mèi;
if their mind is unsettled,
it is called hú yí;
taking the false for the true
is called hú jiǎ;
and a group of cronies
is called a hú qún.
Dear reader,
listen as I explain the two characters for "fox-charm":
Generally, when a vixen wants to entice a man,
she transforms into a beautiful woman.
When a male fox wants to entice a woman,
he transforms into a handsome man.
They all harvest the other's Yin essence and Yang blood
to aid in their spiritual cultivation.
You might ask what magic they use for transformation;
they possess this magical technique by nature.
For instance, if a vixen wants to become a woman,
she must use the skull cap of a deceased woman;
if a male fox wants to become a man,
he must also use the skull cap of a deceased man.
They take it and wear it upon their own heads,
then bow toward the moon.
If it is not the proper time for transformation,
the skull cap will come rolling down;
but if it remains firmly on the head
and they complete the full forty-nine bows,
they will immediately transform into the shape of a man or woman.
They pluck a few leaves and flower petals to cover their bodies,
which then become fashionable garments of five colors.
When people see their beautiful looks and grand attire,
and hear their charming speech and lovely laughter,
even without approaching them closely,
there are none who are not utterly captivated.
Aside from righteous husbands and chaste wives,
nine and a half out of ten others will fall into their trap;
therefore, it is called "fox-charm."
Not only this,
they can also appear as Buddhas when meeting monks
and claim to be immortals when encountering Daoists,
tricking people into worshiping and offering sacrifices to them.
Thus, in the Táng dynasty, there were tales of fox deities,
and every household offered them sacrifices,
not daring to be neglectful.
At that time, there was a proverb:
"No fox, no village."
Although this was news from the Five Dynasties period,
their kind has never been extinguished to this day.
A poem says:
Everything in this world can become false,
how can the demon fox alone be taken as real?
If human nature were free from falsehood and deceit,
the demon fox would surely incur the wrath of Heaven.
It is said that in the first year of the Xiánpíng era of the Great Sòng,
Emperor Zhēnzōng ascended the throne.
At that time, the people were at peace and the nation was prosperous,
which goes without saying.
Now, it is told that in Zǐtóng Village, Āndé Prefecture, Xīchuān,
there lived a hunter
surnamed Zhào and named Yī.
He was originally from a fallen wealthy family,
and because he was the eldest,
people called him Zhào Dàláng.
That Zhào Yī had a wife
surnamed Qián,
who was the daughter of Squire Qián of the prefecture.
She was just twenty-two years old
and was quite beautiful.
Zhào Yī made a living by hunting,
while Qián Shì stayed in their thatched hut,
doing needlework
to help the family get by.
She was chaste and virtuous by nature,
and everyone respected her.
One day she went out to draw water,
and who would have thought she would be spotted by a demon fox.
That beast conceived a lustful heart
and intended to seduce her.
It transformed into the appearance of a handsome scholar,
wearing a set of neat clothes.
Every day it waited for her husband to go out,
then went to her doorstep,
either standing or sitting there.
Sometimes it would pretend to be hungry or thirsty,
asking for a drink or water,
trying to get the woman to speak.
It would also deliberately utter a few flirtatious words,
but the woman's heart was as firm as stone
and she remained entirely unmoved;
thus, it could not charm her.
For two consecutive days,
Zhào Yī ran into that scholar at his own doorstep.
Seeing that his movements were somewhat suspicious,
he asked for his name.
The scholar replied:
"This humble one is surnamed Hú and named Chù.
I am studying in the village ahead
and strolled here for leisure."
Zhào Yī intended to visit the village ahead to inquire,
but there was no such person,
which made him even more suspicious.
Suddenly one day,
Qián Shì rose early to comb her hair
and found that a silver hairpin for securing her bun was missing.
She searched through her shirts,
sleeves,
baskets,
chests,
cosmetic boxes,
and bedding.
There was only a mouse hole at the base of the wall,
which she also inspected several times with a lamp,
but there was no sign of it.
By noon when the rice was cooked,
she lifted the pot lid,
and there was the hairpin, perfectly upright,
inserted into the center of the rice pot.
When she pulled it out to look,
it was once again strange:
inside this boiling hot rice pot,
the hairpin was still cold.
Qián Shì feared her husband would not believe her,
so she kept it to herself and did not mention it.
Another day, she rose early and got out of bed,
and just as she was about to put on her embroidered shoes,
she found one was missing.
Zhào Yī said:
"I suppose a cat carried it off.
Just change into another pair."
That day, Zhào Yī returned shortly after leaving.
He pulled an embroidered shoe from his sleeve to show his wife, saying:
"Is this yours?"
Qián Shì said:
"It is indeed.
Where did you find it?"
Zhào Yī said:
"Three lǐ away,
it was hanging on a pomegranate tree.
Is that not a strange thing!"
Only then did Qián Shì dare to take the matter of the silver hairpin
and speak of it to her husband.
Zhào Yī said:
"This must be the work of mountain spirits or wild demons.
As the saying goes:
'Observe the strange without being startled,
and the strangeness will dissipate of itself.'
Just ignore it."
From then on, strange occurrences in the Zhào family's house continued without end,
but no harm was done.
The couple could do nothing about it
and simply ignored it.
Later they grew accustomed to it
and paid it even less attention.
At that time, the Chóngyáng Festival was approaching.
The winds were high and the grass was withered,
making it the perfect time for hunting.
Zhào Yī and several other hunters,
with their hawks and hounds,
carrying their bows and arrows,
each wielding the tools they were accustomed to,
left Zǐtóng Village
to go hunting in the mountains.
One saw:
Everyone showing off their bravery,
each boasting of their strength.
The brave ones said
a single arrow could pierce two vultures.
The boastful ones said
one man could kill two tigers.
There was barking and baying,
shouting and calling.
The sounds were mournful;
those terrified were none other than wild beasts and birds.
Some were dead,
some were alive;
flesh and blood dripped.
Those bound were always creatures with fur and horns.
Hawks and hounds flatter humans, putting on a show,
while blades and spears are inherently heartless when meeting an object.
They only seek to catch more to make a living,
letting others call them bird-thieves as they please.
Zhào Yī and a group of hunters were hunting in a circle.
As evening approached,
they had caught some game,
muntjacs,
deer,
rabbits, and the like,
and the men divided them equally.
Just as they were about to turn back,
suddenly, from within a hollow in the mountain,
a group of badgers rushed out.
The hunters said,
"Let us each display our skills
to catch those badgers.
To the one who catches one first,
we shall all come forward to offer congratulations."
Zhào Yī said,
"Well said."
He told several unskilled farmhands to guard the hawks and hounds.
Zhào Yī took up a steel fork
and, along with five or six brave men each holding spears or clubs, rushed swiftly upward.
That group of badgers, being pressed hard by the men,
scattered and fled,
so the men split up to pursue them.
Zhào Yī fixed his gaze on an enormous hog-badger
and chased after it with all his might.
After about two or three lǐ of road,
the badger disappeared.
Reluctant to give up,
Zhào Yī ran to a high place to look out.
He saw the badger still among the wild grass below the front mountain slope,
leaping east and burrowing west,
seeking a hole to hide in.
Zhào Yī chased it again with all his might,
turning past several mountain slopes,
but the badger had run off and was gone.
He saw only a large-antlered deer
grazing below the slope.
Seeing someone coming, the deer fled.
Zhào Yī said,
"Though I failed to catch the badger,
if I can get this deer,
it will also serve to save my face."
He hurriedly took off his cloth shirt,
tied it around his waist,
and rushed up the slope, chasing it for a good long way,
but the deer also disappeared.
He heard only the chaotic sound of a spring.
Zhào Yī had run until his mouth was parched;
just as he was looking for a mouthful of water to drink,
he looked at several mountain streams,
but they were all small places
and not very clean.
Following the source of the flowing spring,
he searched his way up.
After walking for another stretch,
he went straight into the mountain hollow,
where a stream of clear spring water
cascaded down like a pearl curtain.
To one side was a pool;
inside the pool were nothing but pebbles,
and it was crystal clear to the bottom.
Zhào Yī put down his steel fork,
scooped up water with his hands,
took several gulps,
and said,
"That is enough."
Seeing that it was already getting dark,
he picked up his steel fork and turned to leave.
He did not realize that he had already traveled more than twenty lǐ.
It was the eighth day of the ninth month;
the sunlight had just faded,
and half a bright moon had already appeared.
Having come in high spirits
and leaving in disappointment,
he took one step after another.
After walking for no more than one or two lǐ,
under the moonlight,
he saw from a distance in the woods ahead
some moving shadows.
Zhào Yī stopped in his tracks,
and when he fixed his eyes to look,
it turned out to be a wild fox
with a piece of a dead person's skull balanced on its head,
bowing incessantly toward the bright moon.
Zhào Yī said,
"Strange!
I have often heard people say
that foxes can transform themselves.
Could it be that this wicked beast is practicing this craft?
I will watch quietly to see what it does."
He saw the fox bow for a long time.
As Zhào Yī watched,
it began to look like a handsome man,
no different from the scholar Hú Chù he had seen before.
Zhào Yī said,
"So that is how it is."
Feeling a great surge of anger in his heart,
he quietly put down the steel fork,
unslung his bow,
and notched an arrow.
Drawing the bow to its full,
the arrow flew swiftly.
Aiming right at the fox's body, the arrow whistled toward it.
He shouted,
"Hit!"
Indeed, an open spear is easy to dodge,
but a hidden arrow is hard to defend.
It struck the fox squarely in the left leg.
The fox gave a loud cry,
clawed the skull down,
returned to its original form,
and fled with the arrow still in it.
Firstly because it was late,
and secondly because he could not help but feel some fear in his heart,
Zhào Yī gave a shiver.
Not daring to pursue,
he hung up his bow,
unfolded his cloth shirt,
draped it over his shoulders,
held the steel fork upside down,
and rushed back along the old path.
It is said that the group of hunters returned to the village,
bought some unfiltered wine,
cooked some game,
and sat eating together in a cooling shed at the foot of the mountain,
waiting for news of Zhào Yī.
One person said:
"Dà láng is late;
he must have succeeded."
Another said:
"Two legs chasing four legs;
there is no certainty in that."
One said:
"Zhào Dà’s skills were formidable to begin with."
Yet another said:
"Since he has not returned by now,
could it be that he failed to catch the badger
and was instead chased by it?"
While everyone was talking and laughing,
one among them with sharp eyes pointed and said:
"Isn't that him coming?"
Everyone walked out of the shed to meet him,
only to see Zhào Yī returning empty-handed.
The group said:
"We have already caught and cooked two hog badgers here;
why did Dà láng take so long to return?
It seemed certain you would have a share of the glory."
Zhào Yī said:
"Although I did not catch that badger,
I encountered a strange occurrence
and resolved a great doubt."
He then related the matter of shooting the fox spirit playing with the moon,
telling the story once through.
The group said:
"It is thanks to you, brother, for removing a local pest.
If it is as you say,
we should instead congratulate you."
Among them, there were many who did not believe him,
saying:
"Zhào Dà láng could not catch the badger,
so he made up this ghost story to trick us.
How could I believe it?
Only if I see it with my own eyes will I accept it as true."
There was also an elder who said:
"It is better to believe it exists
than to believe it does not."
On one hand, he pulled Zhào Yī into the shed to sit,
pouring a large bowl of wine for him,
while on the other, he brought up several stories of fox spirits
to chat with the group.
In the end, the group remained half-doubting and half-believing.
Zhào Yī said:
"I hit its hip with an arrow;
it cried out and fled.
I suspect the blood droplets on the ground can still be verified.
Let us go together tomorrow;
we shall follow the bloodstains to find the fox den.
I expect there are more than just one or two;
we will catch them all,
skin them to make a jacket for the winter—
wouldn't that be fine?"
The group said:
"In that case, there is nothing more to say.
If there is indeed evidence,
we shall invite you out.
If there is none,
then it is a lie,
and you will certainly have to provide a grand feast as our host."
Zhào Yī agreed.
That night they ate for a while,
and then everyone took some game and went home.
When Zhào Yī arrived home,
he told his wife of these matters.
Although his wife answered him,
in her heart she was not entirely certain.
Zhào Yī was sleepless all night;
hoping for dawn,
he jumped up as soon as it came.
He only heard the leaves rustling wildly in front of the door.
Zhào Yī said:
"Today is Chóng yáng, the ninth day of the month;
as expected, the seasonal wind has risen."
When he pushed open the window to look,
he saw a sky full of dark clouds that seemed ready to be wrung for water.
Zhào Yī said impatiently:
"The weather has changed.
While it isn't raining yet, I will go and pull the others to come with me;
it will not be too late for breakfast when we return."
He hurriedly finished washing and grooming,
put on his cotton shirt,
and went to knock on the doors of his neighbors to the east and west.
Every one of them was still tossing and turning in bed.
By the time he got them up,
the one to the east was waiting for washing water,
and the one to the west was waiting to eat breakfast.
They made Zhào Yī wait until he was impatient.
He watched as a day of heavy rain began to fall.
At first, Zhào Yī still hoped the rain would stop,
saying repeatedly:
"It's no matter,
it's no matter."
After a while,
it rained even harder.
Realizing that they could not go out,
he had no choice but to return home,
ate his breakfast,
and sat in the thatched hall,
his eyes staring blankly at the sky.
This rain lasted from morning until night;
when did it ever stop?
There is a "Lyric on Bitter Rain" that puts it well:
Rain,
Rain,
falling so relentlessly.
It is not needed for planting rice,
nor is it needed for watering flowers;
it doesn't wait for you to wash your face,
nor is it used to brew tea.
Hurrying along without a pause,
for what purpose?
Streaming from the eaves,
fast for a while,
slow for a while,
fine for a while,
heavy for a while,
the sound striking the ears with dread,
filling the heart with worries like tangled hemp.
A lively and active person
is trapped like a bird in a cage.
Even with a horse that travels a thousand li a day,
one could not find a place to step.
O Emperor in the imperial palace,
where are you idling and playing?
I resent that Fēng Bó does not raise a fierce wind to blow this away.
O Yǔ Shī,
you exert all your effort,
but what greatness is there in this?
You only earn yourself some curses.
If you must, then rain without end;
then I would have nothing more to say.
I only fear that even you will have your moments of weariness,
and these clouds, thick and thin,
will inevitably have to pack up and return home.
I advise you, Yǔ Shī:
why not pack it up a moment sooner?
Zhào Yī at that time wished he could take a 10,000-fathom bamboo pole,
to push aside the root of the clouds
and reveal the round red sun.
He also wished he could climb up to heaven,
take tens of thousands of pieces of extremely dry cloth,
and for the moisture-laden clouds of the whole sky,
wipe them until not a drop remained.
His wife saw that her husband was reluctant to eat dinner
and was only feeling depressed;
she had stored two bottles of good wine,
which she opened and warmed,
and brought the prepared wild game
for her husband to eat.
Zhào Yī unwittingly became very drunk,
entered the room and did not even loosen his clothes,
nor take off his socks,
but just lay down and slept.
He slept until the fourth watch before waking up,
raised his head and no longer heard the rain,
thinking it had cleared up.
After enduring another watch,
some light gradually appeared on the window;
Zhào Yī got up and went to push open the window to look at the sky,
but it was still pitch black,
yet he was happy the rain had stopped.
Zhào Yī said:
"Those sleepyheads
surely haven't woken up yet;
it won't be too late to go after eating breakfast."
He hurriedly urged his wife to get up, boil water for washing,
and prepare breakfast.
After eating,
when he went out the door to look,
it was again falling with misty, fine rain.
Zhào Yī said:
"This dog-hair rain
won't get clothes wet;
why be afraid?"
Walking a few steps,
seeing the ground was very muddy,
Zhào Yī turned back again, took off his socks,
and put on a pair of wax-soled wooden clogs.
When he went to the eastern and western neighbors to pull them along,
not a single one was willing to set out,
saying:
"What is the urgency?
To drag through mud and water
and run such a long distance—
if there really were a wild fox shot by you,
it would be suffering from its wounds right now
and surely wouldn't move away overnight;
why the rush?"
Zhào Yī saw it wouldn't happen
and felt depressed for another night.
On the third day,
the weather was clear and bright.
Zhào Yī said:
"Today I reckon there can be no excuses."
Early in the morning, he first went to each house to make an appointment,
returned home and finished breakfast,
then went again to invite and pull them from east and west.
A few of the mature ones declined and would not go,
saying:
"On this kind of half-wet, half-dry ground,
let you young folk go."
The rest of the crowd said:
"We will follow Dàláng to catch the fox spirit
and then come back to report."
A group of over twenty people,
each holding weapons.
Zhào Yī led the way in front,
winding and turning;
after walking over many mountain slopes,
the crowd had already become impatient.
By the time they reached the forest
and searched everywhere,
there was not a trace of blood;
it turned out to have been washed away by that day's heavy rain.
Zhào Yī explained it this way,
but how could the crowd believe him?
They said:
"In this dense forest,
with branches covering above,
surely the rain would not wash it so clean.
Even if the bloodstains were washed away,
its burrow must be nearby,
yet where is even a shadow of it now?"
Zhào Yī led the crowd,
searching for a long time as if chasing ghosts and spirits,
only to walk further and further away.
The crowd said:
"Bah!
In broad daylight,
playing such a nonsensical game,
we are not going further;
let's go back and trouble you for a feast instead."
Zhào Yī was so angry he was speechless.
When they arrived in the village,
one would say:
"Zhào Dà is a liar."
Another would say:
"Zhào Dà is talking nonsense;
in this peaceful world,
what fox spirit could there be?
Zhào Dà himself is a lying spirit."
To this day, when people meet a liar,
they still call him "Jīng Zhào,"
or "Luàn Zhào,"
all because of this fox spirit.
There is a poem to prove it:
The demonic fox worshipping the moon was indeed real,
Zhào Yī was never originally a liar.
Rain washed away bloodstains with nowhere to find them,
who in the world can judge such an injustice?
When Zhào Yī returned,
the crowd all sat down in his thatched hall,
wanting him to come out and act as host.
Zhào Yī had no choice
and had to take several pieces of his wife's clothing
to the pawnshop to get some money
to prepare wine for the crowd to drink.
Even several elders were invited,
and the crowd feasted for a while.
Upon leaving, they said:
"Since we have troubled Dàláng,
if others ask in the future,
we will just say there was indeed a fox spirit."
Zhào Yī felt even more indignant,
and from then on, he never again mentioned the matter of shooting the fox.
The story branches out in two directions.
Now, it is said that the male fox who was shot with an arrow
was born of an old white female fox.
This old fox knew not her own age;
she was quite adept at transformations
and had given herself an elegant title,
calling herself Shèng Gūgū.
She made her dwelling in a large earthen cave at the foot of Yàn Mén Shān.
On this mountain, two peaks rose abruptly in the east and west,
their height reaching the heavens.
Wild geese flying from the north to the south
all passed through the gap between these two mountains;
thus, it was called Yàn Mén.
Shèng Gūgū had given birth to one male and one female.
The male was named Hú Chù'ér,
and the female was named Hú Mèi'ér.
It turns out that fox spirits who have existed for five hundred years
mostly take the surnames Bái or Kāng;
those of a thousand years
mostly take the surnames Zhào or Zhāng;
while Hú is their general surname.
That evening, Shèng Gūgū and Mèi'ér were beneath the bright moon,
discussing the arts of alchemy.
They saw Chù'ér limping on a hind leg,
stumbling at every step,
approaching while wailing.
Upon reaching the earthen cave,
he collapsed on the ground, rolling and wailing in pain.
The old fox stepped forward to examine him
and saw that he had been hit by an arrow in his left leg.
When she hurriedly went to pull it out,
she found the arrowhead had entered deeply.
He was in such agony
that he could not move at all.
Shèng Gūgū conceived a plan
and called out:
“Son, endure the pain.”
She then held her breath,
clamped her teeth tightly onto the arrow shaft,
and used both hands to push his leg with all her might.
With a *pū* sound,
the arrow shaft separated from the flesh;
she pulled it out and tossed it onto the ground.
The male fox, however, fainted away.
In truth, this arrow
had struck exactly in the crook of his leg,
and two tendons had been severed.
Furthermore, having struggled back with all his life
and run such a long distance,
how could he not be dying?
Shèng Gūgū wept as she looked at him
and called Mèi'ér to help carry him onto the earthen bed and lay him down.
It was not until two double-hours later that he awoke.
This old fox also knew a few medicinal herbs
and decocted a soup to wash and treat the wound,
but it was completely ineffective.
Two days later,
he appeared to be on the verge of death.
While she was grieving,
she suddenly remembered there was an imperial physician in Yì Zhōu City surnamed Yán,
whose taboo name was Yán Sān Diǎn.
This man possessed the skills to bring the dead back to life.
If his medicine could be obtained,
what would there be to fear?
She instructed Mèi'ér to serve her brother well,
while she disguised herself as a sick old beggar woman,
carrying a hundred-node bamboo staff,
and headed straight toward Chéng Dū Fǔ.
Because of this trip,
the old fox would gain a new level of experience
and stir up endless troubles once more.
Truly it is said:
Methods are obtained when fate allows;
a patient not destined to die will surely find a physician.
Ultimately, how did Imperial Physician Yán apply his medicine,
and did he save the little fox spirit?
Listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
If you wish to cultivate life and accumulate merit,
inquire with an open mind at the Bàn Xiān Táng.
The story goes that in Yì Zhōu there was a famous physician
surnamed Yán and named Běn Rén,
who was a descendant of Yán Jūn Píng.
His way of reading a pulse was different from others:
he would use three fingers to tap lightly,
and then he would know the source of the illness.
The medicine he prescribed
never failed to heal.
Therefore, a nickname was spread, calling him Yán Sān Diǎn.
He was originally an imperial physician in the Imperial Academy of Medicine.
During the Jǐng Dé era,
he was summoned because of the illness of Consort Lǐ Chén Fēi.
He extended his three fingers, gave a single tap, and then left.
Consort Chén Fēi thought he was unwilling to be meticulous or attentive
and informed Emperor Zhēn Zōng.
Zhēn Zōng intended to punish him for the crime of disrespect,
but fortunately, various officials saved him, saying:
“He was taught by an extraordinary person
and cannot be compared to ordinary physicians.”
Although the Emperor spared him further trouble,
he ultimately did not use his prescriptions
and sent him back to his original home.
Because of this, he practiced medicine in Yì Zhōu.
On the fifth,
fifteenth,
and twenty-fifth days of every month, he distributed medicine
without taking a single penny.
Even for those who came for medicine on ordinary days,
if they had money for the medicine, he did not refuse it,
and if they had no money, he did not argue.
Thus, his door was as crowded as a marketplace.
There was something even more remarkable:
while others reading a pulse could only see the patient’s own ailments—
even those proficient in the principles of the Tài Sù pulse
could only see the patient’s own status and lifespan—
he alone, with one tap of his three fingers,
could determine for the entire family—fathers and sons,
mothers and children,
wives and children,
and daughters—
as long as they were close kin,
whether they had calamities or not,
he could judge it all from afar.
Even fortune-tellers
who arranged the twelve houses and stars to calculate in detail
were not as accurate as he.
However, he feared leaking heaven’s secrets
and was not very willing to speak of them easily.
One day,
the Prefectural Governor caught a slight cold
and sent for him to check his pulse.
He tapped the pulse
and said:
“What your excellency suffers from
does not require medicine.
You only need to decoct a bowl of thick Lù Ān tea,
drink it while hot,
and by the third watch you will sweat;
naturally, you will be fine.
Furthermore, I congratulate you that your honored wife
shall soon have the joy of giving birth to a son.
However, your eldest son’s wife
will face childbirth peril in the autumn.”
The Prefectural Governor laughed loudly,
thinking:
“My wife is indeed pregnant;
perhaps someone in the yamen leaked the news,
so he fabricated a fancy phrase
to flatter me with the joy of a son—that is nothing special.
