But my son’s wife is at home in Xiāng Zhōu,
over three thousand lǐ away;
whether she is pregnant or not, even I do not know.
Moreover, a daughter-in-law’s fortune or misfortune—
how could it be seen within the father-in-law’s pulse?
There is absolutely no logic in this.”
That night, the Prefectural Governor drank only a bowl of hot tea,
and his illness was cured.
Later, his wife did indeed give birth to a son,
but the Prefectural Governor still thought it was a coincidence.
In the tenth month, he received a letter from home,
in his eldest son’s own handwriting,
saying that his daughter-in-law had died following a miscarriage on the twenty-seventh day of the eighth month.
From then on, the Prefectural Governor respected him like a god
and called him Bàn Xiān.
Because of this, outsiders also called him Yán Bàn Xiān,
and his name became known throughout the world.
There is a poem to the tune of Lín Jiāng Xiān
solely describing Yán Bàn Xiān’s virtues:
All in the world use three fingers to check the pulse,
but they lose to his one point of immortal insight.
The fortunes and misfortunes of a whole family are entirely known;
to bring back life, one needs but a spoonful of drink,
to extend life, only a tiny measure of medicine.
Questioning, checking, looking, and listening are all unnecessary;
to see internal organs through a wall would not be strange for him.
Illnesses have always avoided a good physician;
if he were made to plant apricot trees,
the blossoms would fill the west of the Jǐn Jiāng.
It is said that the old fox disguised itself as a sick old beggar woman,
walking day and night.
Upon arriving inside the city of Yìzhōu,
she learned that Yán Bànxiān lived near the Hǎitáng Lóu.
This day happened to be the fifteenth of the ninth month,
the scheduled time for the distribution of medicine,
and it also happened to be the Zhīzhōu’s birthday.
Bànxiān prepared several boxes
and went to the prefectural office to offer his birthday congratulations.
The people coming in crowds to have their pulses read and seek medicine
numbered more than a hundred;
they were all scattered about waiting.
Some went up the Hǎitáng Lóu to sightsee
while keeping an eye on the activity in front of the prefectural office.
This tower was located to the west of the prefectural yamen;
it was built by the Tang dynasty Jiédùshǐ Lǐ Huí
as a place for his subordinates to banquet and relax.
Begonias were planted all around,
and they remain lush to this day.
Every time a new official took office,
it would be renovated,
making it extremely tidy and elegant.
That old woman had no heart for sightseeing
and went straight to the entrance of Bànxiān’s residence.
She saw that the storefront was a stretch of wooden palisades;
inside the palisade was a rockery
and four or five ancient osmanthus trees.
Inside were three small hall rooms,
with a plaque inscribed with the three characters “Bànxiān Táng,”
which was a gift from the Zhīzhōu.
On both sides hung boards with a couplet that said:
“Pulse-taking relies on three points;
Expelling illness takes but one dose.”
The old woman’s eyes were sharp,
and she took it all in.
Leaning on a bamboo staff,
she stood under the eaves across from the gate.
At the hour of noon,
she heard people saying,
“He’s coming!
He’s coming!”
Walking into the street and looking out,
she saw Bànxiān riding a white horse,
with a house servant carrying a set of formal robes and several empty boxes,
returning from the east.
Because the Zhīzhōu had kept him for breakfast,
he had returned late.
The crowd had grown impatient while waiting;
of the three parts of the crowd, one part had already dispersed.
There were also many others waiting in front of the prefectural office
who followed behind the horse’s tail as he came.
Bànxiān dismounted at the palisade gate,
and without even entering his house,
he stood directly in the hall.
The crowd pushed and shoved,
swarming forward;
one by one they stretched out their hands,
begging the Great Physician to take their pulses,
and some recounted the origins of illnesses in their families.
Bànxiān examined them one by one like flowing water;
while he dictated prescriptions,
the house servants fetched the medicines.
There were decoctions,
pills and powders,
and treatments for internal and external medicine.
About ten house servants worked separately to dispatch them,
and in less than two double-hours,
everyone had been sent away.
That Bànxiān truly relied on three points for his pulses;
if he were like an ordinary physician
who regulated his breath
and wasted time like a sugar cake maker,
he could never have examined so many pulses.
Furthermore, he used only one dose of medicine;
if he followed the fashionable doctors who opened their medicine chests,
even with two or three bags
and ten or so doses, they still wouldn’t achieve success.
No matter how you piled up medicinal ingredients like firewood,
wrapping for a thousand people
or dispensing for ten thousand,
you could not handle this group of patients.
Bànxiān usually distributed medicine
only until the hour of noon;
after noon, he would not issue medicine.
Because he had gone out late today,
he specifically worked until the hour of Shēn to finish.
There is a poem as proof:
“No divine recluse matches Yán of Western Shǔ,
Divine medicine and divine divination combined in one house.
Because those begging for medicine made his gate like a market,
He also imitated Jūnpíng in lowering the curtain early.”
The old woman saw the crowd pushing and squeezing;
knowing well that she was a bit strange and suspicious,
ancient and odd,
she did not dare rush forward.
She dozed temporarily under the rockery;
by the time the crowd had dispersed,
she hurried forward,
but Bànxiān had already gone back into his residence.
The old woman still hoped he would come out
and leaned blankly against the palisade gate, waiting stubbornly.
As evening approached,
she saw the old steward come out with a large lock in his hand to close the palisade gate.
The old woman became anxious,
rushed forward,
and gave a deep, respectful bow.
The old steward said:
“If you are begging for alms, you must come earlier;
now is the time to close the doors and shut the gates.
What family is so accommodating
as to hold money and wait at the gate to give you alms?”
Hearing this, the old woman
shed tears from both eyes and said:
“This old woman is not here to beg;
I am here to seek medicine.”
The old steward said:
“Even for seeking medicine,
there is a time.
My master has been busy all day
and has only just had half an hour of peace.
He surely won’t, for the sake of one old beggar-woman like you,
break the rules of our house.
Even if I went in to report it,
I would only be asking for the master’s scolding for nothing.”
The old woman said:
“This old body lives in the region of Āndézhōu;
the road I have come is very long,
and I arrived a bit late.
It is only because of a strange ailment
that I seek the Great Physician’s treatment;
I hope you, old grandfather, will do me a favor.
To save a life
is better than building a seven-story pagoda.
Physicians have the heart to slice their own thigh to save others;
if you, old grandfather, would be willing to inform the Great Physician,
perhaps the Great Physician will have pity
and might even be willing to come out to the hall.”
Having finished speaking,
with one hand propped on her bamboo pole
and the other clutching the old steward’s sleeve,
she bent one leg
and knelt down.
The old steward grew irritated
and flared up, saying:
“You old beggar-woman,
how ignorant you are!
I have explained it so clearly to you,
yet you still persist in your pestering.
Even if you have a strange ailment,
I doubt you will die tonight.
Even if it were the old Emperor’s imperial decree summoning him,
he would at least wait until tomorrow to set out.”
Having said this,
he reached out to pull the old woman up,
intending to shove her out.
The old woman jumped with both feet
and began shouting of injustice,
which disturbed Yán Bànxiān inside.
He sent a page boy out with a message,
asking:
“Who is making such a racket?”
Just as the old woman was about to go forward to explain,
she was pulled away by the old steward,
who said to the page boy:
“This old beggar-woman,
neither looking like a human
nor like a ghost,
comes at this time to ask the master for medicine.
I told her to wait through the night but she refused;
I kindly tried to persuade her to leave,
but then she started shouting about injustice.”
The page boy said:
“From where did this old woman come,
so completely unreasonable?
You aren’t some regular customer who has come two or three times
and brought money into our gate.
You aren’t some lady or miss;
even if you died,
it would be just like having one less old bitch around.
The Zhīzhōu is the master of the whole prefecture,
and even when he takes medicine, he must follow the proper time;
he would not dare knock on the door or bang on the house.
Yet you are so unruly and troublesome!
Leave quickly and that will be the end of it.
If you provoke my master,
he will write a three-inch wide note
and send you to the Zhīzhōu’s office.
I’m afraid that while you might not die of illness,
you will be beaten to death.”
While speaking,
he helped the old steward
and used his hands to shove the old woman’s chest.
The old woman began to act out;
giving a loud cry,
she threw her staff aside
and suddenly fell to the ground.
Her face gradually turned yellow,
and her four limbs would not move.
It was exactly as if:
Her body is like withered leaves in late autumn,
her life is like a flickering lamp at the fifth watch.
Even if she might not die immediately,
for now, there is little good fortune and much peril.
The old steward, seeing things were taking a turn for the worse,
instead began to blame the page boy,
saying:
"I, your elder, gave her a piece of my mind,
and it would have been fine if you had just ended it there,
but you had to join in the fun,
scolding her once more,
and then pushing and shoving her.
This sickly old woman,
how could she possibly withstand it!
You go report to the Master yourself;
it has nothing to do with me."
The page boy also panicked,
and had no choice but to report to Bànxiān,
explaining things in such-and-such a way.
Bànxiān was sitting quietly in his study;
hearing this, he was greatly shocked,
and hurriedly went out to the front hall.
When he looked by the rockery,
the old woman had already been awakened by the old steward;
she stared blankly with both eyes wide open,
but remained motionless.
Bànxiān told the old steward to pull up her right hand,
and using three fingers of divine skill,
pressed upon the Cùn, Guān, and Chǐ pulse points on her wrist,
then ordered the left hand to be pulled up and did the same.
He cried out:
"How strange!
This pulse is unlike any ordinary one."
He then turned back to the official hall in the rear and sat down,
telling the page boy to call the Māmā to help the old woman inside,
"I have words for her."
The old Māmā went out and said to the woman:
"The Master says your pulse is somewhat peculiar,
and calls you into the back hall,
to speak with you in detail."
Initially, the woman was still lying stiffly on the ground,
but upon receiving this news,
she was exactly like a wooden jumping-tiger;
once the mechanism was triggered,
she leapt right up.
She picked up her walking stick from the ground,
and without needing any support,
took three steps in two,
and walked briskly into the back hall,
so fast that even the old Māmā could not keep up with her,
falling behind by several paces.
The old steward watched and laughed:
"This beggar woman turns out to be faking death;
she nearly scared us to death."
It is said that Yán Bànxiān was in the back hall,
sitting by a brightly burning candle.
Seeing the woman enter,
he hurriedly dismissed everyone
and called her forward, asking:
"Where do you live?"
The woman said:
"This old woman is from Dé'ān Zhōu."
Bànxiān said:
"Do not try to hide it from me;
I see you have the form of a human,
but the pulse of a beast;
there must be a reason for this."
The woman thought to herself:
"What a fine master; I suppose I cannot hide it from him."
Seeing no one around,
she hurriedly knelt and said:
"To tell the truth,
I am an old fox from the foot of Yànmén Shān.
Because I admire Bànxiān’s great reputation,
I specifically came to seek a pulse reading."
Bànxiān said:
"I already know your pulse;
you suffer from no other illness,
only the illness of wanting to save your children."
The woman was so startled she kowtowed several times before scrambling up and saying:
"The great physician is a true immortal,
far more than just a 'Half-Immortal.'
This old woman has only one son and one daughter left;
now my son has been shot in the left leg by someone,
and he would rather die than live."
She then described the severity of her son's arrow wound
in great detail.
Bànxiān said:
"The wound itself is no matter,
but the tendons and bones are injured;
even if he recovers,
this left leg will not compare to the right;
I fear he will be a cripple."
The woman said:
"If his life is saved,
then losing the use of one leg
is also a minor matter.
When my son's wound has closed,
this old woman will lead him to your residence to offer our thanks."
Bànxiān said:
"That is absolutely unnecessary.
I have something else to say;
according to your pulse,
your daughter also faces a calamity."
At this, the old woman's heart
felt as if it had been struck by a mallet.
Seeing that Bànxiān’s previous words were all miraculously accurate,
and now hearing him say this,
how could she not panic?
She immediately said:
"My daughter's calamity—
when will it occur?
I trouble you, Great Benefactor, to show great mercy
and save her as well;
this old woman shall not forget it in life or death."
Bànxiān said:
"Your daughter's calamity
is indeed very strange;
even I cannot fully deduce it.
It will appear within a year or half a year.
Generally, you beasts masquerade as humans
to deceive the ignorant masses;
you have no learning of transcending form or world above,
and no heaven-shaking, earth-moving arts below.
Once your fate is exhausted and your life ends,
hawks and hounds will all be formidable enemies.
Take your son, for instance:
it was lucky he was only shot in the left leg;
had he been hit in a vital spot,
even Lú Yī or Biǎn Què
could only say the word 'pity,'
and he would have died in vain.
I see the Chǐ pulse on your right hand;
your life-root is firm.
In the Cùn pulse on your left hand,
your mind is quick and perceptive.
You have a great affinity for the Way.
Moreover, you were born in mountain valleys
and have not entered the world deeply;
the seven emotions and six desires
still burden you but little.
Why not take advantage of this time while your energy has not yet faded
to seek a master and inquire of the Way?
Your whole family could shed their furs and skins
and be forever free from suffering and calamity.
Would that not be wonderful?"
These few words
made the old woman weep like rain.
She kowtowed again and said:
"Many thanks to the Great Benefactor for your instruction."
Bànxiān called out a house boy in charge of external medicines
and ordered him to get one pill of Jiǔlíng Xùmìng Dān,
and two plasters.
Each was wrapped well in paper
and given to the woman.
He said:
"This pill should be mixed with good wine and taken;
then naturally all will be well.
However, since the arrow entered the bone,
I fear the arrowhead is still inside.
If it is not removed,
it will cause pain for a lifetime.
You may wash the wound clean with warm water
and apply this Bádú Gāo.
Wait until the purple blood has finished flowing
and fresh blood comes out,
then change it for the Shénxiān Jiēgǔ Gāo.
After a hundred days,
he will be able to move."
He added:
"The words I just exhorted
are all for your good;
you must remember them."
He then called the old Māmā to escort her out.
The woman took the medicine,
thanked him repeatedly,
and followed the old Māmā through the front hall.
She ran into the old steward still guarding the gate;
the woman gave him a deep bow,
asking him not to take offense at the trouble.
After passing through the gate,
she went away full of joy.
Here, Bànxiān was also privately astounded,
but told no one.
There is a poem to prove it:
Bringing the dead back to life is not so strange,
But how could one know a beast's pulse in human form?
Words spoken from the heart are never leaked,
Only then does one know that medical skill is divine providence.
It is said that the old woman left the city overnight.
On the way, she bought a large bottle of high-quality, ash-free wine,
and went straight to the foot of Yànmén Shān in Dé'ān Zhōu.
Here, Chù'ér was groaning incessantly,
and Mèi'ér stayed by his side, never leaving for a moment.
The brother and sister were waiting with great anxiety.
As soon as they saw the old woman crawl into the earthen cave,
they were immensely overjoyed.
The old woman heated the bottle of wine until it was boiling hot,
and mixed the Jiǔlíng Xùmìng Dān into a thin paste with the wine inside a ceramic bowl.
She propped up Chù'ér and poured the medicine into him,
then gave him a little more wine to rinse his mouth,
and applied the Bádú Gāo to the affected area according to the proper method.
They saw Chù'ér face toward the inner side of the earthen bed,
fall into a deep sleep,
and remain unconscious for a full three shíchén.
The old woman and Mèi'ér kept watch over him,
and both said:
"He has not closed his eyes for several days.
Now that he has fallen asleep,
he must no longer be in pain;
this shows the power of the medicine."
They saw a mass of pus and blood flowing from the bend of his leg,
and the medicinal plaster had floated off by itself.
Fearing they might startle him from his sleep,
they did not dare to move.
After a while, Chù'ér woke up
and cried out:
"The sore is so incredibly itchy and unbearable!"
When the old woman peeled back the plaster to look,
within the pus and blood,
something was faintly visible.
The old woman used fine grass to wipe away the filth,
and when she used her nails to poke at it,
a shovel-headed arrowhead came out with a touch.
It turned out that Zhào Yī had used a shovel-headed arrow;
at first, only the arrow shaft had been pulled out,
while the arrowhead had pierced into the bone
and had not been removed.
At the time, they were in such a state of panic and confusion
that they did not look closely.
Only now did they realize the height of the Bàniān's insight
and the excellence of the Bádú Gāo.
The old woman decocted some detoxifying herbal soup
and gently washed it clean for him.
She saw that the bone was damaged and the tendons injured,
the flesh gaped and the skin was rotten,
and fresh blood flowed out profusely;
it was unspeakably pitiful.
She hurriedly warmed the Shénxiān Jiēgǔ Gāo and applied it,
then used some cloth and silk
to slowly bind it up.
After a night had passed,
she unwrapped and tended to it again the next day.
After seven days like this,
the pus and fluid were completely gone.
From then on, they did not disturb it,
and after nursing him for forty or fifty days,
new flesh grew from within,
the tendons and meridians became smooth,
and he could just manage to struggle to his feet.
He spent his time half-lying and half-sitting,
not daring to go outside the earthen cave.
When the full hundred days were up,
the plaster was removed,
and he felt no pain at all.
Only, at the spot where the plaster had been applied,
there was raw, bare flesh,
and not even half a hair would grow.
When he walked,
his left leg was already two inches shorter than his right leg.
The old woman was still delighted and said:
"Yán Bàniān said
he feared you could not avoid becoming a cripple,
and so it has turned out.
You can change your name to Zuǒ Qué'ér
to acknowledge the Bàniān's achievement."
From then on, he was called Zuǒ Qué,
and also Zuǒ Chù,
having discarded the surname Hú.
One day,
Zuǒ Qué'ér left the earthen cave
to go for a stroll.
He walked into the forest,
to the very place where he had been struck by the arrow before.
He thought:
"How can I not avenge this enmity!"
He ran back to discuss it with the mother fox.
The old woman was sitting leaning against an earthen table;
upon hearing these words,
she suddenly shed tears.
Do you know why?
This was where the mother fox's karmic affinity with the Dào was deep.
Just as it is said:
Within the arena of wealth and rank,
one instead invites the calamities of Yīn and Yáng.
Where disaster is suffered,
the karmic connection to virtue and the Dào instead opens up.
Ultimately, what words will the old woman say,
and will this cripple's revenge be successful or not?
Please listen to the next chapter for the explanation.
I ask you not to harbor thoughts of vengeance;
everywhere the spring breeze blows in a heaven of natural ease.
It is said that Zuǒ Qué'ér remembered how his body had once been whole,
but because of a single arrow,
he had become a cripple.
When walking, his right was long and his left was short,
limping along;
it was quite unsightly.
How could he not avenge this enmity!
The old woman said:
"Enmity should be resolved rather than tied.
You were careless yourself,
revealing a flaw to others
and suffering this ordeal.
By heaven's luck, you had an affinity with Yán Bàniān,
who saved your life.
Even though you lost the use of a foot,
it is merely an external appearance.
In the past, during the time of the Qī Guó, the military strategist Sūn Bìn
and the Prime Minister Lóu Shīdé of the Táng Dynasty
were both lame.
Even among the Bādòng Shénxiān of the upper realms,
there is a Tiěguǎi Lǐ among them.
My son,
this is nothing to be ashamed of."
Because she mentioned the name Yán Bàniān,
she suddenly remembered the words he had enjoined upon her,
and unconsciously she shed mournful tears.
Zuǒ Qué'ér said:
"Mother,
I will listen to your words
and simply not harbor a grudge.
But why are you shedding tears?"
The old woman said:
"For all those who have attained the Dào,
spirits cannot control them,
ghosts cannot bring them disaster,
and humans cannot harm them.
We possess no Dàoist arts ourselves,
merely adorning ourselves in human form
to delude the ignorant masses;
inevitably, our allotted time must end.
If after this there is some other misfortune,
we cannot rely on the Imperial Physician forever to survive.
Moreover, Yán Bàniān said
that both my children would face calamities,
and I do not know how it will all end."
She then took the words of the Bàniān advising her to seek a master and the Dào
and recounted them in detail.
Her words made her two children tremble with fear.
At that moment, the old woman wanted to leave the earthen cave
and go out to seek the Way.
Qué’ér and Mèi’ér
both wished to follow.
The three of them discussed which path would be best.
Qué’ér said:
“There is only Dōngjīng Biànzhōu,
which is the place where the current Emperor established his capital;
it is a world of flowers and brocade,
densely populated,
and many extraordinary people are there.”
The old woman said:
“In such a prosperous place,
I fear your spirits will be unsettled
and stir up some sort of trouble.
I have heard that in the Yǐngzhōu area,
there are the scenic beauties of the Three Rivers and Seven Marshes.
Your grandfather passed down four lines saying:
‘If you wish to be a king within the Law,
you must go to Miǎnyáng;
if you wish to perform within the Law,
you must ask Yúnmèng.’
Yún and Mèng are the names of two marshes
located right in Miǎnyáng,
surrounded by myriad mountains.
I hear there is a Báiyún Dòng there
where celestial books are hidden,
guarded by a White Ape Deity.
Our karmic affinity for the Way and its methods
if we go there,
our hearts will find what they seek.”
Qué’ér said:
“The common saying goes, ‘a place of origin is not as good as a gathering place.’
Dōngjīng is where the Three Religions gather.
If we go there,
even if we cannot transmit the Way or obtain the Law,
we can at least see some fine scenery
and eat some good food.”
The old woman said:
“Such talk is not that of someone focused on seeking the Way.”
Mèi’ér said:
“It is very far from here to Yǐngzhōu,
and Brother’s leg is currently inconvenient.
To make him travel so much road,
I do not know what year we would arrive.
According to what I say,
if we take the route through Yǒngxīng,
there is the Western Peak Huà Shān,
the place where Mr. Chén Tuán practiced cultivation.
First, we can burn a stick of incense before the Holy Emperor,
and second, visit Mr. Chén
to seek his Wǔ Lóng Zhé Fǎ.
The rest—Zhōngnán,
Tàiyǐ,
Shílóu,
and Tiānzhù, several famous mountains—
are all places where immortals come and go.
We can visit and search them one by one,
and even Dōngjīng will be seventy or eighty percent closer.
Once we reach Dōngjīng,
we can discuss the path to Yǐngzhōu again;
wouldn’t that be killing two birds with one stone?”
The cripple, hearing these words,
found they suited his wishes perfectly
and said repeatedly:
“What Sister says is right.”
He strongly urged it,
and the old woman nodded in agreement.
Immediately, the cripple disguised himself as a village farmer,
Mèi’ér disguised herself as a village girl,
and the old fox was accustomed to disguising herself as an old poor woman,
needless to say.
Leaving the earthen cave,
they headed toward Xījīng.
At this time, it was the beginning of the second lunar month, when the weather was mild,
and one could see:
True mountains and true waters,
famous grasses and famous flowers.
Curving green waves,
rows of tender willows stretching their eyebrows;
towering green peaks,
several peach trees showing their rosy cheeks.
Pairs of white butterflies fluttering,
couples of dragonflies skimming the water.
Weather of sudden sun and sudden rain that nourishes flowers,
days for outings that are neither warm nor cold.
Young men and women on spring outings sing hand-in-hand,
travelers seeking scenic spots get drunk and dance in their sables.
It is said that although Mèi’ér disguised herself as a village girl,
she was naturally enchantingly beautiful.
The cripple’s walking was inconvenient;
where others took two steps,
he took only one,
and he often fell behind.
Before walking even ten li,
he needed to rest his feet.
The mother and daughter
had no choice but to wait for him.
Every time they reached a resting place,
the women in the village,
Auntie Zhāng and Sister-in-law Lǐ,
calling out to each other,
gathered to watch
and all said:
“This old poor woman
has such a fine daughter.
If she were willing to give her to a family as a daughter-in-law,
people would be willing to pay a hundred strings of cash.
I wonder who this cripple is to them?”
Some also said:
“This cripple must be the old woman’s own son,
and this girl must be a daughter-in-law raised in the family.”
There were also busybodies
who went forward to ask them.
Only then did they learn they were brother and sister,
and then they said:
“From the same shop,
two different kinds of goods have come out.
Both came from the same old woman’s belly,
yet the male is so ugly
and the female is so handsome.”
There were also frivolous young men
who intentionally interrogated them and tried to start conversations,
crowding and jostling.
Mèi’ér was quite mature;
she ignored them completely,
only keeping her head down.
Later, becoming annoyed by the pestering,
they only chose quiet and secluded places to rest.
In one day, they could only travel fifty or sixty li.
The three of them were originally fox spirits;
when hungry, they ate flowers and fruit,
when thirsty, they drank clear spring water.
At night, they chose tall forests or thick grass to stay in,
so delaying for a few days on the road
was no great matter.
It was not like humans going on a journey,
where there are many expenses.
Even just eating a bowl of thin porridge during the day
and a straw mat at night,
if one doesn’t have a few coins in their waist pouch, one cannot hope to get them.
Speaking of this,
beasts actually have it easier.
The three fox spirits traveled for several days,
and luckily they encountered mostly clear and mild weather.
Suddenly one day, a strong wind began to blow,
thick clouds covered the sky,
and a whole sky of spring snow fell.
Now, this snow has several names:
single flakes are called “Bees,”
double flakes are “Goose Feathers,”
triple flakes are “Gathered Threes,”
quadruple flakes are “Assembled Fours,”
quintuple flakes are called “Plum Blossoms,”
and sextuple flakes are called “Six-pointed.”
Snow is originally formed from the condensation of Yin energy,
so the six points correspond to the Yin number.
After Lìchūn,
it is all mixed plum blossom flakes,
and no longer six-pointed.
In good weather, this Qué’ér would still totter with every step;
how much more so when encountering such heavy snow.
He was even more unable to move,
and could only cry out in bitterness and grievance.
The old woman said:
“From here, it is not far to Jiànmén Shān.
There must be a convent or temple there at least,
where we can settle down.
I suppose you must endure a few more steps.”
At once they plucked some tree leaves to place on their heads,
acting as bamboo hats for cover.
Qué’ér also could not help but slip,
straining with every step.
After walking for about another two double-hours,
they saw they were getting close to Jiànmén Shān.
Jiànmén was opened by the Wǔ Dīng Lì Shì,
as evidenced by a Xī Jiāng Yuè
poem:
The Great Sword Mountain pierces the sky’s emerald green,
The jagged Small Sword Mountain connects with the clouds.
Naturally steep and precipitous, it separates Xī Qín,
Even with wings, it is hard to fly over the ridge.
Ever since the Wǔ Dīng opened the path,
to this day, merchants and traders pass through.
The King of Shǔ vainly carved the gate of doom,
In the end, the Golden Ox left no trace.
Before reaching the foot of the mountain,
they could only see that in the woods ahead,
the tops of red walls were faintly visible.
The old woman pointed and said:
“Wouldn't it be good to rest for a while at this place?”
The three of them strove to walk forward
and saw that the plaque with gold characters identified it as the Yìyǒng Guānwáng Miào.
In front were three gateway rooms,
with two vermilion doors in the center
half open and half closed.
Squeezing inside to look further,
in the room on the right was a statue of a ferocious soldier
holding the reins of a Chìtù Yānzhī horse;
in the room on the left stood a stone stele,
and both sides were fenced with railings.
The second level was the main hall of three rooms,
extremely grand and magnificent;
a row of vermilion lattice windows were closed.
To the right in front of the hall,
was a large brick furnace for burning paper offerings;
on the left was a well pavilion,
surrounded by low walls and vermilion railings,
leaving only a path for drawing water.
The old woman said:
“There must be Dàoists living inside the hall;
let us not disturb them,
it would be fine to just rest for a while in the well pavilion.”
Several of them entered the pavilion
and saw an octagonal glazed well in the center,
with stone benches set on both sides.
As soon as the three had sat down,
the snow began to fall even more heavily.
The cripple said:
“This weather surely knows how to play tricks on people;
it’s not even the twelfth-month snow that heralds a prosperous year,
so what is the point of falling so much?
We are also quite senseless;
how could it be seen that our time of death is at hand?
Seeking what master,
searching for what Dào?
Now we are suffering such misery!”
The old woman said:
“Back then, the Patriarch Dámó faced the wall for nine years,
even when vines pierced his knees, he did not move.
During those nine years,
he must have endured countless rain and snow;
it’s not as if he had a house to cover him.
This rain and snow are just the general weather of the season,
they are not meant for you alone,
yet you complain about it—
is that not a sin?”
Before she had finished speaking,
they heard the main gate open with a creak,
and the cripple peered through the gaps in the railings
and saw a person walking in from outside:
his head was wrapped in a tattered Táng-style cap,
he wore a brown jacket with a hundred patches,
a yellow rope tied around his waist,
and straw sandals on his feet.
Do you know who it was?
It was exactly the one in charge of incense at this temple, Dàoist Miè.
That man held an umbrella in one hand
and in the other hand he carried a large clay jar decorated with tassels,
which could hold about five or six catties of wine.
He was muttering to himself:
“A monk treats wine as his very life.
In such heavy snow,
he wants me to go to the village to buy this ‘pus and blood,’
running such a long way.
Heaven has eyes;
just let him have a stomachache after drinking it!”
While talking,
he put down the umbrella and the clay jar
and lifted the large door rings to prop open the gate.
The cripple thought to himself:
“In this bitter cold,
it would be good to have some wine to drink.”
This cripple was usually just lazy,
but at this moment he was unusually nimble.
No sooner said
than done,
he left the well pavilion,
hobbled three or four steps,
quickly picked up the wine jar,
and put his mouth to it, gulping it down with a gurgle,
drinking with great delight.
Dàoist Miè heard the sound,
turned around and saw him,
shouting loudly:
“Where did this beggar come from!
Coming here to be a thief and steal wine to drink!
I worked so hard, traveling so far to the village to buy it,
yet you just help yourself!”
The cripple hurriedly put down the wine jar and tried to leave,
but the Dàoist slapped him right in the face,
sending him somersaulting.
He scrambled up,
limping on his leg,
and ran frantically toward the well pavilion.
The Dàoist did not give up
and chased him into the well pavilion,
only to see a mother and daughter
sitting together in a cluster.
The old woman hurriedly rose,
performed a respectful greeting,
and said:
“The three of us, mother and children, were heading to Xījīng to visit relatives.
We encountered heavy snow on the road
and just took shelter here for a moment.
My son Cūn’ér here is a simpleton;
let this old woman apologize for him,
please don't be offended!”
The Dàoist was in the middle of a scowl,
about to burst out with a few more words,
when his eyes glanced behind the old woman
and saw a pretty girl standing there half-hidden;
his heart immediately softened,
and that steaming rage of his
was cast away to the Kingdom of Zhǎwā.
He quickly changed his tone and said:
“Your son is far too unreasonable
to behave in such a way.
Since he is a simpleton,
so be it.
However, he drank quite a lot of wine;
I fear when the Master inside asks,
you, venerable lady, should answer accordingly.”
Leaving the pavilion,
he went back to the front railings to retrieve the umbrella,
shook it dry and tucked it under his arm,
picked up the wine jar,
and toward the eastern corridor of the main hall,
went away with a chuckle and a smile.
Back there, the old woman grumbled at the cripple:
“You are so greedy that you invite trouble.
Heaven punished you with a disability;
if you had been born with two swift legs,
you would have even stolen this stone well curb to trade for wine.”
Mèi'ér teased him:
“With just this skill of somersaulting,
he also managed to get some wine to drink.”
The cripple laughed and said:
“Even though I did a somersault,
at least my stomach is warmer than yours.”
While they were talking,
they heard footsteps along the corridor,
and a young Dàoist came out from inside.
It turned out there was an old Dàoist in this temple
whose surname was Chén and Dàoist name was Kōngshān.
Although not yet seventy,
he suffered from a phlegm-fire ailment
and spent all day in quiet recuperation.
Eating and relieving himself
were all done in his room,
and he never went out.
As for this young Dàoist,
he was the temple master;
his surname was Jiǎ and his Dàoist name was Qīngfēng.
He was only twenty-four or five years old.
Though he was a member of the Dàoist clergy,
he had some character flaws throughout his life;
specifically, a fondness for women and wine.
Because this Jiànmén Shān was a dangerous and remote place,
even if he urgently wanted to see a woman's face,
he could not manage it.
Hearing from Dàoist Miè
that there was a pretty village girl
sitting in the well pavilion,
whether there was much or little wine in the jar
he did not even check,
but hurriedly walked out to the front of the hall,
stepping through the snow,
and went straight into the well pavilion.
He asked:
“You and your family,
where have you come from?”
The old woman said:
“This old woman lives at the foot of Yànmén Shān;
the three of us are close kin.
Because we wanted to offer incense at Xīyuè Huà Shān,
we encountered snow on the way
and have come here to trouble you.
Just now my son Cūn’ér, not knowing how to behave,
stole some wine to drink;
this old woman has been scolding him for quite some time.
I hope your Reverence will not blame him.”
Dàoist Jiǎ said:
“What harm is there in such a small matter?
Do not let it weigh on your mind.”
His two eyes rolled about,
staring fixedly at the little vixen behind her,
his soul leaving his body.
How can this be seen?
There is a lyric titled Zhùmǎ Tīng
as proof:
One must admire the village girl’s temples,
combed into a clever style like dark clouds.
She was born neither tall nor short,
neither thin nor fat,
neither fine nor coarse.
Her face is like a hibiscus, her skin like snow,
and see how neat and elegant her clothes are.
Has she ever stood by a wine furnace?
If Sīmǎ Xiāngrú were to meet her,
he would mistake her for the young bride of the Zhuō family.
Jiǎ Dàoshì spoke again:
“Traveling in this snowy weather
is extremely difficult for people;
you mother and children have suffered much hardship.”
The lame man jumped up and said:
“It is indeed hard;
if I could just get a mouthful of wine down my throat, then all would be well.”
The old woman glared at him with angry eyes,
so he stopped talking.
The Taoist spoke again:
“This well pavilion is not a place to settle either.
It is fine during the day,
but at night the wind howls;
how could you bear it?
Behind the main hall, there are clean rooms
where traveling officials and guests often come to stay.
I invite you, Old Mother, to go inside to stoke some charcoal fires
and dry these damp clothes; that would be good.”
The old woman said:
“There is no need;
we will just spend the night however we can,
and tomorrow we will be on our way.”
Jiǎ Dàoshì said:
“The sky does not look like it is clearing up yet.
Moreover, the mountain roads here are rugged and extremely difficult to walk,
unlike other places.
Even if the snow stops,
the road and soil will still be muddy.
We ourselves are afraid of it;
how could we let this young lady travel?
This temple is a public place;
even if you stay for ten days or so,
who would ask you for room rent?
Just wait for the sky to clear
and the sun to dry things for a few days;
it will not be too late to set out then.”
The old woman said:
“Many thanks, Master,
it is just that it would be an improper imposition.”
The Taoist said:
“What are you saying?
Who walks around with a house on their head?
As the common saying goes:
To give convenience to others
is to give convenience to oneself.
Even if it is just simple tea and plain rice,
this humble Taoist can afford to provide it.
If you do not mind the poor hospitality,
just eat whatever is available,
and there is no need to start your own fire.”
The lame man said:
“Mother!
It is rare for a Master to be so charitable.
Let us go stay in the house;
when we sleep at night,
we might even have a good dream.”
The old woman looked at Mèi'ér and said:
“My child, what is in your heart?”
Mèi'ér said:
“I leave it to my mother to decide.”
Seeing that they agreed, Jiǎ Dàoshì
was overjoyed beyond measure
and said:
“This humble Taoist will lead the way;
follow me inside.”
At that moment, the mother and two children
followed the Taoist down from the eastern corridor,
passed around the main hall,
then passed the refectory,
went through the kitchen,
and arrived at the back.
They saw only two newly built small upper-story rooms,
with several flower bushes and trees planted in the courtyard.
The three of them stood still downstairs.
The Taoist greeted them again,
bowing to each one,
before inviting them to be seated.
He asked:
“Old Mother, what is your honorable surname?”
The old woman said:
“This old woman’s surname is Zuǒ.
This village’s name is originally Zuǒchù,
and because he injured one foot,
he is called Zuǒ Qué'ér.
This young daughter is called Mèi'ér.”
The Taoist said:
“This humble Taoist’s surname is Jiǎ,
and my humble style is Qīngfēng.
Meeting today unexpectedly
is also a matter of fate.”
The old woman said:
“If there is a Master in charge of the temple,
please invite him to meet us.”
The Taoist said:
“My master is old and ill,
and has not seen guests for several years.
Just inside this small side door on the west side behind the hall
is his bedroom.
Now it is only this humble Taoist who manages the temple.”
The old woman said:
“How many companions of the Way are there in total?”
The Taoist said:
“There is also a young disciple,
but his father passed away in the first lunar month,
and he went to his secular home and has not yet returned.
The Taoist who was just buying wine
is surnamed Miè;
he also entered the temple gates not long ago.
In the kitchen, there is also an old incense attendant
who solely manages the fire and cooking;
besides them, there is no one else.
You three have come all this way;
fearing you may be hungry,
there is ready-made vegetarian food that you may use.”
The old woman said:
“There is no need;
we have brought dry rations.”
The Taoist said:
“Keep the dry rations for the road another day.”
The Taoist hurriedly went to the kitchen and busied himself for a while,
preparing some vegetarian dishes, noodles, and rice,
and told the Taoist Miè to carry them out
and set them on a table.
He also went to his own room to fetch several plates of dried fruit and set them out as well.
The old woman thanked him:
“Why go to the trouble of such a grand setting?”
The Taoist said:
“Please do not laugh at these offerings of the mountains.”
Then the Taoist Miè brought a large pot of wine,
along with four porcelain cups
in a set.
The Taoist laid out three cups,
poured them full of wine,
and said to the old woman:
“Please, Old Mother, sit in the center,
the young brother on the left,
and the young lady on the right.
Please relax and have a cup to dispel the cold.”
The old woman said:
“This old woman and her children are boldly troubling you;
please also sit down, Master.”
The Taoist said:
“Fearing the young lady might find it distasteful,
I dare not join you.”
The old woman said:
“What harm is there in just sitting?”
The Taoist said:
“Since I have received the Old Mother’s command,
it is only right for this humble Taoist to hold the pot.”
He then took a stool
and sat down beside Zuǒ Qué'ér’s shoulder.
Mèi'ér was shy
and still stood behind the old woman’s back.
The old woman said:
“Being a guest is not like being at home;
my child, just sit down,
and do not let the Master’s kind intentions go to waste.”
Only then did Mèi'ér sit.
It would have been fine if she had not sat,
but the moment she did,
the Taoist sat diagonally across from her
and saw her with great clarity.
She was even more enchantingly beautiful than before,
and it was as if his three souls and seven spirits
had clearly written a formal note
and sent them all onto her person.
There is a lyric to the tune *Huángyīng'ér*
as proof:
Carefully observing her enchanting beauty,
it makes one’s mind grow weary with longing.
See her without a word, smiling slightly;
her appearance is so lovely.
Her years are still few;
one wonders if she has yet opened her heart to love.
That small waist;
if one were to embrace her,
even if one did not die, his soul would surely dissipate.
The old woman told Chù’ér to also pour a cup of wine
to return the toast to the Taoist priest.
The four of them sat down,
and after several more rounds of drinking
and some idle chatter,
Niè Dào was seen to have neatly put on a new cap
and changed into a clean cotton jacket.
Carrying a pot of wine,
he came downstairs and said,
"The hot wine is here;
please have some more.
If you wish to have a meal,
there is also some in the kitchen."
The old woman said,
"It is enough;
there is no need."
The Taoist then took the remaining wine from the pot,
poured it into a large porcelain bowl,
picked up a baked cake,
and gave it to him to eat.
Taking the pot of hot wine from his hand,
he placed it on the table
and gave the empty pot back to him, telling him to take it to the kitchen.
This was clearly because he found him to be an eyesore
and intended to dismiss him.
Who would have known that although this Niè Dào was not very old,
he was also an improper person.
He was originally a favored page in an official's household in Jiànzhōu;
because he seduced a maidservant of the house,
he was beaten half to death by the local official
and driven out to beg.
When his father, Old Niè, was alive,
he had been an old neighbor
to the temple’s old incense attendant.
Thus, the old incense attendant had spoken up before the Taoist
to take him into the temple.
However, his old nature still remained;
seeing this beautiful, flower-like girl,
how could he be willing to leave?
At that moment, his gaze was fixed upon the little imp;
standing behind the Taoist’s back,
he simply would not go.
The Taoist, also oblivious,
only looked ahead
and ignored what was behind.
After everyone had sat for a while longer,
the old woman rose and said,
"Having been graced with your wine and food, we are both drunk and full.
It is getting late;
we shall take our leave."
The Taoist was staring at Mèier,
lost in a daze;
hearing them bid farewell,
he said,
"Please, one more cup."
He hurriedly took the pot to pour wine,
but little did he know that the wine pot had already been taken from his hand by the Cripple
and drunk until it was empty—
truly, he could not focus on two things at once.
Then, the mother and her two children
left the table and expressed their thanks;
the Taoist also rose to return the courtesy.
He saw Niè Dào holding an empty pot in his hands,
still standing there dazed.
The Taoist asked,
"When did you come?"
Niè Dào replied,
"When did I ever leave?"
The Taoist was full of anger
but could not let it out;
he had to restrain himself and tell him to quickly clean up.
He then said to the old woman,
"These two upstairs rooms
were built by this humble priest himself in the spring.
Though cramped as a snail's shell,
they are extremely quiet and secluded.
Even when passing guests stay overnight,
they only stay in the two side rooms of the vegetarian hall in front
and have never come here.
Because I feared the young lady would want privacy,
I specially opened them for your use."
The old woman said,
"We are much obliged for your excessive kindness;
we have no way to repay you."
The Taoist added,
"There is a cooling bed upstairs,
and here is a small wooden couch;
please make yourselves comfortable as you please."
Pointing to a small door by the side of the lightwell, he said,
"Inside here is this humble priest’s bedroom;
if you should lack anything,
just trouble the young man to call out."
Seeing his extreme solicitousness,
the old woman felt quite uneasy
and said,
"Master, please go about your business;
allow us to thank you again tomorrow."
Not long after the Taoist left,
he hurriedly brought another lamp
and placed it on the table.
He also brewed some tea and said,
"Please, the three of you, have some tea and get settled."
He also told Niè Dào to go to the old priest's room,
borrow a commode, and place it upstairs,
fearing that the mother and daughter might need to get up during the night to relieve themselves.
As it turned out, this Taoist had a paternal aunt
who was over fifty years old and was a nun at Jìngzhēn Nunnery at the Fújiāng ferry crossing,
not far from Jiànmén.
Every few months, this old nun would come to visit her nephew
and stay for a day or two before leaving.
Whenever she came,
she was accustomed to borrowing the commode;
therefore, today the priest did not hesitate.
It is said that Jiǎ Qīngfēng was also wary of Niè Dào’s lecherous looks;
he waited until he had gone downstairs
before he turned to leave.
The old woman said,
"It is rare for this Master to be so thoughtful
and to arrange things so meticulously.
Tomorrow, if there is no snow,
we should leave quickly,
regardless of how slippery and difficult the road may be.
The things of a religious man
are given twofold;
we must not trouble him too much, lest it be unbecoming."
The Cripple said,
"Since we have already bothered him,
we might as well be thick-skinned and stay for a few more days,
simply waiting for a clear, dry day that is good for traveling.
Do not wait until we find we cannot walk and have to turn back,
which would instead make him laugh at us.
If you are stubborn and insist on going,
I shall just stay here and wait for you."
Mèier laughed and said,
"Brother has eaten and drunk happily
and is now unwilling to leave."
The Cripple said,
"Usually when I cannot keep up with you,
you are simply anxious.
On the road from here to Jiànmén,
it is very steep and difficult to travel!
Trudging through mud and water,
what kind of trick would that be?
I am also considering things carefully;
if we can walk, we walk;
if we should stop, we stop.
Yet you say I have eaten and drunk happily
and am unwilling to leave.
It is not as if we have festive feasts here every morning
and Lantern Festivals every night.
This Master is only showing respect to new guests today;
could he possibly spend money like this every day?
You say I drink happily,
as if you haven't moved your own mouth."
Mèier said,
"I was only joking;
you've gone and taken it seriously."
The old woman said,
"The two of you stop arguing;
by dawn, I will have a plan."
Taking advantage of his tipsiness, the Cripple
fell onto the couch and went to sleep.
Carrying the lamp, the old woman
went upstairs with Mèier.
In his room, the Taoist thought to himself,
"Such a naturally beautiful girl!
If she were willing to marry me,
I would willingly return to secular life."
He further thought,
"This girl was shy at first,
but later she became a bit more familiar.
If Heaven is willing to send down heavy snow for a few more days
to keep her here longer,
I have no doubt she will fall into my hands.
I expect traveling will be impossible tomorrow;
I shall further show her some affection
and really hook her.
A human heart is made of flesh;
could it be made of iron?
This old mother is a poor woman,
and the Cripple only lusts after wine and food;
neither is a difficult matter."
That Jiǎ Taoist thought about this for the entire night,
not even closing his eyes once.
This was not yet surprising;
who would have known that Niè Dào was also indulging in wishful thinking,
his soul disturbed and his dreams tossed.
It was clearly a mangy toad dreaming of eating swan meat;
how could it ever reach his mouth?
Truly:
The infatuated Taoist
longs only for intimacy.
The thick-faced incense page
is also overcome by restless lust.
Jiànmén is not the temple on Mount Wū;
he mistakes her for the goddess in King Xiāng’s dream.
What kind of trouble these Taoists and the little vixen will cause after all,
please listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
If the sword of wisdom can strike and sever,
one will become a deity, if not an immortal or a Buddha.
The story goes that because Jiǎ Dàoshì had taken a fancy to Hú Mèir,
his heart was infatuated and his mind was in a whirl,
and he spent a sleepless night.
Before it was even dawn,
he rose and opened his room door,
quietly pacing downstairs to investigate.
He saw only the cripple snoring in deep sleep on the couch;
there was no movement at all upstairs.
Returning to his room,
he could not sit still,
and went out to pace four or five times in succession,
like an ant on a hot pot lid,
with no way to run or place to go.
He ran to the kitchen,
woke up the Lǎo Xiānggōng,
and told him to heat water for washing
and to prepare breakfast.
There was only one rooster in the temple to herald the dawn;
he ordered Niè Dào to slaughter and prepare it for eating.
Niè Dào already knew the Dàoshì’s heart
and busily made preparations.
Lǎo Xiānggōng was still half-dreaming
when he said,
“Āmítuófó!
Wouldn’t it be better to keep him to herald the dawn?
Why take this life for no reason?”
Niè Dào laughed and said,
“The Shīfu has recently learned to wake up early,
so there is no need for a dawn herald.”
Meanwhile, the old woman and Mèir
were discussing upstairs:
“The days we spend traveling are many,
but the distance we cover is little,
all because this cripple slows us down,
preventing us from moving quickly.
This Fǎguān is very well-intentioned;
it would be better to give the cripple to him as a disciple,
to stay here for a while,
while we go on our way.
If we find a renowned master
and have a place to settle,
it will not be too late to come back and call for him.”
At dawn,
they first called the cripple upstairs
and told him of this.
The cripple, who dreaded walking,
felt as if he had been given an exemption
and was boundlessly happy.
After the three had finished their discussion,
they heard the sound of coughing downstairs;
it was the voice of Jiǎ Dàoshì,
saying,
“Has the Pópo risen yet?
I have told the Niè Dào to bring washing water up.”
The old woman replied,
“I have started moving,
let Quér come and carry it himself.”
The cripple went downstairs to carry the water;
before he had even climbed four or five steps of the ladder,
Niè Dào had already delivered it.
The cripple took it,
and they finished their grooming.
Jiǎ Dàoshì went upstairs, bowed, and asked,
“Did you sleep well last night?”
The old woman said,
“Many thanks.”
This time, looking at Mèir’s appearance,
she seemed different from yesterday.
Yesterday she had come through the snow,
still wearing the weathered look of wind and frost;
today her bearing was doubly extraordinary,
truly like a celestial maiden from Táoyuán Dòng
or a beautiful person from Dòushuài Gōng.
When the Dàoshì saw her,
his itch remained unscratched,
and he wished he could swallow her into his stomach in one gulp.
Immediately, he asked with great solicitude,
“What is your venerable age, Pópo?
And what is the age of the Xiǎoniángzi?”
The old woman said,
“I am exactly sixty,
and my daughter is nineteen.”
The Dàoshì said,
“Was she born when you were forty-two?”
The old woman said,
“Exactly.”
The Dàoshì said,
“How old is this young brother?
How did he lose a foot?”
The old woman said,
“Cūn’er is twenty-three.
This foot was injured in a fall while playing in his youth.
Because he cannot walk well,
he delays our pace considerably.”
The Dàoshì said,
“The snow fell heavily yesterday;
for it to melt away completely,
it will take another four or five days
before it is easy to walk.
Since the young brother has difficulties,
there is no harm in staying for some time.”
The old woman said,
“I happen to have something to say, though I do not know if it is appropriate to report.”
The Dàoshì said,
“Speak freely.”
The old woman said,
“My late husband
was originally a Huǒdān Dàoshì,
in the same Dao as the Fǎguān,
though his magic was not profound.
Although this Cūn’er is unsightly,
he has some affinity for the Dao.
Last year, a Quánzhēn Xiānsheng
who understood Mǎyī physiognomy
said he had the appearance of one who should leave the secular world
and wanted him as a disciple,
but I simply could not bear to let him go.
Seeing now that the Fǎguān is so compassionate,
I wish to have my son bow to you as his Shīfu,
to serve you by burning incense and sweeping floors;
I do not know if you are willing to accept him?”
The Dàoshì, who was already plotting to get close to that little fox spirit but had no pretext,
found that this arrangement made them like kin without being kin,
fitting his plans perfectly.
He replied,
“It would be wonderful to have the young brother here as a companion in the Dao.
Truly wonderful.
However, I
also have something to say.
I lost both my parents in childhood
and have no relatives to look after me;
if you do not despise me,
I wish to bow to you, Pópo, as my Gānniáng.”
The old woman said,
“How could I, an old woman, be worthy of that?”
After both sides yielded politely for a while,
the Dàoshì bowed four times to the old woman,
and the cripple also bowed four times to the Dàoshì.
From then on, the cripple called the Dàoshì “Shīfu,”
and the Dàoshì called the old woman “Gānniáng.”
The Dàoshì then bowed twice more to Mèir and said,
“From now on, we are one family of brother and sister.”
Meanwhile, Niè Dào had cooked the chicken,
cut it into two bowls,
and arranged several vegetarian dishes,
setting the breakfast downstairs.
The Dàoshì and the mother and daughter, a family of three, went downstairs
and sat as before.
However, because the cripple had become a disciple,
he yielded the seat of honor to the Dàoshì.
Once seated,
the Dàoshì said,
“In this snowy weather, there was nowhere to buy anything;
I could only slaughter a chicken,
so I hope my Gānniáng and Xiánmèi will help yourselves as you please.”
He then picked out the best pieces from the bowl and offered them with his chopsticks.
The old woman said,
“My daughter and I both observe a vegetarian fast;
only Cūn'er eats meat.
I did not know the Fǎguān would go to such trouble
and neglected to mention it.”
The Dàoshì said,
“How strange!
My Xiánmèi is so young;
why does she eat vegetarian?”
The old woman said,
“She has been vegetarian since before birth.”
The Dàoshì said,
“When she marries into a family in the future,
it will be very inconvenient.”
The old woman said,
“What talk is there of marrying?
She is like a nun with hair,
often thinking of leaving the secular world.”
The Dàoshì thought,
“This is another opportunity.”
He said,
“Leaving the world is a good thing,
but I fear that if it is not done at the right time,
it may not be ideal.
I have a Dígū
who is currently the Zhùchí at Jìngzhēn Ān.
If Gānniáng
and Xiánmèi are willing to leave the dust behind and study the Dao,
you may go there directly to practice.
This nunnery is only forty-some lǐ from here,
and since the young brother is in this temple,
the distance is not great,
making it easy to look after each other
and avoiding worry for both sides.”
The old woman said,
“That would be excellent.
However, my Mèir has made a vow of incense to the Holy Emperor of Xīyuè Huà Shān,
and we must go.
After I have accompanied her to offer incense
and we return,
we will come back to the temple to discuss it further.”
The Dàoshì said,
“That will be easy then.”
After breakfast,
the old woman saw that the Taoist priest was very kind
and that they had already become like one family,
so she was no longer in a hurry to get back on the road.
The priest took a half-new, half-old Taoist robe from himself
and gave it to the cripple to wear,
telling everyone to call him Master Qué.
He also gave an empty room next to his own to the cripple as a bedroom,
called a carpenter to tidy it up
and make some window lattices,
but told the cripple to supervise the work.
At night, the cripple no longer came downstairs to sleep.
The priest also arranged some vegetables and fruit in his own room
and invited his godmother
and worthy sister
to sit and relax in the room.
In the middle of the conversation, he caught a spare moment
and cast a glance at that little fox-spirit.
Mèi'ér only smiled faintly,
and so the priest became even more infatuated for a time.
A poem serves as proof:
A heart full of charm and a partial smile,
Two eyes that enchant the soul like a pair of flowers.
He thought only of being a companion beneath the blossoms of Wǔlíng,
forgetting that he belonged to the household of the Way.
The priest, having become familiar as a "brother" to her,
followed closely at Mèi'ér's heels,
not leaving her side for even half a step;
the two exchanged flirtatious glances,
and felt their feelings were mutual.
After some more time had passed,
they were already pinching hands and feet,
but were hindered by the old woman,
having no place to take action.
It was just like a broken-legged egret standing on the beach,
watching the fresh fish while enduring a hungry belly.
Three days passed in succession,
and the weather had cleared up nicely,
so the old woman prepared to say goodbye and set off.
The priest pleaded for them to stay one more day,
and the old woman, unable to resist his begging,
had no choice but to agree.
The priest returned to his room
and sat gloomily,
thinking that there was only this one day left;
if he didn't try his best to get his hands on her,
then all his efforts would have been for nothing.
He paced back and forth,
knitting his brows
and picking his fingernails,
thinking for six hours,
until suddenly he burst out laughing and said:
"I have a plan!"
Hurriedly, he found two bolts of extremely fine green shuttle-woven cloth in his trunks,
carried them downstairs,
and said to the old woman:
"Godmother,
worthy sister,
I don't know when you will return once you leave,
so I have selected two bolts of cloth
for each of you to make a shirt to wear away,
as a token of my regard.
I have already called for a tailor;
it will be finished tomorrow,
and you can depart the day after."
The old woman said:
"We have received so much from you,
it makes us truly uneasy.
Mèi'ér, thank your elder brother."
The priest turned and went out,
then told Nièdào to go to the village to fetch two tailors,
as they needed to rush some clothes early the next morning.
Nièdào agreed and left.
That Nièdào's lust was not a bit inferior to that of Jiǎ Qīngfēng;
seeing the priest in such a frantic state
but unable to get his hands on her,
he knew he himself couldn't have her either,
yet he kept a daily watch to look for an opening.
"Calling the tailors this time,
he must be up to some trick again;
I'll watch coldly to see what he does."
Our story splits into two paths:
meanwhile, Priest Jiǎ spent another night in vain thoughts.
When dawn arrived,
he again sent Nièdào to hurry the tailors,
who soon replied:
"The tailors have been called to the fasting hall."
The priest hurriedly ran upstairs,
told the old woman to take the cloth out,
and said:
"I don't know the proper length,
so Godmother, you must go yourself to oversee the cutting
and instruct them on how it should be done.
The tailors in this village of mine
are no experts;
if you leave it to them,
I'm afraid it won't be to your liking."
The old woman indeed held the two bolts of cloth
and followed the priest out.
As soon as they reached the fasting hall,
the priest quickly turned back,
ran downstairs,
and taking advantage of Mèi'ér being there all alone,
he went forward and embraced her,
saying:
"Worthy sister,
I have been longing for you for a long time;
take this opportunity
and quickly save my life!"
Mèi'ér said:
"In broad daylight,
it's so embarrassing!
How can this be done?
My mother will be coming in any moment."
The priest said:
"Your mother is dealing with the tailors;
it will be quite a while yet.
A single moment is worth a thousand pieces of gold;
I hope my worthy sister will fulfill her elder brother's wish
and not make things difficult."
He then pressed his face against hers to kiss her,
and Mèi'ér also met him with the tip of her tongue,
crying out:
"Dear brother,
it's not that your younger sister is heartless,
but it is simply inconvenient;
it absolutely cannot be done during the day.
Late tonight, in the latter half of the night,
when my mother is asleep,
I will quietly come downstairs
and meet you on this couch;
whatever you do, do not break your word."
The priest then knelt down and kowtowed, saying:
"If my worthy sister would do this,
I shall never forget this kindness in life or death."
Before he had even finished speaking,
the old incense attendant called out:
"Master Jiǎ!
The old mother in front is asking you for some thread."
The priest hurriedly answered
and urged Mèi'ér again, saying:
"What you just said,
worthy sister, you must not forget."
The priest went to his room to get the thread.
He did not realize that Nièdào was upstairs carrying the night-stools;
hearing Priest Jiǎ's voice,
he had quietly crouched by the stairs to listen.
Although the conversation between the two was not very clear,
he had seen the sentimental scene with his own eyes
and guessed there was a private tryst.
Waiting specifically for the priest to go out,
he then walked downstairs and caught Mèi'ér in his arms, saying:
"I know all about your affair with my master.
I won't expose you,
as long as I get a share as well.
It was I who started everything at the well pavilion;
you must thank the matchmaker."
Mèi'ér, being clever and quick-witted,
knit her brows as a plan came to mind,
and then said:
"Let go of your hands;
I'm afraid it would be embarrassing if someone saw us.
I guarantee there will be something in it for you."
Nièdào indeed let go and asked:
"How are you going to settle with me?"
Mèi'ér said:
"Just now I couldn't get your master to stop pestering me,
so I told him to leave his bedroom door open at night,
and I would go to his room in the middle of the night.
Tonight, wait until your master has entered his room,
and then quietly go and lie down on the couch downstairs first.
When I come downstairs, I'll settle the account with you first
before I go into his room.
Wouldn't that be good?"
Nièdào also kowtowed and said:
"If the young lady truly does this,
it will be the salvation of my life!"
Having said this, Nièdào went out.
Mèi'ér laughed secretly, saying:
"Since the secret is out, it won't work for anyone.
I might as well play a trick on him
and give him a thoroughly disappointing time tonight."
It is said that after the old woman finished giving her instructions to the tailors,
she called the Cripple downstairs
and exhorted him, saying:
“You must behave well while here;
your sister and I will certainly depart tomorrow morning.
If there is any benefit to be found,
then come and bring us along;
do not merely covet wine and food
and make yourself loathsome and base,
otherwise, next time I, your mother, come here, it will be without honor.”
That day, the Taoist came again to accompany them for dinner.
After the two tailors finished making the clothes,
they sent them in.
The Taoist said to the old woman again:
“Gānniáng, since you are definitely departing tomorrow,
there is no need to rise extremely early;
have some breakfast before you go.”
The old woman said:
“I am most grateful for your kind intentions;
I shall thank you properly tomorrow morning.”
Having a secret appointment with Mèi'ér, the Taoist
was extremely happy;
he returned to his room and warmed a pot of good wine.
Having drunk until he was thirty percent intoxicated,
he sat on the Zuìwēng bed to take a nap,
saving his energy to take action late in the night.
Meanwhile, after Miē Dào had finished tidying up,
he found an opportunity to sneak into the courtyard and crouch under a banana tree.
Peering in, he saw that the Taoist’s door was already closed
and that the mother and daughter had also gone upstairs.
He then quietly went to sleep under the daybed,
simply waiting for word from upstairs;
after waiting for an hour, he unknowingly fell asleep.
Here, the Taoist napped for a while,
losing track of the time;
fearing only that he would miss his appointment,
he hurriedly used both hands to lift the door and pull it open gently.
Walking with the 'crane’s step in an empty courtyard,'
he moved forward step by step.
When he reached the daybed and reached out to feel it,
he knew someone was lying there asleep.
He thought to himself:
“This sweetheart is indeed affectionate;
she was already here waiting for me.”
He hurriedly took off his shoes
and lay down to sleep at one end.
Miē Dào was startled awake by him,
and he also thought that the young lady had kept her word
and had indeed come.
The two of them did not speak,
but embraced and first shared a 'sweet mouth.'
Then the Taoist was heard asking in a low voice:
“Who are you?”
Miē Dào already recognized the Taoist’s voice
and replied:
“Shīfu, it is I.”
The Taoist also recognized that it was Miē Dào;
why was he also here?
Surely this clever thief must have heard some rumors
and was here to interrupt my good business.
Consequently, both felt embarrassed
and went back to their own beds.
The Taoist felt as if he had clearly had a nightmare
and did not believe such a thing could happen.
By then, his desire had subsided,
and he fell fast asleep.
When dawn broke
and everyone arose,
the Taoist looked at Miē Dào and did nothing but laugh;
Miē Dào looked at the Taoist and also did nothing but laugh.
That little fox-spirit looked at the Taoist and Miē Dào and also did nothing but laugh.
Truly:
Today they meet without a word,
for it seems they are all 'members of the same club.'
Although the Taoist was disappointed that night,
he still thought that when she returned from offering incense at Xīyuè,
there would still be a day to meet;
thus he refused to cast aside this burden of lovesickness.
At that time, he told Miē Dào to prepare food and wine
and accompanied the mother and daughter while they ate.
The old woman and Mèi'ér each put on one of the two newly made shirts
and packed up to set out.
She also gave the Cripple a few instructions,
telling him to be patient.
The Cripple replied:
“I know all about it.”
The Taoist and the Cripple saw them out the temple gate,
and the old woman politely expressed her thanks again.
The Taoist said:
“Gānniáng, when you return, you must come to my temple to see your little brother.
Tomorrow I will send a letter to the Gūniang at the Jìngzhēn Ān;
should you ever develop the intention to cultivate,
no place is as peaceful as there.”
He then said to Mèi'ér:
“Take care, Xiánmèi;
we shall meet again some day.”
Unconsciously, tears fell from his eyes,
and he nearly burst out crying;
fearing others would notice,
he covered his eyes and hurriedly ran back inside.
Mèi'ér also felt sorrowful in her heart.
Reader, please remember this:
this Zuǒ Chù was a Taoist in the Guānwáng Miào at the foot of Jiànmén Shān.
Meanwhile, the mother and daughter left the temple
and proceeded toward Jiàngé.
This time, without the Cripple to hinder them,
they traveled faster.
Nothing happened on the road;
as they approached the Yǒngxìng area,
it was already late.
They saw a forest far ahead,
about ten lǐ away.
The old woman said:
“Mèi'ér,
let us hurry to that forest to stay overnight;
from there, Xīyuè is not far.”
Mother and daughter had not walked many steps
when suddenly a great black wind rose up, blowing so hard they could not open their eyes
and could not keep their footing.
That wind was very fierce.
Truly:
Shadowless and formless, the cold pierces the bone;
suddenly coming and going, the chill invades the skin.
If it were not the cry of the Demon King of the Underworld,
it must be the howl of a mountain ghost.
When the wind subsided,
they saw two warriors in military attire step forward, bow, and say:
“The Tiānhòu has a decree,
inviting the Shènggū for an audience.”
The old woman said:
“Who is the Tiānhòu?”
The warriors said:
“She is Wǔ Zétiān Niángniang of the Táng Cháo.”
The old woman said:
“Zétiān Niángniang has been dead for a long time;
how can she still be here?
Moreover, I have never met her;
what business does she have calling for me?”
The warriors said:
“The Niángniang currently resides here and has a karmic bond with the Shènggū;
it is fated that you meet,
so please come with us.
Once the Shènggūgū arrives there, she will know the details.”
The old woman felt somewhat afraid
and wanted to refuse to go,
but the two warriors flanked her on both sides;
she had no choice but to walk.
The moment they moved,
their feet did not touch the ground,
and before long they arrived at a place
where ancient trees reached the sky,
vines covered the paths,
a dismal ghostly wind blew,
and the night air was dark and gloomy.
After passing through two memorial arches,
a large palace hall appeared.
The warriors disappeared,
and two maids in palace attire appeared,
carrying purple gauze lanterns
to lead the way,
saying:
“The Niángniang has been waiting for a long time.”
When the old woman entered the hall,
there was a Pánlóng xiāng'àn in the center,
but no one was sitting there.
The maids said:
“Shènggūgū, please wait here a moment.”
After a short while, they came out and said:
“The Tiānhòu has a decree,
inviting the Shènggūgū to meet behind the hall.”
The old woman followed the handmaidens and went straight inside.
She saw only the pearl curtains rolled up high,
and the interior was brilliantly lit by lamps and candles.
Tiānhòu was seated in the center,
with several female officials in purple robes and gauze caps standing on both sides,
who shouted:
"Bow!"
The old woman bowed toward the throne as commanded,
and only then did she rise.
Tiānhòu issued an imperial decree to grant her a seat,
but the old woman modestly declined, saying:
"How could I dare be so bold before the Celestial Countenance?"
Tiānhòu said:
"There is no need to be overly humble.
Today's meeting is no accident.
We wish to discuss our karmic affinity in detail with you,
for how could it be exhausted in a conversation while standing?"
She then ordered a brocade stool to be brought near
and supported her with the Imperial Hand as she sat.
The old woman spoke again:
"A rustic and ugly person like me is despised by others;
since I have been so graciously summoned by Your Majesty,
what instructions do you have for me?"
Tiānhòu said:
"You should not dislike yourself for being common.
You are a solitary person among your kind,
and We are the solitary one among people.
Reading the manifesto of Scholar Luò still chills Our heart even today;
We are actually ashamed before you."
She then recited a poem,
which said:
"We were originally the King of a Hundred Flowers,
ruling from the inner chambers as the Emperor of the mortal world.
In accord with destiny, We rose like a dragon,
Our bearing was not that of a solitary enchantress.
How could the laws of the state not be upheld?
Yet men of letters are also to be feared.
We dare not look into the bronze mirror;
facing you, We still feel shame."
She continued:
"At that time, We greatly cherished the talent of Luò Bīnwáng.
When the captives were presented and We heard his head was among them,
We could not bear to look at it.
Who would have known that the head was a fake,
and Luò Bīnwáng had escaped to become a monk?
Officials have always deceived the Imperial Court;
they are all of this sort.
Outsiders still believe that Our executions were too excessive;
where is the justice in that?"
She sighed again and said:
"Scholar Luò became a monk
and instead ascended to heaven,
while We are still lingering in the underworld.
Consider the rebellion of Huáng Cháo;
Our century-old decayed bones
were again desecrated.
Things like gold and jade were completely unearthed and stolen,
leaving Our jade pendants withered and broken today.
We are truly ashamed to show Our face to you."
When the old woman looked up,
indeed Tiānhòu had her hair in a "Facing Heaven" bun,
but there were no hairpins or earrings at all,
and her imperial robe had no sash.
The old woman said:
"The bandit Huáng Cháo was insolent;
why did Your Majesty's divine spirit not stop him?"
Tiānhòu said:
"Whenever a cycle of slaughter arrives,
Heaven sends a Demon King to the world.
We were born at the beginning of Táng,
and Huáng Cháo was born at the end of Táng.
Though our appearances as male and female are different,
as demons, we are the same.
When We were in power,
who in the world could stop Us?
Could We alone stop Huáng Cháo?"
The old woman asked:
"I heard that during Tiānhòu's reign,
you cast statues and built pagodas,
performing many Buddhist rites.
Your merit was not small;
why do you still linger on the dark path of the underworld?"
Tiānhòu said:
"A person must first give rise to a pure heart
before they can obtain the blessings of charity.
Our intentions were not pure,
so We cultivated the path of a demon.
At that time, We enjoyed all the blessings of a woman,
but Our only regret was not being a man.
Our prayers to the Buddha
were for nothing but this.
Now the time is approaching,
and the Sovereign on High has already sent Us to take a male body."
The old woman said:
"When Your Majesty is reincarnated into wealth and rank this time,
will it be the same as before?"
Tiānhòu said:
"Since I have achieved the demonic path,
I must be born riding the demonic destiny.
If one lacks power and influence,
how can demonic power be exercised?
We were previously a woman and yet became an Emperor;
how much more so as a man?
Your daughter Mèi'ér is destined by the underworld numbers to be Our consort.
She has now been entrusted to Chōngxiāo Chùshì;
do not worry."
The old woman said:
"Since Your Majesty is turning into a male body
and will again call yourself 'Solitary' and 'Widowed',
surely you will not lack beautiful and enchanting women in the three palaces and six courtyards.
Why then choose a girl of a different kind?"
Tiānhòu said:
"There is something you do not know.
Mèi'ér's previous life was Zhāng Liùláng,
who was said at the time to have a face like a lotus.
The affection between Us and Liùláng was not shallow,
and we once privately made a vow, saying:
'In every life and every world, we wish to be husband and wife.'
Unfortunately, things went against Our heart,
and we have been separated like the stars Shēn and Shāng until now.
Now We shall be the Sovereign,
and he shall again be the Empress.
The register of mandarin ducks is already fixed;
how could it be changed?
Our rise to power shall be in Héběi.
Twenty-eight years from now, We shall meet you again in Bèizhōu.
You should refine your Daoist arts to assist Our mandate."
The old woman said:
"My child and I have come precisely to seek the Dao,
but I do not know where the Daoist arts are."
Tiānhòu said:
"We have sixteen characters.
You should remember them,
for they will surely be fulfilled.
They say:
Stop when meeting Yáng;
become enlightened when meeting the Egg.
People will come to seek you;
you shall not seek people."
Tiānhòu continued:
"Within three years, you will surely have an encounter.
Whether moving or staying, there is no need to be impatient.
After you have attained the Dao,
you may go to Dōngjīng to deliver your daughter.
Although her appearance will have changed,
you will naturally be able to recognize her.
Heavenly secrets should be kept secret;
they must not be lightly leaked.
If the Eighty-Year-Old Man hears of this, the disaster would not be small."
The old woman asked:
"Who is the Eighty-Year-Old Man?"
Tiānhòu said:
"He is Zhāng Jiǎnzhī, the Prince of Hànyáng.
He is the head of the Five Princes,
and he has opposed Us for generations.
You should avoid him."
The words were not yet finished,
when only a chorus of shouts was heard in front of the palace.
Attendants reported in a panic:
"Hànyáng Wáng has heard that Niángniáng intends to scheme for the throne again,
and is leading a grand army of one hundred thousand,
killing his way here."
Tiānhòu was so frightened her face turned the color of ash;
she rose from her seat and fled toward the back.
The old woman said:
"Niángniáng, take this old wife along,
and let us find a place to hide together."
In her frantic haste,
she kicked over a brocade stool,
tripped, and fell flat on the ground.
Startled into a cold sweat,
she realized she was lying beneath a great tomb;
the palace halls were all gone,
and Mèier was no longer by her side.
She called out in all directions,
but there was no trace of her;
she simply did not know where she had gone.
After weeping for a while,
she thought:
"Yán Bànxiān said my daughter would face disaster;
indeed, such an inexplicable thing has happened."
Seeing that dawn was breaking,
