she noticed a broken stone lying amidst the brambles in front of the tomb,
with the words "Spirit Way of Zétiān Huánghòu of the Dà Táng" engraved upon it.
The old woman said:
"So it turns out the place I visited in my dream
was the secluded palace of Tiānhòu.
She gave me many instructions;
I remember every single one.
This matter is very strange;
let me see how those sixteen words will be fulfilled.
Even so,
thinking back to when we first left the earthen cave,
there were three of us, mother and children;
we left Chù'er behind at Jiànmén Shān,
and now I have lost Mèier here as well.
Left all alone,
how miserable!
Since it is said that traveling and staying are the same
and one should not be impatient,
I shall find a quiet place at the foot of Tàihuá Shān to stay for a while,
and then decide what to do."
Because of this episode, there is a reason to say:
The lǎo hújīng meets another extraordinary person,
and a new wondrous tale is born.
Truly it is: "You may wear out iron shoes searching in vain,
but when the time comes, it takes no effort at all."
As for where Mèier has gone,
and who will come looking for this Shèng Gūgu,
let us hear the explanation in the next chapter.
In the seats are idle folk fit for telling of ghosts;
if the heart lacks wondrous words, do not chant poetry.
Just use conversation and laughter to pass the clear day;
of idle rights and idle wrongs, one remains unaware.
The story tells that Shèng Gūgu, in a state between dreaming and waking,
met Wǔ Zétiān Niángniáng
and spoke of a karmic connection.
It turned out that Mèier was the reincarnation of Zhāng Chāngzōng;
in that former life, Zétiān Niángniáng was male
and Zhāng Chāngzōng was female, meeting in Bèizhōu,
where they were once again joined as a pair,
being called King and Queen.
Now that Mèier has disappeared,
and it is not known with which Chōngxiāo Chùshì she is,
it is very strange indeed.
Since it was said that traveling and staying are the same,
it clearly tells me to rest my feet.
Now I wonder where a place to stay might be;
after pondering for a while,
she said:
"I have it!
The incense vows for the Huá Shān Yuè Miào
were originally mentioned by Mèier.
I shall go before the Shèngdì in the Xīyuè Miào to burn a stick of incense
and pray for Mèier's protection.
While there, I will see if there is any quiet place
where I can settle down;
I will wait for her for at least three years
before making other plans.
Since the cripple was given to the Taoist as an apprentice,
and seeing that the Taoist is very well-intentioned,
he likely won't be without a place to stay;
that much I can let go of."
Thereupon, the old woman went alone toward Huáyīn Xiàn
to offer incense at Tàihuá Shān.
How does one see the scenery of Tàihuá Shān?
There is the "Xī Jiāng Yuè"
as evidence:
Steep cliffs tower abruptly as if sheared,
perilous precipices and the Immortal's Palm held high from afar.
Lotus flowers spring from the earth like bright stars,
and the winding Azure Dragon lies across the ridge.
Tàibái brings his poems, wishing to inquire;
Chānglí summons his courage to be the first to ascend.
Better to pack away profit and fame
and sleep a Xīyí sleep, never to wake.
When the old woman reached the mountain,
she took up a handful of earth as incense before the seat of the Xīyuè,
bowed several times to the Shèngdì,
kowtowed a few times,
and made her petition for a while,
which was nothing more than praying for an early encounter with Taoist fate
and for the reunion of mother and daughter.
Stepping down from the hall,
she observed the scenery
and inquired about Master Chén Tuán.
Someone pointed the way:
"This Xīyí Xiá is the place where he underwent his liberation from the corpse."
Only then did she know that Chén Tuán had already transcended as an immortal.
The old woman loved the tranquility of this Xīyí Xiá,
so at night she stayed within the gorge,
and during the day she used the pretext of seeking alms
to walk about the front and back of the mountain.
She watched the men and women, wandering monks and Taoists coming and going,
observing their movements.
If she collected a few coins,
she would exchange them for some vegetarian wine and food to enjoy;
this was a regular occurrence.
One day, together with some other poor women of her kind,
she stood idly for half a day,
but had not encountered a single pilgrim willing to give alms.
As the noon hour was about to pass,
she saw two small sedan chairs carrying a lady
and a maidservant
coming up the mountain to burn incense.
The poor women waited for her to come out of the hall and finish burning paper
before stepping forward to beg.
The lady said:
"I haven't brought any money today."
Hearing these words, the old woman dodged to one side,
but because the other poor women had not received a single coin since morning,
and they were certain this female guest would be generous,
how could they let her go?
They pestered her relentlessly,
wanting her to show a charitable heart.
One said this,
another said that:
"What goes out in the light comes back in the dark;
alms in this life bring blessings in the next;
who has ever seen the Sea Dragon King without treasures?"
The lady said irritably:
"I am not Yáng Lǎo Fó
or Yáng Nǎinai;
if you have the ability, go to her place
and enjoy her great hospitality and gifts.
Why bother me?"
She pushed through the crowd, went down the steps,
got into her sedan chair, and was carried away at high speed.
The poor women sighed at their bad luck
and scattered dejectedly.
Seeing one who seemed honest and knowledgeable,
the old woman went to ask her:
"Just now she spoke of some Yáng Lǎo Fó and Yáng Nǎinai—
what does that mean?"
The poor woman replied:
"In this Huáyīn Xiàn, there is a Xúnjiǎn named Yáng Chūn,
known by the name Yáng Lǎo Fó;
they are a very wealthy family.
Both husband and wife are fond of the Way
and offer incense and alms everywhere.
It doesn't matter if it's a monk, nun, or Taoist;
as long as they are capable and they get along,
and speak in a way that aligns,
they will provide for them for years on end.
This Nǎinai comes to this mountain twice a year;
when she sees us,
she gives each of us a full ten coins or so,
and she has large baskets of toasted buns carried up
to distribute to us to eat.
She came once in the second month of this year,
and she will surely come again in the autumn;
you will inevitably see her."
The old woman kept this in mind
and spent the night there.
Tomorrow, rising early,
she dressed herself in the guise of a poor, begging old Taoist nun;
she went down the mountain to the front of Huáyīn County,
inquired after the house of Yáng Xúnjiǎn,
and went straight to the front of his gate.
There she saw the four characters "Enter and Exit with Caution"
posted on the gate,
and there were also two lines on a notice which read:
"All Buddhist monks, Taoist priests, and Buddhist nuns
are only permitted to attend a vegetarian feast at the West Garden on the first day of the first month of each season;
alms are not customarily distributed at the gate of this residence."
The old woman thought to herself:
"How strange."
She saw an old gatekeeper leaning against the stone lion guarding the gate,
unbuttoning his cloth shirt to catch lice there.
Seeing the old woman approach the gate,
he hurriedly threw on his shirt and shouted:
"Quickly, get out!"
The old woman stepped forward and gave a Taoist greeting,
saying:
"This humble nun is from Xīchuān.
I have made a vow to pilgrimage to Xīyuè.
Passing through your esteemed county,
I lack the travel expenses for my return journey,
and specifically seek some alms."
This gatekeeper, Zhāng Gōng, said:
"Old Taoist nun, you have no luck.
If you had come ten days ago, this notice was not yet here,
but now alms are no longer given."
The old woman said:
"I have long heard that the Master Patrol Inspector and his wife love the Way.
Who in all four directions does not speak of the virtuous Yáng Fózǐ
and Yáng Nǎinai?
Why has this charitable heart now turned to ash?"
Zhāng Gōng said:
"The Master and Lady of this residence
were indeed originally happy to give alms.
If Buddhist monks or Taoist priests from all around could lecture on scriptures or explain the Dharma,
they would provide a house for them to live in
and support them regardless of the months or years.
When it was time to leave,
they would also provide travel expenses,
clothing, and such.
At this gate, there were always people seeking donations;
it was not quiet like this.
It is only because one month ago,
a Buddhist nun came from the south road,
about forty years old,
who could speak about karma.
The Lady loves listening to talk of karma,
so she kept her in the residence for over half a month.
Then there was a group of fourteen or fifteen itinerant monks chanting and seeking alms;
some carried bundles on their heads,
some flicked their fingers,
and some lit flesh-lamps.
This residence also provided them a vegetarian feast once
and gave them some money and silk.
Who knew that group was a band of bandits?
This nun was exactly their leader,
secretly leaking information.
At night, they collaborated from inside and outside,
with torches and weapons,
and robbed many things.
The Master and Lady managed to run quickly
and escaped with their lives.
The two elders discussed it
and said they must have owed a debt to those monks and nuns in a previous life,
so they would not report it to the officials to avoid burdening the local neighbors.
From then on, they would no longer give alms,
nor allow anyone through the gate for an audience.
Only in the first,
fourth,
seventh,
and tenth months, on the first day,
will a vegetarian feast be held once at the West Garden.
Now that the first day of the fourth month has passed,
old Taoist nun, you had better go elsewhere.
In this county, besides this residence,
there are few generous donors.
Even if you beg for a coin or two,
what good would it do?"
The old woman said:
"Among those who have left the home life,
good and bad are different;
it is just that the bad ones have burdened the good ones."
Zhāng Gōng said:
"Exactly."
The old woman said:
"This humble nun no longer hopes for alms.
I have only heard that the Master and Lady are two living Púsà of this world,
and specifically seek an audience,
so that one day on the road to the Western Paradise we might recognize each other."
Before she had finished speaking,
she heard someone inside the residence opening the second set of gates and coming out.
Zhāng Gōng said:
"The Master is coming out to the hall!
Hide yourself quickly,
lest you cause us to suffer his anger."
Hurriedly, from a tattered pouch at his waist,
he pulled out a copper coin and placed it on the head of the stone lion,
saying:
"I will give this single coin to you myself;
now go!"
How could the old woman be willing to leave?
She saw a young servant inside
leading a tall white horse to the main gate,
and standing there holding the reins.
Afterward, Yáng Xúnjiǎn emerged,
wearing a gold-threaded Zhōngjìngguān,
a silk Taoist robe with subtle floral patterns,
black boots on his feet,
and holding a Chuān fan in his hand.
Behind him, one young servant held an umbrella,
one young servant carried a folding chair,
and one young servant held a box.
Inside the box were nothing but incense, candles, and the like,
and on top of the box was placed an empty red sandalwood box.
There was also a group of household musicians,
each carrying an instrument and following him out the gate.
The Master Patrol Inspector
stepped onto the folding chair,
straddled the carved saddle,
and the crowd surged forward, heading west.
Zhāng Gōng complained:
"Did you not see the Master go out?
Fortunately he did not see you;
if he had,
he would have blamed me at the gate for not obeying his decree.
I am giving you this copper coin as charity,
and yet you will not take it;
what more do you want?"
The old woman said:
"Why should I make you, elder, lose money?
If there are no alms to be had, then let it be;
this money, this poor Daoist certainly dares not accept."
While the two were pushing and declining back and forth,
suddenly there was Shòu Gē, who habitually sold miniature mountain pavilions,
carrying his shoulder pole,
passing by the front gate.
From the gatehouse on the side,
a boy of four or five years old ran out,
pulling at Zhāng Gōng and calling:
"Grandfather,
I want a mountain pavilion to play with."
Seeing that the old woman was unwilling to accept it, Zhāng Gōng
called out to Shòu Gē to stop his pole,
took the copper coin from the head of the stone lion to buy a mountain pavilion,
gave it to the boy, and said:
"Play with it well,
do not break it,
or I will not buy you another."
The boy ran laughing into the gatehouse.
Shòu Gē shouldered his pole and left.
The old woman said:
"Who is this boy to you, elder?"
Zhāng Gōng said:
"He is this old man's second grandson.
The one who just carried the folding chair to follow the Master is my eldest grandson,
who is that boy's elder brother."
The old woman said:
"No wonder they have similar faces,
born so clever.
It is the merit you have accumulated from doing good, elder."
Zhāng Gōng said:
"Among the many pages by the Master's side,
he only favors my eldest grandson.
Whenever he goes out, regardless of distance,
he must have him follow."
The old woman said:
"Where did the Master go just now?
He even used a band of musicians."
Zhāng Gōng said:
"To welcome the Fànzì Jīnjīng outside the West Gate."
The old woman said:
"Where did this sūtra come from?"
Zhāng Gōng said:
"A monk from Hāmì brought it.
This Hāmì monk was both mute and deaf,
and stayed at the Guānyīn Ān outside the West Gate.
He lived to ninety-nine years old
and died without illness.
He had nothing else with him,
only leaving behind this Fànzì Jīnjīng.
The abbot of the nunnery said:
'If someone builds a shrine to manage his funeral,
they shall take this sūtra with them.'
My Master built the shrine and cremated him,
and invited monks to perform rituals for him.
Today he went to that nunnery to invite this sūtra,
to be enshrined in the Buddha Hall of the West Garden."
The old woman said:
"What sūtra is it?"
Zhāng Gōng said:
"How would I know if it is a Buddhist sūtra,
a Daoist scripture,
or a Kitchen God scripture?
Who could recognize even half a character?"
The old woman said:
"If it is Sanskrit writing,
perhaps this poor Daoist could decipher and translate it."
Zhāng Gōng started laughing
and said:
"I have heard that this sūtra
came from the Tiānzhú Kingdom of the Western Regions,
written entirely in gold ink,
and is different from the scripts of this world.
Therefore, it is called the Fànzì Jīnjīng.
Before, it passed through many eyes in the nunnery,
and no one recognized it.
You, old woman, tell such a lie;
sinful,
sinful."
The old woman said:
"To not hide it from you, elder,
this poor Daoist once received sixteen kinds of heavenly books from Pǔxián Púsà,
so there are no Sanskrit characters in any scripture that I do not know."
It turned out this old fox spirit
had often associated with celestial foxes
and indeed could recognize heavenly books;
saying it was Pǔxián Púsà was just nonsense.
Hearing this, Zhāng Gōng was greatly shocked and said:
"Pǔxián is of the same rank as Guānshìyīn;
how could you have seen him?"
The old woman said:
"This poor Daoist has an affinity with this Bodhisattva,
and we meet from time to time.
If your Master wants to pay respects to him, it is also very easy."
Zhāng Gōng said:
"Is this true,
or false?"
The old woman said:
"A thousand times true, ten thousand times true."
Zhāng Gōng said:
"If it is really so,
when the Master returns,
I will inform him.
But I do not know your name, Female Bodhisattva,
or where you stay?
I fear the Master may return late today,
and you cannot wait and will leave.
If he wants to find you,
where should he invite you from?"
The old woman said:
"This poor Daoist is called Shèng Gūgū.
If the Master wishes to invite me,
call 'Shèng Gūgū' three times toward the southeast,
and this poor Daoist shall come immediately."
After the old woman finished speaking,
she ran off as if flying.
As the saying goes: when one person eats a vegetarian diet,
ten people chant the Buddha's name.
Because this Yáng Xúnjiǎn and his wife loved the Dao,
even this old gatekeeper was a believer.
Seeing the old woman's words were somewhat strange,
he took them seriously.
That day,
Yáng Xúnjiǎn arrived at the nunnery,
bowed to the Buddha statue,
and invited out the Fànzì Jīnjīng.
Removing the old embroidered wrapper,
he opened it to look closely
and praised it for a while.
He re-wrapped it in a bright red Shǔ silk wrapper
and placed it in a sandalwood box.
Carrying it himself,
he sat on his horse.
A band of musicians with pipes and flutes played refined music
as it was welcomed into the Buddha Hall of the West Garden for enshrinement.
Before the Guānyīn Púsà, he burned incense and lit candles,
bowed four more times,
sent the musicians back first,
and then strolled through the garden himself for a while.
Before leaving, he instructed the gardener not to let idle people into the Buddha Hall,
fearing it would be unclean.
Four pages followed him as he rode back on his horse.
There is a poem to testify:
A troop of pipes and flutes surrounds the carved saddle,
Holding the golden sūtra in hand, the heart is filled with joy.
Having understood the true meaning of the Rúlái,
Táng script and Sanskrit characters are just the same.
At this moment, Zhāng Gōng saw the Patrol Inspector Yáng Xúnjiǎn dismount.
He followed him into the hall
and reported:
"Congratulations, Master!
Today, while we were requesting the Golden Scripture,
someone arrived who can recognize Sanskrit characters and seeks an audience."
Yáng Xúnjiǎn asked:
"What kind of person is it?"
Zhāng Gōng replied:
"It is a female Bodhisattva
whose Dharma name is Shèng Gūgū.
She claims to be a disciple of Pǔxián Púsà
and can recognize sixteen types of heavenly scripts.
If Master wishes to meet her,
just call out to her three times toward the southeast,
and she will arrive instantly."
Yáng Xúnjiǎn, skeptical, said:
"Can such a thing be?
Let us wait until tomorrow
and see if she comes to us again."
Yáng Xúnjiǎn entered the inner residence
and related the news about receiving the Golden Scripture and the matters regarding Shèng Gūgū
to his wife, point by point.
His wife said:
"A strange thing just happened,
and I was just about to tell you.
I went to the courtyard to look at the pomegranate blossoms
and saw a patch of five-colored auspicious clouds from the southeast
slowly approaching.
Within the clouds appeared a Bodhisattva,
adorned with golden beads and jade ornaments,
with a solemn and majestic appearance,
sitting upright upon a white elephant.
I thought to myself that Pǔxián Púsà had appeared,
and I hurriedly bowed down in worship.
When I raised my head, it had vanished.
I thought it was just an illusion,
but from what you say, it truly was Pǔxián Púsà
coming with this Shèng Gūgū.
Shèng Gūgū is certainly no ordinary mortal;
based on the Bodhisattva appearing,
it is quite possible she is his disciple.
Tomorrow, just do as she said and call for her.
If she comes,
show her the Sanskrit scripture to see if she can recognize it.
Let us see how it goes.
If she is indeed a disciple of Pǔxián Púsà,
she surely will not lie."
Dear listeners,
who was that Bodhisattva in the clouds?
It was actually Shèng Gūgū transformed.
As mentioned in the second chapter,
she was a fox spirit of many years.
Transforming into humans
or into Buddhas—
she could conjure any demonic illusion,
but she lacked great divine powers,
and thus could not achieve true greatness.
There is a poem as proof:
Entwined vines serve as her jeweled ornaments,
and tree leaves are worn as her Daoist robes.
One can only laugh at the people of the world who lack the Dharma-eye,
mistaking her for a real Bodhisattva and taking refuge.
Nothing more was said that night.
On the following day, Yáng Xúnjiǎn called for the attendant on duty
to prepare incense and candles
and arrange them in the hall.
Having dressed himself in clean, new clothes,
he stepped out in front of the hall,
faced the southeast,
and sincerely called out "Shèng Gūgū" three times.
Before the sound had even died away,
Zhāng Gōng, the gatekeeper, came to report:
"The old Daoist woman from yesterday is already outside the gate."
Yáng Xúnjiǎn was startled and amazed,
and he said:
"Invite her in."
Before he could even finish saying those words,
an old Daoist woman was already standing in the hall.
She bowed toward him
and said:
"Old Benefactor,
this poor Daoist offers greetings."
Yáng Xúnjiǎn knew she was Shèng Gūgū,
yet he had not seen her walk through the gate;
how could she already be standing in the hall?
His heart was filled with both suspicion and fear.
He hurriedly kowtowed
and said:
"What ability do I, Yáng Chūn, have
to dare trouble Shèng Gūgū to descend?
I have been remiss in my welcome."
The old woman said:
"Old Benefactor, there is no need for such excessive courtesy.
Both you and your wife have an affinity for the Buddha.
This poor Daoist received instructions from the Ancestral Master Pǔxián
to come specifically for this meeting."
Yáng Xúnjiǎn observed Shèng Gūgū's appearance:
although her hair was white and her face wrinkled,
her two eyes were like starlight,
and her spirit was quite different from that of an ordinary person.
Though her clothes were ragged,
they were clean.
At that moment, Yáng Xúnjiǎn felt as if he had clearly seen a living Buddha.
Overjoyed,
he led her to the rear hall
and asked his wife to come out and meet her.
The couple bowed to her as their master
and prepared a vegetarian meal to entertain her.
Shèng Gūgū took the seat of honor,
while the couple sat on either side.
During the meal, they brought up the matter of the Golden Scripture.
The old woman said:
"It is not that this poor Daoist is boasting,
but regardless of whether it is Dragon Scripts or Phoenix Seals,
this poor Daoist knows them all."
When the meal was over,
Yáng Xúnjiǎn ordered Āntóng to prepare sedans and horses.
The couple and the old woman used two sedans
and one horse.
Accompanied by male and female servants,
they went straight to the Xīyuán.
Although this Xīyuán was not as prosperous as the Jīngǔ Garden,
it was indeed well-constructed.
One could see:
The grounds bordered the western side,
with the gate opening to the south.
Entering through the tree-lined lane,
two rows of palace willows were interspersed with sparse locust trees.
Stepping into the maze-like paths,
a stretch of bamboo screens wound along the way.
In front stood five halls for feeding monks,
while several guest houses were built in the middle.
The towers looked out toward Huàyuè,
and there was no need to count the stones piled into mountains.
Water was drawn from the Wèichuān,
making it worthwhile to build pavilions overlooking the ponds.
The winding corridors were elegant;
at the study, one might think it the dwelling of immortals.
The clean rooms were quiet and secluded;
beside the Buddha hall, it felt like wandering through a monk’s quarters.
Opening the path to meet guests, it is fitting to set out wine;
closing the door to decline visitors, one can escape into Chán.
Yáng Xúnjiǎn and his wife let the old woman alight from her sedan first,
then ordered the gardener to lead the way
directly to the Buddha hall,
where the three of them bowed together before the Buddha image.
Yáng Xúnjiǎn ordered Āntóng to bring over a small black lacquered table,
wiped it perfectly clean,
and personally held the sandalwood box,
placing it on the table.
He opened the lid,
took out the scripture,
unwrapped the red brocade bundle,
and asked Shèng Gūgū to examine it.
The old woman pressed her palms together and chanted:
"Āmítuófó."
She then unfolded the scripture
and looked through it from beginning to end.
She said:
"It turns out to be a volume of the Bōluómìduō Xīnjīng,
written in the Sanskrit of Tiānzhù.
Furthermore, the five characters 'Pútí Sà-mó-ā' have been omitted at the end,
which is why the people of the world cannot recognize or identify it."
Yáng Xúnjiǎn was not convinced
and ordered a volume of the Táng Dynasty edition of the Heart Sutra to be brought.
He asked Shèng Gūgū to compare them character by character,
and indeed it was missing five characters.
From then on, Yáng Xúnjiǎn and his wife respected her even more.
At that moment,
Yáng Nǎinai wanted to invite Shèng Gūgū
to her home to live in the same room and discuss things morning and night.
The old woman was unwilling,
so they cleaned three quiet rooms behind the Buddhist hall,
arranged the bedding and utensils,
and provided three meals daily
to support Shèng Gūgū inside.
The old woman lived there entirely alone;
at night, she did not even want a maid or servant woman for company.
She also said to Yáng Nǎinai:
"If it is convenient, send some vegetarian food and wine;
if not, there is no need.
I can go ten years without drinking or eating."
Yáng Nǎinai thought:
"Can one go without food and drink for even a single day?
Even if she tightened her belt,
how could she last ten years?
I will pretend to be busy
and not send her provisions for a few days
to see what happens."
She instructed the gardener to say he had business at home,
locked the garden gate,
and for seven consecutive days, not a single person went there.
On the eighth day,
Yáng Nǎinai took a small sedan chair to the West Garden herself,
opened the lock, and went to see her.
She saw Shèng Gūgū in the quiet room,
serene and motionless,
sitting on a cattail mat reciting the Buddha's name.
Yáng Nǎinai asked:
"Is Shèng Gūgū hungry?"
The old woman shook her head and said,
"I am quite full."
Yáng Nǎinai returned to the residence
and said to her husband,
"Shèng Gūgū has not eaten anything for seven days,
yet she is completely unharmed;
she even has more spirit.
It is truly strange."
The husband and wife were even more convinced she was a living Buddha.
From then on, throughout Huáyīn County,
word spread everywhere that the family of Yáng Xúnjiǎn was supporting a living Buddha.
Speaking of reason, if she were a living Buddha,
what would she seek from others,
and why would she accept support?
In the end, those with insight were few.
Men and women of the county
came in crowds every day to the West Garden to seek an audience;
some even wished to take her as their master.
After a month or two had passed,
the news became a sensation;
even neighboring prefectures and other counties heard of it,
and more and more people came.
Yáng Xúnjiǎn feared it would cause trouble and be inconvenient,
so he discussed it with Shèng Gūgū,
saying she would go into seclusion for three years
and would not receive any outside guests at all.
They locked the front door of the Buddhist hall
and pasted two layers of sealing strips.
However, they made a secret, winding path in the back to quietly deliver things.
Yáng Xúnjiǎn also informed the County Magistrate
and requested an official proclamation to be posted,
strictly forbidding outsiders from disturbing her.
When the people saw the prohibition from the county office,
they no longer came to harass her.
Only the old couple of the household
would occasionally come to the garden for leisure,
secretly visiting the quiet room
to discuss karma and Buddhist laws all day and night.
Others could not very well interfere with them.
From then on, this old fox spirit remained in Huáyīn County receiving the support of Yáng Xúnjiǎn's family.
She herself also thought:
"The four words 'Meet Yáng and stop' spoken by Zétiān Niángniang
have already been fulfilled;
I only wonder about the four words 'Meet an egg and become clear'—
what will they mean?"
Listeners,
I have forgotten an important detail:
the whereabouts of Hú Mèi'ér are still unknown;
why has she not been mentioned?
Readers, do not be anxious.
I have only one mouth
and not two tongues;
how can I say a word here
and a word there?
For now, I will set aside the matter of Hú Mèi'ér
and thoroughly explain the four words "Meet an egg and become clear."
It is said that within the boundaries of Sìzhōu City, there was an Yínghuī Shān and Yínghuī Sì.
The abbot of the temple was an old monk named Cíyún;
his lineage was small,
with only three or four disciples.
There was also an old servant named Liú Gǒu'ér.
Elder Cíyún was nearly sixty years old
and was extremely sincere and honest.
One day,
a family in the prefecture invited him to recite sutras.
Elder Cíyún thought:
"The clothes on my body have not been starched or washed for a month,
and I have no change of clothes.
It would be good to boil a pot of hot water to clean them."
He took a bucket
and went to the pool in front of the temple to draw water.
He saw a round object half-submerged and half-floating on the water's surface;
it drifted toward the edge of the bucket.
Following the motion of Elder Cíyún drawing the water,
it rolled into the bucket with a splash.
Elder Cíyún thought it was just an eggshell,
but when he fished it out, he saw it was a whole egg,
resembling a goose egg.
Elder Cíyún said:
"The families near this temple are not known to raise geese;
where did this egg come from?
Let me see if it is fertile or not.
If it is not fertile,
I will give it to the little śrāmaṇera to eat with his rice.
If it is fertile,
the mother hen of neighbor Zhū Dàbó is currently brooding;
I will give it to him to hatch,
and that will be a life saved."
The Buddhist scriptures say that those who enjoy eating eggs will fall into the Hell of the Empty City after death;
if a glutton were to pick it up and eat it,
would that not be a sin?
When he held the egg against the sunlight,
it was full and fertile.
He hurried to Zhū Dàbó's house and told him to place it in the chicken nest:
"If a goose is hatched,
I will give it to you."
Zhū Dàbó agreed.
It would have been fine if it hadn't hatched,
but after seven days of brooding,
when Zhū Dàbó went to feed them,
he saw the mother hen dead on one side,
and a small child six or seven inches long
had broken through the eggshell and emerged,
sitting inside the nest.
The other chicken eggs had all turned into empty shells,
piled up in a heap.
Zhū Dàbó was terrified
and went to report it to the abbot.
Elder Cíyún was shocked when he heard this,
and when he ran to see it,
he cried out repeatedly:
"How strange!
How strange!
It is this old monk who has burdened you.
This nest of chicken eggs is now useless;
next year when the buckwheat is ripe,
I will compensate you with several dou."
Zhū Dàbó said:
"There is no need;
this is everyone's fate.
I only fear that if the word spreads to the neighbors
and alerts the government,
a small matter will turn into a large one.
A family in the front village, Wáng Pó, once raised a litter of piglets,
among which was one whose front legs looked exactly like human hands.
The local constable found out and reported it to the prefecture,
saying there was such a monstrosity among the people.
The prefecture sent several officers to escort the constable to Wáng Pó's house
to take the pig for inspection.
When this group arrived, they demanded wine and food,
and extorted money;
she even sold the mother pig to give to them,
and it still wasn't enough.
Now, Master, quickly take this monster and cast it away;
do not let it bring trouble to my family."
When Elder Cíyún heard these words,
he remained silent.
He could only take off his black robe,
cover the nest, and carry it back to the temple.
He did not tell his disciples,
but went straight to the vegetable garden in the back,
took a hoe and dug up a patch of ground in a corner of the wall.
He used the chicken nest as the child's coffin
and buried it deep.
It is truly said:
A handful of muddy earth
buries an indestructible spirit;
seven days of floating life
are ended in a sudden moment of impermanence.
The two words life and death are both determined by fate;
misfortune and fortune in the three lives are always up to Heaven.
If the child in the egg died,
then the root of disaster would be ended;
but whether the Elder's wish could be fulfilled,
please listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
The story of Yī Yǐn and the Kōngsāng mulberry is questionable;
the matter of Yǎn Wáng being raised from an egg is even more strange.
Scholars shake their heads when speaking of the supernatural,
not knowing that the neighbor to the east has an egg.
It is said that Cí Zhǎng lǎo buried the child in the vegetable garden;
just as he was about to turn back,
he saw the child part the soil,
and a head like a large walnut poked out.
Cí Zhǎng lǎo was thrown into a panic
and hurriedly struck with his hoe,
but he used too much force,
and fell to the ground with a thud,
even knocking the handle off the hoe.
When he scrambled up to look,
the child was sitting upright inside the chicken coop,
beaming with smiles at Cí Zhǎng lǎo.
Cí Zhǎng lǎo felt pity in his heart
and said:
“Little fellow,
it is a pity that you have obtained a human body;
if you had been born into a wealthy family seeking a son or daughter,
even a night-luminescent pearl could not compare to you.
How did you end up crawling into an eggshell?
You have taken the wrong path yourself;
it has nothing to do with this old monk.
This time, listen to my instructions and seek another path for rebirth;
do not become a spirit or a demon
to frighten this old monk.”
He then pressed down with the hoe handle,
overturned the chicken coop to cover him,
added more soil,
piled it up high,
and placed several loose stones on top to press it down,
reckoning that he could not stick his head out
before finally turning back.
Then he thought to himself:
“If a dog happens to come in
and scratches away the stones,
what then?
I shall close the garden gates several times over;
this monster will either suffocate or starve to death.”
Immediately, he pulled the doors shut,
fastened the iron latch,
returned to his room,
and took a new horizontal copper lock to lock it.
He instructed the monks:
“Wait until I come to open it myself.”
This Zhǎng lǎo was somewhat stubborn by nature;
the monks did not know his intent,
and did not go to ask him.
After about ten days had passed,
Cí Zhǎng lǎo was still worried in his heart.
He thought:
“Surely that child is no longer alive;
I will go and take a look,
for I cannot keep the door locked forever,
leaving this garden plot to go to waste,
without eating a single vegetable.”
Immediately, he took the key to open the lock
and pulled open the garden gate.
When he walked to the corner of the west wall to look,
he saw the stones scattered about,
the chicken coop overturned to the side,
and the child was nowhere to be seen inside.
Cí Zhǎng lǎo was startled
and looked all around,
only to see the child sitting naked under a willow tree,
with no injuries on his body.
He had already grown to two feet tall,
looking handsome,
but he could not speak.
Seeing Cí Zhǎng lǎo approach,
he held onto the corner of his cotton robe with one hand, grinning.
Cí Zhǎng lǎo had no choice;
he shook him off,
turned around and ran,
never daring to look back.
Having left the vegetable garden,
his heart was still thumping.
He thought to himself:
“I buried him like that;
what god or ghost could have brought him out?
Surely,
such a tiny fellow
could not have such great strength to struggle out on his own.
Even if he had crawled out of the mud,
how could these stones have been moved away?
Moreover, in just ten days,
he has grown more than a foot;
if twenty or thirty years pass, I fear he will pierce through the heavens!
Such a strange thing
is rare in all of history.
The divine lots of Guānyīn Dàshì in this meditation hall are extremely accurate;
I will inquire about the good or bad fortune.
If he should be kept and raised,
perhaps he is a holy monk,
and it is not for us to destroy him.
If he should not be kept,
then we shall discuss it further.”
It turns out that what was worshipped in the meditation hall
was a statue of Guānyīn Dàshì carved from sandalwood.
A lot-tube was placed before the altar,
and when someone came to seek a lot,
the fortune would be proven true.
Cí Zhǎng lǎo, having no other recourse at that time,
could only take the lot-tube
and kowtow before the pedestal of the Dàshì, praying:
“Your disciple has been a monk for many years,
carefully observing the precepts.
Unintentionally, while drawing water by the pond,
I brought back an egg and gave it to a neighbor's old hen.
Who would have thought it would hatch into a little rascal
who did not die when buried
and remained when starved.
Suddenly growing from one foot to two,
growing so easily and quickly,
his origins are most strange,
his presence most bizarre.
If he is not a demon,
he must be a karmic debt.
If Heaven ordains him to be a monk,
and keeping him will bring no disaster,
I beg for a divine lot of supreme fortune,
so that I may no longer doubt or be terrified.
I make this special plea
and bow again with a sincere heart.”
His verbal petition finished,
he shook the lot-tube upward for a while,
and with a thud, a lot jumped out.
When he picked it up to look, it was Lot Number Fifteen,
and indeed, it was marked with the words ‘Supreme Fortune’.
The verse on the lot said:
‘Few know of the storms outside the gate,
keeping the mínglíng is only temporary.
Coming from where he came, and going where he must go,
fate is predetermined, so do not doubt.’
Cí Zhǎng lǎo carefully examined the words of the lot
and said:
“A mínglíng is an adopted son;
for us monks, a disciple is our progeny.
This lot clearly allows me to take him in,
so I expect no trouble.”
Immediately, he called the old servant Liú Gǒu’ér to the meditation hall
and instructed him:
“I do not know which family in the village had too many sons
and abandoned one in our vegetable garden.
I just went over there and saw him under the willow tree;
he is quite a fine boy,
and it would be a pity for his life to be lost.
It is inconvenient for us monks to raise him,
so you may take him and nurture him by your side.
If he grows to adulthood,
he shall have his head shaved to become a monk,
and you, old man, will have someone to rely on.”
Originally, this Liú Gǒu'ér was a local farmer
whose family had enough to live on.
Because he was old and childless
and his wife had died,
he felt a sense of frustration;
he even paid a few taels of silver
to enter this temple and become an incense attendant.
Since he had no son of his own,
whenever he saw other people's young children in his daily life,
they were like his very life.
Hearing these words from Zhǎng lǎo Cí,
he ran in one breath to the willow tree in the vegetable garden.
When he looked,
it was indeed a fine and handsome child.
He hurriedly took him into his arms,
cradling him in the hem of his cotton shirt.
Just as he turned back to the doorway,
he saw Zhǎng lǎo Cí coming toward him.
Zhǎng lǎo Cí, seeing the old attendant holding the child,
was also happy in his heart
and said to him,
"Take him into your own room,
and I will come shortly."
The old attendant hurried away.
Zhǎng lǎo Cí pulled the garden gate shut,
took the copper lock back to his room,
then picked an old cotton shirt from the rack by his bed
and a skirt,
and brought them to the old attendant's bedroom
to give to him to wrap the child.
The old attendant said,
"I do have a few old clothes here.
I still have a few feet of blue cloth saved,
which will be perfect for sewing a little shirt for him to wear.
Only, there is nowhere to get milk,
and I'm afraid he will starve."
Zhǎng lǎo Cí said,
"Where would milk be convenient?
Just mix some cake soup to feed him morning and evening.
If he is meant to be your son,
he will naturally have the fate to live.
If he has no such fate,
nothing can be done,
but it is better than leaving him in the vegetable garden
to starve to death.
The Heavens and Earth know every thought and intent;
if you, elder, are willing to adopt him,
it is an act of hidden merit,
and the gods will surely protect you.
Earlier, I requested a divination lot before Guānyīn Dàshì,
and it was 'highly auspicious'.
When he grows up, let's call him Jí'ér."
The old attendant said,
"What's delightful is that this boy has a happy countenance;
he only laughs and does not cry.
From the time I carried him in from the vegetable garden
until now, he hasn't made a sound."
Zhǎng lǎo Cí said,
"Children who don't cry are easy to raise."
While the two were talking,
they saw a young novice monk walk in.
Seeing the boy,
he went to report it to his master and senior fellow disciples.
Three or four monks all came running,
crowding the old attendant's small half-room to capacity.
The monks asked,
"Where did this boy come from?"
Zhǎng lǎo Cí said,
"I don't know if he is the son of the Zhāng or Lǐ family;
he was left in my garden.
I saw he was a fine boy
and pitied his life,
so I told Old Liú to adopt him as a son."
Among these monks,
there were some who were kind-hearted
and some who were malicious.
The kind-hearted ones said,
"Ēmítuófó!
If he can be raised, it will also be a hidden merit for our temple."
The malicious ones said,
"Who would be willing to abandon their own child?
It must be a woman without a husband
who did something illicit
and gave birth to this boy;
fearing that people would find out,
she secretly abandoned him.
Why should we provoke trouble
by taking him in?"
The kind-hearted ones said again,
"Do not speak such sinful words.
Who knows whose family he was born into?
Many have astrological fates that clash with their parents
so they are unwilling to keep them,
or perhaps he was born to a maid or concubine
and the main wife was jealous,
so she might have cast him away.
The boy doesn't have the names Zhāng or Lǐ written on his forehead,
so what trouble could there be?"
The malicious ones added,
"Raising him is one thing,
but the sound of a child crying in the temple quarters,
if heard by outsiders,
would not look proper."
The old attendant said,
"This boy has only this one good point:
he never cries at all."
The monks then fell silent.
Zhǎng lǎo Cí said,
"I'm going out to let you all sit on the bed for a while,
just don't crowd this room until it collapses."
Having said this, he walked out of the room.
The monks, seeing that Zhǎng lǎo Cí was displeased,
also dispersed.
A poem serves as proof:
Raising an infant is not in itself strange,
Half the talk is of good deeds, half of scandal.
With faith and integrity, proceed on the straight path;
The voices of the masses can never be made one.
Furthermore, ever since the old attendant took in this boy,
he loved him like his own son.
Morning and evening he mixed cake soup to feed him,
and since that was not always convenient,
he would put some congee or rice in his mouth;
the boy swallowed it down
and suffered no ailments.
From then on, the old attendant saved his own congee and rice every day
to raise this child.
After three to five months passed,
outsiders all knew that the old monk in the temple had found a child in the vegetable garden
and given him to Liú Gǒu'ér to raise,
passing it around as a piece of news.
Zhū Dàbó, a neighbor to the east, heard this news
and thought to himself,
"Where in a vegetable garden could a child be found?
Could it be that monster hatched from the goose egg?
The old monk didn't arrange to kill it
but is raising it there instead.
Back then, because it ruined a brood of my chickens,
he promised to compensate me with several pecks of wheat,
but I haven't seen him give them to me.
Now I will just say I'm short on wheat seed
and borrow some wheat from him for planting,
as a way of reminding him;
I expect he'll find it hard to refuse me.
While I'm at it, I'll go see what that child looks like
and whether it is that monster or not."
At that moment, Zhū Dàbó took a sack,
and carrying it, he walked into the temple.
He happened to meet Cí Zhǎngláo sitting on the threshold under the corridor,
holding a needle in his hand and mending a tattered monk's robe.
Zhū Dàbó said:
"Old Master,
it has been a long time since we last met."
As soon as Cí Zhǎngláo saw Zhū Dàbó, he remembered their old conversation;
hurriedly setting down the robe,
he stood up to offer greetings,
and said:
"The wheat this old monk promised you has not yet been sent over."
Zhū Dàbó said:
"Why say such a thing?
This old man did not come to collect a debt from the Old Master.
Some old wheat I had saved for seed was eaten up by a group of relatives who stayed at my house for a few days;
they ate it all.
Lacking wheat seed,
I must borrow some from the Old Master.
When the wheat grows next year,
I will make steamed buns to give to the Old Master to eat."
Cí Zhǎngláo said:
"Since I promised it, I must give it to you,
regardless of whether you have seed or not.
Just go back for now,
and in a short while, I will have someone deliver it."
Zhū Dàbó said:
"There is no need to deliver it;
this old man has brought a sack here.
If it is convenient,
this old man will carry it back himself."
Having said this,
he lifted the sack to show Cí Zhǎngláo.
Cí Zhǎngláo took it in his hand
and said:
"If that is the case,
stay here under the corridor for a moment.
Wait while this old monk goes inside to get it for you."
Zhū Dàbó said:
"This old man also wants to find Liú Gǒu'ér to have a chat."
Cí Zhǎngláo feared that if the old man went inside,
he would see the child,
and having a loose tongue,
might stir up some trouble;
so he said:
"Gǒu'ér is hoeing the ground in the garden.
Wait for this old monk to call him out."
Cí Zhǎngláo held the sack in his left hand,
and with his right hand, he picked up the unfinished tattered robe from the threshold and placed it on his left arm,
then walked toward the interior.
Zhū Dàbó followed right on his heels,
Cí Zhǎngláo became anxious,
and hurriedly tried to close the door,
but the old man had already thrust a foot in.
Cí Zhǎngláo said irritably:
"This is the meditation hall and the monks' quarters;
what is a layman like you doing coming in for no reason?
It is just for a few decaliters of wheat;
it's not that I'm unwilling to give it to you.
I told you to wait a moment under the corridor,
but you wouldn't listen to me."
Zhū Dàbó broke into a grin
and said with a chuckle:
"This old man heard that Liú Gǒu'ér has taken in a little boy,
and I want to go and see for myself,
to see if he was born from a womb or hatched from an egg."
When Cí Zhǎngláo heard the words "hatched from an egg,"
it touched a nerve;
his face turned crimson,
and he flared up, saying:
"You old man are quite ridiculous!
Whether he was born from a womb or an egg is none of your damn business.
He simply picked up a boy on the road;
at the start, he was already over two feet tall.
Could it be that 'hatched from an egg' means he was brooded out of a Dàpéng?
What are you looking at him for?
Unless you've taken a liking to him
and want to claim him as your own grandson?"
He then threw the sack on the ground
and added:
"Since you want to claim your grandson,
I have no strength to carry wheat for you."
Seeing Cí Zhǎngláo's anger, Zhū Dàbó
said:
"If you don't want me to see the boy, then so be it.
Is it worth turning your face against me like this?
I only fear that this wild seed
will never become your disciple or grand-disciple."
He picked up the sack,
shook it, held it in his arms,
turned around, and left.
Cí Zhǎngláo said:
"If you don't want the wheat, that's up to you.
Do you think this old monk will beg you to take it?"
He gave a cold laugh
and closed the door.
Zhū Dàbó walked out of the temple gate,
muttering to himself:
"I have never seen such a monk;
despite his many years,
his fiery temper still hasn't subsided.
I only asked that bit about being born from a womb or an egg,
and meant it only as a joke,
yet you became so agitated
and said so much.
How utterly absurd."
The neighbors saw Zhū Dàbó coming out of the temple in a huff,
and asked:
"Uncle, what did you ask for that was refused,
to make you so annoyed?"
Zhū Dàbó said:
"It's a long story to tell you.
Last winter,
this Cí Zhǎngláo brought a goose egg
and came to my house while my hen was brooding eggs,
to put it in the nest to be brooded as well.
Who could have known that from inside the egg,
a child six or seven inches long was hatched."
The neighbors said:
"There is such a thing!"
Zhū Dàbó said:
"Even if I say it, you won't believe it.
Hatching a child was not the worst of it;
it even caused the hen to die.
That whole clutch of chicken eggs was also ruined.
I went to call the Zhǎngláo to see it,
and the Zhǎngláo said, 'Do not speak of it;
it is I who have burdened you.
When the wheat ripens next year, I will compensate you with some wheat.'
He then took away the little monster along with the nest.
I thought it would either be thrown into the water or buried in the ground.
Later I heard that Liú Gǒu'ér was raising a boy,
and I suspected it was that thing.
Today I took a sack to the temple to borrow some wheat seed,
and to take a look at what the boy looks like along the way.
If he wouldn't let me see him, that would be one thing,
but to act so nasty and say 'it's none of your damn business,'
and then tell me to go claim him as my own grandson!
As the saying goes, 'A tree may be a thousand feet high, but its leaves return to its roots.'
I fear this boy might not grow up.
If he does grow up,
he will inevitably search for his roots and origins;
won't he perhaps acknowledge me as his grandfather?"
The neighbors said:
"Your mouth is certainly steady, old sir,
for such a strange occurrence happened,
yet we never saw you mention it.
Since this old monk is acting so pretentiously,
just for the sake of his status as a monk,
bear with it a little.
Why should an old man like you get so worked up,
and bring on such unnecessary irritation?
In a few more days,
we will speak to the old monk and ask for some wheat to return to you;
don't be upset."
With everyone saying a word or two,
they persuaded Zhū Dàbó to go home.
There is a poem to prove it:
Do not mention the idle affairs of other families;
for mentioning them invites trouble.
The wheat was not returned, and instead, tempers flared;
would it not have been better not to ask about the child?
To continue, because of this spat with Zhū Dàbó, Cí Zhǎngláo
ordered the old attendant never to bring the boy out again.
When he reached one year of age,
he had the boy's hair ritually shaved before the Buddha.
From then on, the childhood name Jí'ér was discarded,
and the whole temple called him the Little Monk.
Because Zhū Dàbó had told the neighbors about him being hatched from a goose egg,
the story spread in bits and pieces.
The disciples in the temple all found out,
and Cí Zhǎngláo could no longer hide it;
therefore, they also called him Dànzi Héshang.
As the common saying goes,
one only worries about not raising them,
not about them not growing.
Time flies like an arrow,
and Dànzi Héshang was soon fifteen years old.
What was his appearance like?
There is a "Xījiāngyuè"
to prove it:
Bright eyes, thick eyebrows, and a straight nose;
a stout body over eight feet tall.
Born with an extraordinary and dignified appearance,
his speech resonated like a great bell.
He abstained from neither meat nor vegetables,
his brave strength surpassing that of a Jīngāng.
Heaven sent down this king from an egg,
no ordinary monk was he.
Furthermore, he was naturally intelligent;
though he was unwilling to focus on reciting and studying various scriptures,
if he were taught just once,
he could recite them fluently like flowing water.
Some people, not knowing the circumstances,
would bet on memory with him,
and in their leisure time, they would simply lose their wagers to him for nothing.
It goes without saying that the Lǎo Dào cherished him.
Even the heart of Cí Zhǎng lǎo
could not help but be biased toward him.
Dear readers,
do you know why?
Firstly, he loved his intelligence;
secondly, he pitied him for having no secular family to look after him;
and thirdly, there was another thing:
this Dànzǐ Héshang had not abstained from meat or wine since childhood,
and what he liked best was using spears and brandishing staffs.
Although the temple had no such weapons,
he would often practice with the heavy bar of the main gate for a while.
If he were told to hoe the fields or plant the land,
his one day of work was worth more than two days of others'.
However, he had a bad temper;
if someone provoked him, he would immediately curse and fight.
Fortunately, he would listen to reason,
or if the Lǎo Dào or Cí Zhǎng lǎo shouted from nearby,
he would not even dare to breathe heavily in anger.
For these reasons, he won the favor of the Abbot,
who gave him double the care in food and clothing.
Those disciples and grand-disciples
gradually felt a sense of unfairness,
often plotting and discussing how to drive him out.
But they had no pretext;
even when he was somewhat impolite,
the Lǎo Dào would take the blame upon himself
and apologize on his behalf.
Cí Zhǎng lǎo also said he was a solitary, unusual creature,
urging the monks to yield to him a little,
so the monks had no choice but to tolerate him.
When Dànzǐ Héshang heard people say he came out of an eggshell,
he himself thought it strange
and that he must not be an ordinary person,
wanting to find some earth-shattering thing to do in the world.
Behind his back, the monks all called him a "beast-breed,"
or called him a "wild monk,"
"hatched by a chicken and raised by a dog."
Feeling unhappy in his heart,
he often thought of leaving the temple gates
to wander the world,
but because Cí Zhǎng lǎo treated him so well,
and the Lǎo Dào showed him the kindness of a father,
he could not bear to leave.
Suddenly one day,
the Lǎo Dào fell dangerously ill
and was in bed for several days.
Dànzǐ Héshang did not even loosen his belt while caring for him,
serving soup and medicine, but he did not recover,
and alas, he passed away.
Dànzǐ Héshang wept bitterly,
and a coffin was prepared for the burial.
He also asked Cí Zhǎng lǎo for a piece of empty land next to the vegetable garden for the burial.
Cí Zhǎng lǎo agreed,
but the monks were all somewhat displeased,
muttering and grumbling:
"Our Old Master has lost his sense of propriety;
he even gives a piece of burial ground to a mere temple attendant.
If a monk died,
he would need a large tomb;
after two or three generations, we can forget about having even half an acre of vegetable garden left.
Eventually, the whole temple grounds will be ruined
and turned into a graveyard."
Cí Zhǎng lǎo simply pretended to be deaf,
letting them talk to themselves
while he remained silent.
Before long,
an auspicious day was chosen for the burial.
Among the monks, some claimed to have a cold,
others claimed to have a stomachache;
none were willing to come and help.
Only one old monk sounded the cymbals to see off the funeral.
That evening, Cí Zhǎng lǎo arranged for Dànzǐ Héshang to rest in his own room.
On the third day,
Dànzǐ Héshang wanted to prepare ritual food for the Lǎo Dào;
remembering that the old man had been a vegetarian,
he specifically bought a piece of tofu,
placed it in a bowl, and set it in the kitchen.
He then went to buy some spirit money,
but when he returned to get the tofu,
someone had moved it onto a low stool near the fire,
and it had been eaten by a dog.
Dànzǐ Héshang knew perfectly well that the monks had done this on purpose;
he was both angry and miserable,
weeping sorrowfully before the stove.
The monks came out to interfere, saying:
"This kitchen is certainly not the Liú family's ancestral hall or mourning hall;
what the hell are you crying for?
If we had known this piece of tofu was so valuable,
the Old Master should have kept a better watch on it for you.
Now there's no need to weep;
if it wasn't Zhāng's dog that ate it,
it was Lǐ's dog—
no different from your own father."
Dànzǐ Héshang was lectured by the monks, one sentence after another,
rebuked thoroughly,
but he did not talk back.
He abandoned the spirit money,
and walked straight out to the front of the temple,
where he sat down indignantly on a washing stone by the pond.
He thought:
"This bunch of bald donkeys has bullied me enough.
Now that my foster father is dead,
I have no relatives left.
Although the old monk is kind,
at his great age he is like a candle in the wind,
his life hanging by a thread.
In the end, this won't end well;
it would be better to wait until the middle of the night,
set a fire and burn these bald donkeys to death
to vent this grievance.
Only the Elder's life must be spared;
if only I could trick him into leaving the temple gates, that would be best."
Pondering over and over,
the fire in his heart could not be suppressed.
He raised his fist and struck the washing stone once,
smashing one corner of it to powder.
At this time, Zhū Dàbó from the eastern neighbor had also passed away,
and he had a son named Chǒu Hàn.
After the uncle died, the old monk remembered their past relationship
and gave five dou of wheat to help with his funeral,
and also led Dànzǐ Héshang to kowtow before his spirit tablet;
thus, Dànzǐ Héshang and Chǒu Hàn had been acquainted and in contact.
On this day, Chǒu Hàn was by the pond with his head down washing vegetables;
he heard the sound of a stone shattering,
and when he looked up,
he recognized Dànzǐ Héshang
and asked:
"Master Dàn, why are you testing your strength here?"
Dànzǐ Héshang sat there without saying a word.
Chǒu Hàn said:
"Who have you been fighting with to get so upset?
A monk should abstain from wine,
lust,
wealth,
and anger—these four things.
Wine is not so important,
and as for lust and wealth,
where would there be any woman for you to have an affair with,
or money to throw around?
But this anger
is present every day;
it is the first thing you should abstain from."
Hearing these words, Dànzǐ Héshang's
anger subsided significantly.
He said:
"Good words, brother.
I have no other grievance,
except that I cannot bear the bullying of this group of bald donkeys."
Chǒu Hàn said:
"When my father was alive,
he often said you were a good person who would not fall into the blood-basin of hell;
why stoop to their level?
As the old saying goes, if one is bullied, one should endure.
They entered the temple gates before you and are senior;
moreover, you are alone.
Unless you go elsewhere
and stop living in this temple, there is no other way.
If you want to eat from the same pot,
then in the future after Cí Zhǎng lǎo passes away,
you will still have to ask them for basic necessities.
Considering it from all sides,
it is best to be patient."
Having spoken, he took his bunch of vegetables
and went eastward.
Because of this conversation, Dànzǐ Héshang
cast aside the thought of burning the temple down
and decided to go out and wander.
Thinking, "Cí Zhǎng lǎo treated me so well,
how can I go without saying a word to him?"
then he thought:
"If I tell him,
he certainly will not let me go.
It is better to harden my heart
and just leave today."
He entered the temple as before and went to the kitchen;
the spirit money was still on the cupboard.
He took it and burned it before the stove.
He went into Cí Zhǎng lǎo’s room,
and quietly made a bundle of his clothes and bedding.
Waiting until it was dark, he slipped out of the temple gates,
taking advantage of the moonlight,
he lengthened his stride and departed.
There is a poem to prove it:
Distinguishing not north, south, west, or east,
He walks with great strides like the wind.
The road ahead may not all be to his liking,
But for now, he leaves this place of right and wrong.
We shall not speak of Dànzi Héshàng after his departure;
instead, let us tell of Cí Zhǎnglǎo, who that evening did not see Dànzi Héshàng enter the room.
He asked the various monks,
but they all claimed not to know.
One night passed,
and the next day it was seen that his clothes and bedding were all gone.
Feeling doubtful and anxious,
he said to the monks:
"Which one of you had a quarrel with the little monk?
He has packed up his clothes and bedding and gone
without even saying a word to me;
he must have left in a fit of anger."
None of the monks were willing to admit it,
and they all said:
"We had no dispute with him at all.
He has long set his heart on traveling abroad;
he was only concerned about Liú Gǒu'ér.
Yesterday he burned some paper money,
which was a sign of his intention to depart."
The Zhǎnglǎo did not believe them
and ordered the monks to search for him in all directions and bring him back.
The monks agreed with their mouths,
but none actually went to search;
they merely loitered around the front and back of the temple for an hour or so,
then returned to report:
"There is nowhere to find him;
we think he has gone far away."
After eating breakfast,
Cí Zhǎnglǎo urged the monks again to head out separately,
while he himself, leaning on a bamboo staff,
also went for a walk through the village.
Returning to the front of the temple,
he saw his disciples and grand-disciples lined up by the edge of the pond,
picking up tiles and competing at skipping stones for fun.
Cí Zhǎnglǎo burst out in irritation:
"I, an old man, have gone out to search myself,
and yet you youngsters can bear to watch.
Having lived together in this temple for so long,
you have no affection at all,
not even going to look for his whereabouts."
Seeing that Cí Zhǎnglǎo was serious,
the monks became even more indifferent.
One said:
"There is no need to look for him.
Knowing the Old Master is so concerned,
he surely won't go far.
In just two or three days, he will naturally come to see you."
Another said:
"Old Master, though you are concerned for him,
he is not concerned for you.
If his heart were good,
he would not have left;
even if he went, he should have told you."
Another said:
"He is the future master of the temple,
while we are all useless;
so how could the Old Master not be concerned?"
Another said:
"He has no secular home;
he was originally a drifting monk.
The Old Master knows where he came from,
but there is no way to know where he went.
It is not as if we acted as mediators for his adoption into the temple;
how are we to know from which prefecture or county he hails?
It is like fishing for a needle at the bottom of the sea.
Old Master, you must know some clues;
tell us,
and we will write a formal invitation
to ask him to come back, and that will be that."
Assailed by the monks' chatter,
Cí Zhǎnglǎo was so angry he could not speak.
He returned to his room and shed a few tears.
Thereafter, he no longer told the monks to look for him.
Every day, he locked his door
and went out himself to inquire everywhere.
Each time he returned,
the monks would make gestures and pull faces behind his back,
but Cí Zhǎnglǎo only pretended not to notice.
More than a month passed
without any news.
Cí Zhǎnglǎo sought divination lots before Guānyīn Dàshì several times,
but they were all inauspicious.
Recalling the verse of the first lot he had drawn, which said, "The adopted son is only temporary,"
and also, "Whence he came, thither he goes,"
he realized he certainly would not find him.
That lot was the fifteenth lot,
and he had raised him for exactly fifteen years.
Thinking that fate was already sealed
and there was nothing to be done,
he could only sigh and let it be.
Truly, of all the manifold miseries in the world,
none surpass the parting of the dead and the separation of the living;
under heaven, there is no banquet that does not end.
Let us conclude this matter and mention it no more.
To speak again of Dànzi Héshàng, after leaving the temple gates,
he was determined to travel to various famous mountains
to seek out extraordinary people
and be taught world-shaking Dàofǎ.
Begging for alms along the way,
he arrived at Guāngxiào Sì on Xiāng Shān in Quánzhōu
and worshipped the true body of Wúliàngshòu Fó.
Then he went to Héngzhōu to pay homage to the Southern Peak, Héng Shān,
traveling through all of the seventy-two peaks,
ten caves,
fifteen crags,
thirty-eight springs,
and twenty-five streams.
He looked at the mountains when he encountered mountains
and looked at the waters when he encountered waters.
If he met a wandering monk or priest, he would follow him for ten days or a fortnight,
but if he saw they had nothing interesting to offer,
he would abandon them.
This happened more than once.
Suddenly one day,
together with several other monks,
he passed by the foot of Yúnmèng Shān in Miǎnyáng.
They came to a place
where there was no sign of human habitation,
only wild mountains.
Coveting the seclusion,
he just kept walking,
seeing only vast white mists
so that the path ahead could not be discerned.
While he was feeling startled and suspicious,
one monk among them gestured with his hand from behind and said:
"Come back quickly!
You've taken the wrong path."
Dànzi Héshàng turned back with his monk companions
and asked:
"What place is this?"
That monk walked
and talked at the same time:
"I have heard there is a Báiyún Dòng here,
which was built by the Báiyuán Shén.
Because there are Tiānshū and Dàofǎ inside,
fearing people would steal them,
he raised this great mist
to sequester it forever.
Within a year,
only during the hour of Wǔ on the fifth day of the fifth month
when the Báiyuán Shén ascends to heaven
does the mist temporarily recede.
Once that hour has passed,
the Báiyuán Shén returns
and the mist covers it again.
Inside there is a white jade incense burner;
when smoke rises from that incense burner,
it is the proof that the Báiyuán Shén is about to return.
There was once a traveling Daoist
who took advantage of that hour to go inside,
but when he reached the cave mouth,
he saw a stone bridge that was extremely dangerous.
Knowing he could not cross it,
he had to give up.
This mist covers an unknown number of li;
if one enters by mistake
and becomes lost in the mist,
there is no way out in any direction.
Even if one manages to get out,
having taken this mist into one's belly,
one will either die or be sick for a long time.
This Yúnmèng Shān is nine hundred li in size;
even some locals do not know of Báiyún Dòng."
Dànzi Héshàng heard this
and thought to himself:
"So there really is such magic here!
If I have no affinity with it,
then who does?"
A few days later,
he left his fellow monk companions
and went alone back to the old path on Yúnmèng Shān.
Next to where the mist was thickest,
he snapped some dead wood,
plucked some pine branches,
and built a low thatched hut.
By day he went out to seek vegetarian food and beg for meals,
and by night he merely rested in the hut,
specially waiting for the day of Duānwǔ,
intending to go into Báiyún Dòng to steal the Báiyuán Shén's Tiānshū and Dàofǎ.
If they could be seen just by stealing a look,
then anyone could go there,
and the wonders of the Tiānshū would not be apparent.
As it is said:
Only those who endure the bitterest of hardships
can become superior to others.
After all, how will Dànzi Héshàng go about stealing the arts?
Please listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
Dàofǎ and affinity each have their lineages,
but Báiyún Dòng is the most divinely powerful.
With affinity, people can meet from a thousand li away;
without affinity, they will not meet even if face to face.
It is said that the Monk Dànzi lived in a thatched hut at the foot of Yúnmèng Shān,
specifically waiting for the Duānwǔ Festival on the fifth day of the fifth lunar month when the mist would clear,
to go into the Báiyún Dòng to steal the magical methods.
At this time, it was already the beginning of the fourth lunar month,
and by calculation, Duānwǔ was only one month away;
his heart was extremely anxious.
Although his intention to seek the methods was very sincere,
he was still half-doubting,
fearing that what his fellow monk had said
was merely hearsay,
and he did not know if it was true or false.
If it were false,
then where did this mist come from?
He often ran up to the mountain ridges to keep a lookout,
seeing only a vast, boundless expanse of white,
truly not knowing what the scene was like in the middle.
One day,
after eating his fill,
he bought some wine as well
and drank until he was half-drunk,
saying:
"I have heard that for a person who is full and drunk,
the mist cannot harm him.
My head is against the sky,
and my feet are on the ground;
what do I fear from Yuán Gōng or Yuán Pó?
Why wait for Duānwǔ or Duānliù?
I shall simply go and demand the Celestial Book from him."
Taking advantage of his wine-induced spirits,
he braved the mist and set out.
After advancing for about less than one lǐ,
the mist gradually grew thicker,
and he could no longer open his eyes.
He had no choice but to turn back and come out,
only then realizing that the monk's words were not false.
He waited until the day of Duānwǔ,
and watched as the hour of Sì approached;
the mist gradually cleared.
When it reached the hour of Wǔ,
the weather was clear and refreshing.
Monk Dànzi said:
"Thank goodness!
It is true after all.
Today I have caught the moment."
On his feet he wore a pair of non-slip multi-looped hemp shoes,
and in his hand he carried a sandalwood staff.
Rousing his spirits,
he rushed off as if flying.
After walking two or three lǐ,
through heights and hollows,
it was all chaotic mountains and deep marshes,
where the vegetation was thick and overgrown,
and the path could not be discerned,
except for a single thread in the middle,
which felt slightly level and stable,
as if it had been worn down by travel.
Following this path,
after a journey of about ten lǐ,
sure enough, there was a stone bridge
spanning across a mountain stream.
It was a full thirty feet long
but only a bit over a foot wide.
Beneath the bridge, the waves were surging and turbulent,
with jagged rocks scattered everywhere,
like a marshaled array of swords and spears.
When Monk Dànzi first saw it,
he could not help but be terrified.
Then a thought occurred to him:
"Having come this far,
how can I harbor a heart of retreat?
Life and death are fated;
why fear it?"
Keeping his eyes fixed only on the front,
he summoned his courage and simply walked across,
unexpectedly crossing it as quickly as a wisp of smoke.
On the other side was the stone cave,
with the three characters Báiyún Dòng engraved above the cave entrance.
Upon entering the cave,
there was a very vast expanse of land,
a different world altogether.
One could see:
The plains were broad and level,
the ancient trees dense and lush.
Rare flowers and exotic grasses,
blooming in eternal spring throughout the four seasons.
Precious fruits and famous vegetables,
sufficient for the whole year without being planted.
The Chǔ Wáng in his hunting travels
had never galloped here.
Sīmǎ's poetic compositions
could not describe it.
Had those fleeing the Qín lived in this place,
even a fisherman would find it hard to ask for the way.
Monk Dànzi could not see enough of it,
finding more than enough to enjoy.
Walking further ahead,
he saw a great stone peak,
and beneath the peak sat a white jade incense burner,
lustrous, pure, and lovely.
Monk Dànzi said:
"Never mind the Celestial Book and magical arts for now;
just this scenery
and these treasures
are things that people in the world could never dream of.
Arriving here today
is also a stroke of luck from a past destiny."
He climbed to the top of the peak,
and just as he was about to enjoy the view to the full,
he suddenly smelled a fragrance hitting his nose.
Just as he uttered "How strange,"
he saw a wisp of incense smoke from the burner
already curling upwards.
Monk Dànzi said in great alarm:
"Could it be that the hour of Wǔ has passed,
and the Báiyuán Shén has returned!"
He jumped down from the peak with a thud,
not even looking back.
With his heart set only on the path he came, he ran hard,
even forgetting his sandalwood staff.
When he reached the stone bridge,
he saw it was drizzling and misty,
and the fog was gradually rising.
The monk panicked,
and tripped on the bridge,
nearly falling down below.
Fortunately, once he had crossed the stone bridge,
his courage grew strong again.
He broke into a run,
and the ten or so lǐ were covered in an instant.
When he finally turned back to look,
the sky was full of thick fog,
hiding the cave entrance once again.
Returning to the thatched hut, he sat for over two hours,
his breathing only then steadying,
and he felt depressed in his heart, saying:
"I went through such hardship specifically for this,
yet I only saw some scenery,
and didn't get a bit of news;
I still don't know if this Celestial Book really exists or not.
It is exactly: greedily watching the Zhōngqiū moon in the sky,
while losing the night-shining pearl on the tray.
Until the next Duānwǔ,
there are a full three hundred and sixty days;
how can I endure it?"
He thought for a while longer and said:
"The first time one is unfamiliar,
the second time one is practiced.
After waiting another year,
I won't look at any scenery.
I'll run in one breath to the Báiyuán Shén's bedroom,
and no matter how many Celestial Books he has hidden,
I'll carry them out in full shoulder-poles,
to be chosen and used by me as I please;
wouldn't that be fine?"
From then on,
he calmed his heart and mind,
making a long-term plan.
He treated this thatched hut
as his temporary property.
For whole months and days, he went everywhere wandering and begging for alms.
One day,
he walked to a place
called Yǒngzhōu.
In that land, there was a Shíyàn Shān
and a Wú Xī,
both having some remarkable features.
How could one tell?
The mountain was piled full of scattered fragments of stone,
shaped like swallows.
If one looked from afar during times of wind and rain,
they looked just like flying swallows.
If a person walked close,
they would even flutter onto one's body,
but when taken in hand to look,
they were still just pieces of stone.
When the wind ceased and the rain stopped,
they no longer flew.
On the stone cliff of Wú Xī,
a mirror stone was naturally embedded;
it was one foot five inches high,
three feet wide,
and three feet thick,
its color like lacquer,
and unusually clear.
Although it could not compare to the Gall-Reflecting Mirror of the Qín era,
which could reflect one's internal organs,
every single hair of one's beard and eyebrows
was clearly visible and could be counted.
Because Monk Dànzi loved these two historical sites,
he stayed in Yǒngzhōu for a longer period of time.
One day,
when he went again to the edge of the stone cliff to look,
the stone mirror was gone,
leaving only a hollow hole.
Just as he was in the midst of his surprise,
he heard the sound of harness bells below the mountain slope,
and a group of people came galloping forward.
Dànzi Héshàng crouched beside a large pine tree,
and when he peeked secretly,
the leader on horseback
was a young Lángjūn,
with red lips and white teeth,
wearing a Táng Jìnshì cap
and a Wú silk Dàopáo,
riding a melon-yellow horse,
followed by about ten servants.
The Lángjūn dismounted
and walked to the edge of the cliff.
Looking at the hole,
he gestured wildly to the sky and ground,
though it was unknown what he was saying to his servants.
Then four farmhands,
carrying ropes and cords, came bearing a large black stone.
Dànzi Héshàng thought to himself:
"It must be that this Lángjūn took the stone mirror
and has made a stone just like it to fit inside and deceive people."
He saw the farmhands carry it to the cliff edge,
and the servants said:
"Since these ropes are handy,
do not stop your work."
Everyone came forward together to help.
Some pulled from above,
some pushed from below,
and some assisted with poles.
Before long,
they brought that stone
before the hollow,
and checking its form and orientation,
they settled it into place.
As they slowly pulled the ropes,
the stone fit in perfectly.
Everyone let out a great shout.
It turned out that the black stone
was the stone mirror itself.
This Lángjūn's surname was Lěng,
and he was the Gōngzǐ of Mùchù Lěng Xuéshì;
though he was handsome,
he was a mean-spirited person.
His nickname was Lěng Bōpí.
He had a farm estate
within five lǐ of this place,
called Lěngjiā Zhuāng.
Lěng Gōngzǐ loved that stone mirror with all his heart,
and had suddenly ordered people to steal it back to the estate.
Who could have known that this mirror was divine;
once it left the stone cliff,
it became like black charcoal,
without a trace of luster.
Only when it was returned to its original place,
just as it was fitted back in,
did it become as bright as before.
When Dànzi Héshàng heard everyone shout,
he poked out his head to look,
but Lěng Gōngzǐ had already seen him.
He shouted:
"Hey, you Héshàng!
Poking your head about here all alone,
could you be a highwayman?"
Dànzi Héshàng had no choice but to step forward,
and giving a greeting, said:
"This poor Héshàng bows to you.
This poor Héshàng is a native of Sìzhōu Chéng,
and has vowed to visit the famous mountains of every prefecture.
Passing through your honorable land,
I did not know an honorable person was arriving
and failed to avoid you."
The servants said:
"This wandering Héshàng is impolite;
seeing our Dàyé,
he does not even kowtow!"
Dànzi Héshàng was about to reply,
but Lěng Gōngzǐ said:
"A man of religion need not perform such rites.
May I ask what your honorable name is, Zhǎnglǎo?
How long have you been in this humble place?
Where are you staying?"
Dànzi Héshàng said:
"This poor Héshàng was ordained at Yínghuī Sì on Yínghuī Shān,
and am called Dànzi Héshàng.
Although I have been in your honorable land for nearly a month,
I have not stayed in any temple,
but have been dining on the wind and sleeping in the dew."
Lěng Gōngzǐ then said:
"It is a rare fate for us to meet.
My humble estate is not far;
I wish to invite you, Zhǎnglǎo, to have a vegetarian meal there.
You must not refuse."
Dànzi Héshàng said:
"I am deeply grateful for your kind intentions, Dà Tányuè."
Thereupon, Lěng Gōngzǐ mounted his horse and went ahead.
He ordered two servants
to accompany the Zhǎnglǎo
and follow slowly behind.
On the road, the two servants said to the Zhǎnglǎo:
"Our Dàyé favors the Dàojiā
and does not believe in the Fófǎ.
He has never provided a meal for a Héshàng,
nor donated a single coin.
Seeing you today, Zhǎnglǎo,
and inviting you to the estate for a meal
is a sign of great respect
and exceptional treatment."
Dànzi Héshàng asked:
"What is your Dàyé’s surname?"
The servants said:
"The surname is Lěng,
the character Lěng from Lěng, Zǐ, Xīn, and Kàn in the Hundred Family Surnames.
The old master is at court,
serving as a Hànlín Yuàn Xuéshì.
He has only this one Gōngzǐ,
who remains at home to study.
He recently married a young Xiǎo Zhǔmǔ at the estate,
which is why he has been staying at the estate these few days."
While they were speaking,
they arrived at the front of the estate.
When Dànzi Héshàng looked,
it was indeed a fine Lěngjiā Zhuāng.
He saw:
The gates face the solar path,
the mountains connect to the Qīnglóng,
the road is lined with the shade of several locust trees,
and faces a deep pool of pond water.
The threshing floor,
with its flat stone rollers,
is perfect for kicking a ball.
The cattle-grazing slope,
covered in thick grass,
is suitable for galloping horses.
The tiered elegant lodgings
resemble the residence of Qí Mèngcháng for housing guests.
The flower terraces everywhere
are like the guest house of Shí Tàiwèi for entertaining visitors.
It is surely a fine villa of an official family,
and not like a small farmstead of common villagers.
Monk *Dànzi* arrived in the hall,
and *Lěng Gōngzǐ* came out to exchange courtesies again and offered him a seat.
He asked,
"How many years has the *Zhǎnglǎo* been ordained?
What is your age?
You do not look to be of great years."
Monk *Dànzi* said,
"This poor monk has idly passed nineteen *là*.
I have been ordained since childhood.
It turns out that among monks, we do not rank by age,
but only by *là*."
*Lěng Gōngzǐ* said,
"What is your actual surname in the secular world?
Surely it cannot truly be the surname *Dàn*?"
Monk *Dànzi* said,
"This poor monk grew up within the gates of the Buddha,
and has no secular family to recognize.
Just these two characters, *Dànzi*—
they are my surname,
and they are my name."
*Lěng Gōngzǐ* said,
