"I have heard that those whose fate is affected by the *Huágài*
are destined to be monks or Taoists.
Since the *Zhǎnglǎo* entered the gates of emptiness from childhood,
your fate must be exceptionally stern.
This year you are nineteen;
on what month and day were you born?"
Monk *Dànzi* said,
"This poor monk was brought into the temple gates during this month;
speaking of it, it seems to have been around the eleventh month.
As for the day and the hour,
I do not know them at all."
Having finished speaking, a servant came out and asked,
"The vegetarian meal is ready.
Where shall it be set?"
*Lěng Gōngzǐ* pondered for a moment
and replied,
"Set it in the *Cǎiliánhuàng*."
*Lěng Gōngzǐ* rose first and said,
"I invite the *Zhǎnglǎo* to the back garden for the meal."
Monk *Dànzi* said,
"Many thanks."
*Lěng Gōngzǐ* said,
"I neglected to ask just now,
do you perhaps also consume meat and wine?"
Monk *Dànzi* said,
"I have not yet managed to abstain from meat and wine."
*Lěng Gōngzǐ* laughed and said,
"No wonder the *Zhǎnglǎo* is so robust.
If that is the case,
it will be convenient for my small estate.
He instructed the servants to take some prepared fish, meat, and the like,
warm up a large pot of good wine,
and send them along with the vegetarian meal.
He added,
"I have some secular matters to attend to
and cannot accompany you."
Monk *Dànzi* said,
"Do not trouble yourself;
I shall offer my thanks in a short while."
He then took his leave of *Lěng Gōngzǐ*
and followed the servants through a winding path to the back garden.
In this garden was a fish pond,
roughly several *mǔ* in size.
In the very center was a small three-bay pavilion,
modeled after the style of a *Jiāngnán* boat,
built in a linear fashion.
All around the pavilion,
lotus flowers were planted.
It was then the weather of late autumn;
although the flowers were gone,
there were still some withered leaves scattered across the water's surface.
On the pavilion was a plaque
inscribed with the three characters '*Cǎiliánhuàng*,'
with a side note saying it was inscribed by *Tànhuā Féng Zhěng*.
Beside the pond was a large, open three-bay hall,
with lush bamboo on both sides.
In front of the hall, large stones were laid to form a Moon-Viewing Terrace,
and below the terrace, a ferry boat was moored.
The servants invited the *Zhǎnglǎo* onto the ferry boat;
a servant untied the rope
and rowed with a single oar.
In an instant, they reached the side of the pavilion.
They escorted the monk into the *Cǎiliánhuàng*
and then rowed the ferry boat back as before.
When Monk *Dànzi* looked,
it was indeed no different from a boat or skiff.
Each room was partitioned by screen walls,
all of which could be opened or closed.
The first level was a small sitting room;
the second level went deeper,
with tables, chairs, and other items arranged.
Around the sides were vermilion railings,
and mottled bamboo curtains were hung.
On the third level, within the warm windows on all sides, a small couch was set,
clearly making it a bedroom.
Monk *Dànzi* thought to himself,
"If he wanted to treat me to a meal,
I could eat anywhere.
Why send me to the middle of a pond?
Could it be he is afraid I will run away and not accept his hospitality?
Or perhaps,
is it that he does not believe in the Buddhist Law?
Does he blame us monks
and has tricked me here to this dead end to starve to death?"
While he was in a state of hesitation,
he saw two servants
carrying a food box.
They rowed the ferry boat
and delivered it to the middle of the pavilion.
On the table were set a bowl of cured goose,
a bowl of cured meat,
a bowl of pig's trotter,
a bowl of fresh fish,
a bowl of dried bamboo shoots,
a bowl of oil-fried tofu cooked with fragrant mushrooms,
a bowl of green vegetables,
and a bowl of green beans.
He saw there were four meat and four vegetarian dishes.
There was a large pot of wine
and a tin container of white rice.
Monk *Dànzi* offered a word of thanks,
and without standing on ceremony,
he ate and drank to his heart's content.
The others waited for him to finish eating,
cleared everything away,
wiped the table clean,
and were about to turn and leave.
Monk *Dànzi* asked,
"Where is your eldest master?
This poor monk would like to take his leave and go."
The people said,
"The Master has not yet made up his mind;
it seems he intends to keep the *Zhǎnglǎo* overnight."
Having said this,
the people boarded the boat
and rowed away again.
Monk *Dànzi* said,
"What is the meaning of keeping me overnight?
I shall stay patiently for a while
and see what happens."
As evening approached,
two more servants appeared,
one carrying a set of bedding
and the other bringing tea, food, snacks, and the like.
They boarded the ferry boat and came to the pavilion.
While they set out the tea and snacks
and invited the master to have tea,
they also arranged the bedding
and bid him goodnight.
Then the two of them boarded the boat and left again.
Monk *Dànzi* said,
"I shall sleep happily for one night,
and attend to matters again tomorrow."
That night passed without incident,
and when dawn arrived,
the two servants again came to bring hot water
and set out breakfast.
It was neatly arranged with two meat and two vegetarian dishes.
After Dànzǐ Héshang had finished eating,
he said,
"This poor monk has eaten his fill without performing any service.
Today I must certainly depart."
The servants said,
"The young master still wishes to meet face-to-face with the Zhǎng lǎo to discuss some matters,
but these few days he has had no time.
He only told us to treat the Zhǎng lǎo well
and not to be neglectful.
Please stay for a while with a relaxed mind;
what is there to fear?"
Dànzǐ Héshang said,
"What does your young master have to say?
He should speak plainly,
so that I may feel settled staying here."
The servants said,
"The matters in the master's heart,
how could we underlings know?
Perhaps the Zhǎng lǎo fears the quiet of the night
and wants someone to keep him company?
If you want,
let alone anything else,
even getting a woman would be easy.
Last year the young master hosted a Quánzhēn Dàorén
who also stayed in this pavilion
and spoke of some method of Cǎiyīn bǔyáng;
every night he could not do without a woman's company.
The master once called three or four courtesans to accompany him,
and even let us fool around for over a month.
Now he has gone to Luòyáng.
He promised to return this year,
but he has not been seen yet."
Dànzǐ Héshang said,
"This poor monk has never broken the precept of celibacy
and does not fear the quiet.
There is only one thing:
since I have received your master's kind intention to stay,
let me walk leisurely in this garden
to pass the time."
The servant pointed to the open hall on the south side and said,
"Behind this hall is a row of buildings
where the newly-taken concubine lives.
Maidservants often come downstairs to pick flowers,
so it is feared that an outsider walking there would be inconvenient."
Hearing these words, Dànzǐ Héshang
did not speak again.
The story divides in two directions.
It is said that Lěng Gōngzǐ was raised in a wealthy and noble family,
and matters of chasing flowers and wine
were not among his interests.
There was only one immature trait:
he was fond of sorcery and the occult.
From all directions, practitioners were recommended to him,
and there was none he would not receive.
It just so happened that a few days ago,
the son of Wáng Shūmì from the neighboring county recommended a person
named Fēng Jìngyǎn.
He claimed his eyes could see gods and ghosts,
and furthermore, he possessed a technique for cursing people into nightmares,
which was extremely formidable.
During the Hàn Dynasty, there were those Wùgǔ affairs
where wooden figures were carved,
holding wooden sticks,
and buried underground.
At night, ghosts were sacrificed to and incantations were recited,
making the wooden figures go and strike the target person.
During the Táng Dynasty, when Lǚ Yòngzhī was in service under Gāo Pián,
he monopolized power and threw the government into chaos.
He had a small image of Gāo Pián cast in bronze,
with the eyes and ears covered by objects.
It was hidden in a chest
and buried under his own bed
to make the other's ears and eyes confused and muddled,
so he alone could control him.
Now, the technique of Fēng Jìngyǎn
was again different.
When he wanted to curse someone,
he would set up a sacrificial altar in a secluded place,
making offerings to divine generals.
In front of the altar, he would draw a large circle,
and inside the circle, he would place a ceramic jar. The person's name,
place of origin,
birth year,
birth month,
birth day,
and birth hour
would be written and placed inside the jar.
He would write talismans and recite incantations before the altar
to summon their living soul.
If it was not summoned in three days,
he would wait until five;
if not in five days,
he would wait until seven.
When the living soul came,
it was only one foot and two inches tall,
and its face was no different from the person's.
If it walked into the circle,
he would use a command token to draw it into the jar,
seal it firmly with talismans,
and bury it in the northern direction,
and the person would die immediately.
There is a poem to prove it:
In those years, the elderly spoke of Gāo Pián,
and the Crown Prince once suffered the grievance of Wùgǔ.
If cursing a person would make them die,
who would not hold the power of life and death?
These four lines of poetry say that a person's life and death are determined by fate;
even if a nightmare technique causes death,
it is because the person's fate had reached its end and their fortune was exhausted.
As the common saying goes:
At the head of a coffin,
how can there be a cursed-to-death ghost?
Nevertheless,
there is another saying:
There can be an unjust death, but never an undeserved life.
If a person's fortune is in its prime,
even a thunderbolt from heaven would not strike them dead.
If they are of the common sort,
they might generally suffer a premature death;
otherwise, why would the underworld establish the Wǎngsǐ Chéng
and for what purpose?
Let us put aside such idle talk.
It is said that when Lěng Gōngzǐ heard Fēng Jìngyǎn possessed this kind of technique,
he was anxious to learn it,
but he had not yet tested whether it was real or false.
Seeing that this Dànzǐ Héshang was a wandering monk
and did not belong to a monastery,
he focused on coaxing him to his home,
intending to test the technique on him.
He had already asked his name
and place of origin,
but for his birth details, he only had the year and month but not the day and hour.
He then sent someone to Fēng Jìngyǎn's lodging
to invite him over to discuss the matter.
Fēng Jìngyǎn said,
"If there is no birth time,
one must obtain a piece of the person's underclothing,
or their hair or fingernails—it would be the same."
Lěng Gōngzǐ said,
"This is easy then."
He then ordered a servant to take a piece of new cloth and make a shirt to give to the monk,
saying that the young master feared the Zhǎng lǎo's body was not clean
and instructed them to send this cloth shirt
so he could change out of the old one for washing.
He also called a Dàizhào to shave his head,
ordering him to secretly collect the shaven hair and report back,
and not to lose any.
The monk only took it as a kind gesture,
not knowing what was behind it.
Even the servants did not know their master's intention.
Then the servants coaxed him into taking off his under-shirt
and collected the short shaven hair to present to Lěng Gōngzǐ.
Lěng Gōngzǐ was overjoyed
and went with Fēng Jìngyǎn to a grain storage hall on the east side
to set up the altar according to the method,
preparing paper horses, incense, candles, and the like.
He kept only two very young servants to wait on them.
He locked the doors from the outside,
and every day three meals were prepared;
the servants would call out at the door,
and a young page would unlock it to receive the food,
not allowing anyone to peek inside.
Truly, not even a chicken or dog's sound could be heard;
it was extremely secret.
Meanwhile, Fēng Jìngyǎn was eager to kill the monk with a nightmare,
to show the efficacy of his master's magic
which he had taught to Lěng Gōngzǐ,
so as to obtain a large sum of money from him;
thus, he applied himself with total devotion.
He then took a sheet of yellow paper
and wrote down an order to summon and capture the living soul of one Dànzǐ héshang,
a native of Sìzhōu Chéng,
who had entered the monkhood at Yínghuī Sì on Yínghuī Shān
and was now a wandering monk in this area.
He wrapped some of the monk's hair into a small bundle,
and on the monk's undershirt worn next to the skin, he wrote many soul-summoning talismans;
he tied these together and placed them inside a purified jar.
Before the altar, he drew a large circle with lime,
and inside the circle, he placed the purified jar.
Fēng Jìngyǎn offered incense three times a day,
and at night, he wrote talismans and chanted incantations before the altar,
performing the Big Dipper ritual steps,
working until the second or third watch every night.
By the third day, there was no effect on this side,
but on the other side, Dànzǐ héshang already felt some headache and fever.
By the fifth day,
he appeared to fall ill
and was confined to bed, unable to rise.
Fēng Jìngyǎn saw a faint black vapor drifting back and forth outside the circle,
and knew that the wandering soul was wavering.
The next day, he asked Lěng Gōngzǐ to inquire about news of the monk;
learning that he was bedridden and unable to rise,
he exerted himself even more,
using all sorts of cunning tricks and arrangements.
After dusk on the seventh day,
that ball of black vapor moved back and forth very frequently,
spinning incessantly around the edge of the circle.
When it reached the third watch,
sure enough, it condensed into the form of a small monk one foot two inches tall,
sometimes advancing, sometimes retreating,
lingering outside the circle.
Fēng Jìngyǎn widened his strange eyes, struck the table fiercely with his command token,
and shouted:
"Heavenly Generals of the day,
Chénghuáng and Tǔdì!
If you do not follow my legal command at this hour,
what time are you waiting for?"
Before he had finished speaking,
that little monk rolled into the circle
and dove straight into the jar.
Had he not dove in, it might have been fine;
but the moment he dove in,
a strange wind suddenly rose before the altar,
sounding like a thunderclap in the air,
and the jar burst into seven or eight pieces.
Fēng Jìngyǎn spat out fresh blood
and died before the altar.
Alas, having been a sorcerer for a lifetime,
in the end, he failed to harm another
and instead harmed himself first.
There is a poem to prove it:
Evil arts, when effective, harm others;
when they fail, they damage oneself.
The wandering soul outside the circle is still not destroyed,
while Jìngyǎn before the altar was not true.
The magic breaks with the jar, making children laugh;
the spell vanishes with the man, making the young master angry.
In all things, advise people not to be calculating;
three feet above one's head, there are deities.
Later people also have a poem saying:
To destroy others is to destroy oneself;
to curse others is to curse oneself.
It is like fire in a headwind;
it burns oneself first.
If the gods of curses were efficacious,
then prayers for blessings would be bountiful.
Those who govern fate in the darkness,
how could they ever hand over their great power?
May one develop an impartial heart,
then all will be at peace and without blame.
Lěng Gōngzǐ collapsed in shock;
it was a long time before he regained consciousness.
The two young servant boys
were so scared they cried incessantly.
Then Lěng Gōngzǐ hurriedly went to unlock the door himself
and called the servants to clean up the altar and the corpse.
The next morning, he bought a coffin for the burial.
On one hand, he wrote a letter to Wáng Shūmì Gōngzǐ,
saying only that the man had died of a sudden evil affliction.
On the other hand, he sent someone to check on Dànzǐ héshang;
that monk had broken out in a cold sweat,
and his illness was already gone.
Lěng Gōngzǐ felt very disheartened;
although the plot had not been leaked,
he had no face to see the monk again.
He set aside two taels of silver
and told the two servants who had been attending him to send the monk on his way.
He himself pretended to be far away and did not meet him.
Dànzǐ héshang only thought that because he had been ill, they would not let him stay,
not knowing that they had used him to test magic
and had almost ended his life.
Then Dànzǐ héshang accepted the silver
and thanked them a thousand times, saying:
"I am much obliged for the alms."
He shaved his head clean and smooth,
changed into a new undershirt next to his skin,
and left Lěngjiā Zhuāng happily,
continuing his wandering in all directions as before.
Meanwhile, Wáng Shūmì Gōngzǐ received the letter from the Lěng family
and sent back a reply;
he also had to report the news to Fēng's family.
He had a wife and children,
daughters,
sons,
and other relatives; hearing this news,
they immediately hurried in a large group to Lěngjiā Zhuāng,
weeping and wailing by the coffin.
There was nothing to be done with them;
knowing the matter was not upright,
he asked a secretary to come out
and provide some funeral expenses for them,
and also gave some travel money to the crowd.
Among them was a sharp and crafty old man
who talked privately with the secretary;
having gained some personal profit in the middle,
he took full responsibility for the arrangements,
and only when the coffin was carried back was there peace,
though it cost over a hundred taels of silver.
Lěng Gōngzǐ was mean-spirited all his life
and was used to scheming against others,
not realizing that this time he had made a losing deal.
The local neighbors, seeing it was an official family
and that he was the famous "Skin-Peeling Young Master,"
no one dared to speak up,
they only laughed secretly behind his back.
Truly, when the great wind blows down the parasol tree,
others will naturally gossip about its merits and faults;
let us say no more of this.
To speak again of Dànzǐ héshang passing his days wandering;
time passed easily,
and before he knew it, another year had gone by.
Let us skip the idle talk.
As spring turned to summer,
it was again the Double Fifth Festival,
the season of the fifth month.
A month earlier, Dànzǐ héshang had returned to the foot of Yúnmèng Shān,
repaired the thatched hut by adding more thatch,
and stayed there as before.
He prepared some vegetarian provisions in advance,
and from the first day of the month, he did not go out to beg for alms,
but only sat in meditation in the hut
to cultivate his spirit.
Waiting until the Double Fifth,
he rose early and bound his clothes tightly,
with a sash
cinching his cotton shirt firmly,
and wore a pair of multi-looped hemp shoes.
When it was about to be the hour of Wǔ,
he set out, braving the mist.
When he reached the cave's edge,
the mist had just completely cleared,
and Dànzǐ héshang was overjoyed.
This was the second time;
he was even more courageous,
walking casually,
and soon crossed that perilous bridge thirty feet long and one foot wide.
Entering the cave mouth,
he had no heart to look at the scenery
but walked straight toward that large stone peak where the white jade incense burner was offered.
It turned out that opposite the stone peak was a natural stone house,
about the size of five or six civilian houses,
empty and hollow in the middle,
with no furnishings.
Passing through the back of the stone house,
there was another small stone cave.
Dànzǐ héshang entered this cave,
thinking it must be where the Báiyuán Shén kept his books,
and he ducked his head to crawl into the cave.
Truly it is:
Without a plan for the ten-thousand-fathom deep pool,
how can one get the pearl from under the black dragon's chin?
Because of this endeavor,
Dànzǐ héshang would waste his energy once again
and endure another year of hardship.
When he will finally steal the magic,
let us listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
Do not let laziness waste time;
an iron pestle, if diligently ground, can become an embroidery needle.
Stealing the magic three times, he will eventually succeed;
all things in the world fear a determined heart.
It is said that the monk Dànzǐ thought to himself:
"This small cave must be the place where Yuán Gōng hides his books."
Lowering his head and squeezing inside,
he saw that the interior was winding and crooked,
sometimes bright and sometimes dark,
sometimes wide and sometimes narrow,
with several places resembling rooms.
Inside were stone beds,
stone stoves,
stone chairs,
stone tables, and such;
there were also stone brushes,
stone inkstones,
stone bowls,
stone urns,
and various utensils,
all naturally formed in those shapes
and impossible to pick up;
he did not see any books at all.
Going further in,
the cave gradually narrowed,
and the ground was a depression with water about one or two feet deep;
he expected this was the end.
Turning back to look once more,
he knew the Heavenly Book was not inside.
He squeezed out of the cave and went to the stone room in front,
looking carefully all around,
and cried out:
"Oh my!
It is not a thousand miles away,
but right here before my eyes!
These stone walls on both sides are engraved with so many characters—
if this is not the Heavenly Book,
then what is it?
There is only one problem:
these natural stone walls cannot be moved,
and if I want to transcribe it,
I did not bring paper, ink, brush, or inkstone.
What should I do?
I will just rely on my own memory to memorize a few passages into my belly;
then these two arduous trips will not have been in vain."
Just as he stood firm,
wiped the corners of his eyes,
and began to carefully recognize the strokes of the characters from the beginning,
he suddenly smelled a waft of fragrance hitting his nose.
Stepping outside to look,
smoke was already rising from the white jade incense burner.
Startled, the monk Dànzǐ did not dare to look back,
but stretched his legs
and ran across the stone bridge in one breath, his feet barely touching the ground.
Reaching the pine-branch hut,
he sat in meditation for a long time
before his breathing settled.
As the ancient saying goes, "Once the pain has passed, one reflects on the pain."
Thinking of his two visits to Báiyún Dòng,
the many terrors he had endured
and the hardships he had suffered,
without managing to get even a tiny bit into his belly,
he unconsciously began to wail loudly.
He cried for three days and three nights straight,
still lamenting without stop.
He then heard a loud voice outside asking:
"Who is in the hut,
weeping so sorrowfully?"
Hearing a human voice, the monk Dànzǐ
wiped away his tears
and squeezed out of the hut.
When he looked,
it was a white-haired old man.
What was his appearance?
It was seen that:
Snow was smeared on the tips of his eyebrows,
and silk strands hung from his chin.
His voice was like a great bell,
and his form was like a slender crane.
His head was wrapped in a piece of blue silk cloth,
with a large flap hanging behind his head.
He wore a yellow cloth jacket with four-sided borders,
and a slender sash was tied tightly around his waist.
On his feet were square shoes;
he was so ethereal he truly seemed about to soar above the clouds.
In his hand he held a rattan staff;
every step was truly fit to support an elder.
If he were not an old dragon from the bottom of the sea,
he must surely be Tàibái from the edge of the sky.
Seeing his strange appearance, the monk Dànzǐ
hurriedly went forward to give a greeting.
The old man said again:
"Abbot, you are not very old,
why are you living all alone in these desolate mountains?
What grievances do you have
that make you weep and wail so?
Please try to tell me about it."
The monk Dànzǐ said:
"I should let the elder know,
I have been a monk since childhood
and have no relatives.
Because I have set my heart on the Way
and wish to learn world-shaking arts,
I heard that in this mountain there is a Báiyún Dòng
containing the Heavenly Book and Daoist methods.
Therefore, I did not mind the hardship
to seek a glimpse of it.
Who knew that on two Duānwǔ Festivals I reached the cave,
but it was all to no avail."
He then explained how the first time he could not find the Heavenly Book
and the second time he saw it but could not transcribe it,
recounting everything in detail.
After speaking, he began to cry again.
The old man consoled him:
"Abbot, you need not be so sorrowful;
listen to my words.
This Báiyún Dòng,
I, too, visited in my youth."
The monk Dànzǐ turned his grief into joy
and hurriedly asked:
"Since the elder has been there,
you must have seen the Heavenly Book.
I wonder how much you transcribed?"
The old man said:
"Although I saw it,
I had no way to obtain it.
Later, I met a Quánzhēn Daoist in these parts
who told me that this secret method of the Heavenly Court is unlike ordinary books and cannot be transcribed.
If one wishes to receive the method,
one does not use a brush to copy it,
nor ink to print it.
One only needs pure white paper.
Take it before that white jade incense burner,
pray with a sincere heart,
and make a vow to act on behalf of Heaven,
never daring to do wrong.
After praying,
then take the plain paper and rub it against the places on the stone wall where there are characters.
If you have a predestined connection with the Daoist method,
the characters will be rubbed onto the paper.
If there is no connection,
not a single character will appear."
The monk Dànzǐ asked:
"Has the elder ever obtained a rubbing?"
The old man said:
"My energy has already faded;
even if I obtained it, I could not put it into practice,
and therefore I never did."
The monk Dànzǐ said:
"Where does the elder reside?
If I manage to get a rubbing,
I would like to come and seek your guidance."
The old man said:
"I live not far from here;
when I have leisure, I will come to visit you again."
Having said this, he leaned on his rattan staff
and went straight toward the eastern road.
The monk Dànzǐ said, half-believing and half-doubting:
"Once started,
one must not stop.
If one puts in deep enough effort,
an iron pestle can be ground into a needle.
I will wait here for another year of twelve months;
one way or another, I must get some skills into my hands.
Otherwise, if this secret method was not meant to be passed on,
why would it be engraved on the stone walls?"
From then on, he put his other thoughts to rest
and placed his hopes on the coming year.
For four or five days straight, he kept a lookout for the old man's residence,
but there was no trace of him,
and his heart grew idle again.
How could he spend all four seasons in this pine hut?
He could not help but pack a bundle of clothes,
take a short staff for self-defense,
and go traveling outside again to beg for food.
In a few days, he arrived at the region of Chénzhōu.
What kind of place was it?
Overlapping ridges and multiple mounds,
overlooking streams and guarding caves.
Its mountains have the majesty of Èryǒu and Wǔchéng;
its waters have the beauty of Qián Jiāng and Wǔ Xī.
Where Luó Gōng lived in seclusion,
the chirping of birds predicts the rain without error.
Ever since Xīnnǚ was transformed,
the standing stones are no different from people.
At Míngyuè Dòng,
the springs are clear upon the crags.
At Táohuā Shān,
spring fills the mountaintops.
Exquisite colors reaching the sky often join with the clouds;
rank winds from the Dragon Stream often bring the rain.
The monk Dànzi Héshang traveled to and fro in Chénzhōu seeking food
for more than a single day;
let us skip over the uneventful times.
It is said that on this day, he happened to walk to the border of Qiányáng Xiàn
and arrived at a wilderness where the terrain was uneven,
and in every direction, one could see nothing but scattered graves.
At this time, it was the weather of the late eighth month,
and the grass was knee-deep,
appearing extremely desolate.
Having walked for a long while
without finding a place to beg for a bite of vegetarian food,
he saw the sun sinking in the west
and felt hunger in his belly.
Just as he had no way out,
he suddenly saw four or five woodcutters on a high ridge carrying loads of firewood,
walking hurriedly.
Dànzi Héshang hurried a step forward,
caught hold of a steady-looking one, and asked:
"This poor monk wishes to go into Qiányáng Xiàn;
which road is the shortest?"
The woodcutter pointed and said:
"Just head south down this ridge,
and you will reach the main road of Luójiāfàn.
There are several farmhouses there;
you can ask again then.
It is already late,
and we must still rush past Jièkǒu;
we have no time to explain things to you in detail."
Having finished speaking,
he called out to his companions ahead to slow down
and went off like the wind with his load.
Dànzi Héshang could not very well stop them,
so he asked from a distance:
"What is the name of this place?"
He heard a reply of "Luànzànggǎng"
— those three words.
Dànzi Héshang nodded and said:
"No wonder there are so many mounds;
it turns out to be a burial ground for the local people's bones.
A man lives for a lifetime,
and grass grows for an autumn;
if one does not learn some skills
and perform some great deeds
to make a name for ten thousand generations,
then like this pile of yellow earth,
who can tell the wise from the foolish?"
He gave a sigh
and headed south.
After walking a long way more,
the terrain gradually leveled out,
and he saw several plots of grain and millet,
which he supposed must be Luójiāfàn.
Yet he saw no inhabitants;
there were a few scattered thatched huts,
but their doors were all locked,
with no one living inside.
He was forced to endure his hunger and walk on,
watching as the sun set and the sky grew dark,
until he saw a forest of trees across a stream
that seemed to house a residence.
Intending to cross the stream to go there
but not knowing the depth,
he approached the bank,
held up his defensive short staff,
and pushed it into the water
to probe the depth;
unexpectedly, the water was over ten feet deep,
and the staff struck the bottom and sprang up,
then drifted downstream half-horizontal and half-vertical.
Dànzi Héshang could not retrieve it
and was forced to abandon the staff.
He walked along the stream to look
and after about the distance of an arrow's flight,
the stream's surface became narrower,
and there were two pieces of miscellaneous wood tied with straw rope
laid across the water to serve as a floating bridge.
Dànzi Héshang was impatient
and stepped onto it with both feet;
he did not realize that the straw rope had rotted over time,
and as his weight shifted too heavily to one side,
he kicked the two logs apart with one foot.
What a reckless monk!
Unable to pull back his feet in time,
he fell flat down.
Luckily, it was a shallow spot,
and the water only reached his chest,
so he did not swallow a drop of water,
though his clothes bundle was completely soaked.
His left foot was stuck in deep sand;
by the time he pulled it free,
one hemp shoe was already lost.
There was nothing he could do then;
regardless of the consequences,
he dragged himself through the mud and water to the other bank.
He took off his wet cloth shirt, skirt, and trousers,
wrung out the water,
and put them back on as before.
He took off the right hemp shoe as well and threw it away.
Barefoot,
carrying his wet clothes bundle,
he walked toward the distant forest.
When he was roughly half a li from the forest,
he saw several thatched huts.
Approaching them,
he found that their doors were also closed.
Outside a door, by the edge of the thatched eaves, a pile of messy straw was laid out,
and an ascetic was sitting cross-legged upon it in meditation,
with a roll of sutras placed before him,
a bundle placed to his left,
and leaning against a short, eyebrow-height staff bound with iron at both ends.
Dànzi Héshang went forward and called out:
"Old Master,
this poor monk has escaped with his life after falling into the water;
I beg for your mercy and protection."
The ascetic kept his eyelids lowered
and ignored him completely.
Dànzi Héshang called out again:
"This poor monk is hungry;
if the Old Master has brought any dry rations,
I hope you will give some alms
as a present merit."
The ascetic still ignored him.
Dànzi Héshang said:
"Bah!
Are you made of wood or stone,
that you won't even open your mouth?
I shouldn't pester him;
I will go knock on the door instead.
If I can get it open,
it would be good to beg for a bowl of hot soup to drink."
Then he suddenly thought:
"I do not know if anyone lives in this house;
that ascetic is also of the Buddhist path
yet acts in such a way.
If I knock on doors in the dead of night,
who knows what the people's tempers will be like?
I can endure even a beating for just one night;
fortunately, it is not cold weather,
and if these wet clothes are warmed on my body for a night,
they will dry one way or another.
The clothes bundle can be sorted out slowly later without issue."
He tightened his sash around his waist
and also came under the eaves to sit in meditation across from the ascetic.
When the ascetic saw the monk sit down,
he cursed:
"You dead bald donkey!
This space under the eaves is where this Master intends to stretch his back and legs.
You are so ignorant of the situation,
squeezing in here recklessly with your wet clothes;
how is this Master to have any peace?"
Dànzi Héshang thought:
"Where can one find such a man of the cloth,
who curses as soon as he opens his mouth
and is so coarse and reckless?"
Having no choice, he swallowed his anger
and spoke to him again:
"This poor monk took the wrong road
and has not had a bite of food all day;
I also slipped into the stream
and got soaked all over.
Having nowhere to go at night,
I am merely borrowing this space under the eaves to rest for one night
and will leave tomorrow morning;
it will be no hindrance to the Old Master.
I beg for your tolerance."
The ascetic cursed even more fiercely:
"Dead bald donkey, do you not recognize this Master?
This Master is called Shítóutuó,
and my other name is Shíluóhàn.
All my life I have traveled the world;
when I walk, I walk alone,
and when I sleep, I sleep alone;
I am not used to partnering with others.
Who knows if a bald donkey like you is good or bad,
coming here to bother me?
Leave while you can;
if you do not, one blow of this staff will end your life!"
Having spoken,
he stood up
and reached out his hand for the staff.
Dànzi Héshang was both hungry and cold,
and he had no weapon with him;
fearing the ascetic was formidable
and that he would be no match for him,
he hurriedly stood up and said:
"Old Master, calm your anger;
this poor monk shall keep away then."
The ascetic cursed again:
"Dead bald donkey,
I doubt you would dare not avoid me!
You must stay far away from me;
if you are near my side
and this Master catches sight of you, do not expect any mercy!"
Dànzǐ Héshang said repeatedly:
"I wouldn't dare,
I wouldn't dare."
Then, picking up his bundle of clothes, he walked toward the back of the house.
In the darkness, he truly did not know where best to go;
walking aimlessly, he reached the middle of a forest
and saw a large pine tree standing tall and straight, about a hundred feet high.
He thought to himself:
"Up in this tree would be a good place to stay,
but how can I get up there?"
He came up with a plan:
he untied his sash, strapped the bundle of clothes to his waist,
and stepped up onto a small tree next to the pine tree.
Grabbing a pine branch with one hand,
he used his momentum to cross over from that tree
and climbed up several more levels.
Choosing a large fork in the branches,
he curled up and sat there like a magpie.
Just as he had settled himself firmly,
he suddenly heard a sound below.
Dànzǐ Héshang was quick-eyed;
under the starlight, he looked carefully
and saw the Tóutuó carrying an eyebrow-length short staff, walking back and forth around the forest,
peering East and West.
He muttered:
"Where did that dead bald donkey really go?"
After passing through the woods and going some distance further, he returned,
dragging his staff behind him,
and slowly went back along the old path.
Seeing this, Dànzǐ Héshang sighed with relief,
glad that he had not fallen into the man's cruel hands.
But there was one thing:
that Tóutuó was sitting alone at someone's doorstep;
it was quite lone-
ly;
it would have been good to have someone for company;
why was he so dead-set against it?
Even after I yielded to him,
he still came searching everywhere;
I fear he is still nearby
and cannot set my mind at ease.
There must be a reason for this.
Surely he cannot be planning to commit robbery or burglary
and is afraid I will be an eyesore.
What great wealth could there be in this desolate village and thatched hut
to stir his passions?
It is truly hard to understand.
Let me ignore him for now;
I will rest for a while and then decide.
Just as he was about to close his eyes,
he unexpectedly felt a sharp hunger pang in his stomach,
and his intestines began to rumble.
Dànzǐ Héshang said:
"This night will be so hard to endure.
Even if I last through the night, how will I have the strength to jump down from the tree tomorrow morning?
Even if I jump down, I won't be able to run;
if I encounter that rogue Tóutuó,
I will lose my life to him for nothing.
I have heard that immortals eat pine needles and cedar;
I shall try to learn from them."
He picked the tender needles from the pine branches to taste;
though not palatable,
they were fragrant.
After eating a bit,
his spirits rose;
regardless of whether they were old or tender, he put handfuls of them into his mouth,
chewing and swallowing a great deal,
and felt his stomach become somewhat fuller.
Suddenly a gust of wind blew,
and from afar he heard the sound of shouting and weeping.
Dànzǐ Héshang said:
"Strange,
this is not a bustling village;
where is this sound coming from?"
Listening closely again,
the sound was mournful and urgent,
and it sounded like a woman's voice,
clearly coming from that thatched hut ahead.
Dànzǐ Héshang suddenly realized:
"That's it,
that rogue Tóutuó must have committed some unjust and illegal act.
I want to ignore it,
but my heart is so indignant, how can I endure it!
I will go quietly to investigate the situation
so I can put my mind at ease."
He then untied the bundle of clothes from his waist,
tied it to the tree,
tightened his sash around his waist again,
parted the pine branches,
and leaped downward.
His feet touched the ground
without any injury.
Shaking himself,
he walked out of the woods
and edged his way step by step toward the path ahead.
When he was roughly near the thatched hut,
he quietly poked his head out to look under the eaves;
there was no movement at all.
Walking a few more steps
and looking forward,
the Tóutuó was gone.
He went to the eaves and looked carefully left and right;
indeed, he was nowhere to be seen.
Listening closely,
the crying inside had also stopped.
Dànzǐ Héshang felt suspicious
and gently pushed the door.
It turned out to be a pair of old plain wooden doors.
This Shí Tóutuó was inside using a staff to prop it shut,
but it was not propped firmly.
At first, it would not open,
but after he pushed hard with effort,
with a thud, the staff fell to the ground,
and the left door opened.
This thatched house was originally three small rooms wide,
with two sections and a side wing.
In the first section, both sides were filled with mud bricks and timber for building,
as well as several pieces of heavy equipment.
In the middle, a path was left open.
The second section served as an inner room.
In the side wing to the left, a stove was set up.
Shí Tóutuó had stripped to his bare waist
and was at the stove lighting a fire to cook rice;
hearing the sound of the door opening,
he hurriedly got up to look.
No sooner said
than done,
Dànzi Héshang kicked the door open and entered.
Kicking right against the staff,
he bent down and grabbed it in his hand.
Knowing that someone was coming out from within,
he quickly dodged into the pile of timber
and hid.
In the darkness, Shí Tóutuó could not distinguish things clearly;
seeing the main door open,
he slipped outside to look around.
Taking advantage of the light leaking from the lean-to,
Dànzi Héshang slipped inside toward the courtyard.
Having entered, he did not yet know the details of the interior.
In a dark spot inside,
an old woman had already seen the monk
and cried out:
"Aya!
Another Luóhàn has arrived!
I am dead,
I am dead!"
Hearing the voice, Dànzi Héshang
knew something was strange,
but just as he was about to step forward to inquire,
he heard the right leaf of the main door creak;
it was Shí Tóutuó pushing it open with force.
Dànzi Héshang hurriedly retreated
and crouched again by the timber pile.
He saw Shí Tóutuó step inside the door,
turn his body back toward the outside,
and cry out fiercely like a ghost:
"Who is so bold
as to dare come in?"
After shouting once, he crouched down to feel for the staff on the ground,
but little did he know the staff was already in the hands of Dànzi Héshang.
Having a weapon,
the monk's courage grew considerably.
Seeing clearly at that moment,
just as the other squatted down,
he made a "scooping clothes from the water" gesture
and aimed the staff at his buttocks, thrusting upward with all his might.
Caught by surprise, the priest’s
bare scalp fell forward and hit the ground,
and he lay flat on the floor.
Dànzi Héshang was not one to shy away from a fight;
he raised the staff and struck again.
The other man used his right hand to block,
meeting the heavy blow of the staff.
With a single crack,
two fingers were broken,
hanging only by the skin.
Shí Tóutuó cried out in pain:
"Hero, spare my life!"
Dànzi Héshang knew he had the advantage;
holding the staff in his left hand,
he spread the five fingers of his right hand,
grabbed the man in one go,
lifting him by the waist, hips, and belly all together,
and threw him down hard in the courtyard.
The priest screamed like a slaughtered pig.
Dànzi Héshang stepped forward,
pinning him by the chest with his right foot.
He brandished a fist the size of a bushel basket in front of his face
and shouted:
"You thieving priest,
do you want to live or die?"
Only then did the priest recognize him as the monk who had fallen into the water,
and he cried:
"Elder Brother,
I have offended you,
please spare my life."
Dànzi Héshang cursed:
"You thieving priest,
I thought you were a famous hero of the underworld,
an elite fighter from Shàolín Sì,
but it turns out you are such a useless, stupid thing.
Why call yourself Stone Luóhàn?
Even if you were an Iron Luóhàn,
I would melt you down.
That massive laundry stone in front of Yínghuī Sì,
I smashed to pieces with a single punch.
Earlier, I yielded to you repeatedly
because it is my duty as a man of the cloth.
But then you came into the forest to provoke me.
Tell the truth, what business are you doing here
to make this family weep and cry?
Speak quickly and there may be room for discussion;
if there is any ambiguity in your words,
I will not even use the staff—
I will treat you like a laundry stone
and test my fist on you."
Having said this,
he cast aside the staff
and raised his right fist to strike.
The priest panicked,
and with his chest pinned so tightly he was in great distress,
he shouted with all his might:
"Grandfather Buddha, Ancestral Master Buddha,
let me up
and let me explain in detail."
Dànzi Héshang said:
"Thieving priest,
even if I let you up,
I doubt you would dare run."
But just as he was about to relax his foot,
he heard someone call from the darkness inside:
"Master, please right the wrongs of my family!
Do not let him go!"
Dànzi Héshang recognized it as the same voice from before.
Steadying his foot to look,
he saw a white-haired old woman,
hunched and bent-backed,
half-crouching and half-walking as she felt her way out.
Coming into the courtyard,
she faced Dànzi Héshang
and bowed repeatedly,
crying for justice.
Dànzi Héshang said:
"Old woman, no need for such ceremony.
Whatever grievance you have,
speak it quickly,
and I will see justice done for you."
The old woman said:
"This devil
has taken the lives of my daughter-in-law and her child."
This single sentence made Dànzi Héshang’s temper flare;
he stomped his heel hard into the priest's solar plexus.
The priest gave a great cry,
and fresh blood sprayed from his mouth.
A poem serves as witness:
A monk's pure calling is a joy beyond measure;
why then do straw sandals roam the ten directions?
Committing theft and lust brings evil retribution;
it is like cutting a wound into healthy flesh.
Only then did Dànzi Héshang pull back his foot,
help the old woman up,
and ask for the reason.
The old woman began to wail,
pointed toward the lean-to,
and said:
"Master, go and see, and you will know."
Dànzi Héshang, still fearing the priest's treachery,
was about to strike him a few more times,
but seeing him lying stiff and motionless,
not even making a sound when kicked,
he finally felt at ease.
He walked into the lean-to
and trimmed the wick of the wall lamp to make it brighter.
Steam was still rising from the pot;
when he lifted the lid,
there was a pot of fragrant hot rice
that the priest had just cooked.
Dànzi Héshang was in the middle of a hungry urgency,
so he said:
"I will eat two bowls of his rice first,
then I will deal with this."
He picked up a bundle of thatch by the stove and lit it
to find a bowl.
He had just retrieved a porcelain bowl
and a pair of willow-wood chopsticks from a broken cupboard,
when he suddenly saw another person lying in the corner of the wall,
which gave him a start.
Shining the light carefully,
it turned out to be a woman, stripped naked,
dead in a pool of blood.
Just then, the old woman also felt her way in, weeping.
Dànzi Héshang asked:
"Who is this woman to you?
Why did she die?"
The old woman said:
"It is a long story."
Dragging a stool over, she asked the master to sit,
"Wait and let this old woman tell you slowly."
Dànzi Héshang said:
"Don't worry about me;
speak your fill,
I am listening."
He then scooped some rice and began to eat
while listening to the old woman's story.
The old woman sat on the threshold
and told the story from beginning to end, saying:
“My family name is Xíng.
The one who died is my daughter-in-law.
My son is named Xíng Xiào,
and he makes a living farming here in Luójiāfàn.
Because the Xiànlìng of this county was greedy for wealth,
he pressured the Lǐzhèng to provide about a hundred dàn of high-quality cinnabar.
Although this cinnabar is said to be produced in Chénzhōu,
it is not a local product of Qiányáng Xiàn;
instead, it is found within the Lǎoyājǐng of Yuánzhōu.
This well is incredibly wide,
with natural walls of green stone on all four sides.
One must stack dry firewood and set it ablaze
to burn those stone walls until they crack open;
only then does the cinnabar appear.
When the farmers here in Luójiāfàn are idle from their fields,
they are all accustomed to doing this line of business.
The Lǐzhèng extorted silver from the common people
and hired men to go there to pay the land fees
and extract the cinnabar to curry favor with the Xiànlìng.
Several farming households in this valley accepted the wages,
but those who had wives sent them to stay with relatives.
Only my daughter-in-law was five months pregnant
and could not travel;
furthermore, I am over seventy years old, so the two of us stayed together for company
to watch over this house.
A month ago, when Xíng Xiào was still at home,
my daughter-in-law suffered from a bout of abdominal pain,
and we could not find a doctor in a hurry.
Just then, we encountered this Tóutuó coming to the door to beg for alms.
My son replied to him:
‘There is a sick person at home right now;
I am in no mood to give you alms.’
He asked what the illness was,
and my son unwisely replied to him:
‘My wife is five months pregnant
and is currently suffering from abdominal pain;
I fear she might miscarry.’
The Tóutuó said:
‘I am called Shí Tóutuó,
the Shí Luóhàn.
Not only can I chant scriptures,
but I also understand some medical principles.
I have a herbal prescription;
if she takes it according to my instructions, the abdominal pain will stop immediately,
and it can also stabilize the fetus.’
My son had no other choice
and had to allow him to untie his bundle,
boil a few herbal medicines, and pour them down her throat.
Indeed, the abdominal pain stopped.
That day, we treated him to a full meal of alms;
he didn't want any money
and simply left.
We only thought he was a good man.
Yesterday, he came here again to beg for alms.
My daughter-in-law replied to him:
‘The man of the house is not at home;
please come back another day.’
He refused to leave
and began to harass my daughter-in-law with his words.
My daughter-in-law closed the door and came inside,
ignoring him.
He sat at the doorway chanting scriptures
and just would not go away.
By the middle of the night,
I had gone to sleep,
but my daughter-in-law was still in the central room spinning hemp.
That Tóutuó knew there was no man in the house;
he quietly forced the door open
and walked right in.
He grabbed my daughter-in-law
and threatened her, saying that if she made a sound, he would kill her.
He then raped her;
but that was a minor matter.
He then ordered her to boil a pot of scalding water,
saying he wanted to take a bath.
My daughter-in-law had no choice but to boil the water for him.
He then ordered her to pour
half of it into a tub.
That murderous scoundrel actually did not want a bath;
he opened his bundle, took out a pill of white medicine, and made her swallow it,
saying it would facilitate childbirth later.
After swallowing it, she immediately felt some abdominal pain.
He then untied two new straw sandals and soaked them in the pot,
saying to my daughter-in-law:
‘I want to borrow something from you
to compound an elixir of immortality.
When the medicine is ready, I will give you some to eat,
and we will all ascend as immortals.’
My daughter-in-law asked:
‘What do you want to borrow?’
He said:
‘I want your five-month-old bloody fetus.’
My daughter-in-law was terrified
and wept, bowing to beg for mercy.
That murderous scoundrel held her firm with both hands,
stripped her until not a thread remained,
bound her hands and feet,
pressed her onto the tub,
and rubbed her belly with the hot water.
My daughter-in-law was in extreme pain
and pleaded repeatedly,
but he would not grant her mercy.
He then took the two hot straw sandals from the pot and rubbed them alternately over her belly.
Pitifully, the bloody fetus fell out,
and my daughter-in-law died of a hemorrhage on the spot.
I was frightened out of my wits and crouched in the back,
not daring to make a sound.
I only heard that murderous scoundrel say:
‘It turns out to be a male fetus.’
He then took rice from his cloth bag to cook a meal,
intending to leave as soon as he had eaten.
Unexpectedly, he encountered the arrival of you, Master,
who dealt with him.
Truly, heaven’s justice is manifest;
evil people will be reaped by their own kind.
Dànzi Héshang asked:
“Where is the bloody fetus he took?”
The old woman said:
“I think he has packed it away inside his bundle.”
Because the old woman's story was long,
Dànzi Héshang did not know how many bowls of rice he had eaten;
he had emptied the pot completely,
leaving only the bottom.
The Héshang put down his bowl and chopsticks
and searched for the bundle on the upper shelf of the cupboard.
When he opened it on top of the pot lid to look,
there was another small cloth packet inside.
When unwrapped, it was a cloth skirt
wrapping the blood-clumped little boy and the placenta within.
There was also a packet of over ten taels of broken silver.
Additionally, there was a bolt of fine white cloth wrapping a Lièhuǒ Jiāshā,
a monk's robe,
and various items of clothing.
There was another cloth bag containing two or three shēng of mixed rice.
Dànzi Héshang looked at the bloody fetus
and thought to himself:
“I don’t know if his recipe for immortality is true or false,
what drugs it is paired with,
or how it is used.
It is a pity that such a sin was committed;
it is useless now and must be discarded.”
He recited the name of Āmítuófó
and handed the bloody fetus and the cloth skirt to the old woman.
When the old woman saw them,
she began to weep for her flesh and blood all over again.
Dànzi Héshang opened the silver packet,
picked out several large pieces
totaling about five or six taels,
and gave them to the old woman, saying:
“Take this silver
to arrange your daughter-in-law's burial.
The rest I shall keep for myself.”
By this time, the sky was gradually brightening.
He walked out into the courtyard
and saw the Tóutuó’s face was yellow;
he had already stopped breathing.
On his feet was a fine pair of blue cloth monk's shoes,
which Dànzi Héshang stripped off and put on.
He used his iron-capped, eyebrow-height staff to shoulder the bundle
and called out:
“Old one,
that thief of a Tóutuó is dead;
all is peaceful now.
He was about to leave.
The old woman said:
"Master, you cannot go."
Dànzǐ Héshang indeed stopped in his tracks
and asked:
"Why can I not go?"
The old woman said:
"Although you have removed this harm for me,
you have left behind two corpses;
how am I supposed to manage this?"
Dànzǐ Héshang said:
"That is also true.
I will first cast the thief monk’s corpse onto the wild outskirts
and then decide what to do."
He set down his staff and bundle,
grasped the dead monk’s waistband with one hand,
lifted the corpse just like a small chick,
went out the door,
and headed straight into the woods.
By this time, the sky was fully bright;
he recognized that large pine tree from the night before
and was just waiting to drop the corpse
and climb up to retrieve his bundle of clothes.
Suddenly, he heard someone shouting from afar:
"In this peaceful world,
from where has a monk killed someone
and dumped them in this place?"
When Dànzǐ Héshang fixed his gaze to look,
there were seven or eight villagers behind the woods,
each carrying a bundle on their back,
wearing a waist saber,
and carrying a pǔdāo staff-knife,
rushing toward him as if flying.
Dànzǐ Héshang unhurriedly dropped the corpse on the ground,
already having climbed up the tree,
and took the bundle of clothes in his hand.
The villagers surrounded the large pine tree in a circle;
Dànzǐ Héshang called out from the tree:
"This poor monk is not a murderer;
I am the one who killed that murderous thief.
Everyone, step aside
and wait for this poor monk to come down and meet you."
Having finished speaking,
he gave a sudden leap,
jumping outside the circle of people.
The villagers surrounded the monk once more,
questioning him about the reason.
Dànzǐ Héshang said:
"Sirs, please tell me where you have come from?"
The villagers said:
"We have been commissioned by the Lord County Magistrate
to go to Yuánzhōu to collect cinnabar.
Last night we reached the county and handed it over to the village head;
this morning we set out at the fifth watch and walked to this place."
Dànzǐ Héshang said:
"Among you sirs, is there one named Xíng Xiào?
This poor monk has news to give him."
A short, dark man stepped out from among the group,
came forward and said:
"I am indeed Xíng Xiào."
Dànzǐ Héshang pointed at the corpse and said:
"This thief monk is your enemy of seven lifetimes."
When Xíng Xiào finished hearing these words,
it was as if a thousand mallets were pounding wildly at his heart;
his complexion changed completely,
and he grabbed the monk, saying:
"Explain it clearly to me."
Dànzǐ Héshang said:
"If I tell you now,
you will not believe it.
Your noble residence is not far from here;
sirs, do not disperse,
let everyone go and be witnesses."
The people said:
"Brother Xíng, do not panic.
Since we are going together to your residence,
naturally things will be clarified."
At that time, the group followed the monk along the way;
although their toes all pointed forward together
and their heels all pointed backward together,
yet there were three different states of mind.
Dànzǐ Héshang’s heart was joyful,
like a boatman entering a harbor against the wind;
he had reached a conclusion.
The villagers’ hearts were full of doubt,
like people watching a performance,
not knowing what story would be presented.
Only Xíng Xiào’s heart was filled with terror,
like a suspect being escorted to the Inspectorate,
with only punishment and no reward.
Indeed: "One steals wine to drink behind others’ backs,
but its cold or warmth only oneself knows."
It is said that when the old woman saw the monk had gone,
fear grew in her heart.
With effort, she went to the bed to pull a sheet
and covered the woman’s corpse on the ground with it.
She groped her way to the door,
looking in both directions,
yet not knowing which way was the path.
Gazing this way and that,
she only waited for the monk’s arrival to handle this matter,
never dreaming that her son would return.
While her old eyes were blurred and could not yet see clearly,
Xíng Xiào took a step ahead;
he had already seen her
and called out:
"Old Mother,
why are you alone outside the door looking for someone?
Where is my wife,
why is she not accompanying you?"
As soon as the old woman saw her son,
she grabbed him and wailed loudly, saying:
"My son, if you had returned one day earlier,
it might not have happened that your perfectly good wife was killed by some Shí monk or Shí Luóhàn."
Xíng Xiào said:
"What are you saying?"
The old woman cried:
"She died so miserably!"
When Xíng Xiào rushed inside the door to look,
the others all arrived shortly after,
crowding forward,
and pushed the old woman to the back.
They saw Xíng Xiào pick up his wife together with the sheet,
placed her in the middle of the back room,
and wailed while beating his chest.
All the villagers were sorrowful,
and they asked Dànzǐ Héshang:
"How did this matter happen?"
Dànzǐ Héshang said:
"Wait until Brother Xíng has finished crying,
then ask the old mother and you will know."
Xíng Xiào said:
"My mother is an aged person;
the Elder must explain it clearly for me."
Dànzǐ Héshang then related how he had fallen into the water and sought lodging until he killed the monk,
and afterward how the old mother of the house spoke to him thus and so,
recounting the details in full.
Xíng Xiào could not stop the tears falling down his cheeks.
Everyone ground their teeth in rage.
The old woman reproached her son, saying:
"It is all because you listened to the nonsense of that one who deserves to be killed by Heaven,
taking some herbal prescription for calming the fetus,
which drew that thief monk to our door
and caused this matter.
Now one life has become two lives;
is it not as if you yourself harmed your wife and child?"
The villagers advised:
"Old Mother, speaking of it now is of no use.
Fortunately, we encountered this Elder
who has avenged the wrong,
so the deceased may rest in peace.
However, now one is lying in the woods
and another is lying in the house;
this is not right,
and we should quickly make a plan.
Is there rice in the house?
We can cook some rice and eat it,
then we shall trouble the Elder to go with us to the Lord County Magistrate to report the matter.
Wait for him to dispatch an official to conduct an inquest,
and take the opportunity to bring down a coffin for the burial,
lest some time passes and the constables see the corpse in the woods
and then spread rumors and cause trouble,
making a profit out of the local area."
Dànzǐ Héshang said:
"I have heard that the County Magistrate is a corrupt official;
why report it to him?
If you want to bury them,
just bury them yourselves and be done with it."
Xíng Xiào said:
"That would never do."
Immediately they struck fire and cooked rice;
the people each took out some dried vegetables they had prepared,
brought them all out,
and waited for the rice to be cooked so everyone could eat their fill.
The old woman handed the silver to Xíng Xiào
and told him the reasons;
Xíng Xiào bowed again to thank the monk.
The people said:
"The old mother must also go once."
Xíng Xiào prepared a 'sheep-head' small cart,
had his mother sit on it,
locked the door,
and asked a close fellow villager to help push the cart.
Dànzǐ Héshang took up his staff,
combined the two bundles into one to carry on his back,
and the group crowded together to Qiányáng County.
After waiting a short while,
the County Magistrate was just ascending to the evening court.
The group presented the bundle containing the bloodied fetus in the court,
reporting a case of homicide in the locality.
The Magistrate interrogated each person involved one by one,
recorded their testimonies,
and ordered a County Lieutenant to go to the countryside to conduct an inquest.
By the evening court of the next day, the report returned with no discrepancies,
and the official’s verdict was:
Shí Tóutuó was a vagabond monk with no fixed registration.
Although his crimes were heavy,
as he was already dead, his corpse would not be investigated.
The local authorities were ordered to have him buried.
Shěn Shì was told to have Xíng Xiào personally handle the funeral and burial.
Dànzi Héshàng was exempted from punishment because he had killed and wounded out of righteous indignation.
The rest of the people were all sent back home.
Only Dànzi Héshàng was kept at the county office to receive instructions.
After the court session adjourned,
the Xiànlìng called the Héshàng to the study in the rear hall.
He dismissed his attendants,
praised him with a few words,
and then said:
"I have an important letter and some gifts
that I wish to send to a relative in Qìngyuán Fǔ.
The journey is long and distant,
and I have no one I can entrust with this.
I just heard that you have such a sense of righteousness
and are heroically capable.
If you are willing to perform this service for me,
I will reward you generously upon your return."
Dànzi Héshàng said:
"I am but a traveling Héshàng;
there is no place I do not go.
Since Your Honor has entrusted me with this, I dare not fail you."
The Xiànlìng was greatly pleased
and called his confidant Wú Kǒngmù to escort the elder to stay at the Chénghuáng Miào.
Two strings of full cash were drawn from the treasury and given to the Dàoshì,
instructing him to provide for the monk while waiting for the letters to be finished
before he set off.
It is not mentioned how the Xiànlìng entered the yamen to pack gold, pearls, and silver,
or the matter of arranging the boxes and trunks.
Now, when Dànzi Héshàng and Wú Kǒngmù arrived at the Chénghuáng Miào,
an official messenger had already informed the Dàoshì.
He welcomed them into the guest hall to sit.
Dànzi Héshàng saw that the temple was dilapidated,
the buildings were in disrepair,
and the Dàoshì’s clothes were ragged.
So he asked:
"Is the incense at this divine temple flourishing?"
The Dàoshì said:
"The deity is extremely efficacious,
and the incense never ceases."
Dànzi Héshàng remained silent.
After tea was finished,
Wú Kǒngmù handed the two strings of cash over to the Dàoshì,
then stood up and instructed him to treat the monk well.
The Dàoshì then gave three hundred coins to Wú Kǒngmù
as a substitute for a banquet
and saw him out the door.
The Dàoshì asked Dànzi Héshàng if he consumed meat or wine,
then hurriedly ordered the temple caretaker to buy various things.
Having prepared everything properly,
he set it out inside the bedroom
and invited him to sit.
He also moved his own bedding out
to let the Héshàng rest in this room.
While Dànzi Héshàng was drinking wine,
he asked:
"Since the deity is efficacious
and the incense is flourishing,
why is the temple in such a wretched state?"
The Dàoshì sighed and said:
"Although that is so,
for this humble Dàoshì, there is harm but no benefit."
Dànzi Héshàng asked in a low voice:
"Could it be that the Xiànlìng makes things difficult for you?"
The Dàoshì's face turned red,
and he did not dare answer.
Dànzi Héshàng said again:
"I am not originally acquainted with this Xiànlìng.
It is only today that he wanted me to make a trip to Qìngyuán Fǔ and keep me here.
I momentarily agreed,
but I do not know what kind of letter it is.
I have heard that the Xiànlìng is a corrupt official
who exploits the common people.
You must know the details.
Do not be suspicious of me;
just speak freely.
We who have left the secular world,
could we possibly go along with a corrupt dog?"
The Dàoshì saw that his words were sincere,
so he used two fingers to make a circle like a coin
and said:
"What the Xiànlìng Lǎoyé loves is that thing.
Never mind other matters;
just in this Chénghuáng Miào,
regardless of whether the month is long or short,
one must pay him ten strings of incense money.
When it falls short of the amount,
I even have to make up the difference myself.
If any grain or supplies are donated here,
the county office immediately comes to take them for use.
That is why I have no resources to repair the gates or the corridors.
Because he wears an official's cap,
even the deity is snobbish toward him.
Although the deity's power is said to be awe-inspiring,
it only works its effects on the common people.
When it encounters an official, there is no retribution at all."
Dànzi Héshàng said:
"Where is he from,
and what relatives does he have in Qìngyuán Fǔ?
If it's just a letter, what does it matter?
Why must he use me?"
The Dàoshì said:
"He is indeed a native of Cíxī in Qìngyuán Fǔ,
surnamed Hóu, given name Míngzǎi.
He has been an official here for four years.
Every year he amasses a certain amount of illicit gains and ships them home.
Fearing any mishap,
he insists on having someone capable to escort them.
Last year, he used the wrong person,
and the goods were robbed at Dòngtíng Hú.
I heard that this time he wants to take the land route,
and he is keeping you, Chánshī, surely for this reason.
He was originally from a poor scholarly background,
but just through this term of office,
he has opened several pawnshops back home.
Yet his greed is still not satisfied.
Chánshī, would you say he is cruel or not?"
Dànzi Héshàng said:
"So that's how it is."
The Dàoshì said:
"Just now the Chánshī questioned me,
and I have spoken too much.
On the road, in front of their stewards or official runners,
you must not mention any of this."
Dànzi Héshàng said:
"There is no need to tell me."
That night, after the wine and food were finished,
the Dàoshì left.
Dànzi Héshàng thought to himself in the room:
"This wealth swindled from people,
he actually wants me to deliver it for him.
This will not do,
it will not do."
He slept until the fifth watch,
then pretending to relieve himself,
he took his bundle and staff, left the temple gate,
and vanished in a puff of smoke.
The next day, when the Dàoshì found the monk gone,
he was thrown into a panic
and informed the Xiànlìng.
The Xiànlìng said:
"Fortunately, I had not yet entrusted him with the task.
This traveling Héshàng has no trustworthiness at all."
He did not blame the Dàoshì,
but only demanded those two strings of cash be returned to the treasury.
The Dàoshì had no choice but to borrow money and go into debt
to make up the amount,
ending up losing three hundred coins
and a meal of wine and food.
Later, Xiànlìng Hóu used many bribes
and was promoted to a capital post.
He had a living shrine built for himself in the county.
After he left his post, the common people at midnight carried away the clay statue from that shrine,
broke its legs,
and threw it into a manure pit.
On his journey, the Xiànlìng was thrown from his horse when it was startled,
broke his leg, and died.
It can be seen that the Way of Heaven does not err.
This is a later part of the story.
There is a poem to prove it:
No matter how much one eats, it is not much;
Why then greedily seek with such bitterness?
Just see how the corrupt official must eventually fall;
Even if he escapes human execution, he will be rebuked by ghosts.
Now, it is said that on the day Dànzi Héshàng left Qiányáng Xiàn,
he departed from Chénzhōu
and traveled once again towards the Húběi and Jīngnán route.
Seeing mountains when meeting mountains,
seeing water when meeting water,
lingering over the scenery,
another year passed before he knew it.
Seeing the plum blossoms white and peach blossoms red,
and soon the plums turning yellow and apricots purple,
Dànzi Héshàng kept his original purpose in mind.
He bought a hundred sheets of clean, pure cotton large paper in advance,
and brought them back to his straw hut at the foot of Yúnmèng Shān.
He pre-numbered the sheets one, two, three, four,
wrapped them with the piece of fine white cloth from Shí Tóutuó into a bundle,
and went to the Qīngshuǐ Tán to take a purifying bath.
By the day of Duānwǔ,
he rose early to cook rice in the earth stove and ate his fill;
just as he was preparing to tie his gear together,
he saw clouds darkening the mountain peaks,
and a heavy rain began to fall.
Monk Dànzǐ said:
"Is this not bad luck!
This rain has not fallen for days,
yet it specifically starts today to see me off."
He had no choice but to kowtow toward the empty sky within the pine shed and pray, saying:
"I, this humble one, have the karmic opportunity today to see the face of the Heavenly Script;
I beg for the clouds to gather and the rain to cease,
and for the red sun to quickly appear."
After enduring until the hour of Sì,
the rain finally stopped.
The monk was overjoyed beyond measure;
he took the cotton paper,
grabbed his eyebrow-height staff, and set off.
This was the third time,
and he was familiar with the path.
However, the mountain ground was wet,
rugged and uneven,
and moreover, traveling through the mist,
he feared he might be delayed.
Hurrying forward,
by the time the mist was about to dissipate,
he reached the stone bridge.
When Monk Dànzǐ looked up,
he was startled.
It turned out that this bridge was a single naturally formed bluestone;
after the rain,
it was as slippery as oil.
No matter how careful you were at every step,
how could you keep your footing?
Someone might ask:
"With those three hundred and sixty days of thick mist,
could it be that the stone bridge had no dampness at all,
and only waited for this heavy rain?"
Dear readers, you may not know.
Ordinary mist
is the ascent of earthly vapors
that are not met by heavenly vapors;
it is formed by a dense and chaotic aura,
and thus it wets one's clothes
and moistens stones upon contact,
lingering without dispersing.
The mist of the Báiyún Dòng
is sprayed from a misty curtain;
it is merely a dry mist.
It is clearly a mirage;
visible from afar,
but having no trace when approached.
Therefore, during the previous two times, the stone bridge was not damp at all,
but after this rain, it was difficult to cross.
If it were only three or four feet,
a few steps would be fine,
but it was over thirty feet long!
Below was an unfathomable abyss;
it was no joking matter.
It is just as the saying goes:
"Unless one sprouts wings and flies across,
one is sure to fall as soon as they move their feet."
If that were the case,
the third trip would have been in vain again.
But isn't it said that when the wind is fierce and rain arrives,
urgent situations give rise to cleverness?
In the end, what plan did he use?
Please listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
The twin spinning balls turn as fast as a shuttle,
in a glance, the years have already passed.
When there is work to be done, one must do it quickly;
for who can hold back the Lǔyáng Gē?
It is said that on Monk Dànzǐ's third trip on the day of Duānwǔ,
after encountering the rain,
the stone bridge was wet and slippery,
and he could not walk across;
a plan formed in his mind.
He put down his eyebrow-height short staff,
took the bundle of cotton paper,
bound it tightly to his back,
laid his body down,
and gripped the stone bridge with both hands.
The underside of both sides of the bridge
unavoidably had some edges and corners,
unlike the smooth surface of the bridge;
his feet could find purchase
and he pushed himself forward step by step,
crossing in an instant.
Monk Dànzǐ climbed up,
pressed his palms together, and cried out:
"Thank Heaven and Earth!"
Then he hurriedly entered the Báiyún Xiāndòng.
Coming before the white jade incense burner,
he knelt on both knees,
kowtowed, and reported:
"This poor monk has come here for the third time;
I beg the spirits to have pity
and transmit the Daoist methods.
I am willing to act on behalf of Heaven;
if I commit evil or wrongdoing,
may Heaven strike me down and the Earth destroy me."
After making his vow,
he went into the stone chamber,
untied his bundle,
took out the paper,
spread it out on the ground,
picked up each sheet,
and arranged them in order from number one and number two.
Starting first from the left wall,
he held the paper steady with his hands,
from beginning to end,
wherever there were characters,
he rubbed over them in sequence,
totaling thirteen sheets.
On each sheet, he tore off a corner
to identify them.
He turned to the right side
and rubbed them one by one.
The characters on the right were dense and long;
by the time he had rubbed twenty-four sheets,
he felt the fragrance arrive.
There was still one more section at the end,
but he didn't have time to rub it.
Hastily, he took the thirty-seven sheets he had rubbed,
rolled them into a messy bundle,
wrapped them in the cloth, and carried them.
The remaining paper he discarded,
having no time to collect it.
He rushed out of the stone chamber,
and a great amount of smoke billowed from the white jade incense burner.
In a panic, he ran out of the cave,
and bound the bundle to his back as before.
Still using his hands and feet for leverage,
like a monkey climbing a tree,
he clambered across that thirty-foot long,
one-foot wide,
mirror-bright,
and oil-slippery stone bridge.
Generally, for those who travel,
the journey there feels slow,
while the return feels fast.
Monk Dànzǐ was delighted that he had succeeded this time,
and moreover, the dangerous place had been passed.
He picked up his staff from the ground,
strode out with big steps,
and before long,
he reached the thatched hut.
Without waiting to catch his breath,
he untied the bundle of paper
and spread it out to look.
It turned out that while in the cave,
he had been in such a frantic rush
and his mind so dazed
that it only seemed like there were some dark, faint traces of characters.
Now as he looked,
they were actually sheets of plain paper;
how could there be a single dot or stroke?
He checked every sheet,
and they were all the same.
This left Monk Dànzǐ staring in dumbstruck amazement,
his hands paralyzed and his legs weak.
This disappointment
was beyond description.
He thought about seeing gods and ghosts;
all this time,
it had all been a fruitless endeavor.
He had endured three rounds of hardship
and nearly lost his life,
yet he was so lacking in karmic fortune
that he could not even obtain a line or two by luck.
Although the first two times were in vain,
the matter was still unsettled;
now all hope was lost,
and there was no longer any plan to pursue.
In a fit of anger,
he threw the sheets of paper all over the ground;
the more he thought, the more bitter he felt,
and his heart began to ache;
tears welled up like pearls,
and he unconsciously began to wail loudly.
After a bout of crying,
he intended to head to the pool to find a way to end his life.
As he emerged from the straw hut
and had walked only a few steps,
he happened to encounter the white-bearded old man from the previous year,
who met him and asked:
“Elder, your quest for the Dào has been arduous.”
Dànzi Héshàng, his face full of shame, replied:
“It is hard to tell you, Elder.
My fate lacks the affinity;
a bundle of paper was taken and brought back in vain,
with not a single word upon it.
With such a wretched fate, it is better to die.”
Having finished speaking,
his tears fell like rain.
The old man said:
“Elder, do not be sorrowful for now;
whether there is affinity or not is yet to be determined.
Since this Tiān Shū was not produced by brush and ink,
how could the traces of writing come from them?”
Dànzi Héshàng asked in great shock:
“Last year you instructed me not to use brush and ink,
so why do you speak this way now?”
The old man said:
“The Tiān Shū is no ordinary object.
Moreover, that which is openly bestowed belongs to Yáng,
while that which is secretly taken belongs to Yīn.
Under sunlight, Yīn energy remains hidden
and naturally cannot be seen;
this is the principle of Yīn and Yáng overcoming one another.
If you wish to distinguish whether you have affinity or not,
you must wait for the three double-hours of Xū, Hài, and Zǐ,
choose a night when the moon is full,
and in an open wilderness where no one is present,
hold the paper up to the moonlight.
Faintly, green characters will appear;
this means the opportunity has arrived.
If there are no characters,
then there is no affinity.”
Dànzi Héshàng felt as if awakening from a dream,
or returning to life from death,
and said:
“I am deeply grateful for your guidance, Elder,
but I do not know if there will be a moon tonight.”
The old man said:
“The moonlight is insufficient in the first decade of the month.
You must wait until the five days from the eleventh to the fifteenth,
when the moon gradually becomes full.
Inspect it according to the method;
if you see the characters,
then use brush and ink to trace them accordingly.
I shall come to meet you again when the time arrives.”
Dànzi Héshàng thanked him endlessly.
The old man bid the monk farewell
and turned the corner, departing.
Dànzi Héshàng was overcome with joy;
he returned to the straw hut
and once again
picked up the papers from the ground.
Following the secret marks for the east and west,
he arranged them in numerical order
and rolled them into two bundles,
hiding them safely within a cloth wrap.
Following the old man's instructions,
he waited until the eleventh day.
He prepared a bowl of ink in advance,
and at dusk, he carried it to the highest mountaintop.
Selecting a level spot,
he opened the cloth wrap and spread it on the ground.
First, he took the papers traced from the left wall
and inspected them one by one against the moon,
but as before, there was not a single word.
Dànzi Héshàng was no small amount of panicked;
settling his mind,
he then took the papers traced from the right wall to inspect them under the moon.
Indeed, green characters faintly appeared.
The fine characters were the size of copper coins,
while the thick ones were the size of a palm,
but most were Léi Wén and Yún Zhuàn scripts,
of which he did not recognize a single bit.
He was simply glad that the characters had been passed down
and would figure out the rest later.
He then used the brush and ink to trace over the original papers according to the patterns.
By the latter half of the night, as the moon sank to the west,
the characters became unclear.
He packed up and returned;
the next night he came again.
For five consecutive days, the weather was clear and bright,
as if it were destined to be so.
By the fifteenth day, all twenty-four sheets of paper had been traced,
and he placed them inside the cloth wrap.
Back in the straw hut, he did not sleep all night,
thinking:
“I wonder who can recognize the writing of this Tiān Shū?
The old man promised to meet me when the time came,
yet he hasn't appeared;
this is truly vexing.”
It was not until the fifth watch that he closed his eyes.
He heard a voice outside the straw hut,
sounding like the old man, saying:
“To distinguish the Tiān Shū,
one must seek Shèng Gū.”
Dànzi Héshàng leaped up in his dream
and asked:
“Who is Shèng Gū?”
By then, the sky was already dawning.
When he rushed out of the hut to look,
there was no sign of anyone.
Dànzi Héshàng said:
“How strange!
Someone was clearly speaking;
how has he vanished?”
After thinking for a while, he said:
“That’s it!
This white-haired old man must be an incarnation of Bái Yuán Shén.
Because my heart in seeking the Dào is sincere,
I have moved him,
