and he has come here twice to guide me through my confusion.
Calling to me in a dream tonight
is indeed proof.
There must be a Shèng Gū
somewhere who can distinguish the Tiān Shū.
I only do not know where she lives.
How can I meet her at the ends of the earth?
I must go everywhere to search for her;
waiting here like 'watching a stump for a rabbit'
is surely of no use.
This straw hut is no longer needed.”
He then packed the Tiān Shū wrap and his belongings into his bundle.
He cooked and ate some rice,
took his bundle and staff,
stoked the fire in the earthen stove,
and used pine needles to set the straw hut ablaze.
He decided he would walk in whichever direction the hut collapsed,
for he had no plan of his own
and treated the straw hut as if leaving it to the Mandate of Heaven.
A poem serves as proof:
Seeking the truth three times, he suffered all hardships,
yet in the end, he could not distinguish his own affairs.
This time he must wander the ends of the earth;
where is the person who can read the script?
On this day, a northeast wind blew;
the flames were fanned by the wind,
crackling as they burned away the roof of the straw hut.
With a loud crash,
several pillars collapsed toward the north-northwest.
Dànzi Héshàng said:
“The wind is blowing from the south,
yet the hut's pillars fell toward the north instead;
how very strange.
North-northwest
is precisely the region of Guān Zhōng.
That is where the emperors established their capitals,
and many extraordinary people dwell.
Perhaps Shèng Gū is there; it is hard to say.”
He then bowed
toward the direction of Bái Yún Dòng,
thanking Bái Yuán Shén,
and set off with great strides toward the north.
Later people wrote a poem in the ancient style
specifically describing Dànzi Héshàng's three quests for the Dào;
the poem says:
Thick clouds lock the depths of the grotto-heaven,
incense from the jade brazier curls around the thousand-year fire.
Within, Yuán Gōng is steeped in the Sù Shū;
the stone walls are engraved with transmissions divided between left and right.
The Buddhist monk was originally a child from an egg,
who suddenly conceived heaven-startling and earth-shaking thoughts.
Swinging his arms, he left home without looking back,
wandering to the ends of the earth in search of a master.
At the ferry of confusion, he happened upon Yún Mèng;
a passerby pointed the way to the immortal's cave.
Every year on the Duān Wǔ festival he went to pay homage,
but the incense faded and mists rolled in, leaving him empty.
The marvelous book and spiritual traces caused his soul to soar;
dining on wind and sleeping in rain, how devout his sincerity!
To the thousand-fathom abyss, he was willing to cross the sea;
on a three-foot precarious beam, he lightly ascended to heaven.
Coveting the scenery, the smoke from the brazier rose;
his period of hardship became like flowing water.
Coming again to circle the cave in search of the Tiān Shū,
he found the Tiān Shū but had no brush to record it.
The Tiān Shū is not transmitted by rabbit-hair brushes;
tracing the stone wall in vain, he grieved over lack of affinity.
Pitying his tears of blood, the Divine Elder guided him;
through a thousand shocks and ten thousand terrors, three years passed.
Three years of terror nearly cost him his life,
yet alone in the empty mountains, his heart remained firm.
Clearly, green Léi Wén characters appeared,
at midnight on the peak when the moon was like a mirror.
To distinguish the Léi Wén, there is Shèng Gū;
who calls out to his sorrowful breast within a dream?
Bidding farewell to the mountain spirit, he becomes a traveler,
a solitary journey gazing toward the road to Cháng’ān.
Cháng’ān has been a realm of prosperity since ancient times,
where famous mountains are forever home to immortal companions.
On this journey, meeting a teacher, he will master all laws,
and not let the three years of bitter determination be in vain.
It is said that the monk Dànzi Héshang traveled to Nèixiāng Xiàn in Wǎnqiū.
It was then the middle of the fifth month,
and the weather was scorching hot.
Thinking that it would be best to have a fan to use,
he had not walked many steps when he happened to see a fan shop.
At that time, folding fans were not yet in fashion;
the shop sold five types of fans.
What five types?
They were:
paper or silk round fans,
black or white feather fans,
fine bamboo splint pouch-fans,
cattail leaf fans,
and plantain leaf fans.
Dànzi Héshang said that feather fans were quite nice,
but one could not write characters on them.
Round fans did not seem like something a monk should hold,
so he bought a fine bamboo splint pouch-fan,
intending to write the three characters "Seeking Shènggū" upon it.
Should he encounter someone on the road who knew of her origins,
it could serve as a guide.
Walking to the storefront,
he called to the shopkeeper to bring the pouch-fans for him to see.
He selected one that he liked,
and after negotiating the price, he bought it for five cents of silver.
It turned out that the back half of this shop had a small three-partition seating area
where a table was arranged
with a few chairs.
Near the table was a half-window,
and outside the window was a small courtyard
where a few stalks of slender bamboo were planted.
On the table were laid out items like brushes and inkstones.
Dànzi Héshang caught sight of them
and said:
"I am sorry to trouble your esteemed shop,
but I would like to borrow the brush and inkstone for a moment."
The shopkeeper said:
"The master is not here,
but there is no harm in using them out here."
He hurriedly brought them out and placed them on the shop counter.
Dànzi Héshang had just ground the ink
and had not yet put brush to paper
when he heard a voice from within:
"Who took the brush and inkstone away?"
The shopkeeper answered:
"There is an elder here
who borrowed them to write a character;
they will be returned shortly."
He then said to the monk:
"Write quickly,
for the master is coming out."
Before he had finished speaking,
a man walked out from within,
his head wrapped in a wàn-character kerchief
and wearing a single-layered tunic.
Seeing that the monk was writing the three characters "Seeking Shènggū"
on the fan,
he cupped his hands and asked:
"Where does the elder come from,
and why do you wish to seek Shènggū?"
Dànzi Héshang said:
"This poor monk has come from Yínghuī Sì in Sìzhōu Chéng.
I have heard that Shènggū possesses great spiritual power,
so I have come specifically to seek her."
The man said:
"Sìzhōu Chéng is in the Lǐngnán region;
even from such a distance, you know of Shènggū."
Dànzi Héshang was secretly surprised and said to himself:
"So there truly is a Shènggū."
He then asked:
"Has the benefactor ever met Shènggū?"
The man said:
"I have met her before."
Dànzi Héshang asked:
"Where is she now?
I trouble the benefactor to guide me."
The man said:
"Please come inside and sit down;
allow me to explain in detail."
Dànzi Héshang walked into the seating area,
and the man said again:
"Pardon my lack of ceremony in this hot weather.
Please sit;
I shall go pour a cup of tea for the elder to drink."
The man went inside.
Dànzi Héshang saw several miscellaneous books on the table,
one of which was damaged and incomplete.
By chance, he picked it up and saw the title was Bàopǔzǐ.
One entry within said:
"The Dān Shuǐ produces cinnabar fish.
If one watches for them on the night ten days before the Xiàzhì,
the fish will all float on the water,
their red light glowing like fire.
If one takes their blood and smears it on the feet,
one can walk upon water without drowning."
Dànzi Héshang said:
"In this Nèixiāng Xiàn there is a Jútán,
and also a Dān Shuǐ.
I have only heard that the banks of Jútán are covered in natural sweet chrysanthemums
and that those who drink this water live long lives.
I did not know that the Dān Shuǐ produced such a strange creature.
Had I learned of this method earlier,
why would I have suffered the hardship of falling into the water at Luójiāfàn?"
While he was thus reflecting,
he saw the man himself carrying a tray
with two bowls of brewed tea on it.
Placing them on the table, he said:
"Elder, please have some tea."
Dànzi Héshang said:
"I ought not to trouble you."
The two sat and drank tea.
The man spoke, saying:
"My surname is Qín,
and my given name is Héng.
Last year, I went to offer incense at Xīyuè Huà Shān in Huàyīn Xiàn.
I heard many people in the streets saying:
'In the household of Patrol Inspector Yáng of this county,
a living Buddha is being supported.'
Over there,
she is called Shèng Gūgū.
I asked them:
'How can she be seen as a living Buddha?'
They said:
'Patrol Inspector Yáng's family has obtained a Golden Sutra in Sanskrit script
which no one else can recognize,
but only Shèng Gūgū can explain it.'
Patrol Inspector Yáng reveres her like a god
and supports her in the Xī Yuán.
Almost everyone in the county has gone to pay respects and take her as their teacher;
I also went twice to join in the merit.
Later, because her fame spread everywhere
and more and more people went,
she went into seclusion and stopped seeing outsiders.
Now I hear she is still over there,
having lived there for more than a year now."
Dànzi Héshang said:
"She only knows the Sanskrit script;
does she have any other spiritual arts?"
Qín Héng said:
"I have heard she also has some extraordinary traits;
she can go a whole month without eating
and not feel hungry.
She also frequently communicates with Bodhisattvas,
though we have never tested her."
Dànzi Héshang said:
"Since the benefactor has personally seen Shènggū,
what does she look like?"
Qín Héng said:
"She is just an old woman.
But her spirit is different;
she seems to have an immortal air and sage-like character.
If the elder goes now,
I fear she may not yet have emerged from seclusion
and you will not be able to meet.
If you do meet her,
I beg you to mention my humble name
and say that I shall come to pay my respects again soon."
Dànzi Héshang said:
"I shall do so,
I shall do so."
Having thanked him for the tea,
he asked for the route to Huàyīn Xiàn and took his leave.
He searched until he reached the edge of Jútán,
where there was indeed a pool of clear water.
Dànzi Héshang said:
"Although it is not the season for chrysanthemums,
I must not miss this chance."
He cupped his hands and drank a few mouthfuls of water,
stripped to his bare waist,
took a bath,
put on his clothes,
and asked the way to Dān Shuǐ.
This year had an intercalary seventh month,
so the Xiàzhì was on the second day of the sixth month.
At this time, it was the twenty-first day of the fifth month.
Dànzi Héshang remembered this clearly
and stayed overnight in the grass nearby.
On the twenty-second day, it was exactly ten days before the Xiàzhì.
Dànzi Héshang came to the water's edge
and saw it was a large river.
He asked a local and learned that it was originally a connecting canal,
and only within these two or three lǐ of the river did the fish all appear red,
without any others mixed in,
which is why it was called Dān Shuǐ.
It can be seen that even aquatic creatures have their boundaries;
this is indeed a wonder of creation.
Because these cinnabar fish were few and small
and not good for eating,
there were absolutely no fishing boats upon the Dān Shuǐ.
Dànzi Héshàng went specifically to the lower reaches,
hired a small fishing boat,
and moved in to stay.
He bought plenty of wine and food to eat with the old fisherman,
and said to him:
"Tonight I must trouble you to cast a net;
when we obtain a few dānyú,
I shall teach you a magic trick to play with."
The fisherman asked:
"What kind of trick?"
Dànzi Héshàng said:
"Take the blood of these dānyú and smear it on the soles of your feet,
recite an incantation,
and with a puff of breath, walk upon the surface of the water
as if walking on dry land."
The fisherman said:
"This method is of vital use to me as a fisherman;
please, you must pass this secret formula to me."
Dànzi Héshàng said:
"If we have the fish,
it will be easy to teach you."
Carried away by the wine, the fisherman
hurried to the stern to get the net.
The fisherman’s wife saw that he was drunk
and refused to give it to him.
The two of them had a row,
but he snatched the net away,
tidied it up,
and was about to cast it down.
Dànzi Héshàng said:
"Wait a moment.
I still have an incantation;
wait a while for the fish to float to the surface on their own,
then you may take them."
The two of them chatted on the boat for a while,
and the fisherman, being drunk, unconsciously fell asleep.
Dànzi Héshàng stared intently at the water's surface;
he heard the sounds of swimming and nibbling,
but saw no red light.
He waited until late in the night,
when the moon rose from the east,
and saw that indeed all the fish were floating on the water's surface.
The dānyú reflected the moonlight,
their color like fire.
Dànzi Héshàng hurriedly woke the fisherman,
but the fisherman was still not sober from his wine;
shouting out gambling cries, he cast a net into the empty air
and caught only a few small fish.
When he cast the net again,
the fish were mostly startled and scattered.
Altogether they obtained about ten fish,
but when killed, they did not have much blood.
Dànzi Héshàng thought to himself:
"I have intended to make use of this wonder,
so I shall let the fisherman try it first.
If it is effective,
it will not be too late to come back next year and take more for use."
He told the fisherman to stretch out his feet,
smeared some fish blood on the centers of his soles,
feigned the chanting of an incantation,
blew a breath, and shouted:
"Ji!"
He told the fisherman to walk quickly onto the water.
The fisherman was honest;
he truly jumped onto the water with both feet,
and with a "plop," he sank over his head.
The fisherman’s wife saw this from the stern
and began to cry out in grievance.
Dànzi Héshàng also became flustered
and frantically threw wooden planks and bamboo poles from the boat into the water.
Fortunately, the fisherman knew how to swim;
he had entered the water at the bow
but climbed up at the stern.
The old couple clung to Dànzi Héshàng,
nagging and scolding him without end.
Dànzi Héshàng had no words to answer
and could only admit his fault,
willing to make amends.
At dawn the next day, he took a piece of silver from his bundle,
weighing about two qián,
and gave it to him to buy wine to settle his nerves;
only then did they stop and let the monk go ashore,
and the fishing boat went on its way.
Dànzi Héshàng sighed and said:
"The ancients said:
'To believe everything in books is worse than having no books.'
The magic passed down in the world is all just chasing shadows,
false and without truth.
Even the heavenly script of Bái Yún Dòng,
although I visited three times personally
before believing it to be true,
I have not yet discerned or tested it,
so I still do not know how it truly is."
Because Dànzi Héshàng was too curious
and too eager to seek the truth,
upon happening to see this passage in the book Bào Pǔ Zǐ,
he wanted to test it,
but when it was not effective,
he even began to doubt the heavenly script of Bái Yún Dòng.
A poem serves as proof:
The magic tricks of the world are never truly real,
what is recorded in books also deceives people.
Why was the foolish monk so particularly easy to convince?
The fisherman at least gained silver for his shock.
There are also those who refute this poem, saying that the words of the ancients must surely have a basis;
it is only that people do not receive the proper transmission,
so one cannot directly call it false.
A poem says:
The transformations of the world are full of wonders,
what Bào Pǔ passed down is not necessarily empty.
It is simply that the practice lacked the secret formula;
even now, the Dān Shuǐ produces dānyú.
Dànzi Héshàng saw that the weather was scorching hot,
and as he passed Qiū Lín, he saw its springs and rocks were elegant and beautiful;
his heart was delighted, and he said:
"According to what Qín Héng said,
Shènggū is in seclusion,
and I might not necessarily be able to see her.
I should not wait until I get there and be in a dilemma.
I shall stay through the sixth month
and wait for the autumn coolness before traveling; it will not be too late."
The monks in this mountain temple saw the three characters "Visiting Shènggū" on his fan;
there were some who did not know of her
and questioned him incessantly,
and there were those who knew, saying she was that old woman in Huàyīn Xiàn.
Dànzi Héshàng heard the monks recognized the name
and felt even more at ease.
The story now splits in two directions.
To speak again of Shènggūgū staying in Inspector Yáng’s West Garden;
it was in the fifth month of last year.
This year it was already the seventh month,
over a year later.
She suddenly thought:
"Mèi'ér’s whereabouts are unknown.
Tiānhòu said someone would come to find you,
but I do not know in which year or on which day.
Here, inside and outside do not communicate.
Even if Lǚ Chúnyáng or Zhāng Dàolíng appeared in the world,
who would knock on the door at midnight or the third watch
specifically to seek you out for these divine secrets and wondrous methods?
It is better to connect with outsiders
to facilitate the search."
She heard that Madame Yáng had caught a cold and was gravely ill,
and all doctors were ineffective.
Inspector Yáng was in an anxious state,
so taking this opportunity,
she advised him to hold a Wúzhē Dàhuì to pray for the Madame's health;
at that time, monks and Daoists would gather,
and she would surely hear something.
That evening, when the servant who delivered supplies arrived,
she told him the words about establishing an assembly for protection.
She further said:
"If the master is willing to set his heart to it,
I shall seek the holy water of Pǔxián Púsà this very night
to save the Madame,
and I guarantee everything will be fine."
The servant went back and related this to Inspector Yáng.
Inspector Yáng stamped his feet and said:
"I had completely forgotten Shènggūgū;
with such a fine physician, why not go seek her?"
He then told the old matron in charge of the household
to quickly go to the West Garden and seek her holy water,
and regarding the proposed ritual of protection,
she should proceed according to the regulations she set.
The old matron went to the West Garden and saw Shènggūgū,
relating everything Inspector Yáng had instructed.
How could that old fox spirit have any holy water?
She secretly went into the bedroom and urinated into a porcelain bowl,
then put on an air of mystery as she carried it out of the room
and handed it to the old matron.
The old matron took it in her hands
as if she were holding a jade cup of sweet dew,
trembling with fear that she might lose a single drop.
She asked for a box to hold it and took it back,
presenting it to Inspector Yáng.
Yáng Chūnpíng's belief was such
that he did not suspect any fraud.
He truly took it for a celestial elixir and wondrous medicine
and told the maidservants to lift the Madame’s head,
personally pouring this bowl of fox urine into her mouth.
Now, in the pharmacopoeia Yàoxìng Běn Cǎo, there is an entry for fox urine,
which primarily treats cold-heat fevers and malaria,
and it happened to coincide by chance.
By midnight, Madame Yáng suddenly felt refreshed
and asked for soup to drink.
Yáng Chūn's joy was like a gift from heaven,
and he praised Shènggūgū without ceasing.
At that time, even if there were someone with clear insight
who told him it was the foul urine of an old female fox,
how could his family ever believe it?
This was also because the fox spirit’s fate was approaching;
she naturally had such fortune,
just as all things in the world are.
A poem serves as proof:
When luck has not arrived, the truth becomes false;
when the time is right, the false becomes true.
Do not brag of your skills before others;
one still fears that fortune is not as good as another’s creation.
The next morning, the Xúnjiǎn Yáng Chūn went in person to Xīyuán.
He entered via a private back path to see Shèng Gūgū
and thanked her repeatedly.
He then asked her about the rules and procedures for the ritual of protection and prayer.
The old woman said,
“This ritual is called the Wúzhē Dàhuì.
One way is to lecture on the sutras
to clarify the mind and see one's true nature.
Another is to chant the name of the Buddha
and specially cultivate the path to the Western Pure Land.
The spiritual capacities of people in the world
are mostly dull and rarely sharp.
For now, it is better to speak of cause and effect
to persuade and transform people into chanting the name of the Buddha.
Regardless of whether they are laymen or laywomen,
living at home or in monastic life,
anyone willing to come may listen.
As the patron of this house,
you shall prepare vegetarian meals to host them.
Those who come to eat and still have hair do not count toward the total;
only the bald monks must reach the number of ten thousand.
On the day the number is full,
we shall perform a dedication of merit,
and the blessings will be immeasurable.
Not only will the Lǎo Tányuè and his wife live long,
but Guānyīn Púsà will also deliver a son,
and Wénchāng Dìjūn will fill your records with prosperity.
There will be wealth and honor for generations;
only then will my humble intent to repay you be expressed.”
As it happened, the Xúnjiǎn Yáng and his wife
got along extremely well;
they were truly like fish in water,
perfectly harmonious in every way.
Although he had a son by a concubine, he was not pleased;
he only wanted the Mistress to have a child of her own
to be fully satisfied.
Hearing these words,
how could he not be delighted?
He immediately took a calendar and consulted it.
He chose the third day of the eighth month to invite Shèng Gū to end her retreat
and the eleventh day for the ritual to begin.
He first went to report this to the Xiànyǐn,
then wrote a public notice himself
and posted it at the entrance of Xīyuán.
It read:
“Due to unrest within the family, this household
has resolved to establish a Wúzhē Dàhuì.
It will begin on the eleventh day of the eighth month
and continue for seven consecutive days.
Laymen and laywomen from all directions,
as well as monks, nuns, and Taoists who sincerely wish to come and chant the Buddha’s name,
will be provided with vegetarian meals and offerings as per custom.
If any scoundrels take this opportunity to cause a disturbance
or disrupt the Buddhist grounds,
they will surely be sent to the officials for punishment without mercy.
Special Notice.
Seventh month of the second year of Tiānxǐ,
[Day].”
It is said that after Mistress Yáng took the holy water,
her illness gradually subsided.
Although her spirit had not yet fully recovered,
she was happily out of danger.
Grateful for Shèng Gūgū’s life-saving kindness,
she made a green silk nun’s hood,
a purple patterned fine cloth monastic robe lined with white silk,
a plum-green brocade skirt with subtle patterns,
and a pair of cloud-patterned monastic shoes.
On the second day, she sent two maids following an old matron via the private back path into Xīyuán
to give them to Shèng Gūgū, saying,
“The Mistress sends her many regards
and thanks Shèng Gūgū for her life-saving grace.
Fearing she cannot come in person tomorrow when you leave retreat,
she has specially prepared this set of new clothes for worshipping Buddha.
We hope you will not decline them.”
Shèng Gūgū said,
“I disturb your household every day;
how could I let the Mistress go to such trouble again?”
Since she could not refuse,
she had to accept them.
She then said,
“When you return, give my regards to the Mistress
and tell her to be patient and take care.
When the ritual begins on the eleventh,
the Mistress will be healthy by then.
Please come early to offer incense.
On the day the merit is complete,
I will also ensure the Mistress gains a son!”
The old matron said,
“The Mistress is satisfied with everything
except for one thing.
She has had five pregnancies, both boys and girls,
but they did not survive.”
Shèng Gūgū asked,
“How old is the Mistress this year?”
The maid said,
“The Master is forty-one,
and the Mistress is two years younger;
she is thirty-nine this year.”
Shèng Gūgū said,
“This illness was also the bad luck of a year containing a nine.
Now that it has passed, there will be no more trouble.
Looking at her, she does not have the appearance of someone childless;
she is destined to have a good son,
he just arrives a bit late.”
They talked for a long while,
and after exchanging many thanks, they bid farewell and left.
On the third day,
the Xúnjiǎn Yáng went to Xīyuán himself to remove the seal
and unlock the door.
He ordered people to clean the monks' dining hall
and repair the stoves and ovens.
He then invited Shèng Gūgū into the Buddha hall
to discuss the arrangements for the ritual
and the necessary equipment.
Aside from vegetables,
tea, and water which would be prepared daily when the time came,
everything else—rice, wheat,
bean flour,
oil,
salt,
sauce,
vinegar,
as well as tables, stools,
bowls, and plates—was transported there in advance.
At this time, it caused a stir in Huáyīn County;
who wasn't talking about Yáng Lǎofó’s family feeding the monks?
There were vagrants and beggars,
as well as street-wandering women,
who usually never ate vegetarian for a single day or chanted the Buddha’s name once,
yet they also learned to wrap Táng-style caps
and don nun’s hoods,
preparing to come to the ritual on the day the meals began to get a free bite and join the crowd.
When the eleventh day arrived
and the sky just began to brighten,
people were already coming and going to watch.
One could see:
The garden gates were wide open,
and the Buddha hall was grandly opened.
Under the glass lamps,
oil candles stood in rows on the stands.
In front of the lion-shaped censers,
boxes full of fine incense sat on the altar.
On the platform for chanting Buddha's name,
a high Dharma throne was set up to sound the call,
specifically for making offerings to the Buddha.
In the monks' dining hall,
tables were arranged for placing alms bowls,
inviting only the clergy.
Chopping wood and cooking rice,
the fire-tenders shouted for axes.
Washing vegetables and boiling oil,
the cooks only complained about the lack of helpers.
It is a pity that what a rich family spends on a single day's feast
could suffice a poor household for an entire year.
After a short while,
Yáng Xúnjiǎn brought a troupe of family musicians
and went to Xīyuán to inspect the front, back, left, and right areas.
These Buddhist monks and Daoist friends,
men and women,
came in a continuous stream.
There were also idle men and children
who, though not chanting Buddha’s name or seeking vegetarian meals,
all came to watch the excitement.
These were the most numerous,
making it seem all the more like a sea of people.
One only heard from the meditation room
a total of three bell tolls.
The first toll:
Shènggūgu rose to wash and comb her hair.
The second toll:
Shènggūgu had her morning vegetarian meal and changed her clothes.
The third toll:
the musicians all began to play.
One saw painted candles all lit in the hall,
and incense smoke curling up.
Several maidservants and nurses crowded around Shènggūgu,
all neat and tidy;
wearing a suit of new clothes, she swayed forward
and offered incense and bowed before the Buddha.
Yáng Xúnjiǎn followed and bowed as well.
A troupe of wind instrument players greeted them into the front hall;
that old woman showed no humility at all
and went straight to sit on a high seat.
Yáng Xúnjiǎn called her "Master"
and prostrated himself in a bow.
Among the crowd, some had bowed to her last year,
and some were newcomers;
regardless of gender,
everyone in the Buddhist assembly
kowtowed along with him,
yet that old woman remained seated and unmoved.
It turned out that in this Buddha-chanting assembly,
the leader is called the "Buddha Head";
if they speak,
the crowd listens quietly;
if they chant Buddha's name,
the crowd joins in harmony.
Such a person becomes arrogantly self-important,
acting as if no one else were around;
there has always been this custom,
and this old woman was merely following the precedent.
After the bowing ended,
Shènggūgu ordered the men to the left and women to the right to sit in groups.
Yáng Xúnjiǎn, seeing the noisy crowd,
retreated into a nearby study
and sat for a while before going back first.
This group of old and young women,
Zhāng Yí and Lǐ Mā,
tugging and pulling at each other,
each found their companions and sat down on the right side.
However, the monks and laymen were all on the left side.
There were also those claiming to be nun-monks
who squeezed in to sit on the right,
and in the haste, one could not distinguish truth from falsehood.
There were also those who could not squeeze in
and only stood on both sides.
Other traveling monks seeking vegetarian meals were scattered outside,
either sitting or standing.
Shènggūgu struck the gavel three times sharply on the table,
ordering the virtuous friends not to make a sound
and that each should listen quietly:
"Impermanence is swift,
time does not wait;
to escape the cycle of rebirth,
hurriedly chant Buddha's name."
The gatha says:
"In the West, there is a path good for cultivation,
Āmítuófó.
I urge you to embark, but you refuse,
Nāmó Āmítuófó.
If you embark, I will assist you,
Āmítuófó.
You only need to chant Buddha's name a hundred or thousand times,
Nāmó Āmítuófó."
Every time the Buddha's name was praised
and after the crowd joined in harmony,
Shènggūgu said:
"I, this poor Daoist, have come from Xīchuān to here
and am grateful to the master of this residence for letting me stay
for over a year.
Today I emerge from seclusion to open this place of practice:
firstly, to ensure the country is well-governed and the years are bountiful,
the people are at peace and the Way is prosperous;
secondly, to ensure the safety of the household in this residence,
that their blessings and official salary may be far-reaching;
thirdly, to ensure the Bodhi hearts of the masses from all directions are awakened
so they may early discern their future path.
Today I, this poor Daoist, will not speak of any scriptures or laws,
but will rather tell the origins of the various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas
for the masses to hear.
Do you know what Guānyīn Púsà's origin is?
The gatha says:
Guānyīn the Ancient Buddha was originally a man,
Āmítuófó.
To save the women of the world, he transformed into a female body,
Nāmó Āmítuófó.
He was the third child of Emperor Miàozhuāng,
Āmítuófó.
Not enjoying glory and wealth, she endured hardship,
Nāmó Āmítuófó."
That old woman then took Guānyīn Púsà's nine sufferings and eight hardships,
and the deeds of leaving home to practice cultivation,
and elaborated on them.
She spoke for a while
and chanted for a while,
making these simple men and women's eyes turn red and their noses stuffy,
ceaselessly wiping away their tears.
When it came time for the midday vegetarian meal,
Shènggūgu finished the session, left her seat, and went to the meal.
Among the crowd, some stayed to eat the vegetarian meal,
and some went home directly.
Only the monks in the dining hall
sat down together in order,
each with a large bowl of rice,
topped with a bunch of dried vegetables,
two large pieces of tofu,
two large steamed buns,
and a string of longevity cotton thread
with thirty cash of lining money threaded on,
distributed per person in seven or eight batches.
This was the first day,
and those who came were still few,
only a little over two hundred people;
the steward recorded it clearly.
The leftover rice
was put in large baskets for those bloated Daoist priests
and mangy beggars to eat their fill in large bowls as they pleased;
the next day was the same.
The number of people increased day by day,
and the supplies could no longer keep up;
after reporting to Yáng Xúnjiǎn,
another announcement was issued
that all traveling monks
should receive their vegetarian meals and money at various nunneries and temples,
the residence having pre-allocated the funds and grain
and sent people to various places to take charge of the registration.
The dining hall in the residence
would exclusively serve Daoist friends from all directions.
He also ordered the heads of the nunneries and temples to carefully investigate:
if among the monks and Daoists there were any of extraordinary virtue
or those with magic arts that surprised the masses,
they should immediately inform the residence
for special treatment.
This was Shènggūgu's idea.
To cut the story short.
Moving on, Dànzi Héshang had stayed at Qiūlín Shān for two months,
and seeing the weather had turned cold,
he packed his bags and set off toward Yǒngxīng.
Inevitably, he begged for food by day
and sought lodging by night;
on the road, people were telling that an official's family in Huàyīn Xiàn had opened a Great Assembly Without Distinction
to urge people to chant Buddha's name.
Dànzi Héshang guessed:
"It must be Shènggū who started this,"
and hurried his pace toward it.
Within a few days,
he arrived in Huàyīn;
it was exactly on the seventeenth day of the eighth month,
and it was the seventh day of the ritual here.
Day by day, the old woman took the incarnations of Wénshū, Pǔxián, and the various Buddhas;
she recounted those as if she had seen them with her own eyes,
and who would dare to challenge her or say no?
By the time Dànzi Héshang arrived, he knew the details;
his heart was set on seeing Shènggū,
so how could he be bothered to go to the nunneries or temples to receive the standard meal and money?
Wanting to go to Xīyuán, he also feared being blocked at the gate;
after pondering for a while,
he went straight to the gate of Yáng Xúnjiǎn's residence
and sat cross-legged by the stone lion, chanting Buddha's name.
The gatekeeper, Zhāng Gōng, said:
"You, Elder, must have no ears;
this residence is currently providing meals for monks,
yet you do not go to the nunneries or temples to receive them;
why are you sitting here idly?"
Dànzi Héshang raised his fan and said:
"I, this poor monk, have no ears,
but you, old Bodhisattva, have eyes.
How can you not see the words written on this fan?
I, this poor monk, have come to seek an audience with Shènggū,
not to beg for a meal and money."
Before he had finished speaking,
two elderly women were seen walking out from the inner gate of the residence,
followed by Āntóng carrying a double-tiered food box.
Do you know who those women were?
One was the old housekeeper in charge of the rooms,
and the other was a female companion.
Why was she called a female companion?
For example, just as a scholar in a gentleman's house has a study companion,
or a man of leisure has a hanger-on,
those who keep company with female family members are called companions.
They were not female tutors,
nor were they seamstresses;
day after day they only engaged in pure conversation and idle play,
perhaps drinking tea or wine, playing chess or pitch-pot.
If they encountered one who was devout in Buddhism, they would accompany her in burning incense and making offerings;
great households often have them.
Zhāng Gōng pointed at them and said:
"Monk, if you want to see the Shènggū,
just ask these two elderly people to lead you in,
and then you may meet her."
Dànzi Héshàng hurriedly rose
and gave a greeting, saying:
"Female Bodhisattvas,
this poor monk bows in greeting.
This poor monk wishes to see the Shènggū
and bothers you to lead me in."
The old housekeeper first stopped her pace,
and the female companion and Āntóng also stopped.
The old housekeeper asked:
"Monk, where have you come from?
Why do you want to see the Shènggū?"
Dànzi Héshàng said:
"This poor monk is a native of Sìzhōu City and hails from the Yínghuī Temple.
Last year I contracted a terminal illness,
and in a dream, I was saved by that Shènggū.
I have come specifically to visit her,
not expecting her to be here.
I have heard of your esteemed residence's notice
that all traveling monks from afar should go directly to the various nunneries and temples to receive their alms
and are not allowed to disturb the Buddha Hall.
Could it be that those in the assembly are mostly female Bodhisattvas?
The gate of Buddhism is wide;
if you could take this poor monk along to kowtow once,
it would also be a karmic blessing."
The old housekeeper said:
"Generally there are also men there.
At first, the monks were all together to receive alms,
but later the crowd became too large,
so they were separated.
Now, if only one person goes,
it would be no problem."
The female companion then said:
"Fortunately the Mistress is not over there,
so there is no hindrance."
The old housekeeper said:
"The Mistress has been ill lately,
and she was also saved and cured by the Shènggū.
This ritual arena was also established for her protection and recovery.
Because the Mistress's body is not yet robust enough for her to go,
otherwise she would also be there offering incense and bowing to the Buddha.
The snacks, tea, and fruit in this food box
were ordered by the Mistress for me to bring to the Shènggū for her use."
Dànzi Héshàng, seeing that the old woman was both amiable and talkative,
then asked:
"I have heard that the Shènggū's literacy is most profound
and that she once identified some Sanskrit Golden Sutras in your esteemed residence.
Is this truly the case?"
The old housekeeper said:
"It is absolutely true.
This sutra passed through many famous monks who did not understand it,
yet she, a woman, was able to recognize every character.
For this reason, the Master respects her greatly."
While their mouths spoke,
their feet moved,
and before they knew it, they arrived at the West Garden.
They saw inside and outside the gate
a bustling coming and going
of no fewer than a thousand people.
They all said that by walking once upon the Buddhist ground,
one would not lose a human body in future lives.
Because of such heretical talk,
Buddhist gatherings gather people very easily.
The old housekeeper said:
"Monk, please stay a while in the Hall for Feeding Monks.
Wait until I have reported to the Shènggū
before I come to call you to meet her."
After walking a few steps,
she turned back and said:
"I forgot to ask what your Dharma name is?
So that I can speak of it."
Dànzi Héshàng said:
"This poor monk has no surname and no name;
since childhood, I have only been called Dànzi Héshàng."
The old housekeeper said:
"That is indeed a bald-headed nickname."
She walked inside with a smile.
On this day,
the Shènggū happened to be speaking about the karmic causes and effects of Luóbo saving his mother.
After speaking, she chanted the Buddha's name,
and after chanting, she spoke again.
By the time of the noon hour, she finished.
The old housekeeper placed the brought tea and fruits in the clean room,
which were nothing but white cakes,
oil cakes,
steamed pastries, sesame balls, as well as hazelnuts,
pine nuts,
dates,
chestnuts, and the like.
Waiting for the Shènggū to come in,
the female companion greeted her
and said:
"You have worked hard for several days;
the Mistress is very concerned.
She specially prepared some coarse snacks
and asks the Old Bodhisattva to take some."
The Shènggū offered her thanks.
The female companion pushed the Shènggū to sit in the guest seat
while she herself sat in the host seat,
also pulling the old housekeeper to sit with them.
The old housekeeper refused repeatedly,
but the Shènggū said:
"In the gate of Buddha,
there is no distinction of high or low;
just sit, it does no harm."
Only then did the old housekeeper take a small stool, place it to the side,
and sit down with bold resolve.
Attentively serving tea and fruit,
during their conversation,
they mentioned the Mistress's request for a child.
The female companion asked:
"Old Bodhisattva,
did you have a son in the past?"
The Shènggū said:
"I have a son
who left home in a distant place to be a Dàoshì."
The female companion asked:
"Why did he not become a monk
but instead became a Dàoshì?
That is not proper for a female Bodhisattva."
The Shènggū said:
"The myriad laws are originally not of two principles,
and the Three Teachings are originally of one source.
Even I myself speak of Buddhist law
as well as Daoist law."
The old housekeeper chimed in:
"Old Bodhisattva, you also speak of medical methods;
otherwise, how could you cure people's illnesses?"
The Shènggū smiled and said:
"The Mistress's illness was cured thanks to the holy water."
The old housekeeper said:
"And you can also go and save people in their dreams;
is there really such a thing?"
The Shènggū said:
"No."
The old housekeeper said:
"Just now there was a monk from Sìzhōu City;
he said you went and saved him from illness in a dream.
He came specifically to find you.
In his hand, he carries a fan made of fine bamboo strips
with the three characters 'Seeking Shènggū' written on it.
His name is also strange;
he is called something like Tuánzi Héshàng."
The female companion said:
"You're wrong;
he is called Dànzi Héshàng."
Just this "Dànzi"
struck directly into the Shènggū's heart.
That old fox spirit had the quickest of wits
and immediately told a lie:
"That monk is my brother from a previous life.
Throughout his life, he was most filial to me.
Once when I was ill, he cut a piece of lean meat from his thigh to make a broth for me to eat,
and then I recovered.
In this life, it was right for me to go and save him;
it is exactly one kindness repaying another.
Where is he now?
Lead him here to see me."
The old housekeeper agreed and went.
It is said that the person in charge of the vegetarian meals at Xī Yuán,
who originally did not serve wandering monks,
because he saw that he was brought by the head Lǎo Mó Mo and the female assistant,
provided both a meal and a gift as usual.
Dàn Zi Hé Shang finished his meal
and was leaning against the door with his eyes closed
when he heard a call:
“Dàn Zhǎng Lǎo,
your sister from a past life is calling for you.”
Dàn Zi Hé Shang turned his head and saw it was the Lǎo Mó Mo,
and asked:
“Who is this poor monk’s sister?”
The Lǎo Mó Mo then took the words spoken by Shèng Gū Gū,
recounted them once,
and said she was calling him to meet now.
Dàn Zi Hé Shang clearly knew it was a farce,
but he had to play along with the mistake,
so he straightened his monk’s robe
and followed the Lǎo Mó Mo straight into the clean chamber.
Shèng Gū Gū rose first to receive him,
and as soon as Dàn Zi Hé Shang saw her, he set down his staff and
bundle of clothes,
kowtowed, and offered his thanks.
Shèng Gū Gū hurriedly helped him up
and recognized him as her brother.
She then took a stool
and told him to sit beside the Lǎo Mó Mo.
The two of them had no connection whatsoever,
so they inevitably exchanged a few words of nonsense.
Because of this meeting,
there is a story to tell:
A clever monk who stole the dharma also discerns the celestial Kē Dǒu script;
A demonic crone in meditation suddenly gains the supernatural powers of the Dì Shà.
It will deplete some of the fortune of Yáng Xún Jiǎn,
and cost Zhào Guǎn Jiā a great deal of scheming.
Truly:
A single stalk possesses a momentum of a thousand fathoms,
A foot of water can raise waves ten thousand feet high.
To see it clearly,
listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
With a thousand schemes, the heart is like thirst,
if it is not fate, it is all in vain.
Willows planted without intent grow into shade,
but flowers planted with care do not survive.
It is said that Dàn Zi Hé Shang and Shèng Gū Gū recognized each other as flesh and blood from a past life;
how absurd!
The Lǎo Mó Mo and the female assistant, however, took it for truth
and went back to report it to Yáng Chūn and his wife.
The couple only thought it was strange,
and did not suspect it to be false.
Previously, Shèng Gū Gū had always stayed in the clean chamber
all alone.
Because a ritual ceremony was being held these few days,
Yáng Nǎi Nai assigned several maidservants and nurses
to serve there.
Dàn Zi Hé Shang saw people around
and did not dare to talk in detail,
only asking:
“What is the style of that Sanskrit Golden Sutra,
and how does the Shèng Gū recognize it?”
The old woman boasted that she had once met an extraordinary person
and had received sixteen kinds of Tiān Shū.
Whether dragon patterns or phoenix seals,
there were none she did not know.
That Sanskrit script comes from Tiān Zhú
and is one of the forms within the Buddhist gate.
Originally, the scriptures of the Dà Zàng Zhēn Jīng were all in Sanskrit,
but after Chén Xuán Zàng, Jiū Mó Luó Shí, and others translated them,
changing them into Táng characters and Táng sounds,
only then did the current versions exist.
To this day, in famous mountains and ancient temples,
there are still Sanskrit volumes handed down.
Dàn Zi Hé Shang said:
“Your humble brother also met an extraordinary person,
who passed down twenty-four pages of strange documents.
When shown to others,
not a single word could be recognized.
I have brought one page with me here;
please, Shèng Gū Gū, see what kind of language it is.”
The old woman said:
“I would like to have a look.”
Dàn Zi Hé Shang had previously pulled out one sheet and kept it separate,
so he took it out from his bundle,
unrolled it, and placed it on the table.
The old woman was greatly shocked upon seeing it,
and said falsely:
“This is yet another script from a foreign land overseas;
I do not recognize it either.”
She stole a glance at Dàn Zi Hé Shang.
The monk understood,
and hurriedly folded it up,
and wrapped it as before.
After the evening meal,
the garden keeper was seen leading a servant to the room.
From a felt bag, he took out a new cloth robe
and a new cloth lined quilt,
saying:
"The master heard that the Púsà encountered a brother from a previous life;
it is truly a wondrous destiny.
These two humble items
are sent to the Elder
as a small token of his regard.
Tomorrow morning, he will come in person to meet you."
The old woman and the monk thanked him in unison.
The servant then instructed the garden keeper to sweep out the side room within the front hall
to serve as a bedroom for this Elder.
The monk took the robe,
the quilt, and the bundle,
cradled them in his arms,
took up his staff,
and followed the servant out,
where he settled in the side room.
He thought to himself:
"That old woman gave me a look;
there must be a reason.
I intended to wait until late in the night
to slip into the quiet chamber to ask her,
but I fear being seen by the attendants,
which would not be proper."
He pondered back and forth,
hesitant and undecided.
As dusk turned into night,
he heard three strikes of a stone chime in the distance,
and gathered it was the routine for retiring in the quiet chamber.
He stepped out of the side room
and went quietly straight into the Buddhist hall.
He saw only the cold and lonely light of a glass lamp,
flickering dimly.
Behind the Buddhist hall was a row of rooms, one of which was the quiet chamber,
its two doors tightly shut.
Listening intently,
there was no sound inside;
unable to set his mind at ease,
he paced for an hour
before turning to leave.
Just then, he saw the light in the Buddhist hall
brighten from its dimness,
and Shèng Gūgū came walking out,
calling out:
"Virtuous Brother, where have you been?"
Dànzǐ Héshang was startled,
thinking that this old woman was indeed no ordinary person.
He cupped his hands and replied:
"I was just coming to seek Shèng Gūgū for guidance."
The old woman said:
"The twenty-four sheets mentioned earlier,
let me have a look at them."
Dànzǐ Héshang dared not hide them:
"In truth, they are all here."
The old woman said:
"This is the secret method of the Jiǔtiān,
lightning scripts and cloud seals.
Virtuous Brother, where did you obtain them?"
Seeing that she had spoken correctly, Dànzǐ Héshang
recounted the three attempts to seek the Dao at Báiyún Dòng,
and the divine words from his dream.
The old woman then related her dream of meeting Empress Wǔ Zétiān.
She pressed her palms together and said:
"Thank heaven and earth!
Clarity comes through Dàn,
and only today do I finally understand.
This book could not have been taken by anyone but Virtuous Brother,
and could not be recognized by anyone but me.
With nothing hidden from each other,
let us cultivate the Supreme Dao together
to fulfill this wondrous omen."
She then took down the glass lamp and placed it on the floor.
Dànzǐ Héshang went to the side room,
brought in the bundle,
opened it upon a prayer mat,
took out the twenty-four sheets of the Celestial Book,
and handed them to the old woman.
The two sat on the ground;
the old woman, from beginning to end,
looked through them once
and said:
"This book is named the Rúyì Bǎocè;
it is the seventy-two transformations of the Dìshà.
There are also thirty-six Tiāngāng transformations;
why did you not take those as well?"
Dànzǐ Héshang said:
"I rubbed copies from both walls,
but on the thirteen sheets from the left wall,
there was not a single word."
The old woman sighed:
"It is fate!
It is destiny!"
Dànzǐ Héshang asked:
"Between the Tiāngāng and the Dìshà,
what is the difference?"
The old woman said:
"Heaven is Yáng,
Earth is Yīn;
Heaven is ethereal,
Earth is substantial;
Heaven is noble,
Earth is lowly;
Heaven is simple,
Earth is complex.
If the Dìshà method is mastered,
one can command all sentient and physical things,
but it only exhausts the transformations of the human world,
and in the end, one cannot avoid being confined by heavenly fate.
If the Tiāngāng method is mastered,
the spirit wanders the celestial palaces,
one's name outranks the ranks of immortals,
and even the Shàngdì cannot control you!"
Dànzǐ Héshang asked:
"Can they both command gods and employ ghosts?"
The old woman said:
"Gods and ghosts are also sentient beings;
why could they not?"
Dànzǐ Héshang said:
"The Tiāngāng must be similar then.
Since you, Shèng Gū, have not seen it,
how do you know it is superior to the Dìshà?"
The old woman said:
"Heaven can encompass the Earth,
but Earth cannot encompass the Heaven.
Based on the sixteenth entry being the Hútiān method,
the heaven within the pot
is not the heaven above the heavens;
this is merely the essence of Dùnjiǎ and shrinking the earth.
The seventy-second entry is the method of the Dìxiān;
it does not say Tiānxiān,
but Dìxiān.
Judging by this,
its inferiority to the Tiāngāng is clear.
Even so,
its divine powers are not insignificant.
Our meeting today
is an extraordinary blessing!"
Dànzǐ Héshang said:
"Regarding the Dìshà transformations,
are these twenty-four sheets complete?"
The old woman said:
"They are complete."
Dànzǐ Héshang said:
"There was another section of text at the end
that I did not rub;
I wonder what method that was?"
The old woman said:
"The main text is finished;
there is no need to ask about the rest."
Dànzǐ Héshang asked:
"There were many large characters at the beginning;
what were those?"
The old woman said:
"Those are the talismans used for the seventy-two methods,
not words."
Dànzǐ Héshang asked:
"Before the talismans, there were several dozen lines of text,
which were not within the seventy-two entries;
what were they?"
The old woman said:
"To cultivate these methods,
one must first establish an altar and summon generals;
those are the essential opening words."
Dànzǐ Héshang had been as if in a dream,
and only now did he finally awaken.
Unconsciously, he knelt and kowtowed, saying:
"If your humble brother had not met Shèng Gū's guidance,
my three arduous efforts would have been in vain;
like uncarved jade that knows not the chisel,
or a clam that knows not the opening.
What use would it have been?
Today, please by all means take me along to cultivate together."
The old woman raised him with both hands, saying:
"This is a natural course;
no need for further entreaties!
But as for cultivation,
it takes but a sentence to say,
but it is not easy to do.
First, we must choose a location.
The site must be extremely spacious,
yet extremely secluded;
where no chickens or dogs are heard,
and human footprints are rare,
so it can be kept secret.
This allows gods and ghosts to come and go without hindrance.
Second, we must gather wealth.
During cultivation,
which spans months and years,
supplies must be complete.
This is a minor matter,
but the necessary items,
such as metals and general goods,
various medicinal ingredients,
and all sorts of utensils,
must be fully prepared without exception,
so they are convenient to use when needed.
This will cost a great deal of money and goods,"
It cannot be done without a thousand pieces of gold.
Third, there must be a unity of heart.
Suppose two people go to study the Way together,
but their hearts are not unified;
if one person gives up halfway,
the other person will also be unable to achieve anything."
When Dànzǐ Héshang heard this,
he began to shed tears and said:
"I have endured a thousand kinds of hardship
to get the Heavenly Books into my hands,
which was a stroke of ten thousand-fold good fortune.
I sought and obtained an audience with Shènggū,
not hoping to become a Heavenly Immortal,
but even to be an Earthly Immortal for a single day,
I would die with my eyes closed in peace.
According to what Shènggū says,
the third matter, unity of heart,
is not difficult.
The first matter, choosing a location,
whether entering deep mountains or remote valleys,
there are still secluded and quiet places.
However, this second matter, gathering wealth—
I am not an official
and I am not a thief;
from where will these thousand pieces of gold come?
Most likely, this is again drawing a cake to satisfy hunger
or gazing at plums to quench thirst!"
The old woman said:
"Do not be anxious yet.
As the proverb says:
'One guest does not trouble two hosts.'
Wait until the merit-making ceremony here is completed.
This host will inevitably be needed;
we must still arrange matters through Yáng Xúnjiǎn."
Dànzǐ Héshang pressed his palms together and bowed, saying:
"I rely entirely on Shènggū's guidance!"
When he straightened his back,
the old woman had already disappeared.
Dànzǐ Héshang rubbed his eyes,
looked around at the surroundings, and said:
"Could I be dreaming?"
When he went to the door of the quiet room to look,
it was as silent as before.
Recalling the many words spoken,
every sentence was orderly and logical,
and he then realized the old woman originally possessed magical arts.
If she wanted to take away these twenty-four pages of the Heavenly Books
and keep their beauty for herself alone,
what difficulty would there be?
She clearly left them in my care
to set my mind at ease.
Shènggū is truly an extraordinary person,
beyond reach."
He immediately gathered the Heavenly Books,
wrapped them as before,
and put them back into his bundle.
He then pulled up the glass lamp to hang it high,
took his bundle,
and returned to the side room to rest.
There is a poem to prove it:
A single glass lamp's light does not fade,
On a prayer mat, they subtly discuss the secrets of the Immortals.
A thousand gold pieces are still to be spent by the host,
But once the dharma is achieved, he will not bring the host along.
At dawn,
Yáng Xúnjiǎn went in person to the West Garden
to request an audience with Dànzǐ Héshang.
He asked about his background
and offered a few words of praise.
Then he went with him into the quiet room;
they met Shènggū,
and he thanked her for her seven days of labor in preaching the Dharma and chanting the Buddha's name.
He mentioned that he had hosted monks at various places,
but the total number was still not yet four thousand;
he did not know on which day it would be completed.
The old woman said:
"The moment the old benefactor makes the vow,
it is completed.
Simply take the expenses for the feast and alms of ten thousand monks
and distribute them among the various nunneries and temples;
that will fulfill the old benefactor's heart's desire.
Tomorrow is an auspicious day for the feast;
here, we shall simply perform the merit of dedicating the virtues."
Yáng Xúnjiǎn said:
"That is very good.
All the documents and petitions for the vegetarian ritual
have already been ordered for preparation at the Guānyīn Ān.
Your younger brother, the elder monk,
must surely have a pure and noble path of conduct;
I shall trouble him to preside over the proceedings."
Dànzǐ Héshang said:
"This humble monk is young
and can only follow the group and offer my services."
The old woman said:
"This poor practitioner has received the kindness of your noble house
and has no way to repay it.
Tomorrow, I shall also invite the Patriarch Pǔxián to descend to the ritual site
to pray for blessings for the old benefactor and his wife."
Now, ever since Yáng Xúnjiǎn first met Shènggū
and heard the lady say that Pǔxián Púsà had appeared,
he had longed for a glimpse.
He had also told Shènggū several times,
but she only gave verbal promises
and his wish could not be fulfilled.
Hearing now that the Bodhisattva would descend to bestow blessings,
his joy came as if from heaven.
He then said:
"If I, Yáng Chūn, could look upon the Bodhisattva's precious image,
my life's wish would be satisfied!"
At that moment, he hurriedly dispatched his personal attendants
to the Guānyīn Ān outside the West Gate to give orders for the next day's dedication
and to invite only six elder monks.
After Yáng Xúnjiǎn rose and departed,
that night in the Guānyīn Ān,
the prepared petitions,
musical instruments,
and ritual implements were sent ahead by the Daoist attendants.
Buddhist statues were already present in the garden,
so there was no need to bring more.
Shènggū only said that the room must be pure and quiet
for the Bodhisattva to be willing to come to the assembly,
so the several serving maidservants and nurses
were all sent back.
At dawn the next day,
the six elder monks invited from the Guānyīn Ān met with Dànzǐ Héshang,
making seven monks in all.
Together they beat the drums and clashed the cymbals,
chanting scriptures and proclaiming the holy names,
all according to the usual regulations for merit-making,
which need not be detailed.
Yáng Xúnjiǎn also arrived early,
wearing his formal robes to worship the Buddha.
Mrs. Yáng, newly recovered from illness,
heard that the Bodhisattva was descending
and also wished to pay her respects.
She forced herself to take a small sedan chair
and went in person to the garden to offer incense.
Seeing the quiet room tightly closed,
she already understood the situation
and did not disturb them.
Yáng Xúnjiǎn then told the old nannies and others to escort the mistress to the study to sit quietly,
while he himself moved back and forth to observe.
He waited with eager anticipation for Pǔxián Púsà to descend,
intending to invite the mistress to pay respects together.
The monks collectively offered incense three times
and partook of the vegetarian meal twice;
seeing the sunlight sink in the west
and the candles turn to ash and incense to dust,
there was not the slightest sign of news.
Looking at that quiet room, its double doors were tightly shut;
listening within,
there was absolutely no movement.
Mrs. Yáng grew impatient from waiting;
although she loved the Buddha,
after enduring the whole day,
she felt physically exhausted
and had to return first.
Yáng Chūn ordered more incense and fresh candles;
he once again donned his ritual cap and round-collared robe,
kowtowing repeatedly before the Buddha
to state his piteous plea.
When the monks saw the host acting thus,
not a single one dared to be negligent.
They continued in a bustle until the third watch,
when even Yáng Xúnjiǎn thought it would be impossible,
so he ordered the petitions and paper offerings to be burned
and prepared to bid farewell to the Buddha and end the gathering.
Everyone was burning ritual paper in the courtyard,
when suddenly a gust of wind arrived
and swept the fire and the paper up into the air.
Yáng Xúnjiǎn and the crowd looked up to watch,
and as the light of the fire dispersed,
it transformed into five-colored auspicious clouds.
Upon the clouds appeared a Púsà,
adorned with golden pearls and tassels,
with a solemn and dignified appearance,
sitting upright upon a white elephant.
Yáng Xúnjiǎn was startled;
he could not utter a single word of prayer
and hurriedly prostrated himself in worship.
Dànzǐ Héshang also took it for the truth
and followed the monks in kowtowing incessantly.
As for the other attendants and servants,
none dared not to kneel and worship.
The Púsà did not speak,
but moved slowly and steadily,
going straight to the meditation room where he descended and vanished.
It was the nineteenth day of the eighth month,
and the moonlight was still bright,
so they saw everything clearly.
Yáng Xúnjiǎn thought to himself:
"The Púsà must be conversing with Shèng Gūgū tonight.
We mortals
definitely dare not intrude into the meditation room to seek an audience;
just this appearance in the clouds
is a source of extraordinary joy."
All the monks said:
"It is entirely because your lordship’s noble household has always loved doing good
that it has moved the Shìzūn,
allowing us humble monks to also gaze upon him;
this is truly a blessing from three lifetimes."
Yáng Xúnjiǎn was modest for a while,
then kowtowed before the Buddha in thanks,
took his leave of the crowd, mounted his horse, and returned first.
The monks went to the front hall to eat the vegetarian meal,
and once the incense ritual was finished,
they packed their things and returned to the nunnery.
Dànzǐ Héshang stayed as before in the side room.
Early the next morning,
Dànzǐ Héshang returned the visit to Yáng Xúnjiǎn.
Yáng Xúnjiǎn kept him for tea
and thanked him for his efforts the previous day,
then mentioned the matter of the Púsà's manifestation,
saying:
"I told my wife about it when I got home,
and she regrets that she lacked the karmic connection
and was not in good health,
so she could not wait longer."
Dànzǐ Héshang said:
"This morning I received instructions from Shèng Gū,
who wishes to trouble the Madame to come to the garden for a meeting
to discuss something."
Yáng Xúnjiǎn said:
"I was just about to see Shèng Gū
to ask about the meeting with the Púsà last night.
Since it is so,
I will not go.
If you, Elder, stay at my humble home for a vegetarian meal
while my wife goes to Shèng Gū's place to receive instructions,
would that not be well?
Please be so kind as to sit comfortably in the eastern hall for a while, Elder,
and I will come to keep you company."
Having spoken,
he rose and went inside
to inform the Madame.
The Madame joyfully prepared herself,
and attended by her maidservants, she departed in her sedan chair.
Dànzǐ Héshang did not originally abstain from meat or alcohol,
but seeing that Yáng Xúnjiǎn’s whole household had been observing a vegetarian diet for days,
he had to pretend to eat vegetarian food.
That day in the eastern hall,
Yáng Xúnjiǎn accompanied him for a vegetarian meal,
which is not further discussed.
Now, Madame Yáng arrived at the western garden
and went straight into the meditation room.
By calculation, it had been two months since she last met Shèng Gūgū;
this meeting
brought doubled joy.
They exchanged greetings for quite some time.
Madame Yáng said:
"Last night, Shèng Gū invited the Púsà's true form to descend.
This disciple lacked the karmic connection
and could not pay respects,
which I deeply regret!"
The old woman said:
"The Patriarch Pǔxián said that Madame had already met him once."
Madame Yáng said:
"That was in the fifth month of last year,
before I had met you, Shèng Gū."
The old woman said:
"The Patriarch said that you and your husband
were originally the Jīntóng and Yùnǚ reborn.
Only because at a Buddhist assembly
you two played by striking banners and canopies against each other
were you banished to the mortal world
to become husband and wife.
Because you came from a good place,
you love the Dào in this life.
If your merits and practices are complete,
you can still ascend.
I wish to build a Pǔxián Buddhist Temple
right here
and cast a golden body for worship,
where I will reside constantly to read sutras and chant the Buddha's name,
to protect and help your couple to ascend to the heavens together,
I wonder what your thoughts are?"
Madame Yáng said:
"I am very grateful for Shèng Gū's kind intention.
My humble home’s eastern estate has a piece of vacant mountain land,
about forty or fifty mǔ.
There was originally a nunnery there in the past,
which has been abandoned for many years.
However, starting work to cast a statue
will require much money and grain;
even if my family gives alms with all our might,
I fear it will not be enough."
Shèng Gūgū said:
"It will not cost your noble household a single penny.
I have a son
named Zuǒ Chù,
who is currently a Dàoshì at the Guānwáng Miào in Jiànmén Shān.
Since childhood, he has been passed down the alchemy method,
and is skilled at turning white into yellow.
Only because he has not met a person of great fortune
has he not dared to try it lightly.
This fortune
is no ordinary fortune,
but an immortal fortune.
If he transforms gold,
the high grade,
if made into vessels for eating and drinking,
will make one’s complexion never age,
cure all illnesses,
cause a spiritual light to appear above one’s head,
and after a long time, one can ascend.
As for the lower grade,
if exchanged with others,
there is still a ten-fold profit.
Your noble household need only provide some capital,
and wait for us mother and son to transform gold for use.
Any surplus from the construction
will also have interest added to be repaid.
If more is produced,
it would also be good to give it as alms to the poor.
Yesterday, I already consulted the Patriarch about this,
and the Patriarch repeatedly exclaimed: 'Excellent!
Excellent!
Boundless merit.'
If you did not have this immortal fortune,
the Patriarch would certainly not have granted permission so lightly.
But this matter must be kept entirely secret;
if it leaks out,
not only will the task be difficult to complete,
but it will instead become unpleasant."
Madame Yáng said:
"Please allow this disciple to discuss it with my husband and report back."
Madame Yáng returned home and told her husband.
Yáng Xúnjiǎn’s heart and soul
had long been muddled by Shèng Gūgū;
seeing this fake Púsà,
he became even more utterly devoted.
Even if she wanted him to cut off his own head
and tricked him by saying it would not hurt,
he would have taken a knife to it.
Moreover, alchemy is a common occurrence for immortals;
how could he not believe it!
At that time, he left the hall,
and after giving his promise in front of Dànzǐ Héshang,
he told him to go back first to deliver the message.
He himself rode a horse to Dōngzhuāng to inspect it for a while.
Then he went straight to Xīyuán to see Shèng Gūgu
to ask about the matter of turning dross into gold and building the convent.
The old woman said:
"Other things are not difficult.
I only need a clean room
in a remote wilderness,
where neither chickens nor dogs can be heard
and human footprints are rare;
only then will the work inside be efficacious."
Yáng Xúnjiǎn said:
"I have just visited my estate to inspect it;
the grounds are quite spacious
and sufficient to establish a Daoist convent.
As there is an urgent need for a clean room,
you might as well stay at my estate.
This estate,
according to legend, was originally the villa of Guō Lìnggōng of the Táng Dynasty.
There are still several ancient cypresses,
and the house has thirty-four rooms.
Whichever few rooms Shèng Gū finds to her liking,
we can simply wall them off.
The estate servants stay in the outer section
and will have absolutely nothing to do with the interior.
I will instruct them,
and they will naturally not let anyone come to disturb you."
The old woman said:
"Wait until my son Zuǒ Chù arrives;
then we shall go together to choose a convenient place to use."
Yáng Xúnjiǎn asked:
"Where is your son?
I will send someone tonight to fetch him."
The old woman said:
"My son has a diseased leg,
and his nickname is Qué'ér.
He is at Jiànmén Shān,
which is quite far from here.
Since he has difficulty walking,
he will need a mount.
There is another thing:
in that Guān Wáng Miào,
they rely entirely on my son's bit of Daoist arts
to maintain the establishment.
If the Daoists there hear that your noble house is bringing him here,
they will certainly not let him go.
Only if I personally write a letter
and instruct the steward thus and so,
will my son be able to get away quickly."
Yáng Xúnjiǎn said with great joy:
"I trouble Shèng Gūgu to quickly write a letter;
I will send someone tomorrow morning.
The mount for the journey is no problem;
it can be hired with money."
The two took their leave.
Shèng Gūgu hurriedly wrote the letter and sealed it,
telling Dànzǐ Héshang to deliver it to Yáng Xúnjiǎn's place.
Yáng Xúnjiǎn summoned Yáng Xīng, who was experienced in running errands,
and gave him Shèng Gūgu's family letter with detailed instructions.
He set a deadline for him to depart the next day.
He gave him over twenty taels of silver for travel expenses,
and told him to hire a horse for Zuǒ Fǎshī to ride along the way,
to serve him carefully,
and to go and return quickly.
Yáng Xīng accepted his master's order
and packed through the night.
His wife, seeing the large bundle of silver,
clung to him desperately,
wanting him to make her a new cloth shirt
and buy a jade hairpin.
Yáng Xīng could not shake her off,
so he had to give her one or two pieces
weighing about five or six qián.
The next morning, he went to the pawnshop to redeem his clothes, bedding, and other items.
Everyone knew he was going on a long journey in a hurry,
and heard that he had been given ample travel money.
Those to whom he owed some small debts
all came to collect.
He had no choice but to pay them back,
which cost him a few more taels of silver.
Fearing he would run out of funds,
he lived frugally on the road,
economizing on every detail.
For the round trip,
he still hoped to save a little
to tuck into his belt as private savings.
This is common human nature,
and need not be discussed further.
There is a poem to prove it:
"Willingly spending wealth to refine elixir,
waiting only for success to transcend the nine heavens.
Gazing toward the horizon for the Lame Zuǒ,
wondering which day he will be brought back."
It is said that the Daoist Jiǎ Qīngfēng of the Guān Wáng Miào,
since parting with Mèi'ér in the second month of last year,
had been pining for her in his dreams,
as if drunk or dazed.
Every day he asked Qué'ér for news,
asking when she would return.
Qué'ér could only answer him:
"She will return after offering incense."
Afterward, he kept asking frequently,
two or three times a day.
Qué'ér also lost his patience
and said irritably:
"Master, you are quite funny!
I am here with you;
who among us is Shùnfēng'ěr
or Qiānlǐyǎn
to know about things in distant prefectures?
Her two feet are grown under her own belly;
whether she is fast or slow is up to her.
If not,
could I have pulled her here with a thin hemp rope?
You say she is my godmother and godsister,
yet as if my own kin weren't in my heart's concern.
Even if you ask from morning till night,
she over there won't know,
so isn't it all in vain!"
Daoist Jiǎ was in a bad mood,
and having been lectured like that,
he had nothing to say in reply.
Remembering that he was Mèi'ér's relative,
he didn't dare to clash with him too much
and had to be patient.
After a few days,
he unexpectedly asked again.
Qué'ér simply did not answer,
which was quite embarrassing.
As half a year and then ten months passed
without any news,
Daoist Jiǎ could not settle his mind.
Thinking she would come,
so much time had passed
that she should have returned.
Thinking she wouldn't come,
her own son was here;
surely the old woman's heart wouldn't be completely without concern.
He went privately to various places to seek divinations;
some said she was coming,
some said she wasn't.
Some said the traveler was slow,
while others said she would be fast,
even predicting the hour and day.
This made Daoist Jiǎ's heart happy for a while,
sorrowful for a while,
hopeful for a while,
pensive for a while,
guessing for a while,
and resentful for a while.
A group of frivolous young men heard this story
and composed several short lyrics
to sing amusingly:
"Last year I caught a glimpse of that beautiful face,
it hooked my soul, ah,
it hooked my soul.
Looking fixedly at her flowery face without blinking,
I was thrilled to death,
I was loved to death.
Hurrying to offer service, ah,
hurrying to offer service.
The new building is not for ordinary people to stay,
especially lent to the passionate one, ah,
especially lent to the passionate one.
Morning and evening meals I provided,
ease your mind,
and take your time on the journey.
Wait for the sky to clear, ah,
wait for the sky to clear.
The godmother acknowledged us as brother and sister,
adding a bit of affection, ah,
adding a bit of affection.
As we gradually get to know each other, the matter can be settled.
She has a heart,
I have a heart,
no need for a matchmaker, ah,
no need for a matchmaker.
Qué'ér was sent to supervise the work,
half of the progress, ah,
half of the progress.
Only the meddling old woman is an eyesore,
a thorn in the eye,
annoying to death,
she won't leave, ah,
she won't leave.
Sewing clothes with oil-green cloth,
to show a bit of sincerity, ah,
to show a bit of sincerity.
Fearing the tailor wouldn't satisfy,
deceiving the mother,
I supervised it myself.
Secretly having an affair, ah,
secretly having an affair.
Hurrying to the tower to embrace the beauty,
a moment is worth a thousand pieces of gold, ah,
a moment is worth a thousand pieces of gold."
If you are willing to fulfill it, then fulfill it quickly;
wait a little longer
until dusk.
Make a promise in the heat of the moment,
make a promise in the heat of the moment.
Walls have ears and the secret is out;
Zhāng and Yīng are torn apart,
Zhāng and Yīng are torn apart.
Tomorrow the beauty must travel far again;
seeing her out the door,
the pain is hard to bear.
Pearly tears are secretly shed,
pearly tears are secretly shed.
Burning incense, we agreed to meet again;
I look forward only to the return journey,
look forward only to the return journey.
Waiting for the time to renew old vows,
I feel grateful for the love,
and cry out once,
"O Savior from Suffering, Jiùkǔ Tiānzūn!"
"O Jiùkǔ Tiānzūn!"
Qīngmíng passes and Chóngyáng arrives;
the time has been wasted,
the time has been wasted.
Incense was burned and the vow was fulfilled; she should return.
That little enchantress,
for what reason
is there no news at all,
no news at all?
This feeling is hard to tell others;
there is only personal bitterness,
only personal bitterness.
Better to just give me a final, decisive rejection;
let me curse once,
open my heart,
and then I would be happy,
then I would be happy.
Though Guān Wáng does not concern himself with private affairs,
I still go to report to him!
I still go to report to him.
Longing by dusk and thinking by morning for this person;
words are unreliable,
talk is unreliable.
I rely entirely on the divine spirits,
rely entirely on the divine spirits.
A Daoist priest has fallen ill with lovesickness;
it is a wonder of the world,
a wonder of the world.
Delusional and obsessed, he pines for a woman.
He lacks seriousness;
his old roots are weak.
He is ashamed to face Tiānzūn,
ashamed to face Tiānzūn.
Generally, unfulfilled secret love is of two kinds:
One kind is when the man has talent and the woman beauty,
they desire and love each other,
sending letters and messages,
making a thousand promises and ten thousand appointments,
but someone comes between them to obstruct,
so they cannot be together.
Before the flowers, they long for each other;
under the moon, they pity one another.
This is called "mutual longing."
Another kind is when either the man longs for the woman,
but she does not care for him at all;
or the woman longs for the man,
but the man does not think of her at all.
Nevertheless, the heart is entangled and the mind is confused;
with short sighs and long laments,
it is a sheer waste of effort.
This is called "one-sided longing."
Today, the spirit of Mèi'ér
is nowhere to be found.
Jiǎ Qīngfēng still looks with yearning eyes, hoping she will come
to renew their vows as mandarin ducks
and fulfill the joys of clouds and rain.
Is this not one-sided longing?
This foolish Daoist priest has contracted the disease of one-sided longing
and has no heart for any business.
Sitting as if asleep,
sleeping as if drunk,
he neither chants scriptures
nor performs rituals.
Even on the first
and fifteenth of every month,
he no longer goes to tend the incense and candles before Guāndì.
The household provisions
are left entirely to Mièdào to manage haphazardly.
After Mièdào had managed things for a few days,
he began to act like an arrogant master
and gradually grew discordant with the Quézi.
This foolish priest could not care less about it.
After more than a year,
he gradually felt pain in his body,
heat in his bones,
his flesh became lean,
and his face turned yellow;
it developed into a consumptive illness.
Originally, this kind of illness has no pain or itch,
it is neither death nor life,
and it is the most difficult way to pass the days.
At the Fùjiāng ferry, there was a Jìngzhēn Nunnery.
The old nun was Daoist Jiǎ's aunt.
Hearing that her nephew was ill,
she came specifically to the temple to see him,
bringing an extremely ugly young female acolyte to serve him.
Jiǎ's lustful heart burned like fire,
so he flirted with her again,
and within a few days they were entangled.
When the aunt found out, she was furious
and gave her nephew a scolding.
As she left, she said
she vowed never to come to the temple again.
Do not speak of the foolish priest's illness,
let us only describe the Quézi.
At first,
the priest favored him with good wine and good food,
and he ate happily.
Later, things gradually grew lax.
By the time the priest fell ill with consumption,
there was no one at all to look after him.
When there was some food or drink,
it was first enjoyed in secret by Mièdào.
Even when something reached his mouth,
it was leftover plates and scrap water,
truly insufficient.
Moreover, there was a lack of this and a shortage of that;
even several of the Quézi's clothes
were pawned for money and rice,
and who was there to redeem them?
Seeing the situation was bad,
the Quézi could not help but think of his mother.
He said:
"Mother!
Three of us left home,
and only because my legs were inconvenient
was I temporarily left here.
You said once there was a place to settle,
you would send a letter to call for me.
Now it has been a year and a half;
surely you aren't still wandering on the road?
Here, I have no tea and no rice,
no proper meals,
and no one to care for my pain;
how could you know!
If my hands and feet were functional,
I would run out of the temple gates
and become a wandering priest
to feed myself.
Why must I be caught in between,
in this dilemma?
Truly, people are not good for a thousand days,
and flowers are not red for a hundred.
And they say if human hearts remained as they were when first they met,
in the end, there would be no heart of resentment.
Let us speak no more of the Quézi's complaints,
but rather of Yáng Xīng, who followed his master's orders.
On the road, he disguised himself as an official messenger delivering a letter.
Resting by night and traveling by day,
in no time he arrived at Jiànmén Shān.
Taking the path, he went straight to the temple of Guān Wáng,
pretending to be thirsty
and asking the temple for some water to drink.
Mièdào saw first that he was an official messenger
who could not be neglected.
Since Daoist Jiǎ was bedridden with illness,
he hurriedly scooped a bowl of rice water,
placed it on a tray,
and told the little monk with the scabbed head to hold it,
while urging the Quézi to go out and keep him company.
In this world, only a lame person is the easiest to recognize,
and Yáng Xīng knew it as soon as he saw him.
After bowing, the Quézi asked:
"Where does the honorable official come from?"
Yáng Xīng said:
