"I have been sent on a mission from Huázhōu."
The Quézi presented the rice water and said:
"This desolate mountain lacks tea;
I fear this is not fit to drink."
Yáng Xīng said:
"It is enough to quench my thirst!"
The little scab-headed monk took the bowl back inside.
Yáng Xīng then stood up,
and the Quézi saw him out of the temple gates.
Yáng Xīng said:
"Master, might your surname be Zuǒ?"
The Quézi said:
"It is indeed!"
Yáng Xīng said:
"Let us step aside to speak."
The Quézi stood with him outside the temple gates,
about a hundred paces away.
Yáng Xīng said:
"I am sent from the household of Master Yáng the Inspector of Huáyīn County, Huázhōu.
I have here a letter from your mother, Shènggūgū,
telling you, Master, to travel with me this very night;
there must be no delay."
When the Quézi took the letter and opened it to look,
there were indeed four lines of poetry.
The poem said:
I am staying at the Yáng residence in Huáyīn.
The master is worthy and wise, truly hard to encounter.
He wants you to cultivate the Great Dào Elixir with us.
Set out on your journey with great speed and do not look back.
Quězi recognized the old woman's handwriting
and was overjoyed beyond expectations.
He was about to turn around to pack his bundles,
but Yáng Xīng said:
"No need for that!
Whatever items you lack,
just ask me.
Even if things are not perfectly prepared on the road,
once we reach the house, everything will be there."
Quězi said:
"It is a long way to Huázhōu,
and I have difficulty walking.
If I cannot keep up with you,
what should I do?"
Yáng Xīng said:
"Once we reach Jiànmén Shān,
we can hire mules and horses along the road,
so there is no need to trouble your esteemed feet."
That Quězi thought of the temple;
Miè Dào was detestable,
and Jiǎ Qīngfēng had fallen ill,
so he had no sentimental attachments.
Regarding when they first met,
the three of them, mother and sons, had received his kindness.
Now that his mother's letter had arrived,
he ought to inform him.
However, it was only a single letter
and he had not sent a single thing to thank him;
how could he bring it up?
It would be better not to see him at all.
As for the few pieces of winter and summer clothing,
he had already picked out the good ones and put them in the pawnshop.
That man called himself "this humble one,"
so the master of the house must have ordered him to come and escort me.
Why should I delay further?
He let out a sigh
and then said:
"Since my mother has told me to set out with all speed,
I shall leave right now.
I fear if my masters find out,
it will cause another delay."
Thereupon, Yáng Xīng assisted Quězi as they hurried toward Jiànmén Shān.
Along the way, whether by mule or horse,
they were hired for Quězi to ride.
Yáng Xīng was accustomed to walking;
if they went fast, he followed fast;
if they went slow, he followed slow.
They proceeded along the road toward Huázhōu.
The story splits into two paths.
To speak again of Miè Dào,
on this day he did not see Quězi come in to eat,
which he found strange.
He waited until evening,
but he still did not return,
so he had to inform Dàoshì Jiǎ.
Dàoshì Jiǎ asked:
"When did he leave?"
Miè Dào said:
"In the morning, a messenger arrived asking for soup and water.
He saw him out the door
and has not been seen back since."
Dàoshì Jiǎ said:
"That courier,
where did he come from?"
Xiǎo Làlì, who was nearby, replied:
"I was bringing out the tray with rice soup
and heard him say one thing,
that it seemed he was from Huázhōu."
When Dàoshì Jiǎ heard the two words "Huázhōu,"
his infatuation was stirred once again,
and he said:
"Huáyīn is exactly where Huà Shān of the Western Peak is located.
Godmother and Sister are currently there offering incense;
how could he not tell me
so I could ask for news!"
Miè Dào laughed and said:
"Huázhōu is a large prefecture and a large city,
not some tiny three-house village
or a one-legged town.
When two women go to the mountain to offer incense,
how would that courier have paid them any heed!"
Dàoshì Jiǎ, easily irritated in his illness,
cursed him:
"You son of a dog!
What do you know?
As the saying goes, 'Two leaves of duckweed return to the great sea;
where in life do people not meet again?'
The mother and daughter are currently offering incense in Huáyīn Xiàn.
You say the courier couldn't have met them,
but this Quězi is in a remote place like Jiànmén Shān,
so how did he come to meet the courier?
Now that this Quězi has gone off with the courier,
there must have been some news that arrived.
Either his mother is nearby and called for him,
or they are in another place and sent for Quězi instead;
either way, it is not certain.
You didn't bother to question him
and instead say such useless things.
Are you not just farting?"
Panicked, Xiǎo Làlì was the first to run out of the room.
Miè Dào, seeing him becoming fierce,
intentionally said:
"Master is right.
I will go look for that courier tomorrow to question him, then we will know."
Dàoshì Jiǎ said:
"When he was at the door, you kept your bird-beak shut and didn't ask;
now that he’s gone,
where will you find him?"
Miè Dào said:
"As Master said, 'Where in life do people not meet again?'"
Dàoshì Jiǎ, seeing him talk back,
was so angry his face turned purple.
He lifted his head from the bed,
wanting to pull Miè Dào over to beat him,
but suddenly he felt dizzy
and fell back down as before.
Miè Dào grumbled and muttered
as he walked out.
Once outside, he scolded Xiǎo Làlì for being talkative
and gave him several raps on the head.
Xiǎo Làlì whimpered and cried incessantly.
Dàoshì Jiǎ was extremely infuriated hearing this,
but he only regretted his dizziness and physical weakness,
as he was unable to crawl or move.
By dusk,
no one even came to light a lamp.
It was then the eighteenth day of the ninth month;
the moon rose early.
Dàoshì Jiǎ, holding his breath in anger,
lay silently on the bed.
Seeing the moon rising over the window lattice,
a myriad of thoughts
and a thousand kinds of sorrow filled him.
He wondered where at this moment
Sister Mèi'ér might be.
Only this round, bright moon could see her clearly wherever she was.
"How I wish Cháng'é would conveniently send me a message."
Just as he was lost in wild thoughts,
he suddenly saw Xiǎo Làlì run in to report:
"Master Quě is back!
He is outside the door with Godmother and the others, three in all."
Hearing this, Dàoshì Jiǎ
turned his bubbling anger into a sky full of joy
and hurriedly asked them to be invited in.
He tried to struggle out of bed,
but feeling heavy-headed and light-footed,
he lay back down again.
He only heard the hubbub of voices
as the three of them entered the room.
The old woman asked about the cause of his illness
and spoke a few words of comfort,
then hurriedly went back out, saying:
"Wait until this old body has finished packing the luggage,
then I will return to talk."
Quězi also ran out.
Only Hú Mèi'ér remained, sitting on the edge of the bed with a beaming smile,
saying:
"Brother, we have been apart for a long time;
I did not know you had this honorable illness."
Dàoshì Jiǎ, seeing there was no one around,
poured out his heart, saying:
"This illness was caused by you, my worthy sister.
Now that I see you,
I would have no regrets even in death."
He reached out his hand to hook around Mèi'ér’s neck.
Mèi'ér lowered her head
and made a pouting face.
Dàoshì Jiǎ had already woken up;
it turned out to be a dream.
Opening his eyes to look,
he saw a silent, empty room,
with only the moon's soul across half the window,
and a chill invading the air.
Dàoshì Jiǎ's eyes were filled with desolation;
he let out a sigh,
and unconsciously, tears fell like rain.
It is just as the saying goes:
"The same moon as always before the window,
yet it shines specifically on the sorrowful, making their sorrow grow."
I do not know what will become of Dàoshì Jiǎ's life;
let us listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
In the ancient cave, the heavenly book records no years;
who will pass on these half-walls of text to others?
Once the thunder-script is discerned,
when cultivation is complete, one intends to become a superior immortal.
It is said that Jiǎ Daòshì kept Quézi by his side,
hoping to anchor the old woman’s heart,
as this was the crucial link for reuniting with Mèier.
For reasons unknown, Quézi suddenly departed;
Jiǎ’s heart was both vexed and pained.
With his spirit in disarray,
he fell into this delusional dream.
Upon waking, he sighed and lamented,
spending a night in bitter sorrow.
The next day, when he asked about Quézi, his clothes and bedding were all still there;
thinking he had not gone far,
he sent people to search in all directions.
Someone reported seeing Quézi hiring a beast of burden at the foot of Jiànmén Shān,
and that a man from afar
had gone away with him.
From then on, Jiǎ’s anxiety grew,
his illness worsened,
and every night he dreamed of that little vixen coming to haunt him.
After several such emissions,
he developed the ailment of chronic spermatorrhea.
During the day, his internal fire would flare up unexpectedly,
and the essence would leak out from below.
Thereafter, whenever he closed his eyes, he saw Mèier;
eventually, he became as thin as a stick of wood.
Knowing he would not recover,
he sighed:
"Mèier,
oh, between me and you!
If we cannot be companions playing the flute in this life,
we shall be husband and wife in the next."
He spoke to Miē Daò and Xiǎo Làlì;
his words were all the bleak talk of a final farewell.
The Lǎo Daòshì, who usually never left his room,
also came to visit him several times.
The illness had reached a critical state,
and preparations for his funeral were unavoidable.
Lingering until the onset of spring,
the oil was dry and the fire extinguished;
alas, he passed away.
He was exactly twenty-seven years old,
truly a case of "coveting flowers and not reaching thirty."
An ancient writer once penned a short lyric
titled "Qīng Jiāng Yǐn,"
which describes it perfectly:
All manner of illnesses can be cured,
but never succumb to lovesickness.
Suddenly, pain pierces the heart;
all day long, the soul is absent,
and only at the final breath does one realize it was a karmic debt of grievance.
Even as this foolish Daoist was dying,
his heart was still firmly tied to the little vixen;
thus, his spirit did not dissipate.
In the next life, Mèier was reborn into the Hú family
and named Yǒng'er;
the Daoist was reborn into the Jiāo family
and named Hānggē.
Although they did not grow old together,
it could be considered a marriage of youth;
in the Register of Marriages,
the old debt was cleared.
But this is a later story and will not be discussed further.
Meanwhile, Quézi and Yáng Xīng hurried along their way,
eating when hungry and drinking when thirsty,
resting at night and traveling at dawn.
In a few days, they arrived in Huáyīn Xiàn.
First, they passed by the gate of Yáng the Inspector;
Yáng Xīng and Quézi entered the residence to report to the master.
Yáng Chūn hurriedly came out to meet them.
Amidst their greetings,
Yáng Chūn spoke a few words about alchemy to test Quézi.
Unexpectedly, Quézi understood nothing at all;
he only stared with wide eyes
and did not answer a word.
Yáng Chūn only suspected that Quézi was unwilling to discuss the matter lightly
and did not press him.
After serving tea,
Yáng Chūn ordered Yáng Xīng to take Quézi to Xī Yuán to meet Shèng Gūgū.
When Quézi entered the garden gate,
he first met Dànzi Héshàng
and thought to himself:
"My mother is truly indecent;
how could she take in a wild monk to live with her?
Can it be that at her age,
she still needs a monk to rouse her?"
Upon entering the quiet chamber and seeing the old woman,
he immediately asked:
"Why is my sister Mèier not living here?
And who is that wild monk in the front?"
The old woman said:
"It is a long story!
First, while hiding from the wind in the forest,
I dreamed of Zétiān Niángniáng,
and it was like this and that;
when I woke up, Mèier was gone.
Later, I met Dànzi Héshàng,
which precisely matched the words in the dream about 'meeting an egg and gaining enlightenment.'
He brought with him a Heavenly Book
that only I can recognize;
it contains the secret methods of the Nine Heavens.
To cultivate them,
one needs a thousand pieces of gold.
I pretended to want to build a monastery for the Ancestral Teacher Pǔxián,
saying my son Zuǒ Chù can transmute base metals into gold and silver.
Using these words,
I enticed some riches out of him,
and took the opportunity to bring you here
so we can practice together.
Isn't that wonderful?"
Quézi laughed and said:
"No wonder when Yáng the Inspector saw me,
he immediately talked about furnaces and fire.
It was lucky I didn't answer;
otherwise,
wouldn't the ruse have been exposed?"
While they were chatting,
Yáng the Inspector came to pay his respects to Master Quézi.
He presented a set of new clothes
and a set of bedding.
He then invited the mother and son
to go to Dōng Zhuāng tomorrow to look at a house and land.
The old woman said:
"To purchase medicinal ingredients and handle various errands,
I must rely on my brother Dànzi.
If we use someone else,
I fear they might not be tight-lipped.
He must also make the trip tomorrow."
Yáng Chūn agreed and left.
Shortly after,
people brought the evening meal
and set out a table of vegetarian dishes.
Quézi whispered to the old woman:
"Mother,
how can we get some meat and wine to eat? That would be better."
The old woman said:
"This is the famous household of Old Buddha Yáng;
meat and wine are never heard of here.
You must not indulge your palate;
when the cultivation begins tomorrow,
you won't be allowed to touch meat for a whole year!"
Quézi was stunned
and stuck out his tongue in surprise.
Nothing more happened that night.
After breakfast the next day,
Yáng the Inspector ordered a small sedan chair,
two horses,
to go to Xī Yuán to receive the three of them.
He went ahead to Dōng Zhuāng to wait.
The old woman rode in the sedan chair in front,
while the monk and the Daoist followed on horseback.
Led by the steward,
they hurried towards Dōng Zhuāng.
Looking around as they traveled,
it was indeed a fine place.
One could see:
Fields stretched to the horizon,
and trees covered the hills.
Fields stretched to the horizon,
where farmers lived in scattered dwellings.
Trees covered the hills,
where woodcutters walked in lines.
In a mountain hollow,
there was a broad stretch of idle land,
which had once been a ritual site for Buddhist nuns.
On a high elevation,
stood a large, exquisite manor house,
no longer the old estate of Guō Lìnggōng.
If one were to build a Buddhist convent or Daoist temple here,
though it might have a thousand gates and ten thousand windows,
one would fear it might not match the grandeur of the legendary architecture.
If used as a lair for ghosts or a shrine for spirits,
even if one lived there for half a year or a full year,
truly, not even the crowing of a cock or the barking of a dog would be heard.
Most pleasing is that the master loves to host guests,
allowing the birds in the deep forest to nest in peace.
The old woman saw Yáng Xúnjiǎn and hurriedly thanked him:
"Since you, the old benefactor, have such faith,
it is all due to causes from a past life."
Yáng Chūn said:
"Did you see that piece of land on the way here?"
The old woman said:
"I have seen it,
and I am very satisfied.
Outside this noble villa,
the landscape is also quite excellent.
I just don't know what the buildings inside are like?"
Yáng Chūn said:
"Let us go together and have a look!"
He then led the group,
winding and turning,
and walked through every part.
It turned out that although it was called a villa manor,
it was built with great style.
Inside the gate wall was a large open field,
a place for stacking firewood and grain.
Warehouses were set up on both sides,
and in the center were three large open halls,
with several miscellaneous rooms flanking them on the left and right.
The rooms on the left were the residence of the manor manager.
Behind the hall, a very large fish pond was dug
to prevent fires.
Looking to the right,
there were all sorts of pavilions, terraces, flowers, and trees.
Three ancient cypress trees slanted and were half-rotted,
supported by vermilion wooden frames.
On the left was a stretch of winding corridor;
at the end of the corridor,
there was another side gate.
After entering the side gate,
there were another three and a half rooms.
Inside were study rooms and multi-storied buildings,
with medicine stoves and tea hearths,
all fully equipped.
Every year when Yáng Xúnjiǎn collected rent and settled accounts,
he would come here to stay for ten days or half a month.
Therefore, it was kept neat and tidy.
If the side gate were closed,
it clearly became a separate residential compound.
Yáng Chūn said:
"Could these few humble rooms
serve as a temporary residence?"
The old woman said:
"How could such refined rooms be necessary?
It is too much of a blessing, too much!"
She also said:
"Let us stay here starting tonight!
Better to remain still than to move.
Only regarding the principal silver we are to borrow,
I hope you will please attend to it quickly."
Yáng Chūn said:
"I will gather it and send it within three days.
The daily supplies for the three of you
can be drawn from this small manor.
I'm only afraid that for cooking,
you might still need a young servant."
The old woman said:
"That is not needed at all!"
Before departing, Yáng Xúnjiǎn
called over the manor manager, Lǎo Wáng, to give instructions:
"All supplies
must be provided by you;
they must be complete.
Just open the accounts for me to see every month."
He also ordered that the two walls behind the open hall be closed off
and sealed with paper strips.
"When sending supplies,
go through the winding corridor from Lǎo Wáng's house,
and do not allow others to move about."
He then gave the keys to the side gate to Shènggū,
for her to open and close as she pleased.
Thereupon, he took several manor guests
to the West Garden to fetch the luggage of the three people.
The old woman moved into the house
and was thoroughly satisfied.
After a short while,
the garden caretaker and several manor guests
delivered the luggage.
Dànzǐ Héshang’s bundle contained the Heavenly Book;
he never let it leave him, whether walking or sitting,
and had already kept it on his person.
Only the bedding and staffs
were in the side room,
and these were all brought together.
At sunset,
the old woman told Dànzǐ Héshang to lock the side door,
and the three of them gathered to consult.
Dànzǐ Héshang was experienced in wandering,
so for all purchasing and necessary items,
he was the one to run errands.
Zuǒ Chù's leg was inconvenient,
so he was specifically in charge of guarding the ritual altar,
burning incense and lighting candles,
as well as simmering and cooking the three daily meals and tea.
The old woman focused on teaching them how to draw talismans and chant incantations,
and to practice cultivation at the appointed times.
The preliminary assignments were completed.
As for things like firewood and rice,
they were drawn monthly from Lǎo Wáng's place,
to avoid daily disturbances.
Early the next morning,
Yáng Nǎinai sent the senior maid in charge of the household to take a small sedan chair to the East Manor specifically to see Shènggū.
She knocked on the door, came in, and said:
"Nǎinai heard that your religious kin are living together,
and feared it might be inconvenient,
so she felt it inappropriate to come herself.
She told me to convey her many regards!"
The old woman said:
"I am very grateful for Nǎinai's concern!"
The senior maid looked at the Lame One and smiled, saying:
"Is this person your son, the Lame Dharma Master?
Since Shènggū is so well-acquainted with Pǔxián Púsà,
why not entreat the Bodhisattva to command the Heavenly Physician to heal this leg?"
The old woman said:
"Each person has their own form,
and it cannot be changed.
For instance, Guānshìyīn has a thousand hands and a thousand eyes;
when has she ever disliked them and removed a few?
Mílè Zǔshī has a large belly
that hangs down to his knees;
when has he ever said it was inconvenient and taken medicine to dissolve it?"
The senior maid said:
"Shènggū is right."
She added:
"There is a small official's chest in the sedan chair;
I must trouble Master Dàn to fetch it."
Dànzǐ Héshang fetched it
and placed it on the table.
It was a gold-painted box,
locked with a small white-copper lock.
The senior maid, acting mysteriously, said:
"I have some private words to say;
I ask the two masters to step away for a moment!"
From her sleeve, she pulled out an old handkerchief the color of pig's liver,
with a small key tied to the corner,
and opened the lock.
She took several packages of things from the box
and placed them in a pile.
She said:
"This silver totals two hundred taels.
It is Nǎinai's private money,
and she told me to give it to Shènggū to help with miscellaneous expenses.
Do not mention this in front of others."
The old woman expressed her thanks
and stored it inside a desk drawer.
The senior maid cautioned her again:
"It would be best to put it in a safe place!"
The old woman said:
"It is no matter."
The senior maid said:
"I am just being careful;
don't blame me for speaking too much."
She added:
"In the future, when Shènggū sees Pǔxián Púsà,
please also register my name for me.
I am Sūn Shì,
and I have observed a vegetarian fast for over twenty years!"
The old woman said:
"Certainly!
Certainly!"
The senior maid said:
"I am only here because my husband died
and my children are not filial,
so I spend my days alone by Nǎinai's side.
In that next life, I only seek to have good children—that would be enough!"
Having finished speaking,
she locked the empty box as before.
The old woman called the Lame One to escort her out,
and she boarded the sedan chair and left.
The Lame One locked the side gate and came back in;
having already known Nǎinai sent silver,
he excitedly wanted to buy this and that.
The old woman said:
"Nǎinai sent this secretly;
for now, be slow to act.
Wait until what Yáng Xúnjiǎn sends arrives,
and see how much or how little there is,
before making any further arrangements."
There is a poem to prove it:
Women have always been quite stingy,
and many good deeds are wasted because of it.
Yet they are greedy for blessings in the name of the Buddha,
willing to give their private wealth to a Daoist woman.
It is said that Dànzi Héshang saw that things had happened coincidentally,
and his heart was filled with joy.
He then wanted to take the twenty-four sheets of the heavenly book
and ask Shènggū to translate and explain them.
The old woman said:
"Now that the three of us are cultivating together in one place,
you cannot hide things from me,
and I cannot hide things from you.
On these large sheets,
it is not very convenient to read the characters.
You should take plain paper and bind it into a book the size of a palm;
I shall translate the text into the Tángyīn,
and you, Worthy Brother, shall transcribe it carefully.
This way, when it comes time to perform the magic,
it will be easy to flip through."
Dànzi Héshang said:
"That would be most wonderful.
Tell me, how much paper, ink, brushes, and inkstones
will be needed in total?
I will buy them all at once;
it would do no harm to finish this small task today."
The old woman said:
"Forty-nine sheets of good paper for each person.
We need ten brushes,
five sticks of ink,
two small inkstones,
and three liǎng of cinnabar.
For three people, we will need triple that amount.
As for transcribing the small book,
it will not consume much paper;
adding five more sheets,
one brush,
and one stick of ink
will be sufficient."
When the old woman was at Xīyuán,
some people had originally given her some money;
she took it and told Dànzi Héshang to go and procure these things.
Because this was previously arranged,
Quétzi did not dare to interfere.
Within a short time,
Dànzi Héshang had bought all the four treasures of the study.
The old woman took the five extra sheets of paper and cut them,
each sheet making more than twenty pages.
Except for the talisman shapes which were traced as they were,
all other text was translated into Tángyīn
and written in tiny "fly-head" characters.
As Dànzi Héshang wrote one line,
he understood one line,
and rejoiced for one line.
It is truly said: although he had not yet obtained divine powers to use,
he was no longer a man of divided mind.
In one day and one night,
all was finished.
The old woman proofread it once;
there was not a single mistake.
At dawn on the third day,
they took the original twenty-four sheets
and burned them to ashes with fire.
For this secret version of the heavenly book
can have only one copy and not a second.
There was also the fear that if it remained in the human world,
it might lead to desecration,
and the guilt would fall upon them.
After breakfast,
Yáng Xúnjiǎn arrived at Dōngzhuāng.
He brought a leather chest of silver,
amounting to a full thousand pieces of gold,
and handed it to the old woman for safekeeping.
He said:
"When the gold is produced,
exchange it for silver and produce more again;
then it will be infinite!"
The old woman said:
"Exactly so!"
Yáng Chūn said again:
"Now that I am parting from Shènggū,
I dare not ask to see you again!
But I wonder approximately on which day the elixir will be completed?"
The old woman said it depends on the timing of fate.
At most a year,
at least half a year,
and then there will certainly be good news in reply.
Even if it is slow,
do not be impatient.
Yáng Xúnjiǎn took his leave.
The old woman instructed Dànzi Héshang
to first take earth from the five directions.
Use this manor to temporarily represent the center,
and for the others—East, South, West, and North—
all should be taken from ten li away.
Each should be placed in a cloth bag.
Other items for use in the world:
precious ones like gold and pearls,
cheap ones like wood and stone,
edible ones like beans and wheat,
combustible ones like coal and charcoal,
coarse ones like jars and vats,
fine ones like needles and thread,
pure ones like tea and wine,
and miscellaneous ones like medicinal ingredients;
every kind must be fully prepared.
While Dànzi Héshang was procuring these things,
the old woman cleaned the ground floor to set up an altar.
First, they observed fasting and bathing.
Choosing an auspicious hour on a Liùjiǎ day,
they positioned the cloth bags of earth according to the five directions,
each about a foot apart.
All around, they built up new bricks
to a height of about one foot and five inches,
and filled the empty spaces with five types of grain.
Above, three bright lamps were placed,
burning day and night without ceasing.
Outside, a divine canopy made of yellow cloth was used to cover it.
In front, an incense altar was set up,
where Jiǎmǎ and Cloud Cranes were enshrined,
and three kinds of offerings—tea, wine, and fruit—were set out daily.
Every morning, they recited the Mouth Purifying Incantation once,
the Body Purifying Incantation once,
the Dharma-realm Purifying Incantation once,
the Earth-pacifying Incantation once,
and the Soul-settling Incantation three times;
after that, they performed the magic according to the method.
These are standard procedures
and need not be described in detail.
It is said that on the day after the altar was established,
first the paper, ink, brushes, inkstones, and other items required by each person
were arranged beneath the Liù Jiǎ altar.
The old woman began;
her feet trod upon the characters Kuí and Gāng,
her left hand formed the Thunder Seal,
and her right hand formed the Sword Gesture.
She took a breath of the life-giving essence from the east,
recited the Spirit-Connecting Incantation once,
and burned one talisman.
Dànzǐ Héshang and Zuǒ Chù both followed the old woman's actions.
Although they recited the incantations
and burned the talismans in the same way,
the forms of these talismans had all been drawn by the old woman’s hand.
After forty-nine days in this manner,
the paper,
ink,
brushes,
and inkstones all became spiritually charged;
then they discussed summoning the generals.
Dànzǐ Héshang wanted to write the talismans himself.
The old woman said:
“Writing talismans is the most difficult task.
One must use qì to encompass the form
and use the form to encompass the qì.
Suppose a talisman has a certain function;
then you must perform a corresponding visualization.
If you wish to raise clouds,
then visualize a bit of yīn energy
arising from the dāntián,
gradually feeling your entire body filled and obstructed by cloud-like essence,
billowing out from your seven orifices
and permeating heaven and earth.
If you wish to summon thunder,
then visualize a point of yáng energy
arising from the dāntián,
gradually feeling your whole body swirling with thunderous fire,
bursting forth from your seven orifices
and shaking heaven and earth.
When the visualization is complete,
quickly channel this qì into the ink
and complete it in a single stroke.
This is what is called joining spirit with spirit
and joining qì with qì.
It is precisely about taking my own spirit and qì
and connecting them with heaven and earth;
only then will this talisman be effective.
At first, it takes effort to focus and gather,
but once the skill is mastered through practice,
the spirit gathers as soon as you close your eyes,
and even a talisman drawn in the air will be effective.
This is the marvelous secret for penetrating heaven and earth.
If you merely trace the shape of the talisman,
your own spirit and qì will first become scattered,
so how could you move the gods and ghosts?
As the proverb says:
‘If the written talisman is not effective,
it will be laughed at by ghosts;
if the inscribed talisman is not spiritual,
it will instead startle the gods.’
I will now first write for you to see:
where to start,
how to structure it,
and how to concentrate the spirit and circulate the qì.
Once you have observed until it is thoroughly familiar,
then you may take up the brush.
If one method is mastered,
ten thousand methods are mastered;
if one method is not mastered,
then ten thousand methods will not be mastered at all.
You must never be careless or flighty,
lest you ruin the opportunity yourself.”
Dànzǐ Héshang and Quézi
responded with repeated "yeses"
and asked in unison:
“The method of writing talismans
we have already received your instruction on.
Now we wish to summon the generals,
but we do not know if they will be able to come?
If they do come,
how should they be treated?”
The old woman said:
“I was just about to explain this to you in detail.
Only when there are internal generals
can one summon external generals.
Dèng,
Xīn,
Zhāng,
Táo,
Gǒu,
Bì,
Mǎ,
Zhào,
Wēn,
and Guān
are the ten external generals.
The eyes,
ears,
nose,
tongue,
intent,
heart,
liver,
lungs,
spleen,
and kidneys
are the ten internal generals.
First, refine your own ten internal generals
until they are unified and not in disorder,
preserving the spirit and stabilizing the qì,
as if the external generals are solemnly lined up before you.
Then they will respond as soon as they are called
and obey as soon as they are commanded.
At first, they may appear half-bodied,
and later appear in full.
If you see their divine countenances are fierce and evil,
you must not be afraid;
if they are ugly and grotesque,
you must not laugh.
You must respect them like parents,
be close to them like friends,
and employ them like servants.
If you do otherwise,
you will surely provoke the gods’ wrath.
Furthermore, whenever you wish to summon a general,
you must first predetermine the task to be performed
and the questions to be asked.
If they are summoned for no use,
the generals will not consider you reliable,
and thereafter they will not come even if summoned.”
The two, the monk and the Daoist,
had never seen the generals before;
having first heard these words,
they were clearly like elementary students first entering a schoolroom,
still not knowing what the teacher’s rules were.
Their bellies were full of trembling and apprehension,
and they were shivering to their very bones.
Each went to sit in devout meditation,
concentrating their spirit and nurturing their qì.
When it came time for the old woman to write the talismans,
she first called the two of them to look at the patterns.
Dànzǐ Héshang was clever after all,
and he learned it after seeing it once.
The cripple also constantly traced the patterns in the air with his hand.
It was also because their destiny had arrived;
though he had always been lazy,
he became diligent and industrious at this point.
Because he applied himself so intensely,
he eventually managed to catch up.
Together they performed the Paces of Yǔ and stepped on the Big Dipper,
reciting incantations and burning talismans.
They practiced for one seven-day period,
two seven-day periods,
until the third seven-day period,
and there were slight manifestations.
Sometimes they heard the sound of swords and jade pendants,
or saw the colors of robes.
It turned out these were not yet the true generals,
but rather the subordinates of the generals,
who were sent to inspect the altar.
By the fourth seven-day period
and the fifth,
the true forms finally appeared.
Sometimes they were half-bodied,
sometimes whole-bodied;
sometimes walking alone,
sometimes riding together followed by a crowd.
Sometimes many,
sometimes few,
they just came and went,
without stopping in the courtyard.
The storyteller asks,
why was this so?
It turns out the heroic spirits of these generals
are everywhere.
It is only because the essence and qì of ordinary people
do not resonate with them,
so mortal eyes cannot see them.
Today, being constrained by talismans and incantations,
when they traveled,
they could not help but pass by the ritual altar.
Moreover, meeting the focused gaze of those with utmost sincerity,
how could they not be seen!
As for their just coming and going,
it was because the ritual's effect was not yet full,
and the magic power had not yet reached its peak.
By the forty-ninth day, the seven-sevens,
the generals stood in the courtyard,
bowing with hands clasped to receive orders.
They crowded around on all sides
as if with the might of thousands of soldiers and horses,
yet they did not feel the courtyard was narrow at all.
The old woman was in front,
the monk and Daoist were behind,
standing upright with solemn expressions.
The old woman spoke and commanded:
"The three of us
are the kin of the Shàngdì.
Obeying the divine decree of the Empress Jiǔtiān Xuánnǚ Niángniáng,
we have obtained the Jiǔtiān Rúyì Bǎocè
and celestial talismans.
To propagate the great Daoist methods,
we have specially summoned you to come and assist,
and to obey my commands.
On the day the work is accomplished,
we shall report to the Shàngdì,
recording your merits for transcendence and ascension."
The generals bowed, acknowledged the command, and withdrew.
In an instant,
the courtyard was silent.
There is a poem to prove it:
They all say money can make ghosts work,
but know also that without arts one cannot communicate with gods.
Behold the divine generals lined up in the courtyard,
only because the celestial book and incantations are true.
It is said that Dànzǐ Héshang, seeing the divine generals coming and going,
was initially somewhat restrained,
but later gradually became accustomed to it.
However, every time it was the old woman in front,
with the two of them following her heels to work.
Although they were doing the same,
the old woman was always the one leading.
Dànzǐ Héshang was impatient
and had excessive confidence;
he wanted to try it for himself.
So he quietly got up at the fifth watch,
stepped before the altar,
and pinched the mudras and recited the incantations according to the method.
Only a loud sound was heard,
and a heavenly general descended into the courtyard.
What did he look like?
There is a "Xī Jiāng Yuè"
poem to prove it:
Eyes large as copper bells,
face like a purple crab and beard like steel.
A golden head-wrap emitting rays of light,
an embroidered jacket with coiled dragon patterns.
Holding a black banner in one hand,
summoning wind and calling for rain in his movements.
Heroic and fierce, who would dare face him?
The envoy is the heavenly general named Zhāng Shǐzhě.
Zhāng Shǐzhě bowed and came forward,
saying:
"My master has summoned me;
what is the divine decree?"
Dànzǐ Héshang was so flustered his face turned red and his heart pounded;
he hurriedly steadied his soul
and answered:
"Behind this building at the north window,
a few large trees are lacking for shade.
Only in the west garden are there four very large pear trees;
you may quickly move and plant them here."
The divine general responded and left.
In a moment,
only a great wind was heard,
with flying sand and dancing tiles,
and the sound of army horses galloping in the ears.
By dawn the wind subsided;
when Dànzǐ Héshang went to look behind the building,
the four large pear trees had been planted in a row.
This was done by the divine soldiers sent by Zhāng Shǐzhě.
The old woman, knowing Dànzǐ Héshang had done this,
gave him a real scolding,
saying:
"These heavenly generals are not to be compared to mortal men;
you should not lightly command them for unimportant matters.
Moreover, the Daoist arts are not yet completed
and you have no real skill of your own;
if you provoke their anger,
your life will be hard to save."
Dànzǐ Héshang said:
"I just tested it once;
I will never dare to do it again."
Now, about the gardener of the west garden:
because of this great wind,
he lost four large pear trees,
and hurriedly went to report it to Yáng Xúnjiǎn.
Yáng Chūn was just being surprised
when Lǎo Wáng of the east manor also came to report:
"This morning at the fifth watch the wind rose,
and behind the building where Shèng Gūgū lives,
several large trees have been added."
Yáng Chūn said:
"The side gate is locked shut;
how did you see it?"
Lǎo Wáng said:
"These trees are so high they reach the clouds;
I saw them from the outside.
They were never there before,
so I reported it."
Yáng Chūn knew it was another of Shèng Gūgū’s divine powers
and secretly marveled,
then said:
"I see,
you must not spread this to outsiders."
He rewarded each with wine and food
and sent them back, saying no more.
Now, the old woman consulted with the two, saying:
"Now that the generals have been trained,
we can take the seventy-two transformations of the Dìshà
and practice them in order.
Every time a method is practiced,
it must take forty-nine days.
Some of them are simple,
so we can just combine the days.
Within about three years,
we must aim to complete them."
Seeing that she spoke so readily,
the two were infinitely joyful;
from then on they applied themselves with double the effort.
Performing the Paces of Yǔ and stepping on the Big Dipper,
drawing talismans and reciting incantations,
they never wasted a moment.
Having practiced for one forty-nine-day period,
they could first secretly transport firewood, rice, and such,
no longer going to Lǎo Wáng to draw supplies.
Lǎo Wáng said:
"Since they don't come to draw,
it must not be because they lack anything;
I might as well enjoy some myself."
When he went to check the amount of firewood and rice,
it still decreased month by month.
Lǎo Wáng was greatly surprised
and went again to report to Yáng Chūn;
Yáng Chūn just told him not to say anything and see what they would do.
Time flies like an arrow,
and soon three years were nearly complete.
The three of them, including the old woman,
had mastered all seventy-two types of Daoist arts
As for their supernatural powers and transformations,
how were they in general?
One could see:
Above, they could scale the clouds like a ladder;
below, they could shrink the earth.
Wherever their fingers pointed,
mountains opened and cliffs split;
when they exhaled,
rocks rolled and sand flew.
Hiding their forms and changing their appearances,
they made people right in front of them completely bewildered;
capturing ghosts and summoning souls,
they commanded them at will in the void.
From bean-men and grass-horses,
they added an air of awesome power on the battlefield.
With paper tigers and belt-snakes,
they performed miraculous wonders in times of trouble.
Wind, clouds, thunder, and rain were used at their whim,
and water, fire, knives, and spears dared not harm them.
The mountain-founding Immortal Matriarch Kāishān Xiānlǎo had great supernatural powers,
and the Chaos-World Demon King Hùnshì Mówáng had high magical arts.
It turns out that these arts of the Báiyún Dòng,
at the highest level, were not like those of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
who through countless kalpas of cultivation
realize the samadhi of the void
and attain effortless supernatural powers.
At the middle level, they were not like the True Immortals of the thirty-six caves of Pénglái,
who spend decades balancing water and fire,
exchanging marrow and shifting tendons,
before they can transcend form and the world
to play with creation.
They merely relied on talismans and incantations
to seize power for a moment,
stealing the essence of heaven and earth
and borrowing the operations of ghosts and spirits.
In Buddhism, this is called the heterodox method of Jīngāng Chán;
in Daoism, it is called illusionary arts.
Therefore, Yùdì was cautious,
not allowing the divine seal to be opened privately
and passed down to the mortal world.
Even so,
a person of great brilliance
could utilize these magical arts
to protect themselves and stay away from harm,
using them as a bridge to the immortal path.
When entering mountains to gather herbs,
they would not fear tigers or wolves;
when seeking a master a thousand miles away,
they would not need the expense of carts and horses;
it is indeed a shortcut.
For this reason, the Báiyún Dòng left behind this lineage
to await those with a fated connection.
The cave master, the White Ape God Báiyuánshén, added a postscript at the end,
requiring them to swear an oath to the Dipper constellation every year:
"If I cause trouble and harm the people,
Léishén will not forgive me."
Only because the smoke from the jade incense burner rose a bit too early,
Dànzi Héshàng missed copying the final seventy-six characters,
and thus he never saw these words about the consequences.
Having successfully completed the cultivation today,
they considered it earth-shaking knowledge
and a gateway to immortality.
Later on,
they indeed caused trouble and harmed the people,
stirring up years of warfare in the Héběi region,
causing people to curse their demonic names
for a thousand autumns without end.
This is a story for later.
Let it be said that Shèng Gūgū’s cultivation this time
only required the use of Yáng Xúnjiǎn’s silver.
As for the two hundred pieces of gold from Yáng Nǎinai,
they remained untouched,
and she dispatched a clever spirit to return them to her.
She thought back to when she first left the earthen cave at the foot of Yànmén Shān;
at that time, the mother and sons were only three in total.
Although they had now added Dànzǐ Héshang,
they were ultimately missing Hú Mèi’ér,
which was a deficiency;
she would inevitably have to seek her out in the future
to pass on the teachings to her—
this was the most important matter in the old woman’s heart.
The talk about building a nunnery and casting statues
was originally not her true intention,
so there was no need to mention it further.
However, there was one more thing:
"The three of us
have received long-term sustenance from Yáng Xúnjiǎn and his wife,
and also gained the help of their gold and silver;
to leave suddenly without saying goodbye
feels indifferent.
Each of us should display our divine powers
to leave a remembrance for them."
The cripple jumped up and said:
"I will give them a tiger to guard the manor."
The old woman said:
"I originally promised to transmute gold for him;
now I will take this Tàihú stone in front of the tower
and transmute it into a family heirloom for him."
The cripple said:
"Wonderful!
My tiger will then guard the gold for him,
so that thieves will not dare to have any ideas."
Dànzǐ Héshang said:
"This humble younger brother is untalented,
but I wish to summon a superb sculptor
to fashion images of the three of us
here beneath the tower,
so that his descendants
may pay their respects morning and night."
The cripple said:
"Not good,
not good!
If my crippled leg is sculpted,
you will surely mock it."
Dànzǐ Héshang laughed and said:
"If that is the case,
we shall just have seated statues sculpted!"
At that moment, the old woman muttered incantations under her breath
and sprayed once toward the stone;
her saliva scattered like a fine mist.
She quickly rubbed it with her palm,
and wherever her palm reached,
it all turned the color of purple gold.
In no time at all,
a Tàihú stone weighing a full thousand catties
was transformed into a dazzling mountain of gold.
The cripple cut out a paper tiger,
muttered incantations,
and blew it with the wind.
He shouted:
"Swiftly!"
The paper tiger was seen pouncing on the ground and jumping twice,
then becoming a yellow-striped tiger.
It roared fiercely,
no different from a real tiger.
The cripple commanded:
"Tiger,
tiger,
listen to my words:
Guard the golden mountain
and do not allow it to be taken.
If anyone tries to take it,
tiger, chase them away."
After speaking,
he flicked his sleeve,
and it was still a paper tiger.
The cripple saw an empty space beneath the golden mountain
and placed the paper tiger inside.
Dànzǐ Héshang captured the living soul of a skilled craftsman
and confined him beneath the tower;
in one night, he sculpted three full-length figures
that were extremely lifelike.
Shèng Gūgū was in the center,
Dànzǐ Héshang was on the left,
and Zuǒ Chù was on the right.
When Dànzǐ Héshang saw them,
he was overcome with joy.
He then said:
"These are the statues I had sculpted;
I will start by bowing first."
The cripple said:
"If the wild monk bows,
who will return the courtesy?"
Dànzǐ Héshang said:
"If they stood up to return the courtesy,
I fear someone with an inconvenient leg
would be exposed."
The cripple also burst out laughing.
The old woman said:
"Stop the idle talk.
Thinking of the reasons for attaining the Way today:
'Stop when meeting Yáng'
and 'Be enlightened when meeting Dàn'
were all instructions from Tiānhòu in a dream.
She said that after twenty-eight years,
I should flourish in Héběi,
and she invited me to go to Bèizhōu to assist her.
This is the destiny of Heaven.
Firstly, we must not go against Heaven;
secondly, we must not forget the kindness of her guidance.
Starting from today,
each of us shall roam as we please;
when the thought arises,
we shall meet immediately.
When the day of our destiny arrives,
do not have a change of heart,
lest you violate the Heavenly Way."
Having finished speaking,
the old woman rose into the air
and beckoned the two of them with her hand from the sky.
Dànzǐ Héshang threw his brow-high short staff into the air,
which transformed into a golden bridge ten thousand fathoms long,
and he strode up it.
The cripple said:
"I shall go play in the Calabash Heaven for a while."
He then picked out an empty wine bottle from a corner
and placed it steadily on the ground.
He called out:
"I am coming down!"
and with both feet, he jumped into the mouth of the bottle,
and it was unknown where he went.
It is truly said:
Since ancient times, only immortals have joy;
when magic is high, one yields to no one.
After all, where will the three of them meet,
and where will Hú Mèi’ér turn up to stir things up again?

Kindness is better than reading the classics;
with frugality, there is no need to transmute gold.
There is no logic in riding a crane with wealth around one's waist;
alas, the foolish waste their efforts in vain.
Let it be said that when Shèng Gūgū first arrived at Dōngzhuāng,
she originally agreed with Yáng Xúnjiǎn that in half a year or a year,
there would be a response.
Who would have thought that with one boast,
she would close the side gate for three years.
Yáng Xúnjiǎn already had full confidence,
and seeing the moving of trees and transport of rice,
such divine powers,
he felt there must be some miraculous use.
For this reason, he only instructed Old Wáng, who managed the manor,
to secretly inquire about news,
while he himself no longer dared to knock on the doors
to ask for information.
Suddenly one day,
Yáng Nǎinai opened a clothes chest
and saw many things piled up inside.
When she took them out to look,
it turned out to be the two hundred pieces of private silver she had asked the old nurse to give to Shèng Gūgū three years ago,
lying inside untouched.
Nǎinai was startled
and hurriedly called the old nurse to identify them;
indeed, they were the same.
This was clearly the work of a clever spirit,
the same method as moving firewood and transporting rice.
How could they know the truth?
They could only guess wildly,
saying:
"This clothes chest has been locked for a long time without being opened;
why is the silver inside?
And when was it sent back?
We must send the old nurse to Dōngzhuāng to investigate."
The Lǎo Māmā sat in a small sedan chair,
arriving at the house of Lǎo Wáng in Dōngzhuāng,
to inquire about the situation.
Lǎo Wáng said:
"In the past, during the middle of the night,
I often heard a great commotion in the courtyard,
sounds of shouting and calling out.
Now, for several days, I haven't heard a sound.
I don't know the reason why."
The Lǎo Māmā said:
"Go get a ladder,
wait for me to climb up onto the roof,
to take a secret look
and see what is going on!"
Lǎo Wáng, seeing she was the Māmā in charge of the household,
naturally wanted to be extra attentive;
furthermore, she had been sent by the Nǎinai,
so how could he refuse?
In a rush, he went to the open hall to fetch a long ladder.
After struggling for a while,
he brought it into the building
and leaned it against the eaves of the corridor.
The Lǎo Māmā first climbed up onto the roof,
took a look,
then came down the ladder
and said:
"The courtyard is deathly still,
with no movement whatsoever.
My legs are weak and I cannot stand steady;
I'll let you, old sir, have a look!"
Lǎo Wáng indeed went up the ladder,
stretched out his head to look,
and there was not a single person.
He climbed onto the roof ridge himself,
looking carefully front and back,
when suddenly he saw a shining, brilliant yellow mountain of gold.
In his heart, he was both shocked and delighted.
Coming down the ladder,
a plan formed in his mind.
Hiding the truth from the Lǎo Māmā,
he only said:
"I didn't see anything.
I think they must have left through the back gate!"
After the Lǎo Māmā turned and left,
Lǎo Wáng ran as fast as an arrow into the city.
He reported to his master, Xúnjiǎn Yáng, to let him know:
"It was like this and like that.
I think it is your Excellency's great fortune,
so I have come specifically to report the good news."
Xúnjiǎn Yáng shouted:
"Who told you to go and look?"
Lǎo Wáng said:
"It was the Nǎinai who sent the Lǎo Māmā
and told me to go look;
it was not my own doing.
Because for several days no sound was heard from the courtyard,
I thought they were no longer there,
so I became bold.
Otherwise,
I wouldn't have dared."
Yáng Chūn pondered in his heart,
then ordered an Āntóng to prepare a horse
and personally went to Dōngzhuāng.
He peeled off the seal on the back wall of the open hall,
and when he went inside to look,
there was no one coming or going.
Weeds grew in wild tangles,
and the small corner gate under the corridor was still tightly closed.
Xúnjiǎn Yáng went over and knocked a few times,
but there was no response.
He ordered an Āntóng to pick up bricks and throw them;
they threw for an hour,
but it was as if they hadn't thrown at all.
Xúnjiǎn Yáng grew impatient
and ordered the villagers, sedan chair carriers,
and followers to use their strength together to break the door open.
Xúnjiǎn Yáng ordered the crowd to step back,
taking only four Āntóng to follow him.
He did not go to the study, the hall, or the living quarters,
but went straight out to the rear building to look.
He saw the Tàihú stone standing below the building
had already turned into a large piece of purple gold.
Yáng Chūn thought secretly to himself:
"The divine power of the Shèng Gūgū is truly not small!"
Turning his head,
he suddenly saw Shèng Gūgū, Héshang Dànzǐ, and Zuǒ Chù—the three of them—
sitting upright and properly below the building.
Yáng Chūn was greatly startled
and hurriedly knelt down at the steps to bow,
reporting:
"Your disciple has long lacked your guidance.
Hearing that Master's transformation is complete,
I have come specifically to pay my respects!"
An Āntóng said:
"Master, do not bow.
Those sitting above are dead.
Otherwise,
why wouldn't they return the greeting?"
Yáng Chūn stood up and went forward to look;
it turned out they were all statues.
Their entire bodies looked exactly like living people,
and he praised them endlessly.
Looking in the various side rooms,
there were all kinds of goods and utensils piled up,
still worth four or five hundred pieces of gold.
The clothes and luggage of the three
were all gone.
The four large pear trees in the back
were indeed moved from the Xī Yuán,
planted neatly.
Only, he did not know for what reason
they had left without saying goodbye.
He thought that perhaps Pǔxián Zǔshī was unwilling to build a temporary palace here,
and Shèng Gū found it hard to explain,
so she left on her own.
Yáng Chūn sighed for a while,
then told an Āntóng to go and welcome the Nǎinai.
Before long,
Yáng Nǎinai arrived.
Yáng Chūn led her to see the statues,
saying:
"They were sculpted by Shèng Gūgū herself."
The Nǎinai bowed four times,
then turned and saw the mountain of gold,
exclaiming:
"Gold of the human world,
how could it have such a pure red color!
It's just a pity that the transformation made it too large,
making it difficult to move."
Yáng Chūn said:
"We will bring many more people to move it home
to be a family treasure."
Seeing a yellow cloth canopy under the curtain by the incense table,
he went to get it himself
and covered the mountain of gold.
He ordered an Āntóng to call the villagers, sedan chair carriers,
and followers together,
to get poles and ropes,
and enter all together—
there were no fewer than thirty or forty people.
This group of people, hearing the Āntóng's call
and asking the reason,
already knew.
Seeing it wrapped in the canopy,
they all went to take a secret peek,
and every one of them was surprised and delighted.
They discussed it among themselves;
some said seeing such a rare object
would increase one's lifespan by twelve years.
Some said,
"After all, the fortune of an official is great;
the God of Wealth follows him."
Some said,
"Heaven's heart is also unfair;
with all this gold,
it doesn't distribute even a tiny bit to us poor men,
but gives it to that wealthy man instead."
A few strong ones,
who always took the lead,
took the ropes and went to bind the mountain of gold.
When they weren't touching it, everything was fine,
but as soon as they laid hands on it,
suddenly from beneath the mountain of gold,
a wild wind arose,
and a yellow-spotted tiger
pounced out with a leap.
Terrified, the crowd cried out:
"Āyà!"
and fled in all directions for their lives.
Xúnjiǎn Yáng grabbed one of the Nǎinai's arms
and ran up the stairs,
closing all the doors and windows.
After a while,
hearing no movement below,
he peeked through a hole in the window,
and the tiger was already gone.
Xúnjiǎn Yáng pushed open the window and called for people,
but not a single person answered.
He had no choice but to summon his courage and walk downstairs.
He saw the maidservants and wet nurses
still hiding under the table with the divine statues,
and some had run outside,
peering in with the Āntóng through the doorway for news from inside.
Xúnjiǎn Yáng shouted:
"Where is the tiger?
Why are you still acting as if you've seen a ghost?"
Only then did the Āntóng and the wet nurses feel safe enough to come in.
Xúnjiǎn Yáng ordered an Āntóng to prepare the horse
and call all the sedan chair carriers
to take the Nǎinai back to the residence.
After arriving home,
the husband and wife said:
"This Shèng Gū is efficacious.
Since her whole body has been sculpted,
she must want that golden mountain as an offering
and does not allow people to move it;
that is why she manifested a tiger to frighten people.
Now if we do not move it,
naturally there will be no trouble."
Having reached a consensus,
they moved back all the stored goods and utensils.
The ground floor of these three rooms was called the Shèng Gū Táng.
Every year, on the first day of the first,
fourth,
seventh,
and tenth months,
a vegetarian feast was set in the Xīyuán;
Yáng Xúnjiǎn would burn incense and light candles once,
and then it would be locked up,
not allowing outsiders to enter and look.
For the rest of the months,
even the members of the household were not allowed to enter.
He also instructed Āntóng and the estate workers
not to wag their tongues in front of outsiders.
As the saying goes:
What you can catch is the hand,
but what you cannot cover is the mouth.
Even though the master had given such instructions,
there were still those whose mouths were not firm
and who, treating it as news or a strange occurrence,
spoke of it abroad.
All the people in the county were in an uproar, saying:
"In Yáng Xúnjiǎn’s estate, a golden mountain has appeared,
and there is also a yellow-striped tiger."
There were also peers and relatives
who came specifically to ask Yáng Chūn about this matter,
but Yáng Chūn simply denied it.
Later, this Shèng Gū Gōng remained until after the rebellion in Bèizhōu,
when the Shūmìyuàn issued documents
to search everywhere for sorcerers and the remaining followers of
Dànzi Héshang
and Zuǒ Chù.
By this time, Yáng Xúnjiǎn had already passed away,
and the lady was old and bedridden with illness.
The steward informed the young master,
who privately called the estate tenants to destroy these three clay idols overnight.
When they looked at the golden mountain,
it was still just a piece of Tàihú stone.
The tiger was made of paper cutouts
and had already rotted away.
This is a later story.
Just as it is said:
When luck comes, even iron glows;
when fortune recedes, even gold loses its luster.
There is a poem as proof:
How laughable that Yáng Chūn’s insight was so crude,
mistaking a fox spirit for a true immortal.
Gold did not serve as a mountain to guard his home,
nearly causing his descendants to become a wicked sect.
This part of Yáng Xúnjiǎn’s story
is finished and will not be mentioned further.
Dear readers,
now if you wish to know the whereabouts of Mèi’ér,
it is necessary to take a wide detour
and start another topic.
The story specifically describes a man surnamed Zhāng, named Dàpéng,
a native of Xī’ān Fǔ.
He studied from childhood,
but lost his parents at twelve
and followed a Quánzhēn master
to wander abroad.
While at Yāndū Dàfáng Shān, he happened to contract an epidemic disease,
and the Quánzhēn master abandoned him and left.
Fortunately, he met a strange person from abroad
who cured him.
Seeing that his hand bones were extraordinary,
the stranger taught him a set of magical arts:
being able to summon wind and rain,
and command ghosts and spirits.
If compared with the magic of Báiyún Dòng,
it was about half a pound to eight ounces,
more or less the same.
Throughout his life, he was close to a person in Dōngjīng
and became sworn brothers with him,
often staying at his house.
That person was surnamed Zhū and named Néng,
and he had a mastery of martial arts.
Speaking of that matter,
it was still during the first year of the Xiángfú era,
when the Emperor Zhēnzōng was annoyed that the Qìdān barbarians treated the Central Kingdom with contempt.
A sycophantic official named Wáng Qīnruò memorialized:
"If one is not the true Son of Heaven ordained by fate,
one cannot ascend Tài Shān.
Thus, though Qín Shǐ Huáng was such a hero,
he was beaten down by wind and rain.
If Your Majesty wishes to overawe the four seas
and show off to the foreign tribes,
you must invite heavenly blessings and auspicious signs
and perform the sacrifices at Tài Shān;
only then can you be called the sagely ruler of the era."
Zhēnzōng asked:
"How many times has Tài Shān been enfeoffed?"
Wáng Qīnruò memorialized:
"Seventy-two times."
Zhēnzōng granted the petition.
It was placed upon Wáng Qīnruò
to require him, within three days,
to report seventy-two kinds of auspicious signs,
and every matter had to have evidence.
Wáng Qīnruò withdrew from court
with a worried expression.
In a moment he had spoken too much,
for within three days,
how could there be seventy-two kinds of auspicious signs?
Even if one spoke of Ganoderma,
sweet dew,
Qílín,
and phoenixes,
though they currently exist in the world,
they could not be brought forth within three days.
Zhū Néng was serving as a house guest under Wáng Qīnruò,
and knowing what was on his mind,
he said:
"This matter is not difficult.
According to Zhū Néng,
only one kind of auspicious sign is needed
to match those seventy-two kinds."
Wáng Qīnruò joyfully asked for the plan.
Zhū Néng said:
"Signs from plants, trees, birds, and beasts
all come later
and are not considered rare.
Only in the time of Fúxī of high antiquity
did a dragon-horse emerge from the river carrying a diagram,
and Heaven revealed the Yīn and Yáng trigrams;
it was called the Heavenly Script.
This is the ancestor of all auspicious signs.
Now, if the Heavenly Script were to descend
and be announced both within and outside the court,
the sacrifice at Tài Shān could be accomplished."
Wáng Qīnruò said:
"How can the Heavenly Script be made to descend?"
Zhū Néng said:
"There is no need for Your Excellency to trouble yourself;
Zhū Néng has his own clever strategy.
I will present it tomorrow morning!"
That night, Zhū Néng returned home
and consulted with Zhāng Dàpéng.
Zhāng Dàpéng said:
"It is not that this humble brother is boasting,
but relying on the Taoist arts I have learned throughout my life,
I will send the message of the Heavenly Script into the old Emperor’s palace tonight!"
Zhū Néng said:
"For me, this time
will be the stepping stone for my career;
I entirely rely on you, worthy brother, to assist with this!"
Immediately, Zhāng Dàpéng performed a method of planting a dream.
While Emperor Zhēnzōng was sleeping in the palace,
he dreamed of a red light illuminating the room
and a divine person
wearing a Seven-Star Crown
and dressed in crimson robes,
holding a book in his hands,
who announced:
"By the command of the High God,
three volumes of the Heavenly Script of Dàzhōng Xiángfú are bestowed.
Your Majesty should receive them with sincerity
so that the sacred reign may last ten thousand years!"
Just as he was about to reach out his hand to take the documents,
he suddenly woke up.
The bells of the fifth watch rang,
and Emperor Zhēnzōng ascended the hall.
It is truly:
The gates of the Nine Heavens open to the palaces,
the robes and caps of ten thousand nations bow to the crown and tassels.
The sunlight has just reached the moving immortal palms,
and the incense smoke drifts near the floating dragon robes.
The hundred officials had finished the morning court assembly.
The Emperor then summoned the Zǎixiàng Wáng Qīnrùo to an audience,
and regarding the dream of the previous night,
spoke to him about it.
Wáng Qīnrùo memorialized:
“This is because my Emperor’s will and vital energy are moved as one,
and are in communication with the heart of Heaven,
thus resulting in this dream omen.
Regarding these Tiānshū, ever since the time of Fúxī when the dragon-horse bore the chart,
until now,
they have not been seen again.
If they indeed descend,
it would be the supreme auspicious omen for the nation.
Not to mention the seventy-two kinds of propitious signs—
even if there were ten thousand kinds,
they could not surpass this.
I beg my Emperor to swiftly issue an imperial edict
to be proclaimed throughout the nine gates and investigated everywhere for news of the Tiānshū.”
Emperor Zhēnzōng granted the request.
At that moment, he took some dragon and phoenix patterned floral stationery,
spread it out on the imperial desk,
lifted a jade-handled rabbit-hair brush,
and with his own imperial hand wrote:
“I, in the depths of the palace,
respectfully and silently contemplate the Way.
In a dream, there was a divine man,
with a starry crown and crimson robes,
who relayed the command of the Celestial Emperor,
stating that three chapters of the Dàzhōng Xiángfú Tiānshū shall descend.
If anyone finds them first,
regardless of whether they are military or civilian,
they should swiftly come to the palace gates and present them,
and they shall be promoted and employed immediately.
If it is an official,
they shall be granted higher rank and increased salary.
Respect this and do not be negligent.”
The fifth year of Jǐngdé, the first month,
[blank] day,
by the Imperial Pen.
Wáng Qīnrùo held this imperial edict respectfully,
took his leave from court and departed.
He then ordered the document office to copy nine identical sheets,
dispatched men to post them at the nine gates,
and put the imperial handwriting into storage,
honoring it as a supreme treasure.
Attendants reported that Zhū Néng had come for an audience;
Wáng Qīnrùo hurried to invite him in.
After they had finished meeting,
Zhū Néng said:
“Your Excellency was just about to memorialize regarding the Tiānshū,
and it just so happens there is this imperial edict;
it can be called the height of coincidence!”
Wáng Qīnrùo said:
“Based on His Majesty’s dream,
could it be that there really are Tiānshū descending?”
Zhū Néng said:
“Never mind whether it is real or not;
it only depends on Zhū Néng.
I guarantee there will be Tiānshū for Your Excellency.
I only need to be temporarily appointed to the post of a Xúnguān,
so that it may be convenient to search and inquire.”
Wáng Qīnrùo said:
“I only fear that such a lowly post does not match your great talent;
what difficulty could there be!
I trouble you to apply your mind,
and on the day the matter is accomplished,
I will certainly memorialize to ensure you are heavily employed.”
At that moment, he sent a man with a name card to the Bureau of Military Affairs
to appoint Zhū Néng to the post of Xúnguān in the Huángchéng Sī.
Zhū Néng hung his ivory tablet at the Zǎixiàng's residence and came out.
He said to Zhāng Dàpéng:
“The Emperor indeed had a strange dream;
this is all thanks to your divine power, Worthy Brother.
However, as for the three chapters of the Dàzhōng Xiángfú,
where are we to seek them?”
Zhāng Dàpéng said:
“The Tiānshū is just a name.
I have already imitated the meaning of Lǎozǐ’s Dàodé Jīng
and scribbled three chapters.
I do not know if they can be used?”
He then reached into his sleeve and pulled out the drafts,
giving them to Zhū Néng to see.
Zhū Néng was originally not very well-versed in literature,
yet he praised them as wonderful with a full mouth
and said:
“Then I trouble you, Worthy Brother, to write them out.
What kind of paper should be used?
I will go and get it.”
Zhāng Dàpéng said:
“The year before last when I went to Gāolí, I brought back some hide paper,
and there is still some left.
I will write each chapter as one scroll
and wrap them in yellow silk.
Tomorrow at the fifth watch,
you, Elder Brother, go directly to strike the Dēngwén Drum,
and report that Tiānshū have descended upon the owl-tail ridge of Chéngtiān Mén;
just follow what I say.”
Zhū Néng said:
“The court is not a place for joking.
If the imperial carriage arrives at Chéngtiān Mén
and there are no Tiānshū,
the crime will not be small.”
Zhāng Dàpéng said:
“I will certainly not fail you in your matter, Elder Brother.”
At the fifth watch the next day,
Zhū Néng first went to knock on Zhāng Dàpéng’s door
to urge him about this matter again.
Zhāng Dàpéng replied from his bed:
“It is already settled!”
Zhū Néng knew of Zhāng Dàpéng’s skills
and thus had no doubts.
In one breath, he ran to the Dēngwén Yuàn
and beat the drum with a chaotic thundering.
The drum official on duty reported it to the academy;
the Yuànshǐ interrogated him about his origin
and took him to the court waiting room,
where he first met the Zǎixiàng Wáng Qīnrùo.
When Wáng Qīnrùo heard that there were Tiānshū,
his joy was beyond measure.
In a moment,
the purifying whip cracked three times,
and the Emperor ascended the hall in the palace to receive the court.
Wáng Qīnrùo led the Yuànshǐ of the Dēngwén Yuàn and memorialized:
“Tiānshū have descended at Chéngtiān Mén.
The Huángchéng Patrolling Official Zhū Néng has come to report it
and is awaiting the imperial command outside the court gates.”
Zhēnzōng heard the memorial
and ordered Zhū Néng to be summoned to the hall.
After Zhū Néng had finished his bows and dances of obeisance,
Zhēnzōng asked:
“Where are the Tiānshū?
And how do you know of it?”
Zhū Néng memorialized:
“Ever since your servant saw the imperial edict at the nine gates the day before yesterday,
I have not dared to rest by day
nor sleep by night.
I thought that the Celestial Emperor’s commands and heavenly words
must descend upon a high and towering place.
Furthermore, heavenly secrets are mysterious
and surely would not descend during the day.
This morning when your servant was patrolling below Chéngtiān Mén,
I saw yellow silk trailing out from the owl-tail ridge.
I reckoned it must be the Tiānshū
and did not dare not to report it.”
Zhēnzōng’s celestial countenance was greatly pleased.
He hurried down from the imperial throne
with a dragon's gait and a tiger's step,
straight to the Chéngtiān Mén.
The civil and military officials of the entire court were startled;
regardless of their orderly ranks like mandarin ducks and egrets,
they descended the hall one after another to follow him.
Zhū Néng pointed out the owl-tail ridge for Zhēnzōng to see,
and Zhēnzōng then dispatched two inner attendants to take a ladder and climb the roof.
It turned out to be a small yellow cloth bundle,
with two ribbons wrapped around the owl-tail ridge.
They untied it and brought it down.
Wáng Qīnrùo received it in his hands
and knelt to present it to Zhēnzōng.
There is a poem to prove it:
The starry crown and owl-tail are all deep mysteries,
Without sound or scent, how could there be a book?
Monarch and minister were both as if in a dream,
Who was it that deceived, using the mouth to speak for Heaven?
Zhēnzōng bowed again toward Heaven,
held the bundle in his imperial hands and walked back to the hall.
He gave it to the Hánlín Xuéshì Chén Yáosǒu
to open the seal and read it aloud.
It was indeed the upper,
middle,
and lower chapters of the Dàzhōng Xiángfú.
The chapters were all filled with Daoist language.
After the reading was finished,
all the officials shouted “Long Live the Emperor.”
Zhēnzōng ordered the inner attendants to bring a golden casket to hold them,
and they were temporarily sent to the Jǐnglíng Gōng to be enshrined before the altar of the Sacred Ancestor.
He awaited the construction of the Yùqīng Zhāoyìng Gōng to specifically enshrine the Tiānshū.
He then ordered Chén Yáosǒu to draft an edict
to be proclaimed throughout the world,
changing this year to the first year of Dàzhōng Xiángfú.
An auspicious day was chosen to set out,
and the Emperor personally went to Tàishān to perform the sacrificial rites.
He enfeoffed Wáng Qīnrùo as the Yǎnguó Gōng,
and Zhū Néng as the Patrolling Inspector of Jīngnán.
Within three years,
he was promoted directly to the post of Jiédùshǐ.
Knowing clearly that this wealth and honor
were all created by Zhāng Dàpéng,
whenever they met,
he was afraid that Zhāng might mention the previous cause,
and thus he showed quite a bit of neglect and rudeness.
Zhāng Dàpéng guessed this intention
but did not expose him;
he simply stopped associating with him.
From this, one can see the meager virtue of Zhū Néng.
Later on, memorials from fifteen circuits and prefectures
all reported having Heavenly Books;
the Emperor did not know which ones were real or fake
and began to have suspicions.
There was a Participant in Determining Governmental Matters, Dīng Wèi,
who gained favor through flattery and cunning
and contended for power with Wáng Qīnruò.
He discovered that Zhū Néng used deceit to cheat the Emperor
and secretly reported this to Zhēnzōng.
Zhēnzōng then replaced Wáng Qīnruò's position with Dīng Wèi
and sent an envoy to arrest Zhū Néng for trial.
Zhū Néng, relying on his martial skills,
killed the envoy
and led his troops in rebellion.
He was defeated and captured,
and eventually confessed the name of Zhāng Dàpéng.
The imperial decree ordered Zhū Néng to be executed by slicing
and issued a nationwide warrant
for all to capture the villain Zhāng Dàpéng.
Consequently, Zhāng Dàpéng drifted to Jiāngnán again,
changed his name to Zhāng Luán,
and called himself Chōngxiāo Chùshì.
Having a body full of magical arts,
there was nowhere he could not go.
As the common saying goes:
"No official business stays urgent for more than three days."
After a few years had passed,
this matter became neglected.
In the world of rivers and lakes, Zhāng Luán heard that the prince born to Zhēnzōng
had now grown up
and that the prince was the reincarnation of the Barefoot Immortal, Chìjiǎo Dàxiān.
How could this be seen?
It turns out that Zhēnzōng ascended the throne at the age of twenty-one,
but there was still no imperial heir in the palace.
He personally composed a prayer,
promulgated it throughout the realm,
and ordered famous mountains and temples everywhere
to perform fasts and sacrificial rites
to pray to Shàngdì.
At that time, Yùdì was gathering with the host of immortals
and asked who was willing to go,
but none of the immortals responded.
Only the Chìjiǎo Dàxiān gave a small smile.
Yùdì said:
"Those who smile cannot help but have feelings."
He then ordered him to be born in the palace
as the son of Lǐ Chénfēi.
After he was born,
he cried incessantly day and night.
An imperial placard was issued to recruit doctors;
a Daoist said to an eunuch:
"This poor Daoist can stop the child's crying."
Zhēnzōng summoned him into the palace,
the prince was carried out,
and the Daoist was told to examine him.
The Daoist whispered into the prince's ear:
"Do not cry,
do not cry;
how much better it would have been if you had not smiled at the start!"
The prince immediately stopped crying.
Zhēnzōng was greatly pleased
and asked for the reason;
after the Daoist finished explaining the circumstances,
he walked out of the palace gate,
transformed into a gust of clear wind, and vanished.
Who was this prince?
He was the Rénzōng Emperor, who ruled for forty-two years of peace and virtue.
While in the palace,
he liked to go barefoot
and never liked wearing shoes or socks;
this was the proof.
Zhēnzōng, feeling that the fasts and rites had been efficacious,
became even more devout
and restored Daoist temples everywhere.
Zhāng Luán heard this news,
and since the prince was the reincarnation of a great immortal,
he thought there must be a karmic affinity with the Daoist path.
Previously, when he was in Dōngjīng,
he had been acquainted with the eunuch Léi Yǔnggōng
and was held in great respect by him.
That Léi Yǔnggōng was favored and powerful,
holding the office of Xuānzhèngshǐ,
and was in league with Prime Minister Dīng Wèi, connecting the inner and outer courts.
For this reason, Zhāng Luán returned to Dōngjīng,
met with Eunuch Léi,
and told him about being wronged in the past.
He then entrusted him to pull strings with Prime Minister Dīng,
hoping to promote Daoism
and obtain an imperial title for himself.
Generally, for those of the sorcerer class,
no matter how much gods admire or ghosts obey you,
one always needs to rely on an imperial investiture
to avoid punishment from the Heavenly Court.
Léi Yǔnggōng said:
"Old matters from years ago
need not be worried about.
Master, simply take up residence in my Shújǐng Yuán.
Currently, the Crown Prince is selecting a consort
under the instructions of the Empress Dowager's decree,
and things are very busy.
When there is a bit of leisure,
we will go together to see Prime Minister Dīng
and then we can discuss further."
Zhāng Luán thanked him.
A subordinate led him to stay in the study of Shújǐng Yuán.
According to what is recorded in the Sòngshǐ,
the Zhēnzōng Emperor changed his era name five times in total:
Xiánpíng for six years,
Jǐngdé for four years,
Xiángfú for nine years,
Tiānxǐ for five years,
and Qiánxīng for one year.
At this time, it was the middle of the second month of the ninth year of Xiángfú.
One night, Zhāng Luán
saw that the moon was as bright as day
and took a stroll in the garden.
Suddenly, black clouds obscured the moon,
and a gust of strange wind
came from the west.
Zhāng Luán said:
"How strange!
What deity is passing by now?"
He formed the Wind-Settling Hand Seal
and watched intently.
In a moment,
after the wind had passed,
the clouds parted and the moon shone brightly.
Only a loud crash was heard,
and a woman fell from mid-air.
There is a poem as proof:
"Knowing full well that no one lives in the heavens,
how could a beauty fall from the nine skies?
Gusts of clear wind dazzle the eyes of the Daoist;
if she is not a lunar spirit, then she is a flower demon."
That woman was none other than
Hú Mèier, that little vixen.
This chapter connects directly to the plot of the sixth chapter.
She and Shènggūgū had left Jiànménshān
and traveled together along the way
to the Yǒngxīng area.
Because it was late,
they hurried to a forest to lodge for the night.
As they were walking,
a black wind arose from the opposite direction,
blowing so hard that one could not keep their footing.
That old woman was invited away by the Empress Wǔ Zétián
to meet in the dark palace.
This little vixen was swept up into mid-air by the wind,
drifting and fluttering,
all the way to Dōngjīng, falling into Eunuch Léi's garden.
What the Heavenly Empress said about entrusting her to Chōngxiāo Chùshì
refers to this situation.
Zhāng Luán saw that this girl's origin was mysterious.
When he approached to look,
she had already been half-frozen by the cold wind.
He immediately supported her into the study,
revived her with hot soup,
and asked for her name and surname.
She replied:
"Your humble servant is from Āndé Zhōu,
surnamed Hú,
and my childhood name is Mèier.
I was traveling with my mother to Huá Shān of the West Peak to offer incense,
when unexpectedly we encountered a gust of strange wind midway,
which blew me into the air.
At that time, I was unconscious,
hearing only a divine voice in my ears saying:
'A daughter of the Hú family, an empress for the Wáng family,
delivered to the Recluse of Chōngxiāo to receive.'
In a moment,
like rolling remnant clouds,
like drifting fallen leaves,
truly not knowing how many miles I had traveled,
I fell to this place.
I beg you, honorable official, to save me!"
Zhāng Luán looked closely at the girl;
she was extraordinarily beautiful and seductive.
Moreover, in her responses,
she was detailed and articulate,
calm and unhurried.
He sensed she was not a human being.
Having also heard the strange divine words,
he thought secretly:
"Could it be that this girl truly has the destiny of a consort or empress?
Now that the Palace Eunuch Léi is selecting palace women,
beauty such as this
is surely hard to come by;
this is truly a rare commodity worth hoarding!"
He then said:
"If you wish to ask for the Recluse of Chōngxiāo,
that is none other than this poor Daoist.
Little lady, you must identify yourself as my niece;
only then can I keep you here."
Mèier hurriedly bowed and said:
"Having received the grace of saving my life,
even if I were to serve you,
I would still be willing.
Since we are to be uncle and niece,
how could I dare not obey your command?"
Zhāng Luán helped her up
and settled her in a small back room to rest.
The next morning, he went to see Léi Yǔngōng
and said:
"I have a niece
named Mèier,
who is quite beautiful.
Because her parents recently passed away,
leaving her with no one to rely on,
