I have now brought her to my lodging.
If the Grand Marshal finds her to his liking,
please register her name.
If by any chance she is fortunate,
it would make me a relative of the imperial house."
Léi Yǔngōng was greatly pleased
and went with Zhāng Luán to Shùjǐng Yuán.
Just as it is said:
When one attains the day of mutual understanding,
that is the time when fortune flows.
What happened in the end?
Please listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
Both the talented man and the beautiful woman are greedy;
a mismatched marriage is always difficult to bear.
Unsatisfactory matters occur eight or nine times out of ten;
those that can be shared with others are not even two or three.
To continue, Eunuch Léi arrived at Shūjǐng Yuán,
and Zhāng Luán led Hú Mèier out to pay her respects.
Eunuch Léi saw she was exceedingly beautiful and seductive;
with a face full of smiles, he asked:
"How many years is your youth?"
Mèier said:
"I am just sixteen years old."
Eunuch Léi fixed his eyes on her,
pondered for a while,
praised her several times,
then mounted his horse and left.
After a short while,
he sent an official
to invite Zhāng Luán to his residence for a conversation.
Léi Yǔngōng was waiting in the hall;
when it was reported that Zhāng Luán had arrived,
he hurriedly descended the steps to welcome him.
Zhāng Luán was one who could read faces and discern moods;
he thought to himself:
"His manner today is twice as attentive as usual;
there must be some benefit."
After sitting down in the hall,
he asked:
"The honorable official has summoned me;
what instructions do you have?"
Léi Yǔngōng said:
"Just now I saw that your niece has very fine talent and appearance,
but the Prince is only fourteen years old;
your niece’s age is older,
so I fear she would be difficult to select as a consort.
If she only becomes a palace maid,
would that not be undignified for her?
I have an idea:
I wish to become a relative by marriage with you, Master,
but I do not know your thoughts?"
Zhāng Luán said:
"Is the marriage for your younger brother,
or your nephew?"
Eunuch Léi smiled and said:
"Neither brother nor nephew,
but for myself."
Zhāng Luán said:
"The honorable official is a close attendant of the palace;
please do not joke."
Léi Yǔngōng said:
"There is something you do not know, Master.
Although we have been purified,
our seven emotions and six desires are just like those of ordinary people.
The nights are too lonely;
one often desires a partner to sleep with.
Whenever there is cold weather or a cold moon,
having a young page-boy warm my back or feet
is of little interest.
There are also those who associate with prostitutes in outside residences
to have companionship from time to time,
but after all, that is not a permanent way.
Even if it is good, it is not ideal.
It is better to marry a wife
to stay together for a long time;
would that not be wonderful?"
Zhāng Luán said:
"Can such a thing be done?"
Yǔngōng said:
"Eunuchs of the inner palace taking wives
has precedents in previous dynasties.
Shí Xiǎn of the Hàn Dynasty had a wife and son;
Gāo Lìshì of the Táng Dynasty married a woman of the Lǚ family;
Lǐ Fǔguó married a woman of the Yuán family;
these are recorded in history books and can be cited.
Master, do not decline.
I have looked at the calendar;
tomorrow is an auspicious day for marriage.
In the morning, I will offer some modest betrothal gifts,
and in the evening, I will come to personally welcome the bride.
I trouble you to take charge,
and first inform your niece.
After she crosses my threshold,
she will only enjoy wealth and comfort."
Zhāng Luán saw that he was very insistent;
although he was unhappy in his heart,
he could only agree.
He took his leave from Eunuch Léi,
returned to Shùjǐng Yuán,
and told Mèier these words.
Mèier said:
"Uncle, if you marry me to a eunuch,
what future is there in that?"
Zhāng Luán said:
"I thought the same,
but he currently has power and influence,
and cannot be disobeyed.
Just go with a peaceful mind;
I will have my own ways."
Nothing more was said that day.
On the following day,
Eunuch Léi’s house hung up red silks in the morning,
with great fanfare of drums and music,
preparing the wedding banquet.
In the morning, he first sent the betrothal gifts;
the gifts were:
one golden phoenix pearl crown,
one set of crimson silk python-patterned robes,
one green jade belt with small floral patterns,
two pairs of gold hairpins,
two pairs of gold bracelets,
and all other personal new clothes,
every item in pairs,
along with festive flowers, red silks, sheep, and wine,
which need not be detailed.
They were displayed in Zhāng Luán’s lodging like a piece of brocade.
There is a poem as proof:
Festive silks, sheep, and wine are all spread out;
the eunuch is joyfully getting married tonight.
Having power and wealth, he acts as he pleases;
how many people in the world must sleep alone?
By evening,
Eunuch Léi Tàijiàn, wearing python-patterned robes and a jade belt,
riding a purplish-brown horse,
and escorting a five-colored decorated bridal sedan,
arrived with the music of sheng, flutes, and drums
at the garden to personally receive the bride.
At that time,
Zhāng Luán took a new undershirt,
performed a hand gesture and wrote a talisman,
recited some incantations in his mouth,
and told Mèi’ér to put it on.
He then taught the formula to Mèi’ér,
so that whenever she wanted to put it on,
she would recite a "Body-Locking Incantation,"
and if she wanted to take it off,
she would recite an "Undressing Incantation."
Mèi’ér learned them all.
At that moment, she was dressed up to look like a heavenly being,
and she entered the decorated sedan and departed with Eunuch Léi Tàijiàn.
Zhāng Luán saw them out of the garden gate and returned home.
It is said that Eunuch Léi Tàijiàn and Mèi’ér performed the ritual bows and were married,
but there were no maidservants or old matrons to serve them,
only some young eunuchs
carrying candles
who led the couple into the bridal chamber
to drink the nuptial cup.
At this time, the weather was still cold;
red woolen carpets were spread on the floor of Eunuch Léi Tàijiàn’s room,
marten-fur curtains were hung,
and there were brocade quilts and embroidered mattresses—
everything was luxurious.
When it was time to go to bed,
he likewise knew how to say a few flirtatious words.
However, there was one strange thing:
after Mèi’ér had removed her flowery crown and embroidered jacket,
when she reached the undershirt next to her skin,
it could not be undone.
It was clearly as if it were her own natural skin,
and even her lower garments were tightly wrapped by the shirt.
Even when Eunuch Léi Tàijiàn tried his own hand,
he could only look at it.
Thus, he had no choice but to sleep with her with his clothes on.
He could not achieve any skin-to-skin
intimacy.
This was the magic of Zhāng Luán.
Early the next morning,
the household officials,
personal attendants,
and idle hands
all came to kowtow,
wishing to pay their respects to the lady,
but Eunuch Léi Tàijiàn dismissed them all.
He instructed the young eunuchs to call her "the bride" for the time being
and not to address her as "the lady,"
lest it invite ridicule.
After a short while,
Zhāng Luán also came to the door to offer congratulations.
Eunuch Léi Tàijiàn invited him into the study to sit
and told him about this strange occurrence.
Zhāng Luán said,
"This is because the predestined affinity has not yet arrived;
perhaps in Your Honor’s seventh palace of fate,
there is another auspicious marriage,
and my niece has no fortune to serve you."
Eunuch Léi Tàijiàn said,
"Let us see what happens tonight."
He then kept Zhāng Luán for a meal of wine and food before he left.
When it was time to sleep that evening,
Mèi’ér took off her clothes,
but it was the same as before.
Now, Eunuch Léi Tàijiàn was someone who loved comfort;
he was like a silk knot rolled out from a pile of brocade,
unable to endure even one knot against his body;
if one pressed against him,
it felt like a massive lump.
Only because he loved Mèi’ér’s appearance
did he endure sleeping a night with her while she was dressed,
but it was clearly a night of suffering.
On the second night, he could not manage it anymore,
so they had to use separate quilts.
By the third night, another room was prepared,
and Mèi’ér was sent to sleep by herself.
Zhāng Luán also knew they could not get along
and that she would surely be sent away.
Who would have thought that although he was unhappy in his heart,
he still could not bear to send her back.
Zhāng Luán thought to himself with hesitation,
"It is not appropriate for me to speak of this matter;
what should be done?
Now I shall capture a true likeness of Mèi’ér;
later, looking for a convenient opportunity
and devising a plan,
I will persuade him to present her to the Sovereign.
Should she receive his favor,
perhaps she could win a title.
That would be better than being nameless and aimless
as a eunuch's nominal wife."
That night, he performed the "Method of Summoning Immortals to Capture a Likeness."
Dear reader,
how do you think this method works?
If one wishes to capture someone's true likeness,
sweep a clean room,
prepare paper on the table,
brushes,
and various colors,
and set out wine and fruit as offerings.
Write a detailed petition describing the circumstances,
and along with an "Immortal-Summoning Talisman"
and a "Soul-Capturing Talisman," burn them.
Recite the "Immortal-Summoning Incantation"
and the "Soul-Capturing Incantation" once each,
and then lock the door.
No matter how far or near the person is,
their living soul can be summoned;
it leaves after the painting is finished.
At that time, the living person
is just like someone talking in their sleep.
Even for ghosts long dead,
one can summon their wandering souls,
and they are no different from when they were alive.
Therefore, their appearance and mannerisms
are captured with lifelike accuracy.
Once the Painting Immortal arrives,
one hears the brushes and ink moving about;
when the sound of putting down the brush is heard,
the immortal has already departed.
Slowly open the door and enter,
and the true likeness is already captured.
Generally, for those who summon Poetry Immortals,
those who come are mostly ghosts skilled in poetry.
For those who summon Painting Immortals,
those who come are ghosts skilled in painting.
If by chance a true immortal descends,
the poem will be exquisite
and the painting will be divinely inspired.
That night, Zhāng Luán was in Mèi’ér’s bedroom
and summoned a Painting Immortal according to the method.
At midnight,
the sound of a brush being put down was heard.
Zhāng Luán unlocked the door
and went in to look;
the cheeks were painted like flowers,
and the eyes seemed about to dart,
just like a living person.
On it were three words in cursive script: "Brush of Sēngyóu."
Thus he knew it was Zhāng Sēngyóu of the Jìn dynasty who had descended.
This was the man of the saying "Sēngyóu paints a dragon but does not dot the pupils;
if he dots the pupils, the dragon will fly into the sky."
It was indeed that man,
a truly immortal brush.
Zhāng Luán was delighted,
and the next day he used silk and paper to mount it as a small scroll,
which he hung in the inner chamber.
He waited only for the next time he met with Eunuch Léi Tàijiàn
to sound him out
and then use persuasive words to convince him.
It is said that Mèi'ér was feeling neglected and listless at the house of Léi Tàijiàn.
From that night, she talked in her sleep,
and by morning she felt dazed and depressed;
feeling her spirits decline,
she then asked a young palace attendant:
"Are there any here who can perform Pínghuà?"
The young attendant replied:
"There is a Qú Xiāzi who tells them best;
his voice is resonant
and his plots are clear.
He lives right under the eaves of this mansion."
Mèi'ér said:
"Call him here for me to pass the time!"
The young attendant reported this to Léi Tàijiàn,
summoned Qú Xiāzi,
helped him into the central hall,
and excused him from performing formal bows.
A small table
and a small stool were brought,
and he was told to sit outside the threshold,
while Mèi'ér sat in the middle,
listening from behind a curtain.
She instructed that he need not be given a specific topic,
but should just pick something pleasant to hear.
Qú Xiāzi then cleared his throat,
struck his wooden clapper on the table,
recited four lines of an introductory poem,
and entered the main story.
It turned out he was telling the story of Zhòu Wáng and Dájǐ.
As the story goes, Dájǐ was a beauty betrothed to Zhòu Wáng.
While she was being escorted mid-journey,
a wild wind blew,
the sky darkened and the earth grew dim,
and all the attendants fell down in shock.
When the wind passed
and they struggled to their feet to look,
only Dájǐ sat upright and unmoving.
Zhòu Wáng said she was blessed with good fortune,
established her as his primary consort,
and favored her immensely.
But little did he know that Dájǐ was no longer the real one,
but a jade-faced fox spirit of many years;
she had raised that strange wind,
carried the beauty away,
and transformed herself into her likeness.
With all kinds of bewitching charms,
she deluded Zhòu Wáng.
Just because Zhòu Wáng doted on this consort,
he engaged in drinking bouts through the long night,
making a pool of wine
and a forest of meat.
He executed loyal ministers who gave counsel
and acted with wanton lawlessness.
At that time, the people sighed with resentment,
prompting Zhōu Wǔ Wáng to raise an army to punish his crimes,
defeating Zhòu Wáng at Mùyě
and killing Dájǐ in the palace.
After telling this part,
he recited another four lines of poetry.
The poem said:
"All say the Shāng Wáng's favor was extraordinary,
but who knew Dájǐ was a demon fox?
Even if a fox's wit could be wise and virtuous,
would it not still surpass the likes of Lǚ and Wǔ in the human world?"
Mèi'ér heard this
and sighed, saying:
"The ancients said:
'If in life one cannot fulfill one's heart's desires,
even living a hundred years is like dying young.'
If one can have one's way for a single day,
one can die without regret."
She then ordered a string of cash to be given to Qú Xiāzi, and he left.
She thought to herself:
"Being of the same kind of fox-bewitchment,
she could usurp Dájǐ's position
and win the favor of a ruler.
With my spiritual illusions,
how could I be inferior to her?"
That night she slept alone in her room.
She dreamed she was selected to enter the imperial palace,
received immense favor from the court,
was invested as Huánghòu,
surrounded by palace maids,
in extraordinary wealth and honor.
Her mother, Shèng Gūgu, was titled Guótài.
Her brother, Zuǒ Chù,
was also appointed as a high official.
The whole family of relatives was incomparably prosperous.
Suddenly she woke up
and it was but a Nánkē dream.
The sunlight on the gauze window was already bright red.
She saw the young attendant holding a silver basin for washing,
placing it on a vermilion washstand.
He reported:
"Today is the third round of the grand selection of imperial consorts;
Lǎo Gōnggōng left early for the Lǐbù.
Please, young lady, get up to wash and have breakfast;
after we have served you,
we also want to take leave to go and have a look!"
Mèi'ér said:
"My body is weary
and for now, I will not wash or comb my hair.
If you want to go see it, go ahead!"
When the group of boys heard this,
it was just like a village teacher dismissing school;
the whole bunch of them ran off.
Mèi'ér said:
"Since it is the third round of the grand selection,
the beauties of the entire city
must all be gathered in one place.
I will also go and see
what it is like."
She got up and washed,
and looking into the bright mirror, she said:
"With a complexion like mine,
it is rare even among humans.
Yet I am stuck here;
would that not be a waste of my clever heart and skillful nature!"
She took a piece of blue cloth and wrapped it around her head down to her eyebrows,
disguising herself as a village girl.
She bolted the door of her room.
Using her old fox-spirit tricks,
she climbed over the wall behind the room and went out.
She opened the back gate
and hurried away like a puff of smoke.
Going straight to the entrance of the Lǐbù,
she squeezed into the crowd.
She saw the gates of the yámén wide open,
and from afar she could see Léi Tàijiàn and the officials of the Lǐbù,
all sitting in the hall.
A group of official matchmakers led the girls from respectable families across the hall,
and names were called according to the register.
They entered through the east corner gate
and exited through the west corner gate.
There were also parents of beloved daughters from poor families,
following them themselves,
waiting outside the gate.
There were also young ladies from official families,
followed by lines of servants and nurses.
The total number was far more than a hundred!
They were all thirteen or fourteen years old.
Among them, those with clear brows and elegant eyes,
and red lips and white teeth were quite numerous.
But there was not one with an extraordinary charm
or outstanding beauty.
Mèi'ér looked at them one by one
and said:
"As the ancients said:
'A true beauty is hard to find.'
In a flowery and splendid Dōngjīng,
the talents are only such as these!"
The crowd jostled and crowded,
only dispersing in the afternoon.
Mèi'ér hid in the Tǔdìtáng,
and by evening she did not return home.
A wild idea struck her,
that she wanted to go to the Dànèi
to see for herself how prosperous and noble the Sāngōng Liùyuàn were.
Do you know why she had this foolish idea?
Firstly, her true soul had been captured by a celestial brush,
and thus her spirit was in disarray;
secondly, the three characters "Wáng Jiā Hòu" were churning within her belly.
Having heard the story of Dájǐ,
her heart grew increasingly restless,
and unable to restrain herself,
she slipped into the Huángchéng under the cover of night.
Although she was a fox demon using enchantments,
arriving without leaving a track
and departing without a trace,
yet the interior of the Huángchéng
was different from the world of common folk,
and was no place for trifles.
Seeing the guards at the front gate were strict,
she could not help but feel afraid
and did not dare to barge in.
She turned toward the Hòuzǎimén.
It so happened that a group of craftsmen were repairing the Yùhuāyuán,
and had just finished their work.
A eunuch was there questioning the foreman about something,
holding two gauze lanterns
and two torches,
lighting the area as if it were day.
Mèi’ér slipped in during the bustle
and went straight into the Yùhuāyuán.
After walking for a long time,
she suddenly saw the palace walls were high and steep,
difficult to scale.
She shuddered once more
and sat down for a moment to deliberate.
Suddenly she remembered
that the Huángtàizǐ lived alone in the Dōnggōng,
and his vital energy was not yet settled.
If she could manage to meet him,
he would surely feel affection for her.
She had heard he was the reincarnation of the Chìjiǎo Dàxiān,
with an extraordinary nature;
if she could obtain a bit of his true essence,
it would be a stroke of luck for her.
Turning her steps eastward,
she advanced windingly.
After crossing the Jīnshuǐ Qiáo,
she wanted to crawl in through the Yùgōu,
but she feared the deep water,
and there were copper pillars blocking the way, which was inconvenient,
so she had to continue forward.
She heard the palace clepsydra marking the night watch;
the moon had not yet risen.
Seeing a few points of firelight in the distance,
she ran forward to look,
and it was four or five young eunuchs
carrying red gauze lanterns,
coming out together to relieve themselves.
Mèi’ér said:
"Since they have a door to exit,
I am not afraid of having no door to enter."
Taking advantage of the firelight to look quietly,
there was indeed a side door open.
Mèi’ér squeezed her way in,
looked for a convenient spot,
climbed onto the eaves,
and passed through several courtyards.
She then heard the sound of reading from below;
Mèi’ér did not come down yet,
but removed several glazed tiles from the roof,
dug open the ceiling boards,
and peered down.
It turned out this place was called the Zīshàn Táng,
the place where the Huángtàizǐ studied.
This Huángtàizǐ was naturally intelligent and fond of learning;
even though it was late at night,
he was still sitting there by candlelight.
Several attendants
were leaning against tables or walls in all directions,
slumping this way and that,
all dozing off.
Mèi’ér said:
"If I miss this chance,
when will another come?"
She then flew down from the opening.
She saw several old palace women in the back hall guarding the tea stove,
brewing tea there.
On the table were arranged carved lacquer tea trays,
silver bowls, gold spoons, and such things.
Mèi’ér removed her headscarf,
wiped her face,
and transformed into a young, beautiful, and peerless palace maid.
Suddenly she stole a tray of tea
and a silver bowl,
and spat some saliva into it.
She blew on it with her breath,
and it became fragrant hot tea.
In truth, fox saliva is a drug that charms people;
if someone drinks it,
their heart and mind will be deluded.
Regardless of being man or woman,
once they fall for her trick,
even if you were Lǔ Nánzǐ,
it would be hard to remain untempted,
and even the chaste woman in the Lùjīn Cí
would crawl into the bed curtains.
Mèi’ér held the tea tray,
walked out of the back hall in a seductive manner,
and just as she was about to present it to the Huángtàizǐ,
she suddenly saw a deity flash out from behind the Huángtàizǐ.
What did he look like?
There is a "Línjiāngxiān"
as evidence:
Eyebrows like reclining silkworms and phoenix eyes,
a face like heavy dates, bright red.
A steel blade, the Yǎnyuè, dancing like a green dragon,
wearing a battle robe of green brocade,
his fine title is Rángōng.
A heart of loyalty suspended like the sun and moon,
assisting the Liú family to support the Hàn dynasty's success.
His divine spirit spreads his heroic fame through the ages,
beheading demons, he is called the Shàngjiàng,
protecting the nation and manifesting divine powers.
This deity was precisely the Yìyǒng Wǔ'ān Wáng, the demon-beheading Great General, Guān Shèng.
Since ancient times, the Sagely Son of Heaven has been protected by a hundred gods;
on this day, it was Guān Shèng’s turn to guard the carriage from the void.
Seeing Mèi’ér practicing her sorcery and displaying illusions,
about to make contact,
his holy heart was greatly enraged,
and he manifested his divine might,
taking the Qīnglóng Yǎnyuè Dāo
and cleaving down from her head.
Mèi’ér gave a great cry,
dropped the tea tray,
and fell backward.
The Huángtàizǐ heard the fox’s shriek
and was startled.
The attendants were all startled awake,
carrying painted lanterns to look around everywhere.
They only found a vixen,
her skull split open,
dead on the ground.
Her clothes, like a cicada’s sloughed skin,
had slipped to the side.
In the chaos, everyone lit their lanterns and torches;
fearing there might be other foxes in the group,
they searched everywhere front and back,
but there was absolutely no sign,
and they truly did not know where it had come from.
That night, they carried the fox corpse out the back.
The next morning,
the Huángtàizǐ entered the palace and reported to the Emperor.
The Sītiānjiàn was ordered to divine the omen.
The Sītiānjiàn reported:
"Fox demons assuming human clothes
happens from time to time.
But in the inner grounds of the Imperial Palace,
how could it have stolen in?
This is an extraordinary monster!
Yesterday, the Wěihuǒhú was on duty,
and there happened to be a fox monster;
the palace should be careful to prevent fires.
However, the fox died as if struck by a ghost or god,
which is a blessing for the Huángtàizǐ for a thousand years,
and will not be a great misfortune.
Later, the fire disaster did not occur,
and the Emperor did not investigate further.
Later generations have a poem that says:
Vainly they say the Sītiān acts on true principles,
who among them is truly of help?
They only use vague words for common responses,
when has the Xuānshì ever truly asked about ghosts and gods?
The story now splits into two branches.
To continue, that evening Eunuch Léi Tàijiàn returned from the Lǐbù,
and ordered the bride to be invited to accompany him for wine.
The little eunuch attendant reported:
"The bride has kept her room door closed since morning
and has not opened it yet.
She does not answer when called;
I do not know the reason."
Léi Tàijiàn went himself and knocked a few times,
then called several times,
but it was silent inside.
Losing his temper,
he ordered the door to be forced open.
They looked on and under the bed,
but where was there even a trace of a person?
He thought to himself:
"Seeing that I did not treat her very intimately,
perhaps she has run away.
However, a young woman's arched shoes and socks are small,
and with walls like these and no ladder,
how could she have gone?"
After hesitating for a while,
he said again:
"If she went anywhere, it would only be to her uncle's place.
Order someone to go see and then we will know for sure."
He then dispatched an official attendant overnight to Zhāng Luán’s residence at the Shújǐngyuán
to see if the bride was there.
Zhāng Luán saw the official attendant arrive
and state his purpose.
Zhāng Luán said in great shock:
"Your Master Léi Tàijiàn is mistaken!
Since my niece married him,
in life or death she is a member of his household.
Where could a young girl go?
She must surely be in the Master's house.
It cannot be that after losing one,
you want me to compensate you with another?"
The attendant took these words
and returned to report back.
That night, Zhāng Luán felt suspicious;
he closed the door
and immediately wrote talismans and recited incantations,
intending to summon Mèi'ér’s soul for questioning.
In the past, the soul would arrive as soon as the talisman did,
but this time it was not effective.
Zhāng Luán cried out:
"How strange!"
Then, before the portrait of Mèi'ér,
he focused his mind and concentrated for a while,
and burned another Soul-Pursuing Talisman.
He saw a gust of cold wind pass,
and from within the painting, there seemed to be a soft sobbing sound;
suddenly she stepped down—
it was indeed Mèi'ér’s demonic soul.
She grabbed Zhāng Luán and wailed loudly.
Zhāng Luán comforted her
and asked for the reason.
Mèi'ér told him:
"I dare not hide anything now;
I am actually a fox spirit from the foot of Yànménshān.
I followed my mother, Shènggūgu, wandering to seek the Way,
but midway we encountered a windstorm,
and I was blown to this place.
I was taken in and raised by the Immortal Official,
treated like his own flesh and blood,
for which my gratitude is not shallow.
Unexpectedly, I was forcibly wed by the Léi family,
ruining my whole life.
The night before last, after some sleep-talking,
I felt my spirit dissipating.
Yesterday, hearing that the Lǐbù was selecting consorts,
I stole away to see.
Thinking that my beauty was second to none,
I slipped into the Imperial Palace,
hoping to beguile the Emperor.
Unexpectedly, in the darkness, I provoked the wrath of Guānshèng
and met the edge of his blade;
my soul was immediately dispatched to Fèngdū to be interrogated for my crimes.
I pleaded again and again,
and Guānshèng checked the ledgers,
saying that by my predestined fate in the underworld, I am due to receive a human body.
In the future, I will rise to prominence in Bèizhōu
and have the destiny of an Empress of the Central Palace.
Within this very month, I should go to the local Member Hú Yuánwài’s house to be reincarnated.
Just as I was about to be released,
I happened to encounter the Immortal Talismans summoning me several times,
and so I came here.
Only then did I realize my soul was already within the portrait.
Now that the three souls are reunited,
by relying on the Immortal Official's power
to send the painting into Member Hú Yuánwài’s house,
that will be my place of birth!
Regarding the future events in Bèizhōu,
the Immortal Official is also among those named.
If you encounter my mother, Shènggūgu,
please send her a message."
Having finished speaking, she walked back into the painting.
Zhāng Luán then recalled when Mèi'ér was blown here by the wind,
he had heard two lines of divine words from the air:
"The daughter of the Hú family shall be the Queen of the Wáng family,
given to the Chōngxiāo Chǔshì to receive."
I only thought her surname was originally Hú,
but it turns out there is also this part about being reincarnated in Member Hú Yuánwài’s family.
According to those three words, 'Queen of the Wáng family,'
she is no longer the daughter-in-law of the Zhào family.
I do not know about the Bèizhōu business
or what that is about.
While traveling the rivers and lakes,
I have also heard of a Shènggūgu with great supernatural powers,
but at this moment, I don't know where she is.
If I meet Shènggūgu,
this matter will naturally become clear.
He thought about it all that night.
Early the next morning,
Léi Tàijiàn came to the garden in person;
fearing that Zhāng Luán would demand her back from him,
he came first to offer apologies.
Zhāng Luán did not explain it to him
but only gave evasive answers with polite clichés,
asking him to search diligently.
After a short while,
word spread throughout the capital
that last night a vixen died in the Zīshàntáng of the Eastern Palace
and this morning she was carried out through the Hòuzǎimén.
Zhāng Luán understood it in his heart
and secretly found it marvelous.
How could Léi Tàijiàn think of connecting it to Mèi'ér?
He only instructed official attendants,
private servants,
and idle fellows
to search in all directions,
offering a thousand strings of cash as a reward.
These people took it as a business opportunity;
acting as if they saw ghosts and gods,
they probed here and asked there,
but where was there any news?
It is truly said:
Scooping the moon from the water—when was it ever there?
Searching for a needle in the ocean—in the end, there is none.
This need not be discussed further.
To continue, after breakfast, Zhāng Luán
dressed himself neatly.
Wearing an iron Taoist cap
in the shape of a fish tail,
and a fiery scarlet robe with black borders,
he rolled up Mèi'ér’s portrait
and placed it in a wicker basket.
Holding the basket in his left hand
and a palm-bark fan in his right,
and having learned that Member Hú Yuánwài lived on Píng'ānjiē,
he headed straight for that road.
It is just as the saying goes:
White clouds are originally mindless things,
yet they are drawn out by the clear breeze.
In the end, how did Zhāng Luán get this painting into Member Hú Yuánwài’s house?
Please listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
You do not yet know who Yǒng'ér is;
she is the Hú Mèi'ér of that time.
Once the demonic womb bears its fruit,
the ruin of families and the harm to the nation all stem from this.
It is said that during the peak of the Dà Sòng,
in Biànzhōu of Dōngjīng Kāifēng Fǔ, the city was as beautiful as a tapestry of flowers.
Outside the city, there was an outer wall thirty-six lǐ in circumference,
with twenty-eight city gates.
There were thirty-six lanes of flowers and willows,
and seventy-two buildings for music and song.
If there were any vacant land,
it was surely used for planting flowers or playing cùqíqiú.
As for the powerful officials within that city of Dōngjīng,
we shall not speak of them;
just the wealthy Yuánwài alone,
their numbers were beyond knowing.
There was Yuánwài Wáng of the dye-works,
Yuánwài Lǐ of the pearls,
Yuánwài Zhāng of the seafaring trade,
Yuánwài Jiāo of the colorful silks—
there were more Yuánwài than could be named.
Among them was one Yuánwài
whose family was immensely rich;
truly, his money reached higher than the Big Dipper,
and his grain rotted in the old granaries.
His family operated three pawnshops:
the pawnshop on the left
specialized in taking damasks and silks;
the pawnshop on the right
specialized in gold, silver, pearls, and jade;
the pawnshop in the middle
specialized in zithers, chess sets, books, paintings, and antiques.
In each pawnshop,
there was one manager
and three supervisors.
This Yuánwài was surnamed Hú,
named Hào,
and styled Dàhóng.
He had only his wife, Yuànjūn Māma Zhāng shì.
Because this Yuánwài was a man who, in his daily life,
indeed had a pair of eyes,
but not a single child.
Because in his daily life, this Yuánwài
focused his heart only on building his household,
calculating capital and interest.
Turning one into ten,
turning ten into a hundred,
he never gave a thought to the matter of children.
That Yuànjūn also had a certain flaw:
she was devoted to jealousy and sourness,
and would not allow the Yuánwài to take concubines or purchase maidservants.
Ten years ago, the Yuánwài had secretly trifled with a maidservant;
when the Yuànjūn found out,
she immediately beat the maidservant half to death,
handed her over to a supervisor,
and ordered him to find someone to sell her.
She also quarreled with the Yuánwài,
bickering,
and making scenes;
for a full month, there was no peace.
Therefore, the Yuánwài gave up such hopes
and spent his days merely rolling in money and coins.
There is a poem as evidence:
In this world, only women are foolish,
Being jealous and sour without end.
They do not think that joy and pleasure are easily scattered,
And it is the child who is the family incense for a hundred years.
Time flies like an arrow,
and Yuánwài Hú unknowingly reached the age of fifty.
The three managers of his family's pawnshops
consulted together to raise money,
prepared a formal gift of sheep and wine,
and went in early in the morning to raise their cups and offer birthday wishes.
The nine supervisors formed another group,
and the remaining domestic servants and pages
formed yet another;
they all came to kowtow.
Other Yuánwài of similar standing in the city,
and families he knew,
some came in person to offer a toast,
while others sent servants with gifts.
He could not help but order the attendants to prepare a banquet,
write out colored invitations,
and invite people to eat noodles and drink wine.
In the midst of it, he only heard among the guests and friends
the exchange of toasts between various in-laws,
all speaking of family matters and children.
The Yuánwài thought of himself having neither son nor daughter,
and his heart was silently unhappy.
When the banquet ended,
the various guests took their leave and departed.
In the chamber, the Yuànjūn prepared a separate box of delicacies
and invited the Yuánwài to drink three cups in celebration.
The Yuánwài looked at the Yuànjūn,
and suddenly the thought struck him;
his eyes brimmed, and tears fell.
When the Māma saw this,
she rose and said to the Yuánwài:
"Yuánwài,
in this house we have plenty to eat
and plenty to wear;
everything is abundant,
enough for you to enjoy.
Though it does not compare to the wealth and glory of being a Qīng or a Xiàng,
you are still a wealthy man envied by thousands and admired by tens of thousands.
Moreover, today is your birthday,
a good day;
why are you so distressed?"
Yuánwài Hú said:
"I am not concerned about food or enjoyment.
Although our family estate is substantial,
unfortunately, you and I have no son or daughter;
who will we rely on in the end?
Just today at the banquet,
everyone had relatives to converse with,
all brought together by their children,
while I alone am solitary.
As the common saying goes:
'Raise a son against old age;
store grain against famine.'
Next year I will be fifty-one,
looking toward the sixty-year mark.
The matter of bearing children
is becoming increasingly unlikely;
therefore, my heart is grieved."
The Māma said:
"In the eastern village there is a Wáng lǎoniáng
who gave birth to her firstborn at forty-eight.
I am only forty-seven this year,
not yet considered old;
could it really be that I cannot give birth?
Or perhaps the fate of having children arrives late—
one cannot say for sure.
If I reach fifty and still have no children,
then I must surely marry a maidservant to you to be your concubine.
There is also another way:
I have heard that the current Huáng Tàizǐ was also obtained by the Huángdì through prayer.
Is it possible that in our commoner's house,
we cannot obtain one through prayer?
Now in the Bǎolù Gōng within the city,
the Běijí Yòushèng Zhēnjūn
is extremely efficacious.
Why don't I choose an auspicious day and hour with you,
bring plenty of incense, candles, and paper horses to pray to the Zhēnjūn,
and ask for an heir?
Regardless of whether it is a boy or a girl,
they will be the one to worship at our graves.
I will have the maidservants prepare hot wine
to relieve the Yuánwài's boredom."
The couple drank several cups,
cleared the dishes, and retired to rest.
After several more days,
just as they met an auspicious day and hour,
they ordered the attendants to buy incense and paper,
and prepared the palanquin and horses.
Followed by maidservants,
they went directly to the gates of Bǎolù Gōng and stepped down from the palanquin.
Entering the palace,
they went to the main hall and burned incense;
they did not fail to burn it everywhere in the two galleries as well.
Coming to the Zhēnwǔ Diàn,
Yuánwài Hú piously prayed, stating his birth date,
asking for a son or a daughter
to be a descendant of the Hú family line.
The Yuánwài bowed as if a mountain of gold were collapsing
or a pillar of jade were falling,
clacking his teeth and kowtowing;
the Māma likewise bowed several times as if inserting candles.
After the prayer, they burned the paper offerings,
left the temple, and returned home;
of this, no more need be said.
From then on,
on the first
and fifteenth of every month,
they went to burn incense and pray for a child;
half a year passed in this way.
Suddenly one day,
in the twelfth lunar month,
it was the day for settling accounts in the pawnshops.
Moreover, as the end of winter approached,
those who needed to pawn were pawning,
and those who needed to redeem were redeeming.
The managers and supervisors had to attend to customers
and also prepare to clear and hand over the accounts;
how busy they were!
Only the pawnshop in the middle,
which dealt in antiques,
was after all a bit more idle than the others.
As the supervisor was in the pawnshop calculating the accounts of principal and interest for the items pawned and redeemed throughout the year,
the cloth curtain was suddenly lifted,
and a xiānshēng entered.
That xiānshēng wore a fish-tail iron Daoist cap
and a scarlet robe with black borders and flame patterns.
In his left hand, he carried a basket made of brambles,
and in his right, he held a fan made of tortoise shells.
His legs were wrapped in gaiters, and he wore multi-eyed hemp shoes.
He had an ethereal, otherworldly appearance;
clearly, he had the look of an immortal.
It turns out that immortals have four qualities:
they walk like the wind,
stand like a pine,
lie like a bow,
and have a voice like a bell.
He saw that gentleman lift the cloth curtain and enter,
looking at the Zhǔguǎn.
The Zhǔguǎn saw that his Daoist appearance was uncommon
and hurriedly stood up to welcome him into the pawnshop.
After performing salutations with the gentleman,
they sat on stools as host and guest.
The Zhǔguǎn said,
"Master, what instructions do you have for me?"
That gentleman said,
"I inform you, Zhǔguǎn,
does this pawnshop here
specialize in pawning qín, chess, books, and paintings?"
The Zhǔguǎn said,
"Indeed!"
The gentleman said,
"I, a poor Daoist, have a small painting
and wish to pawn it for some silver
to be redeemed later."
The Zhǔguǎn said,
"May I borrow it for a look
to see how much it is worth?"
The Zhǔguǎn thought someone followed him carrying the painting,
but he only saw the gentleman reach into a thorn-wicker basket,
put in his hand and pull out a painting
less than a foot wide,
and hand it to the Zhǔguǎn.
The Zhǔguǎn took it in his hand;
though he said nothing,
he thought to himself,
"Could the gentleman be playing a joke?
How much could this little painting be worth?"
He could not help but use a painting fork to lift it for inspection;
it was not even five feet long.
Upon looking at it,
it turned out to be a plain painting of a beautiful woman
with the three characters 'Sēngyáo Bǐ' written on it.
The painting was indeed well-executed,
but it was a bit small
and not worth much money.
The Zhǔguǎn put down the painting fork,
turned around and asked,
"Master, how much do you want to pawn it for?"
The gentleman said,
"This painting is no small matter;
I want to pawn it for one hundred taels of silver."
The Zhǔguǎn said,
"Master, do not joke;
as for this small painting,
it is worth no more than five or six hundred coins.
To pawn it for a hundred taels of silver
is a difference of many times over;
how can it be pawned!"
The gentleman said,
"This was painted by Zhāng Sēngyáo of the Jìn Dynasty,
a thing rare in the world."
The Zhǔguǎn said,
"From Zhāng Sēngyáo until now, it has been over five hundred years;
yet this painting of a beautiful woman
is still brand new.
There are many fake paintings in the world today;
what you say is far too excessive."
The gentleman said,
"Since you cannot recognize its authenticity,
let it be pawned for only fifty taels then!"
The Zhǔguǎn said,
"Even for five taels it cannot be pawned!"
The gentleman insisted on pawning it,
but the Zhǔguǎn simply refused;
when told to leave, he refused to go.
The two argued about fake and real,
complaining of too much or too little.
While they were in the midst of arguing,
the sound of shoes was heard
and footsteps rang out;
where the central cloth curtain was raised,
the Yuánwài strolled out.
He asked the Zhǔguǎn,
"Has the noon incense been burned yet?"
The Zhǔguǎn said,
"I inform the Yuánwài,
the noon incense has been burned!"
That gentleman looked at the Yuánwài and said,
"Yuánwài,
I salute you!"
The Yuánwài said,
"Master, please be seated.
Serve tea!"
The Yuánwài only thought he was there to collect alms.
He saw the Zhǔguǎn lift the painting with the fork
and present it to the Yuánwài, saying,
"This Master has this small painting
and insists on pawning it for fifty taels of silver;
I do not dare to make the decision."
The Yuánwài took a look
and laughed, saying,
"Master, although this painting of yours is good,
it is not worth so much;
how can it be pawned for fifty taels!"
That gentleman said,
"Yuánwài,
you only know one thing
but not the other.
Although this painting is small,
it has a wondrous quality."
The Yuánwài said,
"I would like to hear the details."
The gentleman said,
"This is not the place to talk;
please step aside
so that I may speak in detail."
The Yuánwài and the gentleman held hands and walked directly into the study,
where there was no one around.
The Yuánwài said,
"What is wondrous about this painting?"
The gentleman said,
"This painting is not like ordinary artwork;
it is from the brush of an immortal.
In the stillness of late night,
without letting a single person see,
hang the painting in a private room,
burn a stick of fine incense,
light two candles,
give a cough,
and tap three times on the table,
inviting the celestial maiden to descend and drink tea.
As a gust of wind passes,
the celestial maiden in the painting will come down."
Hearing this, the Yuánwài
thought to himself,
"If it is so,
it truly is a celestial painting.
Only I fear it may not be so!"
Seeing him hesitate, the gentleman
then said,
"If the Yuánwài does not believe it,
leave the painting here for now.
Try it tonight
and come to collect the pawn price tomorrow."
The Yuánwài said,
"Since you say so, Master,
it surely is not a false claim.
May I ask your honored surname?"
The gentleman said,
"I, a poor Daoist, am surnamed Zhāng,
named Luán,
with the pseudonym Chōngxiāo Chǔshì."
The Yuánwài nodded
and immediately came out with the gentleman,
instructing the Zhǔguǎn:
"Pawn it for Mr. Zhāng then."
The Zhǔguǎn said,
"If he does not come to redeem it in the future,
it will be none of my business."
The Yuánwài said,
"I don't need you to worry.
Just make a note in the ledger
saying I pawned it myself, and that's that."
While inviting the gentleman to a vegetarian meal, the Yuánwài
tucked the painting into his sleeve,
and then entered the back hall with the gentleman to sit and finish the meal.
The Yuánwài saw the gentleman out;
the Zhǔguǎn weighed out exactly fifty taels of white silver and handed it to the gentleman,
who bid farewell and departed.
That is all to be said of that.
At home, the Yuánwài was restricted by his wife;
ordinary women
could not even come near him.
Moreover, having heard she was a celestial maiden,
enchanting and beautiful,
someone the likes of whom he had never met in his life,
how could his soul not be shaken as at Luòpǔ,
and his spirit not wander at Yángtái?
That day, he wished he could knock the sun out of the sky with a single punch,
and stand on the watchtower to urge the drum to start beating immediately.
Just as it is said:
Eyes watching for the victory banner,
ears listening for good news.
Before it grew dark,
he first ordered the servant on duty to sweep the study
and arrange the incense burner,
candlestick,
tea stand,
hot water pot, and such.
Having devised a plan in advance,
he said to his wife:
"I have some accounts that are unclear;
tonight I must go to the study to calculate them carefully.
Quickly, have dinner brought for me to eat."
His wife believed him without suspicion,
and indeed prepared dinner early,
which the couple finished.
The Yuánwài said,
"Wife, please rest first;
I will be back shortly."
Unnoticed, the tower drum sounded,
and the temple bell rang;
it was already the hour of the first watch.
One only saw:
At the crossroads,
human shadows gradually thin out.
Clouds in the nine heavens
darkly lock away the mountain light.
Travelers from the eight directions
disperse into groups to find lodging at the "East House."
Seven bright stars—
see the Běidǒu hanging high and tilted.
Shouts over the Liùbó game beneath the moon
are none other than playboys and drinkers.
Diligent recitation of the Wǔjīng before the lamp
are all talented men and scholars.
Drum sounds from four sides hasten the night,
and three parts of cold air pierce through the heavy curtains.
Two painted candles, the fragrant chamber is quiet;
a single Chán lamp, the Buddhist temple is pure.
Hú Yuánwài went straight to the study,
pushed open the window,
and stepped inside.
He instructed the attendant on duty:
"You wait outside.
Turn back and close the window and door.
Once the lamp is lit,
and the water in the pot on the stove is bubbling and boiling."
Yuánwài took some high-grade Lóngtuán tea cakes
and placed them in the pot.
He burned a censer of incense
and lit two candles.
He took the painting fork,
and hung the painting up;
she was truly a bewitchingly beautiful woman who looked as if she could be plucked from the paper.
Yuánwài gave a cough,
and tapped three times upon the table.
By the side of the table,
a gentle breeze began to stir.
This gust of wind
was truly:
Good at gathering the grass before the courtyard,
able to part the duckweed upon the water.
Moving the curtains with deep intent,
extinguishing the candle with utter ruthlessness.
The ancient temple transmits the sound of the bell,
and the high tower sends forth the beat of the drum.
Only the roar of a thousand trees is heard,
not a sliver of its form is seen.
Where the wind passed,
the beauty in the painting
made a vivid leap
onto the table.
With another leap,
she was on the floor.
From head to toe,
she stood five feet and three inches tall,
born as fair as a flower or jade,
beautiful beyond words.
It was truly:
Add a finger and she is too long,
subtract a finger and she is too short.
Applying rouge makes her too red,
applying powder makes her too white.
Without makeup, her natural state
cannot be captured even by the finest paints.
She possessed a chén yú luò yàn countenance,
and a bì yuè xiū huā beauty.
The woman looked at Yuánwài
and gave a deep wànfú bow.
Yuánwài hurried to return the gesture.
He went to the pot on the stove,
poured a cup of tea and handed it to the woman,
then poured another for himself to accompany her.
When the tea was finished
and the cups were returned to the stand,
not a word had been spoken.
With a gust of wind, the woman
returned once more into the painting.
Yuánwài was overcome with joy
and said:
"This painting is indeed spiritual.
For this first time,
I shall not pester her.
I will wait for the second time;
it will not be too late to converse with her in detail."
Then he rolled up the painting scroll himself
and called the attendant to put away the utensils.
Yuánwài returned to his bedroom to rest.
This needs no further mention.
On the second day,
he again said he was going to settle accounts.
Hurriedly he urged for dinner to be eaten
and went to the study again.
Meanwhile, Zhāng Yuànjūn thought to herself:
"Yuánwài managed the accounts last night,
and he is settling accounts again tonight.
I do not believe there are so many accounts to settle.
If there are accounts to settle,
where did his daytime efforts go?
Yet he is so pressed for time at night!
This matter is suspicious."
She told a maid to carry a lantern in front
while she followed behind straight to the study.
Near the window, she heard what sounded like the voice of a woman inside.
She walked softly to the window,
dipped her little finger in some saliva,
and gently poked a hole in the paper window.
Peering through,
she saw a woman sitting across from Yuánwài and speaking with him.
Two streaks of fury shot from the soles of her feet to the top of her head.
A nameless fire in her heart
rose three thousand rods high.
Unable to restrain herself,
she reached out her hand,
pushed open the window and door,
and burst into the study.
Yuánwài was startled
and stood up, saying:
"Madam, what are you doing?"
She was a ball of rage
and said:
"What am I doing?
You old beggar,
you ignorant old man,
you've done a fine thing!
You shameless old man,
for two nights in a row,
you used the excuse of settling accounts
to carry out this heartless and unrighteous business here.
This vile creature of unknown origin—
who lured her here?
Speak quickly!"
In the midst of the clamor,
a gust of wind passed and the woman had already returned into the painting.
Madam cried out in fury:
"Méixiāng,
come,
find her for me!
I'll teach you not to panic."
Yuánwài said nothing,
but thought to himself:
"Even if you turn this study upside down,
you will find nowhere to look."
When she could not find the woman,
her anger piled up.
Raising her head suddenly,
she saw the painting of the beauty hanging on the wall.
She grabbed it and tore it down,
then burned it over the lamp
and threw it on the floor.
Seeing her in such a great rage,
Yuánwài did not dare to snatch it away.
The painting burned brightly,
and the paper ashes rose from the floor and whirled around,
eventually swirling to her feet.
Fearing the fire would burn her clothes,
she stepped back two paces,
only to see the paper ashes surge directly into her mouth.
She gave a loud cry
and suddenly collapsed to the ground.
A poem serves as witness:
The spirit accidentally entered the romantic record,
and with the flames, returned to the Líhèntiān.
Because the demonic energy was not fully extinguished,
it returned to this house of fire to form a marriage bond.
Hú Yuánwài was flustered
and ordered the maid to help her up.
Sitting her on the floor,
he poured some hot water from the pot
and poured it into her to wake her.
They helped her up
and settled her into a chair.
Madam cursed again:
"Ignorant old man,
you've done a fine thing!
Call the servant girl to help me to the bedroom to recover."
She slept until the middle of the night,
feeling somewhat unwell.
From then on,
her eyebrows lowered and her eyes became slow,
her breasts swelled and her belly rose;
she was pregnant.
Hú Yuánwài was very happy,
but there were two things
that made him unhappy.
First, it was a pity this immortal painting
was burned by his wife,
and he would never see the immortal woman's face again.
Second, he feared the gentleman would come to redeem it in the future,
and how could he return the painting to him?
This needs no further mention.
Time flies like an arrow,
and days and months move like a shuttle.
After a year had passed,
the wife was nearly ready to give birth.
Hú Yuánwài went before the family hall to burn incense and make a vow.
Suddenly, he heard a commotion at the gate.
An attendant reported to the Yuánwài:
"The gentleman who painted the portrait before is at the gate."
When Hú Yuánwài heard this,
he felt as if he had been punched in the heart.
He had no choice but to come out and welcome him, saying:
"Master,
another year has passed without us meeting.
I did not dare to inform you,
but today my wife is currently in labor.
It is by fate that you, Master, have arrived."
He saw the gentleman laugh loudly and say:
"Your wife is in distress today;
I, a poor Daoist, have some medicine here."
From within a thorn-branch basket,
he took out a small gourd,
poured out a single red pill,
and handed it to the Yuánwài.
He instructed him to have her swallow it with pure water,
and she would give birth immediately.
The Yuánwài took the medicine
and invited the Master to stay for a vegetarian meal.
The Master said:
"The household is busy and pressed for time today;
I do not dare to trouble you.
I shall come another day to offer congratulations and enjoy a meal!"
Having finished speaking,
he took his leave and departed,
without mentioning the matter of redeeming the painting.
Leaving the Master aside,
let it be told that the Yuánwài gave the medicine to his wife to take.
In no time at all,
she gave birth to a daughter,
and the Yuánwài was greatly pleased.
After the old midwife had attended to her,
they inevitably performed the three-day bath, the hundred-day celebration,
and at the one-year anniversary, they gave her a childhood name. Because she was conceived when the paper ashes surged up,
and she was carried in the womb from that,
she was therefore named Yǒng'ér.
Later, they disliked the character 'Yǒng' for 'surge' as unsuitable,
so they changed it to the 'Yǒng' meaning 'eternal.'
Time passed swiftly,
and before they knew it, Yǒng'ér had grown to the age of seven.
She was born exceptionally refined and beautiful,
with a fair face and black hair,
bright eyes and white teeth,
just like the Dragon Girl who sits at the side of Guānyīn.
The husband and wife
cherished her like a pearl in the palm
or jade in a casket.
The Yuánwài invited a professor to the house
to teach Yǒng'ér how to read.
This professor was surnamed Chén and named Shàn.
He was an honest and mature man,
a long-experienced teacher of punctuation and reading.
Once the Yuánwài had invited him to the house,
the husband and wife
treated him with great respect.
It is truly said:
Though the kind mother protects her precious daughter,
she is glad to find a virtuous host for the fine guest.
Let this part of the story be set aside for a moment.
Now let it be told that since the day Eunuch Lěi lost the bride,
he had sent people in all directions to search for her,
but there was no trace.
Fearing that Zhāng Luán might turn hostile,
he went to great lengths to apologize and flatter him.
Zhāng Luán already knew it was not the Lěi family's doing,
so he was happy to accept his respect.
However, because Chancellor Dǐng was sycophantic and treacherous,
he did not get along well with the Crown Prince.
In his later years, Emperor Zhēnzōng
suffered from a paralytic stroke
and could not attend court.
Therefore, although Eunuch Lěi was very much inclined to recommend Zhāng Luán,
there was no place to exert his influence.
Zhāng Luán had also listened to the nonsense of the little demon spirits;
moreover, seeing that Hú Yuánwài's family had actually conceived and given birth to a daughter,
it appeared there was some divine efficacy to it.
As for the matter of his own career advancement,
he did not consider it very urgent.
He simply used Shùjǐng Yuán as his lodgings
and wandered leisurely inside and outside the city of Dōngjīng.
Firstly, he wanted to find and meet Shèng Gūgu,
and secondly, he wanted to observe the whereabouts of Hú Yuánwài's daughter.
Time flies like an arrow,
and before long, it reached the first year of Jǐngdé.
Emperor Zhēnzōng passed away,
and the Crown Prince ascended the throne;
this was Emperor Rénzōng.
Because he commissioned Lěi Yǔnggōng to manage the construction of the imperial tomb,
and Lěi mistakenly moved the imperial chamber to an ill-fated location,
he was impeached by Scholar Wáng Zēng,
who also exposed many wicked deeds of Chancellor Dǐng's internal and external collusion.
Emperor Rénzōng's dragon countenance flared in great anger;
he demoted Dǐng Wèi to the position of military commissary of Yuǎnzhōu.
Lěi Yǔnggōng was immediately executed,
his family property was confiscated,
and even Shùjǐng Yuán was seized as government property.
Because Zhāng Luán had lived in this garden for a long time,
he feared being implicated in any trouble,
so he extricated himself in advance and went far away,
wandering through the rivers and lakes.
Suddenly one day,
he traveled to the region of Pùzhōu in Shāndōng.
It was then the season of the fourth lunar month,
and there was a severe drought.
Every county had issued notices widely summoning masters of the law to pray for rain,
but none were successful.
He heard that there was a female Daoist nun
who had taken down the notice in Bópíng County to establish an altar
and set a date to pray for rain.
Zhāng Luán thought to himself:
"This must surely be Shèng Gūgu;
I shall go and see what is happening!"
He quickened his pace
and headed straight for Bópíng County.
It is truly said:
A long drought will surely meet with sweet rain;
do not say that one only meets an old friend in a distant land.
In the end, upon this journey of Zhāng Luán,
would he meet Shèng Gūgu or not?
Please listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
The third month of spring and the fourth of summer are good for planting rice seedlings,
ten thousand eyes gaze anxiously, hoping for rain and sun.
We only hope the virtuous chancellors of the world
will diligently harmonize the elements to avoid disaster.
The story says that when Zhāng Luán heard there was an old Daoist nun in Bópíng County ascending the altar to pray for rain,
he suspected Shèng Gūgu was there
and ran there like a trail of smoke.
Entering the city gate of Bópíng County,
he saw a proclamation hanging inside the gate.
On a small stool beside the proclamation, an old man sat blankly.
Although many people were coming and going,
few stopped to look at the notice.
Zhāng Luán stepped forward
and read it from the beginning:
"Chúnyú Hòu, the Magistrate of Bópíng County,
regarding the matter of praying for rain:
This county has suffered a long drought,
the fields have been abandoned,
and prayers for rain have gone unanswered.
If there are any travelers from the four directions,
regardless of their status,
who can perform the rites to bring down rain
and save the people,
let them take down this notice and come forward;
this county will treat them with the rites due to a master.
On the day the rain falls,
this county has already collected one thousand strings of cash in the treasury
to be given immediately as a reward;
we shall certainly not treat you with neglect.
This notice is hereby issued.
April, the third year of Tiānshèng.
Issued."
After Zhāng Luán had finished reading,
he cupped his hands toward the old man and said:
"When did it last rain in your honorable county?"
Seeing that his Daoist appearance was extraordinary,
the old man quickly stood up and replied:
"Since the eleventh month of last year
until now, there has not been a single drop of water.
It has been a severe drought for nearly six months!"
Zhāng Luán said:
"I heard that a female Daoist from afar
took down the official notice to pray for rain;
is this news true?
Where is she now?"
The old man spread his hands
and curled his lip, saying:
"Where is she? She’s long since vanished!"
Zhāng Luán laughed and asked:
"But why is that?"
The old man said:
"This female Daoist's surname is Xī;
she calls herself the Nǚ Shénxiān.
She is over fifty years old.
The disciples who follow her,
both men and women,
number about ten in total.
The women are called Xiāngū,
and the men are called Xiānguān.
According to her, she came from the Mansion of Chief Administrator Lè in Dàwàngǔ,
and she is skilled at summoning wind and rain.
When she first took down the notice,
the Xiànzhǔ Xiānggōng showed her great respect.
She wanted to go ten lǐ outside the North Gate
to choose a high mound
and establish a rain-altar
named the Wǔlóngtán.
She fashioned dragon shapes in the five colors of green,
crimson,
red,
white,
and black,
arranging them according to the directions.
She also forced the Xiànzhǔ Xiānggōng to demand one thousand guàn of cash from the local area as a reward;
only after the full amount of money was collected and stored in the treasury
did she finally ascend the altar.
The Magistrate agreed to everything.
The ritual she performed was something called the Method of Yuèbèi.
She required every ward
and every neighborhood
to report the birth dates of pregnant women.
Based on her calculations, she singled one out and designated her the Bámǔ,
saying that she carried a Hànbá in her womb.
Without allowing any explanation,
she ordered the county office to bring the woman before the altar.
This female Daoist sat above,
directing her disciples to beat gongs and drums,
spray water, and recite incantations.
They made the woman lose consciousness
and then stripped her completely naked,
laying her on a wooden door panel,
with her two feet,
two hands,
and her hair
all immersed in five basins filled to the brim with water.
An Xiānguān faced the north with disheveled hair and a sword,
stepping on her belly with his right foot,
while his mouth chanted unknown words.
The other male and female disciples—
some waving flags,
others striking tiles—
made a great clamor.
After a day of such chaos,
this pregnant woman was tormented nearly to death,
yet not a single cloud appeared in the sky.
When the sun set,
they had to end the session.
She claimed the Lóngwáng was not at home today
but promised there would surely be rain tomorrow.
She told the Magistrate to give three guàn of 'shame-covering money' to the woman's husband
and ordered them to take her back.
On the second day,
another Bámǔ was chosen
to be brought before the altar for the ritual.
The common people were filled with indignation
and instantly gathered three or four hundred people
who threw bricks
and hurled tiles,
shouting like thunder,
wanting to beat the master and disciples to death.
This Daoist Xī was terrified,
and she and her group changed their clothes
and fled from behind the altar.
The Magistrate did not pursue the matter
but issued this other official notice
to be posted at every gate.
I am the local Lǐzhèng;
fearing that someone might come to take down the notice,
I must stay here and watch."
Zhāng Luán laughed heartily and said:
"So that's how it is!
I, this poor Daoist, will spend a moment of my time
to pray at an altar for a bit of sweet rain for your amusement."
Having finished speaking,
he took down the notice with one hand.
The old man came forward, grabbed him, and said:
"You are bold to take down the notice;
do you truly have some real ability?
Do not boast big words only to have a small result,
having only a beginning
and no end,
like that Nǚ Shénxiān who went up to the altar
and fled from the back."
Zhāng Luán said:
"How much rain do you want
to cause such a fuss?"
The old man said:
"We only need three chǐ of sweet rain,
and it will be enough for both high and low ground."
Zhāng Luán smiled:
"I thought you wanted to overturn the riverbeds
and sweep the sea's edge;
that would have cost me a few hours of deliberation.
For just this little bit of rain,
what difficulty could there be?"
Then, the old man left his stool at someone's house
and led Zhāng Luán along the road in front of the county office.
The common people saw the Lǐzhèng leading a Daoist into the city;
thinking he must be the one who took the notice to pray for rain,
everyone was delighted
and followed to watch.
It happened that Bópíng Xiàn had seen no rain for nearly six months,
and the drought was extraordinary.
One could see:
Dust rose from the riverbeds,
and cracks appeared in the fields.
Trees took on a scorched and withered color,
and wells held only muddy sludge.
Under the blazing white sun,
the heavens seemed to glare with menacing power.
Amidst the rolling yellow dust,
the grass seemed to bow its head and lie down.
People carried money to exchange for water,
with families competing to buy it first.
When welcoming guests with tea,
mostly they called out in vain for what could not be produced.
It was just like the days of the drought in the Hàn era,
or like the time before the Shāng king’s prayer.
Travelers on the road were parched as if burning,
and the hidden dragons at the bottom of the wells slept and would not rise.
There were also several temples and monasteries in this county;
the monks and Daoists each followed their own liturgical traditions,
setting up altars and performing fasts,
chanting scriptures and praying.
The County Magistrate, Chúnyú Hòu,
went every morning to the Chénghuáng Miào to offer incense,
but there was no response at all.
The people made up a chant, saying:
"Pray in the morning, pray in the evening,
praying until the sun dries everything.
Beg in the morning, beg in the evening,
begging until not a drop of water flows."
The Magistrate had no plan left
and could only leave things as they were.
This day, after the offering of incense,
the morning court session had just ended.
While resting in the private residence,
a clamor of voices was heard in the hall,
and the court drum was being beaten wildly.
Startled, the Xiànlìng had no time to put on his official cap and belt properly
and ran out to the back hall in his plain clothes.
The doorman reported:
"Today, a Daoist from a distant land
has taken down the notice for rain prayers,
and the common people are crowding around him as they come forward."
The Xiànlìng ordered the Lǐzhèng to lead the people to wait outside the gate,
and invited only the Daoist to meet in the back hall.
Zhāng Luán held a thorn-woven basket in his left hand
and a palm-leaf fan in his right
as he entered gracefully.
Seeing the Xiànlìng,
he set down the basket
and gave a formal bow.
The Xiànlìng hurriedly returned the greeting
and asked:
"What is your honorable surname, Master,
and your title?
From where have you come?"
Zhāng Luán said:
"Your humble servant's surname is Zhāng,
my name is Luán,
and my style name is Chōngxiāo Chùshì.
I have come here from the sea.
Just now, seeing the notice for rain prayers,
I have come specifically to offer my services."
The Xiànlìng said:
"Is it not the Yuèbèi method that you practice, Master?"
Zhāng Luán said:
"It is not the Yuèbèi method;
it is the Rìhēi method.
If the sun is not made dark,
how can rain be obtained?"
The Xiànlìng also laughed.
He asked again:
"An Yùtán has been built outside the North Gate;
I wonder if it can be used?"
Zhāng Luán said:
"Since there is already an existing Yùtán,
then let us use that one."
The Xiànlìng said:
"In approximately how many days
can the rain be brought forth?"
Zhāng Luán said:
"If I ascend the altar in the morning,
there will be rain in the morning;
if I ascend the altar in the evening,
there will be rain in the evening."
Because Xī Dàogū had once made a fool of herself,
the Xiànlìng did not fully believe him
and said:
"You boast quite boldly, Master.
I just do not know what ritual objects you still require
so they may be prepared in advance."
Zhāng Luán said:
"I do not use ritual objects at all;
just instruct the monks and priests of the various temples and monasteries in this county who are praying for rain
to go first and sweep the altar and wait."
The Xiànlìng said:
"That is easy!
I shall give the orders tonight,
and you, Master, shall stay for a night in the Chénghuáng Miào,
and ascend the altar tomorrow morning."
Zhāng Luán said:
"I shall obey your command.
Only there is one thing:
any vacant official residence will do
for me to rest for a night.
If I go to the Chénghuáng Miào,
I fear it might trouble the deity to receive me,
making us both uneasy."
The Xiànlìng said:
"There are plenty of official residences."
Although he agreed with his mouth,
in his heart he did not think it was true.
Zhāng Luán had already sensed this
and said intentionally:
"I came here this morning on an empty stomach;
I seek some ready-made wine and food."
The Xiànlìng said:
"There is plenty of wine,
but it is only vegetarian food."
Zhāng Luán said:
"I am accustomed to eating fresh meat with my wine;
I do not eat vegetarian food."
The Xiànlìng said:
"I will not hide it from you, Master;
because of the matter of praying for rain,
there has been a ban on slaughter for over three months.
I myself eat only vegetables,
and it is not convenient to get fresh meat."
Zhāng Luán laughed and said:
"The government's ban on slaughter
has always been a mere formality.
As the saying goes:
'The government bans it, but the private citizens do not,'
which only serves to benefit the runners and the Lǐzhèng.
If you do not believe me,
at the thirteenth house in the east of the county,
the butcher Lǚ slaughtered a seventy-jīn pig this morning.
Next door, Sūn Kǒngmù is hosting guests for his son's first birthday;
he bought fifteen jīn of it,
which is now boiling in the pot.
Also, at the Gù wine shop in the west of the county,
they killed a sheep last night to sell;
there is still one cooked sheep's hoof left,
covered with rushes in a small bamboo basket
placed on the rice bucket in front of the bed.
You may ask them according to my words,
say the government will not hold it against them
and buy it from them at a fair price;
they will surely be willing to give it."
The Xiànlìng said:
"I do not believe such a thing exists!"
He summoned the buyer on duty
and, according to the Master's words,
asked to buy five jīn of pork
and a sheep's hoof from those two houses.
The runner was gone for only a short time
before he obtained the pork and the sheep's hoof
and reported:
"At first, those two houses denied it,
but after I exposed them according to your words,
they became flustered
and immediately sent out the meat,
and even dared not take the payment."
The Xiànlìng said:
"What kind of divination do you use, Master,
to be so efficacious?"
Zhāng Luán said:
"It was just a lucky hit!"
Only then did the Xiànlìng realize the Master was not like ordinary men,
and he looked upon him with new respect.
A moment later,
the runner brought a large vessel of warmed wine, about six or seven jīn,
twenty or so large Mómo,
along with the pork and the sheep's hoof,
and laid them all out on the table.
Zhāng Luán cupped his hands and said:
"I shall not stand on ceremony!"
He ate in large bowls and large chunks without restraint,
and in an instant,
he finished it like a wind sweeping away clouds,
leaving only three empty plates
and a single pot.
He said:
"I have received your gift and had a snack.
I will eat again when I get to the temple."
At that moment, the crowd was all dumbfounded and said:
"We have never seen such an eater;
what a pair of large intestines and a stomach!"
Standing behind the Xiànlìng was a handsome young servant
who chimed in:
"Without large intestines and a stomach,
how could he match that big mouth?"
Zhāng Luán heard this,
pointed a finger at the boy,
and said:
"Your mouth is not small either."
Immediately, the boy's face with vermilion lips,
unable to control itself,
stretched open all the way to the roots of his ears,
round like a vermilion lacquered bowl;
once opened, it would not close,
and he could not speak,
only shed tears.
It turned out this boy was only fifteen years old,
with hair just covering his eyebrows,
and very handsome;
he was the personal attendant most favored by the Xiànlìng.
Seeing him acting so strangely,
the Xiànlìng knew it was because he had offended the Master,
and hurriedly bowed to apologize, saying:
"Master, have pity on his youth and ignorance.
For my sake,
please forgive him!"
Zhāng Luán said:
"I did not trouble him at all."
The Xiànlìng said:
"This boy originally had a fine face!"
Zhāng Luán pointed and said:
"Now he still has a fine face!"
When the Xiànlìng turned to look,
the boy's mouth was as good as before.
A Yāsī standing by said in a low voice:
"This is the trick of blurring the eyes."
Zhāng Luán had already heard it
but did not call him out.
He asked the Xiànlìng:
"What is this Yāsī's surname?"
The Xiànlìng said:
"His surname is Lù,
and his name is Mào."
Zhāng Luán said:
"What a fine Lù Yāsī!"
Registrar Lù Yā-sī was so terrified that he hid to one side.
The County Magistrate sent men to escort Zhāng Luán to the official guest house to rest,
where wine and food for morning and evening
would be provided by the staff of the guest house.
Upon parting, Zhāng Luán made an appointment for the County Magistrate to rise early
so they could go together to the Yùtán to offer incense.
The County Magistrate said:
"This is my duty,
so naturally I shall accompany you!"
That evening in the court hall,
the County Magistrate ordered the monks and Daoist priests of all the temples and monasteries
to sweep the Five Dragon Altar clean
and arrange the furnishings neatly.
At the fifth watch tomorrow, they were to wait at the altar in advance
to welcome the Master.
He also ordered the county clerks and runners to assemble at dawn,
and assigned an official horse
to go to the guest house to wait for the Master to set out.
That night, the whole of Bópíng Xiàn was in an uproar.
The next day, as the east began to brighten,
the County Magistrate came out of the hall,
and just as he was about to enter his sedan chair,
he saw Zhāng Luán holding a palm fan in his right hand
and carrying a bramble basket in his left hand,
swaying as he walked in.
The County Magistrate met him
and asked:
"Why has the Master favored me with another visit?"
Zhāng Luán said:
"We had an appointment yesterday,
so I have come specifically to invite you to walk together."
The County Magistrate said:
"It is ten lǐ away from here;
I have already dispatched a horse to wait for you.
Has it arrived yet?"
Zhāng Luán said:
"The horse is there.
But this poor Daoist is capable of walking;
I have no use for it."
The County Magistrate asked:
"Have you had breakfast?"
Zhāng Luán said:
"I have."
The County Magistrate said:
"If that is the case,
please go on ahead.
I shall follow shortly."
Zhāng Luán said:
"This poor Daoist does not know the way to the Yùtán;
I must trouble Lù Yā-sī to accompany me."
The County Magistrate ordered Lù Mào
to lead the way properly for the Master.
Lù Yā-sī took the order from the County Magistrate
and walked closely alongside him.
In the blink of an eye,
the Master suddenly vanished,
leaving the Registrar so panicked he was at a loss.
Realizing the Master had not fallen behind,
he hurried forward to look,
and saw the Master was already about twenty or thirty paces ahead.
The Registrar thought:
"It is fine as long as he is here.
But if he were a wandering Daoist
who made grand boasts
that could not be proven,
and then slipped away at the last moment,
how could I report back?
Or if he really does not know the road
and goes the wrong way,
and the County Magistrate arrives at the Yùtán first,
it will make me look incompetent."
He exerted himself to speed up,
wanting to catch up to the Master.
He saw the Master walking slowly ahead,
yet despite his best efforts, he could not catch up.
No matter how fast or slow he walked,
the distance remained twenty or thirty paces.
The Registrar was panting from the walk
and shouted out:
"Master, slow down!
I cannot keep up with you!"
Zhāng Luán laughed loudly ahead:
"This poor Daoist is not used to walking slowly.
If you do not come to the front to lead the way,
I shall walk up into the sky
and will not pray for rain for you!"
In a panic, the Registrar ran for his life again,
his eyes fixed ahead,
but he still could not reach the Master's heels.
A poem serves as proof:
In the Art of Dùnjiǎ, the Earth-Shrinking technique is supreme;
though he walks slowly, the far distance is covered.
The talkative Registrar now labors on foot,
toyed with until sweat pours from him like water being poured.
The Registrar's sweat fell like rain,
and he was gasping for breath;
he could only shout out:
"I now know the Master's divine arts!
Please spare me!"
Zhāng Luán said:
"This poor Daoist is using a trick to deceive the eyes;
what divine art is there!"
Only then did the Registrar realize this was punishment for his slip of the tongue yesterday,
and he kowtowed to apologize.
Zhāng Luán gave a wave of his hand,
and just like a magnet attracting iron,
the Registrar found himself standing behind the Master.
The Registrar grabbed the Master
and would not let go for anything.
After only a few more steps,
they arrived at the Five Dragon Altar.
The group of monks and Daoist priests were already there.
Hearing that the new Master had arrived,
they divided into two groups and descended the altar to welcome him.
Zhāng Luán looked at this Yùtán;
it was very high and open,
surrounded by a grove of trees.
The five dragons set up by Daoist Nun Xī were still there;
they were all made of bamboo frames and paper,
painted with five-colored scales.
In the center, a large oilcloth canopy was erected,
with tables, chairs, and such provided.
After a short while,
the common people from inside and outside the city arrived in crowds,
numbering more than a thousand.
Still not seeing the County Magistrate arrive,
Zhāng Luán thought:
"This County Magistrate refused to walk with me
but put on airs,
telling me to go first
while he intends to come by sedan chair.
You are praying for rain for the people;
even if you walked this once,
you would not lose face,
yet you are so pretentious!
I shall play a trick on him this time."
He then said to a young Daoist priest:
"The County Magistrate has not arrived;
I must trouble you to go and urge him!"
He pulled the young man's left hand over,
formed a sword mudra himself,
and drew an invisible talisman on his palm.
He quickly told him to clench his fist tight
and instructed:
"When you see the County Magistrate,
deliver my words:
'Please, County Magistrate, come quickly to welcome the rain.'
If he hesitates,
open your palm as proof.
Do not open it to look on the way."
He also took off the young man's two shoes,
drew a talisman on the soles,
told him to put them on and walk fast,
and if he wanted to stop,
to shout the two words 'Duò tuì!'
As soon as the young Daoist put on his shoes, his feet felt as if they were being carried by someone,
and he sped away like the wind against his will.
After traveling about four or five lǐ,
he met the County Magistrate's vanguard arriving.
He shouted out:
"Duò tuì!"
His feet felt light,
and he was able to stop.
He saw the County Magistrate sitting in a cool sedan chair with vermilion and green gauze curtains,
with four bearers and four assistants,
walking under a green silk umbrella.
The young Daoist knelt before the sedan chair and reported:
"The Master sent me to invite you to come quickly to welcome the rain."
The County Magistrate said:
"Under such a blazing sun,
where is the rain?"
The young Daoist clenched his fist and said to the County Magistrate:
"Fearing you might hesitate,
he ordered me to open my palm as proof."
Having spoken,
he opened his fist.
Suddenly, a crack of thunder
erupted from his palm,
and the poles of the sedan chair were snapped clean in two by the shock.
The County Magistrate was so terrified he could not cover his ears in time;
his face turned the color of ash,
and he tumbled straight out of the sedan chair.
Everyone was thrown into confusion,
and even the young Daoist was stunned.
After a while,
