just as the County Magistrate was about to send people to nearby houses
to borrow a mule or a horse to ride,
he saw a group of monks
leading many common people towards him,
urging the County Magistrate to go to the altar to offer incense.
The County Magistrate, having suffered this fright,
did not dare to delay.
At this moment, he could only have his attendants support him as he walked to the altar.
Meanwhile, he sent someone back to the county seat to get another sedan chair and horse
to wait at the Yùtán for his return trip.
Zhāng Luán saw the Xiànlìng arrive,
went to the hall to greet him,
and asked:
"Xiànggōng, why did you not come by sedan chair?"
The Xiànlìng recounted the incident of the thunder striking the sedan chair poles
and said:
"So it turns out you possess such supernatural powers and techniques, Master;
praying for rain today will not be difficult,
and it is the good fortune of the ten thousand people!"
Zhāng Luán said:
"It is not that this humble Daoist is boasting, but
wind,
thunder,
clouds,
and rain
are all things inside my waist pouch.
Let me perform a small trick
for Your Honor to see.
I beg to borrow a large umbrella."
The Xiànlìng ordered a three-layered blue silk umbrella to be handed to the Master.
The Master took the umbrella in his hand,
spun it twice,
suddenly tossed it upward,
and shouted:
"Rise!"
He blew a breath, and the umbrella gradually ascended
to the highest point,
transforming into a dark cloud
that covered the sunlight
and completely dimmed its red glow.
Everyone looked up at it,
and then Zhāng Luán beckoned with his hand.
The dark cloud fell straight to the ground,
becoming a blue silk umbrella again,
and the scorching sun shone through once more.
The Xiànlìng felt both joy and fear in his heart;
he invited the Master to the seat of honor
and prepared to bow in supplication,
asking him to quickly bestow sweet rain
to save the region from its plight.
Zhāng Luán said:
"There is no need for excessive ceremony.
Ten days ago,
while passing through Nánmín Shān,
I encountered heavy rain.
This humble Daoist collected those rain clouds and kept them here;
today I shall give them away to form a karmic bond with your county!"
He reached into his bramble basket,
took out a small gourd,
placed it before the altar,
and instructed the Xiànlìng to burn incense and pray.
Zhāng Luán formed mudras and chanted incantations;
when the ritual was complete,
he pulled out the gourd’s stopper
and lightly fanned it several times with a palm-leaf fan.
Suddenly, a great wind arose before the altar,
a stream of black vapor came out of the gourd,
shot straight into the nine heavens,
and became a sky full of thick clouds.
Zhāng Luán put away the gourd,
walked to the side of the black dragon made of bamboo and paper,
and commanded:
"Black Dragon,
Black Dragon,
assist my divine powers.
Ride the clouds swiftly,
make the rain fall heavily.
Three feet of sweet rain
to comfort the farmers.
Those who obey me shall be fortunate,
those who oppose me shall face calamity."
Then the black dragon's scales and whiskers all moved,
and it suddenly soared into the sky.
In an instant,
lightning flashed wildly,
thunder roared fiercely,
and raindrops as large as fists began to fall.
The common people were so frightened they scattered in all directions.
The Xiànlìng also wanted to descend from the altar,
but the sedan chair from the county office had not yet arrived,
so he could only hide with the clerks, attendants, monks, and Daoists
under the cloth canopy.
Shortly,
the rain poured down like a deluge.
Fortunately, the canopy was thoroughly soaked in oil
and propped up on high poles,
so it prevented leaking from above and dampness from below.
However, there was no shelter on the four sides;
everyone tilted tables and chairs to shield themselves from the rain.
Some had brought parasols
and opened them against the wind.
In the midst of the chaos,
golden snakes of lightning flickered wildly,
and thunderclaps sounded continuously,
not leaving the Rain Altar
but circling around it.
The Xiànlìng said:
"May I ask the Master,
why is the God of Thunder angry today?"
Zhāng Luán said:
"I suppose he has set his eyes on a few villains!"
Then Zhāng Luán shouted loudly:
"Léibù, hear my command:
if there are truly corrupt officials or clerks,
monks who have broken their vows,
or Daoists of filthy conduct,
only then are you permitted to strike.
If there are none such as these,
you should retreat immediately."
At that moment, the thunderclaps became even more continuous;
the terrified Xiànlìng was the first to prostrate himself in worship,
confessing his faults.
Among the clerks, attendants, monks, and Daoists, those who had spoken boastfully
were all in a panic,
bowing together in a heap.
Zhāng Luán laughed until his eyes were but narrow slits.
After about two hours,
the sound of rain finally ceased,
and the thunder and lightning also stopped.
Only then did everyone feel at ease
and climbed back up.
Looking down from the altar,
they saw the mountains echoing and rivers roaring,
ponds full and ditches overflowing;
there were a full three feet of sweet rain.
Just as the Xiànlìng was praising the Master’s merit,
someone below the altar shouted sternly:
"What beginner
dares to show off his tricks here
and intimidate everyone?
Could it be that you want to swindle them out of these one thousand strings of cash?"
When Zhāng Luán looked,
it was a lame Daoist.
He was short in stature,
his clothes were filthy,
and he held a Qīnglí Zhàng.
He limped up to the altar step by step through the heavy rain,
yet not a single thread on his body was wet.
Arriving at the altar,
he put down his staff
and bowed to the Xiànlìng with hands clasped.
The Xiànlìng and the others were all terrified.
Zhāng Luán said:
"This humble Daoist has bestowed an altar’s worth of sweet rain
to save living beings;
you, this beggar Daoist, come here to cause trouble—
do you dare to compete in magic with me?"
The lame one laughed and said:
"What magic do you think you have
that you dare to compete with this master!"
Zhāng Luán was furious;
he tossed his palm-leaf fan
and shouted:
"Go quickly and strike that beggar Daoist!"
The fan flew slowly through the air,
heading straight for the lame one’s head.
The lame one laughed heartily
and tossed his head;
his tattered headscarf bobbed up twice,
popped off his head,
and went to meet the fan.
It was clearly like two eagles wrestling,
one above and one below.
The lame one shouted:
"Where is my staff?"
Suddenly, the Qīnglí Zhàng lying on the ground leaped up
and jumped step by step to strike Zhāng Luán.
Zhāng Luán flicked his sleeve,
and the bramble basket at his side
rose from the ground to meet it.
Like a rattan shield parrying a staff,
they went back and forth.
Everyone was so frightened they hid to one side;
even the Xiànlìng did not dare to step forward.
The two sides competed,
neither winning nor losing,
and both withdrew their magic.
Zhāng Luán was greatly enraged,
and summoning his spirits,
he muttered incantations in his mouth.
He raised his hand and beckoned toward the north,
shouting loudly,
"Black Dragon, come quickly!"
When the lame man heard this,
he struck once on the head of the Yellow Dragon upon the altar.
Then the Black Dragon that had previously flown off to bring rain was seen
flying toward the altar amidst clouds and mist.
Here, the Yellow Dragon
bristled its mane and spread its scales,
leapt up from the ground,
and met the Black Dragon to fight in mid-air.
Since ancient times it has been said
that Earth can overcome Water;
thus the Black Dragon was no match for the Yellow Dragon.
Zhāng Luán called out again,
"Azure Dragon, go quickly and help!"
The lame man gave the White Dragon another blow with his palm,
and just as the Azure Dragon flew up,
the White Dragon went to meet it.
This so annoyed Zhāng Luán that he gnashed his teeth in rage
and hurriedly called the Vermilion Dragon for help.
Five dragons danced wildly in the air,
exactly according to Jīn,
Mù,
Shuǐ,
Huǒ,
and Tǔ, the five elements,
generating and overcoming one another
as they became tangled together in a mass.
A fierce wind rose up,
and the cloth awnings and frames were all blown down.
While everyone was struggling to keep their footing,
a monk suddenly stepped out,
with gold rings hanging from his ears
and wearing a fiery red kashaya,
holding a crystal alms bowl in his hand.
No one knew where this monk had come from;
he shouted,
"You two fellow cultivators,
do not harm the harmony between you.
Let this poor monk mediate for you."
He threw the crystal alms bowl in his hand forcefully into the air,
and it transformed into a brilliant five-colored pearl.
The five dragons all came to play with this pearl,
and forming a circle and a formation, they departed.
The lame man had already recognized him as Dànzǐ Héshang;
he secretly rejoiced,
but neither of them gave the secret away.
The monk was seen clapping his hands and saying,
"The two of you were gambling with magic,
with no winner or loser.
Whichever one can retrieve the crystal alms bowl and return it to this poor monk,
I shall judge him to be the elder brother."
Zhāng Luán and the lame man replied in unison,
"What difficulty is there in that!"
The two of them secretly chanted spells
and withdrew their magic.
The dragon shapes made of bamboo frames and pasted paper
returned to their original places as before,
just as if they had never moved,
yet no one saw where they had flown back from.
Zhāng Luán was seen taking a crystal alms bowl from his sleeve
and returning it to the monk.
The lame man said,
"His is a fake;
the real one is with me."
Sure enough, he also took one out from his waist,
identical in size.
The monk accepted neither of them
but instead felt around in his own sleeve and produced an alms bowl.
He laughed and said,
"This poor monk's is right here;
you two should stop teasing me!"
It turned out that Zhāng Luán's alms bowl
was transformed from a gourd in his sleeve,
and the lame man's alms bowl
was transformed from a willow ladle at his waist.
Now that the real alms bowl had appeared,
both objects returned to their original forms.
Each of them laughed loudly
and took their things back.
Zhāng Luán was also inwardly shocked
and thought,
"This beggar-Daoist's skill
is not inferior to mine,
and I do not know where this boorish monk came from,
who is even more formidable."
There is a poem to prove it:
Sūn and Páng pitted their wits, but were not true rivals;
The struggle between Chǔ and Hàn is not worth boasting of.
How can they compare to the display of magic at the Rain Altar,
where everyone watched until their eyes grew blurred.
Only the noisy chatter of the people below the altar could be heard;
the common people arrived in an endless stream,
everyone holding incense to welcome the masters into the county.
The sedans and horses from the county office had also arrived.
The Xiànlìng finally dared to show himself and asked,
"Just now, this lowly official saw that all three masters possess techniques that could shake heaven and earth,
being of equal caliber.
In my opinion,
the Three Teachings share the same source;
let us not quarrel over formalities.
Please come to my humble county,
where I shall honor you all.
Horses have been prepared here;
please mount them,
and I hope you will not refuse."
The lame man, seeing the horses below the altar,
intended to ride one.
Zhāng Luán still felt some lingering resentment
and, deliberately taking advantage of the man's lameness,
grabbed him and said,
"We are not permitted to ride;
let us all go on foot
to see who is faster."
The lame man said,
"Are you perhaps a fool?"
Zhāng Luán asked,
"How am I a fool?"
The lame man said,
"If you aren't a fool,
why would you leave the horses to go on foot!"
Everyone burst out laughing.
The Xiànlìng said,
"Since the three of you are unwilling to ride horses,
it is only proper for this official to accompany you on foot."
Dànzǐ Héshang said,
"The ground is muddy;
it would not be fitting for the officials to lose their dignity.
I and my two Daoist friends
shall go ahead and wait for you in your esteemed county."
Having finished speaking,
he took the hands of the two Daoists
and walked down from the altar.
At first, the common people only recognized the master who had prayed for rain,
but now suddenly a monk and a Daoist were added,
and they did not know where they had come from.
It was very strange;
they parted on both sides,
making a path for them to lead the way.
Dànzǐ Héshang was in front,
Zhāng Luán was in the middle,
and the Lame One was behind.
After walking not more than a few steps,
the Lame One intentionally limped and said:
“You two walk slowly,
the ground is so hard to walk on!”
Zhāng Luán, exactly in agreement with his intent,
pulled Dànzǐ Héshang along,
and they walked even faster.
They only heard a cry from behind:
“Oh my!”
When they looked back,
there was a small puddle by the roadside;
the Lame One’s right foot had fallen in.
When he lifted it,
his left foot couldn't hold its grip,
and with a "plop," he tumbled headfirst into the water.
Zhāng Luán exclaimed:
“How regrettable!”
Dànzǐ Héshang said:
“Don't mind him,
let’s just go to the county office and wait for him.”
By the time the two entered the county gate,
they saw a person on the county hall leaning on a green goosefoot staff,
limping down,
calling out:
“Why are you two so late?”
Zhāng Luán was greatly shocked;
that person was none other than
the Lame One.
Only then did he realize that tumbling into the puddle
was the technique of Water Escape.
At this point, Zhāng Luán
was finally convinced in his heart.
On the county hall, they exchanged formalities again,
and only then did he ask for their names and titles.
The Lame One said:
“My humble surname is Zuǒ and my given name is Chù.
Because my left leg was injured,
I changed my name to Zuǒ Qué.
Among my fellow cultivators, I am called Master Qué Shī.
This is my senior dharma brother,
whose title is Dàn Shī,
and his illusory name is Dànzǐ Héshang.”
Zhāng Luán said:
“Could you two be the ones practicing the Dao with Shèng Gūgū at the house of Yáng Xúnjiǎn?”
The Lame One said:
“How do you know this?”
Zhāng Luán said:
“I have been to the Yǒngxīng area
and have often heard people mention your great names,
but I never had the chance to meet you.
Today, fortunately, we have met;
I have been quite offensive!”
Having said this,
he bowed down to the ground,
and Dàn Shī and the Lame One hurriedly returned the bow.
They asked:
“Who are you, senior brother?”
Zhāng Luán stated his name and title.
Dànzǐ Héshang said:
“So it is the Chōngxiāo Chùshì;
Shèng Gūgū very much wishes to meet you.”
Just as Zhāng Luán was about to ask further,
it was reported that the County Magistrate had returned.
The County Magistrate already knew the masters had arrived first,
so he got out of his sedan chair
and walked into the county gate.
The group of monks, Daoists, and common people
all followed him in.
The County Magistrate ordered red rugs to be laid out
and first invited Zhāng Luán to accept a bow of thanks,
but Zhāng Luán would not agree.
The County Magistrate said:
“I, the humble official, kneel for the sake of the ten thousand people;
it is only proper!”
After yielding to each other several times,
they finally exchanged two bows.
Next, he invited the other two to meet.
Those two asked to have the red rugs put away,
and guest and host exchanged salutations.
Below the steps, the group of monks, Daoists, and common people
all bowed down together,
their cheers sounding like thunder.
Zhāng Luán spoke a few words of comfort
and asked the County Magistrate to dismiss them.
The monks went to perform their merit-dedication rituals,
the Daoists went to slaughter chickens to thank the divine generals,
and the rest of the people
each dispersed and returned home.
The County Magistrate had previously ordered a banquet to be prepared,
set out in the back hall,
to entertain the three of them.
The County Magistrate did not yet know the names of Dànzǐ Héshang and Master Zuǒ Qué,
so in the back hall, he asked one by one,
and Zhāng Luán answered for them.
The County Magistrate said:
“How do you know, sir?”
Zhāng Luán said:
“They are people I have long admired;
I only just found out after we spoke.”
The County Magistrate smiled and said:
“I advised the three of you not to dispute over formalities,
and it was for this very reason.
Since you three are already kindred spirits,
for today’s seating,
I, the humble official, dare not presume the order;
please determine your own seating.”
Dànzǐ Héshang said:
“Mr. Zhāng is the one who achieved merit today;
he naturally should take the first seat.”
The County Magistrate was of the same mind.
Zhāng Luán could not refuse the modesty
and had to agree.
The Lame One let Dàn Shī sit in the second seat
and sat in the third seat himself;
the County Magistrate took the accompanying seat below.
The County Magistrate said:
“Does Master Dàn perhaps observe a vegetarian diet?”
Dànzǐ Héshang said:
“I am not restricted by meat or vegetarian food.”
The County Magistrate thought to himself:
“I have never seen such a group of monks and Daoists.”
At that moment, three rounds of wine were served,
and two sets of food were offered.
The County Magistrate rose to offer a cup,
and ordered a payment voucher for one thousand strings of cash to be brought,
handing it personally to Zhāng Luán, saying:
“This is a meager reward from this locality;
please do not consider it light or disrespectful.
When your crane-carriage departs,
you may withdraw it at your convenience;
the treasury will immediately deliver it.”
In those Sòng Dynasty times, one string of cash was worth one tael of silver;
one thousand strings were worth one thousand taels.
Even if it were a thousand taels of silver,
one person could not carry it,
let alone a thousand strings of copper coins—
how could they receive it?
The County Magistrate had spoken beforehand,
merely to show favor,
calculating that the gentleman would certainly decline,
and even if he accepted, he could not take so much.
Unexpectedly, just as Zhāng Luán was about to decline,
the Lame One whispered in his ear:
“This money will be useful in the future;
you should accept it.”
Zhāng Luán nodded
and asked for paper and brush to be brought,
writing:
“Temporarily deposited in the treasury of the City God of Bópíng County.”
He then requested the county treasury clerk
to burn this paper in the incense burner inside the temple,
and these one thousand strings of cash
were to be carried and placed under the divine seat.
The County Magistrate was silent for a while
and had no choice but to order the treasury clerk accordingly.
The treasury clerk answered and came out,
thinking to himself:
“Who ever saw a City God manage wealth for people?
Even if it is sent there,
it will just be taken by others for nothing.
Why not take advantage of this dark night to carry it to my home
and see what he does?”
Then he thought again:
“These one thousand strings of cash are no small matter;
whose eyes and ears could I deceive?
Moreover, in official matters,
if there is an inquiry at the City God Temple,
it would not be safe.
I will first carry it to the temple
and discuss it with the Daoists,
and everyone can split it.
If the officials ask,
we will just say Lord City God took it away;
where would they check the records?
A good plan,
a good plan!”
That night, the laborers of the town were called together,
with large and small poles,
to carry those one thousand strings of coins to the center of the main hall of the Chénghuáng Miào.
First, they informed the Dàoshì,
and after burning the Fǎshī’s own handwritten charms,
they then took the one thousand strings of coins
and piled them on both sides of the incense burner,
like two earthen mounds.
The Treasury Clerk privately agreed with the Dàoshì that after dusk,
they would all divide the money.
The Treasury Clerk then returned to report.
The Dàoshì also developed a deceitful heart,
thinking:
“The common saying goes, ‘If you see something and do not take it,
you will instead suffer blame.’
The wealth and money now delivered to my temple,
how could I share it with others!
Behind the temple is a large fish pond;
I might as well call my disciples to help
and transport them there one after another,
throwing them into the pond.
I will simply say the Chénghuáng Yé took them;
it will be invisible and traceless,
and would that not be clean?
After waiting for a long time,
I can take them out at leisure to enjoy.”
He quickly closed the temple gates,
gathered all the disciples,
prepared the equipment,
and got ready to carry the poles.
The Dàoshì had just taken one string of coins in his hand
when he felt something wriggling in his hand.
When he lifted it to look,
it was actually a red-banded snake,
and he hurriedly let go.
Immediately the disciples began to shout,
only to see the two piles of coins moving wildly,
all transforming into snakes,
massing together and twisting in clumps,
and rolling into the deity’s shrine.
At this time, it was the fourteenth day of the fifth month;
after the rain had cleared,
the moonlight was twice as bright.
He only heard a knock at the door;
when he opened it to see,
it was precisely the Treasury Clerk.
The Dàoshì then told him about the transformation into snakes.
The Treasury Clerk was not at all willing to believe it;
he took a torch to look into the deity’s shrine,
but he did not see the shadow of a single snake.
The Treasury Clerk was certain the Dàoshì had hidden the money,
and though he searched everywhere, he found nothing,
leaving his heart very resentful.
He then went to report this matter to the Xiànlìng.
The Xiànlìng was furious,
gave the Treasury Clerk twenty strokes of the board and dismissed him,
and expelled the Dàoshì from the temple gates,
not allowing him to stay.
This is a later story.
There is a poem to prove it:
The Treasury Clerk was greedy and the Dàoshì was cunning,
plotting for the thousand strings as private wealth.
The division failed and only the greed remained;
it was not a heavenly disaster, but one of their own making.
Meanwhile, Zhāng Luán and the other two ate until the time of bright moonlight,
stood up to thank the Xiànlìng,
and took their leave to depart.
The Xiànlìng said:
“Since the three of you have graced us with your presence,
pray stay at the guest house for a night,
for tomorrow I still wish to seek your guidance.”
Dànzǐ Héshang said:
“This poor monk has a thatched hut,
and I venture to invite your Excellency to come with us
for a visit.”
The Xiànlìng said:
“Where is this jade monastery?”
Dànzǐ Héshang said:
“Not far from here.”
The Xiànlìng saw them out of the front hall,
and Dànzǐ Héshang said:
“I beg for a bowl of pure water.”
A young servant brought the water.
Dànzǐ Héshang took it in his hand,
chanted an incantation,
and took a mouthful of water and sprayed it downward.
One could only see the sound of water before the steps,
transforming into a river,
with surging waves,
reflecting the moon like silver.
Zuǒ Chù untied a willow gourd from his waist and cast it down,
and it transformed into a small boat.
Because of this, there is a lesson:
The heterodox gather in groups,
narrating a case of life and death.
Enemies meet,
turning into waves of poverty and wealth.
I do not know where the three of them went by boat,
listen to the next chapter for the explanation.
The production and destruction of the Five Elements are fundamentally profound,
the spiritual connection of the single breath makes all dharmas complete.
Spraying water to form a river, a gourd can cross it;
where else would one seek immortals?
The story says that Dànzǐ Héshang sprayed water to form a river,
the Lame Master threw down the willow gourd,
transforming into a small skiff,
and wanted to invite the Xiànlìng to board together.
When the Xiànlìng looked at this boat,
from bow to stern,
it was not even eight or nine feet long;
how could it accommodate so many people?
He declined repeatedly and would not go.
Dànzǐ Héshang let Zhāng Luán go down first,
to sit in the middle,
Dànzǐ Héshang was at the bow,
and the Lame One was at the stern.
The three of them cupped their hands in thanks to the Xiànlìng.
Zhāng Luán held up a palm-leaf fan
like a sail,
let out a long whistle,
and they went away as if flying.
In the blink of an eye,
both the boat and the water disappeared,
returning to the sight of the path and gates before the steps of the hall.
The Xiànlìng was so startled he was left staring blankly,
just as if he had had a strange dream.
Although he had prayed for an altar of sweet rain
to save the myriad people,
he himself bore endless caution and fear.
He did not know if it was immortal arts
or demonic arts;
it was very difficult to judge.
Fearing they would come again to disturb him,
he ordered the Wǔlóng Tán to be abolished.
Three days later,
word spread through the various counties that Bópíng Xiàn had an itinerant Dàoshì
who could instantly bring rain.
They were all in the midst of a severe drought,
and all prepared gifts to welcome him.
The Zhīzhōu of Púzhōu also sent a document down to the county.
Xiànlìng Chúnyú Hòu could no longer hide it,
and was forced to vaguely report the three monks and priests whose names he did not know,
their prayer for rain and contest of magic,
and their departure by boat,
among many other strange events,
reporting them in detail in his reply.
The Zhīzhōu, seeing they could not be invited,
was very displeased.
The various counties went to pray for rain themselves but received no response;
seeing that Bópíng Xiàn had sufficient rain,
they all harbored jealousy
and came before the Zhīzhōu again,
everyone shouting confusedly:
“According to what the document says,
they are clearly a gang of sorcerers.
The county official should not have associated with them,
for fear that familiarity would breed trouble
and burden the locality.”
The Zhīzhōu heard this
and instead severely reprimanded Bópíng Xiàn,
ordering them to investigate the names and hideouts of the sorcerers,
while also reporting the matter to the Shūmì Yuàn.
The Shūmì Yuàn petitioned the imperial court;
as the area of Dōngjīng was vast,
they feared there were demonic factions hiding and causing trouble.
They issued a proclamation to inform the public
that if anyone with suspicious movements was found,
they should immediately report to the officials
and were not permitted to hide them.
From then on, it spread throughout Dōngjīng
that itinerant monks and priests
dared not enter the city.
Later generations had a poem lamenting the injustice toward Chúnyú Hòu,
the poem said:
Conspiracies and jealousy arose among colleagues,
failing to bring rain, they instead condemned it as sorcery.
Simply because there is little justice on the perilous path of life,
men of high character simply wish to grow old as fishermen and woodcutters.
The story branches out.
To continue, Zhāng Luán and the other two boarded a small boat,
traveling with the wind,
and in an instant, they reached the shore.
Monk Dànzǐ led Zhāng Luán ahead,
while the Lame Master followed behind.
After only a few steps,
they arrived at a place
of dense forests and tall bamboos,
where cranes and deer gathered in herds.
In their midst, an exquisite thatched hut appeared.
Zhāng Luán asked:
"Is this Master Dàn's place for practicing meditation?"
Monk Dànzǐ said:
"Throughout my life, I have not practiced meditation,
nor do I have a permanent dwelling.
Like idle clouds coming and going,
it is merely by chance."
Zhāng Luán sighed in admiration.
Monk Dànzǐ said to the Lame Master:
"Since Mr. Zhāng is here,
why not invite Shèng Gūgū to meet him!"
The Lame One looked up at the moon
and called out "Shèng Gūgū" three times.
Suddenly, a ray of golden light flew out from the moon,
descended all at once,
and transformed into an old woman.
That woman had a weathered and ancient appearance,
with snowy temples and bushy eyebrows.
She wore a star-crown on her head
and a crane-feather cloak on her body;
she truly possessed an ethereal and world-transcending air.
Zhāng Luán, knowing she was Shèng Gūgū,
stepped forward, announced his name, and bowed.
Shèng Gūgū addressed him as "Sir" and hurriedly returned the salute,
and both expressed their mutual admiration.
Shèng Gūgū saw that Zhāng Luán was eight feet tall,
with a majestic frame and a long beard.
His face was as red as sprayed blood,
his eyes were like bright stars,
and his elegant spirit was unlike that of ordinary men;
she secretly marveled at him.
That night, the moonlight was as bright as day.
All four entered the hut and took their seats:
Shèng Gūgū took the seat of honor at the top,
Zhāng Luán was next,
the Lame One sat to the side,
and Monk Dànzǐ accompanied them from the lower seat.
Shèng Gūgū asked:
"Where did my daughter, Mèi’ér,
meet with you, Sir?"
Zhāng Luán then recounted how, thirteen years ago in Shūjǐng Yuán, the wind had blown Mèi’ér down,
through to her reincarnation and upbringing in Squire Hú's household,
detailing the whole story once.
Shèng Gūgū expressed her gratitude, saying:
"If not for your constant care, Sir,
my daughter would have been eternally severed from a human form!"
She then said to the Lame One:
"Do you remember the words of Yán Sāndiǎn?
Truly a divine physician!"
Zhāng Luán asked:
"Could it be Yán Bànxiān of Yìzhōu?"
Shèng Gūgū said:
"Have you met him as well, Sir?"
Zhāng Luán said:
"I once stole a labor-inducing pill from an official's household in Dōngjīng
and gave it to the mistress of Squire Hú's house
to deliver her from the perils of childbirth.
I knew it came from the family of Imperial Physician Yán of the Bànxiān Táng,
but I have only heard his name
and have never actually met him."
The Lame Master said:
"You have set aside the main business and do not speak of it,
instead engaging in idle chatter."
Zhāng Luán then asked about the matters of Bèizhōu,
and Shèng Gūgū recounted the episode of meeting Empress Wǔ Zétiān in a dream.
She added:
"This is the decree of Heaven;
it cannot be forced."
Zhāng Luán again mentioned the saying about the Hú family's daughter and the Wáng family's queen,
saying:
"Now that she has been reincarnated into Squire Hú's house,
the first half of the prophecy has been fulfilled.
But I do not know how she will become the queen of the Wáng family."
Shèng Gūgū said:
"When we go to Bèizhōu in the future,
it will naturally become clear."
Zhāng Luán asked:
"When shall we begin this matter?"
Shèng Gūgū counted on her fingers and said:
"Fifteen years from now,
the true person shall emerge.
You, Sir, are the first to set it in motion,
and there should be several others to assist.
Let us see what the karmic conditions bring;
everyone should diligently seek and attract them
to achieve this success."
After talking for a long time,
Monk Dànzǐ called for a young novice to serve tea.
A thin young novice came out from within,
carrying a vermilion tray
on which was a plate of apricots,
larger than pears
and more yellow than oranges.
Monk Dànzǐ said:
"These are golden apricots produced in Línzī.
Hàn Wǔdì loved them most;
even now, scholars call them 'Hàn Emperor's Fruit.'
Please accept them as a modest offering in place of tea."
There happened to be exactly eight golden apricots,
and the four people each took two to eat.
The young novice, seeing everyone eating the apricots from the side,
began to salivate,
and let the vermilion tray slip from his hands; it fell to the ground and shattered to pieces.
Monk Dànzǐ was furious;
he grabbed the young novice with one hand,
walked out into the courtyard,
and threw him high into the sky,
where he tumbled through the air.
Just as Zhāng Luán was about to step forward to mediate,
he saw the young novice fall from the sky.
With a loud sound,
he fell stiffly to the ground and did not move.
When Zhāng Luán looked,
it was actually an eyebrow-height short staff.
Looking again at the vermilion tray,
it was a cluster of pomegranate flowers.
Shèng Gūgū shouted:
"In the presence of a great master,
why show off your axe!"
These words clearly meant that since Zhāng Luán was also a master of magic,
one should not play tricks on him.
Zhāng Luán said:
"Master Dàn's divine powers are vast,
beyond what I can achieve."
At this time, the moonlight was sinking in the west,
and the east was about to brighten.
Shèng Gūgū rose and said:
"This old one is now going to Dōngjīng to see my daughter.
I will call for you from time to time,
and then we shall meet."
Having spoken, she ascended into the air and departed.
Zhāng Luán and the other three also dispersed at once,
and no one knew where they went.
There is a poem as proof:
Moonlight at the thatched hut at night is clear as water,
Perfect for hermits to sit close and converse.
Coming and going of their own accord, truly at ease,
How many can fathom such wondrous magic?
To continue, Squire Hú of Dōngjīng had invited a pedantic scholar to his home
to teach Yǒng'ér her studies.
This Yǒng'ér was clever and intelligent,
surpassing any male;
she mastered what she read
and understood what was explained.
She soon grew to be thirteen years old,
born with a face as beautiful as a flower;
moreover, she was proficient in both writing and calculation,
and was incomparably clever.
Many families of similar squires,
admiring her talent and beauty,
sent go-betweens to propose a match,
wishing to betroth her as a daughter-in-law.
Squire Hú cherished her too much;
picking and choosing,
he simply would not agree.
It is truly that marriages are predestined;
timing is not up to man.
This will not be further discussed.
To continue, since Shèng Gūgū arrived in Dōngjīng,
she had wandered in and around Squire Hú's house several times.
Because she came without a trace
and left without a shadow,
how could his family know?
She had seen for herself that Yǒng'ér had grown up clever,
and her heart was filled with joy;
she intended to teach her magic.
Considering that the girl lived in such wealth and honor,
ensconced within deep chambers and embroidered rooms,
how could they meet?
Even if they met,
how would she be willing to believe and learn!
"It would be better to use divine power
to spirit away her family's vast wealth,
leaving them displaced and destitute.
When the girl reaches the point of extreme poverty and suffering,
then I will find a way to entice her,
and she will surely follow."
Setting Shèng Gūgū aside for now.
To continue, every year on the Mid-Autumn Festival in the eighth month, Squire Hú's family
would prepare a banquet
and invite Scholar Chén to admire the moon and drink wine.
That year, because Yǒng'ér was older,
Scholar Chén declined.
With no outside guests,
he ordered wine to be prepared at the octagonal pavilion in the back garden,
for the three close family members to enjoy.
That night the sky was clear and bright,
and the moonlight in the east rose like a jade plate.
One could see:
The moon rises from the ocean peaks,
and cloud leaves scatter across the celestial thoroughfare.
Colorful clouds illuminate ten thousand lǐ like silver;
the Jade Rabbit reflects upon a thousand mountains like water.
A single bright and pure orb
is capable of making the universe clear and limpid.
Throughout the four seas, all is reunified,
and it can make heaven and earth bright and clear.
Shadows sway across the open wilderness,
startling the solitary roosting crow.
Light pierces through the secluded window,
shining upon the resentful woman sleeping in solitude.
The icy wheel crushes through the three thousand worlds,
and the jade soul swallows up ten thousand lǐ of autumn.
Hú Yuánwài dismissed the pawnshop managers and supervisors early
to go home and enjoy the Zhōngqiū Festival.
He instructed the servants to securely bolt all the doors and gates
and to be careful with fires and candles.
He himself, along with Māmā and Yǒng'ér, went to the octagonal pavilion in the back garden to sit and drink wine,
attended only by the wet nurse and maidservants
with no young boys present.
As they sat until the first watch of the night,
they saw the gatekeeper rushing in hurriedly to report:
“Yuánwài, disaster has struck!”
Yuánwài said:
“From where does disaster come?
Where is the trouble?”
The gatekeeper said:
“A fire has broken out in the pawnshop in the middle of the outer area!”
Yuánwài, Māmā, and Yǒng'ér were greatly shocked.
When they all stood down from the pavilion to look,
indeed, it was a massive fire.
How could one tell how big this fire was?
At first like a firefly's light,
then like the light of a lamp.
A thousand candles' force would be hard to withstand;
ten thousand water basins could not rival it.
Atop Líshān,
one might expect Bāo Sì to be showing off her prowess.
At the head of the Yángzǐ Jiāng,
it was not as good as Zhōu Láng executing his brilliant plan.
Dense purple mists rose into the sky;
flickering red clouds pierced through to the earth.
The multi-story buildings looked like broken lanterns;
the earthen storehouses were just like iron firecrackers.
This fire started in the pawnshop
and spread into the central hall and inner chambers.
If it had burned inward layer by layer in order,
one could still have made preparations;
but this fire was a celestial fire sent down by Shèng Gūgū using her divine powers.
It was capable of piercing through walls and penetrating barriers,
toppling pillars and collapsing beams.
Even the fuse on a firecracker
would not transmit as quickly as this.
Furthermore, a great wind began to blow;
the wind followed the fire's momentum,
and the fire took advantage of the wind's power,
crackling and popping as it kept burning.
Yuánwài stamped his feet and cried out in bitterness,
calling upon the gods
and invoking his ancestors.
On one hand, he told the wet nurse and maidservants
to open the back gate
and told the houseboys to spread the word
that he was willing to give a heavy reward
to hire people to fight the fire.
On the other hand, he told the men and women of the household to go into the inner chambers
to snatch up some small valuables and furniture
and essential chests and trunks.
That group of local neighbors
at first also had many people carrying grappling hooks
and bearing water buckets.
Like a swarm of ants,
they climbed ladders onto the roofs;
how could they possibly extinguish it!
In a short time,
the flames flared up
with a sound like heaven collapsing and the earth splitting.
The crowd gave a shout and all fled.
The houses all around, front and back,
in an instant,
turned into masses of smoke and lumps of fire.
Not one of the men or women could take a step forward.
Māmā and Yǒng'ér held their heads and wept.
Yuánwài, seeing the mother and son in such grief,
instead went to comfort them, saying:
“You two, do not panic for now.
Even if everything is burned to ashes,
it will not make us poor for the rest of our lives!”
At that time, one only saw flames surging up,
rising higher and becoming fiercer,
burning for a full night.
The three family members had no choice but to rest temporarily in the Octagonal Pavilion.
When dawn broke,
they ordered people to rake through the scorched ground.
As everyone raked it open to look,
their mouths opened and could not close,
their eyes opened wide and could not shut.
As the saying goes:
"Though man has a thousand calculations,
Heaven has but one."
If Heaven allowed man's calculations to prevail,
there would be no poor men in the world.
Hú Yuánwài never expected this heavenly fire would burn everything to the point that not a blade of grass remained;
the front hall,
the rear tower,
the corridors,
the main rooms,
and the side rooms were all burnt to ashes.
He only hoped that the gold and silver vessels and the bronze and tin utensils,
though melted,
would still be in the ground,
and gathering them together would still provide a small bit of family property.
When he ordered people to rake and look,
unexpectedly, they had all been taken away by Shèng Gūgu.
In the first half of his life, he had the fortune to enjoy wealth;
now his fortune had receded.
They raked through the whole site,
but did not find a single trace.
Truly, a wealthy family of millions was made poor by a single flame.
Hú Yuánwài and the three members of his family lived in the pavilion;
the group of managers and stewards
all resigned.
The male and female servants in the house had no rooms to live in
and no food to eat,
so they all had to be sent away.
A few maidservants and nurses remained,
who inevitably had to be resold to others.
Because the Mistress was habitually jealous and petty,
she had only employed low-grade, ugly maidservants,
so even when sold to others, they did not fetch much money.
Moreover, his wealthy man's temperament remained;
he could not endure extreme austerity.
Aside from coal,
every single other thing had to be bought.
Before long,
everything in his hands was completely spent.
As he looked at his three daily meals,
none could be provided.
Well-meaning relatives, neighbors, and friends
sent things once or twice,
but then they also stopped.
It was also unavoidable to go and borrow some rice and firewood,
but that could only be done once or twice;
three times in one day,
nine times in three days,
and after half a year or a full year,
things to eat in the mouth,
things to wear on the body—
every single item was gone.
He entreated someone to act as a middleman,
willing to sell the vacant land at a low price to the neighbors on either side.
But they said:
"Land scorched by heavenly fire
has no vitality for ten years.
Land that has undergone heavenly fire
suffers from being withered and scorched for ten years."
Because of these common taboos,
who would want it?
Seeing himself reduced to rags,
he went to seek help from old acquaintances.
Those who were at home
simply said they were out.
Those who knew him in ordinary times
acted as if they did not know him.
If they bumped into him on the street,
they covered their faces with fans,
pretending not to see.
As it has been said since ancient times:
"A poor man living in a bustling market has no one to ask after him;
a rich man in the remote mountains has distant relatives."
It is also said:
"If one brings the spring breeze,
there will be summer rain."
Hú Yuánwài usually calculated one to get ten,
and ten to get a hundred;
he was originally a man who managed his household with harsh frugality.
Regarding those who were as poor as he was now,
in his whole life they had never received a cent of kindness from him.
As for wealthy men of the same class as him,
they were always jealous of each other;
even today there are those who delight in talking about his misfortune,
who would be willing to say the word "pity"?
Even his old acquaintances,
it was only because he had money and notes
that they associated with him;
where would there be a bosom friendship like that of Guǎn and Bào?
Therefore, a poor man of integrity
will instead have people to support and raise him up;
but a wealthy family with no character
often meets with a crushing defeat.
That Hú Yuánwài lived in the pavilion,
which had no walls on any side.
It was fine during sunny days,
but if there were wind, rain, or snow,
how could he settle himself?
He had no choice but to move to the Bù Sī Qiú Yuàn,
which was just like a modern-day home for the elderly.
It was then mid-winter;
dark clouds were densely packed,
the north wind was biting cold,
and a great snow fell from the sky in drifting profusion.
How could one see that the snow was great?
One saw only:
drifting willow catkins,
flakes like goose feathers.
In the air, white herons fly in flocks;
on the river, white gulls wheel about.
A thousand mountains paved with jade,
enough to make the woodcutter lose his path.
Ten thousand households dressed in silver,
breaking the hearts of many travelers.
The poor scholar who fears the cold
prays to the Lord of Heaven to let three parts less fall.
The prince who enjoys the scenery
wishes for Téng Liù to add several more feet.
Truly it is said that it is an omen of a bountiful year,
but what of this omen of a bountiful year?
There are poor people in Cháng’ān,
for whom the omen is fine, but it should not be too much.
Those who love the snow are the young masters in high towers,
and those who dislike the snow are the poor folk in lowly alleys.
In the capital city of Dōngjīng, there was a certain Hú Yuánwài who had recently fallen on hard times.
He was originally a very wealthy man,
but because a fire from heaven reduced him to ruin,
dissipating his family wealth,
he moved to live in the Bùsīqiú Yuàn.
It happened to be winter and snow was falling;
the three members of the family sat huddled together around a stove,
and even at noon, they still had no breakfast to eat.
The mother pointed her finger at the Yuánwài’s head,
and Hú Yuánwài raised his head and saw her,
saying:
“Mother,
it is nothing!”
The mother said:
“The heavy snow falls,
and there is no rice for food in the house.
You and I once had plenty of clothes and food
and enjoyed ourselves;
even if we endure hunger and starvation today,
it is only fitting.”
Pointing at Yǒng’ér:
“He is only fourteen years old this year;
what prosperity has he ever seen?
To make my son suffer such bitterness,
how can we as parents have the heart!”
Hú Yuánwài said:
“There is no way out;
what would you have me do?”
The mother said:
“You are the provider for the family.
It has just started snowing outside;
if it freezes up in half a day or so
and it becomes impossible to go out in a hurry,
surely the three of us cannot just wait to starve to death!
Go out while you still can
and find one or two acquaintances to beg for three or four hundred coins to bring back;
that will get us through a few days.”
The Yuánwài said:
“As for the ways of the world lately,
you surely know them.
If I go out this time,
who is there worth seeing?”
The mother said:
“Even so,
one day of shamelessness
for three days of a full stomach.
If you do not go out,
surely I cannot go out.”
Hú Yuánwài, unable to withstand the mother’s pressure,
stood up and said:
“Let me tighten my belt a bit;
I do not know if this will take half a day or a whole day.
In the world today,
they only add flowers to brocade;
who is willing to send charcoal in the snow?
Is it not easier to capture a tiger barehanded
than to open one’s mouth to beg from others?
You all be patient
and do not think this will be very easy.”
Having finished speaking,
with a pool of tears in his eyes,
he opened the door and went out.
He took two steps forward
and fell back three steps.
He said:
“So cold!
The cold wind hits the face like arrows,
and the biting chill pierces a person like a knife.”
Driven back several steps by the northwest wind,
he wanted to turn back around,
but the mother had already shut the door.
With no other choice,
he could only brave the wind and snow to walk on.
Walking out of Bùsīqiú Yuàn to beg from others
is not further mentioned.
There is a poem as evidence:
Dark clouds spread thick and snow falls in flurries,
the ground covered in jade-white and the road indistinguishable.
Wishing to beg for coins to provide for wife and child,
who before my eyes is a Mèngcháng Jūn?
Hú Yuánwài wanted to find acquaintances
and could not afford to be ashamed,
so he could only wander the streets near his old residence.
Many people in this market recognized him;
when they saw him coming,
they pointed and gestured, saying:
“This is the end of a wealthy man.”
There were also those frivolous ones
who sang softly:
“Hú Yuánwài,
heaven sent disaster;
the good days are gone,
and the bad days have come.”
There were also those who had suffered losses at his Jiěkù,
who then said:
“Giving out by light weight
and taking in by heavy weight;
fake silver going out
and pure silver coming in;
in this world, only those who run pawnshops have deceptive hearts.
I only wish every one of them were like Old Man Hú,
receiving retribution in this very life.”
The Yuánwài kept walking with his head bowed,
when he bumped into someone face-to-face
holding a small umbrella in his hand,
who called out:
“Yuánwài,
where are you going in this snowy weather?”
When the Yuánwài looked,
it was Chén Xuéjiū, Chén Shàn, who had formerly been invited to his home to teach Yǒng’ér the classics.
Hú Yuánwài, full of shame,
made a bow
and said:
“To not hide it from you, Xuéjiū,
things at home are truly difficult;
I have no choice but to come out and find an acquaintance.”
Chén Shàn then said:
“Since you are in such dire straits,
why not go and seek help from that person under the Sìpáifāng?”
Hú Yuánwài asked:
“Who is it?”
The Xuéjiū whispered a few words into his ear.
Hú Yuánwài was overjoyed
and cupped his hands, saying:
“I rely entirely on your support and recommendation, Xuéjiū.”
Chén Shàn said:
“Of course, of course.”
Then he pulled Hú Yuánwài under the small umbrella,
covering them both.
Hú Yuánwài took advantage of the umbrella
and turned back from his old path towards the south to seek that person under the gate tower of the Sìpáifāng.
It turned out that man was surnamed Mí and named Bìdá,
a native of Dōngjīng.
Originally of idle-man background,
he won the favor of an official in the Shūmìyuàn,
who supported him in becoming a Tíxiá.
Three years ago, wanting to seek a promotion,
he was short of some funds for expenses.
Because Chén Shàn was his old friend
and knew he was teaching at Hú Yuánwài’s house,
he asked him to borrow three hundred taels of silver
to handle official matters at the yamen
and was promoted to the position of Dūjiān of Jìzhōu.
After serving for over two years,
because of discord with his colleagues,
he was transferred to Qīngzhōu to take up office,
bringing his family along the way to his post.
Having just returned home,
he had only been back for two days.
Originally, the loan contract had the signature of the guarantor, Chén Xuéjiū;
today, although Hú Yuánwài had lost the contract in the fire,
fortunately the guarantor was present.
Furthermore, it was a debt of gratitude;
there was no reason it should not be repaid.
Today Chén Xuéjiū was just going to pay a visit.
With his introduction,
it would be convenient for both parties.
So Hú Yuánwài went along joyfully,
and upon arriving at the entrance,
many official and private attendants were going in and out,
quite a bustling scene.
The gatekeeper, seeing the Yuánwài in ragged clothes,
looking clearly like a beggar,
began to shout and scold him;
who would be willing to let him in?
Chén Jiàoshòu explained,
but they wouldn’t accept it,
so he had to give him the small umbrella
and told him to stand on the street corner for the time being:
“Wait until I go in and see the Dūjiān,
he will surely invite you.”
The others said again
that a man looking like a beggar standing on the street
would damage the official’s dignity,
so they drove him away until he was under the eaves of the opposite house.
Now it is said that Chén Xuéjiū entered the hall to meet Mí Dūjiān,
exchanging greetings and congratulatory words,
and after tea was finished,
Mí Dūjiān invited Chén Xuéjiū to sit comfortably in the study.
Chén Shàndào said:
"There is another friend outside
who has specifically come to pay his respects."
Mí Dūjiàn said:
"Who is it?"
Chén Shàndào said:
"He originally had dealings with you, Dūjiàn;
his name is Hú Dàhóng."
Mí Dūjiàn said:
"Could it be Yuánwài Hú, who ran the pawnshop on Píng’ān Street?"
Chén Shàndào said:
"Indeed."
Mí Dūjiàn said:
"Quickly, ask him in."
The house boy hurriedly relayed the message
and invited Yuánwài Hú to come in and meet.
The doorkeeper said:
"I have never seen any Yuánwài Hú arrive."
Yuánwài Hú heard this while standing under the eaves across from the gate,
and he walked over, saying:
"I am Yuánwài Hú."
The men laughed and said:
"We have traveled through all four hundred prefectures,
and we have never seen a Yuánwài like you.
If a face like yours is called a Yuánwài,
then people like us should all be called Shàngshū."
The doorkeeper blocked him
and would not let him in.
Yuánwài Hú then loudly called out for Xuéjiù Chén.
Just then, an old man came out of the residence;
his surname was Liú and his given name was Yì.
He was the old servant of the Mí family,
a man who was honest and kind-hearted.
He had always followed his master to his posts
and had only recently returned.
Originally, when Mí Bìdá borrowed silver from Yuánwài Hú’s house,
he was the one who personally handled the delivery,
and he had visited several times.
Although the Yuánwài’s appearance had changed today,
his face was still recognizable.
He shouted at the doorkeeper to stop
and went forward to welcome the Yuánwài.
Yuánwài Hú then told him the brief story of his misfortune
and his intention for coming today.
Liú Yì said:
"Since the master invited you,
there must be good intentions."
He then led the Yuánwài into the hall.
Xuéjiù Chén saw him and hurriedly stood up,
but when Mí Dūjiàn saw that he was a ragged and poor fellow,
he intended to look down on him
and remained seated.
Yuánwài Hú walked near the chair
and made a very respectful bow, saying:
"Honorable official,
it has been a long time."
Mí Dūjiàn merely gave a slight wave of his hand from his chair
and sat back down as before,
asking Xuéjiù Chén:
"Who is this person?"
Chén Shàndào said:
"It is Yuánwài Hú Dàhóng."
Mí Bìdá intentionally squinted his eyes
to take a look
and then said:
"We have been apart for three years,
and I simply didn't recognize you."
He did not return the bow,
nor did he say "please sit,"
nor did he gesture toward a chair.
It was Xuéjiù Chén, acting half as host and half as guest,
who pulled over a chair for them to sit together.
Yuánwài Hú saw that Mí Dūjiàn remained silent,
so he had to speak first, saying:
"I have a few words to say, though I know not whether it is proper."
Mí Bìdá pretended to be ignorant
and asked:
"What advice do you have?"
Yuánwài Hú said:
"Three years ago,
when I still ran the pawnshop
and my family affairs were quite prosperous,
you, honorable official, once established a contract
and took three hundred taels of silver from me,
with an interest of twenty percent added to the agreement.
When you were serving your term in Jìzhōu,
I did not dare to mention it.
Recently, because my fortune has turned poor
and I suffered a fire from heaven,
everything was burned away
until not a blade of grass remained.
I lack food and my clothes are thin;
it is truly difficult to survive.
Fortunately, I met with you, honorable official, upon your promotion and return to the residence,
so I have specifically come to pay my respects.
I no longer dare to count the interest;
I only hope you will grant me the principal silver
to serve as capital for my livelihood;
it would be just as if you were bestowing a gift upon me."
Mí Bìdá said:
"When I first served as Tíxié,
I did borrow a hundred taels for use,
but I didn't borrow that much.
After a year in Jìzhōu,
both principal and interest were sent back.
How could there be any silver still owed?"
Yuánwài Hú said:
"Noble people have short memories;
it was truly three hundred taels,
and it was never returned."
Mí Dūjiàn said:
"Since it hasn't been returned,
there must be a loan contract.
Bring it out for me to see, and we shall know."
Yuánwài said:
"The contract was also burned in the fire."
Pointing at Xuéjiù Chén, he said:
"There is a guarantor here to bear witness."
Chén Shàndào said:
"I was the one who handled it;
it indeed has not been returned.
I think you, Dūjiàn, have remembered incorrectly."
Mí Bìdá’s face changed, and he said:
"As the common saying goes,
where there is writing, there is no need for verbal dispute.
Since there is no original contract,
what proof is there?
If you two say it's three hundred,
then it's three hundred?
If you said three thousand,
would it be three thousand?"
Chén Shàndào still thought he had simply forgotten
and said:
"Dūjiàn, do not be so stubborn.
By the laws of heaven and conscience,
if it exists, it exists;
if it doesn't, it doesn't.
Please think it over slowly."
Yuánwài Hú said with a smile:
"Now I do not dare to say three hundred or two hundred;
I only rely on whatever you, honorable official, are pleased to give."
Mí Bìdá was furious,
stood up, and said:
"The two of you are playing in harmony,
conspiring together
to extort people's money.
This is quite uncalled for!
If you had the original contract,
I would return even three thousand taels to you.
Without the original contract,
do not expect to get even half a copper coin."
Having finished speaking,
he walked directly into the inner residence.
The old servant Liú Yì had previously seen that his master’s tone was unpleasant,
and fearing that if he were asked about whether the debt existed or not
it would be hard to answer,
he hid himself in advance.
He was, however, quite conscientious.
He waited at the main gate,
and seeing Yuánwài Hú and Xuéjiù Chén walking out in a huff,
Liú Yì said:
"Yuánwài, do not be anxious.
Allow me to calmly speak to the master again;
there will surely be a resolution.
You have been here for half a day
and must be hungry.
If you do not despise my low status,
please come to a tavern to have three cups.
I would also like to invite the Jiàoshòu to go with us;
what do you think?"
Chén Shàndào was full of anger
and had no desire to eat anything from Liú Yì.
But seeing the look of hunger on Yuánwài Hú’s face,
he feared that if he declined,
he would cause him to have nothing to eat as well.
He could only pull Yuánwài Hú along
and urge him to go together.
Liú Yì then led Yuánwài Hú
and Xuéjiù Chén
to a quiet tavern nearby.
This time, Yuánwài Hú truly found life in a desperate situation
and was saved from the brink of death.
Truly it is said:
Three full meals are not particularly precious,
but a single mouthful when hungry is truly difficult to come by.
How exactly did Yuánwài Hú return home?
Please listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
Lately, provisions in the kitchen are scarce,
the infant cries, and the rice basket is empty.
The mother leans in to whisper to the child:
"Father has written a new poem to visit the Xiànggōng."
It is said that Mí Dūjiān relied on his wealth to bully the poor,
seeing Hú Yuánwài’s impoverished state and wretched appearance,
he refused to repay his debt.
Hú Yuánwài went to him despite the snow,
only to meet with a cold reception,
leaving his heart full of anger and bitterness.
However, the old steward of the Mí family, Liú Yì, saw his look of hunger and cold;
unable to bear the sight,
he pulled him to a secluded place
and into a small tavern.
Choosing a clean table,
he invited the Yuánwài to the seat of honor,
while Chén Xuéjiū sat below to keep him company.
He called the wine steward and instructed:
“Bring two measures of wine;
they must be heated until boiling hot,
but do not use small cups.
If there is good food to go with the wine,
just bring it out.”
The wine steward said:
“There is only freshly steamed beef,
nothing else for sale.”
Liú Yì said:
“Wouldn't it be better if you slaughtered a fat chicken?”
Hú Yuánwài said:
“One dish is enough;
why go to such great expense?”
Liú Yì said:
“Do not laugh at this humble offering.”
Liú Yì went to the jars himself to taste the wine, and once satisfied,
only then did he have the wine steward heat it.
The wine steward sliced a large, full plate of beef,
and along with small dishes of pickles, salt, and vinegar,
set them all down.
Placing three large bowls,
he was about to pour the wine.
Liú Yì snatched the wine pot from him and said:
“Let us help ourselves;
you go and slaughter the chicken
and cook it quickly.”
Hú Yuánwài said to Liú Yì:
“You, venerable elder, should also sit down.”
Liú Yì said:
“With the Yuánwài and the Teacher above me,
how could a humble man like me dare to sit?”
Chén Xuéjiū said:
“If you do not sit,
then neither the Yuánwài nor I will feel at ease sitting.”
Liú Yì said:
“Since such are your instructions,
I shall sit to the side to pour the wine;
please do not take offense at my boldness.”
He poured two large bowls full and offered them to the Yuánwài and the Xuéjiū to drink.
Hú Yuánwài had left home on an empty stomach;
after drinking two bowls of hot wine,
he felt his face flush and his heart race.
He said:
“I cannot drink anymore;
if there is rice, I would like a bowl.”
Liú Yì feared he was hungry
and did not press him further.
He then instructed the wine steward:
“When the chicken is cooked,
first bring a bowl of rice for one person;
I will keep the Teacher company for another pot of wine.”
The wine steward cooked the chicken,
chopped it into a plate,
and brought it along with the wine.
He then went to get a bowl and serve the rice,
bringing it over while offering to refill and asked:
“Which one will have the rice?”
Liú Yì told him to place it before Hú Yuánwài
and said, “Please!”
The Yuánwài held the rice bowl in his hand,
but as he had just swallowed a mouthful,
he thought of his wife and daughter at home,
who were waiting expectantly.
Now that he was returning empty-handed,
even though he had this bowl of rice to eat,
their rice
was still nowhere to be seen,
and who knew when it would reach their mouths.
Unconsciously, two lines of pearly tears fell.
Chén Xuéjiū already knew what he was thinking
and said:
“It was my fault for talking too much at the start,
leading the Yuánwài to spend money only to be insulted;
I also never expected that the Mí family would be such people.”
He then said to Liú Yì:
“The master of your house
used to be close friends with me in our youth,
like a single person.
He would consult me on everything,
and he was kind and righteous.
Today, now that the official's gauze cap is on his head
and people call him Lǎoyé,
it is as if he has changed into a different person before King Yánluó;
even his heart, liver, and five internal organs have all changed.”
Liú Yì said:
“Even the Yellow River has days when it runs clear;
how can a person never have a time when luck turns their way?
The Yuánwài may be lonely and frustrated for now,
but there will eventually be good days.
Please eat your fill for now,
and then we shall consider the matter further.
If my master ultimately refuses to acknowledge the debt,
I will somehow manage to provide a string of coins to the Yuánwài to help with your livelihood.”
Hú Yuánwài said:
“Then I thank you very much.”
After eating two bowls of rice,
he put down his chopsticks.
Liú Yì said:
“Please have some more.”
Hú Yuánwài said:
“I have had a bit too much wine;
I truly cannot eat any more.”
Liú Yì looked at Chén Shàn and said:
“Since he won't have more rice,
shall I encourage another cup of wine?”
Chén Shàn said:
“The Yuánwài has always been a moderate drinker.”
Hú Yuánwài said:
“Since falling into hardship,
I can tolerate it even less.
It is truly a case of ‘wine falling into a sorrowful heart’;
having received the kind sentiments of you two today,
it is already more than enough.”
Chén Shàn and Liú Yì both finished their wine and rice.
Chén Shàn then stood up,
reached into his sleeve for three hundred copper coins,
and gave them to the Yuánwài, saying:
“Take this string of coins
back home however you can
to buy some snacks.
I only regret being a poor teacher
and cannot be more generous.”
Liú Yì called the wine steward and settled the bill;
there were more than a hundred coins left over,
which he also gave to Hú Yuánwài,
saying:
“This humble servant's gift is meager,
but please accept it as a small token of respect for tea.”
Hú Yuánwài thought of the suffering at home
and saw that both were acting out of absolute sincerity;
he had to accept it,
bowing and offering his thanks.
Truly it is:
Intentionally planting flowers, the flowers do not bloom;
unintentionally planting willows, the willows form shade.
There is a poem to prove it:
The deceitful official loses to the poor man,
the kindhearted servant is better than his master.
Good and evil both spring from the heart;
they have never depended on wealth or poverty.
Charity has never been about the amount;
what matters is that it comes at a time of distress.
In the city of Dōngjīng, there was the famous Hú Yuánwài who had piled gold and accumulated jade;
today, amidst his hardships, seeing these three hundred-odd copper coins,
he was greatly delighted
and a hundred times more grateful.
It can be seen that being a good person is originally easy;
it only highlights the character of Mí Dūjiān,
who is actually inferior to Chén Xuéjiū and Liú Yì.
The story now follows two different paths.
Let us tell of Zhāng Yuànjūn and her daughter, who were sitting together in cold desolation.
Yǒng'ér said,
"Father has gone out to ask people for help;
I wonder how it is going?"
Her mother said,
"The ways of the world follow fortune and status;
people’s faces change accordingly.
Your father had no choice but to brace himself and go ask for help;
who knows how it will turn out?"
Yǒng'ér spoke again,
"Mother!
The snow is falling heavily
and the wind is cold.
Whom did Father go to ask?"
Her mother said,
"My child!
There is no money in the house.
If we did not have your father go out,
we simply could not survive these hungry days.
My child!
Go search by the bedside for a few copper coins,
then go out of the alley to buy some snacks to eat.
When your father returns,
we will then decide what to do."
At that moment, Yǒng'ér went to the bedside and searched high and low,
finding only eight copper coins.
Her mother said,
"My child!
Take them all and buy a few steamed cakes;
just eat a few to stave off your hunger."
Yǒng'ér, dragging along a broken shoe
and using her lapel to cover her head,
stepped through the snow and out of the Bùsīqiú courtyard.
The marketplace was not like the deep mountains or open fields;
with many people coming and going,
the snow on the ground did not pile up
but was all trampled into slushy mud,
making it extremely difficult to walk.
Yǒng'ér had just turned a corner
when she stepped on uneven ground
and took a fall.
The copper coins in her hand
were scattered all over the ground,
and her clothes were stained with mud.
Yǒng'ér scrambled up,
and regardless of her clothes,
she picked up the copper coins from the mud;
there were only seven,
for the remaining one had been tossed who knows where.
She searched for a while but could not find it,
so she had to give up.
Walking to the main street where steamed cakes were sold,
Yǒng'ér gave the shop assistant a polite greeting
and said,
"Uncle,
I would like to buy seven coins' worth of steamed cakes."
When the assistant took the money in his hand to look,
one of the coins was broken,
so he picked it out and refused to take it.
Yǒng'ér tied it to her sash
and said,
"Then I will just buy six coins' worth!"
The assistant took a fresh lotus leaf,
wrapped up six steamed cakes,
and handed them to Yǒng'ér.
Yǒng'ér took them
and returned by her former path;
it was already the hour of Wèi.
While Yǒng'ér was walking along the eaves of the houses,
she came to an open space
and saw an old woman leaning on a bamboo staff,
with a basket hanging on her arm,
approaching quickly from behind.
What did that old woman look like?
One saw:
A bent waist and a curved back,
a thin face and loose skin.
Her eyebrows were like two streaks of clouds;
her hair was wound in a messy nest.
Her eyes were like autumn waters, slightly turbid;
her hair was like the light clouds of the Chǔ mountains.
Her form was like a flower at the end of the third month;
her fate was like a chrysanthemum after the frost of the ninth autumn.
It turned out to be an old beggar woman,
who looked at Yǒng'ér and gave a polite greeting.
Yǒng'ér returned the courtesy.
The old woman said:
"What did you come to buy?"
Yǒng'ér said:
"My mother at home told me to buy steamed buns."
The old woman said:
"My child!
I will let you know
that I had no dinner yesterday.
Would you be willing to treat me to a steamed bun?"
Yǒng'ér did not speak,
but thought to herself,
"My mother also had no dinner yesterday
and no breakfast today.
This old woman is of such an advanced age,
I really cannot bear to see her like this."
She then unwrapped the lotus leaf package
and handed one steamed bun to the old woman.
The old woman took it in her hand,
looked at the steamed bun, and said:
"It is good enough,
but how can this one bun fill me up?
Why not give them all to me?"
Yǒng'ér said:
"I tell you, Grandma,
it is not that I am unwilling to give them all to you,
but the three of us at home have not had a meal for two days.
Mother told Father to go out and ask others for help,
leaving only eight copper coins,
and told me to come out and buy steamed buns.
On the way, I dropped one coin,
and was left with one broken coin,
so I could only buy six steamed buns.
Mother will eat two,
I will eat two,
and I am saving two to wait for Father to return.
I am afraid he has not eaten anything
and want to give them to him to relieve his hunger.
Because you are old, Grandma,
I could not bear it,
so I had to give one to you."
The old woman said:
"When your mother asks why you bought fewer buns,
what will you say?"
Yǒng'ér said:
"When Mother asks,
I will just say I was hungry
and ate one on the road first."
The old woman said:
"Since you need to take the buns back,
give this broken coin to me instead!"
Yǒng'ér showed no sign of reluctance at all;
she truly untied the coin from her belt
and handed it to the old woman.
The old woman said:
"If your mother asks about the money,
how will you answer then?"
Yǒng'ér said:
"I will just say the streets were muddy
and I dropped and lost two coins."
The old woman said:
"It is rare for my child to have such a good heart
and to be so clever.
To tell you the truth,
I am not hungry
and do not want to eat this bun;
I am giving it back to you."
Yǒng'ér said:
"I gave it to you to eat, Grandma,
so why are you giving it back to me?"
The old woman said:
"I was only testing you;
it is rare to find such a compassionate and filial heart.
I was just teasing you!"
She took the broken coin and tossed it in her palm,
blew a breath on it,
and it changed into a perfectly round and good coin,
which she handed into Yǒng'ér's hand.
She asked:
"Is this trick good?"
Yǒng'ér said:
"What a trick!
Grandma, please teach it to me."
The old woman said:
"This small trick is nothing extraordinary;
if you are willing to learn,
there are many other fun things.
I will teach them all to you at once.
Do you know how to read?"
Yǒng'ér said:
"I know a few words."
The old woman said:
"My child!
Then there is indeed a karmic affinity."
She reached into her basket and took out a purple silk pouch.
The outside was tightly bound with a thin hemp cord.
Looking at Yǒng'ér, she said:
"You may keep this."
Yǒng'ér took the pouch
and said:
"Grandma, what is this thing?"
The old woman said:
"This is called the Rúyì Bǎocè.
Many fun tricks
are all inside it.
You must keep it safe.
If you are ever in urgent trouble,
you can unroll the scroll to look for a solution.
If there is anything you do not understand,
just secretly call for Shèng Gūgū,
and I will come to teach you.
Do not let anyone else know."
Yǒng'ér tucked the scroll into her bosom.
She took the coin that had been changed into a good one
and threaded it onto her inner skirt sash.
She thanked the old woman and started to leave.
Before she had gone a few steps,
when she looked back,
the old woman had suddenly vanished.
There is a poem to prove it:
A single steamed bun reveals the heart,
A silk pouch and heavenly book repay virtue deeply.
Know that a good heart brings a good reward;
why be stingy with kindness, even if it costs a thousand gold?
Yǒng'ér carried the steamed buns home.
Her mother said:
"My child, why have you returned so late?
Your clothes are all stained with mud;
could it be that you had a fall?"
Yǒng'ér said:
"Mother!
The streets were snowy and slippery, making it hard to walk.
I also fell and lost two coins,
so I could only buy six steamed buns."
Her mother sighed and said:
"My child!
A bitter fate is just bitter.
Steamed buns worth two more coins
would not keep us full for a lifetime anyway,
so let it be.
Do not touch these mud stains;
wait until they are dry,
and then just brush them off."
The mother and daughter each ate two steamed buns.
The remaining two were wrapped in the lotus leaf
and put aside.
Not long after,
Yuánwài returned.
Māmā saw that his face was flushed
and asked:
“You have been gone for this half a day,
whom did you see,
and where did you get wine to drink?”
Yuánwài recounted the whole story of meeting Chén Xuéjiù on the way and going together to the house of Mí Dūjiàn,
and then said:
“Fortunately, Heaven does not block every road for a person.
Thanks to the righteous intent of the old steward of that house,
and his kind heart,
he invited me to an inn to have wine and food,
and also pooled over three hundred coins with Chén Jiàoshòu to help us.”
Māmā was delighted
and told Yuánwài to go buy some rice
and some firewood and charcoal;
they would get through three or five days
and then make further arrangements.
Mother and daughter divided and ate the remaining steamed cakes.
Waiting for the rice to arrive,
they would inevitably cook some to eat.
When they went to sleep that night,
Yǒng-ér could not fall asleep,
thinking:
“During the day, when that old woman gave me the booklet, she said
that in times of urgent need,
I could open it and look.
Now, although Father has bought some rice,
how many days of use will it be enough for?
Inevitably, there will be hunger again,
which can also be counted as an urgent need.
I will go and open it to see
if there is a method to save us from hunger.”
Yǒng-ér got up slowly,
put on her clothes gently,
and walked out of the room.
As it turned out, the house Hú Yuánwài lived in
consisted of one main room and one lean-to.
It was nothing more than wattle and earth;
the lean-to on the side was broken down
and could only serve as a makeshift place for cooking.
The main room was partitioned
into two bedrooms.
The front part was close to the outer street,
where the old couple lived,
and the back part was given to the daughter as her room.
However, a path was carved out on the left side,
leading to the courtyard by the kitchen.
That night, when Yǒng-ér opened the door and went out,
although she did not pass by her parents’ bedside,
she was right against the wall,
so how could they not be startled awake?
Māmā asked:
“Where is my child going?”
Yǒng-ér said:
“I have a stomachache
and am getting up for some business.”
Māmā said:
“My child, I think you have caught a cold.
When you get up,
be careful to avoid the wind,
wear an extra piece of clothing,
and do not let the illness become serious.”
Yǒng-ér said:
“It is no matter.”
She got off the bed and slipped on her shoes,
and went into the broken lean-to on the side.
She saw the snow light shining
like broad daylight.
The earthen stove, earthenware pots, flour basins, and the like in the kitchen
were all visible.
Yǒng-ér took out the purple silk bag from her bosom,
untied the fine hemp rope,
gave it a shake,
and shook out the booklet to look.
Because Hú Yǒng-ér looked at this booklet,
it was destined that:
A young maiden of the inner chambers
would turn into a strange and monstrous demon;
a luckless beggar
would once again become a wealthy Yuánwài.
It truly caused:
the year-titles of the thirty-six prefectures to be changed,
and for five, six, or seven years, the dust of war to fly.
How Yǒng-ér transformed and achieved this,
let us listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
The Jiǔtiān secret manual is truly astounding,
but I fear its contents might not be transmitted truly.
If it is well-transmitted and well-used,
it can easily make one suspect ghosts and spirits.
That night, Hú Yǒng-ér untied the hemp rope wrapped around the outside of the purple silk bag,
shook out that booklet,
and walked out of the lean-to.
Looking closely,
the title on it was:
“Rúyì Bǎocè.”
Opening the first page to look,
the first line read:
Money Transformation Method.
Take a string and thread it through a copper coin,
tie a knot,
place it on the ground,
and cover it with an object.
Scoop a bowl of water into your hand,
recite the incantation seven times according to the spell,
take a mouthful of water and spray it downward,
and shout "Jí!"
When you lift the cover,
it will have turned into a string of a thousand copper coins.
Yǒng-ér said:
“So this is the method!”
She took the hemp rope she had just untied
and untied the single good copper coin that the old woman had transformed during the day from her sash,
threaded it onto the rope,
tied a knot,
and placed it on the ground.
She covered it with a flour basin.
She scooped a bowl of water from the water jar into her hand
and recited the incantation seven times according to the spell.
Taking a mouthful of water, she sprayed it downward
and shouted "Jí!"
Setting down the water bowl,
she lifted the flour basin.
Taking a look,
there was a pile of copper coins like a blue snake!
Yǒng-ér was quite startled
and did not know what to do.
She pondered:
“If I take this to Father and Mother,
they will surely ask where it came from.
How should I answer?”
Yǒng-ér then devised a plan;
she gently opened the back door
and tossed them onto the snowy ground within her own fence.
She would just say that someone had secretly aided her poor household.
Then she closed the back door,
entered the room,
and hid the booklet.
Māmā asked:
“Does your stomach still hurt, daughter?”
Yǒng-ér said:
“It does not hurt anymore.”
She then got back onto the bed to sleep again.
When dawn broke,
the three of them got up
and heated water to wash their faces.
Mother opened the back door to pour out the waste water.
Suddenly she saw a string of coins on the snowy ground.
She was startled
and hurriedly picked it up and said to the Yuánwài:
"I do not know who left this string of coins on the snowy ground in the back,
but I have picked it up here."
Hú Yuánwài said:
"Mother, it is better to be purely poor
than to be foully rich.
Our daughter is grown up,
and I fear some improper young men might come to provoke her
and use these copper coins to flirt with her.
This is currently a time when I have no luck;
if we take and use it for a moment,
it will lead those young men to come to our house and cause a disturbance,
and we will have no way to deal with them."
Mother said:
"How little sense you have!
In the city of Dōngjīng, there are many wealthy people who do good deeds,
helping the poor and alleviating suffering.
Seeing such heavy snow,
they take pity on the many in this courtyard who have nothing to eat.
It is not impossible that they left this in someone's home during the night as charity for the poor."
The Yuánwài only shook his hand and said:
"Hard to say!
Hard to say!
I too was once a wealthy man;
when did such a thing ever happen?"
Mother grew irritated
and scolded him:
"You ignorant old man!
It truly is that when a person is poor, their wisdom is short.
Since ancient times it has been said
that the virtuous and the foolish are not the same;
there are those willing to give
and those unwilling to give.
Why must everyone be the same as you?
You were burned by heavenly fire,
but how is it that other wealthy men
are not also burned by heavenly fire?
Those who do good deeds are good in the end.
Regarding your own daughter,
you are being suspicious of her with all sorts of doubts.
My daughter has not even gone out once or twice,
so what kind of people could she know?
Yet you talk such nonsense!"
Scolding the Yuánwài into silence, he nodded and said:
"What you say is also true.
Yesterday I went out to beg people for two or three hundred coins
and still could not get any.
Now that we have this string of coins,
let us buy five hundred coins' worth of rice,
three hundred coins' worth of firewood,
and use two hundred coins to buy some salt, sauce, and vegetables to eat with the rice;
then for now we will not worry about the falling snow."
The three of them spent the day very happily.
When night came and they went to sleep, around the second watch,
Yǒng'ér thought to herself:
"It was good to conjure a string of coins last night;
