tonight I will arrange things again and see."
She had this intention during the day
and had found a cord in advance
and hidden it on her person.
Yǒng'ér rose slowly
and put on her clothes.
Mother asked:
"What are you doing, my child?"
Yǒng'ér said:
"My stomach hurts again;
I need to go have a bowel movement!"
Mother said:
"How pitiful!
In the past few days, my child,
you had one meal and then none;
these past two days we have had firewood and rice,
and not knowing hunger,
you have just gone and overeaten.
Tomorrow I will tell your father to go out and buy a dose of medicine for you to take."
Yǒng'ér got off the bed
and came under the dilapidated lean-to,
just as she had arranged the night before.
Using the method to thread the coins with the cord,
she covered the washbasin,
chanted the incantation,
and spat a mouthful of water.
When she lifted the basin to look,
it was just like the night before;
there was another string of coins.
Yǒng'ér opened the back door, threw this money onto the snowy ground again,
closed the back door,
and went into the room to sleep.
At dawn,
Mother got up to heat water and wash her face;
she opened the back door to pour out the water
and saw another string of coins.
She was incredibly happy
and brought it back.
Hú Yuánwài said:
"How strange;
the origin of this money is unclear."
Mother said:
"Do not talk nonsense!
I am not afraid!
This is the local deity who cannot bear to see the three of us suffer
and is providing relief to us.
Once again, this string of coins has been placed in our home."
The Yuánwài saw that Mother had been irritated yesterday
and this time dared not say more;
he could only answer vaguely:
"Mother is right;
keep it in the house
and use it sparingly."
After three or five days had passed,
the snow finally melted
and the weather was clear and fine.
Mother said to the Yuánwài:
"While there are still a few days of food in the house,
you should go out for a walk.
If you happen to run into an acquaintance,
earning one or two hundred coins would be good too."
Hearing this, the Yuánwài
had no choice but to go out.
Mother, feeling relaxed and having nothing to do,
went to a neighbor's house to drink tea and gossip.
Yǒng'ér saw her mother go out
and that there was no one in the house.
She closed the front door,
took out her booklet,
and when she opened it to the second page,
written at the top was the Method for Conjuring Rice.
Yǒng'ér said:
"Thank Heaven and Earth!
Since I can conjure rice,
why worry about having nothing to eat!"
At the head of her mother's bed, there was originally a rice bucket
and a rice vat.
When Yǒng'ér went to look,
they both contained rice.
She thought for a while
and then combined the rice from the bucket into the vat.
As for the rest, she spread a bedsheet on the floor
and poured it all out,
leaving only a dozen grains of rice in the empty bucket.
She carried it into the lean-to,
covered it with a piece of clothing,
chanted the incantation,
spat a mouthful of water,
and shouted:
"Jí!"
She saw rice gushing out from the bucket.
Yǒng'ér panicked,
for she had not yet chanted the counter-spell.
The rice surged up rapidly.
The bucket hoops were old
and rotten.
Suddenly there was a sound,
the bucket hoops snapped,
and rice spilled all over the floor.
Later people heard of this matter of conjuring money and rice,
and playfully composed a poem saying:
When the cord is full of coins and the house is full of rice,
what kind of incantation can be so swift and divine?
If someone were willing to pass the incantation to me,
in life I would serve them, and in death I would mourn them.
Yǒng'ér saw this,
and cried out in distress!
Mother was in the next room,
and hearing her daughter cry out,
she hurried over to see.
Once the rice was disturbed by an outsider,
it stopped growing.
She saw that the floor of the lean-to was covered in rice.
Mother was startled
and said:
"How is there so much rice?"
Yǒng'ér quickly came up with a plan,
called a "deceptive ruse," and said:
"I must let Mother know,
a large man carrying a sack of rice on his back
pushed open the back door,
poured it out here and left.
I was startled by him,
and that is why I cried out."
Mother saw that the bucket hoops had fallen apart
and asked:
"This rice bucket is from my room;
why did you bring it out,
and where did the rice in this bucket go?"
Yǒng'ér said:
"I poured it inside the room;
I wanted to use this empty bucket
to hold the rice under this lean-to.
I did not expect the bucket hoops to be so old that they would break."
Mother said:
"But who was that large man,
and what was his reason?"
While she was nagging,
Zhāng Dàsǎo next door heard her;
not knowing the situation,
she knocked on the wall and called out:
"Hú Māmā!
How can you be so ignorant?
It must be those wealthy Yuánwài and rich men,
seeing that it has rained and snowed for many days.
Knowing that there are thousands in the compounds with nothing to eat,
they do such good deeds
without letting anyone know.
Leaving money and rice in people's homes
is secret merit.
If they gave it openly,
they would fear being pestered.
This is not worth mentioning."
Because Zhāng Dàsǎo had heard them,
Mother stopped speaking.
She told her daughter to hurry and tidy up,
and she came to help as well.
The two were still tidying up,
when the Yuánwài happened to return.
Seeing the mother and daughter sweeping rice on the ground,
he grew irritated and said:
"Where did you two learn such ways?
We only have enough rice for a meal or two,
and yet you choose to waste it!"
Māmā said:
"How could I be willing to waste it?
Look for yourself!
In the vats,
in the jars,
in the tubs,
and in the basins,
all are filled to the brim.
There is still so much left here and no more containers to hold it!"
The Yuánwài looked in astonishment and said:
"Where did this rice come from?"
Māmā said:
"After you went out,
I was having tea next door
when I heard our daughter crying out in distress.
When I rushed back,
I saw that the floor in the lean-to was covered in rice."
The Yuánwài said:
"This is indeed strange.
Where did this rice come from?"
Māmā said:
"Yǒng'ér said she saw a large man
carrying a sack of rice,
who pushed open the back door,
dumped the rice in the house, and left."
That Hú Yuánwài was an observant man.
When he opened the back door to look,
there were no footprints of anyone coming or going inside or outside the fence.
Feeling suspicious in his heart,
he closed the back door,
came back in and took a staff in his hand,
and repeatedly called for Yǒng'ér!
Yǒng'ér saw that things looked bad,
so she hid in her own room
and did not dare to come out.
The Yuánwài dragged her over.
Māmā said:
"Nothing happened, so why are you beating the child?"
The Yuánwài said:
"Keep your mouth shut!
This matter is very serious.
The two strings of cash the other day came in a strange way,
and today this rice has come in an unclear manner.
Tell this girl to speak the truth to me,
and I will not beat her;
if even one word is untrue,
I will beat her to death.
I am asking her
why those two strings of cash were on the snowy ground,
why this rice is in the house,
and who that large man was.
Even if it were some wealthy house performing good deeds,
would they specifically look after my family?
There must be a reason for this!"
At first Yǒng'ér denied it,
but later, unable to endure the beating,
she was forced to confess the origins of that large man.
This was a celestial injustice
that she could not bear,
so she had to tell the truth:
"I will not hide it from Father
and Māmā!
She said that on the day it first started snowing,
Father went out.
Māmā told me to go out and buy steamed buns.
On my way back, I ran into an old Pópó
who looked at me and said she was hungry,
and asked me for a steamed bun to eat.
I could not bear to refuse,
so I gave a steamed bun to that Pópó.
She said,
'I don't want to eat yours;
I was only testing you,'
and she gave it back to me.
She said it was rare to find such compassion, filiality, and kindness.
Then she gave me a purple gauze bag
with a booklet inside,
saying:
'If you want money or rice,
according to the incantations in this booklet,
they will all appear.'
I did not believe it at first,
so for two nights in a row, I followed the incantations in that booklet,
and money was indeed conjured up.
Today, while Māmā went to the neighbor's house,
I tried the method for conjuring rice,
and indeed, rice appeared once more."
When Hú Yuánwài heard this,
he stomped his feet and cried out in distress:
"Now the government has posted notices
to capture sorcerers,
and you have implicated me!
If I beat this girl to death,
I might escape punishment myself."
He picked up the staff and began to beat her.
Yǒng'ér cried out for someone to save her!
When the neighbor Zhāng Dàsǎo heard the beating of Yǒng'ér,
she came over to intervene
but found the door locked.
Zhāng Dàsǎo shouted from outside the door:
"Yuánwài, please spare the child!
Usually you aren't so irritable;
why are you beating her?
Māmā!
Why aren't you trying to stop him?"
The Yuánwài replied in a huff:
"Sister, it's because this girl was hiding a booklet—"
Having said half a sentence,
he stopped.
Zhāng Dàsǎo said:
"What is written in the booklet?"
The Yuánwài said:
"It's all just nonsense."
Zhāng Dàsǎo misunderstood,
thinking it was some secret love letter,
and called out:
"Your daughter is young
and does not understand such things.
It must be those idle young men on the street
who have provoked her with their talk.
If it is something improper,
you just need to burn this booklet
and forbid her from doing it again.
Why get so angry
and beat the child so severely?"
The Yuánwài was actually reminded by her words and
responded:
"Sister is right."
Looking at Yǒng'ér, he said:
"Bring the booklet to me so I can see it."
Yǒng'ér then took the booklet from her bosom
and handed it to her father.
The Yuánwài took it and said:
"Do you remember the words in it?"
Yǒng'ér said:
"I beg Father's forgiveness,
I cannot remember them.
But if I look at them,
I can read them out."
The Yuánwài told Māmā to light a bundle of firewood
and burned it together with the purple gauze bag.
Looking at Yǒng'ér, he said:
"Today, for the sake of the neighbor Gānniáng's face,
I will spare you this time.
If you ever do this again,
I will beat you to death!"
Yǒng'ér said:
"I beg Father's mercy!
I will never dare to do it again."
The Yuánwài said to Māmā:
"It is because our husband and wife's fortune is strong
and only we know of this.
If outsiders were to hear of it,
it would be a terrible disaster."
Māmā had been thrown into a state of confusion by the Yuánwài's outburst,
not knowing what was right or wrong,
so she simply let him have his way.
There is a poem to prove it:
In years past, the Māmā burned the immortal painting,
And now the Yuánwài burns the precious booklet.
Since they are so accustomed to using fire,
How could the fires of heaven be willing to spare them?
As for the storyteller,
I have a question to ask:
In the thirteenth chapter of this book,
it says Shènggūgū, Dànzǐ Héshang, and Zuǒ Chù refined their magic
for three years before succeeding.
How difficult that was!
Today, Hú Yǒng'ér conjures money and rice
so easily;
isn't this a contradiction between the beginning and the end?
The reader may not know
that when they first refined gods and ghosts,
they were novices at the task.
But today, it is Shènggūgū who has devised a plan to deliver her daughter,
secretly assisting her from the void.
If it had seemed very difficult at the start,
Yǒng'ér would not have been willing to learn.
Look, the first page of this booklet is the method for conjuring money,
and the second page is the method for conjuring rice.
These were specifically chosen to move her heart by providing what was lacking in Yǒng'ér's home.
These were all the means by which Shènggūgū enticed her through the gate.
Enough of idle talk.
Let it be said that Hú Yǒng’ér was beaten by her father,
who forced her to give up the booklet and burned it.
She was extremely upset
and went off by herself to weep.
Her mother saw this
and consoled her.
After a night had passed,
on the next day,
the Yuánwài went out again.
Her mother once more went next door to Sister-in-law Zhāng’s house to chat.
Yǒng’ér closed both the front and back doors
and sat gloomily in her room thinking:
"This booklet
is worth more than a thousand pieces of gold.
That old woman had such kind intentions
in giving it to me.
Even if I only conjured some money and rice to pass the days,
it would save me from begging others.
Yet it was burned by father;
what a pity I hadn't seen the rest of it
and don't know what kind of tricks were there.
That old woman instructed that if I didn't understand,
I should call for Shèng Gūgū,
and she would come to teach me.
Although I no longer have the booklet today,
I will try calling out once
to see if she comes or not.
If she is willing to come,
perhaps she still has a copy kept
and I can ask her for another one.
I only fear that when the old woman comes,
she might startle mother,
which would be unsafe."
She then went into the courtyard,
looked up at the sky,
and called out softly:
"Shèng Gūgū!"
She saw the old woman carrying a bamboo staff,
descending from the eaves,
and entering straight into the lean-to
without a sound.
Yǒng’ér followed her into the room
and offered her greetings.
She then told her about the matter of her father burning the booklet
and finished her explanation.
The old woman said:
"The booklet was not burned;
I had originally taken it back here!"
She then pulled the booklet out from her sleeve;
it was still wrapped in the purple silk bag,
completely undamaged.
Yǒng’ér was shocked
and hurriedly knelt down to beg her.
The old woman helped Yǒng’ér up and said:
"My child!
I was actually your biological mother in a past life!
Now, pitying your suffering,
I have specifically come to deliver you.
If you want this booklet,
you cannot practice it at home,
so it would be useless.
You must follow my words:
sleep during the day
to restore your spirit.
At night, do not take off your clothes.
Wait until dusk when everyone has settled down;
whenever you hear the cry of a crane,
that is what I have sent to welcome you.
You then quietly leave the room,
come riding the crane,
and I will meet with you;
you will return by the fifth watch.
The magical arts in this booklet,
I will teach them to you one by one.
On the day you attain the Way,
your divine powers will be vast,
and you will be free and happy
beyond what can be fully described."
Yǒng’ér said:
"That is very good,
but I fear my parents might notice at night
and start looking for me;
finding me gone,
when I return in the morning,
how could I deny it?"
The old woman said:
"That is easy!"
She handed the bamboo staff in her hand to Yǒng’ér
and instructed:
"My child, hide this staff well;
when you set out at night,
place it in your sleeping spot
and cover it with the quilt.
If your parents come,
it will look exactly as if you are asleep.
This is the immortals' technique of a substitute body."
Yǒng’ér took the bamboo staff in her hand.
The old woman flew up to the eaves
and suddenly vanished again.
Yǒng’ér was finally joyful;
she hid the staff under the mat
and, following the old woman's words,
she did not take off her clothes.
When dusk arrived,
sure enough, she heard the cry of a crane.
Yǒng’ér then took the staff from under the bed mat and placed it within the quilt,
and quietly stepped out into the courtyard.
She saw an immortal crane
stretching its neck to welcome her.
Yǒng’ér straddled the crane's back
and flew off into the sky.
After a short while, they reached a place to stop.
She saw the old woman was already there,
but she was no longer dressed as before;
on her head she wore a star crown,
and on her body a crane-feather cloak,
looking very refined.
The old woman gave a beckon with her hand,
and the crane then ducked into her sleeve.
When she took it out to look,
it was actually an immortal crane cut from paper.
This startled Yǒng’ér, who knelt down again.
The old woman helped her up and said:
"My child, do not be afraid."
Yǒng’ér felt that the place where she stood
was very high and steep.
She asked:
"Where is this place?"
The old woman said:
"This is the highest level of the pagoda in the Dà Xiāngguó Sì;
no human tracks reach here,
so it is the perfect place to teach you.
First I will teach you the art of hiding your form,
so you can pass through windows and enter crevices,
entering and leaving without needing to open doors.
Next I will teach you the art of flight;
sit astride a wooden stool
and recite an incantation.
This stool will change as you wish
and rise into the air.
You will come and go on your own every night;
how convenient that will be!"
Yǒng’ér learned these arts
and from then on went out at dusk and returned at dawn,
understanding the Rúyì Bǎocè step by step.
Firstly, Yǒng’ér was intelligent and gifted,
so in drawing talismans and reciting incantations,
she learned as soon as she was taught.
Secondly, most of these were arts that Shèng Gūgū had already refined and completed
and handed over to her;
she only needed to be shown how to use them,
which was very effortless.
Leaving aside Yǒng'ér's study of magic,
and speaking instead of the time when Hú Yuánwài burned the book:
there was rice in the bucket to eat
and money by the bedside to spend.
As the ancients said:
sitting and eating will empty a mountain;
standing and eating will sink the ground.
One day three,
three days nine;
before ten days or half a month had passed,
the food in the bucket gradually became shallow,
and the bedside money gradually grew short.
After some more time,
the rice was exhausted and the money gone;
once again, they had one meal
followed by none.
They pleaded with people,
but had nowhere to turn for help,
and as before, they had no food to eat.
Māmā thought once again of Yǒng'ér conjuring money and rice,
and with sharp and bitter resentment, she grumbled to her husband:
"You went and beat Yǒng'ér,
and burned her book as well.
Today you deserve to starve to death,
dragging me and our daughter into suffering.
How can you be such a man,
starving to death while leaning against the rice vat,
making us mother and daughter endure hunger and starvation!"
The Yuánwài said:
"Now that things have come to this,
there is nothing to be done.
Why do you keep blaming me?"
Māmā said:
"As soon as there was some rice to eat,
you stirred up all this trouble.
Since you were bold enough to beat her,
you should have had some way to provide money and rice.
Now our poor lives are still here,
yet that book has been burned by you."
The Yuánwài said:
"It was my momentary lack of foresight;
it was a thousand times, ten thousand times wrong to burn it.
Had I known, it would have been better to keep that book."
Māmā said:
"By the time you realized it, it was too late."
The Yuánwài said:
"It can't be helped;
I will swallow my pride and entreat my daughter;
I expect she still remembers it,
and can conjure some more money and rice
to rescue us.
You go and ask her for now."
Māmā said:
"Ever since the daughter was beaten by you,
she has not come near her father or mother again.
During the day she stays only in her room,
moping and dazed, dozing off.
When she goes to bed at night,
she is just like a piece of wood,
senseless and unconscious.
The night before last, I got up in the middle of the night to relieve myself
and saw that the back room door was not closed tightly;
it had been blown open by the wind.
I was afraid the daughter would catch a chill,
so I lit a lamp to look;
she was sleeping soundly, tightly wrapped in her quilt.
No matter how I shook her,
she simply would not wake up.
A perfectly fine and clever child
has been beaten into a stupor by your fists.
As if she would still remember some book!
If you want to ask her,
go into her room and ask her yourself;
I do not have the face for it."
The Yuánwài indeed walked into the room
and, with a conciliatory smile, said:
"My child!
Your father asks you something:
do you remember the methods for conjuring money and rice from the book?"
Yǒng'ér said:
"I tell you, Father,
I do not remember."
The Yuánwài said:
"My child!
Rescue your father and mother;
it is not as if you are rescuing strangers.
Do not be stubborn;
it was your father who was in the wrong."
Yǒng'ér simply did not speak.
Māmā stepped into the room,
gave the Yuánwài a shove,
and cursed:
"Get away, you useless man!"
The mother went forward and said:
"My child!
If not for your father's sake, then for your mother's,
try to remember some of the magic, however little,
to save your mother's life."
The Yuánwài said:
"From now on, I will never beat you again."
Yǒng'ér said:
"Because Father beat me before,
I have forgotten everything.
I vaguely remember a little bit,
but I do not know if it will work.
Father!
Go get a stool and sit down firmly.
I will let you see."
The Yuánwài obeyed his daughter and sat on the wooden stool,
only to see his daughter's mouth chanting incantations.
She shouted, "Swiftly!"
and the stool rose straight into the air.
Māmā was terrified and dazed.
The Yuánwài's head was pressed against the roof beam
as he cried:
"Help!
I cannot get down!
If not for this house,
I would have gone straight up into the middle of the sky!"
Truly:
Before she had even displayed her divine powers,
she first played a trick on her own father.
It is not yet known how Hú Yuánwài came down;
listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
Few know the Wǔléi Zhèngfǎ,
yet the spread of heterodox paths through the world is also strange.
Do not act with a deceitful heart or betray Heaven and Earth;
divine powers and playful games stem from immortal roots.
It is said that Hú Yǒng'ér was playing a trick on the Yuánwài.
As he sat on a bench,
the bench suddenly flew up
and went straight to the roof beam.
At that moment, the Yuánwài was terrified.
He looked at his daughter and said,
“What kind of magic is this?
Please let me down.”
Yǒng'ér said,
“Let it be known to Father!
I have forgotten all the magic for conjuring money and rice.
I only remember this magic,
which cannot save one from hunger
nor provide relief in an emergency.”
The Yuánwài said,
“This is terrifying!
Just let me down for now.”
Yǒng'ér muttered some incantations
and shouted,
“Speedily!”
The bench then descended.
The Yuánwài said,
“That was close!
I almost fell.
Even if I hadn’t died,
I would certainly have ended up with several bruises.”
Yǒng'ér asked,
“Father,
do you truly want money or not?”
The Yuánwài said,
“My child!
You are talking nonsense.
Your father and mother haven't had a full meal for two or three days.
Even if I could do without money,
could I possibly do without my life?”
Yǒng'ér said,
“Since Father wants money,
go find two ropes,
and I will transform them into one or two strings of cash for us to use.”
Although the Yuánwài remained silent,
he thought to himself,
“I had intended to ask my daughter but hadn't done so yet;
it is better not to trouble two hosts for one guest.
While she is willing,
I should find more ropes.
I will have her transform them into several hundred strings of cash
to make me happy.
If the matter is discovered by officials,
I will deal with it then.”
When he went to look by the bedside,
there were only three ropes left.
The Yuánwài felt this was too few,
so he walked straight out of the alley
to the Líhuòpù of his acquaintance Zōu Dàláng on the main street and asked,
“Dàláng!
I want a large bundle of fine hemp rope.”
Zōu Dàláng asked,
“What is it for?”
The Yuánwài was an honest man,
so he replied,
“It is for stringing money.”
Zōu Dàláng laughed and said,
“The Yuánwài has struck it rich again,
having so much money to string!
There are plenty of ropes;
just bring the money and pay for them.”
The Yuánwài said,
“I do not have any money on me.”
He then took off the old cloth cloak he was wearing
to offer it as temporary collateral.
Zōu Dàláng thought to himself,
“He doesn't even have money to buy rope,
so how could he have money to string?
It is clearly a lie.
He is so destitute
that he lacks food to eat;
who knows what kind of trick he intends to pull with those hemp ropes?
If he causes some trouble tomorrow,
it will implicate me.”
So he said,
“My small shop has little capital and tiny profits;
I only sell for cash.
There is no need to take off your clothes.”
The Yuánwài said,
“Just leave it here for a moment;
I will come back shortly to redeem it.”
But Zōu Dàláng would not agree to it.
The Yuánwài had no choice but to step down from the shop entrance.
He thought,
“If even an acquaintance behaves like this,
other shops will surely be unwilling as well.
It just goes to show how ill-fated I am.
I will just take those three ropes
and transform them into three strings of cash first, then decide what to do.”
He hurriedly ran back to the courtyard
and ducked into the room.
He frantically searched by the bedside,
but the ropes were nowhere to be seen.
His wife and Yǒng'ér saw this
and could not help but laugh.
His wife said,
“You old fool!
What are you so busy with?”
The Yuánwài said,
“I had set aside three ropes here;
why have they disappeared?”
His wife said,
“I gave them to our daughter and she transformed them into these three strings of cash here.
Where on earth did you run off to?”
The Yuánwài said,
“I thought that since I was going to ask our daughter anyway,
I should find over a hundred ropes
and turn them into money
for our long-term use.
Unfortunately, Zōu Dàláng, who runs the Líhuòpù,
insisted on cash before he would sell anything.
I took off this cloak to give to him as collateral,
but he refused time and again.”
His wife said,
“You shouldn't be so greedy.
If we have one or two strings of cash at home every day,
it will be enough for the rest of your life without having to ask anyone for help.”
The Yuánwài asked,
“Where is the money?”
His wife said,
“It’s covered up under the quilt.”
The Yuánwài was overjoyed
and took some Chìlíguǒ to buy firewood.
The next day, he and his wife went together again to beg Yǒng'ér to conjure money.
From that day forward,
Yǒng'ér would transform things into money from time to time,
and there was always rice in the jar.
The Yuánwài himself
often had money to buy wine and food,
and he gradually acquired new clothes,
so his appearance became more respectable than before.
One day,
the Yuánwài returned from buying things.
Yǒng'ér said,
“Father!
I want to show you something.”
She reached into her sleeve and pulled out a silver ingot.
The Yuánwài took it in his hand to weigh it
and saw that it was about twenty-four or twenty-five taels in weight.
The Yuánwài asked,
“Where did this silver ingot come from?”
Yǒng'ér said,
“Early this morning, I saw an old man selling incense and paper goods passing by with his cart.
On it were gold and silver ingots made of paper;
I used one coin to buy one from him
and transformed it into a real one.”
The Yuánwài said, “Transforming things into a hundred or so strings of cash
isn't worth much.
If you can transform things into gold and silver,
the three of us will be wealthy once again.”
He went to a Zhǐshǒupù,
bought three strings of paper gold and silver ingots, and returned.
Looking at his daughter, he said,
“If you only transform one or half an ingot,
it won’t be enough.
You might as well transform twenty or thirty of them,
so we can live happily for the rest of our lives.”
Yǒng'ér took those gold and silver ingots
and placed them on the ground.
She untied her skirt from her waist and covered them.
She muttered some incantations,
spat out a mouthful of water,
and shouted,
“Speedily!”
When she lifted the skirt to look,
there was a pile of gold and a pile of silver on the ground.
When Hú Yuánwài saw this,
his joy went without saying;
it was all through his daughter's power that so much gold and silver had been conjured.
The Yuánwài looked at his wife and Yǒng'ér
and suggested,
“Now that we have gold and silver
and are wealthy,
we cannot possibly stay only in the Bùsīqiú Yuàn.
My intention is to find a house in a bustling area
and open a Cǎibópù.
What do you two say to that?”
His wife said,
“We had no food to eat all winter
and had to beg people all day long.
If we suddenly open a Cǎibópù now,
I am afraid it will arouse people's suspicion.”
The Yuánwài said,
“No matter.
Among my peers and acquaintances,
I will go and tell them:
‘Recently an official has taken care of me
and lent me some capital.’
I will buy half the goods through a broker
and take half on credit.
Then they won’t be suspicious.”
His wife said,
“That is a good point.”
On that day,
Hú Yuánwài dressed himself neatly,
and went out to see several acquaintances, saying:
"I have recently received the patronage of an official,
and have borrowed some capital,
intending to open a small shop.
All of you acquaintances,
are you willing to assist me?
I only ask to buy half on credit and half with cash;
I hope you will help this humble one succeed!"
The people said:
"No problem!
No problem!
It is all on us."
Once the acquaintances had agreed,
he went to the local marketplace and rented a building,
set up some cabinets and furniture,
and chose an auspicious day to open the shop front.
Although it was said he would buy half on credit
and half with cash,
in truth, this was just a pretense;
how could he have collected so many goods?
It was all thanks to Yǒng’ér, who would listen in the shop to what was needed,
and then go inside to conjure them up.
Because there was no cost for capital,
for goods worth one guàn,
they sold them to others for only nine hundred wén,
adding a ten percent discount.
People always want a bargain,
and seeing that they could buy cheaply,
and that the goods were better than those of other shops,
everyone came to buy.
The goods in the shop,
every single item sold well,
and the Yuánwài was immensely delighted.
The family wealth gradually grew;
they employed a manager in the shop,
two attendants,
and two maidservants.
In less than two or three years,
the household finances became very abundant.
One after another, houses were built on the vacant lot in Píng’ān Jiē where the fire had broken out, just as before.
Although they were not as tidy as in the old days,
they still had halls and rooms,
and flowers and plants were planted in the back garden.
Truly it is said:
Suddenly a new atmosphere opens up,
restoring the old family reputation.
At that time, neighbors from the east and west
all came to offer congratulations.
Households that had cut off contact for several years
now once again sent trays and boxes of gifts,
and resumed their relationship as acquaintances.
Hú Yuánwài had lived at Bājiǎo Tíng and in that Bùsīqiú Yuàn
for nearly two years;
renting a house and opening a shop,
another three years passed,
totaling five years.
Returning to his old home,
he was once again Hú Yuánwài.
This is indeed:
Even the Huáng Hé has days when it runs clear;
how can a person not have times of success?
There is a poem to prove it:
Wealth and poverty, rise and fall, are all destined by fate;
family assets taken away return once more.
To whom should I entrust a word for Mí Dūjiàn?
The wealthy man now has wealth again.
When other shops saw people coming to buy from him,
they began to suspect, saying:
"How strange and bizarre!
All the goods are brought out from the back by the owner."
The managers also suspected, saying:
"Why are the goods not kept in the cabinets,
but instead brought out from the back?"
Hú Yuánwài realized the meaning of their suspicion and jealousy,
and thought to himself:
"My family hasn't even bought them;
it is my daughter who conjures them up.
Now that others are suspicious,
what should I do?"
After a day passed,
in the evening when the shop was closed,
he went inside and ordered dinner to be prepared.
The maidservants brought it out,
and while the three of them were drinking wine,
the Yuánwài instructed the maidservants:
"You go and rest;
we need to discuss some household matters."
Hearing his words, the maidservants
each went their way,
which goes without saying.
The Yuánwài said to Yǒng’ér:
"Child!
Our entire family's livelihood and wealth
all come from you.
We have gold, silver, and bolts of silk
beyond counting.
Outside we have attendants,
inside we have maidservants,
and in the shop there are managers.
As for the silk people come to buy,
they suspect because they only see it being sold,
and never see it being supplied.
From now on,
you must not come to the front of the shop.
Hearing about sales worth a hundred or so guàn,
what is that worth?
If any traces of our handiwork are revealed,
and people see through it,
it would be a great disaster,
and our livelihood would all be lost.
From now on, do not conjure anything up anymore."
Yǒng’ér said:
"I beg of you, Father,
I will stay inside,
and simply not come out;
I will just listen to the business at the front."
The Yuánwài said:
"If that is the case,
very well!
Call for the meal,"
and after they had eaten,
the daughter went back to her room.
Since instructing his daughter that evening,
they sold whatever silk was available in the shop,
and for what they didn't have, they went to other shops to buy;
previously, they would have conjured up whatever was missing.
Now the girl no longer came to the shop to listen.
Hú Yuánwài felt very much at ease.
After more than a month had passed,
Hú Yuánwài suddenly realized:
"These past few days I have only looked after the business at the front,
and have not looked after my daughter at home.
It would be fine if she stays settled and behaves herself,
but if she acts recklessly,
and the maidservants find out,
that would be disastrous!"
On that day, Hú Yuánwài had the thought to go see his daughter.
He came to the central hall,
but could not find his daughter;
he looked in the rooms but still could not find her.
He walked into the rear garden,
yet still did not find her.
As he passed by the door of the woodshed,
he saw that the door was open.
The Yuánwài said,
"Could she be in here?"
He moved his body and stepped forward,
entering the woodshed door.
He saw Yǒng'ér sitting on a small stool in an open space,
with a water bowl placed before her
and a vermilion gourd in her hand.
The Yuánwài said to himself,
"I looked for her everywhere else to no avail,
so what is she doing here?"
He did not dare to startle her,
so he stood still to see what she would do.
He saw Yǒng'ér pull the stopper from the vermilion gourd and give it a tip;
out poured about two hundred red beans,
along with rice straw cut into inch-long pieces, onto the ground.
She muttered incantations under her breath,
took a mouthful of water and sprayed it out,
then shouted,
"Swiftly!"
They all transformed into men and horses three feet tall.
All had red helmets,
red armor,
red robes,
red tassels,
red flags,
and red insignias;
the red horses circled on the ground,
forming a battle array.
The Yuánwài said to himself,
"Around the tenth of that month,
I warned her sternly,
so she did not dare to transform things,
yet here she is practicing her magic arts.
Let me see how she intends to proceed."
He saw Yǒng'ér pull the stopper from a white gourd and give it a tip;
out poured about two hundred white beans,
along with rice straw cut into inch-long pieces, onto the ground.
She muttered incantations under her breath,
took a mouthful of water and sprayed it out,
then shouted,
"Swiftly!"
They all transformed into men and horses three feet tall,
all with white helmets,
white robes,
white armor,
white tassels,
white flags,
and white insignias.
The white horses were like a wall of copper or iron,
also forming a battle array.
How much space could this woodshed have?
Yet it accommodated over four hundred men and horses;
with two arrays deployed, there was still room for a battlefield,
and it did not feel cramped in the slightest.
The Yuánwài watched until his eyes were dazzled,
as if in a dream.
He saw Yǒng'ér pull a gold fine-toothed comb from her head,
shout "Transform!"
and the comb in her hand became a precious sword.
Pointing it at the two sides of troops,
she shouted,
"Engage in battle!"
He saw the troops from both sides clash,
their battle cries shaking the heavens.
Hú Yuánwài was so shocked he stood there like a block of wood,
saying,
"It is good that I am the one who saw this;
if others were to see it,
it would be a major disaster,
and I would eventually be implicated by this girl.
If I want to be free of trouble,
it is better to act early,
regardless of our father-daughter bond."
The Yuánwài watched, feeling extremely agitated;
he walked out of the woodshed door,
went to the kitchen to find a heavy cleaver for chopping bones,
and turned back.
Meanwhile, Hú Yǒng'ér held the sword,
commanding the troops to circle and join from left and right,
engaging in a "Dragon Gate" battle.
He saw the left and right sides in a confused melee,
with no victor yet decided.
After a long while,
the battle arrays moved apart,
and the red and white troops separated into two groups.
Yǒng'ér gave a wave of her sword,
and shouted "Retract!"
He saw the red and white troops
return to their original forms as red beans,
white beans,
and inch-long straw.
Yǒng'ér collected them back into the red and white gourds.
Hú Yuánwài, from behind,
raised his cleaver;
seeing Yǒng'ér clearly,
with just one blow,
her head fell with the blade,
and as her corpse lay on the ground,
there is a poem as witness:
How could a father's nature bear to kill his child?
But he feared her demonic arts would bring calamity.
Pity the two troops of cloud-like cavalry
could not save their general from her death.
The Yuánwài saw Yǒng'ér's head and body in different places,
and in his heart he felt great bitterness,
great melancholy,
and great panic.
He then threw the cleaver aside,
dragged the corpse to a secluded spot and covered it,
then left the woodshed and locked the door with a lock.
Dejected and listless, he walked out to the silk shop and sat down,
thinking to himself,
"What a sin!
My daughter had managed so many of our family's affairs,
yet in a sudden moment just now,
because I saw her doing something improper,
I destroyed her;
yet I cannot be blamed.
If I had looked out for her,
I would surely have ended up involved in a lawsuit.
It was better to destroy her
so that we, husband and wife,
could be safe.
If her mother finds out,
how could she not be furious?
It cannot be that she goes unseen for a whole day;
by evening, how will I explain the reason for killing her when she asks?"
Hú Yuánwài was restless,
pacing in and out over a hundred times.
By evening,
the shop was closed,
and the managers all left.
He ordered the maidservant:
"Prepare some wine;
I shall drink three cups with Māmā."
Neither Yuánwài nor Māmā mentioned their daughter.
After the two of them had drunk five or seven cups of wine,
Yuánwài was seen to let out a sigh,
and two lines of tears fell pattering down.
Māmā said:
"There is nothing wrong,
so why are you crying like this?"
Yuánwài said:
"I have a matter to tell you,
and it is my fault.
You and I, husband and wife, were just beginning to enjoy a happy life,
but I saw our daughter's behavior was improper,
and in a moment of short-sightedness,
I killed her.
I fear you will blame me;
please do not be distressed."
Māmā said:
"Yuánwài, why do you speak such words?
What strange thing did the child do again?"
Yuánwài recounted the matter of Yǒng'ér transforming things into men and horses
from beginning to end.
When Māmā heard this,
she beat her breast and stamped her feet,
crying out:
"Have you forgotten three years ago when we lived in the Bùsīqiú courtyard,
enduring hunger and cold?
If it were not for my daughter,
how could we have today?
Yet you could actually strike
and kill my child!"
Yuánwài said:
"It was simply a moment of irritation on my part,
but it was also because our family's safety was at stake,
so I had no other choice.
Do not resent me,
and please consider our long-standing relationship as husband and wife."
Māmā said:
"You killed my daughter,
how could I not be distressed!"
Māmā then wondered:
"Just now I saw my daughter safe and sound in her room,
so why do you say she is dead?"
Thus she asked:
"When did you kill her?"
Yuánwài said:
"I killed her during the day."
Māmā said:
"If she was killed during the day,
let me show you someone."
Māmā went inside and after a short while,
pulled her out by the arm.
When Yuánwài looked closely,
he was startled and said:
"It really is my daughter!
During the day I hacked her with a knife,
so how is she alive here?"
Yuánwài was so frightened that his heart was in a panic,
and he thought:
"In the end, I will be implicated by this monster-like girl.
I must use a small trick
to save the lives of us two."
Just because Yuánwài had this thought,
it was destined that:
Yǒng'ér would bring about a strange marriage
that would cause a stir throughout the prefecture of Kāifēng.
Truly:
Only constant peace is true fortune;
all kinds of strange phenomena are never auspicious.
As for what kind of trick Yuánwài would use,
listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
Many words lead to hatred, few words to foolishness;
the evil are detested, and the good are bullied.
The rich suffer from jealousy, the poor from humiliation;
consider which of these accords with Heaven's plan.
It is said that Māmā led Yǒng'ér out by the arm.
When Yǒng'ér saw her father,
she turned her face away, gave a formal greeting,
and said to her mother:
"Father is fine,
so why did you call me out?"
After saying this,
she went back into her room as before.
Hú Yuánwài saw with his own eyes that his daughter was safe and sound there,
and instead his face was full of shame,
his mouth open and unable to close.
Having been rebuked by Māmā,
Yuánwài could only confusedly pass the night.
Getting up early the next day,
he went to open the woodshed door to look;
Yuánwài was so frightened he was dazed.
He saw the knife on one side,
and the hacked corpse
was actually a bamboo broom cut into two pieces.
Yuánwài said:
"Yesterday it was clearly I who struck,
how could it be a broom?
Since she has become a monster and makes trouble like this,
I definitely cannot keep her.
I must simply have her leave my house."
Yuánwài hesitated for a day,
and when evening came and he had dinner with Māmā,
he discussed it, saying:
"As the common saying goes, when a son grows up he should marry,
and when a daughter grows up she must be wed.
Now Yǒng'ér is fully grown;
just keeping her at home
is not a long-term plan.
Her life
will also remain unsettled."
Māmā said:
"Today's family wealth was all earned by our daughter,
how could I have the heart to push her out!
Moreover, you and I have no other child,
so we should instead bring in a son-in-law to live here and help manage the household,
so you and I can have 'half a son' to rely on."
Yuánwài said:
"Māmā!
My initial intention was also like this.
However, the daughter has been pampered and spoiled since childhood,
and what she likes is playing around."
He then sent away the maidservant
and told Māmā about the battle between the bean-people and grass-horses in the woodshed,
saying:
"Practicing such tricks,
if it should happen to fall into the eyes of others
and they speak of it,
wouldn't that bring an end to your life and mine!
It is better to choose a good match
and marry her off.
Being with parents-in-law
is ultimately not like being with one's own parents;
she will surely have to restrain herself a bit.
After three or five years,
when she is older and more mature,
we can bring her back along with the son-in-law;
wouldn't that be convenient for both?"
With just this speech,
he coaxed Māmā,
and she replied:
"What Yuánwài says is also right."
At dawn the next day,
he told the attendant to go to the front streets and back alleys to call for two matchmakers.
The attendant went and after a short while,
called for two matchmakers.
There is a short lyric titled "Zhù Yún Fēi"
specifically describing the conduct of a matchmaker:
Pitiful matchmaker,
her two feet move back and forth as fast as a shuttle.
A person's fate depends entirely on her making,
and ages are passed on incorrectly.
Ha!
Stirring up storms upon her tongue,
she turns poverty into wealth,
bringing about a deal,
regardless of whether it ruins a life.
She only wants many gifts from the groom's family,
only hoping for many rewards and gratitude.
Of those two matchmakers,
one was called Kuàizuǐ Zhāng Sānsǎo,
and the other was called Lǎoshí Lǐ Sìsǎo.
The two arrived at the front hall
and greeted the Yuánwài and the Māma with wishes of boundless blessings.
The Māma asked them to be seated
and invited them for tea.
After tea,
wine was prepared to entertain them.
Zhāng Sānsǎo rose to address the Māma and the Yuánwài, saying:
“You summoned us,
but we do not know what orders you have?”
The Yuánwài said:
“Sit for a moment!
Have you two ever seen my daughter?”
Zhāng Sānsǎo said:
“We saw the Xiǎoniángzǐ once before;
what a fine Xiǎoniángzǐ she is!”
The Yuánwài said:
“My family has raised only this one daughter,
just nineteen years of age,
and we wish to arrange a marriage for her.
We have specifically invited you two to discuss the matter.”
Zhāng Sānsǎo said:
“Thank you, Yuánwài and Māma,
for looking after us.
Since the Xiǎoniángzǐ is to be betrothed,
we do not know whether you wish to take in a son-in-law
or marry her out?”
Yuánwài Hú said:
“I only wish to marry her out.”
Lǐ Sìsǎo said:
“If she is to be married out,
then matches are indeed available.”
The Yuánwài took out two taels of silver
and said:
“Take this for now as travel money for the two of you.
If the marriage is successful,
I shall naturally thank you most generously.”
The two said:
“We have not yet exerted the slightest effort;
how could we receive such a generous gift beforehand?
It is improper to accept.”
Though they spoke thus,
both reached out their hands to take the silver.
Zhāng Sānsǎo was the first to receive it.
They gave thanks and left,
going into a silk and fabric shop
where they borrowed a děngzi scale and shears to divide the silver equally.
The two discussed it on the road, saying:
“Where is there a good family of matching status?
It would be best to go and propose while the matter is hot.”
Lǐ Sìsǎo said:
“Such a match is hard to find in a hurry;
it all depends on our luck.”
Zhāng Sānsǎo said:
“It is settled today;
you must not hide things from me,
and I will not hide things from you.
Let us search separately,
and if one of us finds a prospect,
we two shall speak together,
share the money,
and drink the wine together.”
Lǐ Sìsǎo said:
“Well said.
If I find one, I will tell you,
and if you find one, you will tell me.”
The two made their agreement and went their separate ways.
Zhāng Sānsǎo thought to herself:
“On the West Street, at the large shop of Yuánwài Zhāng, there is an only son,
just seventeen years of age.
They only want to find a good daughter-in-law;
I shall pay them a visit.
I only fear they might mind that the Hú family’s daughter is older;
regardless of success, I’ll get three bottles of wine,
so it is well to go and coax a cup to drink.”
Zhāng Sānsǎo then went straight to the house of Yuánwài Zhāng.
Yuánwài Zhāng saw a matchmaker enter
and asked:
“What business brings you to my house?”
Zhāng Sānsǎo said:
“There is a good marriage prospect,
which I have come specifically to propose.”
The Yuánwài said:
“Many matchmakers have come to propose,
but none have been successful.
Now, I wonder whose daughter it is?”
Zhāng Sānsǎo said:
“It is the daughter of Yuánwài Hú, who runs the silk and fabric shop;
she is as beautiful as a flowering branch.”
Yuánwài Zhāng said:
“I once saw her at Jīnmíng Chí;
she is indeed beautiful.
But I do not know her age?”
Zhāng Sānsǎo said:
“Nineteen years old,
and an only daughter.”
Yuánwài Zhāng said:
“Being two years older doesn’t matter;
I only fear they are unwilling to marry her out.
I have only this one son,
and I am unwilling for him to be a live-in son-in-law.”
Zhāng Sānsǎo said:
“Yuánwài Hú is also willing to marry her out.”
Hearing this, Yuánwài Zhāng
was greatly pleased.
He ordered wine to be prepared for Zhāng Sānsǎo to have three cups.
He took out one tael of silver to give her,
saying:
“If the marriage is successful,
there will be another generous reward.”
Zhāng Sānsǎo took the silver,
thanked him, and went out the door.
Having drunk wine from both families,
she muttered tipsily to herself:
“Today is a good day;
everything is going smoothly.
This marriage match
is sure to succeed.
After tonight, I’ll rise early before dawn tomorrow
and go to the Hú family to propose,
without letting Lǐ Lǎoshí know.”
Meanwhile, Lǎoshí Lǐ Sìsǎo,
having passed by the gate of Yuánwài Táng’s house in Jīnshā that day,
thought:
“He has a son,
just twenty-one years of age,
who was previously betrothed to the daughter of Xú Dàhù.
Because the girl suffered from consumption,
the marriage was never completed.
The girl died in the second month,
so Táng Xiǎoguānrén is in urgent need of a marriage.
If I propose the daughter in Yuánwài Hú’s residence,
they will surely follow through gladly.”
She walked to the gate of the Táng house;
it so happened that Yuánwài Táng was sitting leisurely in front of the gate.
Seeing Lǐ Sìsǎo approach,
since they were old acquaintances,
he said:
“Where is Sìsǎo coming from?”
Lǐ Sìsǎo said:
“I have something to say and have come specifically to your residence.”
Yuánwài Táng said:
“Since you have something to say,
please come inside to speak.”
Lǐ Sìsǎo followed the Yuánwài inside,
sat down,
and asked:
“Is the Xiǎoguānrén at home?”
Yuánwài Táng said:
“He has gone out to collect some small goods and hasn’t returned yet.”
Lǐ Sìsǎo said:
“The Xiǎoniángzǐ of the Xú family is gone;
have you secured another good match?”
Yuánwài Táng said:
“Not yet.
If you see a good prospect, please arrange it for us.”
Lǐ Sìsǎo said:
“There is one right here,
whom you will surely find to your liking.”
Yuánwài Táng said:
“Which family is it?”
Lǐ Sìsǎo said:
“It is the daughter of Yuánwài Hú, who runs the silk and fabric shop,
just nineteen years of age.”
Upon hearing this, Yuánwài Táng
smiled and said:
“I know of Yuánwài Hú’s daughter,
and she is indeed born clever and sharp.
Back when the Hú family ran a pawnshop,
my family sent someone to propose,
but Yuánwài Hú wanted to take in a son-in-law.
We were unwilling to do so,
so we settled on the match with the Xú family instead.
I only wonder if Yuánwài Hú has changed his mind;
how is it that you come to propose this?”
Lǐ Sìsǎo said:
“Yesterday Yuánwài Hú sent for me,
gave me one tael of silver,
and gave me three cups of wine to drink.
He wants a match of equal status
and is willing to marry her out.
Therefore, I have specifically come to your residence to propose.”
Hearing this, Yuánwài Táng
was greatly pleased
and immediately ordered wine to be prepared.
After Lǐ Sìsǎo drank,
he also gave her one tael of silver
and said:
“If the marriage is successful,
there will be another generous reward.
Please take care and put in the effort.”
Lǐ Sìsǎo thanked Yuánwài Táng and left.
All along the way she was full of joy,
and also planned to keep it a secret from Kuàizuǐ Zhāng Sānsǎo,
to act as the sole matchmaker tomorrow.
It is said that the next day, the household of Hú Yuánwài opened the main gates.
Zhāng Sānsǎo was the first to arrive,
and just as she was about to enter the door,
she saw someone coming from the east in the distance
who looked like Lǐ Sìsǎo.
Zhāng Sānsǎo said,
“Where is this old woman going so early in the morning?
I will hide to one side and watch her.”
She saw Lǐ Sìsǎo arrive at the Hú family’s gate,
look both ways,
and slip straight inside the gate,
where she came face-to-face with Zhāng Sānsǎo.
Truly:
Rising early after sleeping through the night,
there are those who do not sleep at all.
Both of them were startled
and felt quite embarrassed.
Zhāng Sānsǎo said,
“What business brings you here?”
Lǐ Sìsǎo said,
“Seeing you here,
I came in specifically to accompany you.”
Zhāng Sānsǎo said,
“I also thought you would certainly come here,
so I came early to wait for you.”
The two of them shared a laugh.
Lǐ Sìsǎo said,
“Āmǔ!
Tell the truth,
have you found a good prospect?”
Zhāng Sānsǎo said,
“I won’t hide it from you;
I have an excellent candidate
who is guaranteed to succeed nine times out of ten.”
Lǐ Sìsǎo asked,
“Which family?”
Zhāng Sānsǎo said,
“It is the seventeen-year-old son of Dàpù Zhāng Yuánwài, a young gentleman as fair as a flower.”
Lǐ Sìsǎo said,
“Āmǔ, don’t take offense!
I say that when the man is older and the woman younger, they stay together until old age;
but in this case, the female is two years older,
so I fear it will not suit this household’s wishes.”
Zhāng Sānsǎo said,
“You’d better shut your mouth!
As the common saying goes:
If the wife is one year older,
there will be rice to eat;
if the wife is two years older,
there will be much profit;
if the wife is three years older,
wealth will be piled in the corners of the house.
Now she is exactly two years older,
which is precisely the omen for profit,
bringing wealth and prosperity to her husband.
How could that be bad!
You dislike my prospect,
but what other prospect could possibly beat this one?”
Lǐ Sìsǎo said,
“The one I have is much better.
He is the son of Jīnshā Táng Yuánwài,
the eldest son of the primary branch.
If the deal is made now,
the betrothal gifts can be sent and the wedding performed immediately.”
Zhāng Sānsǎo said,
“Is it that cursed fellow who brings bad luck to his betrothed?
Whose daughter is a sturdy bronze basin
that would be willing to be paired with such an iron broom of ill fortune!
With a prospect like that,
it is better not to speak of it,
to save some complaints later on.”
Lǐ Sìsǎo said,
“I will make a wager with you;
the Yuánwài will definitely agree to my match.”
Zhāng Sānsǎo said,
“There is no need to bet.
Let it be said now:
if yours succeeds,
I will not come to dispute it.
If mine succeeds,
you should not expect a single share of the reward.
We will just have a cup of wedding wine and be done with it.”
The shop manager heard this
and interjected,
“That is well said!
There is water under each person’s boat;
everyone sails their own.
Wasting your saliva in an argument
is also useless.
No one knows which match our Yuánwài will like.
Marriages are decided five hundred years in advance;
they cannot be forced.”
Only then did the two of them stop talking,
and together they walked into the guest room and took their seats.
There is a poem to prove it:
The matchmakers’ two feet are like the shape of boats,
each sailing their own way where there is water in the river;
in vain they deceived each other and competed to rise early,
for who would have known that the Yuánwài would not agree?
It is said that Hú Yuánwài happened to walk out to the guest seats,
and the two matchmakers met him.
The Yuánwài asked them to sit and said,
“It is rare that you are so diligent;
I spoke of it yesterday, and today you are here.”
Zhāng Sānsǎo did not wait for Sìsǎo to speak,
but rushed to respond,
“There is a good match
that I have found.
On Xī Jiē, the family of Dàpù Zhāng Yuánwài has an only son, just seventeen years of age,
with outstanding talents.
He is truly very clever;
he can write with one hand
and calculate with the other.”
Hú Yuánwài heard this and said,
“Set this match aside for now!”
Lǐ Sìsǎo said,
“The one I am speaking of is another prospect,
from the family of Jīnshā Táng Yuánwài.
He is a fine young gentleman,
twenty-one years old,
exceptionally clever,
proficient in both writing and calculation.
Five or six years ago,
he had come to this house to ask for a hand in marriage,
but it did not succeed;
now he has come to ask once again.”
Hú Yuánwài shook his head and said,
“Set this match aside as well.
When there are other matches,
I will trouble you two to come and speak again.”
Both matchmakers said,
“With such good matches,
how can you let them pass?
Yuánwài, pray discuss this with the Yuànjūn.”
Hú Yuánwài said,
“In my heart, I am simply not interested,
and the Yuànjūn certainly cannot decide.”
He then reached into his sleeve and pulled out one tael of silver,
gave it to the two of them,
and said,
“The day is early, so I won’t detain you;
take this for some tea.
I must trouble you to diligently look for a sincere young gentleman.
It will only be good when it suits my heart.”
The two matchmakers accepted the silver,
and could only rise and leave,
saying,
“Even though the matches didn’t succeed,
at least this early rising wasn’t for nothing.
Looking back on it,
this job as a matchmaker is not something one can do alone.
From now on, we must harmonize our efforts;
if we all urge and encourage together,
we need not fear that he won't listen.”
The two of them then split the one tael of silver
and each went their separate ways.
From then on, the two matchmakers were truly as harmonious as honey and water,
walking together on a single gangplank.
To keep the story brief,
whenever there was a good match to propose,
if they heard that the young man was clever and sharp,
they would let it pass.
This went on for who knows how many times.
After another few days had passed,
the two matchmakers discussed:
"It is rare to find someone like Hú Yuánwài.
Whenever we go, there is always wine and silver;
we have never left empty-handed.
The two of us have had seven or eight good matches to propose,
but he just refuses.
I wonder what the reason is?"
Lǐ Sìsǎo said:
"I said we should find a young gentleman;
could it be that he dislikes them for being too intelligent and handsome?"
Zhāng Sānsǎo said:
"Today we have nowhere else to go.
I will go with you to Hú Yuánwài's residence to trick him into giving us a few cups of wine.
We can also trick him out of two handfuls of silver,
and we can all have a good laugh together."
Lǐ Sìsǎo asked:
"What match do you have to propose?"
Zhāng Sānsǎo said:
"Don't you worry about it.
Just come with me,
and I'll see to it that you get your wine."
The two arrived at Hú Yuánwài's house,
and it happened that the Yuánwài was in his shop.
The two sat down and had tea.
The Yuánwài asked:
"What match have you come to propose?"
Zhāng Sānsǎo said:
"I beg your pardon, Yuánwài!
There is a Jiāo Yuánwài who, like you, owns a silk and fabric shop.
He has a son who is extremely honest;
my only fear is that he is a bit too honest."
The Yuánwài asked:
"How old is his son,
and how is he in other respects?"
Zhāng Sānsǎo said:
"Although Jiāo Yuánwài's son is already nineteen years old,
his nǎizi still has to put his clothes on for him
and feed him his three meals a day.
Saliva is always dripping from his mouth,
and he doesn't understand worldly matters much at all.
Everyone in the household calls him Hāng Gē."
Hearing this, Hú Yuánwài said:
"This match actually suits my intentions perfectly.
I must trouble you two to put your hearts into arranging it.
Do not tell the truth to the Yuàn Jūn;
just praise him and leave it at that."
When the two matchmakers heard this,
they said nothing,
but thought to themselves:
"Thousands of good matches,
and young men as beautiful as flowers,
were all passed over.
Yet he wants to take this fine daughter
and marry her to this madman."
The two drank several more cups of wine,
each received two taels of silver,
and after thanking the Yuánwài, they went out.
Opposite the house was a tea house,
and the two went in to have tea.
Lǐ Sìsǎo said:
"You were so reckless;
I could hardly keep from laughing
and was breaking out in a cold sweat.
I was only afraid that Hú Yuánwài would get angry
and it would involve me too.
What would be the point of that?"
Zhāng Sānsǎo said:
"I proposed so many matches to him,
and he rejected them all.
I was just teasing him;
if Hú Yuánwài had gotten angry,
I would have simply said I was joking.
Who would have thought he'd actually agree?"
Lǐ Sìsǎo said:
"It seems it caught his fancy.
If it hadn't,
why would he have given us four taels of silver today,
which is even more generous than usual?"
The two hurried along together,
walking
and laughing as they went.
They headed straight for the Guózǐmén to see Jiāo Yuánwài.
Jiāo Yuánwài asked them to sit and have tea.
The Yuánwài said:
"You two coming to my door are like xǐchóng'ér;
what good news have you brought?"
Zhāng Sānsǎo said:
"I beg your pardon, Yuánwài!
The two of us have come specifically to ask for wine to drink
and to propose a match for the young Yuánwài."
Jiāo Yuánwài said:
"My son is a simpleton
who knows nothing of worldly matters.
Whose daughter would be willing to marry him?"
Lǐ Sìsǎo said:
"In the residence of Hú Yuánwài, who like you owns a silk and fabric shop,
there is a young lady as beautiful as a flower.
She is just nineteen years old.
Many families have gone to propose a match,
but he refused them all.
Just now, when we mentioned your household,
Hú Yuánwài was willing to accept
and specifically sent the two of us to speak with you."
Jiāo Yuánwài was greatly delighted in his heart
and said:
"If the two of you can make this match a success,
I will reward you handsomely."
The two drank several cups of wine,
were given two taels of silver each,
and after leaving Jiāo Yuánwài's house,
they went straight to see Hú Yuánwài.
Lǐ Sìsǎo said:
"When Jiāo Yuánwài heard about the young lady of your residence,
he was extremely happy
and sent us back to report
that he wants you to choose an auspicious day and hour
to present the betrothal gifts.
As for what arrangements are needed,
they will follow your residence's instructions."
When Hú Yuánwài heard this,
his joy was beyond measure,
and he personally called the matchmakers to speak to Zhāng Yuàn Jūn.
When the Yuàn Jūn asked for details,
they only said the young gentleman was of a robust and prosperous build
and was a man of good fortune.
It was only that he had been pampered and spoiled since childhood,
so he still required others to wait on him while dressing.
Being born into such a wealthy family,
he certainly lived a life of ease.
The Yuàn Jūn also consented.
The matchmakers returned to the Jiāo family to report.
To keep the story brief,
they couldn't avoid sending the matchmakers to deliver the betrothal gifts
and exchange the traditional ritual letters.
Because Jiāo Yuánwài knew his own son was incompetent,
he was generous in every matter.
After some time,
an auspicious day and hour were chosen
to complete the marriage.
Meanwhile, Jiāo Yuánwài and his māmā called the nǎizi to instruct her:
"When the young gentleman gets married,
the matters of the bedroom
will all rest upon your shoulders.
If you make the husband and wife live in harmony,
I will reward you handsomely."
The nǎizi said:
"Many thanks, Yuánwài and māmā;
the nǎizi has her own ways."
The māmā said:
"If that is the case,
you must slowly teach him well."
The nǎizi and the māmā went into the room to see Hāng Gē and said:
"Hāng Gē!
Tomorrow we are getting you a wife."
Hāng Gē also said:
"Tomorrow we are getting you a wife."
The nǎizi added:
"What a joy!"
Hāng Gē said:
"What a joy!"
The nǎizi said nothing aloud,
but thought to herself:
"Our Yuánwài is so senseless!
Why fetch a wife for such a madman?
What is the point?
It is just cruelly harming someone's daughter!
And that Hú Yuánwài is also lacking judgement.
I hear people say
that this girl is extremely beautiful
and is also smart and wise,
capable of both writing and arithmetic.
Yet he marries her off to this madman;
I wonder what the reason is."
That night passed,
and the next day the Jiāo family prepared for the wedding,
which need not be further discussed.
In the evening,
Hú Māmā escorted the bride through the door.
Naturally, there were rituals of bowing to the gods,
attending the banquet, and ceremonial seating.
The nǎizi helped Hāng Gē out,
and when Hú Māmā saw him,
she was startled.
She saw:
His face was caked with layers of grime,
and saliva flowed from the corners of his mouth.
A polished cap was perched crookedly over his twin hair-buns,
and a new robe was pulled haphazardly across his frame.
With shrunken eyebrows and hollow cheeks,
he had protruding ears and squinting eyes.
His boots were worn lopsided,
and his steps were stumbling and unsteady,
supported by six or seven people.
Snot hung from his upturned nose,
and his lips were filthy,
wiped clean by a pair of sleeves.
He stared at people with wide eyes without a single word,
appearing exactly like a ferocious beast being led out.
Short hairs joined his sideburns in a thousand bristles,
looking much like a summoned ghost or demon.
His clumsy frame could hardly stand on its own,
like a gnarled tree on a desolate cliff swaying in the wind;
his hideous face turned toward the divine presence,
like a demonic fox in a deep valley bowing to the moon.
He saw only the festive lanterns,
having no understanding that tonight was for the nuptial cup.
Though he had met his mate,
he did not know that this night they were to be wed.
The departing guests were startled by the sight,
and the whole hall was doubled over with laughter.
In the bridal chamber with the flowered candles,
it was clearly Zhī Nǚ meeting Nà Luó.
Behind the swaying red curtains,
it was just as if Guān Yīn had encountered Bā Jiè.
Even Mómǔ would have found him loathsome,
and even Wú Yán would be ashamed to be his match.
That night, the nanny supported Hāng Gē to perform the ritual;
his bows were not bows,
and his prostrations were not prostrations.
Usually he was accustomed to parroting what others said,
but arriving at this point, he had no one to follow,
and only muttered incoherently.
When Hú Māma saw the new son-in-law in such a state,
she could not help but let her tears fall piteously,
secretly lamenting in her heart:
"You old fool!
To take this piece of my own flesh
and ruin her with such a man.
My daughter's entire life—
how can this be the end of it!"
When she wanted to summon the two matchmakers to vent her anger,
that Lǐ Lǎoshí had already slipped away to one side.
Zhāng Kuàizuǐ, seeing that the lady's expression was far from kind,
took the lead to intercept her with words, saying:
"Lǎo Yuànjūn!
Regarding this marriage,
we juniors would not have dared be so bold;
everything followed the instructions passed down by Lǎo Yuánwài.
When Lǎo Yuànjūn goes back and asks Lǎo Yuánwài,
it will naturally become clear.
Today is a day of great joy,
and all the distinguished relatives are here;
we hope the Yuànjūn will be most forbearing,
concealing the faults and highlighting the virtues."
With just these few words,
Zhāng Yuànjūn found it hard to open her mouth further.
It was truly like a mute slowly tasting the bitterness of coptis;
hard to speak of the bitterness in one's mouth to others.
Having no choice, she stayed with the many relatives,
playing host and drinking for the night.
The next morning,
she had to leave her daughter behind,
bid farewell to the various relatives, and return home.
As soon as she saw the Yuánwài,
her anger reached the heavens;
she pulled at her hair bun,
lunged into his arms,
and began to wail to heaven and earth.
The Yuánwài said:
"On such a good and auspicious day,
why are you acting like this for no reason?"
Māma said:
"I only thought you were the master of the house,
and that all matters depended on you.
Who knew you were an old beast,
a man without a heart!
This fine daughter of mine, who could manage a household and start an estate—
hundreds and thousands of marriage offers came,
and you simply would not agree.
Why did you pick this madman to marry her to?
What is the reason?"
Hú Yuánwài said:
"If our daughter stayed at home,
she would surely bring trouble to our family in the long run.
Even if she married into another house,
if she married a clever and sharp husband,
he might not be able to stabilize her,
and some traces of the 'chisel and axe' might be revealed,
which would again be a hardship for me.
Now, by marrying her to a blockhead of a husband who knows nothing of human affairs,
even if there is some 'leakage,'
he will not be able to perceive it."
Māma said:
"Such a fine daughter,
married to such a crazed idiot.
Does this not ruin my daughter's whole life?"
Yuánwài said:
"That she has left my house
is a blessing from heaven for her.
Why do you care about her so much!"
Māma only wept for her own flesh and blood,
scolding for a while,
and weeping for a while;
they made a ruckus for an entire night,
of which no more need be said.
Now, when Hú Yǒng'ér saw that her mother had left,
her tears fell uncontrollably;
her suffering was beyond words.
One by one, she saw the relatives out the door.
After the evening meal was finished,
she thanked her mother-in-law,
said her goodnights,
and followed the nanny into the bedroom.
Seeing Hāng Gē sitting on the bed,
the nanny said:
"You sleep with the young lady."
Hāng Gē said:
"You sleep with the little lady."
The nanny said:
"You sleep with the young lady, now!"
Hāng Gē said:
"You sleep with the little lady, now!"
The nanny thought to herself:
"If he just keeps parroting me,
when will it ever end?
I might as well arrange for the young lady to sleep myself."
The nanny first helped Hāng Gē take off his clothes,
assisted him onto the bed to lie down,
and covered him with the quilt.
Then she looked at Yǒng'ér and said:
"Please undress and go to sleep, young lady."
Seeing the nanny inviting her to sleep,
Yǒng'ér thought with two rows of pearly tears:
"Father!
Mother!
How have I failed you,
that you would marry me to a madman?
Have you forgotten the suffering we endured in Bù Sī Qiú Yuàn?
As for the wealth and honor you have now,
you do not know whom you owe it to!
Enough!
Enough!
I understand my father's intention now;
he feared that if I married a clever husband,
I might teach him something.
Because he saw through this beforehand,
he married me to this madman."
Wiping away her tears,
she bid the nanny goodnight.
She took off her outer garments
and lay down with Hāng Gē.
The nanny returned to her own room.
Having climbed into bed, Yǒng'ér wrapped the quilt tightly around her body,
sleeping by herself on one side,
not sharing the quilt with Hāng Gē.
She thought in her heart:
"I have long had the intention of following Shèng Gūgū away.
Only because my parents were hard to forget,
I could not cast them aside for a moment.
Since they have no other child to rely on,
how could they have the heart to marry me off
and match me with this piece of junk?
I wonder if Shèng Gūgū knows of this or not."
After sighing for a while,
she drifted off to sleep
and dreamed of Shèng Gūgū arriving riding a crane.
Because of this visit,
there is a reason to tell:
Yǒng'ér found peace of mind,
and some more time passed.
As the saying goes:
"Husband and wife are destined from a previous life,
do not resent the east wind or sigh in vain."
As for what Shèng Gūgū said in the end,
let us hear it explained in the next chapter.
A fine horse is used to carrying a village boor,
and a clever wife is destined to sleep with a clumsy husband.
Marriage is all a debt from a former life;
do not complain to the east wind or blame the heavens.
It is said that Hú Yǒng'ér dreamed of Shèng Gūgu riding a crane, arriving there.
She called out:
"My child!
I heard that you have married a new bridegroom,
and I have come specifically to see you."
Yǒng'ér then recounted all the bitterness in her heart.
Shèng Gūgu said:
"Your life's ultimate outcome
naturally lies in Bèizhōu.
This place was never meant to be your permanent home."
Yǒng'ér said:
"I would rather follow you, My Lady, and leave right now!"
Shèng Gūgu said:
"Your karmic debts from previous lives are not yet fulfilled;
it is not yet time to free yourself."
Yǒng'ér asked:
"What karmic debt could I possibly have with that madman?"
Shèng Gūgu said:
"In your previous life when you were my daughter,
I took you to the Guān Wáng Miào in Jiànmén Shān to seek shelter from the snow.
There was a young Daoist priest named Jiǎ Qīngfēng,
who exchanged flirtatious glances with you.
Although nothing ever came of it,
you did not decisively break things off with him either.
That priest pined for you
and fell ill and died.
Only because his infatuation was so deep,
he was reincarnated in this life
as a simpleton.
But the roots of his affection
were planted deeply.
It must bloom and bear fruit in this life.
Being husband and wife with him today
is a way of repaying that debt.
When your fate with him is ended,
there will naturally be a parting.
You must also be patient,
and must not display your supernatural powers,
to avoid arousing suspicion.
If you find yourself in desperate trouble,
you can come to Zhèngzhōu to find me."
Having finished speaking,
she departed on her crane as before, riding the wind.
When Yǒng'ér woke up,
she remembered every single word in her heart.
Knowing this was a matter of past karma,
her mind became settled.
On the second day after Lady Zhāng Yuànjūn returned home,
her heart was entirely preoccupied with her daughter,
wondering how her daughter had spent this night.
Her eyes must surely be red and swollen from crying.
She sent two nursemaids to check on her.
They returned and said:
"She is there quite happily."
The mother did not believe it
and went to look several times;
the reports were always the same words.
The mother sighed
and set her mind at ease,
no longer quarreling with the Yuánwài.
As for Jiāo Yuánwài and his wife,
they were only afraid the new bride would be unhappy.
Seeing the two of them being filial and obedient,
they were naturally overjoyed,
which goes without saying.
Jiāo Yuánwài went in person to his in-law Hú's house to express his thanks,
and from then on, all was well between the two families.
To speak further of Yǒng'ér and Hāng Gē, though they were husband and wife,
in reality, they were like people separated by a thousand miles while sharing the same bed.
Hāng Gē had never understood human affairs
and did not pester his wife.
Yǒng'ér was also glad to keep him at a distance,
though she usually felt a sense of pity for him.
She took care of him in various ways,
much like she had gained a child to nurse.
Sometimes she would close the bedroom door
and perform magic for fun.
Hāng Gē would stare blankly at her,
not saying a word,
so they lived together in peace for some time.
Time slipped away,
and before they knew it, three years had passed.
It was during the sixth month,
and that year the weather was exceptionally hot.
When evening came, Yǒng'ér
went to the front hall to say goodnight,
then came to the courtyard with Hāng Gē to enjoy the cool air.
Yǒng'ér said:
"Hāng Gē!
Are we very hot?"
Hāng Gē said:
"Are we very hot?"
Yǒng'ér said:
"I will go with you to a place to enjoy the cool air;
do not be afraid."
Hāng Gē said:
"I will go with you to a place to enjoy the cool air;
do not be afraid."
Seeing Hāng Gē's chaotic state,
Yǒng'ér felt quite stifled in her heart.
That night, Yǒng'ér and Hāng Gē sat together on a stool.
Yǒng'ér chanted an incantation,
and the stool transformed into a great tiger with hanging eyes and a white forehead.
Carrying Yǒng'ér and Hāng Gē on its back, it rose into the air
and went straight to the top of a city gate tower.
This tower was called the Ānshàng Dàmén tower.
Yǒng'ér shouted:
"Stop!"
The tiger stopped right on the roof ridge.
Yǒng'ér said to Hāng Gē:
"Is it cool here?"
Hāng Gē said:
"Is it cool here?"
The two of them enjoyed the cool air until the fourth watch.
Yǒng'ér said:
"Let us go back!"
Hāng Gē said:
"Let us go back!"
Yǒng'ér chanted an incantation,
and the tiger rose into the air,
descending right into their courtyard at home,
where it turned back into a stool.
Yǒng'ér said:
"Hāng Gē,
let us go to sleep!"
Hāng Gē said:
"Let us go to sleep!"
From that night onward,
Yǒng'ér and Hāng Gē rode the tiger every night to the roof ridge of the Ānshàng Dàmén tower to enjoy the cool air,
returning at the fourth watch.
There is a poem to testify:
The magic of the Báiyún Dòng is great and divine,
A wooden stool can be made to turn into a tiger.
If you don't believe it, look toward the land of Wú,
The 'Leaping Tiger of the Western Mountains' is a remaining trace.
Suddenly one day,
Yǒng'ér said:
"We should go enjoy the cool air now."
Hāng Gē said:
"We should go enjoy the cool air now."
Yǒng'ér chanted an incantation,
the stool turned into a tiger,
and they rose into the air,
going straight to the Ānshàng Dàmén tower to enjoy the cool air.
That night there was no wind.
Yǒng'ér said:
"It is so hot today."
She held a white paper fan shaped like the moon in her hand,
fanning herself incessantly.
At that time, the moonlight was somewhat dim.
Two soldiers on night duty came out to patrol the city;
they were none other than Zhāng Qiān
and Lǐ Wàn.
After the two of them had patrolled once,
they returned to the base of the city gate tower.
Zhāng Qiān suddenly raised his head to look at the moon,
was startled, and said:
"Lǐ Wàn!
Do you see that?
There are two people sitting on the roof ridge of the gate tower!"
Lǐ Wàn said:
"If they are people,
how could they have gotten up there?"
Zhāng Qiān fixed his gaze and said:
"They really are two people."
Lǐ Wàn said:
"From where I see it,
they are just two crows."
That night, the two on the roof ridge never stopped fanning with their hands.
Lǐ Wàn said:
"If they aren't crows,
how could they be flapping their wings up high?"
Zhāng Qiān had sharp eyes and said:
"From what I see,
one looks like a man and one looks like a woman.
Now, I don't care if it's a person or a crow,
I'll let it taste one of my arrows!"
He went to his quiver, gripped his bow, and took an arrow.
Nocking the arrow,
he drew the bow to its full extent.
Taking careful aim, he shot a single arrow,
which went neither left nor right,
but struck Hāng Gē right in the thigh.
Hāng Gē gave a loud cry
and came tumbling down from the roof ridge,
falling like a rotten melon.
Zhāng Qiān and
Lǐ Wàn
went forward to look;
it was indeed a man.
Fortunately, he had not been killed by the fall,
so they bound him.
When they looked up again,
the other one was gone.
By the early morning of the next day,
he was escorted to Kāifēng Fǔ.
The Zhīfǔ ascended the hall,
and Zhāng Qiān and Lǐ Wàn brought Hāng Gē under guard to kneel down,
reporting:
"The two of us are night patrol soldiers.
At the third watch last night,
we patrolled to the Ānshàng Grand Gate.
Suddenly raising our heads,
we saw two people sitting on the ridge of the gate tower roof,
waving white paper fans.
At that time, the moonlight was not very bright;
approximately one looked like a man,
and one looked like a woman.
We calculated that,
for such a tall building,
and seeing no ladder,
how could they have gotten up there?
They must be villains who fly over eaves and walk on walls.
Immediately, we took bows and arrows and shot this man down.
When we looked up again,
that woman had indeed disappeared.
Now we have escorted this man before the dais;
we request your Excellency's instructions."
After the Zhīfǔ finished listening,
he asked Hāng Gē:
"What kind of person are you?"
Hāng Gē also said:
"What kind of person are you?"
The Zhīfǔ said:
"Speak the truth
to avoid suffering."
Hāng Gē also said:
"Speak the truth
to avoid suffering."
The Zhīfǔ was greatly enraged
and cursed:
"This fellow is detestable!
How dare he pretend to be mad with me!"
Hāng Gē also stared and said:
"This fellow is detestable!
How dare he pretend to be mad with me!"
Everyone crowded in the hall could not help but laugh.
The Zhīfǔ was helpless
and called for everyone to come and identify him,
to see where he was from.
Everyone came forward and looked for a while,
then all said:
"We do not recognize this person at all."
The Zhīfǔ pondered:
"The Ānshàng Grand Gate tower is as high as a sheer cliff;
how could these two have climbed up?
Even if they could get up,
the one who looked like a woman,
why was she not seen coming down,
but instead vanished secretly?
Surely that one who looked like a woman
is an elf or a demon
who bewitched this man
to go onto that rooftop;
not expecting these fellows to shoot him down,
she simply went her own way.
Now, seeing this person talking nonsense,
