he is still not yet awake.
But not knowing this person's name or hometown,
how can this official matter be concluded?"
After reflecting for a while,
he shouted:
"For now, put this person in a cangue at the crossroads of the main thoroughfare."
Looking at Zhāng Qiān
and Lǐ Wàn, he said:
"I order the two of you to stand guard;
if anyone comes to inquire of him,
immediately bring them to see me."
Before long,
the jailer took a cangue and put Hāng Gē in it.
When Zhāng Qiān
and Lǐ Wàn supported him to the crossroads,
people from the main streets and small alleys were stirred up,
crowding shoulder to back,
competing to see.
Meanwhile, the nurse and the maidservant of Jiāo Yuánwài's household
went into the room at dawn to deliver washing water,
and seeing that Hāng Gē
and Yǒng'ér were missing,
they were startled
and hurriedly reported it to the Yuánwài and the Māmā.
Both the Yuánwài and the Māmā were stunned
and said:
"The gates were not open,
the doors were not open;
where could they have gone?"
Jiāo Yuánwài walked in and out,
having no idea what to do.
Suddenly he heard people on the street
talking in groups of twos and threes:
"Last night on the roof ridge of the Ānshàng Grand Gate tower,
there were two people sitting up there;
the patrol soldiers shot one down,
and one escaped."
Others were saying:
"Aren't they displaying him in a cangue at the crossroads now?"
When Jiāo Yuánwài heard this,
it was as if someone had pushed him out the door;
he went straight to the crossroads,
parted the crowd,
and squeezed forward to look,
and it was indeed his own son.
He then began to wail loudly
and asked:
"How did you get up onto the gate tower?
Where is your wife?"
When Zhāng Qiān
and Lǐ Wàn saw Jiāo Yuánwài come to inquire,
without allowing any explanation,
they dragged and pulled him roughly into the prefecture gate.
The Zhīfǔ asked:
"What is your surname and given name?
Who is that person in the cangue to you?
Why did he go straight up to sit on the prohibited city tower?
What evil deed did he intend to do?
What is his connection with that woman who escaped?
If you speak the truth,
I will pardon you."
Jiāo Yuánwài bowed and knelt, saying:
"Your servant's surname is Jiāo and given name is Yù,
a native of this prefecture.
The one in the cangue is your servant's son.
He has lived in vain for over twenty years,
without knowing the slightest bit of human affairs.
Even for dressing and eating,
he constantly needs someone.
If people ask him something,
he simply answers by mimicking their words;
therefore, he was given the childhood name Hāng Gē.
I only had the nurse who attended to him in his childhood look after him;
even beyond the middle gate,
I did not dare let him out a single step.
Three years ago, a matchmaker happened to come to discuss a marriage for him.
I wanted to take a wife for him,
but feared it would wrong someone else's daughter.
Yet if I did not take a wife for him,
I only have this one son,
and there would be no one to continue the ancestral line.
Fortunately, there is a certain Hú Hào in this locality
who did not mind my son's stupidity and married his daughter, Hú Yǒng'ér, to him.
Furthermore, she was born beautiful and clever.
Unexpectedly, after having dinner last night,
the pair went into the room to sleep.
This morning the gates were not open,
the doors were not open,
yet my son and daughter-in-law
had both disappeared.
I do not know how they could have gone out the door to that high place on the gate tower.
Nor do I know why my daughter-in-law was not seen coming down
but was able to leave."
The Zhīfǔ shouted:
"Stop talking nonsense!
If they are your son and daughter-in-law,
how could they have come out without opening the gates or doors?
You must have hidden the daughter-in-law in your home;
quickly call her to see me."
Jiāo Yuánwài:
"Your servant is a law-abiding and simple man;
how would I dare to lie?
Even if you beat your servant to death,
you would truly be killing me out of a grievance!"
The Zhīfǔ heard that his words were sincere,
and moreover, Hāng Gē's manner of mimicking people's speech was also genuine.
He then dispatched two more men to seize Hú Yǒng'ér's father for interrogation,
so that her whereabouts might be known.
The runners took the official warrant,
and rushed like flying to Hú Yuánwài's house.
Now, it is said that Hú Wǎiyuán heard the streets clamoring about this matter,
and he already knew it was his own daughter’s doing,
which had harmed Hāng Gē,
so he and the Māmā were at home secretly lamenting their misfortune.
Suddenly, two runners came running in
and shouted, “Is the Wǎiyuán here?”
The Wǎiyuán was so startled his soul nearly left his body,
and he had no choice but to come out to meet them,
asking,
“What instructions do you have for me?”
The runners said,
“We have received the strict command of the Zhīfǔ Xiànggōng to summon you;
please set out immediately.”
Hú Wǎiyuán said,
“I have never meddled in idle affairs or done wrong;
I do not know what matter troubles you two to call for me?”
The runners said,
“The Zhīfǔ Xiànggōng is waiting right now;
once you go, you will know the details.”
The Wǎiyuán then took ten taels of silver from the shop
and gave them to the two men, saying:
“Please use this for wine and food;
if I return without trouble,
I shall thank you again.”
The two runners took the silver
and, without allowing him to turn around, they pushed and pulled him out the door,
going straight to the government office.
The Zhīfǔ was waiting anxiously,
and seeing that Hú Wǎiyuán had been brought,
he spoke of how Hāng Gē had been shot down from the city tower,
then how Jiāo Wǎiyuán mentioned that Yǒng'ér and Hāng Gē’s accounts did not match,
and explained the reason why Yǒng'ér must come out for interrogation.
Hú Wǎiyuán only feigned ignorance.
The Zhīfǔ said,
“I have heard your daughter is extremely clever and sharp,
while your son-in-law is so dull and foolish.
There must surely be another lover
doing some unfair and unlawful things.
You are afraid I will trouble her into revealing the truth,
so you insist on hiding her at home
and come here to cover it up.”
Jiāo Wǎiyuán, kneeling over there, interrupted,
“If she is at your house,
bring her out quickly
to save my son’s life!”
Hú Wǎiyuán said,
“In this world, it is only men who abduct women to do things.
It is clearly you who, for some unknown reason, took my daughter
and sent her off to who knows where.
You deliberately bribed the patrol soldiers
to say they were together on the roof ridge of the city tower,
and that one was shot while the other escaped.
My Lord, consider this:
The city tower is high in the sky,
and there was no ladder;
could it be these two grew wings and flew up there?
If they truly were up there together,
why did the tiles make no sound,
and how could she escape so quickly?
A woman’s feet are bound in small shoes and socks;
how could the patrol soldiers not catch her,
and instead just watch her come to hide in my house?”
The Zhīfǔ listened to his words,
finding every sentence to be reasonable.
He shouted:
“Take Hāng Gē’s father
and Zhāng Qiān and Lǐ Wàn and put them all in the finger-presses!”
Pointing at Jiāo Wǎiyuán, he said,
“This matter is likely your family’s plot to murder his daughter,
yet you, with Zhāng Qiān
and Lǐ Wàn, devised this strategy,
using this mad son as a pretext to enter and exit.
Unless beaten, how will you confess?”
He ordered the three of them to be severely tortured.
The attendants on both sides set to work together,
beating them until their skin split and flesh tore,
and fresh blood flowed.
Jiāo Wǎiyuán could not bear the suffering
and pleaded,
“I beg your Lordship, as a Just Official, to judge this;
I truly did not murder Hú Yǒng'ér.
Allow me to draw Yǒng'ér’s likeness,
and I am willing to offer a reward of three thousand strings of cash.
If only your Lordship will issue a warrant for arrest,
to be sent to every prefecture and county,
displaying the likeness and offering the reward.
If there is truly no news of Yǒng'ér,
I am willing to pay for the crime.”
The Zhīfǔ saw that the three of them would rather die than confess,
and his heart softened.
Moreover, Hú Wǎiyuán was also acting indifferent and not pressing for a conviction,
so he said,
“This also makes sense.”
He released the three men,
and then brought Hāng Gē into the office,
removed his cangue,
and ordered everyone involved to provide bail and return home for now to await further notice.
He also ordered the Jiāo family to draw Yǒng'ér’s likeness
and issued a warrant to be posted everywhere.
There is a poem to prove it:
Since ancient times, courtrooms have seen many injustices,
none so much as when litigious mouths deceive people.
By the time the high official changes his mind,
a round of severe torture has already been endured.
These four lines of poetry speak of the difficulty of hearing lawsuits;
if both sides speak as if they have reason,
one must see which side’s reasoning is slightly superior
and listen to them.
Yet, when there is such reasoning,
there may not necessarily be such an occurrence.
Just as with Hú Wǎiyuán’s defense in court,
how convincing it was!
The Zhīfǔ because of this had Jiāo Yù and the patrol soldiers beaten together,
yet who knew they were all wronged?
Therefore, those who sit in court
must never rely solely on their own cleverness and observation
to lightly resort to torture.
To return from the digression,
it is said that Hú Yǒng'ér, seeing Hāng Gē hit by an arrow and falling down,
began to chant an incantation
and rose into the air.
Returning home alone,
she thought,
“I have lost Hāng Gē;
it is no longer possible to stay here.
At my father and mother’s house,
it is also not good to go;
what should I do?”
She remembered the night of her marriage,
when she dreamed of Shèng Gūgū saying to her,
“This is not a place for you to settle;
if there is an emergency,
you may come to Zhèngzhōu to find me.”
“Now that I have no place to stay,
it would be better to go to Zhèngzhōu and seek refuge with Shèng Gūgū
to see how things go.”
Immediately, she put on several layers of clothes
and took her magical ritual objects.
As before, she straddled a stool,
flew out into the air,
and went straight to an empty field where no one was,
where she slowly descended and abandoned the stool,
then set off on her way alone.
At this time, the sky was just brightening,
and she happened to meet her former teacher, Chén Xuéjiū,
Chén Shàn.
He was hurrying from the countryside into the city early
to attend to some business.
Recognizing his female student Hú Yǒng'ér,
he was startled
and asked,
“Why are you walking alone here, my worthy student?
Where are your father and mother?”
Yǒng'ér performed a bow
and replied,
“My husband’s family has met with disaster,
and I have escaped alone,
without time to inform my parents.
From her side, she took out a small, smooth, square pillow made of white clay
and handed it to Chén Xuéjiū, saying,
“I trouble you, Shīfu, to deliver this pillow to my parents
to slightly express my concern for them.
This is the Jiǔ Tiān Yóu Xiān Zhěn;
it brings pleasant dreams to the soul,
and sleeping on it cures all illnesses.
Shīfu, you must deliver it.”
Chén Xuéjiū took it in his hand
and asked,
“Worthy student!
Where are you going now?”
Hú Yǒng'ér pointed ahead,
“There is a relative up ahead
waiting for me to go to their home together.”
As Chén Xuéjiū looked toward the front,
Yǒng'ér used an invisibility spell
and suddenly vanished.
Chén Shàn wiped his eyes,
spat out a mouthful of saliva,
and shouted, "I've seen a ghost!
Could it be that Yǒng'ér is already dead,
and her soul just appeared?
This pillow made of mud
clearly is not something used in the world of the living.
I was about to throw it away,
but then I thought:
'She went out of her way to send this to her father and mother
and repeatedly urged me.
Could it be ghostly talk?
I should not care whether it is true or false;
I will just take it and ask for news.
Why should I fear her?'
He then wrapped the pillow in his sleeve
and hurriedly walked into the city.
Suddenly he thought again:
'Today I have urgent matters of my own
and no time.
Moreover, Píng'ān Jiē is not on my way;
walking around with this pillow
is quite inconvenient.'
Just as he was passing by Fèi Jiàngshì's gate,
a young servant called out:
'Where are you going, Master Chén?'
It turned out that Chén Shàn had once taught at the Fèi family's home,
and this young servant was an old student of his.
Scholar Chén handed the pillow to him and said:
'Keep this for me for a while.
I am a bit busy today;
I will come to get it tomorrow,
and I will visit the Jiàngshì then too.'
After saying this, he left.
The servant looked at the earth-made pillow
and did not think much of it.
He took it into the house
and tossed it onto his own bed in the side room.
After breakfast, Fèi Jiàngshì went out to visit guests.
The servant boy had nothing to do,
so he went to his bed to sleep.
Seeing the pillow was convenient,
he used it.
It happened that this young servant had a predestined connection from a past life;
what a fine Jiǔtiān Yóuxiān Zhěn!
Many princes, dukes, and noble relatives
had never laid eyes on it,
nor had their ears heard of it,
yet he was the one to try its method and enjoy it.
Truly it is said:
Before the yellow millet is even cooked,
one dream reaches Huáxū.
While the servant boy was in a deep sleep,
two other boys of his kind
came looking for him to play a game of "Ascending to Officialdom" together.
They looked into the side room
and saw him snoring loudly.
One went to tickle the soles of his feet,
while the other twisted a piece of paper
and stuck it into his nostril.
The servant boy let out a few sneezes in a row,
then began to dance about as if possessed by a wind demon,
shouting wildly:
'What joy!
What joy!'
The two boys each grabbed one of his ears
and woke him up,
asking:
'What joy?'
The servant boy said:
'I had just gone to sleep
when I suddenly saw two doors open on the wall of the pillow.
A strange fragrance hit my nose,
and a troupe of female musicians came out playing instruments.
Every one of them had a face like the moon and features like flowers;
they welcomed me to wander in the immortal realm.
Within a few steps,
there were indeed immortal mountains,
immortal waters,
immortal flowers,
and immortal birds—
the scenery was extraordinary.
One fairy held a pitcher,
and another held a cup,
repeatedly urging me to drink three cups of immortal wine.
I had not even finished the third cup
when you two noisy fellows woke me up!'
One said:
'I don't believe it!
I don't believe it!'
The other grabbed the pillow.
Looking at it,
they saw on one side of the pillow wall
the five words Jiǔtiān Yóuxiān Zhěn written in gold-painted mud.
On the other side were painted two doors,
with a horizontal plaque above them saying "Xiānjiè."
Looking closely,
they finally realized the dream was because of this pillow.
One said:
'I don't know if you are telling the truth or not.
Tonight, I will take this pillow
and sleep on it for a night
to see if there is a dream or not.'
The other said:
'Don't be selfish!
Let's all enjoy it together.
You take the first half of the night,
and I will take the second half.'
Fèi Jiàngshì had just returned from visiting guests
and was passing by the side room
when he heard them talking about dividing the first and second halves of the night for enjoyment.
Thinking they were plotting something wicked,
he kicked open the door.
He saw the three boys
clustered around a small, smooth, square pillow made of white earth,
talking nonsense there.
Fèi Jiàngshì flew into a rage,
grabbed the pillow with both hands,
and without even looking at it,
he hurled it high into the air.
It smashed to pieces on the bluestone floor.
Alas, the priceless Yóuxiān Zhěn
turned into a patch of dust before the steps.
Could it be that this pillow was just like an ordinary one,
breaking at the touch of a hand
without showing any spiritual signs?
To know the details,
listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
An immortal dream upon the Yóuxiān Zhěn
far surpasses the ancient skies of Huáxū.
Who will gift this pillow to me?
I would willingly spend my whole life in deep slumber.
It is said that Fèi Jiàngshì, without listening to any explanation,
hurled the pillow into the air.
The servant boy had just cried out "Ayā!"
when the pillow fell before the bluestone steps
and smashed to pieces.
At the moment the pillow shattered,
with a resounding *huáng* sound,
a group of things appeared—
they were not bees,
and they were not butterflies;
they had shadows but no solid form,
and they flew up onto the eaves.
When Fèi Jiàngshì walked down the steps to look,
he saw a troupe of fairies about three inches tall,
holding musical instruments—
pipes, flutes, and strings,
nothing was missing.
Some held pitchers,
some held cups,
some held fans,
and some held Rúyì scepters.
There were more than twenty in total,
looking like a troupe of puppets.
Each one was glamorously dressed and heavily made up,
incomparably beautiful.
The troupe of fairies stood in a line on the eaves,
and all together gave a deep bow to Fèi Jiàngshì.
They chirped like orioles
and spoke like swallows,
saying:
"We were originally palace maids of the inner court in the previous dynasty,
and were imprisoned here by the command of Jiǔtiān Xuánnǚ Niángniáng.
Now, thanks to your protective grace,
we are released to roam freely;
this is truly a ten-thousand-fold stroke of luck."
After speaking,
they all began to play their instruments;
the melody was harmonious
and plaintively beautiful to hear.
They slowly walked across the roof ridge
and gradually disappeared toward the north.
Fèi Jiāngshì had never seen such a strange thing before;
he stared blankly for a long while.
When he carefully picked up the broken pieces of the pillow to examine them,
the inside was smooth and clean, all painted with delicate mountains and waters,
pavilions, and trees.
This pillow was fashioned from a single piece of white clay,
and there were no seams on the outside;
he did not know how the painter's hand could have moved within.
Was it not an immortal's pillow?
Fèi Jiāngshì then shouted for the three young servants to come and kneel,
asking about the origin of this pillow.
The other two servants pointed at Xuétóng and said:
"He said that Mr. Chén Xuéjiù left it with him,
promising to come and get it tomorrow;
we knew nothing of the matter.
We only heard him say that when he slept on it,
he experienced many pleasures and enjoyments.
What he saw was a fairy realm,
what he heard was celestial music,
and what he drank was immortal wine.
We saw five golden characters written on the side of the pillow: 'Jiǔ Tiān Yóu Xiān Zhěn,'
and our hearts were suspicious;
we were just discussing it here
when unexpectedly you, Old Master, returned."
He asked Xuétóng again, and it was indeed so.
Fèi Jiāngshì simply did not believe it
and locked the three servants in an empty room.
He intended to wait until Chén Xuéjiù came the next morning;
once the truth was clarified,
he would then forgive them.
To speak of Chén Shàn, on the next day
he was at leisure
and intended to go to the house of Hú Yuánwài on Píng'ān Street.
First he came to see Fèi Jiāngshì,
planning to ask for the pillow at the same time.
When Fèi Jiāngshì heard that Chén Xuéjiù had arrived,
he quickly invited him into the inner study to meet and sit down.
Fèi Jiāngshì first asked:
"Professor, did you leave a pillow with the young servant?"
Chén Shàn said:
"I did not tell him to mention it to you, Master Jiāngshì;
how did you know of it?"
Fèi Jiāngshì said:
"This pillow has some strange features.
Professor, tell me the truth:
where did it come from?
I also have something to tell you."
Chén Shàn said:
"I formerly lived as a tutor in the house of Hú Dàhóng on Píng'ān Street;
there was a female student named Yǒng'ér,
who married when she grew up
and has been away for three years.
Yesterday morning I suddenly met her outside the city;
she said her husband's family had met with disaster,
so she had fled.
She entrusted this to me to send to her parents,
as a token of her feelings.
Because I was busy with some matters yesterday,
I did not examine it closely either
and did not know it had anything strange about it."
Fèi Jiāngshì said:
"If that is so,
then it is fortunate that you did not deliver it for her!
He then told him how Xuétóng had dreamed—this and that,
thus and so—
and how he himself had smashed the pillow,
and the strange sights that followed.
Now the government has issued a proclamation,
offering a reward of three thousand strings of cash
to capture the sorceress Hú Yǒng'ér.
If you had taken this pillow,
it would have served as evidence,
and you would surely have been embroiled in a lawsuit.
Fortunately, I smashed the demonic object early,
and it is just as well that it has vanished without a trace."
Chén Shàn was scared out of his wits
and thanked him, saying:
"Because I live in a remote village
far from the city,
I knew nothing of the government's affairs.
If you had not explained it, Master Jiāngshì,
I would have been dangerously misled.
I only wonder how the government knew Hú Yǒng'ér was a sorceress;
surely you must know the details?"
Fèi Jiāngshì then recounted how Zhāng Qiān
and Lǐ Wàn had shot down Hāngē from the roof of the Ānshàng Main Gate,
and the whole story of the Jiāo and Hú families' testimony in court.
He related it all once.
Hearing it made Chén Shàn's hair stand on end.
At that moment Fèi Jiāngshì kept him for wine and a meal;
Chén Shàn thanked him repeatedly and departed,
returning home directly
without going to the house of Hú Yuánwài.
Fèi Jiāngshì unlocked the door
and let out the three servants, instructing them:
"From now on,
you are never to mention the matter of the pillow again.
If any outsiders hear of it,
I will hand you three dog-slaves over to the officials as sorcerers."
The three servants repeatedly said they would not dare.
From then on, no one mentioned the matter of the Jiǔ Tiān Yóu Xiān Zhěn.
The story splits into two directions;
to speak of Hú Yǒng'ér again, after she left Chén Xuéjiù,
she traveled alone for a day.
When it was late,
she came to a shaded shed
and saw an old woman serving tea.
Yǒng'ér went into the tea shop, sat down and rested her feet;
the old woman served a cup of tea for Yǒng'ér to drink.
Yǒng'ér asked the old woman:
"What place is this,
and where does the road ahead go?"
The old woman said:
"Ahead is Bājiǎo Town in Bǎnqiáo;
beyond it is the main road to Zhèngzhōu.
Young lady, why are you traveling
all alone to that place?"
Yǒng'ér said:
"My father and mother are there;
I am going to visit them."
The old woman said:
"It is late.
You should stay for a night at an inn in Bājiǎo Town before continuing;
it is lucky there is such a place to stay,
for it is inconvenient to walk alone at night."
Yǒng'ér conjured a dozen or so coins
and paid for the tea.
She thanked the old woman and walked another two lǐ,
where she saw a young man:
under six feet tall,
twenty-two or twenty-three years of age;
with a fine beard in three strands covering his mouth,
a narrow waist and broad shoulders;
wearing a headscarf with a papaya-heart knot,
a white gauze shirt like silver silk,
a red and green spider-spotted belt,
and a pair of yellowish multi-eye leather shoes.
He was carrying luggage
and an umbrella.
As the young man was walking,
he saw that Yǒng'ér wore no flowered crown
but had her hair in buns
with two gold hairpins;
though in simple clothes,
she had some beauty.
He stepped forward and greeted Yǒng'ér, saying:
"Where is the young lady going?"
Yǒng'ér said:
"Brother!
I am going to Zhèngzhōu to seek refuge with relatives."
That fellow was a profligate son of a family,
so he said:
"I am also going toward Zhèngzhōu,
and it is difficult to travel alone.
You are a woman;
how can you walk alone?
I will walk with you!"
He also used some frightening words to startle her.
Arriving before a forest,
the fellow said:
"Young lady!
This forest is most dangerous;
tigers often come out.
If two people walk together, it's no problem.
If you walk alone,
a tiger will come out and carry you away!"
Yǒng'ér said:
"Brother!
If that is the case,
I will need your strength to help me along!"
That fellow bought snacks along the way whenever they came across a wine shop.
After the two had eaten,
he would pay the money.
They walked and rested,
sat and rested,
as they watched the sky grow dark.
Yǒng'ér said,
"Brother!
It is late.
Is there an inn ahead to stay in?"
That fellow said,
"Little Lady!
I should let you know,
one month ago,
two spies from the Dádzi state were captured here.
The government issued a decree
that inns are not permitted to accommodate single individuals.
Neither you nor I will be able to get a room."
Yǒng'ér said,
"If we cannot get a room,
where shall we stay tonight?"
That fellow said,
"If you follow my word,
we can get a room."
Yǒng'ér said,
"I will just follow your word then, brother."
That fellow said,
"Little Lady!
It will not be for real;
we will just pretend that we are husband and wife,
and then we can get a room."
Yǒng'ér said nothing,
but thought to herself:
"This fellow and I have never met before;
meeting by chance like duckweed on water,
he has not said a single good word,
but only uses ghostly talk to frighten me,
wanting to take advantage of me by force.
Am I, Hú Yǒng'ér, one who is afraid of trouble?"
Yǒng'ér said,
"Brother!
It would be fine even to just tag along and sleep for one night."
That fellow said,
"That is good then!"
They arrived at Bājiǎo Zhèn,
and passed by several good inns.
Then they came to an inn at the edge of the market.
That fellow entered the inn's door and called out,
"Host,
are there any vacant rooms?
We two, husband and wife, want a room to rest in."
The waiter said,
"Do not take offense, Dàláng,
there are no rooms left!"
That fellow said,
"How bitter!
I travel back and forth often,
and only stay at your house.
Why are there no rooms today?"
The waiter said,
"They are all full;
there is only one room
with two beds laid out.
A bearded man who makes leather shoes just settled in.
I fear it might be inconvenient for you two, husband and wife."
That fellow said,
"Lead me to take a look first."
The waiter went ahead,
and that fellow followed with Yǒng'ér.
The waiter pushed open the door
and showed it to that fellow.
That fellow said,
"What is there to fear?
He is over there himself.
We two, husband and wife, will be on the opposite bed."
The waiter said,
"If that is the case,
you two go into the room yourselves."
The waiter handed over the room.
Yǒng'ér thought to herself:
"How intolerable this fellow is!
I do not even know you.
Yet you make me play your wife to get a room.
I will just let him experience a wife's methods."
There is a poem to prove it:
Ridiculous is the flashy and frivolous man,
who happens upon a woman and takes her as his wife.
Gold, powder, and wine in high towers—
who says these three things are not intoxicating?
Have you not heard what the ancients said:
Do not love another's wife,
do not ride another's horse.
How can one, meeting a beautiful woman on the road, give rise to wicked thoughts?
That fellow looked at the waiter and said,
"Get some water to wash our feet."
The waiter said,
"Yes!
Yes!"
Then the waiter spoke to the master artisan, saying,
"This husband and wife came from Dōngjīng.
The rooms in the inn are all full.
There is still one bed in this room,
so I have no choice but to let them stay for one night."
The master artisan said,
"I only need one bed to sleep on.
If someone comes to stay,
let them be as they please."
Yǒng'ér entered the room,
greeted the master artisan with a blessing,
and the master artisan returned the gesture.
That fellow looked at the bearded man and said,
"Sorry for the intrusion!"
The master artisan said,
"Please, make yourselves comfortable."
The master artisan thought to himself:
"The speech of these two does not sound like people from Dōngjīng.
Traveling in such a peculiar manner,
the two do not seem like husband and wife;
they are not of one mind,
and there is something suspicious about their appearance.
But what business is it of mine?
Let them be."
The bearded man said,
"Make yourselves comfortable."
That fellow and Yǒng'ér sat on the bed.
The waiter brought the foot-washing water.
That fellow washed his feet,
asked for a lamp with oil, and lit it.
The bearded man did not work at night;
he called out his goodnights,
and slept facing the inner part of the bed.
That fellow said,
"Sister!
In our haste on the road,
we did not prepare food.
I will go out and buy some wine and food to eat."
He turned and left the room.
Yǒng'ér said,
"How truly intolerable and rude this fellow is!
He has gone to buy wine;
I will play a trick on him for fun."
She mumbled something under her breath,
exhaled and blew toward the bearded man's bed,
then touched her own face.
Yǒng'ér then turned into a bearded man
with a purplish-brown complexion,
exactly like the master artisan who made leather shoes,
while the master artisan turned into Yǒng'ér.
The fake master artisan also lay down on the bed and pretended to be asleep.
It is said that fellow bought some wine,
purchased some side dishes,
and brought them into the inn.
He thought to himself:
"I have good luck today,
meeting such a beautiful woman.
Everyone in the inn knows I am her husband;
tonight I shall happily sleep with her for a night."
That fellow pushed open the room door,
placed the wine bottle on the table,
trimmed the lamp wick,
and when he looked at the bed,
it was the shoemaker Dàizhào.
He wondered in doubt:
"What is the reason for this?
How did he end up sleeping in my bed?"
Looking at the bed opposite,
the woman was sleeping there.
The fellow said:
"Perhaps she was tired from walking during the day
and fell asleep here as soon as her head hit the pillow."
He stepped forward and shook the woman with both hands,
calling out:
"Sister!
I've bought wine;
get up,
get up!"
Suddenly, the shoemaker Dàizhào leaped up,
grabbed him by the head, threw him down, and started beating him.
That fellow cried out:
"Why are you beating your husband?"
The bearded man shouted:
"Who is your wife?"
When the fellow looked closely,
it was indeed the shoemaker Dàizhào.
Hurriedly he cried:
"It's my mistake!
Don't blame me, don't blame me!"
Diànxiǎo’èr heard the commotion and made a fuss,
entering the room to ask:
"What's going on?"
The Dàizhào said:
"This fellow actually came and shook me,
calling me 'sister'."
Diànxiǎo’èr said:
"You're not blind;
your bed is right here."
Diànxiǎo’èr broke them up,
and the Dàizhào went back to bed to sleep as before.
Having taken a few punches, the fellow
said:
"How unlucky I am!
With my eyes wide open, it was a woman,
but it turned out to be the Dàizhào."
Seeing the young woman sleeping on this bed,
he called out:
"Little lady!
Get up and drink wine."
As soon as he looked closely,
she had vermilion hair,
emerald green eyes,
and blue fangs.
He screamed "Ghost!"
and suddenly collapsed to the ground.
Diànxiǎo’èr was eating in front of the door
when he heard the cry of "Ghost" in the room.
When he came in to look,
he saw the fellow fallen on the floor.
He hurriedly helped him up,
which also startled the shoemaker Dàizhào awake.
The people resting in the inn
all got up to rescue him.
Some sprayed water on him,
and some bit his thumbs.
After being fussed over all night,
his three souls returned
and his seven spirits were reborn.
The fellow woke up and said:
"How terrifying!
There's a ghost!
A ghost!"
Diànxiǎo’èr grabbed him, spat twice in his face, and said:
"This place of mine is a clean and quiet establishment.
What ghosts are there in an inn?
Who sent you here to ruin my livelihood?"
He brought the lamp over and said:
"Where is the ghost?"
The fellow said:
"That woman on the bed is a ghost!"
Diànxiǎo’èr said:
"This fellow is just making things up!
This is your wife;
how can you say she is a ghost?"
The fellow said:
"She is not my wife.
I ran into her on the road
and we agreed to come here to get a room,
pretending to be husband and wife.
Just now I went out to buy wine;
when I came into the room to see her,
it was a bearded man.
I mistakenly called the Dàizhào
and took a beating from him.
When I looked at her again,
she had vermilion hair,
emerald green eyes,
a blue face and fangs;
she turned out to be a ghost!"
Everyone was startled,
but when they looked at the woman under the lamp light,
she was a beautiful woman, pretty as flowers and jade.
They all said:
"Your eyes are playing tricks on you!
Such a fine woman,
how can you say she is a ghost?"
Yǒng’ér said:
"Everyone is here;
this fellow is truly unreasonable.
I was headed to Zhèngzhōu to seek my father and mother.
This fellow met me on the road
and insisted on traveling with me.
All along the way, he used terrifying words to scare me.
He also said:
'Several spies have been caught,
the inn doesn't allow single people to stay,'
and forced me to pretend to be husband and wife
to get a room.
Now that we've arrived here,
he keeps calling me a ghost.
He's been talking nonsense all night;
I don't know what this fellow is planning."
The people and Diànxiǎo’èr all cursed:
"This fellow
is intolerable to reason.
Make him leave my inn immediately.
If he doesn't go,
we will all beat him up together
and smash your bones to pieces!"
They drove the fellow out in a heated rush
and closed the inn door.
The fellow went outside,
but it was pitch black and he dared not travel.
Fearing the patrolling soldiers would catch him and he'd face a lawsuit,
he had to huddle in a quiet spot in front of someone's door outside all night.
When dawn came,
the fellow said:
"I'll just leave."
Leaving the inn door,
he walked for six or seven lǐ,
and just as he was about to pass through a grove of trees,
Hú Yǒng’ér stepped out from the grove,
looked at the fellow and said:
"Brother!
I'm sorry for last night;
you helped me stay in the inn for a night,
so why did you say I was a ghost?
Now in broad daylight,
look at me and see if I am a ghost or not?"
The fellow saw that Yǒng’ér was as beautiful as flowers and jade
and couldn't make up his mind, thinking:
"Could it be that my eyes really played tricks on me last night?"
The fellow said:
"Sister!
I was going to travel with you,
but last night I was frightened twice because of you.
I think you're not a good person;
just go your own way!"
Yǒng’ér said:
"Last night it was you who wanted me to be a fake wife,
and now you are afraid of me.
I'm a bit afraid of the loneliness;
I want you to travel with me."
The fellow said:
"What's there to fear in daylight?"
Yǒng’ér said:
"Brother, you said yesterday there are tigers coming out to hurt people."
The fellow said:
"That was just talk;
how could there really be a tiger?"
Yǒng’ér pointed her hand
and said:
"Isn't that a tiger coming?"
Before she had finished speaking,
a white-browed tiger with bulging eyes leaped out from the grove
and pounced right at the fellow.
The fellow gave a great cry
and fell flat on the ground.
The fellow closed his eyes,
thinking to himself:
"My life is over this time!"
After a long time with no activity,
he slowly opened his eyes to look;
the tiger was gone,
and the woman was gone too.
That fellow said,
“I have always liked to tease people.
Yesterday I should not have provoked that woman;
I received a beating from the bearded man’s fists,
and was startled by him again,
making my soul leave my body.
This morning she summoned a tiger out again.
I thought my life was over,
but it turns out she just wanted to scare me.
I don’t know if this woman is a demon or a ghost.
If I run into her again up ahead,
it will be disastrous!
It would be better for me to return to Dōngjīng.”
That fellow turned around as before and left.
Later generations have an ancient-style poem as evidence:
The beauty’s face is as delicate as a flower,
Walking alone, sighing from time to time.
On the roadside, she suddenly meets a young man,
Who courteously asks whose house she seeks.
She replies she is visiting her parents in Zhèngzhōu,
But the inns do not take in solitary travelers.
Pretending to be a couple in hopes it becomes real,
Who would have thought the pleasure would turn into a prank?
Facing each other across the bed, her spirit is hard to fathom,
His eyes dazed by her beauty, truly a shameful sight.
It is not that a beauty once turned into a ghost;
A beauty is inherently a living Rakshasa.
Suffering the cruelty of heavy fists and vicious hands,
The next morning in the woods, he is startled once more.
When did the beauty ever conjure a tiger?
The beauty was a “Rouge Tiger” all along.
A young man greedy for lust lacks self-restraint,
At a sudden meeting, he hopes to form a wild union.
Even heroes find it hard to escape a beauty’s hands,
Let alone an ignorant young lad.
To continue, Hú Yǒng'ér had turned into a tiger to scare him;
he would never dare come this way again.
“I shall head toward Zhèngzhōu myself,
traveling slowly along the road.”
At this time, the weather was scorching hot,
so she walked and rested by turns.
When it was nearly the hour of Sì,
she saw a large tree providing good shade to rest under,
and sat for a while.
While she was sitting,
she heard the rumbling and clattering of a cart.
She saw a traveler wearing a Fànyáng felt hat
and a traveling cloth shirt.
A hand-towel was tied around his waist,
leg-wraps bound his calves,
and he wore straw sandals.
He pushed the cart under the tree
and prepared to rest.
Seeing this, Yǒng'ér stood up and said,
“Greetings, traveler!”
The traveler returned the greeting and asked,
“Where is the young lady going?”
Yǒng'ér said,
“I am going to Zhèngzhōu to seek my father and mother.
My feet are sore
and I can walk no further,
so I am resting here.
What precious goods are you trading, traveler,
and where are you pushing that cart?”
The traveler said,
“I am a native of Zhèngzhōu.
I went to sell honey locusts in Dōngjīng and am now returning.”
Yǒng'ér said,
“Since you are passing through Zhèngzhōu, traveler,
if you could carry me in your cart,
I will give you five hundred cash for wine.”
The traveler thought to himself,
“My goods are already sold,
and Zhèngzhōu is on the way;
I might as well earn those five hundred cash.”
The traveler said,
“That will be no problem.”
He told Yǒng'ér to sit in the cart.
That traveler pushed the cart with all his might;
he did not speak to Yǒng'ér,
nor did he cast a glance at her.
With his head down,
he focused only on pushing the cart forward.
Yǒng'ér thought to herself,
“This traveler is an honest and simple man;
rare indeed, rare indeed.
Thinking of that fellow last night who provoked me with his words all along the way,
I used a bit of minor magic on him.
Although I did not take his life,
I gave him a good scare.
For a traveler such as this one,
it is just right to deliver him;
he may be of use in the future.”
The traveler pushed the cart
all the way to the East Gate of Zhèngzhōu,
and asked Yǒng'ér,
“Where is the house of your father and mother?”
Yǒng'ér said,
“Traveler!
I do not know the name of the place,
but once I am there, I will recognize it.”
The traveler pushed the cart through the East Gate
and came to a crossroads.
Yǒng'ér said,
“This is my home.”
The traveler set down the cart
and saw an empty house that was locked.
The traveler said,
“Young lady!
This is an empty house that is locked.
How can you say it is your home?”
Yǒng'ér jumped off the cart
and gave a shout!
The iron lock then fell off.
She pushed open a door with her hand
and went inside.
The traveler waited outside the door for more than an hour,
but saw no one come out.
The sky was turning dark,
and he kept craning his neck to look inside.
Unexpectedly, a person behind him said,
“What are you looking at that gate for?
Who opened this gate?”
Startled, the traveler turned around quickly.
He saw an old man
and hurriedly bowed, saying,
“I must inform you, venerable sir,
a moment ago at the crossroads ten li outside the city, I met a young lady
who said her feet were sore
and she could walk no further.
She promised me five hundred cash
and urged me to carry her here. She went inside
and has not come out.
She has kept me waiting for half a day.”
The old man said,
“This residence is the official quarters of Diāo Tōngpàn.
I am the caretaker.
It was originally sealed and locked;
who opened it?”
The traveler said,
“If that is the case,
I trouble you, venerable sir, to go into the house and say a word,
so as to get some silver to pay me.”
The old man said,
“I ask you,
who opened the gate?”
The traveler said,
“It was your young lady who opened it herself.”
The old man said,
“This is a locked, empty residence
with no one living here at all.
Where would a young lady come from?
You are speaking such ghostly nonsense;
are you perhaps deceiving me?”
The traveler said,
“This makes no sense!
I carried your family’s young lady home.
She promised me five hundred cash
but has not paid me.
Instead, you call it ‘ghostly nonsense.’
Let me go inside;
if the young lady is not there,
I am willing to offer my humble apologies.”
The old man said,
“Since you have said this,
if she is not found,
do not think of leaving!”
The old man opened the door wide
and told the guest to enter.
They went to the front hall and the winding corridor,
straight to the back parlor,
where from afar they saw Yǒng'ér sitting in the parlor.
The guest pointed and said:
"Isn't this the young lady?"
The Lǎo Yuànzi was feeling suspicious in his heart,
wondering where this woman had come from!
He saw the guest walk forward and shout:
"Young lady, why don't you come out and return my silver?
What is the reason for this?"
When Yǒng'ér saw the guest coming,
she quickly stood up and fled toward the back.
The guest immediately strode to the back parlor.
Seeing him chasing closely
and that there was no place to hide behind the parlor,
Yǒng'ér ran straight to the side of a well,
looked into it,
and jumped down.
Seeing this, the guest
was so frightened he could only cry out in misery!
"Oh, misery!"
Just as he was about to flee,
he was grabbed by the Lǎo Yuànzi,
who said:
"You don't even know this woman.
You came here with her yourself,
and yet you forced her down the well.
In this peaceful world,
under the vast heavens,
you have driven someone to their death,
and yet you want to escape.
If this woman's family finds out
and comes here seeking her life,
where will I find you to answer for it then?
This matter cannot be dropped!"
Holding him tightly,
he called out to the neighbors and others,
bound the guest with a rope,
and delivered him straight to Zhèngzhōu.
Because of this event,
it is said:
An honest guest
ends up in a phantom lawsuit;
A corrupt official
turns to deceitful methods.
It truly makes
an ordinary man stomp his feet
and a brave man beat his chest.
As for what happened next,
listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
In such a vast world, what does not occur?
A universe within a jar, a realm within a well.
If one can turn somersaults from here,
then they are a true man of the human world.
The story continues: the Lǎo Yuànzi and the neighbors
bound the guest with a rope
and delivered him straight to Zhèngzhōu.
It happened that the Tàiyǐn was in the hall presiding over cases.
The local Lǐjiǎ and others
brought the guest to kneel down
and related how the man, at the residence of Diāo Tōngpàn,
had chased a woman of unknown name
down the Bājiǎo Well.
The Tàiyǐn interrogated the guest.
The guest confessed:
"I am a native of this prefecture,
surnamed Bǔ and named Jí.
Because I was returning from selling soap pods in Dōngjīng,
I traveled past Bǎnqiáo and Bājiǎo Town, and fifty lǐ beyond, under a large tree,
I met a woman of unknown name.
She said her feet were in pain and she could not walk,
and wished to rent a cart to go to her father and mother's house at the Crossroads of the East Gate of Zhèngzhōu,
willing to pay five hundred coins.
I, Bǔ Jí, carried her to this house;
she opened the door and entered,
but never came out.
I waited for a long time
until the Lǎo Yuànzi came out
and said, 'My house is the residence of Diāo Tōngpàn,
it is a vacant house with no one living in it,'
and she refused to return the money.
After a while,
I went inside with the Lǎo Yuànzi to search for her.
Unexpectedly, when the woman saw me,
she jumped into the well herself;
it was not a matter of me forcing her."
The Tàiyǐn ordered Bǔ Jí to be detained in prison
and to be taken the next day to Diāo Tōngpàn's residence to salvage the corpse from the well.
The next day, the Tàiyǐn appointed an official
who took Bǔ Jí out of prison
and, together with the neighbors and others,
escorted him to Diāo Tōngpàn's residence.
The people watching on the street
were crowded shoulder to shoulder and back to back;
everyone said:
"In the residence of Diāo Tōngpàn,
divine songs and ghostly weeping are often heard inside.
No one dares to live there."
Some said:
"Let's see how the salvaging of the corpse goes today."
The official sat on a folding chair
and ordered Bǔ Jí to kneel before him.
The official questioned the Lǎo Yuànzi and the four neighbors
about how Bǔ Jí had chased the woman into the well.
Bǔ Jí pleaded:
"The woman jumped into the well herself;
I never chased her down."
The official called out:
"Bring the divers forward!"
The divers bowed in acknowledgement
and put on their water vests.
The official said:
"By the decree of the Tàiyǐn,
I have been appointed to oversee you going down the well.
You must salvage it carefully!"
A diver said:
"Just now I went to examine the well;
it is about thirty to fifty zhàng deep.
If I just go down like this,
it will be of little use.
We must use a windlass with a claw attachment;
if there is an emergency,
I can be heard when I call."
The official said:
"Whatever items are needed,
I will order them to be prepared immediately."
The diver said:
"I need a windlass with a claw attachment,
thirty zhàng of rope for the frame,
a large bamboo basket,
a large bronze bell,
and twenty laborers.
If there is an emergency,
I will shake the bell,
and those above can pull me up."
In a short while,
all the items were procured and ready.
The diver prepared the windlass,
the bronze bell,
and the bamboo basket.
When all was ready,
he said:
"I request the Lángzhōng's command
to go down the well to salvage."
The official said:
"From among you divers,
let one who is skilled in the water go down."
Four or five men held the windlass,
and a diver sat in the bamboo basket.
Two or three people lifted the basket into the well curb,
and four people released the windlass.
After lowering it about twenty-odd zhàng,
they suddenly heard the bronze bell ringing frantically.
The official ordered everyone to step back
and hurriedly had them wind the windlass to bring the basket up.
When everyone saw it,
they all let out a shout.
Looking into the basket,
it was something unheard of since ancient times
and rare to see today.
That diver, when he first went down,
was a man of healthy complexion;
now, as he was wound up and seen,
his face was as yellow as wax,
and his limbs were stiff and rigid;
he had died in the basket.
The official ordered him to be carried to one side
and told the diver's family to take him home for the funeral rites;
let this not be spoken of further.
The Wěiguān said:
"It certainly won't do for only one to go down,
leaving the official business unfinished,
and just letting it be.
Send another sailor down."
The sailors all appealed together, saying:
"Lángzhōng above!
We all have elders and children at home.
Did you see how it was just now?
For what reason
should we treat our lives like skipping stones on water?
We absolutely dare not go down.
If Lángzhōng insists that we subordinates go down,
we would rather be taken before the Zhīzhōu Excellency;
even if we are beaten, it would be dying on land.
It is truly impossible to go down."
The Wěiguān said:
"This is also not to be blamed on you.
But how are we to get this woman's corpse up?
You lot stay here and guard Bǔ Jí,
while I go report back to the Zhīzhōu Excellency to discuss the matter."
The Wěiguān entered his sedan chair,
recounted the matter,
and the Zhīzhōu also had no idea what to do.
The Wěiguān said:
"The local people
all say that Diāo Tōngpàn’s manor is haunted;
unexpectedly, another sailor died today.
Who would dare go down again?
But if we cannot salvage that woman's corpse,
how can we settle Bǔ Jí's case?
In my humble opinion,
it is better to just use Bǔ Jí
and order Bǔ Jí to go down and salvage it.
Even if he dies in the well,
he can be considered as paying for the life."
The Zhīzhōu said:
"That is well said;
you go and handle the matter yourself."
The Wěiguān took his leave of the Zhīzhōu and returned to the well-side,
brought Bǔ Jí forward,
and said:
"It was you who drove the woman down the well;
you must go down yourself to salvage the corpse.
I have reported to the Zhīzhōu Excellency
to grant you a pardon for your crime."
Bǔ Jí said:
"I am willing to go down,
I only need a short knife for self-defense."
Everyone said:
"Well said!"
They immediately removed the cangue,
took off the wooden shackles,
and gave him a short knife.
They put Bǔ Jí in a basket to sit
and lowered the windlass.
After a long time,
it did not seem to reach the bottom.
The crowd raised a cry, saying:
"When the previous sailor went down,
the bell rang after only twenty or so zhàng of rope;
this time the rope on the windlass is nearly exhausted,
is it not strange?
So much rope has been let out,
yet it still hasn't reached the bottom."
Before they finished speaking,
the windlass stopped moving
and the bell did not ring.
Not speaking of the crowd above the well for now,
but of Bǔ Jí reaching the bottom of the well.
When he raised his head to look,
he saw a speck of light at the well mouth.
When he felt around the outside,
there was no water.
When he stepped down,
it was solid ground.
Feeling his way along,
he walked forward.
After walking about one or two lǐ,
he saw a bright place.
Feeling it, there were two cave doors.
He pushed them open,
slipped inside to look,
and again saw the light of day.
Bǔ Jí said:
"How can there be such a place at the bottom of a well?"
While walking with his knife held high,
he saw a large tiger crouching in the middle of the road.
Bǔ Jí said:
"The one that harms people must be this tiger.
Even if you eat me,
I'm dead either way!"
He strode forward,
and slashed at the tiger,
shouting a command!
With a loud bang,
sparks flew in all directions,
and his hand was jolted numb for a long while.
Looking closely,
it was a stone tiger.
Bǔ Jí said:
"There must be another place further in."
After walking a few more steps,
he saw pine trees on both sides,
with a path in the middle
all paved with pebbles.
Bǔ Jí said:
"Since there is a road,
there must be a place ahead."
Wielding his knife, he entered the pine-lined path.
After walking one or two hundred paces,
a place revealed itself,
so startling that Bǔ Jí did not dare approach.
Looking intently:
He saw:
Golden nails on vermilion doors,
green tiles on carved eaves.
Flying dragons coiled around pillars play with bright pearls,
paired phoenixes on screen curtains cry to the morning sun;
Red-plastered walls,
imperial willows amidst palace flowers.
Towers and terraces in emerald mists,
faint auspicious light shrouding lucky shadows.
Windows in tortoise-shell patterns,
a fragrant breeze gently wafting through yellow gauze.
Curtains of fine bamboo rolled up,
the bright moon like a sphere hanging from purple silk;
If this is not the mansion of immortals in the heavens,
it must be the home of an emperor in the human world.
Bǔ Jí said:
"What place is this,
with its doors shut?
Could it be a grotto-dwelling of immortals?"
He wanted to push the door but dared not;
he wanted to go back,
but had no proof.
"I surely cannot just say I saw a stone tiger;
how could the Zhīzhōu believe me?"
While he was hesitating,
the door suddenly creaked open,
and a young girl in blue clothing walked out.
The girl called out:
"Bǔ Dàláng!
Shèng Gūgu has been waiting for you for a long time!"
Hearing this, Bǔ Jí
thought to himself:
"How does this girl know me,
and what Auntie has the surname Shèng?
Among my relatives of three clans,
none have this surname.
And why is she waiting for me?"
Bǔ Jí had no choice but to follow the girl to a certain place.
He saw a palace hall,
on which stood two immortal boys
and an immortal girl.
In the center chair,
sat an elderly woman.
When Bǔ Jí stole a glance,
he saw that the woman had:
An ancient and weathered appearance,
white hair and a youthful complexion.
Eyes dim like the autumn moon shrouded in mist,
eyebrows white as the morning frost reflecting the sun;
Wearing embroidered robes and a jade belt,
resembling Zǐfǔ Yuánjūn,
with a phoenix bun and dragon hairpins,
like Xīchí Wángmǔ.
Even the most righteous immortal guest could not depict her,
and her majestic image is hard for a painting to capture.
Bǔ Jí thought:
"This must be a dwelling place of immortals;
I must be destined by fate to arrive here."
Bǔ Jí then bowed and said:
"I appeal to the True Immortal!
The guest Bǔ Jí respectfully pays his respects."
He bowed four times.
The Pópo said:
"My place here is extraordinary;
your fortune and fate have a share in this.
To be able to reach this place,
you must be a person of merit and practice.
Please come up the steps and be seated."
Bǔ Jí repeatedly refused to sit.
The Pópo said:
"You are a person of destiny;
there is no harm in sitting!"
Only then did Bǔ Jí dare to sit.
The Pópo called for tea to be served.
After the girl attendant finished presenting the tea,
the Pópo said:
"Your coming to this place
was not easy.
For what reason did you come here?"
Bǔ Jí said:
"I inform the Gūgu!
This humble merchant was transporting soap pods to Dōngjīng to sell,
and was pushing an empty cart back,
when on the road I saw a woman sitting under a tree
who said:
'I want to go seek refuge with my parents,
but my feet ache;
I promise you five hundred wén,
if you carry me to the front of the residence of Vice Prefect Diāo Tōngpàn inside the East Gate.'
The woman said:
'This is my home.'
She got off the cart, pushed the door open, and went inside,
but she did not come back out.
Seeing me searching inside,
she then jumped into a well.
Because of this, the local authorities seized me
and sent me to the magistrate.
The officials sent men down the well to salvage her,
and another sailor died.
The Zhīzhōu had no choice but to order me down;
I saw that inside the well there was a path and no water,
and I wandered aimlessly until I arrived here."
The Pópo said:
"When you came down into the well,
what did you see?"
Bǔ Jí said:
"I saw a stone tiger."
The Pópo said:
"That creature has been a vessel for many years
and has harmed many people.
Any mortal who reaches here and sees this tiger
will surely be eaten by him.
But you went as far as to strike him with a blade;
you will certainly achieve success in the future.
Bǔ Jí!
I shall let you see someone!"
Looking at the green-robed girl attendant, she said:
"Tell her to come out!"
Not long after the girl attendant went inside,
the woman who had jumped into the well came walking out;
she looked at Bǔ Jí, gave a greeting of ten thousand blessings,
and said:
"The guest elder was very helpful yesterday."
When Bǔ Jí saw that woman,
anger rose from his heart,
and malice was born from his gallbladder.
He then cursed:
"You spine-beaten thief of a lowly woman!
How intolerable!
Seeing you say your feet ached and you could not walk,
I kindly carried you such a long distance.
You did not even give me the fare,
but walked into a residence
and jumped into a well.
You caused me to be seized by the magistrate,
wearing a cangue on my neck
and shackles on my arms,
suffering in prison.
How can this injustice be explained?
I thought I would never see you again in this life,
yet you are actually here!
When enemies meet,
their eyes open exceptionally wide!
'I shall let you taste my blade!'"
He pulled out a knife from his side,
and stepped forward to seize her by the chest and strike.
Hú Yǒng'ér gave a shout,
which froze his hand;
Bǔ Jí's body and feet could not move at all.
Hú Yǒng'ér said:
"I consider the favor of you carrying me all along the way on your cart.
If not for that,
I would chop you into meat paste.
Because I saw you were pure, kind, and steady,
I intended to deliver you,
yet you are so rude
as to dare to take a knife to strike me,
and yet you cannot strike me after all."
The Pópo rose and advised:
"Do not harm him;
in the future there will be a use for him;
we still need them to come and assist you."
The Pópo looked at Bǔ Jí's face and gave just one puff of breath,
and his feet could move.
Bǔ Jí looked at the Pópo and said:
"The young lady is a person of magic."
The Pópo said:
"If I were not here,
your life would be over.
From now on do not be rude again."
Bǔ Jí said:
"I am fortunate
to have met you, Gūgu.
If I can be saved from the suffering of prison,
get out of the well,
and return home without trouble,
I will burn incense and set up an altar every day
to worship you, Gūgu."
The Pópo said:
"You are fated to be here,
so do not leave just yet;
follow me to drink a few cups of wine,
and then I will send you back."
Bǔ Jí followed her inside,
and was startled, saying:
"I am but a person from the countryside,
how could I have ever seen such a wonderful place?"
Everything was arranged in perfect order;
one could only see:
Incense burning in precious tripods,
flowers placed in golden vases.
Emerald curtains and shark-silk hangings on the four walls.
Gold and silver utensils arranged on a single table.
Inside crystal jars
was entirely the jade nectar of the Zǐfǔ;
within amber cups
was fully filled with the jade liquid of the Yáochí.
On hawksbill platters
were piled immortal peaches and exotic fruits;
in glass bowls
were served bear paws and camel humps.
Fish slices cut like silver threads,
fine tea brewed from jade buds.
The Pópo invited Bǔ Jí to sit,
but Bǔ Jí did not dare to sit.
The Pópo said:
"Bǔ Dàláng, sit down;
in another day, wealth and honor shall be your share!"
Only then did Bǔ Jí sit down.
Then wine was served,
and then food was served;
when had he ever seen such a display?
Two green-robed girl attendants continuously poured wine and served him.
Every cup was poured full,
and every goblet was drained.
When the wine had made him half-drunk,
Bǔ Jí pondered:
"I came a long way from the top of the well to here,
saw such a place,
met an immortal lady,
and saw this woman again.
Who knows if they are immortals or demons?
Staying here is not a long-term plan."
He then rose and spoke to the Gūgu and the young lady:
"I want to go to the well to look after my cart and money;
I fear they may be taken by someone."
The Pópo said:
"What are money and goods worth?
I shall have you take an object up with you,
and your wealth and honor will be beyond words.
I wonder what is in your heart?"
Bǔ Jí said:
"I thank you, Gūgu, for your kind intention.
Never mind if it is a valuable object;
even if it is worthless,
taking it above to serve as evidence
would also clear me of my crime."
The Pópo called Yǒng'ér to come close to her ear and whispered in a low voice.
Not long after entering,
a young girl in green clothes was seen emerging from within, carrying an object with both hands,
and she gave it to Bǔ Jí.
Bǔ Jí received it in his hands
and felt it was somewhat heavy.
He thought to himself:
"What kind of thing is this,
wrapped in a yellow silk bundle?"
Bǔ Jí said:
"I beg you, Gūgū,
for what purpose is this given to a lowly person like me?"
The Pópó said:
"You must not open it.
Carry it up the well,
and do not give it to anyone else.
Simply say that the deity of this prefecture
has kept this item for a thousand years
and is now bestowing it upon the Zhīzhōu;
then you may be pardoned for your own crime.
There is one more matter I must instruct you on:
whenever you are in an urgent or difficult situation,
you may call out loudly for 'Shèng Gūgū,'
and I shall come to save you."
Bǔ Jí heard these words
and committed them all to memory.
The Pópó ordered the green-clad girl to see Bǔ Jí out,
and he returned by the original path to the earthen tunnel.
Upon reaching the side of the bamboo basket,
he stepped inside and sat down.
He shook the rope,
and the bell rang;
those above heard it and turned the windlass to pull him up.
When the crowd looked,
they did not see the woman’s corpse,
but only saw Bǔ Jí clutching a yellow silk bundle
as he came to meet the Wěiguān.
Bǔ Jí said:
"No one move!
This object
was delivered by the deity of this prefecture to be given to the Zhīzhōu;
it must not be opened until it is before the Zhīzhōu."
The Wěiguān boarded his sedan chair,
and the entire group surrounded and escorted Bǔ Jí,
heading straight into the Zhōuyá.
It happened that the Zhīzhōu was presiding in the hall,
with clerks and attendants lined up on both sides.
The Wěiguān stepped forward and reported:
"Bǔ Jí went down the well for half a day.
Afterward, the bell was heard to ring,
and he was immediately pulled up.
Bǔ Jí was seen clutching a yellow silk bundle
wrapping an object,
claiming it was from the deity of this prefecture
to be given to the prefectural official.
I did not dare to act on my own authority
and have brought him for your Excellency's decree."
The Zhīzhōu ordered Bǔ Jí to be brought forward.
The Zhīzhōu said:
"What object is within the yellow bundle,
and how did you obtain it?"
Bǔ Jí said:
"I beg to inform your Excellency!
When I went down into the well,
I found no sign of the woman's corpse at the bottom.
There was no water,
but there was a path,
and after walking about two lǐ,
I finally saw the light of day.
I saw a tiger
and was nearly killed by it.
I struck it once with my knife,
but sparks flew everywhere,
and when I looked closely,
it was a stone tiger.
There was another path through the pines leading inward,
where I saw a palace.
Outside was a green-clad girl
who led me into the hall,
where I saw an immortal.
The immortal claimed to be the deity of this prefecture;
after giving me wine and food to eat,
she brought out this object
and told me to deliver it to the prefectural official to be received,
and forbade me from leaking the secrets of heaven."
The Zhīzhōu took the yellow bundle
and placed it on the official desk;
he felt it was heavy.
The Zhīzhōu thought:
"A treasure has appeared in the world,
and it is only right that it meets me."
He ordered his subordinates to withdraw,
and opening the yellow bundle with his own hands to look,
he said:
"No wonder it is so heavy;
it is a golden tripod with three legs and two ears."
Nine characters were cast upon it, saying:
"He who encounters this object
shall surely have great wealth and rank."
After the Zhīzhōu finished reading,
he wrapped it in the yellow bundle again
and called for his personal servants from his household to take it inside
to be kept as a treasure of the treasury.
The clerk stepped forward and reported:
"Bǔ Jí awaits your Excellency's verdict."
The Zhīzhōu pondered:
"If I were to release Bǔ Jí,
all the people in the prefecture know he chased a woman into the well;
and when it came to the recovery,
a sailor's life was also lost.
If I release him just like that,
the people of the prefecture will surely criticize me.
If I want Bǔ Jí to forfeit his life for the woman's,
yet her corpse cannot be found anywhere,
and instead he brought a golden tripod to offer to me.
What then is the best course?"
Suddenly, he raised his brush to write the judgment:
"Bǔ Jí..."
There is a reason to say:
The Zhīzhōu died an unnatural death instantly,
and not a single person in the city of Zhèngzhōu found any peace.
Truly:
When luck is high, one can buy wine on credit at the shop;
when disaster strikes, one meets a person of karmic debt.
As for what happened in the end,
please listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
The Sovereign is distant and Heaven is high, both are unresponsive;
corrupt officials and dirty clerks dare to run rampant.
The sword at the waist is like autumn water,
seeking to sever the injustice of the human world.
It is said that the Zhīzhōu hesitated in his heart for a good while,
then took up his brush and passed judgment:
"Bǔ Jí inappropriately tried to force payment of cart fare,
causing a woman of unknown name to flee in panic
and accidentally fall into a well.
The well is within an abandoned house that has long been closed,
and has always been full of sinister hauntings;
moreover, the failure to recover her body
is indeed a strange matter.
Since Bǔ Jí originally had no intent to coerce with violence,
it seems difficult to demand a life for a life.
However, the accidental death of a person
was not without cause.
He shall receive twenty strokes on the back
and be tattooed and exiled to the penal camp of Mìzhōu in Shāndōng to serve as a soldier."
Thereupon, twenty strokes were administered in the hall,
and a tattoo artist was summoned
to brand two rows of golden characters.
The official documents were signed,
and two escort officers were dispatched;
one was Dǒng Chāo,
and the other was Xuē Bà.
Having taken custody of Bǔ Jí in the hall
and received the documents,
they led Bǔ Jí out from the front of the prefectural office.
Bǔ Jí stopped his steps outside the office
and turned back toward the interior, saying:
"I, Bǔ Jí, have been greatly wronged!
The woman jumped into the well herself;
I did not use force against her.
Moreover, she was no ordinary person,
but the Tǔshén of this prefecture,
who told me to go down and obtain this treasure to present to you.
Since you received the treasure,
you should have naturally pardoned my crime.
Instead, you have unjustly sentenced me to be tattooed and exiled to Mìzhōu.
If I struggle and return with my life,
I will take the matter of your concealing the treasure
to the Imperial City,
beat the Drum of Grievances,
and I must settle the score with you!"
Seeing that his words were improper, Dǒng Chāo
simply pushed Bǔ Jí along.
Xuē Bà said:
"If you spout such words here,
it will implicate the two of us,
and that would be serious."
They hurriedly left the prefectural office.
Coming to a tavern,
the three of them went inside together and sat down.
Dǒng Chāo said:
"Bring two measures of wine."
Xuē Bà said:
"Bǔ Jí,
although we two are carrying out official orders
to escort you to Mìzhōu in Shāndōng,
the journey is very long.
You will need travel expenses on the road,
and we do not travel with people who bring no money.
Do you have any relatives or acquaintances
to arrange some silver
for use on the road?
We do not want your money for ourselves."
Bǔ Jí said:
"Honorable officers!
I originally had some money,
but when I was caught in this lawsuit,
I don't know who made off with even my cart.
Now, whom can you ask me to seek?
I am a lone man,
without any relatives,
and there is truly no place to arrange travel funds."
Xuē Bà said irritably:
"We have escorted many fierce and stubborn criminals,
but none with a face like yours.
You say you have no travel money,
but even the Pagoda-Bearing Heavenly King Lǐ
would have to leave his armor behind;
we would squeeze juice even out of raw ginger.
Once someone is the 'merchandise' in our hands,
we do not let them off lightly."
After talking for a while,
they paid for the wine.
The two escorted Bǔ Jí out through the west gate of Zhèngzhōu.
As they were walking,
they heard someone behind them call out:
"Dǒng Chāo!"
When Dǒng Chāo turned to look,
he recognized Wú Kǒngmù of the prefecture.
He told Xuē Bà to lead Bǔ Jí ahead
while he lagged a step behind
to meet with him.
Wú Kǒngmù said:
"I have been commissioned by the Lord Zhīzhōu.
Just as Bǔ Jí was sentenced and sent out,
that fellow was being unruly in front of the office.
I now bring the command of the Lord Zhīzhōu:
he wants you two to find a way
to finish him off in a secluded place
and bring back the golden tattoo from his face as proof,
and you will be heavily rewarded."
Dǒng Chāo agreed
and caught up to inform Xuē Bà.
They decided to finish him in the forest ahead.
The two escorted Bǔ Jí to the front of a deserted forest.
Dǒng Chāo said:
"I am a bit weary today
and cannot walk further;
let us sleep for a while in this forest."
Xuē Bà said:
"We have just left the prefectural office
and have not walked even thirty lǐ;
why do you want to rest already?"
Dǒng Chāo said:
"I got up a bit too early today
and need a rest.
I'm only afraid Bǔ Jí might escape,
for there's no apothecary shop where I can buy another 'you' if you are lost.
Let us bind him up;
then even while sleeping, our hearts will be at ease."
Bǔ Jí said:
"If you officers want to bind me, then bind me;
I certainly will not run."
Dǒng Chāo took a long rope and bound Bǔ Jí to a tree branch.
He took the end of the rope and hung him upside down from a large branch,
then took his staff and said:
"Bǔ Jí!
We have received the command of the Lord Zhīzhōu
to kill you;
it has nothing to do with us.
This time, this day, this month of next year
will be the anniversary of your death."
Bǔ Jí was so terrified his soul left his body,
tears fell from his eyes,
and he pleaded:
"You two!
I have no immediate grievance with you,
nor any old enmity.
Even with the Lord Zhīzhōu,
I have committed no offense.
Why must you take my life?
I hope you two will show a heart as vast as heaven and earth,
spare my remaining life,
and in every life to come,
I shall serve you as a dog or a horse in return."
While speaking,
his tears fell like rain.
Dǒng Chāo said:
"Crying is of no use.
The Lord Zhīzhōu is angry that you were unruly in front of the office
and wants to finish you off.
He is the master of the prefecture;
who dares to disobey him?
If you want your life,
would I not have to return and receive the poisonous staff in your stead?"
Xuē Bà said:
"Brother Dǒng Chāo!
Why waste your energy talking to this barbarian?
Finish him early to release him early,
so he can quickly seek a good reincarnation before King Yánluó."
Having spoken,
he snatched the staff from Dǒng Chāo's hand
and prepared to raise it to strike.
Bǔ Jí said:
"How bitter!
How bitter!
My life is at its end!"
Suddenly he remembered the Shèng Gūgū who gave him the treasure,
who once said that if he were in dire trouble, he should call her.
So he cried out: "Shèng Gūgū, save me!"
Before his cry had even faded,
someone outside the forest shouted loudly:
"Escort officers, do not strike!
I have been listening here for a long time."
Dǒng and Xuē were startled
and hurriedly ran to the edge of the forest to look;
it was a Xiānshēng.
What did he look like?
There is a Xījiāngyuè
as proof:
His radiant spirit was extraordinary,
with a dignified seven-foot stature.
His face was like purple jade with a handsome beard,
and his two eyes were like bright stars, truly remarkable.
His hair was bound in an iron crown with a ruyì,
and he wore a red robe with a yellow sash at his waist.
A Tiānshī named Zhāng come from the heavens,
lacking only a tiger cub to ride upon.
That Daoist priest shook his fists and strode forward,
rushing into the woods
to look at the two constables and say:
"The Zhīzhōu ordered you to escort him.
Why have you hung him up to take his life?
What is the reason for this?"
The two constables were flustered and panicked
and said:
"Xiānshēng!
We are following the orders of the Zhīzhōu Xiànggōng
and have no personal grudge."
The Xiānshēng said:
"You speak nonsense! Nowadays the official proceedings are as clear as a mirror,
so why would you take his life if he is innocent?
I am a man of the cloth
and originally should not meddle in others' business.
But just now I heard a loud cry of 'Shèng Gūgu' in the woods;
what was the reason for that?
For now, let him down
and wait for me to question him."
Dǒng Chāo had no choice but to untie Bǔ Jí.
Bǔ Jí said:
"I beg you, Xiānshēng!
Listen to what Bǔ Jí has to say.
Because I went to Dōngjīng to sell soap pods
and was returning after the sale,
on the road I saw a woman crying that her feet hurt and she could not walk;
she promised me five hundred cash to rent my cart to carry her.
When we arrived in front of an empty residence inside the East Gate of Zhèngzhōu,
this woman jumped off the cart and walked inside.
I did not see her come out,
and when I went in after a while, the woman jumped down a well on her own.
The local people said I forced her into the well
and seized me to be sent to the authorities.
The Zhīzhōu ordered me to go down the well myself to recover the body.
When I went down, it turned out there was no water in the well,
but there was a path,
and I saw a palace.
I encountered an immortal Xiāngū who gave me a treasure.
She told me to give it to the Zhīzhōu to be pardoned of my crime.
As I was about to set out, she instructed me
that if I were in urgent trouble, I should call for Shèng Gūgu."
When the Xiānshēng heard this,
he said:
"So that is how it was."
Looking at the two escorting constables, he said:
"This Bǔ Jí should not die
since he has met this humble priest.
Come with me to the village tavern outside the woods to drink three cups of wine,
and I will also provide you with some travel expenses
so that you may look after him well until you reach your destination."
Dǒng Chāo and Xuē Bà said:
"We thank you, Xiānshēng!"
The four of them left the woods together.
After walking about half a lǐ,
they saw a wine shop.
The four of them entered the wine shop and sat down,
and the waiter came and asked:
"Zhāng Xiānshēng!
How much wine shall I pour?"
The Xiānshēng said:
"Pour four jiǎo of wine,
and if you have a roasted chicken, bring one for us to eat."
The waiter said:
"The marketplace is far
and there is no place to get roasted chicken."
The Xiānshēng said:
"If there are no vegetables either,
how can we have anything to go with the wine?"
The waiter said:
"The wine is here."
The four of them each drank a bowl.
The Xiānshēng said:
"I have the heart to treat guests,
yet there is no food to accompany the drink."
Looking east and west,
he saw a water vat by the wall.
When the Xiānshēng looked at it,
it was a vat of clean water.
From his sleeve, the Xiānshēng took out a small gourd,
pulled out the stopper,
shook out a pill of white medicine,
and placed it in the water vat.
He then went back to sit on his stool as before
and called the waiter over, saying:
"How can the four of us drink wine with nothing to eat!
Just now I put the food in your water vat;
take it out and cook it for me."
The waiter said:
"Zhāng Xiānshēng!
You four came in empty-handed;
I did not see any food."
The Xiānshēng said:
"Go and look in the water vat yourself."
When the waiter went to look,
he only saw the water moving;
reaching in with both hands to fish,
he pulled out a carp three feet long
and said:
"Isn't this strange!"
He had no choice but to clean the fish for them,
put it in the pot to boil it thoroughly,
added some salt, soy sauce, pepper, and vinegar,
and placed it on a plate to bring to them.
While the four of them were drinking wine,
Dǒng Chāo said:
"Thank you for your kindness, Xiānshēng."
Xuē Bà said:
"This fish tastes very good;
it would be wonderful if we could have another one to eat."
The Xiānshēng said:
"This is not enough of a courtesy.
I, this humble priest, usually enjoy a drink;
it is rare to meet you two,
and within the four seas,
all are acquaintances.
If you do not mind,
come together to my temple
where we shall drink until we are drunk
and you can set out tomorrow.
I wonder what you two think?"
Xuē Bà had the temperament of a young man
and said:
"It is rare for the Xiānshēng to kindly invite us,
and it is getting late today,
so let us go to your temple to stay for the night.
It's just that we shouldn't trouble you."
Dǒng Chāo, being older after all,
was more experienced;
he called Xuē Bà to a quiet spot and said:
"This Xiānshēng is a person who performs strange feats.
For what reason
should we go to his temple with him?"
Xuē Bà said:
"Dǒng Dàgē!
You have lived all these years in vain
and do not understand things.
The owner of this wine shop also knows him;
if anything goes wrong,
we can just hold the wine shop responsible for him."
Dǒng Chāo said:
"That is also true."
The Xiānshēng paid for the wine,
and the four of them left the wine shop.
Chatting along the way,
they did not know how far they had walked.
Then the Xiānshēng pointed with his hand and said:
"This is my small hermitage."
When Dǒng Chāo looked,
what a fine thatched hermitage!
It was not very large
but built compactly.
There were no other houses in front of or behind the hermitage,
and the two of them felt a bit suspicious.
The **Xiānshēng** opened the door,
invited the three people in,
and they sat down in front of the door.
The **Xiānshēng** said:
“You three, do not worry;
there is plenty of room to lodge here.
Tonight, just rest happily for a night,
and you can set off early tomorrow.
At this time, it is mid-June,
and the moon rises early.”
The **Xiānshēng** fetched a table out
and placed it outside.
He went inside to prepare meat, vegetables, and the like,
and spread them on the table.
The **Xiānshēng** said:
“I treated the two of you in the tavern just now,
but it was not enough to show proper courtesy.
Let us drink to our hearts’ content right here until we stop.”
The two constables looked at each other
and whispered:
“This **Xiānshēng** treated us to food in the tavern.
Now that we have come to the hermitage,
he has prepared so much food and wine again.
If we choose not to eat,
our bellies are hungry.
If we eat his food,
we do not know what his purpose is.”
**Xuē Bà** said:
“The two of us are escorting this criminal,
and the responsibility is not small.
We have only traveled one stage from **Zhèngzhōu**,
and we have encountered this strange **Zhāng Xiānshēng**.
If there is some emergency,
we both have elders and children at home;
this is no joking matter!”
**Dǒng Chāo** said:
“The guest does not decide when to come,
but once he arrives, he is at the host’s mercy.
Since we have come here,
let us eat his food for now
and see what he does.”
The **Xiānshēng** brought out the wine,
and each person drank more than ten cups
until they were all full.
The two constables said:
“We thank you, **Xiānshēng**, for the wine and food,
but we can eat no more.
The three of us will borrow lodgings for the night,
and set off early tomorrow.”
The **Xiānshēng** said:
“This weak wine is not enough to show courtesy;
why bother with thanks?
You two, please sit for a moment.”
That **Xiānshēng** got up and went inside; before long,
he brought out two ingots of silver,
each weighing fifty ounces,
and said:
“You two each take one ingot;
do not despise them for being small.”
**Xuē Bà** did not say a word.
**Dǒng Chāo** said:
“We are grateful to the **Xiānshēng** for bestowing wine and food;
it was already too much trouble.
We absolutely dare not accept this silver.”
The **Xiānshēng** said:
“You two take it for now;
it is just a token of my regard.”
The two men could not resist the **Xiānshēng**'s insistence
and each took one ingot.
The **Xiānshēng** said:
“This humble Daoist has a matter to tell you;
I wonder if you two would be willing to comply?”
The two thought to themselves:
We have drunk the wine
and taken the silver;
how could we not comply?
So they said:
“**Xiānshēng**, do not speak of one matter;
we would comply with ten matters for you.
Feel free to speak.”
The **Xiānshēng** said:
“You two have each taken fifty ounces of silver
to support your families.
Consider that **Bǔ Jí** is a person who has suffered a grievance and been wronged;
I do not know him,
but I only have compassion and a love for life in mind.
Listen to **Bǔ Jí**'s story;
he is an innocent man,
yet he was forced into this wrongful legal case.
I hope you two will somehow make it convenient
to leave him here in the hermitage to accompany me.
My name is **Zhāng Luán**.
If the **Zhīzhōu** asks,
just say that **Zhāng Luán** wanted to save **Bǔ Jí**, and that will be that.
I wonder what you two think?”
