**Dǒng Chāo** did not dare make a sound.
**Xuē Bà**, however, cried out, saying:
“**Xiānshēng**!
How ignorant you are!
Under the whole of heaven,
there is no land that is not the King's.
To the shores of the earth,
there are no people who are not the King's subjects.
Although you are a man of religion
living within the borders of **Zhèngzhōu**,
you are also under the jurisdiction of the **Zhīzhōu**.
This man is a criminal sentenced by the local official;
who would dare to harbor him?
You think that because we took your silver,
you can coerce us.
Your silver is here untouched;
please take it back yourself.”
The **Xiānshēng** said:
“There is no need to be agitated.
If you are willing to leave him, then leave him.
If you are unwilling,
you two keep the silver,
and I will offer another cup of wine.”
**Dǒng Chāo** said:
“We have troubled the **Xiānshēng** for wine and food,
and you have bestowed silver on us.
Why must you keep urging us to drink?”
The **Xiānshēng** said:
“I am not just urging wine;
I have a small art
that I will present for you two to see.
From the **Zhīzhōu** above
to the common people below,
I will have them all admire a pair of moons.”
The **Xiānshēng** took a piece of paper from his bosom,
and with scissors in hand, cut the paper into a round moon.
He dripped wine onto the moon
and shouted, “Rise!”
The paper moon was seen rising into the empty air as it was blown.
The three people cheered together:
“Excellent!”
Two moons were seen in the sky.
There is a poem to prove it:
Pity that **Bǔ Jí** was originally innocent,
presenting the tripod instead led to danger and harm to his person.
Just because the basin was overturned, it was hard to see clearly,
therefore the double moons shine upon the muddled mess.
The **Xiānshēng** said:
“For the sake of this bright moon of mine,
please have a cup of wine.”
Here the four people were drinking wine.
Meanwhile, in **Zhèngzhōu**, from the **Zhīzhōu** above
to the common people below,
the residents inside and outside the city were stirred up;
they all saw two bright moons in the sky.
Some knowledgeable people said:
“There is only one moon;
how can there be two moons?
This must be a demonic moon.”
We shall not speak for now of the stirring among the crowd.
It is said that this Priest was about to finish drinking wine and enjoying the moon with the three men.
The Priest said:
"Do me a favor, you two.
Give *Bǔ Jí* to this poor Daoist."
*Dǒng Chāo* and *Xuē Bà* said:
"We each have elderly and young at home;
we cannot compare to you, Priest.
If the *Zhīzhōu* finds out,
it would be truly difficult for our two families to explain."
The Priest said:
"The *Zhīzhōu* instructed you
to arrange for his death;
that matter is quite easy.
I will have you two take back a piece of evidence
to show the *Zhīzhōu*."
Then the Priest was seen tying the sleeve of his Daoist robe into a knot
and tucking it behind his back.
With both hands, he grabbed *Bǔ Jí*,
used a rope to tie *Bǔ Jí*’s hands behind his back,
and bound him in the thatched hall.
*Xuē Bà* said:
"Priest, you wanted to save him this morning;
why do you want to bind him now?"
The Priest said:
"I am having you two take an object of his to see the *Zhīzhōu*."
*Dǒng Chāo* said:
"I do not know what object you are having us take?"
The Priest said:
"Since the *Zhīzhōu* wants to take his life,
now I, this poor Daoist, will act for you to cut open his belly and take his heart
to take to the *Zhīzhōu*,
to demonstrate your capability."
*Dǒng Chāo* said:
"That must not be done!
This is a sentenced criminal.
That the *Zhīzhōu* wants to harm him
is the *Zhīzhōu*’s private intent.
If we now carry the heart and liver there,
those who know the truth
would say the Priest killed him.
Those who do not know
would only say we two murdered him for his property.
This case of wrongful official business
is more than the two of us can bear."
The Priest said:
"So it turns out you are afraid of official trouble.
I was also just joking with you."
He then untied *Bǔ Jí*
and arranged for the three men to sleep.
The Priest said:
"If you two return to the prefecture,
say that I, *Zhāng Luán*, wanted to save *Bǔ Jí*;
you must remember this well."
The three of them settled into their spots
and stayed the night outside;
the Priest went inside by himself.
*Dǒng Chāo* and
*Xuē Bà* slept straight through until dawn.
When they opened their eyes to look,
the two of them were startled.
*Bǔ Jí* was gone from their side,
and neither the convent
nor the Priest was to be seen.
Instead, they were sleeping inside a temple of the Mountain God,
amidst a pile of paper money.
The two looked at each other and said:
"What misery!
What misery!
The two of us were ignorant
and let the criminal escape.
How should we proceed?"
*Dǒng Chāo* said:
"Let us not panic;
let's go and inform the *Zhīzhōu*."
They went straight back to *Zhèngzhōu*,
just as the *Zhīzhōu* was ascending the hall for the afternoon court session.
The two officers came before the hall and knelt down.
The *Zhīzhōu* then asked:
"The two of you were escorting *Bǔ Jí* to *Shāndōng*;
why have you returned today?"
*Dǒng Chāo* and
*Xuē Bà* said:
"We report to you, *Xiànggōng*:
yesterday we escorted *Bǔ Jí* onto the road.
Over thirty li away,
we encountered a Daoist priest
who invited us into a convent
to seize *Bǔ Jí*;
we subordinates argued with him.
That Daoist is an extraordinary man;
he cut out a paper moon,
blew it into the air,
and then two bright moons were seen."
Hearing this, the *Zhīzhōu*
immediately said:
"How strange!
Last night, because two moons were seen,
the prefectural city was in an uproar all night.
What happened afterward?"
*Dǒng Chāo* said:
"That Daoist told us subordinates to sleep in the convent for the night.
When we woke up early today
and opened our eyes to look,
we were in a pile of paper money in a temple of the Mountain God.
We truly do not know where *Bǔ Jí* and the Daoist went.
That Daoist claimed his name is *Zhāng Luán*."
The *Zhīzhōu* said:
"Since there is a name,
this sorcerer will be easy to catch."
That day, he immediately summoned the arresting officers and gave instructions.
Before he had finished speaking,
a Daoist was seen, wearing an iron crown and grass sandals
and a red robe with black edges,
walking straight up to the front of the hall,
saying in a loud voice:
"I, the poor Daoist *Zhāng Luán*, am here."
He did not even offer a respectful greeting.
The *Zhīzhōu* said in a great rage:
"You are a sorcerer!
How dare you be so insolent!"
The Daoist said:
"You are the master of a prefecture;
how can you wrongfully sentence an ordinary citizen?
*Bǔ Jí* is innocent,
yet you had him tattooed and exiled to *Shāndōng*.
On the road, you even ordered people to take his life
and took his priceless treasure.
What is the reason for this?"
The *Zhīzhōu* said:
"Stop talking nonsense!
What priceless treasure does he have?"
*Zhāng Luán* said:
"The *Jīndǐng* is currently in your treasury.
I will call it out."
The Daoist was then seen calling out:
"*Jīndǐng*! *Jīndǐng*!
I now invite you;
come out quickly,
everyone is waiting!"
The *Zhīzhōu* and the people below the hall were all dumbfounded with fright.
Then the *Jīndǐng* was seen flying down from the sky,
its two ears flapping like wings,
flying straight onto the hall.
Seeing this, the *Zhīzhōu*
said:
"How strange!
How strange!"
Before he finished speaking,
a person climbed out from inside the *Jīndǐng*.
That person was none other than *Bǔ Jí*,
who jumped out of the *Jīndǐng*.
With a sword in his right hand
and grabbing the *Zhīzhōu* with his left hand,
he cut the *Zhīzhōu* into two pieces with one sword stroke right there in the hall.
Seeing the *Zhīzhōu* dead,
everyone was at a loss.
The people on and below the hall all said:
"It cannot be that the *Zhīzhōu* was killed
and it just ends like this!"
They all moved forward to seize the Daoist
and *Bǔ Jí*.
Seeing the crowd coming to seize them, the two
picked up the *Jīndǐng*,
leaped onto the mounting stone, and set it down.
Both stepped into the tripod with their feet,
then called out:
"Farewell, everyone,
we are going!"
They pulled their heads down,
and both of them disappeared.
Suddenly, a wild wind rose up;
where the wind passed, even the *Jīndǐng* disappeared.
Everyone looked at each other and
all said:
"We have never seen such a strange thing."
They then asked the *Tóngzhī* of this prefecture to manage affairs,
along with the clerks of the six bureaus,
to purchase a coffin
and prepare the *Zhīzhōu*’s corpse for burial.
On one hand, they dispatched arresting officers
to search in all directions for *Zhāng Luán*
and *Bǔ Jí*,
and on the other hand, they discussed preparing a memorial to report to the Imperial Court.
Because of this incident,
there is a reason to tell:
A great disturbance in *Héběi*,
and turmoil in *Dōngjīng*.
The Imperial Court mobilized troops and horses,
but could not capture them,
until an upright high official was drawn out
to govern the country and bring peace to the people.
It is just as:
Using for a while the heterodox arts of sorcery,
To entice a man like a dragon or a tiger.
As for how the memorial was presented to the Imperial Court at that time,
please listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
When the monarch rises early, the subjects rise early,
Rushing into the palace gates before the sky is bright.
How many people lying high in the mountains,
Do not hear the morning bells until they are old.
It is said that the officials of Zhèngzhōu prepared a memorial to submit to Huángdì Rénzōng.
Huángdì Rénzōng spread the memorial upon his imperial desk and read it;
he then asked the civil and military officials of the two rows:
“The Zhèngzhōu Zhīzhōu has been murdered by an evil sorcerer;
you all must go to suppress and eliminate him.”
Before he had finished speaking,
an official from the Tàishǐ Yuàn suddenly stepped out from the ranks and reported:
“Last night a demonic star appeared,
shining directly upon the Shuāngyú Gōng,
and looking down upon the land of Wèi;
it portends that there is a sorcerer causing a rebellion.
I beg Your Imperial Majesty’s sagely discernment
to make preparations early.”
Huángdì Rénzōng said:
“Such a thing has just occurred in Zhèngzhōu,
and the Tàishǐ again reports the appearance of a demonic star;
the matter is of grave consequence.
You all must take precautions and handle this.”
The officials collectively reported:
“Currently, the Southern Tribunal of Kāifēng Fǔ is lacking a Zhīfǔ;
one must select a person who is incorruptible, clear-sighted, and upright to fill the post.
Thus he may serve as a model for all directions
and eliminate demonic treachery.”
Huángdì Rénzōng asked:
“Who can be sent to take charge of Kāifēng Fǔ?”
The officials collectively reported:
“The Lóngtú Gé Dàizhì Bāo Zhěng,
courtesy name Xīrén,
is a native of Héféi in Lúzhōu.
He is a man of uprightness and impartiality,
who does not smile lightly.
If anyone sees him smile,
it is like seeing the Huáng Hé run clear.
Only this man is fit to hold this office.”
Rénzōng granted the request
and ordered him summoned before the palace;
after the formal greetings were completed,
he was commanded to take office that very day.
Bāo Zhěng expressed his gratitude for the imperial favor and departed.
The attendants of Kāifēng Fǔ welcomed him to the prefecture,
where the inevitable handover of tallies and seals took place,
and he ascended the hall that same day.
He issued official documents to Dōngjīng
and its subordinate prefectures and counties,
ordering the common people to form a jiǎ for every five households,
and a bǎo for every five-by-five, or twenty-five, households.
No idle or shiftless persons were permitted to be lodged in homes.
If there were people from elsewhere,
it was necessary to inquire about their place of origin and background.
In all the various inns,
it was not permitted to harbor solitary guests.
Dōngjīng has twenty-eight gates, large and small;
at each gate, placards were hung
to clearly notify everyone.
The common people all burned incense and bowed in reverence,
saying:
“What a fine Lóngtú Bāo Xiànggōng!”
He governed the soldiers and civilians of the Kāifēng Fǔ prefecture
so that none were not delighted.
Truly it was that:
Two rows of officials stand as if on spring ice;
The people of the three commanderies dwell within a precious mirror.
Demons and ghosts hide their forms, fearing the thorough illumination;
Imperial relatives draw back their hands to avoid his majestic air.
Travelers yielded the path,
people drummed their bellies and sang;
No one picked up things lost on the road,
and doors were not closed at night.
The whole of Dōngjīng was brought to solemn order;
this needs no further mention.
It is said that in the Back Hòushuǐ Lane,
there was a peddler
surnamed Rèn and named Qiān,
who was the eldest in his family.
Everyone called him Xiǎo Dà Yī Gē,
and he belonged to the "Five Cooked Goods" trade.
What is the "Five Cooked Goods" trade?
Those who sell noodles are called "Soup-cooked,"
those who sell sesame cakes are called "Fire-cooked,"
those who sell pickled fish are called "Pickle-cooked,"
those who sell steamed cakes are called "Steam-cooked,"
and those who sell fried snacks are called "Oil-cooked."
This Xiǎo Dà Yī Gē was a fine peddler
who would compete for dominance among his fellow vendors.
Having spent the day working at home,
his goods for sale were all loaded onto his display rack,
including steamed cakes,
sesame cakes,
steamed buns,
and stuffed cakes, all properly arranged.
Carrying his shoulder pole and baskets, Xiǎo Dà Yī Gē
went out to the crossroads of Mǎxíng Street and set down his burden.
He set up his stall,
greeted his fellow peddlers,
and only after taking a three-legged stool from behind the rack did he finally sit down.
Suddenly, a loud jingling sound was heard,
and a person came running straight to the rack,
but he was not there to buy sesame cakes.
Looking at what made that jingling sound,
the object was called a "Suísù Diànjiā,"
also known as a "Fǎhuán,"
which was shaken as a trademark sign by a Jiěyàn Master.
Shaking the dharma ring, the master
walked to Rèn Qiān’s rack,
looked at Rèn Qiān, and said:
"May wealth be invited,
may profits come,
may harmony arrive,
give me some money."
Rèn Qiān could not help but laugh.
When he looked at the Jiěyàn Master,
he was short of stature
and lame in one leg,
with one step high
and one step low.
His turban lacked a forehead band
and was torn at the top,
revealing hair
that looked like tangled grass.
He wore a tattered cloth shirt with a cape collar
and old cloth trousers,
looking like a lion.
On his feet were tattered leggings and hemp shoes with broken loops,
and a black sash without tassels was tied around his waist.
Rèn Qiān said:
"Be careful, Master Yàn,
watch the ground,
and do not step on a mouse's tail.
Coming to perform exorcisms around the hour of Sì,
you really don't know the time of day."
The lame master said:
"I also said I came out too early,
and have only begged three copper coins."
Rèn Qiān asked:
"Why didn't you come out later?"
The lame master replied:
"Brother, do not be offended!
My mother and I live in a broken kiln,
and even now we have had no breakfast.
Just give me a single coin,
so I can gather enough to buy some rice
for us to cook porridge and satisfy our hunger."
Seeing that he spoke so miserably, Rèn Qiān
wanted to give him a coin.
He felt around his waist
but had not brought any money out with him.
Looking at the lame master, he said:
"Even if I had money, I wouldn't grudge you this one coin,
but today I haven't made my first sale yet."
Seeing him say he had no money, the lame master
then asked:
"Brother!
How much are the steamed cakes?"
Rèn Qiān said:
"Large steamed cakes are two coins each,
and small ones are one coin each."
The lame master then took three copper coins from his bosom and spread them on the tray,
saying:
"Brother!
Sell me a steamed cake for my mother to eat!"
Rèn Qiān took two coins
and returned one coin to the lame master,
saying:
"I will treat this as my first sale
and give you this one coin as alms."
Having received the coin, the lame master
hid it in his bosom.
Rèn Qiān went to the steamer basket,
took out one large and one small cake,
and handed them to the lame master.
The lame master reached out to receive them,
but Rèn Qiān saw that his hands were filthy and pitch black,
and thought:
"I wonder how many days it's been since he washed them?"
The lame master took the steamed cakes in his hands,
looked at them,
and pinched them.
Looking at Rèn Qiān, he said:
"Brother!
My mother is eighty years old,
how can she eat such hard cakes?
Exchange them for a steamed bun for me."
Rèn Qiān said:
"You've made them filthy;
if others see them, they certainly won't want them."
He placed them in the tray in front
and went back to the steamer basket to grab a bun for him.
The lame master took it in his hand,
pinched it again,
and asked Rèn Qiān:
"Brother!
What is inside?"
Rèn Qiān said:
"A bundle of lean meat is inside."
The lame master said:
"Brother!
My mother follows a lifelong vegetarian diet,
how can she eat this?
Exchange it for a bean-paste bun for me."
Rèn Qiān thought:
"I haven't even made my first sale,
and I run into this fellow."
He was about to refuse the exchange,
but saw many people bustling about the rack.
He had no choice but to swallow his anger
and exchanged it for a bean-paste bun for him.
The lame master pressed it in his hand and pinched it again, saying:
"How can this fill her stomach?
Just exchange it back for the steamed cakes."
Seeing this, Rèn Qiān became exasperated:
"No wonder you are left to suffer hunger!
I only made two coins from you,
yet three of my goods are ruined.
I won't exchange them this time."
The lame master said:
"Brother!
Do not be exasperated!
How can two steamed cakes satisfy both my mother and me?
It would be better to just buy rice and cook porridge."
He reached for the copper coins on the rack,
blew a puff of air toward the rack, and walked away.
Rèn Qiān said:
"How intolerable this fellow is,
he ruined three of my goods.
Where do you think you're going?"
He then moved to strike the lame master.
Suddenly he stopped in his tracks,
thinking:
"With a person of this appearance,
how many of my fists or kicks could he take?
If there were some mishap,
I would end up in a homicide lawsuit;
it's better to just let him go."
He turned back
and fixed his gaze on the rack to look,
and Rèn Qiān could only cry out in bitterness.
A rack full of steamed buns and steamed cakes
had all turned black like charcoal.
There is a poem to testify:
Steamed cakes and buns were exchanged at will,
made so filthy they were unpleasant to see.
Even a country man would loathe them,
only a blind man would buy them.
Rèn Qiān said in a great rage:
"This fellow has tormented me for half the day,
and ruined a whole rack of goods.
My business for the day is over,
I must fight him for his life!"
He instructed the other peddlers
to watch the rack,
and with rolled-up sleeves and brisk strides,
he chased after the lame master.
The temperament of a young man—
he chased for half a day without seeing him,
and was just about to return,
when he only heard a *sī-láng-láng* sound ahead.
Rèn Qiān said,
"Could it be that fellow?"
Looking straight ahead to chase and see,
he was gone again.
Going back and forth,
he chased all the way to the gate tower of Ānshàng.
He saw a group of people gathered in front of a meat stall looking at something.
Rèn Qiān said,
"This is the house of my acquaintance Zhāng Tú;
I wonder what is happening
for there to be so many people?"
He stopped his feet
and peered into the crowd.
He saw only a Pópó fallen on the ground.
A young man was supporting her,
constantly calling out, "Niáng!"
After he had called for half a shíchen, she woke up,
but the Pópó kept her eyes tightly shut and refused to open them.
The young man said,
"Niáng!
Relax a bit
and open your eyes!"
The Pópó said,
"Quickly, help me back home."
The young man said,
"Open your eyes!"
The Pópó said,
"I am afraid;
I cannot open them!"
The young man helped the Pópó and left.
Rèn Qiān said,
"I wonder why this Pópó fell here?"
Just then, Zhāng Tú said,
"Everyone disperse!
There is nothing to see!"
Rèn Qiān recognized the man was surnamed Zhāng, named Qí,
the eldest in his family.
Rèn Qiān said,
"Yīláng!
It has been a long time!"
Zhāng Tú said,
"Rèn Dàgē,
where have you been?"
Rèn Qiān said,
"Just attending to some trivial matters."
Zhāng Tú said,
"Rèn Dàgē, come inside,
I will tell you."
Rèn Qiān went inside and asked Zhāng Tú,
"Why was it so lively at your door?"
Zhāng Tú said,
"I have never seen such a strange and bizarre thing.
Just now, a lame Daoist priest,
his head wrapped in a tattered turban,
wearing a torn cloth shirt,
held a ritual ring in his hand.
He was saying,
'May wealth come,
may profits come,
may harmony come,
give me money.'
I said to the Quéshī,
'You really do not know the time;
I suppose your house has no skylight?'
When the Quéshī heard this,
he said,
'If there is no money, then so be it,
but do not make fun of me.'
Unexpectedly, he looked at the pig's head hanging on the counter,
touched it,
and muttered something with his mouth moving.
Shaking his ritual ring, he left.
I did not take it seriously.
Zhái Èrláng, the flower-maker from the side courtyard,
had ordered this pig's head
and sent his Niáng to fetch it.
I took down the pig's head to give to her.
This pig's head twitched its brows and blinked its eyes,
then opened its mouth and bit the Pópó,
scaring her to death on the ground.
I hurriedly told the xiǎo bóshì to call her son,
thinking he could save her life.
If anything goes wrong,
I would have to face a lawsuit.
When her son picked up the pig's head to look,
there was no movement at all.
Zhái Èrláng said,
'The old lady was just seeing things;
how could a dead pig's head twitch its brows and blink its eyes?'
He just helped his Niáng away."
Rèn Qiān heard this
and told Zhāng Tú about the incident where the Quéshī bought steamed buns earlier,
from start to finish.
Zhāng Tú said,
"Strange!
Strange!"
Before he had finished speaking,
he only heard the sound of the ritual ring.
Rèn Qiān said,
"That fellow is still up ahead!"
Zhāng Tú said,
"Spoiling your steamed buns is no big deal
and not very serious,
but he nearly made me pay with my life for that Pópó.
No need for you to do anything;
wait for me to catch that fellow and give him a good beating."
Rèn Qiān said,
"I will go with you to chase that fellow."
The two of them strode out to chase the Quéshī,
but after chasing for half a day, they did not see him.
Zhāng Tú looked at Rèn Qiān and said,
"What should we do?
If we had caught him,
there would certainly be no end to it.
Now that we cannot catch up to him,
let us go back."
Just as they were about to return,
they heard the ritual ring sound again.
They chased for another five or six lǐ,
having traveled more than ten lǐ out of the Ānshàng Gate.
They heard the ritual ring sound,
but simply could not catch him.
The two were about to return
when they saw at the end of the market street, in front of a vegetarian noodle shop,
a man holding a staff and beating a fellow.
Zhāng Tú recognized it was Wú Sānláng, who sells vegetarian noodles,
and stopped his hand,
saying,
"A whole shop of people wanted noodles to eat before their journey;
I told him to quickly light the fire,
but it would not light this way,
nor would it light that way.
For half a day the pot could not get hot,
and everyone left.
If business is done like this,
it would be better to tear down the shop storefront!
I will certainly make his skin split and his flesh flare!"
Zhāng Tú said,
"For my sake, let it be!"
Wú Sānláng said,
"Are you not out for a stroll on your day off today?"
Zhāng Tú then told him about the Quéshī earlier,
relating everything once through.
After Wú Sānláng finished listening,
he was stunned
and said,
"In that case, I have beaten him wrongly.
You two listen to me;
I was at the counter
when I saw a Quéshī shaking a ritual ring
come to my door and shout,
'May wealth come,
may profits come,
may harmony come,
give me money.'
My hands were busy,
so I said,
'You also do not know the time,
coming out at midday to annoy people.
Are you afraid ghosts will catch you if you come out later?
I have no small change,
so skip this turn for now.'
I only saw him blow a breath of air toward my pot
and then leave.
As soon as he turned his back,
I told the xiǎo bóshì to light the fire,
but how could he light it?
It has been the time for two meals,
and it just will not light.
Many people who wanted noodles
could not wait and all dispersed.
That is why I beat him.
If you had not told me,
how would I have known?
How detestable that this fellow is so malicious,
ruining my business for the day."
While they were speaking,
they only heard the ritual ring sound.
Wú Sānláng looked out
and saw that fellow shaking it all along the way ahead.
Wú Sānláng,
Rèn Qiān,
and Zhāng Tú, the three of them together said,
"Let us go chase that fellow!"
The Quéshī saw the three people chasing him
and fled hurriedly.
Because the three of them came to chase the Quéshī,
it results in:
Arriving at a quiet Buddhist temple
and seeing a strange and bizarre thing.
Truly:
Never heard of since the creation of heaven and earth,
and rarely seen from ancient times to the present.
After all, where did the three chase the Quéshī to,
and what did they see?
Listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
The steamed buns are all black but not burnt by fire;
sticking eyes into a pig's head shows great skill.
Just because they wanted to capture Quě Shī,
it led the three men to encounter a female demon.
It is said that at that moment, Quě Shī saw the three men—Rèn, Wú, and Zhāng—coming in pursuit,
and he left in a great hurry.
When they chased quickly, he walked quickly;
when they chased slowly, he walked slowly;
and when they did not chase, he did not walk.
The three of them simply could not catch up.
Zhāng Tú said:
"Let us see where he ends up,
then it will be no trouble to deal with him."
The three left Dōngjīng
and traveled ten or twenty li,
arriving at a place
called Jiāomò.
That road was truly desolate.
There was a temple
called Mòpō Sì.
They saw Quě Shī go straight into Mòpō Sì.
Zhāng Tú laughed and said:
"Excellent!
He has entered a dead end.
Let us see where he can go now.
We shall now pursue him from three directions!"
Rèn Qiān said:
"Well said!
Wú Sānláng, pursue from the middle;
Zhāng Tú, enter and pursue from the left corridor;
and Rèn Qiān shall enter and pursue from the right corridor."
When Quě Shī saw the three men pursuing from three directions,
he dashed straight onto the Buddha hall,
climbed onto the offering table,
stepped on the Buddha’s hand,
climbed onto the Buddha’s shoulder,
and held the Buddha’s head with both hands.
The three reached the Buddha hall together
and looked at Quě Shī, saying:
"Come down properly.
If you do not come down,
we will climb onto the Buddha ourselves
and drag you down!"
Quě Shī said:
"How bitter!
Buddha, save me!"
Then Quě Shī gave the Buddha’s head a shove,
and the Buddha’s head came rolling down with a rumble.
Quě Shī then quickly slipped his body into the Buddha’s belly.
Zhāng Tú said:
"Is this not strange?
There is no path inside the Buddha’s belly;
why did you crawl in there?
This surely cannot be the end of it!"
Zhāng Tú climbed onto the offering table,
stepped on the Buddha’s hand,
climbed onto the Buddha’s shoulder,
and gripped the Buddha’s neck cavity with both hands to take a look.
The inside was pitch black.
Suddenly, a hand reached out from the Buddha’s neck cavity
and grabbed Zhāng Tú by the hair.
Zhāng Tú fell headlong into the Buddha’s belly.
Wú Sānláng
and Rèn Qiān cried out:
"How bitter!"
Not knowing the situation,
the two of them deliberated:
"What should we do?"
Rèn Qiān said:
"It is no matter.
I will go up and have a look
so we can know what happened."
Wú Sānláng said:
"Eldest Brother,
be more careful
so that you do not fall in as well."
Rèn Qiān said:
"I am not like Zhāng Yīláng."
He immediately climbed onto the offering table,
stepped on the Buddha’s hand,
perched on the Buddha’s shoulder,
and gripped the Buddha’s neck cavity to look inside.
It was pitch black.
He called out:
"Zhāng Yīláng,
where are you?"
There was no answer when he called,
but a hand reached out
and grabbed him.
Rèn Qiān was startled
and cried out repeatedly:
"Dear father!
Living father!
Have mercy and spare me;
I will never dare to chase you again.
I specifically came to ask you
if you want steamed buns,
or mantou,
or sweet bean filling;
I will bring them for you to eat."
Then Rèn Qiān, with his head down
and feet up,
tumbled headfirst into the Buddha’s belly.
Wú Sānláng saw this
and said:
"How bitter!
How bitter!
Both of them have fallen into the Buddha’s belly;
how can I return home alone?
I want to go up and take a look,
but I am afraid I will fall in too.
I want to go back myself,
but how can I leave their two lives like this?
I must go up."
Looking at the offering table,
his hands and feet felt numb;
he was trembling all over
and did not dare go up.
He pondered for a long while
and, having no choice,
finally stepped on the Buddha’s hand
and gripped the Buddha’s neck cavity.
He wanted to take a look
but feared falling in.
He could neither advance
nor retreat.
Wú Sānláng then thought to himself:
"How foolish of me.
I only need to find something hard
to break open the Buddha’s belly,
and then I can rescue the two of them."
Just as he was about to get down from the table,
someone grabbed him around the waist from behind.
With a single shove,
Wú Sānláng was also thrown down into the Buddha’s belly.
One of his feet stepped on Rèn Qiān’s head,
and Rèn Qiān cried out:
"You stepped on me!"
Wú Sānláng asked:
"Who are you?"
Rèn Qiān replied:
"I am Rèn Qiān."
Wú Sānláng asked:
"Where is Zhāng Yīláng?"
Then Zhāng Qí replied:
"I am here."
Rèn Qiān said:
"Wú Sānláng!
How did you end up here?"
Wú Sānláng said:
"I went up to the Buddha’s neck cavity to look for you,
but it seemed someone shoved me into the Buddha’s belly."
Rèn Qiān said:
"It also felt to me like someone reached out and grabbed me by the hair to bring me in."
Zhāng Tú said:
"It was the same for me.
The one who grabbed us
must be Quě Shī;
he has played with us enough.
Groping all around,
if we find him,
let us not beat him yet;
just have him lead the three of us out of the Buddha’s belly.
If he refuses to lead us out,
then we must beat him."
At that time,
the three men groped all around
but could not find Quě Shī.
Rèn Qiān said:
"It turns out the inside of the Buddha’s belly is so spacious;
let us take it step by step."
Zhāng Tú said:
"It is dark;
how can we walk?"
Rèn Qiān said:
"I will support you as we walk."
Wú Sānláng said:
"I will also follow you."
They walked gradually for about half a li,
and Zhāng Tú said:
"Is this not strange?
Inside the hall of Mòpō Sì,
how large could it possibly be?
Yet we have walked so far inside the Buddha’s belly."
While they were speaking,
they suddenly saw a point of brightness ahead.
Wú Sānláng [said]:
"So there is actually a path here!"
Walking a few more steps and looking,
they saw a stone gate unevenly set,
and from the gap in the gate shot out a beam of light.
Zhāng Tú went forward,
pushed open the stone gate with his hands,
focused his eyes and took a look,
crying out:
"Wonderful!
Here the mountains are clear and the waters are green,
the trees are dense and the flowers are flourishing—
what a fine place!"
Wú Sānláng said:
"Who would have known there was such scenery inside the Buddha of Mòpō Sì!"
Rèn Qiān said:
"Yet there are no signs of human habitation;
where can we return to?"
Zhāng Tú said:
"No matter;
since there is a path,
there must be human habitation.
Let us just keep going."
After walking another two or three lǐ,
they saw a manor house.
They saw:
famous flowers shining brightly,
tender bamboo lush and green.
The cold stream water reflected people clearly,
and wafts of spring breeze warmed the face.
The thatched study was silent;
swallows carrying mud flitted through the wind.
The courtyards were sparse;
chattering orioles darted through the sunlight.
A yellow-haired child riding a calf
played a short flute without melody;
a dark-skinned farmer carrying a hoe
sang a long song with rhythm.
Scrawny, thin dogs
barked wildly at travelers from behind the bamboo fence;
mountain birds in pairs,
hidden in ancient trees, urged the travelers onward with their calls.
Zhāng Tú said:
"Let me call out to this manor."
At that moment,
Zhāng Tú came and called out:
"We are passing travelers
who have lost our way!"
He only heard a response from inside:
"Coming!
Coming!"
Where the door opened,
an old woman walked out.
The three greeted the old woman.
The old woman returned the greeting
and asked:
"Where do you three come from?"
Zhāng Tú said:
"The three of us are from the city,
and have lost our way to this place.
Firstly, we ask for directions,
and secondly, we ask if there is any food in the manor we might buy?"
The old woman said:
"I am of a village household;
how could I have food for sale?
If passing travelers come here,
what is the harm in having a meal?
Follow me inside."
The three followed the old woman directly to the thatched hall,
and sat down on wooden benches.
The old woman brought a table,
placed it before the three, and said:
"I see you are hungry;
I shall arrange food for you to eat.
If you can drink wine,
each have a bowl of wine first."
The three said:
"We are so grateful to the Mistress of the Manor!"
The old woman went inside,
and after a short while,
brought out a pot of wine
and set out three bowls.
Fragrantly, she brought out a plate of venison
and poured three bowls of wine.
The old woman said:
"It is not as good as the wine in your city;
the wine here is home-brewed,
it is only fit to be used as tea!"
Because the three were hungry and thirsty from chasing the Quéshī
and had not eaten any snacks,
smelling the fragrance of the meat,
the three said:
"Delicious!"
Each person drank two bowls of wine.
The old woman brought out the rice,
and all three ate their fill.
The three said:
"Our thanks to the Mistress of the Manor;
we shall pay as is customary."
The old woman said:
"For a little wine and rice,
how could I want money!"
Meanwhile, she tidied the utensils and went inside.
Just as the three were about to thank the old woman and take their leave,
seeking her guidance to the way out,
they saw a person walk in through the manor gate.
When the three looked,
it was no one else,
but indeed Qué Shī.
Zhāng Tú said:
"We have been annoyed by you scoundrel for half the day,
yet here you are."
The three hurried down to the thatched hall,
like hawks pouncing on swallows and sparrows,
and seized Qué Shī.
Just as they were about to beat him,
they saw Qué Shī cry out:
"Niángniáng, save me!"
The old woman came out from the manor and called out:
"The three of you, do not be rude;
this is my son.
If there is a matter, show some regard for my face!"
She came down to the thatched hall and told the three to let go,
then invited the three to sit in the thatched hall.
The old woman said:
"Just now I kindly prepared wine and food to treat you;
why do you want to beat my child upon seeing him?
You are quite unreasonable!"
Zhāng Tú said:
"Forgive us!
The manor mistress prepared wine to treat us,
and we truly did not know this Qué Shī was the mistress's child;
however, he is not reasonable.
If not for the mistress's sake,
we would have beaten him to a pulp."
The old woman said:
"What did my child do
that you want to beat him?"
Zhāng Tú,
Rèn Qiān,
and Wú Sānláng
all told the old woman what had happened earlier that morning.
The old woman said:
"According to what the three gentlemen say,
it is all my son's fault.
Wait until I have him apologize to the three of you."
Qué Shī stepped forward,
and the old woman said:
"Three gentlemen!
Please, for my sake,
pardon him this once!"
The three said:
"We tell the old woman,
we no longer wish to argue with your son;
just have him escort us out and that will be all."
The old woman said:
"Please sit for a moment.
I think the three of you are all destined people
to have arrived here.
Since you have arrived here,
it wouldn't do to just go back like that.
I have magic arts,
and I will have each of you learn one
to take with you and use for a lifetime."
The old woman looked at Qué Shī and said:
"If only you hadn't gone out!
Going out only causes trouble.
Since you've caused the three gentlemen to come here,
what magic arts do you have?
Show them to the three of them."
The old woman looked at the three and said:
"My child has learned some theatrical arts;
he will perform them for the three of you."
The three said:
"We thank the old woman!"
Qué Shī said:
"I request Niángniáng's command!"
He took out a small gourd from his waist,
muttered incantations in his mouth,
and shouted out:
"Swiftly!"
From the mouth of the gourd,
a stream of water poured out,
and in an instant, waves flooded the ground.
Everyone said:
"Excellent!"
Qué Shī said:
"I shall gather it back for my brothers to see."
Gradually, the water was gathered back into the gourd.
Again, he muttered incantations in his mouth,
and shouted out:
"Swiftly!"
He released a blast of fire,
and in an instant, fierce flames scorched the heavens.
Everyone said again:
"Excellent!"
Qué Shī then gradually gathered the fire back into the gourd.
Zhāng Tú said:
"We tell Qué Shī!
Are you willing to give me this gourd?"
The old woman said:
"My son!
Give this Fire and Water Gourd
to this elder brother."
Qué Shī did not dare defy the old woman's wish,
so he gave the Fire and Water Gourd to Zhāng Tú.
Zhāng Tú thanked him.
Qué Shī said:
"I have another theatrical art for you to watch."
He took out a sheet of paper,
cut out a horse,
placed it on the ground,
and shouted out:
"Swiftly!"
That paper horse stood up,
wagged its tail,
shook its head,
and transformed into a white horse as pure as snow-white silk.
There is a "Xī Jiāng Yuè"
to witness:
Eyes large, head held high, back steady,
A majestic eight-foot frame.
Its coat like a pile of silver,
An incomparable Zhào Yè Yù Shī.
Once competed among the cloud-patterned ranks,
Neighing whenever it heard Bó Lè,
Climbing mountains and crossing ridges as if flying,
Truly travelling a thousand lǐ in a day.
Qué Shī mounted that horse
and shouted out once!
It soared gracefully into the air.
After a long time,
the horse gradually descended to the ground.
Qué Shī jumped down from the horse,
and it was still just a paper horse.
Qué Shī said:
"Which gentleman wants it?"
Wú Sānláng said:
"I want to learn that paper horse magic."
Qué Shī then gave the paper horse to Wú Sānláng.
Wú Sānláng thanked him.
The old woman looked at Qué Shī and said:
"Two gentlemen have magic arts now.
What about this gentleman?"
Qué Shī said:
"By Niángniáng's command,
I would not dare disobey,
but I fear my magical power is small and weak."
While they were speaking,
they saw a woman walk out.
That woman was no one else,
but indeed Hú Yǒng'ér.
Yǒng'ér greeted everyone with a blessing.
Turning to the old woman, she said:
"I tell Niángniáng!
This humble woman will teach this gentleman a magic art,
by Niángniáng's command."
The old woman said:
"I would be glad to see your divine work!"
Hú Yǒng'ér went in and brought out a wooden bench,
placed it on the ground in front of the thatched hall.
Yǒng'ér straddled the bench,
muttered incantations in her mouth,
and shouted out:
"Swiftly!"
They saw the bench transform into a slant-eyed, white-browed tiger.
What was the appearance of this tiger?
There is a "Xī Jiāng Yuè"
to witness:
Neck short, body round, ears small,
Slant-eyed, white-browed, with majestic power.
Paws and hooves lightly spreading as if flying,
Leaping across ravines as if on level ground.
Its shearing tail can startle the deer,
Its roar frightens the foxes to death.
Though Biàn Zhuāng was brave, how could he act?
Even Zǐlù would find it hard to resist.
Hú Yǒng'ér rode the tiger,
and shouted, "Arise!"
The tiger then soared into the air.
She shouted, "Halt!"
The tiger gradually descended to the ground.
She shouted, "Swiftly!"
One could see that the tiger was still just a bench.
Pópó said:
"Rèn Dàláng!
Do you see?"
Rèn Qiān said:
"I report to Pópó!
I have seen it."
Pópó said:
"My daughter can pass this magic spell to Rèn Dàláng."
Hú Yǒng'ér passed the spell to Rèn Qiān,
and Rèn Qiān thanked her.
Pópó said:
"The three of you, perform it once each."
All three practiced until they were proficient.
Pópó said:
"Now that the three of you have magic,
I have a matter to speak to you about.
I wonder if the three of you are willing to follow it?"
Zhāng Tú said:
"I report to Pópó!
We do not know what you want the three of us to follow,
but there is no harm in telling us."
Pópó said, "You must remember it firmly;
should something happen in Bèizhōu one day,
you must come forward to help
and share in wealth and honor."
Zhāng Tú said:
"Since we have received the Niángniáng's instructions,
we will help in Bèizhōu one day.
Now we beg for a path back home."
Pópó said:
"I will have the child send you into the city."
Quéshī said:
"I receive the dharma decree."
The three bowed and thanked Pópó.
Pópó looked at the three and said:
"Today I have the child temporarily send you three Dàláng back.
Tomorrow, you may all come to the Mòpō Temple to meet."
The three bid farewell to Pópó
and Yǒng'ér.
At that time, Quéshī led the way and they walked for about half a li,
when they saw a high mountain.
Quéshī went up the mountain with the three of them.
Quéshī said:
"Dàláng,
can you see the capital?"
Zhāng Tú,
Wú Sānláng,
and Rèn Qiān looked,
and they saw the capital within a hair's breadth.
While the three were looking,
Quéshī suddenly gave them a push,
and they all fell down.
Startled and suddenly waking,
they were in the Buddhist hall.
While Zhāng Tú was still doubting,
he saw Wú Sānláng
and Rèn Qiān also wake up.
Zhāng Tú asked:
"What did you two see?"
Wú Sānláng said, "Quéshī taught us magic.
Is your little gourd there or not?"
Zhāng Tú felt for it,
and it was in his bosom.
Wú Sānláng said:
"My paper horse is also here."
Rèn Qiān said:
"What I learned was the spell to transform into a tiger."
Zhāng Tú said:
"It was as if we were dreaming, yet not dreaming.
That Quéshī, Pópó, and Hú Yǒng'ér are all likely supernatural beings.
They kept saying that one day we should come to Bèizhōu to help;
I wonder what the reason is?"
While the three were at a loss,
Quéshī walked out from behind the Buddhist hall and said:
"Go back for now,
remember the magic arts clearly,
and come to the temple tomorrow to meet."
At that time, the three bid farewell to Quéshī
and went to their respective homes.
There is a poem to testify:
The carefree butterfly truly becomes an illusion,
The wealth and honor of Nánkē are also accidental.
How can it compare to receiving the dharma together in a dream,
Changing at will like an immortal?
There was no more talk that day.
The next day, after eating breakfast,
the three came to Mòpō Temple.
They went into the Buddhist hall to look;
the Buddha's head was serene and motionless.
The three went to the back hall to find Pópó and Quéshī,
but there was no trace of them.
Zhāng Tú said:
"Let us go back!"
While they were speaking,
they heard someone call out:
"The three of you must not lose heart;
I have been waiting here for you for a long time!"
When the three turned to look,
walking out from behind the Buddhist hall
was exactly the Pópó from yesterday.
When the three saw her,
they all bowed and saluted.
Pópó said:
"Why did you three Dàláng arrive so late?
The magic spells passed to you yesterday—
perform them for me once
so they may be used in the future."
Zhāng Tú said:
"Mine is the Gourd of Water and Fire Harmonies."
He muttered an incantation,
and shouted:
"Swiftly!"
A stream of water poured out from the mouth of the gourd.
He shouted, "Withdraw!"
The water gradually withdrew into the gourd.
He shouted again:
"Swiftly!"
A flash of fire
rushed out from the mouth of the gourd.
He shouted again, "Withdraw!"
The fire gradually withdrew into the gourd.
Zhāng Tú said happily:
"I've mastered it!"
Wú Sānláng took out the paper horse from his bosom,
placed it on the ground,
muttered an incantation,
and shouted:
"Swiftly!"
It transformed into a white horse,
its four hooves trotting clatter-clatter.
Wú Sānláng rode it for a while,
then jumped off the horse,
and it was a paper horse once again.
Rèn Qiān went to the back hall and brought out a bench, sat on it,
muttered an incantation,
and shouted:
"Swiftly!"
The bench transformed into a tiger
that roared and ran.
Rèn Qiān shouted, "Halt!"
The tiger gradually retracted
and was a bench once more.
While the three were showing off their magic,
they suddenly heard someone shout:
"In this peaceful world
and vast universe,
you are here performing demonic arts.
Currently, the government has posted notices
to capture sorcerers.
If the authorities find out,
I will surely be implicated."
When the crowd heard this,
they hurriedly turned their heads to look;
it was a monk,
wearing a fiery red cassock,
with gold rings in his ears.
The monk said:
"This poor monk has been watching you from under the corridor for a long time!"
Pópó said:
"Master, please forgive us;
I was here teaching them some minor magic."
The monk said:
"If they are taught well,
then the effort is not in vain.
If they are taught poorly,
it is a waste of mental energy.
Perform for this poor monk so I may see."
Pópó again told the three to perform their magic,
and the three each did so.
Pópó said:
"Master!
How are my three disciples?"
The monk laughed and said:
"As this poor monk sees it,
none of them are good."
Pópó said irritably:
"You monk,
do you dare claim to have world-shaking skills?
What magic do you know?
Perform it for us to see."
Then the monk stretched out a hand,
opened his five fingers,
and from his fingers emitted five rays of golden light.
Within the golden light appeared five Buddhas.
When Rèn,
Zhāng,
and Wú saw this,
they bowed.
In the midst of the three formal bows,
they suddenly heard someone calling out:
“This temple is a temple built by imperial decree.
Why are you here practicing the heterodox arts of Jīngāng Chán?”
The Monk immediately withdrew the golden light.
When everyone looked,
it was a Dàoshì,
riding a fierce beast,
coming toward the hall.
Seeing Pópó, he jumped down from the beast,
pressed his fists together and bowed his head, saying:
“This disciple has come specifically to pay his respects!”
Pópó said:
“Sir, please be seated for a moment!”
The sir and the Monk bowed to each other.
Rèn,
Wú,
and Zhāng also came to bow to the sir.
The sir asked:
“Do these three young masters all possess magical arts now?”
Pópó said:
“They do!”
The sir said:
“This poor Taoist has also guided a disciple here.”
Pópó said:
“Where is he?”
They saw the sir look at the fierce beast and say:
“You may withdraw your divine power!”
That fierce beast shook its head,
swayed its body,
and the beast disappeared.
Standing up,
it was actually a person.
Everyone was greatly surprised.
When Pópó looked,
it was none other than
the guest Bǔ Jí.
Bǔ Jí greeted Pópó with a bow.
Pópó said:
“Bǔ Jí!
Why have you come here?”
Bǔ Jí said:
“I report to Gūgū!
If the teacher Master Zhāng had not saved my life,
I would have nearly missed seeing Gūgū again.”
Pópó asked the sir:
“How did you save him?”
The sir said:
“This poor Taoist was in a forest thirty lǐ outside of Zhèngzhōu,
and heard someone calling, ‘Shèng Gūgū, save me!’
This poor Taoist thought that it was Pópó’s name,
so why was someone calling it?
I rushed in to look,
and saw Bǔ Jí hanging from a tree,
about to be murdered.
This poor Taoist asked the reason,
and Bǔ Jí told me the whole story.
Therefore, I applied a small art to save him from great calamity.”
Pópó said:
“So it was like that.
In that case,
has the sir also taught him magical arts?”
Bǔ Jí said:
“I have them!”
Pópó said:
“Have you all seen my magical arts?”
The Monk and the Dàoshì said:
“We wish to observe your holy work.”
Pópó was seen taking a golden hairpin from her head.
She shouted:
“Swiftly!”
It turned into a precious sword.
She made a stroke across her chest,
set down the sword,
and with both hands, she struck the skin of her torso,
slapping it open.
When everyone stepped forward to look,
they saw:
Golden nails on vermilion doors,
green tiles filling the eaves.
Intertwined emerald cypresses stood at the gate,
and massive green pines surrounded the hall;
immortal children beat drums,
and a flock of white cranes listened to the sutras;
jade maidens rang bells,
and several green monkeys decocted medicine;
it was no different from the fairyland of Pénglái,
just like the Zǐfǔ cavern-heaven.
After everyone saw this,
they said in amazement:
“Wonderful!”
While they were watching,
they suddenly heard a shout from outside the gate,
and a group of people walked in from outside.
Everyone was panicked and said:
“What should we do?”
The Monk said:
“Do not panic,
all of you follow me inside!”
In a screened place,
they hid their bodies.
Looking at that group, there were more than twenty people,
all wearing bows and crossbows at their waists,
and carrying hawks and falcons on their hands.
There were hunters,
official servants,
and private servants.
Seated on a horse was a high-ranking court official,
who came before the hall and dismounted.
He unfolded a folding chair and sat down,
with his attendants standing on either side.
It turned out this official was called Shànwáng Tàiwèi.
That day it was not his turn to go to the palace for duty,
so he had some leisure time
and brought his retinue out of the city for recreation.
He wandered straight to Mòpō Sì in the city,
kicked a ball with the others for a while,
and shot arrows for a while.
He rewarded everyone with wine and food,
drank a few cups himself in the hall,
and then mounted his horse.
The retinue followed him and left.
The group came back to the Buddha hall.
Pópó said:
“I wondered what was happening,
but it was just a group coming to have fun,
and they gave us a fright.
Zhāng Tú,
Rèn Qiān,
and Wú Sānláng said:
“We recognize him as a high official
living in Báitiě Bān,
called Shànwáng Tàiwèi,
who truly loves doing good,
feeds monks, and gives alms.”
Hearing this, the Monk
said:
“Watch me go and annoy him tomorrow.”
Everyone dispersed.
Just because the Monk wanted to annoy Shànwáng Tàiwèi,
about thirty sharp-eyed and quick-handed,
clever and capable observation commissioners from Kāifēng Fǔ
could not find a trace of him;
even when they saw him, they could not catch him.
He threw Dōngjīng Chéng into chaos
and caused a great stir in Biànzhōu Jùn.
Truly it is said that ordinary tradesmen
turned into practitioners of secret societies;
simple and elegant fools
became guests of Jīngāng Chán.
Precisely:
Only because they learned the demonic arts,
did they ruin their dignified six-foot bodies.
How exactly did the Monk go about annoying the man?
Please listen to the explanation in the next chapter.

The methods of Jiǔtiān Xuánnǚ are many,
and when one wishes to learn them, things become clear.
If one can abstain from greed, anger, and lust,
one will clearly be a minor immortal in the world.
It is said that Grand Marshal Shàn Wáng,
after wandering outside the city that day and returning to his manor,
had nothing to do for the rest of the day,
and everyone had dispersed.
The next day,
the official attendants,
private attendants,
and idle fellows all came to pay their respects.
The Grand Marshal said,
"Yesterday I strolled outside the city for the whole day,
so I will not go out today.
I will just arrange for some drinking in the back garden,
so tell everyone not to disperse,
but stay in the garden to watch some plays and amuse themselves."
It turned out that in this garden there was more than just one pavilion,
and there were many places for leisure.
Today they came to this pavilion
called the Sìwàng Tíng.
Everyone went into that pavilion to arrange the Grand Marshal's food and drink.
The Grand Marshal sat alone in the pavilion,
while from the official attendants
and private attendants above,
down to the followers and servants below,
each went to display their skills.
Right in the midst of the drinking,
a sound was suddenly heard upon a pillar of the Sìwàng Tíng pavilion.
From the Grand Marshal above
to his subordinates below,
everyone was startled.
When they looked,
they did not know who
had shot this pellet into the garden.
The Grand Marshal said,
"How insufferable this fellow is!
It was fortunate that it hit the pavilion pillar.
If it had hit me,
it would have been quite serious.
Tell everyone to see who shot it in."
When everyone looked outside the pavilion,
the garden was so vast
and the surrounding walls were so high,
how could it have been shot in?
While they were speaking,
they saw that pellet rolling on the pavilion floor,
bouncing several times with a tuō-tuō sound,
spinning round and round like a thread-spinning roller,
turning hundreds and thousands of times.
The Grand Marshal said,
"Isn't that strange!"
Then, with a single sound,
a tiny little person popped out.
At first he was small,
but as soon as the worldly wind blew on him,
he gradually grew larger
and transformed into a six-foot-tall monk,
wearing a fiery-red cassock
with golden rings hanging from his ears.
When the Grand Marshal and the others saw him,
they were all startled.
They saw the monk walk forward,
look at the Grand Marshal, and say,
"Greetings!"
When the Grand Marshal saw him,
though he said nothing,
he thought to himself,
"What a fine monk,
I must not be disrespectful to him."
He rose to return the gesture
and asked,
"Why has the holy monk come here?"
The monk said,
"This poor monk is a traveling monk from the Wénshū Yuàn
on Wǔtái Shān
in Yànmén County, Dàizhōu.
I have come specifically to pay my respects to the Grand Marshal
and to seek a vegetarian meal."
This Grand Marshal had always respected the Buddhist Dharma
and frequently paid homage to the Three Jewels.
Seeing such a monk come to seek a meal
in such a strange manner,
how could he not be pleased?
The Grand Marshal invited him to be seated.
The monk sat down across from the Grand Marshal
and said,
"I have disturbed the Grand Marshal's banquet."
The Grand Marshal ordered the kitchen to prepare a vegetarian meal at once
and said to the monk,
"Would the master be willing to accompany me in drinking a few cups of wine first?"
The monk replied,
"Many thanks!"
In front of them were laid out all the vessels and delicacies,
all of which were golden cups and plates bestowed by the Emperor.
The monk said,
"If you intend to provide a meal,
how can such small cups make this poor monk happy?"
Hearing this, the Grand Marshal
immediately called for a large golden goblet
and placed it before the monk.
The Grand Marshal drank from a small cup,
while the monk used the large goblet.
The Grand Marshal kept pouring the wine,
and the monk did not refuse.
After drinking about thirty large golden goblets,
the Grand Marshal said joyfully,
"Were you not a holy monk,
how could you drink so much wine!"
The kitchen staff reported,
"The vegetarian food is ready."
The Grand Marshal said,
"Since the vegetarian food is ready,
please have your meal, master."
He ordered it to be brought in
and placed before the monk.
The Grand Marshal sat with him, eating a little in accompaniment.
When the monk saw the vegetarian food,
he picked it up and ate,
never putting down his bowl and chopsticks.
The Grand Marshal told his attendants to go in and bring more.
As for this monk,
when rice came,
when soup came,
or when wine came,
he consumed it all entirely,
making it impossible for the servers to keep up.
The subordinates were all stunned.
The Grand Marshal, seeing how much he could eat,
was also stunned
and said,
"This monk must surely be a holy monk;
after consuming all that wine and food,
I know not where it has all gone."
They saw him finally put down his bowl and chopsticks.
The subordinates said,
"Thank heavens,
there has finally come a day when he has finished eating."
The monk said,
"I am fully sated."
After the vegetarian meal utensils were cleared away,
tea was ordered and served.
After the tea,
the monk stood up and thanked the Tàiwèi.
The Tàiwèi said happily,
"Master!
There is no need to thank me for such a coarse meal.
May I ask where you are going after the meal?"
The monk said,
"I have received the decree of the Head Elder of Wǔtái Shān's Wénshū Yuàn,
instructing me to come and seek donations.
The mountain gate of Wénshū Yuàn has collapsed and is damaged;
it will take three thousand strings of cash to repair and rebuild it.
Today, I had the fortune of meeting the Tàiwèi and receiving a meal.
If the Tàiwèi could spare three thousand strings of cash
to complete this grand undertaking for the mountain gate,
I pray that the Tàiwèi's blessings be increased and his life prolonged,
and that he may plant wide fields of merit."
The Tàiwèi said,
"This is a small matter of merit.
I wonder when you, Master, will come to collect the donation slip?"
The monk said,
"It would be even better if no donation slip were needed;
it would be a great fortune for the monastery."
The Tàiwèi said,
"Master!
What if I give you gold and silver?"
The monk said,
"If you give gold and silver to me,
it will be inconvenient for buying materials.
It would be best to have three thousand strings of copper cash."
The Tàiwèi smiled to himself and said,
"Master!
You are here all alone;
wouldn't three thousand strings of copper cash require many people to carry them?"
The monk said,
"I tell the Tàiwèi,
I have my own way."
The Tàiwèi immediately called the steward to open the treasury,
and ordered the official attendants,
personal servants,
and guards to take turns moving the copper cash,
stacking it on the ground outside the pavilion.
Each stack was one hundred strings,
making thirty stacks in total.
The Tàiwèi said,
"Master!
Here are the three thousand strings of copper cash.
The journey is long,
and it will require many laborers and porterage fees;
how can it possibly reach Wǔtái Shān?"
The monk said,
"No matter!"
He stood up and descended from the pavilion,
thanking the Tàiwèi for his joyful donation:
"There is no need for the Tàiwèi to trouble himself;
I have my own laborers to carry it away."
From his sleeve, he took out a scroll of sutra.
The Tàiwèi said nothing aloud,
but thought to himself,
"Let us see what he does."
The monk said,
"The Buddha's law of the clergy is immense."
He then recited the sutra once to himself
and told the bystanders to step aside.
In the blink of an eye, the monk tossed the sutra scroll into the void,
and it turned into a golden bridge.
The monk gestured toward the air
and called out,
"Practitioners,
cooks,
and laborers of Wǔtái Shān!
I have collected three thousand strings of copper cash in alms from Tàiwèi Wáng of the Shàn family.
All of you come and carry it away!"
Before long,
on the bridge in the sky,
a crowd of practitioners, cooks,
and laborers came down in a bustling throng.
They all arrived below the Sìwàng Tíng
and took the three thousand strings of copper cash;
some hoisted it on their backs,
some carried it on poles,
and some moved it by hand.
Moving back and forth,
in an instant, it was all transported away.
The monk stepped forward and said,
"I thank the Tàiwèi for granting me a meal
and for joyfully donating three thousand strings of cash.
If you should come to Wǔtái Shān in the future,
I shall assemble the monks,
ring the bells and beat the drums,
and with banners and precious canopies,
welcome the Tàiwèi.
I am returning to Wǔtái Shān now."
The monk took his leave of the Tàiwèi
and also walked up onto the golden bridge.
Gradually he went further and further until he disappeared.
A gust of wind rose in the air,
and the golden bridge turned back into a sutra scroll
and was blown away into the sky by the wind.
The Tàiwèi was very delighted,
and ordered his attendants to burn incense and bow in worship,
saying,
"I have been providing meals for monks and giving alms for over fifty years,
and today I have finally met such a holy monk and Arhat."
At that time, everyone arrived
and congratulated the Tàiwèi.
A later poet wrote:
"Giving alms to the school of emptiness to plant fields of merit,
not begrudging three thousand at a single word.
How many hungry and cold people are there in Cháng'ān?
Why not distribute some of that life-saving money?"
From then on,
in the household of Tàiwèi Wáng of the Shàn family,
everyone praised the holy monk Dànzi Héshang.
The name of Dànzi Héshang
spread through the capital in an instant,
and no one knew of his old name spelled with the characters 'Dànzi.'
Nothing happened that day;
the next day was the scheduled date for official duty.
The Tàiwèi rose early and washed,
and with his hall attendants and followers,
he went directly to the palace and entered.
The Tàiwèi arrived a bit early that day,
and while passing the outer waiting pavilion for officials,
he met an official who bowed to him.
This official was none other than Bāo Dàizhì of Kāifēng Fǔ.
Since this Bāo Dàizhì had governed Kāifēng Fǔ,
all the people of that prefecture were delighted.
For they saw him as:
upright throughout his life,
wise and brilliant by nature.
Always harboring a heart of loyalty and filial piety,
and ever maintaining thoughts of compassion and benevolence.
Households increased,
fields were opened,
and the common people sang his praises throughout the streets;
lawsuits decreased,
thieves went into hiding,
and the elders' songs of praise filled the marketplaces.
People clung to his carriage and cut the stirrups to keep him,
his name marked in history to be spread for a thousand years;
inscriptions were carved on stone tablets,
his fame vibrating through the Yellow Hall to be passed down for eternity.
Indeed, his generous writings outshone Lǐ and Dù,
and his virtue and integrity surpassed Gōng and Huáng.
That day, while Bāo Dàizhì was waiting for the morning audience,
he saw the Tàiwèi and invited him to sit for a while.
The Tàiwèi was an upright man,
and the Dàizhì was a clean and honest official;
each had heard of the other's pure virtue.
Although the Tàiwèi was a high-ranking palace official,
he liked Bāo Dàizhì in his heart,
and Bāo Dàizhì also liked Tàiwèi Wáng.
The two sat down in the pavilion.
The Tàiwèi said,
"Whenever one lives in this world,
good and evil both have their retributions."
Bāo Dàizhì said,
"I, Bāo, also act according to my office.
While I, Bāo, have been at Kāifēng Fǔ,
I have judged many legal cases.
Those who commit offenses
must wait for judgment and punishment
before they can change their ways and turn to the good.
For instance, the Tàiwèi is usually fond of doing good;
I wonder what retribution you have experienced?"
Tàiwèi Wáng said,
"Setting other matters aside,
yesterday while I, Wáng, was enjoying myself at the pavilion in my back garden,
a pellet fell from the sky.
From within the pellet, a holy monk burst out.
He claimed to be the alms collector of Wǔtái Shān's Wénshū Yuàn
and asked me for a meal.
I provided him a meal,
and then he asked me for three thousand strings of copper cash in alms.
Without using a single person to carry it away,
he tossed a sutra scroll into the air,
and it transformed into a golden bridge.
He called down practitioners,
cooks,
and laborers from Wǔtái Shān,
and in no time at all,
they had moved it all away.
The monk also went up onto the golden bridge.
How could there not be Buddhas and Arhats in the mortal world!
I, Wáng, have spent my life providing meals for monks and making offerings to the Buddha,
and indeed I have had such a response."
Bāo Dàizhì said,
"Rare indeed, rare indeed."
Although he answered smoothly in this way,
he said nothing aloud
but thought to himself,
"This matter is strange again;
how could such a thing be possible in this world?"
Gradually the sky grew light,
and all the civil and military officials entered the palace.
After the audience ended,
the officials all departed.
Bāo Dàizhì returned to his office,
and without letting other public matters distract him,
he asked for the attendants on duty that day
to see who the arresting officers were.
Only one person below the steps bowed and offered a greeting;
it was the investigation official Wēn Diànzhí.
Bāo Dàizhì said:
"Early this morning while sitting in the waiting pavilion,
I heard Shànwáng Tàiwèi say
that yesterday he was drinking on a pavilion in his back garden.
A pellet was shot in from the outside,
and from the pellet popped a monk
who claimed to be a fundraising monk from Wénshū Yuàn on Wǔtái Shān.
He extorted three thousand strings of copper cash from him and left.
That Tàiwèi said he was a holy monk or an Arhat.
I think if he were indeed a holy monk or an Arhat,
what use would he have for money?
According to my insight,
he must be a demonic monk.
Currently, the Prefect of Zhèngzhōu has been killed by the sorcerers Zhāng Luán
and Bǔ Jí;
a notice has been issued for their arrest,
but they have yet to be captured.
How can the capital’s forbidden grounds
tolerate such a sorcerer?"
Pointing at Wēn Diànzhí, he said:
"You must catch this demonic monk immediately and bring him to the hall to see me."
Wēn Diànzhí could only agree;
having received the official command,
he left the office gate,
passed through Gānquán Fāng and went straight into the messengers' quarters,
where he sat in the hall.
On both sides stood the assembled officers.
Seeing Wēn Diànzhí with furrowed brows,
his face bearing a look of worry,
and his head bowed without making a sound,
one of the officers,
whom Wēn Diànzhí favored most at the time,
whose surname was Rǎn and given name was Guì,
also known as Rǎn Shìsù.
One of his eyes was usually closed,
yet the things in the world that others could not do,
he could do.
He had solved many difficult cases for Wēn Diànzhí,
and for this reason, Wēn Diànzhí liked him.
At that moment, Rǎn Guì stepped forward and said:
"I do not know what matter has occurred,
sir, to make you so troubled?"
Wēn Diànzhí said:
"Rǎn Dà!
Telling you will only make you troubled as well.
Just now the Tàiyǐn called me to the hall and said
that during the morning audience, Shànwáng Tàiwèi of the Bái Tiě rank said:
Yesterday, while drinking on a pavilion in his back garden,
he saw a pellet shot in from outside,
from which popped a monk.
He asked Shànwáng Tàiwèi for a donation of three thousand strings of copper cash.
Shànwáng Tàiwèi said he was a holy monk or an Arhat.
The Tàiyǐn said:
Since he is a holy monk or an Arhat,
why would he want money?
He must be a demonic monk.
He has given me a deadline of today to catch this monk.
I think since he has such great skills,
he must have a place to hide.
Having obtained three thousand strings of copper cash,
he must have gone to another prefecture or province to enjoy himself.
Where can I go to catch him?
Bāo Tàiyǐn is unlike other officials;
moreover, he is difficult to serve.
I could only accept the order and come out.
It is not as if the monk would come and turn himself in.
I have no way out,
and that is why I am troubled."
Rǎn Guì said:
"How is this matter difficult?
Now, give orders to the many officers
to each be diligent and take different routes
around the twenty-eight gates of the capital to catch him.
If we are too late,
I fear he will have scattered."
Wēn Diànzhí said:
"What you say makes sense;
you are older
and indeed have insight."
Looking at the officers, he said:
"You all go separately to handle this,
and each must be diligent."
The crowd agreed and left.
Wēn Diànzhí personally took Rǎn Guì
and two capable confidants,
and they too left the messengers' quarters.
Leaving Gānquán Fāng,
they headed toward Dōngjīng.
Wēn Diànzhí used a warm hat to cover his face,
and Rǎn Guì dressed as an attendant on duty.
His eye was no longer closed
as he watched the people coming and going.
If there was anyone slightly suspicious in tea houses or wine shops,
he would immediately investigate and question them.
Wēn Diànzhí said to Rǎn Guì:
"If he has plunged into the vast Eastern Ocean,
where can we find him?"
Rǎn Guì said:
"Guānchá, do not lose heart;
we shall walk until evening,
and then we will see."
The two walked to the front of Xiàngguó Sì,
where they saw a crowd of people gathered by the wall.
Rǎn Guì said:
"Guānchá, wait a moment
while I go take a look."
Standing on his tiptoes,
among the one or two hundred people,
he saw a man surrounded.
His head was wrapped in a headscarf,
and he wore a peony flower made of silk.
Behind his head were a pair of gold rings as large as basins.
He was wearing a half-jacket,
tied with an embroidered belly band,
and a pair of multi-eared hemp shoes,
revealing a body covered in brocade-like tattoos.
Behind him was inserted a silver spear,
with several small flags standing up,
and he had placed a pair of gold-lacquered bamboo cages.
He was an itinerant practitioner of magic,
drawing this crowd of people to watch him there.
It turns out this man was famous in the capital,
and was called Dù Qīshèng.
That Dù Qīshèng cupped his hands and said:
"I am a person of Dōngjīng.
This is a place where officials and travelers from various circuits, prefectures, and military districts come and go.
There are those who know Dù Qīshèng,
and there are those who do not.
Even if you do not know me by sight, you have heard my name.
Every year I go to offer respects at Dōngyuè,
competing with others,
and I always win the top prize."
Someone asked:
"Dù Qīshèng,
what skills do you have?"
He said:
"Two wheels of the sun and moon,
uniting heaven and earth.
Above the heavens,
and below the earth,
except for my master,
I have never encountered an opponent to challenge me in these arts."
He turned his head and called out:
"Shòushòu, my son,
come out!"
The young lad stripped off his upper garments,
his white flesh like carved jade.
The crowd cheered, saying:
"What a fine boy!"
Dù Qīshèng said:
"I have been throughout Dōngjīng
for many a year.
There are those who have seen me,
and those who have not.
This art of mine
is handed down from the founding master: burning fire and boiling oil,
tempering bowls in a hot pot;
it is called the Head-Reattaching Method.
I place my boy on the bench,
cut off his head with a knife,
cover it with this cloth,
and then reattach the boy's head as it was before.
Honorable spectators gathered here,
first let me sell these one hundred talismans,
and then I shall perform my arts.
These talismans of mine
cost only five coins each."
He began to beat the gong.
The onlookers
soon crowded so tightly they could not move.
There were about two or three hundred people,
but he sold only twenty-eight talismans.
Dù Qīshèng grew frustrated
at not having sold the talismans,
and looking at the crowd,
said:
"Could it be that among you spectators there is someone skilled in these matters
who dares to step forward and challenge my magic?"
He asked three times,
and then three times more,
but no one came down.
Dù Qīshèng said:
"In my art, I have the boy lie on the bench,
perform the magic,
and chant the incantations,
and he is just as if he were asleep."
Just as he was about to perform his magical tricks,
it so happened that in the crowd was a monk who knew this art.
Because he saw the man boasting so loudly,
the monk first chanted an incantation,
shouted "Jí!",
captured the boy's soul first,
and placed it inside his sleeve.
Seeing a noodle shop across the way,
the monk said:
"I am hungry,
so I'll go and eat a bowl of noodles;
it won't be too late to return his son's soul afterward."
The monk walked into the noodle shop and up to the second floor,
and leaning by the window overlooking the street,
he watched Dù Qīshèng and sat down.
The waiter came,
put down chopsticks,
set out small dishes,
asked about the noodles,
and went back down.
The monk took out the boy's soul,
covered it with a small plate,
placed it on the table,
and waited for his noodles.
A poem serves as proof:
Do not boast loudly before others,
for among the strong, there is always one stronger.
The divine art of reattaching heads exists not in this world;
who would have thought a demonic monk would steal the soul away?
The child, like jade, is worthy of pity;
souls coming and going are worth nothing.
The story follows two paths.
Now, Dù Qīshèng chanted the incantation,
raised his knife and chopped;
the boy's head fell,
and the number of onlookers grew even larger.
Dù Qīshèng put down the knife
and covered the body with a sheet.
He held up a talisman,
circled it several times over the boy's body,
and chanted the incantations.
Dù Qīshèng said:
"Spectators, do not be offended,
I have long held this specialty alone;
once this boat passes,
I suspect there will be no other boat to catch.
This treasure of my art is to sell these one hundred talismans."
When he lifted the sheet with both hands to look,
he saw that the boy's head would not reattach.
The crowd cried out:
"Usually when the sheet is lifted,
the child leaps up.
Today it won't reattach;
it’s a failure!"
Dù Qīshèng hurriedly covered it with the sheet again,
deceiving the onlookers with his words, saying:
"Spectators!
It may seem easy,
but I guarantee it will be reattached this time."
Again he bowed and performed the magic,
chanted the incantation,
and when he lifted the sheet to look,
it still would not reattach.
Dù Qīshèng panicked
and looked at the onlookers, saying:
"Honorable spectators,
though our paths may differ,
supporting a family is always the same.
Because I am pressed by the needs of livelihood,
if my words just now were improper,
I hope you gentlemen will forgive me.
Once I have reattached the head this time,
I will go and have a cup of wine.
Within the four seas,
all are acquaintances."
Dù Qīshèng admitted his fault, saying:
"It was my mistake;
it will be reattached this time."
He kept chanting the incantation,
but when he lifted the sheet,
it still would not reattach.
Dù Qīshèng said irritably:
"You are preventing my boy's head from reattaching,
even though I have pleaded with you
and repeatedly admitted my fault,
asking for your forgiveness.
Yet you are so unreasonable."
He then went to the basket in the back,
took out a paper packet,
opened it, and took out a bottle-gourd seed.
Going to the ground,
he loosened the earth
and buried the gourd seed in the ground.
Muttering words under his breath,
he spat a mouthful of water on it
and shouted "Jí!".
Miraculously,
a vine sprouted from the ground
and gradually grew large,
producing branches and leaves,
then blossoming;
then the flowers withered,
and a small bottle-gourd formed.
The crowd saw this
and all cheered:
"Wonderful!"
Dù Qīshèng plucked the little gourd,
holding the gourd in his left hand
and a knife in his right,
and said:
"First you were unreasonable,
taking my child's soul
and making it so I could not reattach his head.
Do not think you shall live in this world either!"
Looking at the gourd,
he struck it across the middle with the knife,
chopping the gourd in half.
It is said that the monk on the upper floor picked up the noodles
and was about to eat.
Suddenly, the monk's head went rolling down from his torso.
All the people eating noodles on the upper floor
were startled.
The timid ones dropped their noodles and ran downstairs,
while the bold ones stood their ground to watch.
The monk flusteredly put down his bowl,
stood up to feel around on the floorboards,
found his head,
grabbed both ears with his hands,
and lifted the head to place it back onto his torso.
Having set it straight,
he felt it again with his hands.
The monk said:
"I was so focused on eating noodles
that I forgot to return that boy's soul."
He reached out to lift up a small plate.
Just as the plate was lifted here,
Dù Qīshèng’s child over there immediately jumped up.
The onlookers let out a great shout.
Dù Qīshèng said:
"Since I started practicing this family magic,
today I have finally met a master."
Now, the people eating in the noodle shop
began talking animatedly,
and some talkative ones said to Dù Qīshèng:
"The one who broke your magic
was a monk on the upper floor of the noodle shop."
Among them, Wēn Diànzhí and Rǎn Guì were there listening to these words.
Rǎn Guì said:
"Guānchá!
Could this monk be the one who swindled Grand Marshal Shàn Wáng Tàiwèi of his copper coins?"
Wēn Diànzhí said:
"I have some suspicions as well."
Rǎn Guì said:
"When you see the rabbit, do not release the hawk;
how can we let this pass?"
Rǎn Guì gave a signal with a flick of his headcloth,
and the group of constables gave a loud shout
and rushed into the noodle shop.
Seeing the monk walking downstairs,
everyone moved to seize him.
The monk pointed with his finger,
and it was destined:
Dōngjīng City would be thrown into a boil,
and Kāifēng Fǔ would be thrown into great turmoil.
The constables were vexed by the demon monk,
unable to capture him,
leading to a greedy young man
meeting an untimely death.
Truly:
Trouble arises only from talking too much;
vexation comes from insisting on poking one's head out.
Ultimately, it is unknown whether the monk was captured then;
please listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
A person should be honest and keep to their poverty;
ill-gotten wealth must not be approached.
When it is in one's fate, it will naturally arrive;
otherwise, good fortune may instead turn into calamity.
It is said that Wēn Diànzhí led the group of constables
and rushed into the noodle shop,
just as the monk was coming downstairs.
Wēn Diànzhí pointed with his iron mace
and ordered the constables to seize the monk.
Seeing the crowd coming to catch him, the monk
pointed with his finger.
Most strangely,
the owner at the counter,
the busy shop assistants,
and the many people eating noodles in the shop
all turned into monks.
Wēn Diànzhí and the constables
were also monks.
The many people looked at one another,
staring back and forth,
all dazed.
The constables looked around,
not knowing which one to seize.
After a period of commotion in the noodle shop,
the noodle eaters all dispersed.
When Wēn Diànzhí looked at the shop owner and the others,
their appearances were the same as before.
Seeing that the monk was no longer in the shop,
Wēn Diànzhí immediately ordered the constables
to pursue in different directions.
He sent messengers to every gate,
saying that if any monk left the city,
he must be seized.
At that time, Wēn Diànzhí returned to the prefecture,
just as the Tàiyǐn was holding the evening court to settle public matters.
Wēn Diànzhí paid his respects in the hall.
Lóngtú Tàiyǐn said:
"I wanted you to capture the demon monk;
how does the matter stand?"
Wēn Diànzhí reported:
"Your servant followed Xiànggōng's decree
to arrest Tánzǐ Héshang.
Just now, in front of the Dà Xiàngguó Sì,
I saw a man performing magic
called Dù Qīshèng.
He chopped off a child's head with a knife.
A monk on the upper floor of the noodle shop across the way took the child's soul,
preventing him from reattaching the head.
Dù Qīshèng was extremely frustrated
and grew a gourd from the ground.
He chopped the gourd in half with one stroke of the knife,
and the monk eating noodles on the upper floor of the shop
then had his head roll off.
That monk felt for his head on the floorboards and reattached it.
Below, the child's head was also reattached.
Your servant, seeing such strange occurrences,
ordered men to capture him.
But the monk simply pointed with his hand,
and everyone in the shop turned into monks.
Even your servant and the constables under my command
also turned into monks,
leaving your servant with no way to proceed.
I report to Xiànggōng,
such a demon,
is truly difficult to capture.
I look to Xiànggōng's decree for a decision."
Lóngtú Tàiyǐn said:
"I am the head of this Kāifēng Prefecture.
If such a demon
is within the city,
I fear other troubles may arise,
causing the Imperial Court to blame me.
He immediately ordered the clerk to write and sign a proclamation
