to be posted at every gate.
All people in nunneries, shrines, and temples everywhere:
if anyone captures Tánzǐ Héshang,
the government will grant a reward of one thousand strings of cash.
If anyone harbors a monk of unknown origin
or hides him without reporting,
the neighbors will be held collectively liable.
Because of this, throughout the capital and its outskirts,
people were talking about it incessantly.
It is said that in the heart of the city of Dōngjīng,
there lived a fruit seller named Lǐ Èrgē.
He and his wife
lived in an inn,
and he had only just recovered from an illness.
Having no capital to conduct business,
he went out to seek his acquaintances,
hoping to borrow two or three hundred coins for his expenses.
That day he could not manage to borrow any,
and he returned home feeling ceaselessly gloomy.
His wife said:
"Èrgē!
How did your borrowing go today?"
Lǐ Èr said:
"I must tell you,
I could not borrow any money today.
The people on the streets were in a great uproar,
and the merchants could not do any business.
They say that yesterday a monk
was eating noodles on the upper floor of a noodle shop.
Suddenly, his head went rolling down to the floor;
he reached out his hand and felt for it,
then grabbed it by the ears with both hands and placed it back on his torso,
reattaching it just as before.
The constables, seeing his bizarre behavior,
went together to seize him.
The monk simply pointed with his hand,
and everyone in the shop turned into the likeness of a monk.
Now, the Kāifēng Fǔ has offered a reward of one thousand strings of cash
for the capture of this monk.
It turns out that three or five days ago,
this monk swindled the Shànwáng Tàiwèi out of three thousand strings of copper coins;
he is called Tánzǐ Héshàng."
His wife said:
"Èrgē!
Is there really such talk?"
Lǐ Èr said:
"I have just seen the posted notice;
why would I lie to you?"
His wife said:
"Èrgē!
Right now, you and I have no food or drink.
If the opportunity arises
to capture this monk
and claim the one thousand strings of cash to start a business,
wouldn't that be wonderful?"
Lǐ Èr said:
"Nonsense!
Dealing with the authorities is no joking matter."
His wife said:
"I guarantee you will claim the one thousand strings of cash, and that is that."
Lǐ Èr said:
"How could you make me claim the one thousand strings of cash?"
His wife said:
"Èrgē!
I must tell you,
this monk is nowhere else;
though he could be a hundred and eight thousand lǐ away,
he is actually right before our eyes."
Lǐ Èrgē said:
"Where is he?"
His wife said:
"In the room next door."
Lǐ Èr said:
"What suspicious sign did you see in him?"
His wife said:
"The monk in the next room came to stay here
three months ago.
I have never seen him go out to beg for alms,
nor have I seen him chanting sutras for anyone.
Every day he sleeps until around mealtime before getting up,
and when he goes out, he returns before dusk completely drunk.
Half a month ago,
because I ate some cold things
and my stomach was upset,
I had a stomachache and needed to go to the back;
our room is narrow and has a foul smell.
I had to go to the latrine at the back of the inn,
and I happened to pass by his door.
It was around the hour of sìpái,
and I saw light shining from his room.
I thought it was strange for there to be a light at that hour,
so I peeked through a crack in the wall,
and I saw the monk sitting on the bed,
with fire bursting out from his whole body.
The monk raised his head to look up,
and it rose from the bed until it touched the roof beam.
I was so frightened that I didn't dare go to the latrine
and returned to our room.
This monk must certainly be the demon monk."
Lǐ Èrgē said:
"Is this the truth?"
His wife said:
"Why would I tell you something false?"
Lǐ Èrgē said:
"Keep your voice low,
and do not let the news leak out."
After instructing his wife,
he went straight out to the officials' quarters,
but then he did not dare to enter.
He just paced back and forth in front of the gate.
A constable saw him
and shouted:
"Lǐ Èr!
What business do you have
that you keep pacing back and forth here?"
Lǐ Èr said:
"I beg to inform your honors,
your humble servant has a confidential matter
and has come specifically to see the Guānchá."
The constable replied:
"Wait here at the entrance;
you may enter only after I have reported this."
It happened that Wēn Diànzhí was just then in the hall.
The constable reported:
"I beg to inform the Guānchá!
Lǐ Èr, the fruit seller, is pacing back and forth at the gate.
I questioned him,
and he says he has a confidential matter to report to the Guānchá."
Wēn Diànzhí said:
"Tell him to come in."
The constable went out and led Lǐ Èr to the hall,
where he bowed respectfully.
When Wēn Diànzhí saw him,
he did not want to alarm him,
and asked with a slight smile:
"Lǐ Èrgē!
What business brings you to see me?"
Lǐ Èr said:
"I beg to inform the Guānchá!
Your humble servant recently fell ill
and could not attend to his affairs,
and went out to look for some work.
I saw the official notice posted;
your humble servant knows a few characters,
and I saw it written that one thousand strings of cash are offered for the capture of the demon monk.
I went home and told my wife,
and my wife said
that the monk staying next door
is the demon monk."
Wēn Diànzhí did not want to cause a stir,
and said with a smile:
"Lǐ Èrgē!
This matter must be handled with care.
What suspicious sign did you and your wife see?"
Lǐ Èr repeated everything his wife had said.
Wēn Diànzhí said:
"This matter must be certain.
Go and prepare a written deposition."
Lǐ Èr agreed and went out.
He asked a constable to draft it,
obtained a sheet of paper,
transcribed it in his own hand,
and went directly back to the hall to submit it.
Wēn Diànzhí asked:
"Is this monk in the inn right now?"
Lǐ Èr said:
"He goes out every day after breakfast
and returns at dusk."
Wēn Diànzhí said:
"Sit here for a while
while I have someone buy some wine for you to drink."
Before long,
the wine was bought,
and Lǐ Èr was given it to drink.
Wēn Diànzhí then came with the constables,
having Lǐ Èr act as the informant.
He led the group away from Wēn Diànzhí’s house
and went to sit in a teahouse to the left of the inn.
He ordered a constable to keep watch outside for the monk.
That day, before it was yet dusk,
they saw the monk stumbling along,
staggering toward them in a drunken stupor.
Lǐ Èr hurriedly went into the teahouse to see Wēn Diànzhí and said:
"I beg to inform the Guānchá!
The monk is here."
Just then, the monk reached the door of the teahouse.
Wēn Diànzhí pointed to the line of constables and said:
"Capture this demon monk!"
The crowd raised a great shout;
it was like a black eagle chasing a purple swallow,
or a fierce tiger devouring a lamb.
They all fell upon him at once,
dragging the monk this way and that,
and bound him with a hemp rope.
Surrounded by the crowd,
he was escorted straight to the official's quarters in Gānquán Fāng.
There is a poem to prove it:
In this world, nothing ruins matters like wine;
one bout of drunkenness can make one forget everything.
Look at the magical Dàn Héshàng;
when was he ever able to escape calamity while drunk?
Wēn Diànzhí said:
“What a relief!
I have managed this piece of official business,
and it will allow Lóngtú Xiānggōng to set his mind at ease.”
Everyone had tied that monk up just like a húntun.
The monk was so drunk he did not wake,
snoring loudly in his sleep.
Wēn Diànzhí immediately entered the prefecture office
and reported to the Tàiyǐn:
“The demon monk has been captured.
He should have been escorted to the hall,
but because this monk is heavily drunk
and unconscious,
he is currently in the officers’ quarters.
I await your Excellency’s command.”
When Lóngtú Tàiyǐn heard this,
he ordered that he be guarded securely
and brought for trial at the morning session the next day.
Wēn Diànzhí left the office
and went to the officers’ quarters to look at the monk;
his wine had not yet worn off.
He instructed all the runners to guard him carefully.
Meanwhile, at midnight, the monk woke from his wine
and felt quite uncomfortable.
He opened his eyes and saw the lamps and candles shining
like daylight.
Sitting on both sides were the runners.
The monk asked:
“Where is this place?”
The runners said:
“This is the officers’ quarters.”
He asked the runners again:
“What crime has this poor monk committed
that you have tied me up here?”
All the runners knew this monk was a demon monk
and did not dare to be harsh with him.
Among them was an older, experienced runner who said:
“Monk!
Do not blame us.
This is our duty.
We each have families at home
and do not wish to stir up trouble for nothing.
It is because Lǐ Èrgē, the fruit seller next door to your inn,
said you stayed for three months
but never chanted sutras for anyone
nor went out to beg for alms,
yet every day you were drunk.
He said your background was suspicious,
so we came to capture you.”
The monk said:
“I have official residences and mansions where I am hosted for meals;
this has nothing to do with him.”
The runner said:
“Monk!
There is nothing to be done.
Wait until dawn
and you can go before the Tàiyǐn to argue your case against Lǐ Èr.”
At the fifth watch,
Wēn Diànzhí ordered the runners to escort the monk to the corridor of the Kāifēng Fǔ to wait.
The Tàiyǐn took his seat in the hall,
and the four departments and six bureaus stood before it.
Then the Tàiyǐn emerged,
and the seating order was very formal.
A pair of crystal dragon lamps
shone like candles lighting up the sky.
The lictors shouted:
“Silence!”
Wēn Diànzhí escorted the monk to the hall
and gave his greeting.
The Tàiyǐn looked at Lǐ Èr’s accusation
and then at the monk,
saying irritably:
“How intolerable! You became a monk
but do not keep to your station
and even dare to deceive people out of their money and property!
Order the jailers to bring a long wooden cangue
and put the monk in it.”
He called two strong jailers over:
“Give the monk a hundred strokes of the staff first,
then I will interrogate him again.”
The jailers gave their greeting,
but before they had struck the monk’s legs even two or three times,
everyone let out a shout.
The doorkeeper shouted:
“Silence!
Stop shouting!”
When the Tàiyǐn looked,
the monk was no longer in the hole of the cangue;
instead, a broom was tied there.
The Tàiyǐn said:
“How can there be such a demonish person?
I just had the monk placed in the cangue here,
yet how has he become a broom?”
While they were speaking,
they heard someone shouting outside the prefecture gates.
The Tàiyǐn asked in surprise:
“What is happening?”
The gatekeeper came to report:
“I report to your Excellency,
there is a monk outside the gate clapping his hands and laughing loudly, saying:
‘What a fine Bāo Lóngtú,
you can do nothing against this poor monk!’”
When Bāo Tàiyǐn heard this,
he was furious and said:
“This fellow dares to be so insolent!
Immediately send men to capture him!
If the demon monk is caught this time,
they shall be rewarded with one thousand guàn according to regulation.”
Then the runners rushed out of the prefecture gate
to catch the demon monk.
When the monk saw people coming to catch him,
he quickly walked onto the market street,
unhurriedly swaying the sleeves of his biǎnshān robe as he went.
When the runners saw this,
if they chased him fast, he walked fast;
if they chased him slowly, he walked slowly;
if they did not chase him, he did not walk.
The runners chased him until they were exhausted
and stopped.
Although they were only ten-odd steps away,
they simply could not catch him.
Everyone chased him to the front of Xiàngguó Sì.
The monk was on the Yán’ān Qiáo,
and seeing everyone coming after him,
he quickly entered the mountain gate of Xiàngguó Sì.
Wēn Diànzhí said:
“This monk has gone into a dead end;
one way or another, we will catch him.”
He ordered half of the runners to surround the front and back gates of the temple,
and half to head to the Buddha hall and the two corridors to search and capture him.
The Abbot of the temple came out to meet Wēn Diànzhí
and said:
“I report to you, Guānchá!
This temple is an imperial house of incense.
For what reason has the Guānchá
brought a group of people
holding weapons into the temple
to cause such an uproar?”
Wēn Diànzhí said:
“I am following the command of the Tàiyǐn Xiānggōng
to capture a demon monk who came into your temple.
Do not hide him;
if you are wise, tie him up and bring him out.”
The Abbot said:
“My humble temple has over a hundred monks,
all of whom have ordination certificates.
When traveling monks arrive,
there is a guest prefect;
we never dare to keep them overnight.
If the Guānchá chased him into the temple, you must recognize this monk;
why didn’t you just catch him then,
instead of coming here to demand him from us?”
Wēn Diànzhí said:
“This demon monk cheated Shànwáng Tàiwèi of three thousand guàn
and has troubled the whole prefecture so they cannot rest.
If you do not send him out,
I will report to the Tàiyǐn
and let your temple suffer the consequences.”
This frightened the Abbot, who panicked
and said:
“I report to you, Guānchá!
The monks of this temple are all respectable;
there is no demon monk.
If you do not believe me,
I will call them all out
and let the Guānchá check them one by one.”
Wēn Diànzhí said:
“Very well!”
The Abbot immediately rang the bell to gather the temple’s hundred-odd monks
and asked Wēn Diànzhí to inspect them.
Wēn Diànzhí and the runners looked,
and said none of them were he.
Wēn Diànzhí said:
“Abbot!
I personally chased him into your temple;
how could he have disappeared?
We must search it.”
The Abbot said:
“I will lead the way
and allow the Guānchá to search as he pleases.”
From the monks' rooms to the kitchen,
the latrines,
and the storehouse,
they searched everywhere but could not find him.
Turning back to the Buddha hall,
they saw a statue of a six-armed deity.
Its three heads were like three green mountains,
its six arms like six steep ridges,
holding six Dharma treasures.
Wēn Diànzhí said:
“Usually temples do not have such statues;
why did you sculpt Nézhā Tàizǐ?”
The Abbot said:
“Nézhā Tàizǐ is the Bùdòng Zūnwáng Fó,
who transforms people through good and evil.”
*Wēn Diànzhí* and the others saw that the hall was empty and desolate,
seeing only *Nézhā* and his group at the hall gate,
when they heard someone on the Buddha hall call out:
“*Wēn Diànzhí*!
*Bāo Tàiyǐn* ordered you to come and catch this poor monk;
now that you have seen me, why do you not catch me?”
When *Wēn Diànzhí* and the others turned their heads to look,
it was *Nézhā Tàizǐ* speaking.
Everyone looked at that *Nézhā Tàizǐ*:
he was fashioned in five colors,
about fifteen or sixteen feet tall,
with six arms holding six different objects.
Of the three heads, the mouth of the middle head was wide open,
dripping with blood and revealing four long fangs,
as he called out:
“*Wēn Diànzhí*!
Come and take me away!”
This frightened the Elder and the crowd, who cried out in great shock:
“How strange!
How strange!”
The crowd wanted to catch *Nézhā*,
but he was made of molded clay;
how could they take him away!
*Nézhā* called out again:
“Why do you not call someone to take me away?”
The crowd discussed:
“Could it be that the clay-molded *Nézhā* has attained a spirit
and come out to trouble people?
Now we must go report to the *Tàiyǐn*;
we must destroy this *Nézhā*,
so that he does not come out to trouble people.”
The Elder said:
“*Guānchá*!
This must not be done.
How can a clay god speak?
It is nothing more than a demonic creature possessing it to cause trouble;
it has nothing to do with the Dharma-body.
The cost of sculpting it was great;
if you destroy it,
it will be difficult to replace in the future.”
*Wēn Diànzhí* said:
“Since that demonic creature is possessing it to cause trouble,
it should be destroyed
to avoid future troubles.”
Among the monks was one of great virtue,
who pressed his palms together before the Buddha and said:
“May the Dragon Kings, Heavenly Beings, and the Triple Gem
protect the Dharma
and cast out the demonic creature,
otherwise I fear the divine statue will be ruined.”
After the prayer was finished,
they only heard someone outside clapping their hands and laughing loudly:
“*Guānchá*!
I am here,
why trouble yourselves?”
The group of constables saw that
it was indeed the monk.
They let out a shout!
Everyone came to catch the demonic monk.
They were only ten or so paces away,
but they simply could not catch up.
That monk led the group
out of the *Xiàngguó Sì*
and ran straight onto the main street.
The merchants could not do their business;
stalls were overturned,
and tables and stands were knocked down.
More and more onlookers gathered;
running back and forth,
they chased him straight out of the city.
Passing the *Yìguāntīng*,
they arrived near the end of the market.
The monk said:
“You all do not need to chase me anymore,
I, this poor monk, shall return on my own.”
Looking toward the *Biànhé*,
he took a leap.
There was only a loud splash,
and the monk dived into the water.
The constables said:
“This time it is good;
since he died in the water by his own hand,
it saves us much effort.”
The water of the *Biànhé* was flowing very swiftly;
everyone said:
“Who knows where his corpse will drift and settle?”
*Wēn Diànzhí* could only go back to report to the *Tàiyǐn*.
It happened that the *Tàiyǐn* was in the hall judging cases.
*Wēn Diànzhí* bowed
and regarding the matter of catching the demonic monk,
he recounted everything from the beginning.
*Bāo Tàiyǐn* heard this and
said:
“How intolerable this fellow was;
he troubled me so much I could do nothing about him.
Since he jumped into the water and died on his own,
so be it!”
Before he had finished speaking,
the voice of a woman was heard below the steps crying out an injustice.
The *Tàiyǐn* asked:
“For what matter do you cry injustice?”
The woman said:
“I petition your *Xiànggōng*!
My husband *Lǐ Èr* was the one who first reported the demonic monk,
who has already been captured and brought to the authorities,
yet you have instead detained my husband.
I do not even wish for the reward money;
I only want my husband released to return home,
to make a living day by day.
I look to your *Xiànggōng*’s command.”
The *Tàiyǐn* said:
“*Lǐ Èr*’s report was truthful;
he should be given the reward money.
Why was he imprisoned?”
*Wēn Diànzhí* said:
“He was not imprisoned;
he has been entertained with wine and food day and night.
He was kept in the emissaries' quarters
awaiting your *Xiànggōng*’s command.”
The *Tàiyǐn* called for him to come out.
*Wēn Diànzhí* immediately went to the emissaries' quarters
and called *Lǐ Èr* to the hall.
The *Tàiyǐn* said:
“Since the notice was posted,
it is right to give him the reward of one thousand strings of cash.”
At that time in *Dōngjīng*, one string of cash was worth one tael of silver.
*Lǐ Èr* was a poor peddler;
gaining one thousand strings of cash for nothing
was no small fortune.
*Lǐ Èr* and his wife received the reward money in the hall;
then the two of them thanked the *Tàiyǐn*,
immediately left the government office,
and returned to their shop.
There is a poem to testify:
Who would get money from the hands of *Lóngtú*?
Usually *Lǐ Èr* relied on his wife’s virtue.
The demonic monk did not fear a man of great wealth;
for how many years could one enjoy such floating wealth?
From ancient times to the present, storytellers are always the same:
if there is no money, the matter ends;
but if there is money, then there will be *Shěn Dàizhào* to encourage it
and *Zhāng Bóshì* to assist.
Lǐ Èr went to the front of Xiāngguó Sì and rented a house,
where he opened a large bázi shop in front of the door.
The husband and wife
had plenty of food and clothing.
It happened to be winter,
and one day around noon,
they had lit a stove of chestnut charcoal fire
and prepared a few cups of wine.
While the husband and wife were facing the fire and drinking wine,
they saw a person walk in
and call out:
"Lǐ Èrláng!
I would like to buy some fine bázi."
The husband and wife recognized him as the monk,
and were startled into a daze.
The monk said:
"Lǐ Èrláng!
If it were not for this poor monk,
how could you be living such a happy life today?
I have come specifically to ask you for a vegetarian meal."
Between the husband and wife,
if there had been one who was sensible,
they would have come out to thank the monk
and given him a meal;
what would that have mattered?
It was not as if he really wanted to eat your meal.
He might have come to test you,
or perhaps you could have dismissed him with a few kind words,
asking him to leave your house, and that would be that.
Lǐ Èr and his wife, however, did not have such insight,
and most unfortunately conceived a thought, saying:
"You demonic monk!
It was said you were pursued and caught by officers,
and that you jumped into the Biàn Hé and died.
Why have you come to my house again to cause trouble?
If you are sensible,
leave quickly.
If you delay even a little,
I will call for the local patrol soldiers to arrest you and take you to court;
do not blame me."
The monk said:
"If anyone could do anything to me,
I would have been caught many days ago.
You reported me to the authorities,
yet I ensured you received a reward of a thousand guàn,
allowing you and your wife to live happily and comfortably.
I come to see you,
and you ought to thank me,
yet instead you show such ill-will
and want to call the officers to arrest me.
You fellow are very unreasonable;
I shall let you suffer some pain."
He pointed with his hand
and shouted, "Swiftly!"
Suddenly, the charcoal brazier Lǐ Èr was facing flew up
and flipped right onto Lǐ Èr's face.
Lǐ Èr gave a loud cry
and suddenly fell to the ground.
His wife hurriedly came to rescue him;
when she helped him up to look,
the chestnut charcoal fire had burned him until he was covered in blisters like watery sacs.
When they looked again, the monk had disappeared.
Lǐ Èr was burned by the charcoal fire so painfully that it was unbearable.
If they had no money,
he would have just had to endure it and that would be the end of it.
But because they had those strings of cash,
they invited a doctor to treat him.
When medicine was applied,
it pained him even more intensely,
and he cried out for three days and three nights.
His wife was so distressed she did not know what to do.
Suddenly, a Dàoshì appeared in front of the door,
wearing a blue headscarf and a yellow robe;
he walked to the counter
and called for alms!
Lǐ Èr’s wife said:
"If my house had no trouble,
I would give you two or three coins,
and what would it matter?
But here, a life is at stake,
and I have no time for you."
The Dàoshì said:
"Lady!
What matter is happening in your house?"
Lǐ Èr’s wife said:
"I should let the master know,
a demonic monk threw fire all over my husband's face,
burning up many blisters.
Applying medicine makes it hurt more;
he has cried for three days and three nights,
and I fear he might die."
The Dàoshì said:
"Lady!
This humble Dàoshì has some medicine for burns;
once applied, the pain will stop,
and the scabs will fall off.
It has been tested many times with success
and has saved many people."
Lǐ Èr’s wife said:
"Do not say it will be completely healed;
if it just stops the pain,
I will certainly thank you generously."
The Dàoshì said:
"Go and ask him to come out,
and get some water."
Lǐ Èr’s wife went in and helped Lǐ Èr out
and handed the water to the Dàoshì.
The Dàoshì took a packet of medicine,
shook some into the water,
and used a goose feather to dip into it
and apply it to the sores.
Lǐ Èr said happily:
"What a miraculous medicine!
It is like pouring water on snow; the pain has stopped."
The Dàoshì said:
"This is not yet miraculous.
If I make the scabs fall off immediately
and leave you with no troubles,
what would you think?"
Lǐ Èr said:
"If it could be so,
I would be grateful to you, master."
The Dàoshì said:
"This is the air of hot poison.
You should go outside to a breezy, cool place to let it blow on you,
and the scabs will then fall off."
Lǐ Èr followed the Dàoshì's words
and went out to the street.
The Dàoshì told Lǐ Èr to sit on a stool,
looked at him, and said:
"Call out three times, 'Scabs fall off!',
and the scabs will fall down."
Lǐ Èr was happy to hear this
and shouted with all his might three times.
Suddenly, the stool Lǐ Èr was sitting on
rose into the air
and went to the top of the ten-zhàng long banner pole of Xiāngguó Sì,
where it perched perfectly straight, neither leaning nor tilting.
When the people on the street saw this,
they let out a great shout.
Lǐ Èr’s wife came out and saw it;
she was shocked and said:
"How bitter!
How bitter!
How will my husband get down?"
The Dàoshì said:
"Do not panic!
I will call him down,
but let me show you who I am first."
The Dàoshì took off his yellow robe
and removed his blue headscarf.
Lǐ Èr’s wife looked closely,
cried out in terror,
not knowing what to do.
It turned out to be the demonic monk.
The monk said:
"Your husband is unreasonable.
With all his heart he only wanted to harm me,
but he could not harm me at all.
I shall let him suffer some terror on the banner pole."
The people on the street were in a hubbub and all came to watch.
Among them, some officers saw it and said:
"The government has clearly posted notices
and offered reward money
to catch demonic people.
This monk is showing off his demonic sorcery here again;
he will surely bring trouble upon us."
The officers and the local lǐjiǎ came together to arrest the monk.
The monk ducked into the crowd and vanished.
Everyone said:
"We have never seen such a strange and bizarre thing."
Lǐ Èr sat tightly on the top of the banner pole;
he could not get down,
and while the crowd discussed how to save him,
they had no ladder that long.
The whole city's soldiers and civilians were stirred up,
and all said:
"This monk is indeed formidable.
How will this man get down?"
It is said that the patrol guards of the local ward rushed like the wind to report to Bāo Tàiyǐn.
Bāo Tàiyǐn immediately took his sedan chair to Xiàngguó Sì and alighted.
He set out the folding chairs
and sat before the main hall.
Lifting his head to look,
he saw Lǐ Èr sitting on a stool atop the flagpole,
shouting loudly for someone to save him.
Bāo Tàiyǐn pondered;
there was no way to save him,
so he ordered Lǐ Èr's wife to be summoned and questioned.
Lǐ Èrsǎo came forward and bowed.
Bāo Tàiyǐn asked,
"For what reason is your husband up there?
You must tell me the truth."
Lǐ Èrsǎo recounted the monk coming for a meal and splashing fire,
and the Taoist's words about applying medicine,
telling everything one by one.
Bāo Tàiyǐn said,
"How detestable that this demonic monk is so unreasonable!
If he is captured this time,
I will certainly not let the matter rest."
Before he had finished speaking,
a monk walked out from the side of the Buddhist hall
and offered a greeting before the Tàiyǐn.
Bāo Tàiyǐn opened his eyes wide and asked,
"Monk!
For what business do you come to see me?"
The monk said,
"This poor monk has a way to get Lǐ Èr down."
Bāo Tàiyǐn said,
"If the Master can save Lǐ Èr and bring him down,
I shall thank you with a vegetarian offering."
The monk was seen lightly gliding up the flagpole,
holding Lǐ Èr with both hands,
and shouting loudly:
"Bāo Lóngtú!
You are an upright and honest official;
I, this poor monk, do not dare to trouble you.
I merely obtained three thousand strings of cash from Grand Marshal Shànwáng;
what business is it of yours
that you want to seize me?
I have nothing to repay you with,
so I return one Lǐ Èr to you."
From mid-air, he hurled Lǐ Èr straight down.
The crowd let out a shout
and looked at Lǐ Èr.
Truly:
His body was like the moon setting behind the mountains at the fifth watch;
his life was like a lamp out of oil at midnight.
As for what happened to Lǐ Èr's life,
listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
Demonic arts are indeed supernatural,
surpassing the refined strategies of the immortals.
Just watch Yǒng-ér's mud candles
burning straight from dusk until dawn.
The story goes that Lǐ Èr, unfortunately because of those one thousand strings of cash,
had informed on the monk.
Having received the reward money,
he used it as capital to open a fruit shop.
When the monk came for a meal,
he should have repaid kindness with kindness,
but instead, he insulted him with harsh words.
On that day, he was hurled straight down from the top of the flagpole by that monk,
right in front of Bāo Lóngtú.
When Lóngtú looked,
he saw Lǐ Èr's head was down
and his feet were up;
his head had been driven straight into his torso.
Alas, he is gone; may he accept this offering!
Lǐ Èrsǎo began to wail loudly,
and it was inevitable that people were called to carry the corpse back for burial,
which will not be further discussed.
Now, that monk was sitting high up on the stool atop the flagpole.
Those watching
were like a mountain of people and a sea of humanity,
growing even more numerous.
Many people began to clamor,
and the subordinates could not restrain them.
Lóngtú watched
but had no way to capture him.
He considered using axes to chop down the flagpole,
but while flagpoles in other temples were made of wood,
only this flagpole at Xiàngguó Sì was cast in bronze.
No one knew how it had been cast ten zhàng long in the first place.
It turned out there were three wonders in Xiàngguó Sì:
A well in the Buddha hall,
thirty zhàng deep.
It had a rope made of hair
and a black lacquered bucket
with vermillion characters reading "For the public use of Dà Xiàngguó Sì."
Suddenly one day the rope broke,
and the bucket could not be found.
Later, someone returned from sailing the sea
and came to Xiàngguó Sì saying,
"While I was a passenger on a ship in the Great Eastern Ocean,
I saw a bucket floating on the surface of the water.
When the sailors fished it out to look,
it had vermillion characters reading 'For the public use of Dà Xiàngguó Sì.'
While we were looking,
a great wind and waves arose,
almost capsizing the ship.
We immediately vowed to return the bucket,
and the wind and waves instantly subsided.
Therefore, I have come to fulfill the vow and return the bucket."
Only then did they know that the well connected directly to the Eastern Ocean.
In front of the gate of Xiàngguó Sì, there was a bridge
called the Yán'ān Bridge.
Looking at the temple from the bridge,
it seemed as if it were in a well.
Yet when looking at the bridge from the Buddha hall,
it was ten-odd zhàng lower than the temple's foundation.
Furthermore, this flagpole was cast in bronze;
it could not be cut
nor sawn.
These together were the three wonders.
The monk was seen atop the flagpole,
taunting Bāo Tàiyǐn with words.
Bāo Tàiyǐn was extremely vexed but had no way to deal with him.
Suddenly he thought of a plan
and ordered a hundred archers to be summoned from the camp.
The attendants called them at once.
Bāo Tàiyǐn ordered them to surround the flagpole and shoot upwards.
Among the archers were those who shot well;
when they shot near the monk,
the monk used his cassock sleeves to block them.
While Bāo Tàiyǐn was at a loss,
Rǎn Guì, a bailiff under Wēn Diànzhí, ran up and reported:
"I have a humble plan to offer
that can capture the demonic monk."
Bāo Tàiyǐn asked,
"What is your idea?"
Rǎn Guì said,
"He is a demonic monk.
One can take the blood of pigs and sheep,
as well as horse urine and garlic,
dip the arrowheads in them, and shoot.
Then that demonic monk's evil magic
will no longer work."
Bāo Tàiyǐn was delighted to hear this
and ordered the blood of pigs and sheep, horse urine, and garlic to be brought.
His subordinates went to fetch them in different directions.
Bāo Tàiyǐn ordered them to be mixed together
and told the hundred archers to dip their arrowheads in it.
At the sound of the clapper,
all the bows fired together.
If they had not shot,
all would have been for nothing.
But as a hundred arrows shot up together,
one or two thousand people inside and outside the temple let out a shout;
they saw the monk fall from mid-air along with his stool.
Everyone said,
"This monk, if not dead, must be crippled."
To the west of the Buddha hall was a urine pit.
The monk fell straight into the urine pit, without leaning or tilting.
The bailiffs immediately dragged him out,
and by the side of the pit, they poured a bucket of pig and sheep blood over the monk's bald head.
They bound him with a rope.
Bāo Tàiyǐn then returned to the prefecture in his sedan chair,
ascended the bench,
and ordered the monk to be brought before him.
Bāo Tàiyǐn said,
"You detestable demonic monk!
To come beneath the Imperial Chariot and use demonic arts
to harass the military and the people!
Now that you have been captured by me,
what do you have to say for yourself?"
He ordered the first-class cangue to be brought
and had the monk shackled in it.
He ordered him to be sent down to the Yòujūn Xúnyuàn
to be interrogated regarding his home district and name.
Fearing there might be remaining accomplices,
it was necessary to investigate and examine thoroughly
so they could all be seized and punished.
Having given the orders, the Tàiyǐn
went to rest.
This monk was covered in urine and blood and bound tight;
he could not use his magic arts.
He was escorted out of the prefecture gate by a group of bailiffs
to the Yòujūn Xún Yuàn.
They relayed the Tàiyǐn’s words to the Tuīguān.
The Tuīguān said:
“I have received the Tàiyǐn’s command
to interrogate you, this demon monk, about your whereabouts.
You must have a monastery where you rest,
and how many people are traveling with you?
It would be better
if I did not have to question you.”
He ordered the jailers to apply the torture.
The jailers hung the monk’s two feet from the tip of the cangue;
he was unable to struggle
and was struck hard with three hundred strokes of the staff.
The monk did not make a single sound,
nor did he cry out in pain.
When the Tuīguān lowered his head to look closely,
he saw only that the monk was snoring loudly in his sleep.
The Tuīguān said:
“Is this not strange?”
He ordered the jailers to keep him in prison for the time being
and bring him out again after a while for interrogation.
He was tortured three times a day,
until the jailers were exhausted from the beating.
The monk remained as if nothing were happening,
simply not making a sound.
Whenever they beat him,
he would fall asleep.
The Tuīguān interrogated him for about ten days,
but could do nothing,
so he had to report to the Tàiyǐn, saying:
“I received your command to interrogate the demon monk.
Now several days have passed,
and he is tortured three times every day.
But whenever he is beaten,
he falls asleep.
Such a demon monk
is truly difficult to interrogate.
If he is kept in prison for long,
I fear there will be future trouble.
I respectfully await your command.”
Bāo Tàiyǐn said:
“Why keep such a demon monk
any longer?”
Immediately the documents were issued,
sentencing the demon monk according to the law
to be taken out to the market execution ground for decapitation.
The Tuīguān ordered the monk to be escorted out,
heading straight for the market execution ground.
On the criminal’s placard was written:
For the unlawful killing of Lǐ Èr,
and for unlawfully practicing demon magic in Dōngjīng
and disturbing and harming the military and civilians,
to be executed according to the law.
The prisoner is one monk named Dànzǐ Héshang.
When the residents inside and outside the capital heard that the demon monk was being brought out,
the merchants stopped their business
and all came to watch.
They saw the criminal’s placard leading the way,
with staves following behind.
The executioners escorted the demon monk
away from the Yòujūn Xún Yuàn.
The onlookers were so crowded they could not be pushed aside.
Meanwhile, as the group escorted the monk
and arrived not far from the center of the market,
the monk stopped in his tracks.
An executioner said:
“Go ahead and be a good man;
why won't you move?”
The monk said:
“Gentlemen,
I, a poor monk, momentarily disturbed the Tàiyǐn and
have received this retribution.
I beg of you!
There is wine in the tavern ahead;
get me a bowl to drink, and then I shall leave this world.”
The executioners, thinking nothing would happen
and pitying him as a man about to die,
had to go to the tavern to get a bowl of wine
and poured it into a wooden ladle for him to drink.
The monk put his mouth to the wooden ladle and drank more than half of it.
The crowd swarmed around as they walked on.
Just as they reached the execution ground,
it turned out the monk was holding a mouthful of wine,
which he sprayed into the air.
Suddenly, under the clear sky and bright sun,
wind and rain came from nowhere.
A gust of wind rose,
and black mist covered the execution ground.
Tiles and stones pelted down upon the people’s heads.
The onlookers all fled.
After a short while,
the wind passed,
and the black mist dispersed.
When the jailers,
executioners, and the supervising official looked for the monk,
his ropes were broken and he was gone.
They searched in all directions,
but there wasn't even a shadow of him.
Truly it is: The Áoyú has escaped the golden hook,
shaking its tail and head, never to return.
There is a poem to prove it:
This monk was born exceedingly strange;
hard to catch, but easy to lose.
Even if a ladle of wine was not allowed to be swallowed,
that bald head would not necessarily have fallen to the ground.
From the supervising official above
to the jailers
and executioners below,
all were distressed that the monk had escaped,
fearing the Tàiyǐn would find them guilty.
“All of us in this group
will have to suffer;
we must return to Kāifēng Fǔ to report to the Tàiyǐn.”
When Lóngtú heard the report,
he immediately ascended the hall.
The supervising official led the group to plead for mercy.
At this time, Lóngtú clearly knew that sorcerers had appeared
and the court would need to mobilize the military.
Unwilling to let people suffer lawsuits for no reason,
he dismissed the group to go their way.
That very night, he wrote a memorial to the imperial court,
saying that it would be easier to manage while it was still early,
but if time passed and the sorcerers gathered in great numbers,
he feared it would be difficult to suppress them.
The imperial court issued an edict
to all circuits, villages, and patrolling inspectors
to diligently investigate and suppress them.
The documents arrived at Bèizhōu in Héběi,
and an official proclamation was hung in front of the prefectural office.
That place was extremely bustling.
There was a woman wearing mourning clothes,
carrying a basket in her hand,
who walked back and forth in front of the prefectural office five or seven times.
If this woman were not good-looking,
no one would have followed her.
Although she was not heavily made up,
she was very beautiful.
Idle men everywhere asked her:
“I have seen you walk back and forth five or seven times;
for what reason?”
The woman said:
“To tell the truth, brothers,
because I lost my husband,
I have no way to make a living.
I have a skill
that I want to sell for three or five hundred coins
to use as travel expenses.”
That person asked again:
“Sister!
What skill do you have to sell?”
The woman said:
“I cannot sell it without an open space;
if there is an open space,
then I can sell it.”
That person cleared the crowd for her,
and with much puffing and blowing said:
“This place is good;
people have performed street magic here before.
Doing it here would be best.”
The woman sat cross-legged on the ground.
The onlookers, firstly seeing how beautiful the woman was,
and secondly seeing her perform street magic,
gathered around her in a group of twenty or thirty,
all saying:
“I wonder what she is selling?”
The woman then took a bowl out of her basket,
looked at the group of people and said:
“Gentlemen!
I am not a traveling performer,
nor can I sell medicine or tell fortunes.
Only because I lost my husband
and have no other choice,
have I had to come out and earn twenty or thirty coins to use.
Which brother will take this bowl and fetch a bowl of water for me?”
A young lad said:
“I will fetch it for you!”
Before long,
a servant boy brought a bowl of water.
Those watching said:
"I do not know what she is selling,
or what the use of asking for water is."
The woman lifted the basket lid
and with a flash, she pulled out a knife.
Many of those watching said:
"Could it be that this woman can perform magic!"
They saw the woman use the tip of the knife to dig up some earth from the ground,
loosening it up;
she poured half a bowl of water into the earth
and mixed it into a lump.
From the basket, she took out several small bamboo sticks,
kneaded a piece of mud,
and molded it onto a bamboo stick into the shape of a candle,
setting it on the ground.
She kneaded another piece of mud
and again molded a bamboo stick into a candle.
In an instant,
she had made about ten of them,
and set them all on the ground.
The onlookers, jostling and crowding one another, sneered:
"For no reason at all,
we have been made fools of by this woman.
After leading us on for all this time,
there is nothing clever about it.
She just molded these ragged mud candles;
what use are they!"
Some people said:
"Just hold your tongues and watch her,
there must be a reason!"
The woman used the remaining half bowl of water to wash her hands,
wiped them clean,
looked at the group of people, and said:
"This young woman has lost her husband
and has no way to make a living.
I do not dare to be greedy;
I only wish to sell them for three coins each.
These ten candles are to be sold for exactly thirty coins.
Each candle,
if lit before the lamps are usually lit,
will burn straight through until dawn."
The onlookers all laughed and said:
"This lady is making fun of us people of Bèizhōu.
Candles made of mud,
just made and still wet—
how could they be lit?
Clearly, she is mocking people."
No one came to buy.
Seeing that no one came to buy, the woman
spoke again:
"You people of Bèizhōu are so untrusting.
Would I lie and cheat you out of three coins?
Which brother will fetch some fire for me?"
There was a certain Shěn Dàizhào, a hanger-on with no proper occupation,
who went to the teahouse for her to ask for a fire starter
and gave it to the woman.
The woman took a piece of sulfur match from her basket,
ignited it on the fire,
and lit the mud candles one by one from the start.
The group of onlookers all cheered, saying:
"What a marvelous feat!
A wet mud candle can actually be lit,
and it only costs three coins each;
where else could three coins be better spent?"
A curious person took three coins and gave them to the woman.
The woman took the money,
took one candle,
blew it out, and handed it over.
In an instant, all ten mud candles were sold.
The woman stood up,
packed the knife and bowl into the basket,
gave a bow of greeting to the crowd,
and left.
On the next day,
the woman came to the open ground again.
People crowded around to watch.
The woman said:
"Yesterday I fortunately sold enough for thirty coins,
which got me through the day.
Today I come again in distress."
The people said:
"It really is strange;
yesterday I bought a mud candle for three coins,
and it burned for exactly one whole night.
It was brighter than a lamp,
and it saved ten coins' worth of oil!"
The woman asked for some water on the grounds,
dug up some mud,
and made ten more mud candles.
The people said:
"No need to light them."
They all scrambled to buy them.
The woman again earned thirty coins
and packed up to leave.
Afterwards, she came to sell them every day;
before she could even finish making them, they were bought up.
Every day she only sold ten.
After selling them for half a month,
the whole of Bèizhōu was buzzing,
everyone saying:
"There is a woman selling mud candles in front of the prefectural office;
they burn a long time
and are bright."
On that day,
while the woman was setting up her spot
and had finished half of them,
a man walked out from the prefectural office.
When the crowd looked at him,
he was a man of status and rank,
surnamed Wáng and named Zé,
currently serving as a Pǎijūn in this office.
What did that man look like?
There is a stanza of Xījiāngyuè
as evidence:
Phoenix eyes and thick brows like a painting,
a yellow beard, a white face, and high cheekbones.
His hands hung past his knees, his shoulders were broad,
and his six-foot frame was robust and strong.
He was skilled at drawing bows and firing crossbows,
and moreover, he was adept with the staff and in wrestling and boxing.
All his life his ambition stood before others.
Wáng Zé, the Dūpái, appeared.
This Wáng Zé’s father
was originally a wealthy man of this prefecture.
Because he believed the words of a fēngshuǐ master,
he set his sights on a piece of burial ground
that was destined to produce noble descendants.
This piece of land had already been used for burial by a neighboring family,
but Wealthy Wáng took advantage of their poverty
by forcing some debts upon them
and deliberately refusing to settle the accounts for several years.
As the debt accumulated and could not be repaid,
he pressured them into giving up the land.
He dug up the corpses and coffins
and took the coffins of his own parents
to bury them there.
After the burial,
his wife, Lady Liú, became pregnant eight times in a row.
Only the first child was a girl,
while the remaining seven were all boys.
That Wáng Zé was born from the fifth pregnancy.
On the night of the labor,
Wealthy Wáng dreamed that Empress Wǔ Zétiān of the Táng dynasty came specifically to his house to stay,
saying:
"Your family is destined to give birth to a blessed son
who will build a foundation and establish a career,
bringing great prosperity to your lineage."
When he woke up,
it just so happened that the mother gave birth to the child.
Wealthy Wáng was overjoyed
and named him Wáng Zé,
with the childhood name Wǔfú’ér,
to commemorate the omen in the dream.
He was clever from childhood;
at the age of five,
he could already read.
One day,
his maternal grandfather, Elder Liú, arrived
and saw the seven grandsons of varying ages standing shoulder to shoulder,
which made him very happy.
Since only Wǔfú’ér was exceptionally bright and handsome,
he proposed a couplet, saying:
"The small child, at five years old, is the most clever in the world."
Wáng Zé replied immediately:
"A great man, once wealthy and noble, will astound the people."
Elder Liú praised this.
He proposed another couplet, saying:
"One mother, eight pregnancies, bearing seven sons;
the younger ones like tigers,
the older ones like dragons."
Wáng Zé replied again:
"With a single spear and a lone horse, leading three armies;
to succeed is to be a king,
to fail is to be a bandit."
Elder Liú said in great alarm:
"Although this child is exceptionally gifted,
he will certainly not be one to peacefully protect the family."
He instructed his son-in-law:
"If Wǔfú’ér grows up,
do not let him be taught martial arts.
I fear he will not keep to his place
and will become a burden to the family."
Another day,
Wáng Zé was playing on the street
and met a passing physiognomist
who stopped and stared at him for a long time,
saying:
"This child’s skeletal structure is extraordinary;
near the age of thirty,
he will surely have a great encounter.
However, his fate of misfortune toward kin is too heavy;
he must bring ruin to all his close relatives
and exhaust his ancestral estate
before he attains fortune."
He looked again and said:
"It is only a pity that there is a beginning but no end."
The wet nurse went inside and reported this to Wealthy Wáng.
Just as Wealthy Wáng was coming out to ask for more details,
the physiognomist had already left.
Sure enough,
when Wáng Zé reached the age of seven,
his father died of an illness.
Afterward, the six brothers fell ill one after another and all died.
His mother, Mother Liú, was overwhelmed with grief
and also died of illness,
leaving him entirely alone.
A poem serves as proof:
Unexpectedly, the many sons all perished,
leaving only Wǔfú to ruin the family gate.
The physiognomist’s words were not without accuracy;
how can a burial site compare to a virtuous heart?
By this time, Elder Liú had also passed away,
and there were no relatives or elders to guide him toward virtue.
By the age of fifteen or sixteen,
he had grown tall and strong;
he did not go to study
but only loved cockfighting, horse racing,
and wielding spears and staves.
He supported many martial arts teachers in his home
and also summoned skilled craftsmen
to tattoo the five characters for "Blessing" on his back.
Furthermore,
he delighted in all kinds of magical arts,
studying them whenever he encountered them.
They were just minor tricks,
for he had never met a famous master
to teach him any great skills.
Despite this,
one knows not how much money he wasted on these things.
Furthermore,
from childhood, he loved female beauty.
If he saw a beautiful woman,
he would rather spend over a hundred taels of silver
to ensure he could have her.
As for brothels and courtesan houses,
that goes without saying.
There was also a group of idlers who helped him spend money,
and one knows not how much money was wasted there either.
After ten years passed,
he had completely exhausted his family estate.
Houses and fields
were all sold and the proceeds spent.
Relying solely on his own skills,
he served as a squad leader in this prefecture.
He rented a small house in the lane behind the prefectural office to live in.
He had married a wife when he was young,
who had not borne children;
two years ago, she too was brought to ruin by his fate,
and he was once again alone.
He only frequented brothels and places of ill repute;
he did not marry another wife.
People saw he was a scoundrel,
and none were willing to give their daughters to him.
Occasionally, there were those willing to give him their daughters,
but he would find fault with them.
Truly, high ambitions are hard to satisfy,
and his late fortune had not yet met its time.
Speaking of which,
he also had one good quality:
he was generous in making friends.
When he had no money,
he would rather tighten his belt to get by.
As soon as he had money in hand,
he and his many brothers would spend all day eating and drinking together.
If things did not go his way,
he would pull out his fists and start hitting.
Thus, everyone both feared him
and liked him.
Enough of these idle words.
One day,
Wáng Zé entered the office at the fifth watch to sign the register;
after finishing his duties, he came out
and saw a crowd of people gathered in front of the prefectural office.
Wáng Zé stood on his tiptoes to take a look
and saw a woman dressed in mourning sitting on the ground.
When he looked closely,
he saw:
She was dressed in plain white silk,
with a hemp skirt tied around her waist.
Without wearing any powder or rouge,
her natural form was enchanting;
disinclined to wear kingfisher feathers or pearls,
she was naturally endowed with heavenly beauty.
With her cloud-like hair partially arranged,
she was like Xī Zǐ clutching her heart when first falling ill;
with star-like eyes shifting like waves,
she was like Wénjūn listening to music while filled with sorrow.
She was just like Cháng’é leaving the Moon Palace,
or the Zhīnǚ descending from the Jasper Pool.
Wáng Zé then asked his followers:
"What is that woman doing here?"
A follower replied:
"I have long heard that this woman sells mud candles here."
Wáng Zé said:
"I am in the government offices every day,
and I have heard talk of this for many days,
saying that a woman sells mud candles.
My fellow officials
have also bought them to light,
and they are quite bright.
I wanted to ask her,
why are they called mud candles?"
The follower said:
"To speak of it is quite startling.
That woman digs up mud from the ground,
mixes it with water,
molds it onto a bamboo stick
like a candle,
and as soon as it touches a flame, it catches fire.
From the time the lamps are lit
until dawn, it burns."
Wáng Zé heard this
and thought to himself:
"This is indeed strange;
I have always been fond of magic tricks.
This one is truly astonishing."
He then squeezed through the crowd
and saw that the woman had finished making them;
she washed her hands with water
and said:
"I sell these candles for three coins each."
Everyone scrambled to buy them,
but Wáng Zé said:
"Wait a moment!
None of you buy any!"
Everyone recognized that Wáng Zé was a Dūpái.
When he shouted not to buy,
no one dared to buy.
The woman raised her head,
saw Wáng Zé,
stood up, and offered a greeting.
Wáng Zé returned the courtesy
and said:
"You take mud to make candles;
how can they be lit?"
The woman said:
"Dūpái,
I have been selling them here for more than half a month.
If they could not be lit,
people would not come to buy from me.
I make ten a day,
and they are always sold out."
Wáng Zé said:
"Do not trick me."
He pulled open his lapel, took thirty coins from his pouch,
and bought them all.
The woman handed the candles to Wáng Zé.
Wáng Zé said:
"Wait a moment.
If I buy them and they cannot be lit,
I have wasted my money.
It is not that I do not believe you,
but I truly have never seen such a thing.
Light one for me to see."
The woman said:
"That is easy.
Dūpái, send someone to get a light."
Wáng Zé ordered a follower to fetch a light
and gave it to the woman.
The woman kindled a splinter
and lit all ten mud candles for Wáng Zé to see.
Wáng Zé watched and praised:
"Indeed,
it is truly startling.
I do not want these ten candles;
those of you who want them can take them."
The crowd took them away.
The woman stood up, packed her knife and bowl,
placed them in a basket,
offered a greeting to the crowd,
and left.
Wáng Zé sent his followers back first
and followed the woman at his leisure.
Wáng Zé said nothing,
but thought to himself:
"This woman is not from our Bèi Zhōu;
I think she lives in the grass market.
I will follow her to her house,
spend some money,
and it would be good to learn this magic."
He saw the woman exit the West Gate,
pass the grass market,
and keep walking.
Wáng Zé said:
"Since she does not live in the grass market,
I wonder where she lives?"
They walked another ten lǐ or so,
and he did not recognize the place.
Wáng Zé said:
"This woman is a strange and mysterious person.
I should go back
and wait until tomorrow when she comes to sell again
to ask for her address."
He turned around to find his way back,
but when he looked,
it was not the old path he had come by.
He saw only towering cliffs and high mountain peaks
blocking his way;
he could not return.
Nor was there anyone walking about.
While he was panicking,
he saw the woman ahead calling out loudly:
"Wáng Dūpái!
It was not easy to get you here;
why do you want to go back so soon?"
Terrified, Wáng Zé trembled as he stepped forward and said:
"Lady!
Who are you?"
The woman said:
"Dūpái!
Shèng Gūgū sent me to invite you to discuss a great matter.
Do not be suspicious.
I will go with you."
Wáng Zé said:
"How strange!
I want to go back,
but unfortunately I have lost my way,
so I must follow her."
They entered a pine forest together,
and after a long time, they emerged from the forest
and saw a manor house.
Wáng Zé asked:
"What place is this?"
The woman said:
"This is where Shèng Gūgū stays;
she has been waiting for the Dūpái for a long time."
When Wáng Zé reached the front of the manor,
two young girls in green clothes came out
and called:
"Is this Wáng Dūpái?"
The woman said:
"It is!"
The girls in green said:
"The Immortal Aunt has been waiting for you for a long time!"
They led Wáng Zé straight to the hall
and announced:
"Wáng Dūpái has been invited here."
Wáng Zé saw an old woman wearing a star crown
and a crane-feather cloak
sitting in the hall.
The woman said:
"This is Shèng Gū;
why do you not pay your respects?"
Wáng Zé bowed in greeting at the hall.
Shèng Gūgū invited Wáng Zé up into the hall.
After the three were seated,
she called for tea to be served,
then Shèng Gūgū ordered the girls to prepare wine and attend to Wáng Dūpái.
Wáng Zé felt bold and spirited
and was very pleased.
He said to Shèng Gūgū:
"Wáng Zé is fated
to meet the Immortal Aunt today.
What instructions do you have for me?"
Shèng Gūgū said:
"Let us drink wine while we deliberate.
Now the time has come,
and you correspond to the heavenly fate;
it is time for you to rise to prominence.
Of the thirty-six prefectures of Héběi,
it is ordained that you shall rule them alone."
Wáng Zé said:
"Immortal Aunt, do not say such things;
the ears and eyes of the government are near.
Wáng Zé is but a soldier in Bèi Zhōu;
how would I dare to become the lord of thirty-six prefectures?"
Shèng Gūgū said:
"If you did not have this fortune,
I would not have sent someone to invite you.
I only fear it would be a pity if you missed the opportunity.
There is one more thing;
I fear you are alone with no one to help you succeed."
Pointing to the woman who sold the mud candles, she said:
"I have this daughter,
whose childhood name is Yǒng'ér.
She is still a maiden
and is your predestined spouse of five hundred years.
I now give this daughter to you as a wife
to help you achieve your goals.
What do you think?"
Wáng Zé was immensely joyful in his heart,
and thought to himself:
"I am twenty-eight years old this year,
my wife died last year,
and I have not yet remarried.
Today the Xiāngū gives this beautiful woman to me;
is this not a miraculous encounter predestined by Heaven?"
Wáng Zé said:
"I am grateful for the Xiāngū's kind intentions;
how would I dare to refuse?
When Wáng Zé was young,
I once met an extraordinary person who read my physiognomy
and said that as I approached the age of thirty,
I would certainly rise to prominence.
Today, having received the Xiāngū's promotion,
his words have indeed come true.
However, there is one matter:
the detestable Zhīzhōu of Bèizhōu has pestered Wáng Zé to procure all sorts of gold, silver, and colorful silks,
but he is unwilling to repay the shops their money,
causing ruin to all the laborers and trades,
so that every single one of them harbors resentment and curses him.
Recently, the two battalions of government troops in this prefecture,
after three months of service,
wanted to draw one month's salary,
but he also refused them.
I wanted to contend with him,
but his power in the imperial court is great,
and I cannot compete with him.
People of the same generation as Wáng Zé,
I do not know how many have suffered from his cruel harm.
If we want to remove an official who oppresses the people,
but do not yet have the strength,
how can we accomplish great deeds?"
Shènggūgu laughed and said:
"If you are alone,
how could you succeed?
You must rely on your wife.
She has a hundred thousand troops under her command to assist you;
you are bound to succeed in your rebellion."
Wáng Zé laughed and said:
"I have heard that moving an army for one day
costs a thousand pieces of gold.
Stopping or moving daily without rest
exhausts the resources of the land.
If there are so many troops and horses,
they would require a vast amount of grain and fodder.
How large can a manor be,
and where would these hundred thousand troops be stationed?"
Shènggūgu laughed and said:
"My troops here require no grain or fodder,
nor do they need a place to encamp.
When they are needed urgently, use them;
when not in use, put them away."
Wáng Zé said:
"If it is like that, then it is perfect!"
Shènggūgu said:
"I shall let you see my troops for a moment."
Shènggūgu called Yǒng’ér to go in and bring out two small baskets.
One basket contained beans,
and the other contained cut rice straw.
Yǒng’ér took a handful of beans
and a handful of rice straw.
She scattered the straw,
shouted "Swiftly!",
and they transformed into about two hundred cavalrymen in front of the hall.
Wáng Zé saw this
and cheered, saying:
"Since you have the skill to turn cut straw into horses
and scatter beans to make soldiers,
why should I worry that the great deed will not be accomplished!"
While they were speaking,
they suddenly heard someone outside the manor shouting loudly:
"What a fine thing you are doing here!
The authorities have now issued a notice to arrest sorcerers.
Yet you are here turning straw into horses
and scattering beans to make soldiers,
intending to start an uprising and rebel."
This gave Wáng Zé a great fright,
as if his skull had split into eight pieces
and half a bucket of ice and snow had been poured over him.
It is truly as they say: "The scheme is not yet complete,
but how could one know a person is listening outside the window?
The plan has just been deployed,
but disaster has already arisen from within."
Indeed:
One may deploy infinite heavenly schemes,
But it is hard to avoid an eavesdropper behind the window.
After all, who was the person who came?
Please listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
People say the heterodox way is not a true art,
Fearing only that its transmission is incomplete.
If the transmission is received with a righteous heart,
Why bother studying to be an immortal outside the world?
It is said that while Wáng Zé was in the thatched hall watching the troops,
and while they were speaking,
he suddenly heard someone shouting:
"Are you here to start an uprising and rebel?"
Wáng Zé was so frightened that his heart panicked and his courage failed.
Raising his head to look,
he saw a person
of strange and eccentric appearance,
wearing an iron crown on his head,
straw sandals on his feet,
and a scarlet robe with black borders on his body.
His face was like sprayed blood,
and his eyes were like strange stars.
Riding a tiger,
he came straight into the manor.
Shènggūgu said:
"Zhāng Xiānsheng,
I am here with Wáng Dūpái discussing matters.
If you come, then come;
why must you make such a fuss?"
The master jumped off the tiger,
shouted "Retreat!",
and the tiger went out the gate.
The master exchanged salutations with Shènggūgu.
Wáng Zé bowed to the master.
The master returned the greeting,
and they sat down.
Shènggūgu said:
"Zhāng Xiānsheng!
This is Wáng Dūpái of Bèizhōu.
In five days, you shall all assist him."
The master said to Wáng Zé:
"This humble Taoist's surname is Zhāng and given name is Luán.
I have often told Shènggūgu that the Dūpái can dominate a region.
I have several times wished to meet the Dūpái,
but fearing you would not agree,
I did not dare to visit.
Shènggūgu!
How did you get Wáng Dūpái to come here?"
Shènggūgu said:
"I sent Yǒng’ér to the front of the Bèizhōu yamen to use some small tricks
to lead the Dūpái here.
We were just about to discuss matters
when you arrived."
The master said:
"I do not know when the Dūpái will start the uprising?"
Shènggūgu said:
"It will be very soon.
Waiting for the army's morale to shift
and break out all at once,
you shall all come to assist in the uprising."
Before she had finished speaking,
they saw a strange beast enter from outside the manor gate.
When Wáng Zé looked,
it was a lion,
which came straight into the thatched hall, circling and roaring.
Wáng Zé saw it
and was both surprised and delighted,
saying:
"This is a heavenly beast;
how can it also exist in the mortal world?
It must be my destiny to see it."
Just as he was about to ask,
Shènggūgu shouted:
"Since this fellow has come to assist the Dūpái,
why act so strange?
You may withdraw your divine power."
The lion shook its head,
the lion disappeared,
and in its place was a man.
Wáng Zé asked Shènggūgu:
"Who is this person?"
Shènggūgu said:
"This man's surname is Bǔ and given name is Jí."
She called Bǔ Jí to meet Wáng Zé.
After the greetings were over,
they sat down in the thatched hall.
Shènggūgu said:
"Wáng Dūpái!
Have you seen the abilities of Zhāng Luán
and Bǔ Jí?"
Wáng Zé said:
"With these two being so formidable,
I am not afraid that the great deed will not be accomplished."
Shènggūgu said:
"We still need one more person to come and help you succeed."
Wáng Zé said:
"Who else is there?"
Just as they were speaking,
they saw a divine crane flying down from the sky.
It landed at the thatched hall,
and a person jumped down from its back.
Zhāng Luán,
Bǔ Jí, and Yǒng'ér all rose to salute that person.
When Wáng Zé looked at that person,
he was lame in one leg
and his stature was no more than four feet.
He wore a tattered kerchief
and a coarse cloth shirt;
his leg wraps were torn and broken.
He wore a pair of broken-eared hemp shoes,
with some straw rope tied around his waist.
Seeing him in such a state, Wáng Zé
did not move
and thought to himself:
"I wonder who this is?"
Shèng Gūgu said,
"Wáng Dūpái!
This is my son, Zuǒ Chù.
Now that he has come,
your great undertaking is assured.
Why do you not rise to welcome him?"
Hearing this, Wáng Zé
hurriedly rose to offer his salutations.
Zuǒ Chù came up to the thatched hall,
gave a greeting to Shèng Gūgu,
and sat down below the others.
He asked Shèng Gūgu,
"I beg to ask, Niángniáng!
Has Wáng Dūpái's business been accomplished yet?"
Shèng Gūgu said,
"My child!
Regarding matters, it is either sooner or later.
We were waiting specifically for you to come;
then this matter will be accomplished."
Zuǒ Chù said,
"Since the discussion is settled,
it is rare for the Dūpái to be here.
We might as well keep him tonight to complete the marriage with my sister, Yǒng'ér.
And we shall trouble Mister Zhāng to act as the matchmaker;
would that not be good?"
Shèng Gūgu said,
"That matches my intention exactly!"
She then ordered the maidservant to lead Wáng Dūpái to the fragrant water bathhouse to bathe.
Wáng Zé took a cleansing bath,
and the maidservant brought a set of new clothes to change him completely.
Shèng Gūgu ordered the dragon robe to be brought out,
along with the jade belt,
the sky-pointing crown,
and the 'free-from-worry' shoes,
and invited him to wear them.
Wáng Zé had never seen such finery before
and did not dare accept them.
Just then, the Lame Master hobbled over
and called out,
"Dūpái!
Do not be humble.
If you have doubts,
I will lead you to the Sān Shēng Chí to show you your origin in this life."
Wáng Zé followed the Lame Master out of the villa
and came to the side of a clear water pool.
The Lame Master told Wáng Zé to look at his reflection in the clear water.
Wáng Zé looked and was greatly shocked;
he saw his own reflection in the water,
wearing the sky-pointing crown on his head,
the billowing dragon robe on his body,
a white jade belt around his waist,
and the 'free-from-worry' shoes on his feet.
His appearance was dignified,
solemnly resembling the Son of Heaven of a dynasty.
The Lame Master said,
"Dūpái!
Do you see?
The mandate of heaven is already fixed;
you cannot be humble."
Only then did Wáng Zé believe it,
and he dressed himself up immediately.
He saw the music of drums and pipes filling the air in the thatched hall,
while eight maidservants with gauze lanterns and palace fans
attended Yǒng'ér as she came out.
With her pearl crown and embroidered jacket,
her attire was exceptional,
just like a consort in the imperial palace.
The two performed the marriage rites in the thatched hall.
How was it?
One could see:
Famous incense burned throughout,
extraordinary colors hung high.
A hundred-year marriage,
smiling words brought about the wedding night.
A scene of joy,
escorted into the orchid chamber by songs and reed pipes.
From whence came this elegant imperial son?
He is clearly Xiāng Wáng in the dream of Wū Shān.
Who could be like the graceful divine lady?
None but the consort in the Tiānbǎo Gōng.
With affection like mountains and devotion like seas, their joy was complete;
in a world of brocade and flowers, their wealth and honor were great.
That night in the bridal chamber,
everything was arranged most neatly.
Wáng Zé thought,
"Could this be a dream?
If it is not a dream,
could it truly be real!"
He added,
"Even if it is not real,
it is still a good dream,
and I might as well enjoy it."
This was because Wáng Zé and Hú Yǒng'ér,
one was the reincarnation of Lady Wǔ Zétiān,
turning from female to male.
The other was the reincarnation of Zhāng Chāngzōng,
turning from male to female.
They had previously made a sincere vow at the Bǎi Huā Tíng,
wishing to be husband and wife forever, generation after generation.
After nearly four hundred years,
they harmonized their old oath again
and formed a new union of joy.
The affection between the husband and wife
needs no further mention.
They stayed together for three days in a row;
it was truly a case of soft jade and fragrant warmth blurring day and night,
with time passing amidst piles of flowers and clusters of brocade.
This goes without saying.
On the fourth day,
Shèng Gūgu invited Wáng Dūpái to discuss matters,
saying,
"The fortune of the times has arrived,
and one should quickly act according to the opportunity.
Do not be greedily attached to the new marriage
and forget the great undertaking!"
The Lame Master said,
"Dūpái, you should return for now.
Tomorrow, I, along with Mister Zhāng and the others, will enter Bèizhōu to initiate the uprising for you."
In his heart, Wáng Zé wished he could stay for a few more days.
On one hand, he was being urged by the others,
and on the other hand, he had not been home for three days to see to things,
fearing that something might have happened in the prefecture.
He had no choice but to thank Shèng Gūgu and bid farewell to Hú Yǒng'ér,
dressing once again in the clothes he arrived in.
The Lame Master led him away from the villa and out of the woods,
pointing to a path and telling him to return.
When Wáng Zé turned his head to look,
the Lame Master was gone.
After walking only a few steps,
he had already reached the gate of Bèizhōu City.
Wáng Zé was startled and said,
"How strange!
Previously, I walked for half a day
to reach the Immortal Lady's villa.
Now, having walked not even several dozen steps,
I have already reached the city gate.
It turns out this group are all extraordinary people,
all capable of magic,
and they have come to assist me.
I must certainly be destined for success."
Wáng Zé entered the city that day,
and it was still around the hour of the sheep.
First, he walked past the front of the prefecture office
to observe the situation.
He saw two or three officers who, upon seeing Wáng Zé,
said:
"Wáng Dūpái!
Where have you been for these several days?
The Zhīzhōu Xiānggōng summoned you but you did not appear;
he is quite irritated!"
Upon hearing this, Wáng Zé
hurriedly ran into the prefecture office
and met with the Zhīzhōu.
The Zhīzhōu asked:
"Wáng Zé!
Where have you been these past few days?"
Wáng Zé said:
"This humble one went to the countryside to visit a relative.
I originally intended to return in one day,
but unexpectedly I caught a chill on the road
and was bedridden for three days.
I only managed to get up this morning.
Hearing that Your Honor had summoned me,
I came specifically to pay my respects
and have not even been home yet."
The Zhīzhōu said:
"Since you were ill,
I will not hold it against you.
Five days ago, I sent you to the shop to fetch colored silks.
The Madam complained that the colors were not bright
and the lengths were short;
they are unusable.
You are to take them
and exchange them for the same number immediately.
I give you until tomorrow to deliver them.
The young lady's auspicious date is near,
and we are waiting specifically to cut the clothes;
do not be late or delay."
He kept him there and called a trusted personal attendant to bring out the colored silks from the private residence,
thirteen bolts in total,
and told Wáng Zé to count the number clearly and take them away.
Wáng Zé complied
and, carrying them with both hands, left the prefecture office.
He went straight to his own house and sat down,
thinking:
"I, Wáng Zé, have such miserable luck!
I just had three days of happiness,
and upon returning, before I could even get a cup of tea,
this corrupt official is pestering me again.
It is you who wants to marry off a daughter;
what does that have to do with us people of Bèi Zhōu?
He refuses to pay the shopkeepers their silver
and forces people to give him credit.
After taking the goods,
he still nitpicks and complains,
making a mess of things
and then sending me to exchange them.
You officials
are truly so tyrannical."
While speaking,
he unfolded the colored silks,
intending to refold them properly.
When he lifted them to look,
he was startled.
When they were sent in before, they were whole bolts,
but now the lengths had been cut.
Checking bolt by bolt,
they were all like this.
He took a ruler to measure them;
each bolt was short by five feet.
Wáng Zé said:
"Missing a bolt or so would be a small matter,
but unfortunately they have all been cut and damaged.
Since they are not the original items,
how could the shopkeeper be willing to exchange them?
It must be the subordinates who are cheating;
how would the official know?
I must go and inform him clearly
to see what he says."
He hurriedly folded them up
and carried them back to the prefecture office.
The Zhīzhōu had already adjourned the court.
Wáng Zé said:
"I will take them back for now;
it will not be too late to report to him tomorrow morning."
The next day, he rose early
and waited for the Zhīzhōu to enter the hall.
Wáng Zé held the thirteen bolts of colored silk
and knelt below.
Seeing him, the Zhīzhōu said happily:
"Wáng Zé!
You are indeed a capable man.
I instructed you yesterday,
and you have already exchanged them this morning."
Wáng Zé reported:
"They have not been exchanged yet.
When Your Honor issued these colored silks yesterday,
they were no longer the original items.
I do not know who,
but five feet were cut from each bolt.
How can this humble one exchange them?
I beg for Your Honor's instruction."
The Zhīzhōu said:
"Yesterday I told you to inspect and receive them in court.
If they were cut,
you should have said so then."
Wáng Zé said:
"In court, this humble one only counted the number of bolts.
When I returned home and looked closely,
only then did I realize they were short.
I hurriedly came to inform Your Honor,
but at that time Your Honor had already dismissed the court.
It was already late,
and this humble one did not dare to send word.
I specifically came to wait this morning."
The Zhīzhōu said in a great rage:
"Nonsense!
Yesterday they were inspected and received clearly,
so they should have been returned to the shop.
But you took them home;
it must be through your own lack of care
that someone in your house cut them,
and this morning you come back here to make this wild report.
If not for your usual diligent service,
I should have given you a severe beating with the staff.
Go immediately and exchange them,
and do not say another word!"
He scolded Wáng Zé until he was speechless.
Wáng Zé could only carry them back as before
and sat at home in low spirits.
While he was searching for a way out but finding none,
he saw three people enter from outside.
When Wáng Zé looked,
they were none other than
Zuǒ Chù, Zhāng Luán,
and Bǔ Jí.
After the four of them finished exchanging greetings,
the three saw the pile of silks on the table
and asked:
"Where did these come from?"
Wáng Zé said:
"It is a long story."
He then explained how the Zhīzhōu had cut and damaged the original items
and the matter of wanting him to exchange them at the shop;
he told them everything in detail.
Zuǒ Chù said:
"What difficulty is there in this?
I, the poor Daoist, will take it upon myself to exchange them for you."
Immediately, he took the thirteen bolts of colored silk,
piled them in a heap on the ground,
and covered them with his coarse cloth gown.
Muttering an incantation,
he shouted:
"Swiftly!"
When he lifted the gown to look,
they had turned into thirteen bolts of bright and fresh colored silk.
Wáng Zé said in great joy:
"I must trouble you three to sit for a moment
while I take these to the prefecture office;
I will return to keep you company."
The three said:
"We have matters to discuss anyway;
go quickly and come back quickly."
Beaming with smiles, Wáng Zé
carried the colored silks to the prefecture office.
There is a poem to prove it:
At the post, no matter how the dowry is prepared,
Silk is cut and damaged, and others are made to pay.
Those with office hope to use their power for a thousand years,
But for their lack of reason, Heaven decrees their ruin in a single day.
The Zhīzhōu returned to the yamen and took his seat,
seeing that the brightly colored silks had been exchanged.
Needless to say, he was delighted.
Wáng Zé counted them out exactly as specified,
and delivered them to the private yamen for receipt.
He quickly hurried back home,
where those three people were waiting for him.
Wáng Zé said,
"I have failed to accompany you;
please do not take offense."
He added,
"Since you three have come here,
it is only proper to serve tea.
However, Wáng Zé is short-handed at home;
please, the three of you, go to the wine shop next door to drink a few cups."
Zhāng Luán smiled and said,
"We haven't yet shared a cup of wedding wine."
Pointing at the Qué Shī, he said,
"Don't mention this elder brother-in-law;
today we should just be treated as the matchmakers."
Zuǒ Chù jumped up and said,
"Let us not talk of relatives or old friends.
Since we have met,
we must drink until we are drunk before we stop."
Bǔ Jí said,
"The Qué Shī still speaks most forthrightly."
Wáng Zé said,
"Today is an off-duty day,
and the colored silks have already been delivered;
it is a perfect time for a long stay."
The four of them went to the upper floor of the wine shop
and sat by the window.
While they were drinking merrily,
they saw groups of official banners and troops passing by below.
Wáng Zé said,
"Today is not a drill day;
why are the government troops from both camps out in full force?"
Zuǒ Chù said,
"Wáng Dūpái!
Go down and ask
what the reason is."
When Wáng Zé went downstairs and out the door to look,
everyone recognized Wáng Zé
and all came to greet him.
Wáng Zé said,
"Where have you all come from?"
The Guǎnyíng said,
"Dūpái!
The Zhīzhōu is making life miserable for those of us who receive pay.
We have served for three months,
but now he won't even give us a single month's pay and rice.
We went to the granary today,
but the granary clerk just beat us back."
Wáng Zé said,
"If it is like that,
then what should be done?"
The Guǎnyíng said,
"If he still won't issue the payment tomorrow,
the crowd will surely revolt."
The Guǎnyíng and the crowd left.
Wáng Zé went back upstairs and repeated the Guǎnyíng's words
to Zuǒ Chù.
Zuǒ Chù stood up and said,
"Hurry and catch up to the Guǎnyíng,
tell them to come back,
and offer to issue one month's pay and rice to them.
This will make the hearts of the troops from both camps submit to you."
Wáng Zé said,
"Sir, where will so much money and rice come from?"
Zuǒ Chù said,
"Just tell them to come back;
I have my own arrangements."
Wáng Zé then caught up with the Guǎnyíng
and told him to stop the men:
"Return, and you will all be given one month's pay and rice."
Hearing this, the Guǎnyíng
called the men back to Wáng Zé's doorstep.
They saw rice piled up like a mountain inside Wáng Zé's house.
Wáng Zé thought to himself,
"How is it that the tables and stools in the house have all disappeared?
And from where did this room full of rice come?"
The Quézi beckoned with his hand and said,
"All of you, if you have the strength,
it doesn't matter if you carry one or two dàn.
Just do not make a racket."
Those paid soldiers came in groups of three and five to carry it;
some could carry one dàn on their backs,
some could carry two dàn,
using all their strength to move it.
Wáng Zé said,
"There are only about a hundred dàn of rice here;
with six thousand people in the two camps,
how can it be distributed to everyone?"
Zuǒ Chù said,
"Do not you mind me;
I guarantee that they will all have rice."
The crowd started carrying from the hour of noon
until the hour of evening,
having carried more than ten thousand dàn,
and there were still four or five dàn left in the house.
The Guǎnyíng and many others came to thank Wáng Zé.
Zuǒ Chù said,
"Wáng Dūpái!
One should not trouble two hosts for one guest.
