Since you intend to grant a favor,
tonight there is moonlight.
Speak to the Guǎnyíng
and tell him to go to the camp and inform everyone
to come tonight and receive one month's pay,
so as to save it until tomorrow
and not do one task in two parts."
When the Guǎnyíng heard this,
he was overjoyed
and went as if flying to tell everyone to come and receive the money.
Wáng Zé said,
"Sir, you have distributed so much rice;
now, where is the money?"
Zuǒ Chù said,
"I have it!"
Zhāng Luán said,
"I have one thousand strings of cash deposited at the City God Temple in Bópíng Xiàn.
I got them this morning,
and they are now under the Dūpái's bed."
Wáng Zé went in to look,
and sure enough, it was packed full under the bed.
He did not know how it had been transported.
While he was marveling,
he felt his foot stepping on the end of a coin string,
looking as if it were buried in the ground.
Wáng Zé bent down
and gave it a pull.
The string came out with his hand,
and closely threaded on the string were high-quality official coins;
it was like a spinning wheel,
being pulled out endlessly.
Wáng Zé became flustered.
Just as he was about to let go,
he heard a great laugh,
and suddenly a monk emerged from the coin string,
wearing gold rings in his ears
and a fiery-red cassock.
Wáng Zé was scared out of his wits
and dropped his hand to run outside.
The monk also came out after him,
calling out,
"This poor monk has arrived late today;
Dūpái, please do not be offended!"
Zhāng,
Zuǒ, and the others saw him
and all recognized him as the Dànzǐ Héshang.
The two said to Wáng Zé,
"This is Dàn Shī;
he is also one of our family,
come to help the Dūpái raise a great undertaking."
Wáng Zé said,
"Could it be the one who offended Lord Bāo Lóngtú in Kāifēng Fǔ?"
Qué Shī said,
"It is indeed so!"
Only then did Wáng Zé feel at ease
and came forward to meet him.
Dànzǐ Héshang said,
"Years ago, I obtained three thousand strings of cash from Shàn Wáng Tàiwèi,
with no place to spend them.
This morning I heard Zhāng Xiānsheng went to Bópíng Xiàn to get money for the Dūpái to reward the army,
so I also brought these three thousand strings to help."
Qué Shī said,
"With six thousand people, give each one a string.
We now have four thousand strings,
so we are still short by two thousand."
Zhāng Luán said,
"I will provide the full three thousand strings."
Bǔ Jí said,
"There is no need to trouble my master's divine power;
the disciple has already prepared it."
The five of them went inside together
and carried it out.
One thousand strings were made into a pile,
until the room was filled with money.
Before they finished piling,
those who were invited were all at the door.
Wáng Zé told them to come in and carry it away,
with each person only allowed to carry one string.
This group was surprised beyond measure,
and none of them dared to ask for more.
By the moonlight,
they carried for about two watches,
and just then everyone from the two camps had their share.
Among these six thousand people and their families,
who did not praise him?
"What a great Wáng Dūpái!
Who would be willing to let others carry away their own money and rice at will?
Provided one is quick of hand and foot
and has the strength,
having received three months' pay and rice
and being settled at home,
what is there to worry about?"
On that day, Zuǒ Chù and the other four finished distributing the money and rice,
bid farewell to Wáng Zé and departed,
agreeing to return the next day.
On the following day, it was Wáng Zé’s turn to be on duty;
at the third point of the fifth watch, he entered the Zhōu office to wait for the Zhīzhōu to ascend the hall.
This Zhīzhōu was surnamed Zhāng and named Dé.
People throughout the commandery cursed him, saying:
“Wrapped in silks and satins, he is a true beast;
fed on a hundred delicacies, he is a mere brute.
How lamentable is the misfortune of this place;
when will this thorn in our eye be pulled out?”
This Zhīzhōu ignored proper affairs every day;
he only wanted money.
On that day, as he sat in the hall,
he summoned the soldier Wáng Zé.
Wáng Zé offered his greetings from below the hall and said:
“I request Xiànggōng’s commands.”
The Zhīzhōu said:
“Wáng Zé!
I heard you are extraordinarily wealthy,
for yesterday you distributed money and rice on my behalf to six thousand people.
Since you wanted to distribute things to them,
why did you not come to report to me first
and wait for me to authorize the release?”
Wáng Zé did not dare to say that someone had conjured them through magic;
just as he was about to give an evasive answer
and before the words had left his mouth,
he saw two men below the steps
wearing purple jackets
with silk sashes tied around their waists;
they offered greetings and reported:
“We inform Xiànggōng!
Although the granary seals were undisturbed,
ten-odd bins of rice have vanished.”
That Zhīzhōu was startled.
While he was still confused,
the treasury manager came out and reported:
“We inform Xiànggōng!
Although the treasury seals were undisturbed,
two thousand strings of cash have vanished!”
It turned out that the rice from Quéshī
and the money from Bǔ Jí
were all transported from the warehouses of this Zhōu.
The Zhīzhōu said:
“I see!
I see!
Wáng Zé!
Rice is missing from my granaries,
and money is missing from my treasury.
Your family has no warehouse,
so how could you distribute money and rice to six thousand people?
Clearly, you used some sorcery of transportation to steal them.”
Wáng Zé, having been found out,
had no words to answer.
The Zhīzhōu ordered the jailers to bring a long cangue,
had Wáng Zé shackled in the hall,
ordered him sent to prison,
and instructed the Sīlǐ Yuàn to interrogate him.
It was because this Zhāng Tàiyǐn put Wáng Zé in prison
that it was fated:
his own head and body would be in different places,
his whole family would meet an untimely death,
and the people of Bèi Zhōu would find no peace.
After all, what disaster did the Zhīzhōu provoke?
Please listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
Liú Chǒng’s pure reputation is known throughout the world;
to this day, his memorial temple remains by the river.
Recently, many capable men on the official path
also follow the master in selecting big coins.
This poem was written by a famous talent named Wáng Shūnéng.
In Qiánqīng Zhèn in Shàoxīng, there is a Qián Tàishǒu Temple;
this Tàishǒu was surnamed Liú and named Chǒng.
During the time of Emperor Huán of the Western Hàn, he served as the Huìjī Tàishǒu.
He was as pure as water,
without a speck of corruption.
On the day he was promoted and about to depart,
many elders of Shānyīn County wept as they saw him off;
each person brought a hundred coins
to gift him as travel expenses.
Liú Chǒng was moved by their intentions
and selected one large coin to accept.
Later generations, remembering his pure virtue,
built a temple to sacrifice to him,
calling it the Yī Qián Tàishǒu Temple;
the town was thus called Qiánqīng Zhèn.
Wáng Shūnéng happened to pass through this town
and bowed before the statue of the Tàishǒu.
Thinking of the corruption on the official path recently,
where they take whatever large sums of money they can get,
he thus inscribed these four lines of poetry.
Although it was well-written,
it is a pity it did not fully capture the meaning.
Nowadays, if an official only picked large sums to seek after,
he would be considered one with high aspirations.
Their calculations
are just like the rules of arithmetic,
without missing a single bit.
Their taking of money
is like those who make mud bricks—
they scrape off even three-tenths of the topsoil.
They do not care whether it is a large sum or a small sum;
they are like those who rake ash or sweep the floor—
whatever they shovel into the dustpan is theirs.
To only say they “select big coins”
surely does not fully capture the meaning.
Another poem says:
“At first, they only picked big coins to pack away;
recently, even the smallest bits enter their bags.
If taking money could be limited to small amounts,
what harm would there be in calling them honest officials?”
Those corrupt officials also have a strategy;
when they get money,
they set aside several parts out of ten to use for securing connections above,
and thus they obtain a fine promotion all the same.
Even if public opinion happens to expose them,
or they offend an opponent
and are dismissed to live at home,
they still become great wealthy landowners.
They end up enjoying abundance for the rest of their lives;
their descendants have fertile fields and beautiful houses,
fine clothes and swift horses—what luxury!
Let the local people curse them as they will,
their ears do not hear it.
For example, an honest official
has no one to support him
and no one to please him;
he is simply written off.
Returning to his hometown with many snivels and tears
that he cannot take home anyway,
he burdens his wife and children with hunger and cold,
and all his relatives complain.
Even if there is a wise emperor,
he is high up in the ninefold palace;
how could he know the details of the outside world?
Speaking of it in this way,
does it not seem that being a corrupt official is more advantageous?
Narrator,
according to what you say, everyone should be a corrupt official then.
Although that is the case,
when those thousands of mouths among the people curse or bless,
could it be that it is entirely useless?
Perhaps their descendants will be born with varying levels of wisdom or folly,
and the family’s fortune will fluctuate unevenly.
Secretly there is retribution;
the Way of Heaven is naturally unerring,
only people at the moment do not know it.
There is one more thing:
if the court’s fortune is as vast as heaven
and the region is peaceful,
then it can be counted as a stroke of luck.
But if the cycle of fortune happens to change
and the region is fated for trouble,
it will certainly be that corrupt official who provokes the disaster.
This disaster will still be faced by him first.
The previous chapter spoke of the Bèi Zhōu Zhīzhōu Zhāng Dé;
if he had not acted so recklessly,
how could he have incited the soldiers’ hearts
and caused such a great disaster?
This is the pattern of a corrupt official.
It is said that on that day, the Prefect saw that rice was missing from the granary
and money was missing from the treasury.
Overwhelmed by anxiety and irritation,
he sent Wáng Zé to the Sīlǐ Yuàn to be interrogated according to the law and reported back.
This investigating officer was surnamed Wáng and named Jiāng.
He questioned Wáng Zé, saying:
"It is said that yesterday you distributed salaries to two battalions.
How large could your house be,
and how could it hold the money and rice for six thousand people?
Today, much money is missing from the state treasury,
and much rice is missing from the granary.
Tell us, how did you produce it all?"
At first, Wáng Zé denied it,
but later, unable to withstand the torture and beating,
he was forced to confess:
"Yesterday was Wáng Zé’s day off duty.
Zé was sitting idly at home
when I saw many who were due for pay passing by my door,
all complaining:
'We have served for over three months,
but cannot even receive one month’s money and rice.'
Then four people came from somewhere unknown.
Without allowing Wáng Zé to explain,
they used my house to distribute money and rice to six thousand people.
Those four left on their own,
and I truly do not know who they were."
The investigating officer said:
"How can there be people whose names you do not know?
You did not ask their origins,
yet allowed them to distribute money and rice for salaries in your home."
He ordered the jailers to drag Wáng Zé down
and apply the finger-crushing rack with great force before beating him again.
Wáng Zé could not bear the suffering
and was forced to confess:
"One was named Zhāng Luán,
one was named Bǔ Jí,
one was called the Crippled Master Zuǒ Chù,
and one was called Master Dàn,
also known as the Pellet Monk (Tánzǐ Héshang)."
The officer provided paper and brush for Wáng Zé to write them down.
Upon seeing them, he was greatly shocked
and thought:
"This Bǔ Jí
and Zhāng Luán are the ones who killed the Prefect of Zhèngzhōu and fled.
The Pellet Monk is the one who swindled Grand Marshal Shàn Wáng out of three thousand strings of cash,
and even Bāo Lóngtú could do nothing against him on several occasions.
Currently, arrest warrants have been issued from both places.
As for that Crippled Master Zuǒ Chù,
I do not know who he is,
but he surely is no good person either.
How did this group all join together as a gang
and gather in Bèizhōu?
This matter is no small thing."
At that time, he had Wáng Zé sign his confession
and kept him imprisoned in the jail as before.
He immediately reported back to the Prefect,
detailing the stakes and consequences.
The Prefect was so frightened that his face turned the color of ash.
He wanted to conduct a serious search and arrest,
but feared these sorcerers could not be easily caught,
and would instead bring disaster upon him.
He wanted to cover it up
and even be lenient toward Wáng Zé,
but the money and rice in the storehouses had been lost and scattered.
Wáng Zé had clearly confessed to four people,
which was common knowledge to all,
so how could he drop the matter?
With such a major event,
to end it half-heartedly
would make it impossible to suppress the military and civilians
or serve as the master of the prefecture.
Thinking it over back and forth,
he could only issue a proclamation,
which stated:
Zhāng, Prefect of Bèizhōu,
Regarding the matter of arrest:
Following the confession of the Sergeant Wáng Zé, the sorcerous thieves Zhāng Luán and others who together robbed the storehouses have not yet been caught.
Should anyone capture the true thieves and bring them forward,
the government will grant a reward of one thousand strings of cash per person.
Those with knowledge who do not report it
will be punished along with them.
Thus publicized.
One is Zhāng Luán,
a wandering Daoist priest,
wearing an iron Rúyì crown
and a scarlet robe with black trim.
One is Bǔ Jí,
dressed as a traveler.
One is the Crippled Master Zuǒ Chù,
who is lame in the leg,
wearing a tattered headcloth
and a coarse cloth shirt.
One is Master Dàn,
also known as the Pellet Monk,
wearing gold rings in his ears
and a fiery-red monastic robe.
Fourth year of Qìnglì,
[blank] Month,
[blank] Day.
The Prefect ordered the clerks to write a dozen copies of the proclamation
and hang them on every gate, in front of the prefectural office,
and at key thoroughfares inside and outside the city.
Meanwhile, he summoned the arresting officers
and set a deadline for the capture;
this need not be further discussed.
Now, the six thousand people from the two battalions and their families all said, "Wáng Zé’s family lent money and rice to us,
yet the Prefect treats it as a crime
and has sent him into the jail to suffer."
Everyone was talking in the teahouses and wine shops;
there was not one who did not curse the Prefect as a dog of a thief
who acted against all reason.
Before they had even finished speaking,
they saw the Crippled Master walking to the front of the barracks,
clapping his hands and shouting loudly:
"Listen, you officers in the camp who are due for pay!
Sergeant-Major Wáng acted improperly in distributing money and rice to you all;
you all saw him carry it out from his own house.
Yet the Prefect has hidden away the rice from the granary
and the money from the treasury,
concealing them,
and instead framed Sergeant-Major Wáng for theft.
He is about to send men to arrest your two Battalion Commanders
to seize your money and rice and return them to the granary and treasury.
I think for you men,
the rice has been eaten
and the money has been spent;
where will you get the compensation to return to the officials?"
When the crowd heard this,
they all broke into an uproar, saying:
"What we ate and used
was not government property.
They refuse to pay us the funds and grain currently due,
yet they want to seize what we have.
In that case,
they are truly forcing us to rebel."
The Crippled Master said:
"Sergeant-Major Wáng distributed money and rice to you with good intentions,
and now he has been beaten by the Prefect until his flesh is torn,
is confined in jail,
and his life is not guaranteed.
If you know how to repay a debt of gratitude,
are you willing to put forth the effort to rescue him?"
The crowd said:
"We also have this intention,
but our strength is not enough,
and we have no leader;
how can we rescue him?"
Zuǒ Chù said:
"Officers!
You speak rightly.
There must be one to take the lead.
I will lead you;
will you officers be willing to help?"
Everyone looked at Zuǒ Chù
and, without saying it aloud,
thought to themselves:
"Looking at how small he is,
and lame in the leg as well,
even if he jumped into a person’s throat,
he couldn't prick them to death.
Following him likely won't accomplish anything;
he's just a false front."
Zuǒ Chù, seeing the crowd was silent,
asked them:
"Why do you say nothing?
Could it be you despise me for being small and weak,
unable to do anything to anyone?
Shall I transform into someone who can deal with people for you to see?"
Zuǒ Chù began to chant a spell under his breath
and shouted:
"Swiftly!"
Revealing his divine power,
the four-foot-tall Crippled Master vanished.
In his place appeared a figure ten feet tall,
with a waist ten spans around,
a head like a carriage wheel,
and eyes like oil lamps,
holding two wind-slashing sabers that looked like two door panels.
The crowd was terrified at the sight
and hurriedly bowed, saying:
"We have eyes but did not recognize Mount Tàishān;
you are indeed a celestial god.
Now we know why, though Sergeant-Major Wáng’s house was not very large yesterday,
it could distribute money and rice to six thousand people."
When the crowd finished bowing and looked up,
it was indeed just the Crippled Master.
The Crippled Master said:
"Do not be half-hearted.
Because you people of Bèizhōu are destined for disaster,
Heaven has sent me to lift you up.
Whether you follow me or not
depends only on today."
Before the words were finished,
two weapons instructors leaped out from the military camp.
One was surnamed Zhāng and named Chéng;
the other was surnamed Dòu and named Wényù.
Each of the two held a staff in his hand
and shouted:
"Wáng Dūpái is a good man,
and it is only right that we rescue him.
Anyone who is unwilling to go,
I will first fight them for a hundred bouts."
The crowd shouted in unison:
"We will all go!
We will all go!"
The Crippled Teacher said:
"It is rare to find two men with such a sense of justice;
I must trouble you to act as leaders
and have them prepare their weapons here.
I will now go alone to rescue our Dūpái.
Once I have dealt with the Zhīzhōu of Bèizhōu,
you then come to reinforce me.
Once we have assisted Wáng Dūpái to become the master of Bèizhōu,
I will ensure you have plenty of food and clothing
and live happily for the rest of your lives."
When the crowd heard this,
they all responded:
"We will come at once to assist you!"
There is a poem to prove it:
"Chóngtóng was stingy with rewards and ultimately lost his state;
Wú Qǐ shared hardships and thus established great merit.
Merely because the rice and money were privately distributed,
in a single day, six thousand soldiers rebelled."
Zuǒ Chù left the front of the camp
and headed straight for the Prefect's office.
It just so happened that the Zhīzhōu was holding court in the hall,
sitting on a tiger-skin armchair,
talking nonsense.
When Zuǒ Chù entered,
he used a spell of invisibility,
so not a single person saw him.
Zuǒ Chù darted forward,
flashing behind the Zhīzhōu.
Seizing an opportunity,
he pulled the armchair backward,
and the Zhīzhōu fell to the ground with a thud.
The crowd hurriedly helped him up.
The Zhīzhōu said:
"I suppose the legs of the armchair have worn out over time;
get another one for me to sit on."
Zuǒ Chù laughed secretly:
"How could this dog of a corrupt official know about me, the Crippled Teacher,
that he also comes to use the term to mock me?
I shall play another trick on him!"
The crowd replaced the armchair,
spread the tiger-skin cushion over it,
and placed it very steadily.
Just as the Zhīzhōu sat down firmly,
Zuǒ Chù struck his gauze cap fiercely from behind.
With a loud thwack,
the gauze cap flew off his head
like an arrow
and landed below the hall.
The crowd thought the Zhīzhōu had released a wood pigeon from his sleeve.
They saw the Zhīzhōu clutching his head
and shouting:
"Quickly, pick up the gauze cap and put it on!"
Only then did the crowd realize it was the Zhīzhōu’s gauze cap.
Just as they were about to pick it up,
Zuǒ Chù, hidden below,
grabbed it first.
Limping grandly up to the hall,
he shouted at the Zhīzhōu:
"Tàiyǐn!
Today you have lost your crown,
and today you have lost your head!"
Holding up the gauze cap,
he added:
"Tàiyǐn, your head has already been picked up here by Zuǒ Chù!"
When the crowd heard the name Zuǒ Chù,
they said:
"We are just now putting up posters to catch him,
yet he comes here to stick his head into the cangue."
The Zhīzhōu, seeing his short stature,
did not take him seriously
and asked:
"Are you that Crippled Teacher?"
Zuǒ Qué slapped his left leg
and said:
"Could this leg be a fake?"
The Zhīzhōu said:
"I was just about to arrest you.
How dare you come here?"
Zuǒ Chù said:
"Knowing Your Honor was offended,
I have come to pay my respects and accept my punishment."
The Zhīzhōu was furious
and cursed:
"I have never seen such a bold demonic rebel."
He ordered his attendants to seize him,
fetch a long cangue,
and lock Zuǒ Chù in it,
then send him to the Sīlǐyuàn
to be confronted with Wáng Zé regarding the money and rice.
The jailers escorted Zuǒ Chù to the investigation hall
and brought Wáng Zé out from the prison.
When Wáng Zé saw Zuǒ Chù,
he was greatly shocked and said:
"Why have you come here too?"
Zuǒ Chù said:
"If I had not come in,
how could I rescue you?"
Wáng Jiāng of the Sīlǐyuàn asked:
"You fellow, give a true account:
the money and rice in the granary—
how did you spirit them away?"
Zuǒ Chù said:
"Investigating Official!
Even you do not understand.
The Zhīzhōu is stupid;
he refused to release the monthly pay and rice to them,
causing the men of the two camps to gnash their teeth in resentment.
I spent four thousand strings of cash to distribute them on behalf of the Zhīzhōu.
Instead of being grateful and thanking me,
he wants to punish me.
What kind of logic is that?"
Wáng Jiāng became irritated
and shouted for the jailers to beat him severely.
The jailers raised their staves,
dragged Zuǒ Chù down, and began to beat him.
But a strange thing happened:
as soon as the first blow landed,
Zuǒ Chù felt nothing at all,
while the one wielding the staff cried out in pain,
as if the blow had landed on his own body.
They changed to several other jailers to wield the staves,
but it was the same for all of them.
Every time a blow was struck,
they would cry out in pain,
drop the boards, and dodge to the side.
Wáng Jiāng did not believe it
and walked down to take the staff himself to strike.
This staff did not seem to hit Zuǒ Chù,
but seemed to hit the investigating official instead.
He too dropped the staff,
covered his backside with his hands, and ran off,
repeatedly shouting that it was a miracle.
Zuǒ Chù laughed loudly
and shouted:
"Jí!"
The ropes on his own body and Wáng Zé's body
snapped as if they were rotten wood,
and the cangues also fell open.
Terrified, Wáng Jiāng said:
"This fellow is truly a sorcerer!"
He hurriedly called for the jailers and the crowd to rush forward together to seize them.
Zuǒ Chù pointed with his hand,
and the feet of many people were frozen
as if they had grown roots;
they could not move a single step.
Zuǒ Chù and Wáng Zé went straight to the hall.
The Zhīzhōu was sitting in the hall;
he had put his gauze cap back on as before
and was sitting in the tiger-skin armchair,
comparing accounts of money and grain.
Zuǒ Chù shouted:
"Zhāng Tàiyǐn!
You have harmed all the people of Bèizhōu;
retribution comes today.
If I do not eliminate this scourge for the people of Bèizhōu today,
I am no great man."
Seeing the two of them coming fiercely,
the Zhīzhōu turned to flee behind the screen.
Suddenly, two men rushed out from inside the hall.
These two were none other than
Zhāng Luán and
Bǔ Jí,
each wielding a blade.
Bǔ Jí stepped forward and seized the Zhīzhōu,
while Zhāng Luán struck the Zhīzhōu with his blade,
severing his shoulder and arm,
cutting his throat and hacking his body,
killing the Zhīzhōu.
The people above and below the hall were so terrified
that they were numb
and could not move.
Wáng Zé said:
"All of you, listen to me.
More than half of you have been harmed by him.
Today I have removed this source of calamity for you,
so the whole prefecture can be happy.
Those of you who suffered under him,
follow me into the office
to seize gold and silver,
and I will make you wealthy."
The crowd heard this,
and all came to assist Wáng Zé.
The instructors of the two camps, Zhāng Chéng
and Dòu Wényù,
led six thousand soldiers
and arrived just in front of the Prefectural Office.
Hearing that Wáng Zé had killed the Prefect,
they rushed inside together
and happened to encounter Wáng Jiāng of the Judicial Office leading his entire family out of the office to escape.
Zhāng Chéng raised his staff
and first struck Wáng Jiāng down;
the crowd fell upon him together
and trampled him into a pulp.
His entire family
also lost their lives.
Hú Yǒng'ér herself went inside the Prefectural Office,
and together with Zuǒ Chù and others, killed the Prefect's entire household.
They also sought out those who were usually the Prefect's trusted confidants in power
and searched for them all to kill them.
They opened the prison gates
and released all the prisoners.
They went into the Prefect's house,
carried out the gold, silver, money, and jewels,
as well as the silks, satins, and fabrics,
piling them like a mountain below the steps.
Even the five-foot remnants cut from those thirteen bolts of colored silk
were wrapped in a bundle
and searched out from the Granny's room.
Wáng Zé said:
"This vast amount of property
is all the marrow of the people of Bèizhōu.
Now it shall be divided into three parts.
One part will be distributed to those in the camps with salaries.
One part will be given to pay off debts to shops
and to the families who were defrauded and harmed by the Prefect.
One part will be distributed to poor peddlers
so they can carry on their trades with peace of mind."
Wáng Zé occupied the Prefectural Office,
posted notices to pacify the common people,
and ordered the soldiers of the two camps
to prepare their weapons,
don their helmets and armor,
and deploy at the four gates
to guard the city walls.
The two instructors then served as the commanders of the troops of the two camps.
This concludes one part of the story;
meanwhile, a great event occurred.
At that time, only two officials escaped.
One was the Vice Prefect Dǒng Yuánchūn,
and the other was the Intendant Tián Jīng.
The two took the official seals,
abandoned their families,
and fled to Dōngjīng
to report to the Imperial Court
and request troops to avenge the Prefect.
Because of this incident,
there is a reason to say:
The general sent to suppress the rebels
wasted his efforts in vain;
the sorcerer plotting for kingship
greatly wielded ten thousand kinds of evil magic.
Truly it is said:
A single lamp can ignite the flames of a thousand houses;
a foot of water can churn into waves of ten thousand fathoms.
In the end, whom did the Imperial Court send to suppress them?
Please listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
Rebellions have always been destined by fate,
but they also arise because the Imperial Court's governance is incomplete.
Witness the days of a sagely and prosperous reign:
cattle are released and horses returned as everyone sleeps in peace.
The story goes that during the Qìnglì era of the Great Sòng,
although Emperor Rénzōng was sagely and enlightened,
he was deceived by the treacherous official Xià Là,
who brought in a group of petty men such as Wáng Gǒngchén
and Yú Zhōuxún.
They fabricated rumors and caused trouble,
plotting against loyal and upright men,
and successively dismissed six virtuous ministers.
Which six?
Wén Yànbó,
Hán Qí,
Fù Bì,
Fàn Zhòngyān,
Ōuyáng Xiū,
and Bāo Zhěng.
All six were mature and experienced,
willing to do good for the state.
Since the six departed,
Xià Là held the post of Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs,
specializing in suppressing the virtuous and envying the capable,
grasping power and accepting bribes.
Therefore, many prefectures and counties had corrupt officials,
and the world was not at peace.
Zhào Yuánhào rebelled in Xīxià,
and Nóng Zhìgāo rebelled in Guǎngnán,
and neither had been suppressed yet.
Today, Wáng Zé has rebelled in Bèizhōu,
also arising because of corrupt officials.
At that time, of all the officials in Bèizhōu,
only Vice Prefect Dǒng Yuánchūn
and Intendant Tián Jīng escaped.
The two went straight to the capital
and reported the rebellion to the Imperial Court.
When Emperor Rénzōng heard the report,
he summoned the officials of the Bureau of Military Affairs for discussion.
Xià Là reported:
"This is because Prefect Zhāng Dé did not release money and rice,
which momentarily provoked the soldiers;
it is not a regional rebellion.
There is no need for Your Majesty to worry;
I recommend one person, the Governor of Jìzhōu, Liú Yànwēi.
This man is the son of a military family,
accomplished in both civil and military arts.
It only requires this man to lead his own troops there
to suppress or pacify as the situation permits,
and we can ensure there is no cause for concern."
Rénzōng granted the request
and immediately sent down an imperial decree
ordering the Governor of Jìzhōu to swiftly lead his own troops
straight to Bèizhōu
to either pacify or suppress,
allowing him to act as he saw fit.
After the matter was settled,
rewards and promotions would be granted based on merit.
This Governor was surnamed Liú and named Yànwēi.
Although he came from a civil service background,
his family was of a military lineage,
and he was well-versed in military strategy.
He wielded a large long-handled saber
and possessed the courage of ten thousand men.
On that day, having received the imperial order,
he invited the Inspector General Rú Gāng to deliberate.
Rú Gāng said:
"I have heard that a group of sorcerers in Bèizhōu are causing havoc
and possess great supernatural powers.
We must proceed according to our strength
and not underestimate the enemy."
Liú Yànwēi laughed loudly and said:
"I have read the classics.
As the ancient saying goes:
'Evil cannot triumph over the righteous.'
I rely on the Heavenly Majesty to punish the rebels;
what is there to fear?
Thereupon, he chose an auspicious day,
mustered five thousand troops of his own division,
with Rú Gāng leading one thousand men as the vanguard.
The Lieutenant Duàn Léi
led one thousand troops as the rearguard,
while he himself led three thousand troops as the central army.
They set out together
and marched toward Bèizhōu.
Meanwhile, a scout from Bèizhōu learned that Liú Yànwēi had raised an army
and rode swiftly to report to Wáng Zé.
Everyone in Bèizhōu was thrown into a panic.
Although Wáng Zé had learned some martial arts,
he had never experienced a battle
and could not help but be afraid.
He hastily invited Zuǒ Chù,
Zhāng Luán,
and Bǔ Jí to discuss the matter.
The storyteller asks:
Where did your Dànzǐ Héshang go?
Readers, there is a reason.
When that monk went to Master Yuán's Báiyún Dòng for the third time to steal the magic,
he had sincerely prayed before the white jade incense burner,
vowing to act on behalf of Heaven
and not dare to do wrong.
Simply because he could not read the Heavenly Book,
he relied on Shèng Gūgū to decipher it.
Then, together with Shèng Gūgū and Zuǒ Chù,
they practiced cultivation together.
Because he heard Shèng Gūgū say
that the thirty-six prefectures of Héběi were destined to change masters,
and they should assist Wáng Zé
to eliminate corrupt officials,
as this was all predestined by Heaven.
Dànzǐ Héshang believed these words,
so he used the three thousand strings of cash from Grand Marshal Shàn Wáng to assist Wáng Zé
by distributing them to the soldiers of the two camps.
Later, when the others went to kill the prefectural officials,
the monk hid away
and did not go with them.
Why was this?
Firstly, because he came from a Buddhist background
and was raised under Master Cízhàng,
he still carried a bit of compassion in his heart.
Secondly, he was quick-witted and clever.
Since he had made a vow,
he always kept the four characters 'Acting on Behalf of Heaven' in his heart.
Even when he troubled Bāo Lóngtú,
it was because Bāo Lóngtú first wanted to arrest him;
it was not that he sought out trouble.
Today, although he believes in the Heavenly destiny,
he also wants to observe the developments
and is unwilling to expose himself to cause trouble and create karma.
While Wáng Zé occupied the city of Bèizhōu,
the monk stayed comfortably in the Gānquán Sì outside the city.
Only Zuǒ Chù and two others worked together morning and night,
so today Wáng Zé only invited the three of them to deliberate.
Qué Shī said:
“Have you found out how many men and horses they have there?”
Wáng Zé said:
“There are five thousand men and horses.”
Zuǒ Chù said:
“Even if he had fifty thousand,
it would not be worth worrying about.
Here in the two camps, there are six thousand men in total;
keep half to guard the city,
and half to face the enemy,
and watch the skills of me, Zuǒ Chù.”
Wáng Zé went in person to the drill ground to inspect the troops,
and saw two newly appointed instructors of the commandery come forward from among the ranks;
one was Zhāng Chéng,
and the other was Dòu Wényù.
After paying their respects,
they reported:
“The soldiers of the two camps have received great kindness from the Commander-in-Chief,
yet have offered not even an inch of repayment.
We are willing to each take fifteen hundred men from our own units out of the city,
taking advantage of the fact that they have not yet settled their camp,
to strike them once,
blunt their morale,
and make them not dare to look directly at our Bèizhōu.”
Wáng Zé was greatly pleased,
and rewarded each with a suit of armor
and a warhorse,
and dispatched three thousand men and horses.
After the rewards were completed,
he ordered them to set out the next day
and to be careful.
A night passed.
The next day,
the two instructors donned their full armor,
organized the troops and horses,
opened the city gates wide,
and charged out in two routes.
Qué Shī saw them go out with such heroic might,
and since he wanted them to test the strength of the coming troops,
he did not stop them.
Now, Zhāng Chéng led fifteen hundred troops in the lead,
and about thirty li outside the city,
at a place called Fùjiātuǎn,
they happened to encounter the troops of Rú Gāng, the vanguard of Jìzhōu.
Just as they were about to deploy for battle,
preparing to fight,
Dòu Wényù’s troops arrived as well.
Rú Gāng, leading his thousand troops, had not yet caught his breath;
how could he withstand the sudden charge of two fresh forces totaling three thousand men?
Moreover, outnumbered as they were,
they could not hold their ground
and fled in all directions.
Rú Gāng cut down several of his own men in succession,
but simply could not hold them back.
Zhāng Chéng
and Dòu Wényù,
seeing the enemy soldiers fleeing in chaos,
urged their two horses forward together
to capture Rú Gāng.
Rú Gāng fought the two generals with all his strength,
without the slightest fear,
and they fought for over twenty bouts;
he saw the Bèizhōu army surrounding him like Mount Tài.
Looking back, only one man and one horse remained of his followers;
with no heart to continue the fight,
he hacked out a path and fled.
Zhāng
and Dòu, the two generals, were just about to pursue,
when a scout arrived reporting that the main Jìzhōu army had arrived,
less than ten li away.
The two generals did not dare press forward,
hurriedly withdrew their troops,
and returned to Bèizhōu.
They stationed the troops outside the city,
and the two generals entered the city to see Wáng Zé,
reporting:
“The vanguard of the Jìzhōu forward unit
has been utterly defeated by us;
we were just about to pursue,
but unfortunately Governor Liú’s main army has arrived.
We could only withdraw our troops,
and are now stationed outside the city,
awaiting the Commander-in-Chief’s orders.”
Wáng Zé said:
“I have heard that this fellow Liú Yànwēi has high skills.
Now that his forward unit has suffered a loss,
his prestige is already dampened.
You two generals shall be credited with the first merit.
Taking advantage of this momentum, you can stay stationed outside the city
to prevent him from attacking the city.
In tomorrow’s battle, I shall have the military advisors assist you.”
The two generals received the order
and that very night, moved ten li from the city
and established two large camps.
Each occupied one camp,
so that if enemy troops came to attack,
they could rescue each other.
Meanwhile, Rú Gāng gathered his defeated and remnant soldiers
and went to see Governor Liú to admit his guilt.
Governor Liú said in a great rage:
“Anyone who leads troops must scout from a distance;
as soon as there is a rumor,
one must prepare in advance.
You were completely careless,
causing the rebels to catch the government troops off guard and throw them into chaos.
Where is the discipline?
By right, I should have you beheaded as a warning,
but since battle is imminent,
I fear it would be disadvantageous for the army.
He shouted for him to be bound and given a hundred lashes,
and punished him by sending him to the rear unit to expedite the grain and fodder,
replacing him with Duàn Léi from the rear unit in the post of vanguard.
When they reached Fùjiātuǎn and set up camp,
the scouts found out that Zhāng Chéng
and Dòu Wényù were leading the rebel forces ten li from the city,
staying in two separate camps.
Governor Liú laughed and said:
“I know these rebels are incapable.
This Fùjiātuǎn is the throat-like pass to Bèizhōu;
if the rebels had taken advantage of their victory
to set up camp here and block the incoming path,
even with an army of a hundred thousand,
how could I even sight the city walls?
Now they have abandoned this and do not guard it,
but have established camps close to the city instead;
I will surely defeat them.
He ordered Duàn Léi:
“Carry banners with the character ‘Liú’ and lead the way;
arrive before their camp at dawn tomorrow to challenge them to battle.
You must only lose and not win.
Lure them toward the Fùjiātuǎn route,
for I have a plan.”
Duàn Léi received the plan and departed.
He also dispatched two captains from his staff, each leading three hundred infantry to move stealthily by night,
to lie in ambush near the left and right sides of their stockades;
waiting until they leave the camp to face the enemy,
to then seize the camp and set it on fire.
He also ordered Rú Gāng to prepare scaling ladders
and cannons as siege equipment.
At noon the next day,
they were to assemble at Bèizhōu City.
Having finished the arrangements,
his own central army inevitably broke camp and set out,
with other orders that will not be mentioned here.
It is said that Zhāng Chéng and
Dòu Wényù, though they were masters of the spear and staff,
were actually ignorant of military strategy.
Having accidentally won their first battle,
they boasted of their own abilities
and became careless.
The next day, they heard that the government army was challenging them to battle,
with the name Liú displayed on the banners.
Zhāng Chéng and
Dòu Wényù both wanted to gain merit,
so they vied to lead the array,
each wielding a fine iron spear
and riding a warhorse,
making a grand display of their martial prowess.
Looking ahead, they saw that the government army had already formed their ranks,
and from the opening in the banners, a general emerged.
He wore an iron helmet
and embroidered armor,
and in his hand, he swung a large Xuānhuà axe.
The two generals said:
"Who is this if not Liú Yànwēi?"
The two generals wasted no words
and charged straight at that general with their spears leveled.
That general met them with his axe,
and after fighting for over thirty bouts,
he feigned a vulnerability
and shouted:
"Let's pause!
He turned his horse's head and fled.
Zhāng
and Dòu, the two generals, signaled their troops
to pursue and kill with all their might.
That general fought as he fled
for about ten lǐ.
Then he turned around and fought for another seventy bouts before fleeing again.
The two generals would not let go
and continued their pursuit.
The government army left gongs and drums scattered all over the ground,
and the rebels scrambled to seize them.
Suddenly, a swift messenger horse arrived like a flying arrow, crying out:
"General, stop the pursuit!
Fires have broken out in two places in the camp behind us!"
Zhāng Chéng and
Dòu Wényù realized they had fallen into a trap
and were thrown into a panic.
They hurriedly led their troops to retreat,
but their ranks were already in chaos.
Before they had gone far,
the sound of continuous cannon fire was heard,
and a troop of soldiers charged out from the side.
At their head was a great general
who, with his blade held horizontally, spurred his horse and shouted:
"Rebel bandits, do not run!
Liú Yànwēi has been waiting here for a long time!"
The two generals had never seen such a fearsome sight before;
they were already panicked and caught off guard.
Liú Yànwēi raised his blade and let it fall,
first decapitating Dòu Wényù beneath his horse.
Zhāng Chéng realized he could not escape,
so he had no choice but to brandish his spear to fight.
Before three bouts had passed,
Liú Yànwēi glared and shouted loudly,
so frightening Zhāng Chéng that his hands grew weak and he could not swing his spear.
Liú Yànwēi's horse arrived in an instant,
and with one hand, he plucked him from his saddle
and threw him to the ground.
The soldiers rushed forward together and ended his life.
Liú Yànwēi directed his troops to slaughter them;
more than half of the three thousand soldiers were lost.
There is a poem as proof:
In military affairs, assessing the enemy is the first priority;
one must know that underestimating the enemy leads to defeat.
How lamentable that the masters boasted of a small victory;
in one day, they fell for a scheme, and their corpses filled the carts.
Meanwhile, Wáng Zé, hearing of the fighting outside the city,
hurriedly invited Zuǒ Chù and the others to climb the city wall and assist.
They saw the defeated soldiers arriving one after another,
crying out:
"Commanders Zhāng
and Dòu have already been killed!
Prefect Liú's army will arrive shortly!
Quickly open the city gates!"
Wáng Zé ordered the guards to let them in.
Upon hearing the details, he was greatly shocked
and said to Zuǒ Chù and the others:
"Liú Yànwēi's reputation as a hero is indeed well-founded.
Do you gentlemen have any way to repel the enemy?"
Zuǒ Chù said:
"I, this humble Daoist, have already calculated it.
For now, let the remnants of the defeated army guard the city.
Pick out one thousand five hundred men;
I, along with Zhāng
and Bǔ, will each lead five hundred.
Relying on the three of us, we will fight them and ensure not a single piece of their armor returns."
Wáng Zé said:
"Five hundred men for each of you might be too few."
Zuǒ Chù said:
"I have celestial soldiers and ghost troops;
the five hundred men are just for show to support the array."
Wáng Zé said:
"I rely entirely on your support
to share in wealth and honor."
Wáng Zé then issued an order to select one thousand five hundred strong soldiers
and divide them into three units.
Before the selection was finished,
the sounds of shouting and killing reached the heavens outside the city;
the government army had arrived.
Liú Yànwēi ordered Duàn Léi
and Rú Gāng to prepare for the siege
while he himself, astride a fine horse that could chase the wind,
stood before the array.
Pointing the tip of his blade toward the city, he shouted:
"If anyone in Bèizhōu understands the situation, bind Wáng Zé and bring him out!
Offer him to the Imperial Court
to save the people of the entire city from slaughter!"
Wáng Zé, seeing his majestic military appearance,
did not dare to make a sound.
Zuǒ Chù, wearing a cloth robe
and wielding a sword,
led five hundred soldiers out of the city on foot.
Pointing the tip of his sword at Liú Yànwēi, he said:
"If you understand the situation, take your troops back to Jìzhōu immediately
and save your head.
If you delay even slightly,
I will ensure your entire group dies by my hand."
Liú Yànwēi said:
"You fellow are a rebel partisan aiding Wáng Zé.
Look at you, without armor
or a horse,
yet you dare to fight me?
It's a pity for a crippled person like you;
you're not even worth one stroke of my blade."
Zuǒ Chù said:
"I will not argue with you;
I'll just show you my skill!"
Liú Yànwēi displayed his blade techniques before the array, underestimating Zuǒ Chù.
Zuǒ Chù pointed with the tip of his sword
and shouted:
"Hurry!"
Immediately, a wild wind whipped up in front of him
and blew toward the government army's array.
Yellow sand pelted their faces,
and for a moment, none could open their eyes.
Liú Yànwēi cried out:
"It's over!"
He turned his horse's head and fled,
pursued by Zuǒ Chù and his troops for a slaughter before they returned.
Liú Yànwēi fled for twenty lǐ
before the wind finally subsided.
Upon counting the soldiers and horses,
one-third had been lost.
Before long,
Duàn Léi
and Rú Gāng arrived with their troops.
When asked the reason,
they reported:
"We were just about to attack the city
when we saw a great wind with flying sand and rolling stones.
Realizing it was the rebels' sorcery
and fearing losses,
we withdrew the troops and returned."
Liú Yànwēi said:
"I did not know the rebels' tricks
and mistakenly fell for their scheme.
We will rest at Fùjiā Tuǎn for three days.
I have my own plan to defeat them.
Order every man in the army to prepare a green gauze blindfold for use."
On the fourth day,
they prepared food at the fourth watch
and set out at the fifth watch.
He selected only five hundred fine horses
and five hundred spearmen,
all carrying blindfolds with them
to protect against wind and sand.
"Upon encountering the rebel army, regardless of the situation,
charge straight through
and stab them with your long spears.
Duàn Léi
and Rú Gāng will lead the troops as the left and right wings.
Once the central army breaks into the rebel forces,
the two wings will surround them.
We must slaughter them completely;
let not a single one escape."
Meanwhile, since Zuǒ Chù had won a battle,
Wáng Zé's mind was somewhat at ease.
Although no movement was seen during several days of scouting,
those guarding the city did not dare to be lax.
On the fourth day,
it was reported that the government army had arrived again.
Zhāng Luán said:
"The other day the Lame Master gained merit;
this time it is my turn."
Bǔ Jí said:
"I, the disciple, shall go on behalf of my Master."
He led five hundred foot soldiers and flew out of the city.
What did Bǔ Jí look like?
His hair was tied in double tufts.
He wore a green brocade robe.
His eyes were fierce, and his eyebrows were knotted.
His face was full of coarse flesh and covered in hair.
Wielding a sword, all the gods submit;
Raising his voice, the hundred beasts are terrified.
In Zhèngzhōu, there is no unlucky traveler;
In the world, there are famous demons.
Liú Yànwēi only thought it was originally this cripple who had come out for battle,
but this time another had replaced him, and he knew not what demonic arts would be used.
He decided not to wait for him to make a move,
but simply to charge forward and be done with it.
He saw Bǔ Jí, unhurried and calm,
murmuring incantations in his mouth.
He cried out:
"Jí!"
and opened both sleeves wide toward the front.
From within the sleeves rushed out thousands upon thousands of jackals, wolves, tigers, leopards, and their kind,
baring their teeth and brandishing their claws,
charging together toward the government army's formation.
Liú Yànwēi’s horse, seeing this, was so frightened it jumped straight up,
throwing Liú Yànwēi to the ground.
Bǔ Jí strode forward, about to advance,
but the left and right wings of the army rushed in together to pull Liú Yànwēi onto a horse and save him.
When the government soldiers saw the strange beasts,
they all cast aside their spears and abandoned their drums,
each fleeing for their lives.
Bǔ Jí took advantage of the momentum to pursue and kill them,
capturing more than two hundred fine horses
and countless military weapons.
Liú Yànwēi suffered another defeat,
with an extremely high number of soldiers killed or wounded,
and he retreated again to Fùjiātuǎn.
He thought:
"In all my life, I have never seen such a demonic person.
I wish to withdraw the troops and return,
but in my heart, I am unwilling.
I wish to fight again,
but I have no good plan.
Moreover, half of my five thousand men have been lost;
if I suffer more losses, will I not be a laughingstock?"
Just as he was hesitating and undecided,
he ordered the army to firmly guard the camp stockades
and not dare to move rashly.
A day passed.
He saw a dispatch arrive from Jìzhōu;
it turned out the Qiānpàn Xià Yǒushǒu had recruited one thousand valiant soldiers
and three hundred warhorses,
and had sent Tǒnglǐngshǐ Táo Bìxiǎn to escort them to assist in the battle.
Táo Bìxiǎn submitted the military register
and performed the formal greeting.
Liú Yànwēi said with great joy:
"Heaven is helping me succeed!"
After sending back the return dispatch,
he then instructed Táo Bìxiǎn to lead the newly arrived thousand troops
and set up a separate camp to form a pincer formation.
He ordered the army's painters to paint three hundred lion designs on cotton cloth,
setting a ten-day limit for the completion of the report.
He told Táo Bìxiǎn to lead the new troops as the vanguard
and to drape the painted lion-cloths over the three hundred warhorses.
"Should the rebel army use demonic arts
and tigers and leopards suddenly appear,
release the three hundred soldiers on lion-clad horses
and sound the gongs behind them.
The lion is the king of all beasts,
and the sounding gongs will resemble its roar;
tigers and leopards will surely retreat upon seeing this."
He himself would lead the main army to follow and advance.
Furthermore, he ordered Duàn Léi
and Rú Gāng to each lead three hundred archers to lie in ambush on the left and right in advance,
just waiting for the rebel troops to leave the city,
then they would come out from behind and fire arrows at them in confusion.
"Even if there be wind, sand, tigers, or leopards, they can only move forward
and not backward."
Liú Yànwēi finished the assignments
and believed it to be a strategy for a great victory.
Meanwhile, Wáng Zé was discussing matters with Zuǒ Chù and two others
when scouts reported the government army had arrived again.
Zhāng Luán said:
"This time, it is necessary for this humble Taoist to go."
He led five hundred men from his own unit out of the city to meet the enemy;
they were cavalry.
Bǔ Jí said:
"That fellow Liú Yànwēi fights battle after battle without retreating;
after resting for a long time, he returns again.
There must be a scheme involved.
This unworthy one wishes to go with the Master to take a look."
Zuǒ Chù jumped up and said:
"Well said.
Today we shall all go
and simply finish him off
to save us from him coming all day and making us uneasy."
Wáng Zé said:
"The success or failure of Bèizhōu will be decided today;
it all depends on the effort of you all."
The cripple and Bǔ Jí both led their troops away,
and Wáng Zé himself went up the gate tower to beat the drums and assist in the battle.
Now, Táo Bìxiǎn, being newly arrived, did not know the enemy's strength;
wielding a wolf-tooth club,
he roused his spirits
and shouted out a challenge to battle.
He saw a troop of men and horses rushing out like flying from below the drawbridge.
At their head was a Taoist wearing an iron crown,
dressed in a crimson robe,
his face like sprayed blood,
his eyes like bright stars,
holding a turtle-shell fan in his hand,
and carrying an ancient pine-patterned sword on his back.
Táo Bìxiǎn was secretly amazed
and thought:
"This fellow carries no weapon in his hand;
he must be relying on demonic arts.
I am already prepared,
so what is there to fear?"
He shouted for the troops to charge forward together.
Facing him, Zhāng Luán murmured incantations
and waved the turtle-shell fan,
crying out:
"Jí!"
A cold wind suddenly rose from the level ground,
blowing so that people's hair and bones were chilled as if in winter.
In mid-air, a dark cloud hovered right over the government army's formation,
and hailstones fell in confusion,
hitting them until their heads were broken and brains injured.
The horses' legs all trembled,
and they could not help but bolt in chaos.
Instead, they collided into Liú Yànwēi’s main army,
leaving it in complete disarray,
and they hastily sounded the gongs to withdraw the army.
When the troops were counted, Táo Bìxiǎn was missing.
It turned out Táo Bìxiǎn had been frightened into a stupor
and had stumbled into the rebel ranks,
and the soldiers had tied him up and taken him away.
Meanwhile, Duàn Léi
and Rú Gāng’s two units of ambushers heard the shouts and killings filling the sky
and knew the battle had begun.
They hastily led their troops to charge out
and clearly saw Zuǒ Chù
and Bǔ Jí in front,
so they pursued with all their might.
In a moment, the sky grew dark,
and one could not distinguish people's forms.
The two units happened to collide,
each mistaking the other for the rebel army.
The six hundred archers fired their arrows together,
all shooting at their own troops.
After a short while, the weather cleared,
and of the six hundred men, only about a hundred or so remained alive;
the rest had all been shot to death.
This was the power of the magic performed by Zuǒ Chù
and Bǔ Jí.
Duàn Léi had hidden in a dirt pit first and was not harmed;
he took off his armor
and escaped by mingling with the remnant troops.
Rú Gāng had been hit by five or six arrows and lay on the ground,
unable to move.
Seeing the rebel troops approaching,
he drew the sword at his side
and committed suicide by slitting his throat.
Later generations have a poem that says:
It was not that the general lacked wisdom or martial skill,
But the gleaming demonic stars were like a pack of tigers.
By the side of Gānlíng City, we mourn the loyal soul,
Under the bright sun and clear frost, enduring for all eternity.
Liú Yànwēi saw Duàn Léi leading the remnant troops back in flight,
and knowing that Rù Gāng had died,
he lamented incessantly.
Having also heard that Táo Bìxiǎn had been captured,
he finally realized how formidable the sorcerer was.
At night, sitting by candlelight,
he was just contemplating whether to stay or go,
when suddenly shouts arose within the camp.
Liú Yànwēi sat calmly without moving
and sent someone to inquire.
They said:
"The abatis densely arrayed before the camp have all vanished at once."
Liú Yànwēi was furious
and restrained the army, not permitting any clamor or reckless movement.
Gripping his blade in hand,
he ordered torches to be lit
and went out before the camp himself to see;
indeed, the surrounding abatis were completely gone.
While he was in the midst of his astonishment,
he heard the simultaneous sound of drums and horns from the east,
with deafening battle cries,
not knowing from where the troops had come.
Liú Yànwēi ordered Duàn Léi to lead troops to the east to meet the enemy.
In a short while, the east became silent,
but in the west, firelight again lit up the sky,
appearing as close as one or two lǐ.
Liú Yànwēi was furious,
and mounting his horse with his blade,
he personally led several hundred men toward the west to meet them.
After traveling about three or four lǐ,
the gongs and drums could not be heard,
and the firelight also gradually faded away.
Liú Yànwēi had no choice but to turn back.
Just as he reached the front of the camp,
he saw the sound of drums and horns rise again to the south,
with battle cries coming very close.
Liú Yànwēi instructed Duàn Léi to patrol the rear camp,
while he himself remained on horseback in the front camp to observe,
no longer going out to meet them.
Torches were lit within the army,
making everything bright red like daytime.
Before long,
the sounds to the south ceased again,
and a murderous aura came from the north.
Liú Yànwēi did not sleep all night.
Just as he was at a loss,
at about the fifth watch,
he heard shouts arise within the camp again,
saying:
"The night watchman has been bitten and taken away by a tiger!"
Liú Yànwēi shouted:
"How could there be tigers in this place?"
Before he had finished speaking,
he saw within the camp
a beautiful woman
wielding a sword in her hand
and riding a tiger, charging straight out.
Liú Yànwēi hastily leaped down from his saddle;
his horse had already collapsed in fright.
Both the woman and the tiger disappeared.
The army had no rest for the entire night.
When they looked at daybreak,
the entire camp was covered with tiger tracks.
The scouts reported:
"The lost abatis are only about a lǐ away,
piled up in a heap over there."
Liú Yànwēi sighed
and said:
"Against such sorcerers, there is nothing even I, Liú, can do."
He immediately struck camp and fled back to Jìzhōu.
He sent a report overnight to the Bureau of Military Affairs (Shūmìyuàn) stating the sorcery was thus,
requesting more troops and generals,
and widely seeking men of wisdom and strategy
to quickly proceed to exterminate them
and eliminate future troubles.
It turns out that there was a rule in the Sòng Dynasty:
whenever someone recommended a border general who then failed or bungled matters,
the recommender would share the punishment.
Therefore, the Commissioner of Military Affairs (Shūmìshǐ) Xià Là concealed this from the court
and did not present the report.
Now, let the story proceed on two fronts.
As for who the woman riding the tiger was,
it was indeed Hú Yǒng'ér.
Seeing that the government troops would not retreat despite repeated battles,
and that there was to be another great fight this time,
she had also gone to the front of the lines to observe.
Knowing that Zhāng Luán had won,
but that the matter was not yet settled,
she went straight to the front of Liú Yànwēi's camp at Fùjiātǔn to disperse ghost soldiers
and torment him all night.
Only because Liú Yànwēi's destiny was not yet ended
was she unable to kill him,
only forcing him to flee.
That night, Zhāng Luán and the others withdrew their troops into the city,
and the soldiers brought Táo Bìxiǎn to claim credit.
Táo Bìxiǎn kowtowed and expressed his willingness to surrender.
Wáng Zé granted it
and appointed him to the rank of Commander (Tǒnglǐng),
leading the troops of Zhāng
and Dòu, the two generals.
When the troops were counted, not a single one was lost.
Wáng Zé was greatly pleased
and overnight slaughtered oxen and horses to greatly reward the three armies.
He then instructed the city-guarding soldiers to be careful and attentive,
while he and Zhāng,
Zuǒ, and the others held a banquet in the prefectural hall,
drinking until they were thoroughly drunk.
As the fifth watch was nearly over,
they heard a loud crash in front of the hall,
and Hú Yǒng'ér stepped inside.
Everyone was greatly startled
and hurriedly rose to welcome her.
Hú Yǒng'ér said:
"You all are drinking and being merry,
but who knows of my night of hard work?
That fellow Liú Yànwēi has already been driven back to Jìzhōu."
She then recounted the matters of how she had tormented him during the night
in full.
Wáng Zé cupped his hands and thanked her, saying:
"Only now does Bèizhōu have the stability of Mount Tài (Tàishān)."
Hú Yǒng'ér said:
"Firmly defending an isolated city will not achieve great things.
Taking advantage of the current military might,
we can now subdue the nearby prefectures and counties."
Everyone said:
"Well said."
Immediately, troops were mobilized again.
Wáng Zé and Zuǒ Chù led the army along the southeast route,
while Hú Yǒng'ér and Bǔ Jí led the army along the northwest route,
leaving only Zhāng Luán to guard the city.
In less than half a year,
they successively captured Qū'ān,
Féixiāng,
Hándān,
Guǎngpíng, and more than ten other county seats.
They recruited surrendered troops,
obtained much grain and money,
and their power became great.
Zhāng Qí, a meat seller from Dōngjīng;
Rèn Qiān, a steamed bun seller;
and the noodle seller Wú Sānláng, having heard that Hú Yǒng'ér was Wáng Zé's wife,
all went to Bèizhōu to join Wáng Zé.
Seeing that the people's hearts were turning toward him,
Wáng Zé established himself as the Prince of Dōngpíng (Dōngpíng Jùnwáng).
He imperially invested Hú Yǒng'ér as Queen (Huánghòu),
Zuǒ Chù as Imperial Uncle (Guójiù),
Zhāng Luán as Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng),
and Bǔ Jí as Great General (Dàjiāngjūn).
Although Dànzi Héshang (the Egg Monk) had not exerted any effort,
everyone praised his high level of skill,
and he was invested as State Preceptor (Guóshī).
Money and rice were sent monthly to Gānquán Temple (Gānquán Sì) for his support,
fearing there might be a place for him in the future.
Below them, Zhāng Qí and the others were all granted seals and official posts,
and their power grew even greater.
They dispatched troops in four directions to plunder;
everywhere people heard that their sorcery was divine,
and none failed to surrender at the mere sight of them.
More than half of the prefectures and counties in Héběi came under Wáng Zé's possession.
Wáng Zé conscripted laborers
to transform the prefectural hall into a royal palace and halls,
matching the systems of the imperial court.
Furthermore, Zuǒ Chù,
Zhāng Luán,
and Bǔ Jí all had administrative offices (yámén) built,
wasting immeasurable money and grain.
They also honored Shèng Gūgū as the Holy Mother Empress (Shèngmǔ Niángniáng)
and built a temporary palace
to prepare for her occasional visits.
The common people worked day and night,
and all sighed in lamentation.
They also searched among the commoners for beautiful girls
to be taken into the palace.
The superior ones became consorts and concubines,
while the lesser ones became palace maids to serve.
They also selected thirty beautiful women
to be bestowed upon Zuǒ Chù and the other two.
Zhāng Luán was naturally a eunuch
and could not approach women,
so he declined and did not accept.
Bǔ Jí, seeing his master decline,
also did not dare to accept any.
Only Zuǒ Chù, who had originally flirted with women
and been wounded in the left leg by an arrow from Zhào Dàláng,
becoming a cripple,
although he had now learned a whole set of magical arts,
his lustful heart remained unchanged.
He took ten beautiful women
to enjoy day and night.
He also personally selected others from various places
to compete with Wáng Zé in his enjoyment.
Because of this, as the saying goes:
An upstart emperor cannot hold onto a peaceful land,
and a crippled sorcerer cannot carry out a thousand tricks forever.
It is exactly so:
Boundless luxury and lust ultimately bring disaster;
many deceptions will surely lead to ruin in the long run.
As for how Wáng Zé's later affairs turned out,
please listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
Learn a bit of cleverness and a bit of foolishness;
to possess both cleverness and foolishness is to have great talent.
Foolishness without cleverness makes it hard to accomplish anything;
cleverness without foolishness makes a task impossible to carry out.
It is said that previously, when Hú Yǒng'ér led her troops to attack prefectures and counties,
her army captured many people.
Among them was a young servant boy
who was born with an exceedingly delicate and handsome appearance.
Yǒng'ér liked him as soon as she saw him.
She asked about his past,
and he replied,
"My surname is Wáng and my given name is Jùn.
I am only thirteen years old.
Both my parents are deceased.
I followed my grandfather out to escape the war,
but we were unexpectedly separated on the way.
I was captured and brought here.
I beg the Niángniáng to spare my life."
Yǒng'ér saw that his speech was quick and clever
and his appearance was pitiable;
moreover, he shared the same surname as Wáng Zé.
She took him into her camp as an adopted son,
never letting him leave her side,
and she loved him dearly.
When Wáng Zé saw him,
he was also pleased
and ordered outsiders to call him the "Little Prince."
Without realizing it, two years passed;
the boy reached fifteen years of age
and had grown even more beautiful.
How could one tell?
His face was like applied powder,
his skin like congealed lard,
his lips like painted vermilion,
and his eyes like dots of lacquer.
His figure was graceful and lithe,
a favored youth not yet ravished;
his manner was enchanting,
like a beautiful woman who had not yet donned a hair bun.
His nature was clear and bright, a true delight;
his words were nimble and sharp, earning people's affection.
On horseback, all were startled by his pellet-slinging;
the master saw again the boy who sold pearls.
Hú Yǒng'ér stayed with him morning and night
and eventually took a fancy to him,
consummating their illicit affair in private.
It turns out that for a woman, it is only the first loss of shame that is significant;
it is difficult to break the precedent.
But once the misdeed has begun,
one might as well go all the way,
and even she herself could not extinguish her own desires.
When Yǒng'ér first followed Shèng Gūgū,
her movements were accompanied by wind and clouds
and she took the mountains and waters as her home;
she was half like a monastic,
and such carnal ways never crossed her mind.
Now living in secluded rooms and deep courtyards,
with brocade clothes and fine food,
she fit the common saying: "Once warm and well-fed, one's thoughts turn to lust."
Seeing that the palace was filled with crowds of "green sleeves"
and ranks of "moth-eyebrowed" beauties,
while she herself was only kept by Wáng Zé—
furthermore, he had three consorts and six concubines
and could not be with her every night—
upon seeing such a powder-faced, jade-carved boy,
how could she not be moved?
The boy did his best to flatter and please her,
but Yǒng'ér's lustful heart was so restless
that her desires remained unsatisfied.
This boy was clever;
whenever he went out and saw a handsome man,
he would inquire about his name
and report it to Yǒng'ér.
Yǒng'ér, being skilled in magic,
would then summon the man to her puppet palace for pleasure.
If he pleased her,
he would stay for several days.
If he did not please her,
she would let him go.
As the ancient saying goes:
"If you want it not to be known,
the only way is not to do it.
If you want it not to be heard,
the only way is not to speak of it."
Wáng Zé lived in the same nest as Yǒng'ér;
even if he hadn't seen it with his own eyes,
how could no rumors have reached his ears?
One night,
after getting dead drunk,
he suddenly thought of this matter.
His anger flared up,
and he grabbed a bronze precious sword to go to the palace to kill Yǒng'ér.
When he reached the gate of the puppet palace,
he suddenly had a change of heart and said:
"If one does not think thrice,
there will eventually be regret.
All this wealth and status
were made possible by Yǒng'ér;
how can I betray her?
Moreover, her divine powers are vast;
if I fail to kill her,
it will only damage our relationship
and make things difficult between us."
He turned toward another courtyard,
threw the precious sword on the ground,
sighed,
and went to sleep by himself.
It so happened that during those few days, Shèng Gūgū was at the Shèngmǔ's traveling palace.
Wáng Zé got up early the next day
and went straight to see Shèng Gūgū.
After some small talk,
Wáng Zé said:
"Recently, thanks to your great protection,
the region has been quite peaceful.
However, I have discovered that among the women of the common people,
many are secretly keeping men,
which corrupts public morals.
How should they be dealt with now?"
Shèng Gūgū said:
"Whenever a man and a woman come together,
it is always a predestined connection from a past life.
Those who become husband and wife have a primary connection,
while those who unite in secret have a secondary connection.
Furthermore,
regarding the seven emotions and six desires,
men and women are generally the same.
If a woman should be a chaste wife,
then a man should also be a righteous husband.
A man has three wives and nine concubines
and still considers them too few.
How can he blame a woman?
Moreover, a woman defers to a man
only because the man manages affairs outside;
all matters
are handled by him.
The woman relies on him for her livelihood,
and therefore she adheres to the man's rules,
remaining faithful to one without straying.
If she is talented and wise,
surpassing men,
she will not be controlled by others,
nor can anyone control her.
Consider the Hàn Emperor Liú Bāng, who executed the Qín and destroyed Xiàng—
what a hero he was!
Yet he allowed Empress Dowager Lǚ to do as she pleased in the palace
and ignored it completely.
He did not regard Lǚ-hòu as an ordinary woman.
In this world, moments of success are hard to come by.
While the times and fortune are good,
take advantage where you can,
and seek pleasure where you can.
Such trivial matters
are not what an enlightened person should be concerned with."
With just this speech,
Wáng Zé was left speechless.
He took his leave and returned to his residence.
Thinking to himself:
"What Shèng Gūgū said
is indeed reasonable.
From now on,
I will not bother her,
and she will not bother me.
Each of us will enjoy our own pleasures—
would that not be wonderful?"
Thereupon, he summoned Zhāng Qí,
Rèn Qiān, and others,
ordering them to search for beautiful women among the common people along the way—
regardless of whether they had husbands or not—
so long as they were exceptionally beautiful.
Within a day,
Zhāng Qí discovered Zhào Wúxiá, the wife of Guān Yí from Guānjiāzhuāng in this prefecture.
She was only twenty years old
and her beauty was peerless.
Wáng Zé then ordered Zhāng Qí to lead soldiers to fetch her
so he could see what her appearance was like.
Zhāng Qí led three hundred soldiers to surround Guānjiāzhuāng,
demanding Lady Zhào at once.
Guān Yí was not at home,
so his entire family, young and old, hid in panic.
Lady Zhào said:
"The bandits have come because they covet my beauty.
If I do not step forward myself,
and they enter the house to search,
it would be even worse."
She took a small dagger,
hid it on her person,
and came out from the central hall to see Zhāng Qí.
When Zhāng Qí saw that she was indeed a heavenly beauty,
he was greatly delighted.
He wanted to pull her onto a horse,
but Lady Zhào shouted:
"General, do not be impolite!
Have you come to take me
for yourself,
or does the Jùnwáng want me?"
Zhāng Qí said:
"The Wángfǔ heard of your beauty, Lady,
and specially sent this minor general to welcome you.
From here you go to extraordinary wealth and honor;
do not hesitate."
Lady Zhào said:
"Since the Jùnwáng wants me,
the Jùnwáng must come himself,
as I have words to say to him face-to-face.
If the Jùnwáng does not come,
I would rather die than go."
Zhāng Qí rode off alone to report swiftly to Wáng Zé.
Wáng Zé mounted a dapple-grey horse
and, leading his attendants from the Wěifǔ,
personally arrived at Guānjiāzhuāng.
When he saw Zhào Wúxiá,
she was truly like a flower that understands speech
and jade that emits fragrance;
Xīzǐ of the Wú Palace was no match,
and Nánwēi of the Chǔ State was far inferior.
Wáng Zé said in great astonishment:
"So there really is such a woman in this world!
You may come forward and converse with me."
Zhào Wúxiá paid her respects
and said calmly and unhurriedly:
"Great King, you are the lord of a region.
Those who serve you
should be virtuous ladies from refined chambers
and beauties from embroidered pavilions.
As for my humble appearance and unworthy body,
I am not fit to disgrace your inner palace.
I hope the Great King will value moral principles
and spare me;
for the Great King’s hidden virtue,
you shall surely live for a thousand years!"
Wáng Zé said:
"What I love
is your beauty.
I shall immediately establish you as Queen;
do not speak such idle words."
Lady Zhào pleaded repeatedly,
but Wáng Zé simply would not allow it.
Realizing she could not avoid it,
Lady Zhào cursed loudly:
"You rebellious bandit!
You are like a fish swimming in a pot,
soon to perish,
yet you still want to defile another's wife!
I wish I could cut off your bandit head with one stroke;
how could I ever follow you!"
She pulled the dagger from her side
and intended to slit her own throat,
but the crowd rushed in quickly
and prevented her from acting.
Zhào Wúxiá cursed incessantly,
seeking only a swift death.
Wáng Zé felt pity in his heart
and ordered Zhāng Qí to disperse the soldiers,
leaving only fifty stalwarts to surround and guard her,
insisting they persuade her to comply.
If she stubbornly refused,
the entire family would be beheaded.
Wáng Zé then returned to his Wěifǔ.
Now, Lady Zhào was kept under watch by Zhāng Qí and the stalwarts
for a day and a night,
unable to find a way to die.
She devised a plan
and said:
"If the Great King truly wants me,
how would I dare remain stubborn
and endanger the lives of my entire family?
However, I have read some books and know the rites;
if I am coerced by force,
I will not obey even if I die.
I have an old mother-in-law in the hall
and a husband who is away;
I must wait to see them one last time before parting.
I shall stay in another room,
and after a day is chosen for the formal betrothal,
then I shall be free from the shame of an illicit union,
and the Great King will also avoid the criticism of a forced marriage.
I hope the General will convey these words favorably."
Zhāng Qí again rode swiftly to convey these words.
Wáng Zé agreed
and let her mother-in-law watch over her.
He only forbade the husband and wife from meeting,
intending to formally marry her into the palace the next day.
Zhāng Qí called the mother-in-law out
and entrusted the daughter-in-law to her.
If anything went wrong,
the whole family's safety would not be guaranteed.
Fifty stalwarts
were stationed to guard the front and back doors,
not allowing her husband to return home to see her.
In fact, Guān Yí had already returned,
but hearing of what was happening at home,
he did not dare enter
and instead stayed in a nearby house,
tearfully seeking news.
The mother-in-law also feared her son would be harmed by the soldiers if he returned
and secretly sent him a message telling him not to come back.
That night, the mother-in-law and daughter-in-law could not bear to part
and wept in each other's arms.
Lady Zhào wiped away her tears and said to her mother-in-law:
"It is not difficult for me to die today,
but I fear involving you.
However, once I arrive at that Wěifǔ,
I will certainly preserve my chastity.
You should prepare your valuables and household goods in advance
and make an appointment with my husband.
After I have departed,
flee quickly to Dōngjīng
to escape the harm of these bandits.
Although my husband and I have been married for two years without children,
my husband is still young
and has a vast future ahead;
he will naturally find another good match.
I only regret my own meager fortune,
which prevents me from serving you to the end.
Now at this moment of life and death,
I am separated by bandits
and cannot see my husband one last time.
Here are two gold rings from my fingers;
please send them to my husband as a memento."
Having finished speaking, she wailed loudly again.
Truly it is said:
Of all the myriad sorrows and bitter things in the world,
none surpass parting by death or separation in life.
Even a man of iron would find his soul shattered,
and even a figure of clay would shed tears.
For the mother-in-law and daughter-in-law, their tears did not dry that night,
and the sound of their weeping never ceased.
When dawn finally broke,
the mother-in-law indeed instructed Wángniáng to pack two bundles of valuables, gold and pearls,
and sent another message to her son,
telling him to find a small cart in advance from a distance
and prepare to flee.
Now Wáng Zé entrusted the matters of the betrothal and marriage
entirely to Zhāng Qí.
Zhāng Qí arrived at the Guānjiā Manor early in the morning
and patrolled it once.
Hearing that nothing had happened during the night,
he was exceedingly joyful.
Soon after, the betrothal gifts arrived:
four ingots each of yellow gold and white silver.
Each yellow ingot weighed forty liǎng,
and each white one weighed fifty liǎng.
There were twenty bolts of colored silk,
a pair of sheep, and a pair of wine jars.
Amidst a great fanfare of drums and pipes, they were delivered to the gate
and arranged in the central hall.
The mother-in-law and daughter-in-law began to weep anew.
The mother-in-law said:
"These things are clearly meant to buy the flesh of my own body;
how could I bear to accept them?"
Zhào-shì said:
"Although he buys my mother-in-law's flesh today,
one day it will be used to buy that bandit's flesh."
The mother-in-law asked:
"What do you mean?"
Zhào-shì said:
"The heavenly troops will surely come for this bandit;
they will capture him and send him to Dōngjīng,
to be sliced a thousand times and cut into ten thousand pieces.
Keep this gold and silver,
and when that time comes, give it to the executioner.
Buy a piece of his flesh from the tip of the blade to sacrifice to your daughter-in-law.
Even in the Yellow Springs, I shall find joy."
Let us speak no more of the sorrow of the two women.
Furthermore, Zhāng Qí urged the mother-in-law to accept the gifts,
while he himself hurried the wedding procession.
One hundred personal guards of the rebel government,
with gongs, drums, banners, and spears leading the way;
about twenty palace maids all riding precious horses,
carrying a golden crown and an embroidered python robe,
a jade belt and a red gown.
Likewise, rebel eunuchs held dragon and phoenix fans,
leading the fragrant carriage and the delicate palanquin.
Over ten troupes of musicians played,
all intending to please Zhào-shì,
so the ceremony was extremely grand.
Zhào-shì bid farewell to the Guān family ancestral hall,
bowed four times to her mother-in-law,
and bowed four times toward the empty air to her husband.
After a bout of weeping,
she boarded the carriage and lowered the curtain,
and the crowd thronged together and departed.
The mother-in-law collapsed on the ground weeping
and was awakened by the maidservant.
Guān Yí, knowing his wife had departed,
only then dared to return home.
Having already wept until he was distraught,
he hurriedly packed his luggage,
abandoned his household property,
and together with the maidservant, supported the mother-in-law as they secretly fled to Dōngjīng.
Meanwhile, Wáng Zé heard Zhāng Qí report:
"The bride has been brought."
Joy descended from heaven;
he hurriedly arranged a great guard of honor
and personally went out to the gate of the manor to receive her.
The soldiers all hoped for rewards,
each full of joy,
lining up in two rows
to let the fragrant carriage enter the manor.
Wáng Zé opened the curtain himself
but saw no movement.
When he lifted her out
and looked, he found a silk cloth tied around her neck.
It turned out she had secretly hanged herself in the carriage;
she was truly a heroic woman.
The historian has a poem in praise:
"Cursing a bandit is not hard, but deceiving one is;
Saving the husband's house from disaster, she rests in the Nine Springs.
Such wisdom and virtue have always been rare;
Not only was her fragrant heart a single inch of crimson loyalty."
Later people also had a poem that says:
"We have heard of Cuī Yuánkǎi's wife cursing the bandit;
