But this woman following the guest to fulfill righteousness is even more remarkable.
How many officials and scholars live only to steal a life,
Not comparable to Zhào and Cuī of Qīnghé."
Qīnghé is the land of Bèizhōu.
At the end of the Suí dynasty, there was a man named Cuī Yuánkǎi.
Cuī Yuánkǎi's wife died while cursing a bandit.
This poem honors the great integrity of these two heroic women,
whom men cannot match.
Wáng Zé's mood was completely dampened that night.
He thought:
"The woman's nature was fierce;
it had nothing to do with the others."
He ordered Zhāng Qí to return the corpse to her original husband
and recover the betrothal gifts.
The next day, Zhāng Qí learned that the Guān family had fled.
He reported this to Wáng Zé,
and she was buried outside the city.
Wáng Zé issued a proclamation:
Any beautiful woman among the common people,
whether parents offer a daughter
or a husband offers a wife,
once selected, the government would provide a hundred liǎng as a betrothal gift.
If anyone hides them and does not offer them,
and they are exposed by others,
the family will be punished.
Consequently, they seized wives and daughters from the common people
in numbers beyond count.
If a commoner took a beautiful wife,
he would say she was an unlucky thing;
but if he took an ugly one, he would instead be joyful.
At that time, there was a saying:
"Do not seek a beautiful face,
An ugly wife is a treasure to a good family.
Do not mind that the officials don't want her,
The husband and wife will stay together until they are old."
To this day, the saying that an ugly wife is a treasure of a good family
originated from this.
Hú Yǒng'ér knew well that Wáng Zé was greedy for beauty and indulged in lust,
but she let him be.
However, when she had her own private affairs
and did not want Wáng Zé to enter the palace,
she would stick a golden hairpin outside the threshold,
and the house would be surrounded as if by a thousand rings of fierce fire.
Or she would stick a silver hairpin outside the threshold,
and the house would be surrounded as if by a great flood;
outsiders could not move an inch closer.
When she was at leisure and nothing was happening,
she would withdraw the magic,
and either invite Wáng Zé to the palace to gather,
or Wáng Zé would come on his own,
and the couple remained on good terms.
It was a pity that this couple,
greedy for lust and obsessed with beauty,
lost their ambition to advance,
which was also because their destiny only reached this far.
Reverend Dànzǐ saw that Wáng Zé's actions were against the principles of Heaven
and that he would eventually fail and achieve nothing,
so he simply left without saying goodbye.
Zuǒ Chù, relying on his status as the national uncle,
acted willfully in all matters.
Zhāng Luán
and Bǔ Jí, though they held their positions,
had no power at all,
yet they enjoyed their leisure.
Wú Sānláng changed his name to Wú Wàng;
he, Zhāng Qí,
and Rèn Qiān all requested regions to govern,
took the office of Prefect,
and enjoyed wealth and honor.
They often led troops to raid neighboring borders,
plundering children and riches
to offer as tribute to Wáng Zé.
It was only because the treacherous official Xià Sǒng deceived the imperial court,
allowing such a great power to develop,
and letting the people of that region suffer,
while he concealed the truth and did not report it.
One day,
Emperor Rénzōng’s imperial carriage traveled to the Western Tàiyǐ Temple to offer incense.
After the ceremony was finished,
just as he was about to return to court,
a newly appointed Imperial Censor suddenly stepped out from the ranks of the hundred officials.
That man’s surname was Hé and his given name was Tán.
He walked forward several quick steps,
grabbed the imperial robe with one hand,
and prostrated himself on the ground, weeping loudly.
Rénzōng said:
"What grievance does my minister have?
Present it to me.
I shall seek justice for you."
Hé Tán reported:
"I have no personal grievance.
It is only a pity that the four hundred prefectures of Emperor Tàizǔ
are being gradually encroached upon and diminished.
Although Your Majesty possesses the natural talent of Yáo and Shùn,
in the future, it will be hard to avoid the disasters of Jié and Zhòu."
Rénzōng was greatly shocked and said:
"Why do you say such words?
You must explain in detail."
Hé Tán reported:
"In Xīxià, Zhào Yuánhào has rebelled;
in Yōngzhōu, Nóng Zhìgāo has rebelled;
and there is no one to subdue them.
Now in Bèizhōu, Wáng Zé has also rebelled,
and the entire Héběi region has become a nest for bandits.
If Your Majesty does not consider selecting good generals
to suppress the rebels and pacify the people,
I fear the territory will shrink day by day,
and the world will no longer belong to the Zhào family."
Rénzōng said:
"I have already ordered Fàn Yōng to campaign against Yuánhào,
and Yáng Tián to campaign against Nóng Zhìgāo,
though I have not yet seen the progress.
As for the mutiny in Bèizhōu,
at the time, I dispatched the Governor of Jìzhōu, Liú Yànwēi, to suppress it.
From where do your words come?"
Hé Tán reported again:
"Fàn Yōng is old
and is held in contempt by Yuánhào.
Yáng Tián has been out for a long time without success,
wasting provisions and fodder.
As for the rebel Wáng Zé in Bèizhōu,
he defeated Liú Yànwēi so thoroughly that not a single piece of armor returned;
he has declared himself king and adopted a title,
and the entire Hédōng region is shaken.
Urgent reports arrived in the capital like snowflakes,
but they were all hidden and not reported by the Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs, Xià Sǒng.
If Your Majesty does not execute Xià Sǒng,
the world will not find peace."
At this time, Xià Sǒng was also before the carriage;
he was scared until his face was the color of earth,
and he stammered, not daring to speak.
Rénzōng said in great anger:
"Xià Sǒng, you treacherous official!
I entrusted you with military power,
yet you did not think of repaying me,
deceiving the sovereign and harming the country.
You truly deserve to be beheaded,
but for now, I shall dismiss you from office to become a commoner."
Xià Sǒng’s face was full of shame;
he could only give thanks and depart.
Rénzōng then asked:
"Who at present can take the post of Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs?"
Hé Tán reported:
"Nowadays, for one whose name is known throughout the world for being upright and selfless,
none is like Bāo Zhěng.
This man once served as the Governor of Kāifēng Prefecture,
governing so cleanly that it was like water.
Only because he refused to attach himself to Xià Sǒng
did he resign his office and return home.
If Your Majesty wishes to select good generals
to suppress the three great bandits,
you need only appoint Bāo Zhěng;
whomever he recommends
will be appropriate."
Rénzōng was greatly pleased
and granted the request.
That same day, he summoned Bāo Lóngtú
and promoted him to the post of Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs.
Bāo Zhěng, hearing the summons at home,
quickly set out for Dōngjīng
and completed his thanks to the Emperor.
Rénzōng asked:
"Now that Xīxià,
Guǎngnán,
and Héběi are in rebellion,
what good strategies do you have to stabilize the state and pacify the people?"
Bāo Zhěng reported:
"In my humble opinion,
Fàn Zhòngyān can be solely assigned to Xīxià,
Dí Qīng can be solely assigned to Guǎngnán,
and Wén Yànbó can be solely assigned to Héběi.
If Your Majesty wants peace in the world,
unless you entrust these three men,
success cannot be demanded."
Rénzōng said:
"In Héběi, it is just a soldier's riot;
how can it be so serious?"
Bāo Zhěng reported:
"Wáng Zé is not worth mentioning.
But he has a group of demon rebels helping him
who can perform sorcery."
Rénzōng said:
"Wén Yànbó is already eighty years old;
why do you specifically recommend him?"
Bāo Zhěng reported:
"I have heard a nursery rhyme that says:
'Eight eyes glinting with anger,
loftily standing as the master of the Three Teachings;
celestial gods act as generals and ghosts as the army.
Not afraid of the military,
only afraid of the civil.'
Beside the character 'zé' in Wáng Zé is the character 'bèi',
and Bèizhōu also signifies the meaning of 'eight eyes'.
Among the sorcerers, there are both monks and Daoists,
yet they all serve Wáng Zé as their master;
hence the phrase 'loftily standing as the master of the Three Teachings.'
Godly generals and ghost armies are sorcery;
these people have more than enough martial power,
but lack civil power.
Thus it is said, 'Not afraid of the military,
only afraid of the civil.'
Now, sending Wén Yànbó
perfectly matches this prophecy.
Furthermore, when the character 'bèi' is combined with 'wén',
it becomes the character 'bài', meaning defeat.
This is why I did not recommend others
but specifically named Yànbó.
Moreover, although Yànbó is old,
his energy has not declined;
his talent and wisdom surpass others,
and he is experienced and steady.
If this man goes,
Wáng Zé will undoubtedly be defeated."
Emperor Rénzōng, hearing the report, was greatly pleased
and issued three imperial edicts,
ordering messengers to go in different directions to summon the three men to the capital overnight for promotion.
There is a poem to prove it:
Xià Sǒng’s treacherous evil was far too heartless,
He wished to catch all the worthy ministers in one net.
But once the day comes that loyal and sycophant are clearly distinguished,
The dust of war will settle on the borders.
Setting aside the matters of Fàn Zhòngyān
and Dí Qīng,
let us specifically describe Wén Yànbó.
This man was from Fénzhōu in Hédōng;
in his youth, he had merit in campaigning against the Western barbarians,
and rose through the ranks to become the Prime Minister.
Because he did not get along with Xià Sǒng,
he insisted on leaving his post
and was reassigned as the Regent of Xījīng.
He was already seventy-nine years old,
but his energy was superior to that of young men in their twenties or thirties.
The messenger received the decree
and arrived at Xījīng in the middle of the night.
Wén Yànbó, along with the high and low officials of the prefecture, went out of the city
to receive the imperial edict at the prefectural office.
After it was read,
the officials rose and faced the palace to give thanks.
Wén Yànbó received the order,
bid farewell to his family,
and traveled at double speed.
In not many days, he reached Dōngjīng,
where officials were waiting at the reception hall
to welcome him into the city.
At the morning audience the next day,
he followed the ranks to see the Emperor.
How can one describe the morning audience?
One sees:
Auspicious clouds drift around the Phoenix Gates,
and propitious vapors shroud the Dragon Tower.
Mist-shrouded imperial willows brush against the banners,
and dew-laden palace peaches greet the swords and halberds.
Amidst the fragrance of heavenly incense,
jade hairpins and pearl shoes gather on the cinnabar steps.
In the sound of immortal music,
embroidered jackets and brocade robes support the imperial carriage.
The pearl curtains are rolled up,
and the golden palanquin appears in the Golden Hall.
The phoenix fans open,
and the jade chariot stops before the white jade steps.
Faintly, the crack of the ceremonial whip sounds three times,
and the two ranks of civil and military officials stand in perfect order.
On that day, the Rénzōng Tiānzǐ summoned Wén Yànbó to his presence.
The Shèngzhǐ stated:
"Wáng Zé has rebelled in Bèizhōu of Héběi.
I now appoint you as the Yuánshuài
to suppress the sorcerous rebel.
How many men and horses should be used?
How many vice-generals?
I leave it to your discretion to decide."
Wén Yànbó memorialized:
"I have heard that Wáng Zé and his faction are also sorcerers.
If the men and horses are few,
I fear victory cannot be won.
I wish to recommend one person as a vice-general;
only with one hundred thousand men and horses can the enemy be overcome."
Rénzōng said:
"The army and horses shall be as you memorialized,
but I do not know whom you recommend as a vice-general?"
Wén Yànbó memorialized:
"I request Cáo Wěi to be the vice-general."
Rénzōng said:
"Is this Cáo Wěi not the descendant of Cáo Bīn, who was the most meritorious in conquering Jiāngnán
and was enfeoffed as a Wáng?"
Wén Yànbó memorialized:
"He is indeed the legitimate grandson of Cáo Bīn."
Rénzōng heard the memorial,
and his Lóngyán was greatly pleased.
He ordered Cáo Wěi to be summoned for an audience.
At the hall, Rénzōng enfeoffed Wén Yànbó as the Tǒngbīng Zhāotǎoshǐ
and Cáo Wěi as the Fù Zhāotǎoshǐ.
He allocated gold, silver, money, and silk from the Nèitǎng
to reward the Sānjūn.
The two thanked him for his grace and left the court,
immediately going to the various camps to review the troops and dispatch the horses.
The Shūmìshǐ Bāo Zhěng prepared wine to see them off,
and privately said to Wén Zhāotǎo:
"Lǎo Xiànggōng, on this journey,
you will surely achieve great merit.
But among the rebels is a sorcerous monk called Dànzǐ Héshang;
this monk has many transformations.
The Xiàngguó should be prepared."
Wén Zhāotǎo said:
"I am much obliged for your guidance."
After three cups of wine were finished,
Bāo Zhěng took his leave.
Wén Zhāotǎo left the capital and set out on his journey that very day,
crossing the Huáng Hé and arriving directly at the borders of Héběi.
The army and horses were then stationed in Jìzhōu.
Truly it was:
Everyone desired to establish the achievements of being enfeoffed as a marquis,
and each one thought of completing the merit of sweeping away the bandits.
After all, as Wén Zhāotǎo campaigns against Bèizhōu,
how will the victory or defeat turn out?
Please listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
Though victory and defeat are not constant for military strategists,
misfortune or fortune is judged by following the heterodox or the orthodox.
If one knows the principles of heterodoxy, orthodoxy, sorcery, and fortune,
turn back early without need for discussion.
It is said that when Wén Zhāotǎo’s grand army arrived and was stationed at Jìzhōu,
the Jìzhōu Tàishǒu Liú Yànwēi welcomed the two Zhāotǎo into the city,
exhaustively describing how Wáng Zé’s sorcery was difficult to withstand.
Wén Yànbó discussed with Cáo Wěi, saying:
"Wáng Zé occupies prefectures and commanderies
and resides in Bèizhōu.
Regarding the current advance of the army,
should we unite our forces and strike Bèizhōu directly,
or divide our forces to attack and seize from four directions?
The Zhāotǎo must have some brilliant plan or divine strategy?"
Cáo Wěi said:
"I, Cáo, am a vice-general;
how would I dare to overstep with strategies?
The commander-in-chief has orders;
I shall solely obey your command."
Wén Zhāotǎo said:
"Not so.
The Zhāotǎo is a descendant of a famous general,
who once established merit on the borders with the late King.
Although I, Yànbó, am the chief general,
I am after all a scholar.
I rely entirely on the Zhāotǎo to complete the royal task together;
there is no need for modesty."
Cáo Zhāotǎo replied:
"Although the prefectures and counties of Héběi have gone over to Wáng Zé,
it is all because they fear his power,
and not because they are truly convinced.
Now hearing that the grand army has arrived here,
they cannot even look after themselves;
how could they have leisure to send troops to assist him?
Relying on the commander-in-chief’s divine majesty,
let us strike directly at Bèizhōu.
If Bèizhōu is conquered,
the rest will not require further military action;
they will naturally submit."
Wén Zhāotǎo said:
"The Zhāotǎo’s insight is extremely clear.
I have heard that the troops in his city do not number ten thousand.
On our side, we have a grand army of one hundred thousand;
furthermore, having the Zhāotǎo’s brilliant plans,
destroying the rebels will be as easy as turning over one's hand."
Cáo Zhāotǎo said:
"I have also investigated and heard that although Wáng Zé and his lot cannot use military or civil arts,
they exclusively practice sorcery.
Previously, when Liú Tàishǒu went to suppress them,
he was countered by Wáng Zé’s use of sorcery;
thus he returned having lost troops and generals.
According to my humble opinion,
the chief general should take thirty thousand men as the central army,
and give twenty thousand men to me as the left wing.
Give twenty thousand men to the Zǒngguǎn Wáng Xìn as the right wing.
Divided into three routes,
we shall form a formation like a long serpent.
Give twenty thousand men to the Zhuǎnyùnshǐ Yòng Gǎo to guard the rear.
Give five thousand men to the Xiānfēng Sūn Fǔ to patrol the various camps.
Give five thousand men to Liú Yànwēi to assist Sūn Fǔ,
acting as guides.
Now Wáng Zé’s troops do not number ten thousand;
they can only oppose one of our routes.
If our army wins,
then all three routes will advance together.
If there is a slight disadvantage,
then the other two routes will surely come to the rescue.
This is a foolproof strategy."
Hearing this, Wén Zhāotǎo
said with great joy:
"With the Zhāotǎo deploying troops like this,
why worry that Bèizhōu will not be broken?"
On this day,
Wén Zhāotǎo divided the men and horses into three routes to take Bèizhōu.
First, he sent a placard ahead;
the placard enumerated ten great crimes of Wáng Zé:
First,
wrongfully inciting a change in the army's morale.
Second,
wrongfully killing prefectural officials on your own authority.
Third,
wrongfully occupying cities and moats on your own authority.
Fourth,
wrongfully gathering a sorcerous faction
and killing or wounding government troops.
Fifth,
wrongfully declaring yourself King and establishing a Queen.
Sixth,
wrongfully bestowing official ranks on your own authority.
Seventh,
wrongfully letting loose troops to invade and plunder prefectures and counties.
Eighth,
wrongfully conscripting laborers privately
and constructing royal palaces and counterfeit offices.
Ninth,
wrongfully committing adultery with the women of the common people.
Tenth,
wrongfully betraying the country, harming the people, and persisting in evil without regret.
Today, one hundred thousand Tiānbīng have come to campaign against you,
seeking only the one chief offender, Wáng Zé;
the rest of the faction shall all be pardoned and not questioned.
If there are those who capture or behead Wáng Zé and present him,
their merit shall be recorded equally.
Should Wáng Zé acknowledge his own crimes,
bind his hands and surrender,
I shall memorialize the court
to grant him life.
If he remains obsessed and continues to resist,
once the troops arrive beneath the city walls,
it will be too late for regrets.
Wáng Zé saw this proclamation,
and was so frightened that he was at a loss for what to do.
He quickly gathered Zuǒ Chù and his group to deliberate.
Zuǒ Chù said:
"The other day, Liú Yànwēi of Jìzhōu was slaughtered so thoroughly that not a single piece of armor returned.
Now Wén Yànbó is already eighty years old,
and has come here on his own to seek death.
Although he has a powerful army of a hundred thousand,
what can he do to us?"
Zhāng Luán said:
"When I, a poor Daoist, was in Dōngjīng,
I often heard the name of Wén Yànbó.
An extraordinary person once calculated his Eight Characters,
saying he would be a general abroad and a minister at home,
and that his life's wealth and honor would be incomparable.
Near the age of eighty,
he would again achieve great merits for the Imperial Court,
bringing peace and stability to the state,
and would die at an age near a hundred years.
This man is a god of fortune from the heavens;
he must not be treated lightly!
Furthermore, a children's nursery rhyme says:
'In Bèizhōu prefecture is a lone tiger,
who fears the Civil (Wén) but does not fear the Martial (Wǔ).'
Now Commissioner Wén exactly matches that surname;
good or bad fortune is hard to guarantee.
According to my humble opinion,
it would be better to take the instances of corruption by the Prefect Zhāng Dé,
explain the detailed reasons and grievances,
use humble words to apologize for our crimes,
and trouble Commissioner Wén to memorialize the Emperor,
expressing our willingness to provide our own military provisions to serve the state,
either by conquering the Xīxià,
or suppressing the Guǎngnán region.
If we can achieve merit and return in triumph,
we would still not lose our positions as Lords or Kings.
I wonder what the Military Counselor's intention is?"
Zuǒ Chù said:
"Having been great, it is hard to be small.
Relying on our magical powers,
even if the Zhào Sovereign himself came,
we would not be afraid.
Why fear a single old man?
Why does the Prime Minister dampen our own spirits?"
Zhāng Luán said:
"When we first rose up,
it was originally because corrupt officials harmed the people,
and the people's hearts were filled with shared indignation,
while it just so happened that treacherous ministers were at court,
hiding the truth and not reporting it,
which allowed us to succeed in our endeavor.
Now the court's governance is clear and bright,
purging evil and employing the worthy,
and they have ordered a high official to lead the troops here;
this is by no means comparable to the past.
If we rely solely on some magic arts,
how do we know there are no people there who understand such matters?
I ask the Military Counselor to think thrice."
Bǔ Jí was at the side but did not open his mouth.
Wáng Zé saw that the two men's opinions differed;
he turned and rose,
and the group dispersed.
Wáng Zé went straight into the false palace
to see Hú Yǒng'ér,
and told her both sides of the argument.
Yǒng'ér said:
"Why should the Great King abandon the enterprise already achieved,
and bind his hands to be controlled by others?
This thousand-catty burden
will naturally be borne by my brother and me.
If you are not at ease,
then invite our mother, Shèng Gūgū, to come,
and there will be absolutely no risk.
The words of Zhāng
and Bǔ
must not be listened to!"
Wáng Zé was overjoyed upon hearing this
and said:
"The Queen's words are correct."
That night they feasted and enjoyed themselves to the fullest,
and he stayed the night in Yǒng'ér's palace.
Now it is said that Bǔ Jí,
though he said nothing that day,
thought in his heart:
"I was originally doing business as a traveler;
because I went down the well for Hú Yǒng'ér,
I offended the prefectural official
and nearly lost my life.
Fortunately, I met my master,
who saved my life
and avenged that grievance.
Who would have known that Wáng Zé would incite the people's hearts
to rebel against the Imperial Court,
greatly violating the laws of heaven.
The other day, Dàn Shī left without saying goodbye
only because he could not bear to see this.
If we do not see the opportunity,
and instead oppose Commissioner Wén,
we will truly be acting against reason."
He then went through the night to see Zhāng Luán,
saying:
"Just now, the Lame One showed great disapproval of my Master's intentions.
If Master stays here,
there will be harm and no benefit.
For our current plan,
it is better to act as the situation dictates
and leap out of this gate of right and wrong."
Zhāng Luán said:
"Your words exactly match my intent.
I have a master living in seclusion on Yùxiāo Peak of Tiāntái Shān practicing the Way;
why not go there together to seek him out,
gather herbs and refine elixirs,
and strive for the true fruit of immortality?
Would that not be beautiful?"
Having finished their discussion,
that very night they left Bèizhōu City
and headed toward Tiāntái Shān.
There is a poem to witness:
"A single thought between purity and evil turns fortune or woe,
A treacherous hero turns his head and is a hero once more.
Today, two wings soar into the sky,
Asking no more of the old war fires of Luòzhōu."
Later, when Emperor Dàojūn was building the Wànsuì Shān,
he sent ten commissioners to Jiāngnán to procure flowers and rocks.
One of these commissioners was at the Yùtíng Cave of Tiāntái,
where he took a fancy to a golden pine.
It turned out that the golden pine was unlike ordinary pines;
its hanging branches were like slender willows,
and its seeds were like green pearls,
produced only in Táizhōu.
This pine grew with even more exquisite loveliness,
its roots and trunk coiling around a clever rock.
The commissioner planted a yellow flag with imperial markings on it,
and chose a day to summon laborers to carry it away along with the rock.
Suddenly, an old Daoist walked out from the cave and said:
"This tree was planted by my late master, the Recluse Chōngxiāo, with his own hands.
I, a poor Daoist, have guarded it here for over seventy years;
I beg you to show mercy
and do not move it."
The commissioner said:
"A drawing of the pine and rock has already been submitted to the Emperor;
how can we stop?"
The old Daoist said:
"Please report back to the Emperor,
and simply say that Daoist Bǔ of Zhèngzhōu begs to keep it as a companion."
The commissioner would not listen
and ordered the laborers to start work.
Just as the shovels were striking,
a loud crash was heard,
the rock fell and split apart,
and the golden pine withered and died instantly.
The commissioner was startled.
The old Daoist again pleaded repeatedly,
and the commissioner agreed.
The old Daoist gently supported the clever rock with his hand,
and the golden tree became lush as before.
When the commissioner returned to court and reported to Dàojūn,
there were those in the court who knew the stories of the Rénzōng era,
who said:
"The Recluse Chōngxiāo was Zhāng Luán, and the Daoist Bǔ was Bǔ Jí."
From the time of Rénzōng to that of Dàojūn,
it had been nearly a hundred years,
and yet Bǔ Jí still lived;
it was suspected that he had attained immortality!
This is a later story.
Furthermore, the next morning Wáng Zé heard a report:
"Zhāng Luán
and Bǔ Jí have both disappeared to places unknown."
He urgently summoned Zuǒ Chù to ask about it.
Zuǒ Chù said:
"Zhāng Luán originally belonged to a different sect than ours.
He likely felt our views were incompatible
and left in shame.
Bǔ Jí is his disciple,
so they left together.
We do not depend on him anyway.
You can summon Zhāng Qí,
Rèn Qiān,
and Wú Wàng, these three, to return for service."
Zhāng Qí and the others were currently serving as officials and enjoying prosperity in various places.
When the news from Bèizhōu arrived,
they each led the troops of their respective regions to come and assist in the battle.
Wáng Zé learned that Wén Zhāotǎo's grand army had arrived,
so he opened the city gates wide
and led his army to deploy in formation near the city.
The cripple stayed close to assist him,
with Wú Wàng on the left
and Rèn Qiān on the right.
He left Zhāng Qí and Táo Bìxiǎn on the city walls to beat drums and shout.
Hú Yǒng'ér personally led troops
to patrol around the city.
Wén Zhāotǎo divided his troops into three routes
and came to the front of the formation
to speak with Wáng Zé.
Wáng Zé saw Wén Zhāotǎo come forward on horseback
and offered a greeting, saying:
"Because the local officials were greedy and corrupt,
I stood up to eliminate the harm for the people.
The masses pushed me to temporarily lead this corner of the land,
and I do not infringe upon others;
why must the imperial court send troops here?"
Wén Zhāotǎo shouted loudly:
"You have committed ten great crimes against Heaven.
Today the celestial army has arrived;
it is only right that you open the gates and surrender.
How dare you resist?
You do not know life from death!"
Wáng Zé said:
"I have long heard of the Zhāotǎo’s great name and advanced age;
you should know when to advance or retreat
to enjoy your remaining years.
If you insist on clashing,
I fear my subordinates will not show mercy;
do not blame me, do not blame me!"
Wén Zhāotǎo was furious and ordered the drums to be beaten.
The vanguard Sūn Fǔ brandished his spear and commanded his troops to storm the city
and capture Wáng Zé.
Seeing the troops charging, Wáng Zé
retreated a step
and allowed Zuǒ Chù’s horse to take the lead.
Liú Yànwēi, beside Wén Zhāotǎo, pointed at the cripple and said:
"This rebel priest is accustomed to using demonic sorcery;
the Marshal should be wary of him."
Before he had even finished speaking,
Zuǒ Chù was seen at the front of the formation gnashing his teeth and performing magic:
dark clouds and fierce rain appeared,
along with thunder and lightning;
chunks of fire rolled about,
and a gust of yellow sand swirled up within the ranks of the troops,
shrouding the sky and darkening the earth.
Inside the yellow sand were people with divine heads and ghostly faces,
leading many jackals, wolves, tigers, and leopards to charge the formation.
The troops could only fight humans;
how could they fight gods, ghosts, and fierce beasts?
The warhorses were so startled they bolted in chaos,
throwing the soldiers and generals off their backs.
Wáng Zé saw that Wén Zhāotǎo's formation was in disorder
and took the opportunity to drive his troops forward for a sudden assault.
Wén Zhāotǎo, along with the vanguard Sūn Fǔ,
was soundly defeated and fled.
Wáng Zé led his troops to pursue them.
The Deputy Zhāotǎo Cáo Wěi
and General Wáng Xìn,
seeing Wén Zhāotǎo's defeat,
each led their own units forward to the rescue.
Wáng Zé saw the two routes of troops coming together
and, fearing a loss,
he urgently ordered his troops to withdraw into the city.
Wén Zhāotǎo led his army thirty lǐ away from the city to Fùjiātuǎn to set up camp.
When they counted the troops,
those killed or trampled to death by their own side were countless.
The two Zhāotǎo, Wén and
Cáo, along with General Wáng Xìn,
gathered the generals to discuss a strategy for attacking the city.
Wén Zhāotǎo said:
"I have fought hundreds of battles, large and small, against the Xīfān Róng troops,
but I have never seen such demonic sorcery as Wáng Zé's.
It is now clear why Prefect Liú lost to this rebel."
Liú Yànwēi said:
"At first, your humble servant was caught in the wind and sand whipped up by the demonic rebel
and lost a battle.
I then ordered the soldiers to each prepare eye covers.
In the second battle, he drove out fierce beasts,
and I lost another battle.
I then ordered the army to paint lions on cloth
and cover the horses' backs.
This was Kǒngmíng’s strategy for defeating the Nánmán.
Unexpectedly, in the third battle, there were freezing winds and hail,
and half of the men and horses froze to death.
This group of sorcerers is truly unpredictable.
We must break their demonic sorcery before we can achieve victory."
Cáo Zhāotǎo said:
"I have heard that there are no more than four or five people in Bèizhōu who know demonic arts;
the rest do not.
However, regarding these demonic spells,
I, Cáo, have a method to break them."
Wén Zhāotǎo heard this and said happily:
"May I ask what clever plan the Zhāotǎo has
to break the demonic sorcery?"
Cáo Zhāotǎo said:
"Wáng Zé's type of magic
is called 'Vajra Zen' by the Buddhists
and 'Heterodox Arts' by the Daoists.
If someone knows both types of magic,
they are called 'Dual Practitioners.'
These are all demonic methods.
What they fear most is the blood of pigs and sheep,
horse urine, dog feces, and garlic.
If even a drop falls on them,
they will be unable to transform into gods or ghosts
and cannot perform their demonic spells."
Wén Zhāotǎo was overjoyed
and ordered that during battle,
the tips of all blades and spears must be dipped in blood.
Cáo Zhāotǎo ordered the construction of five hundred pump-pipes,
all filled with the blood of pigs and sheep.
He selected five hundred tall and strong soldiers to be pump-pipe operators,
pairing them with five hundred archers and crossbowmen.
During the battle,
if they saw gods, ghosts, or strange beasts,
the pump-pipes and crossbows would be discharged all at once.
There is a poem to prove it:
Evil has never triumphed over the upright;
once exposed, how can it last?
No matter how many transformations the demonic crowd has,
today they cannot escape the pump-pipe operators.
Wén Zhāotǎo rewarded the soldiers.
On the following day,
he deployed the troops,
leaving Míng Gǎo to guard the main camp at Fùjiātuǎn.
He ordered most of the others to divide into three units as before,
three lǐ from the city,
and draw up battle formations.
The sound of drums shook the earth,
and the shouts of battle reached the sky.
It turned out that under Wáng Zé,
there were no great heroes or brave men;
their fighting relied entirely on demonic sorcery.
Having won repeatedly,
they did not take Wén Zhāotǎo seriously.
That day, hearing that the army had approached the city,
Zhāng Qí, Wú Wàng,
and Rèn Qiān discussed:
"Since arriving in Bèizhōu,
we have not achieved a shred of merit.
Having learned Daoist arts in vain,
why not demonstrate them today?"
The three of them went together to report to Wáng Zé,
expressing their willingness to lead their own units out to battle.
Wáng Zé said:
"The other day Wén Yànhbó suffered a great defeat,
but his left and right wings of soldiers came to attack and rescue him.
Today, Wú Wàng can lead a detachment of troops to the east to intercept his right army,
and Rèn Qiān can lead a detachment of troops to the west to intercept his left army.
Zhāng Qí shall act as the vanguard
and engage in battle with Sūn Fǔ.
I, the Sovereign, along with the Guójiù
and the Jūnshī, will attack and capture the central army.
We must capture that old man
to eliminate future trouble."
The three received their orders,
led their troops out of the city,
and departed by separate routes.
Now, regarding the vanguard Sūn Fǔ,
leading five thousand men,
he pressed directly to the foot of the city walls to challenge for battle,
where he happened to encounter Zhāng Qí's horses and men.
Zhāng Qí did not know martial arts
and relied only on the Shuǐhuǒ Húlu.
Immediately, he hurriedly recited incantations
and held the mouth of the gourd forward with both hands.
From the left side of the Shuǐhuǒ Húlu, a stream of water sprayed out,
like a waterfall from a high cliff.
From the right side, a stream of fire sprayed out,
like wild flames burning the sky.
Those met by the water had it drenched over their heads and faces;
those met by the fire had their hair singed and eyebrows scorched.
Sūn Fǔ could not withstand it,
and fearing the main army would be thrown into chaos,
he turned his horse and fled diagonally toward the east.
Zhāng Qí directed his horses and men
to pursue him.
Wáng Zé, seeing that the forward army had gained the advantage,
then drove a large force of horses and men forward
and encountered Wén Zhāotǎo's main army.
Beneath the gate banners,
Zuǒ Chù, with disheveled hair and clutching a sword,
drove out many demonic ghosts and strange beasts.
Wén Zhāotǎo shouted for the gates of the formation to be opened,
releasing five hundred pump-operators
and five hundred archers.
Pumping and shooting,
they all broke out at once.
The arrows were all coated with filth,
and those divine ghosts and strange beasts had their magic broken by the filth of pig and sheep blood;
their forms dissolved and their shadows vanished.
Zuǒ Chù was caught off guard
and was greatly shocked.
Before he could make another move,
he was caught by Wén Zhāotǎo's troops who took advantage of the momentum to strike,
and he suffered a great defeat, fleeing into the wild.
Wáng Zé hurriedly led his troops back into the city,
hauled up the drawbridge,
and tightly closed the city gates, not coming out again.
To speak again of Wú Wàng's detachment of troops going east:
they happened to encounter Cáo Zhāotǎo's forward brave general, Dǒng Zhōng,
who raised his spear and went straight for Wú Wàng.
Wú Wàng had also practiced some spear and staff since childhood;
the two began to fight with spears,
back and forth,
for about twenty rounds.
Cáo Zhāotǎo's rear army had already arrived;
Cáo Wěi's double-blade technique was supernatural,
and he personally went to the front of the battle to assist.
Wú Wàng realized he could not match them,
slapped his horse,
soared into the air,
and departed as if flying.
Cáo Zhāotǎo could not pursue him in time.
To speak again of Sūn Fǔ leading his defeated troops east:
he suddenly saw a general on horseback leaping through the air,
several zhàng above the ground.
Guessing it was a sorcerer,
he hurriedly drew his bow
and shot an arrow into the air,
which hit the horse.
That arrow was also dipped in foul blood;
the horse Wú Wàng rode was a demonic horse
originally made of cut paper;
upon being hit by the arrow, it turned back into paper,
and Wú Wàng fell head over heels from mid-air.
Sūn Fǔ turned his horse around
and was just about to capture him,
when Zhāng Qí's troops happened to arrive in pursuit.
Seeing someone fall from the sky,
they recognized it was Wú Wàng
and quickly rescued him.
Cáo Zhāotǎo's main army all arrived,
and Zhāng Qí did not dare linger in battle,
but protected Wú Wàng and fled.
Reaching the drawbridge, they called for the city gates to be opened,
and those inside received them.
Wú Wàng's detachment of troops
was cut off at the rear,
and all surrendered to Cáo Zhāotǎo's command.
To speak again of Rèn Qiān, who turned a wooden stool into a tiger and rode it;
with it shaking its head and wagging its tail,
he considered himself invincible
and led a detachment of troops to the west.
Wáng Zǒngguǎn's forward brave general, Liǔ Chūnshēng,
was originally a hunter by trade
and used an all-iron steel fork.
His subordinates were all infantry.
Liǔ Chūnshēng took it for a real tiger,
raised his steel fork, and prepared to thrust.
Rèn Qiān, seeing the momentum was fierce,
slapped the tiger,
and the tiger leaped over two zhàng high,
baring its fangs and claws,
and pounced toward Liǔ Chūnshēng.
Liǔ Chūnshēng dodged with a flash.
He thrust his steel fork with all his might into the tiger's rear
and shouted:
"Got you!"
With a crackling sound,
the tiger fell to the ground.
Upon looking, it was not a tiger,
but a wooden bench.
This bench was made of wood,
and the steel fork was forged of solid steel;
metal can overcome wood.
Furthermore, the head of the steel fork was also dipped in foul blood;
once it touched it,
the sorcery was dispelled.
Rèn Qiān's heels hit the ground,
and he was already in a panic;
he was thrust down by the steel fork in his shoulder by Liǔ Chūnshēng
and tied up alive.
The rebel troops were without a leader
and each fled for their lives.
In this battle fought by Wén Zhāotǎo,
the three routes were victorious.
They then pressed toward Bèizhōu to set up camp.
Liú Yànwēi, beneath the city,
picked up countless monsters to present.
They were all made of cut paper and grass,
and things like red beans and white beans.
Because they were stained with filth,
they could not be recovered.
The vanguard Sūn Fǔ collected Wú Wàng's paper horse to present.
Cáo Zhāotǎo accepted the surrender of over a thousand soldiers.
Liǔ Chūnshēng, under Wáng Xìn's command, delivered one main rebel, Rèn Qiān, and one bench that had turned into a tiger.
Wén Zhāotǎo recorded each one in the book of merits.
Wén Zhāotǎo personally interrogated Rèn Qiān in detail
and only then learned that there were originally six people including Wáng Zé who started it;
later, there were three others including Zhāng Qí.
Dànzǐ Héshang had already left;
Zhāng
and Bǔ had a disagreement with Zuǒ Chù
and also left.
Now in the city, there were only Hú Yǒng'ér, Zuǒ Chù,
Zhāng Qí,
and Wú Wàng, these four.
There was also Hú Yǒng'ér's mother called Shèng Gūgū,
who came and went irregularly.
When Wén Zhāotǎo was about to depart,
he had heard Bāo Lóngtú say that Dànzǐ Héshang was extremely formidable;
now hearing that he was not in the city,
he let go of one major worry.
After the interrogation was finished,
he ordered him to be put in a prison cart
and sent to Míng Gǎo's place in the main camp to be guarded.
They would wait until Wáng Zé was captured
and send them to the capital together.
Every morning, a bowl of pig and sheep blood was drenched over his head.
Truly, it is as past deeds were done,
misfortune comes all at once.
There is a poem to prove it:
The paper horse's form dissolves, the wooden tiger withers,
years of sorcery suddenly turn to ash.
How is it better than a steady life selling pancakes,
with no right or wrong and no losses.
Wáng Zé lost this battle,
lost many horses and men,
and also lost Rèn Qiān.
It was truly like a sword adding three soldiers,
and men becoming seventy percent complete.
Here, Wén Zhāotǎo's army of one hundred thousand
had their spirits redoubled.
The prefectures and counties of Héběi that had previously been seized by Wáng Zé,
hearing that the government troops were victorious,
all secretly sent messengers to offer surrender;
watching Bèizhōu like tigers, they knew it could be taken in no time.
Wén Zhāotǎo ordered five hundred soldiers to go up the mountain to cut timber
to build siege engines:
cloud ladders, catapult stones,
sky bridges, and fire arrows.
Within a few days, all were ready.
Wén Zhāotǎo ordered the attack on the city.
The soldiers went directly to the city walls to attack,
but they saw dark clouds and black mist over Bèizhōu,
covering the city.
In the air, ghostly faces and divine heads faintly appeared,
along with venomous snakes and fierce beasts.
The soldiers could not attack the city
and instead many horses and men were wounded.
They attacked for two or three days in a row,
but simply could not take it down.
Pacification Commissioner Wén (Wén Zhāotǎo) was feeling uneasy in his tent.
At night, he fell asleep leaning on a small table by the light of a candle.
Suddenly, a gust of cold air passed by,
and he saw a charming and beautiful woman
with a white silk scarf around her neck.
She approached gracefully
and knelt before Wén Zhāotǎo.
Wén Zhāotǎo shouted loudly:
“I follow the King’s command and have led a great army here.
What demon dares to intrude?”
The woman said:
“I am not a demon;
I am Zhào Wúxiá, the wife of Guān Yí from this province.
Wáng Zé lusted after my beauty
and forced me into marriage,
but I remained steadfast in my resolve and hanged myself.
Now my remains are buried in the shallow earth outside the city,
right within the Old Grand Secretary’s (Lǎo Xiàngguó) military camp.
I am disturbed by the clamor of the soldiers and cannot find peace.
I beg the Old Grand Secretary’s pity
to move my bones ten lǐ away.
I shall be grateful in the Nine Springs (Jiǔquán)!”
Wén Zhāotǎo said:
“So the young lady is a woman of great integrity;
I have been disrespectful!
Since your spirit remains unextinguished,
you must know when this rebel can be destroyed.”
The woman said:
“The fate of this rebel demon is nearly exhausted.
But within three days, Old Grand Secretary,
you will face a great calamity.
You must be cautious.”
Wén Zhāotǎo was greatly shocked.
Only because this turn of events had its own explanation:
Ghostly demon kings
will all have their heads shattered by thunder;
evil and rebellious factions
will all be dismembered by swords.
It is just as it is said:
A chaste soul that does not perish eventually becomes formidable;
an ignorant rebel will surely meet with disaster.
To know how it concludes,
listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
Human life is originally a midnight dream;
worldly affairs are entirely like a game of chess.
As long as the field of the heart remains upright,
both peaceful times and chaotic worlds are suitable.
It is said that Wén Zhāotǎo dreamed of this beautiful woman telling him
that within three days
he would face a great calamity,
and he was startled.
When he woke up,
he vaguely saw the figure of the woman drifting away.
Hearing the drums in the army striking the third watch,
Wén Zhāotǎo did not sleep for the rest of the night.
At dawn,
he ordered the military officers to search the camp for the burial place of the martyr Zhào Wúxiá.
Before long,
an officer came to report:
“A soldier named Lǐ Shíbā was just digging the ground to set a cooking pot.
Because the soil was loose, he dug deeper
and found a woman’s corpse
wrapped in straw.
The woman’s complexion was as if she were alive,
with a white scarf tied tightly around her neck,
appearing like one newly hanged.”
Wén Zhāotǎo then ordered a coffin to be prepared for the burial
and arranged the three animal sacrifices.
He personally went before the spirit to offer wine,
and ten lǐ away from the city,
he chose a high mound for her burial.
He personally wrote the seven characters ‘Tomb of the Martyr Zhào of Bèizhōu’ on a stone
and ordered a stonemason to engrave it and set it on the grave to mark it.
This Lady Zhào (Zhào Shì) had been suffering under injustice for three years.
Thanks to Wén Zhāotǎo reburying her and erecting a monument
to honor her as a martyr,
it was as if she had received a formal title of honor,
and the spirit of this martyr was vindicated.
There is a poem as evidence:
Beneath Běimáng Shān, the burial mounds are numerous,
but which one is like this mound in Qīngyáng?
One remembers the place where Lù Gōng inscribed the stone;
year after year, only the cuckoos cry.
Wén Zhāotǎo thought about the great calamity mentioned by the martyr,
fearing that assassins or wicked men
might sneak into the camp.
He ordered careful patrolling
and told the generals attacking the city to rest for a while,
waiting until after three days
to discuss the attack and capture again.
The story branches in two directions.
It is said that within the city of Bèizhōu, a group of sorcerers
commanded spirits and drove ghosts,
practicing their demonic arts regardless of the day.
The demonic energy pierced straight to the Heavenly Court,
disturbing the Yùhuáng Shàngdì,
who dispatched the Tàibái Star Lǐ Chánggēng to investigate.
Lord Star Lǐ investigated the group of sorcerers led by Wáng Zé,
and the whole history of their rebellion,
reporting it all to the Jade Emperor.
The Jade Emperor said:
"The secret volumes of the Heavenly Book are kept in the Báiyún Cave,
guarded by the Báiyuán Shén.
Now that people have stolen the magic,
causing trouble and harming the people,
they should all be punished for their crimes together."
Lord Star Lǐ reported:
"I have heard that sorcery does not arise of its own accord;
it is always incited by humans.
It is only because Zhào Sòng Zhēnzōng
listened to the treacherous official Wáng Qīnruò,
who tempted him three times
to forge a Heavenly Book,
falsely claiming it was from Heaven
and deceiving the common people.
Because of this, the commoners competed to favor sorcerers and shamans,
brewing demonic provocations.
At that time, strange occurrences involving demonic foxes appeared in the palace;
it was a sign that demonic foxes would surely cause chaos
and the world would find no peace.
The Bureau of Astronomy failed in its calculations,
and it happened that when the Heavenly Book of Báiyún Cave appeared
and the demonic magic spread,
continuing until today,
the fox faction became rampant,
truly fulfilling that disaster.
This is a matter of Heaven’s numbers,
and is not the fault of the Báiyuán Shén.
Furthermore, the one who stole the Heavenly Book was the Monk Dànzǐ;
this man once made a great vow,
and was destined to have a connection to the Daoist arts.
The Báiyuán Shén committed no crime of private transmission."
The Jade Emperor asked:
"Who is this Monk Dànzǐ?"
Lord Star Lǐ reported:
"Years ago, there was a Yōupó girl who left home at twelve to practice the path;
for over thirty years, she never broke her vows.
By chance, in a lotus pond,
she saw geese and ducks mating and suddenly felt desire.
From that moment she became pregnant,
and for thirteen months she did not give birth.
One day, passing below Yínghuī Mountain,
her belly became itchy,
and she gave birth to an egg,
which she abandoned in a water pool and left.
A monk from Yínghuī found the egg
and placed it in a chicken's nest, and a small boy hatched from it.
He was tonsured as a monk from childhood
and was named Monk Dànzǐ.
When he grew up, he was brave and diligent,
and his heart was set on the Dao.
Hearing that Báiyún Cave held the secret methods of the Heavenly Book,
after three years of hardship,
he managed to transcribe the seventy-two transformations of the Earthly Fiends.
He requested the old vixen spirit Shènggūgū to identify the characters,
and thus he practiced together with her and her son.
Because the fox girl Hú Yǒng'ér has a predestined marriage from a past life with Wáng Zé,
the fox faction is assisting in the rebellion.
Monk Dànzǐ acts according to the circumstances
and is not involved in these matters."
The Jade Emperor nodded
and ordered the Lǎo Jīnxīng to check Wáng Zé’s lifespan in the three bureaus of Fú, Lù, and Shòu,
and to the Bureau of Good and Evil to investigate Wáng Zé’s past sins
to report back with a detailed discussion.
You storytellers
might say I am lying again.
The people of the world are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
if every single person's lifespan
were recorded in Heaven like a fortune-teller's
detailed ledger of yearly fortunes,
how many rooms would it take to store those books?
With people living and dying every day,
and entries being removed or added,
even tens of millions of scribes would be overwhelmed,
and the three Star Lords of Fú, Lù, and Shòu would be incredibly busy indeed.
Even with a hundred good and evil deeds in a single day of a person's life,
how could the Bureau of Good and Evil remember so many?
Readers, you do not understand.
Suppose they are common folk
with no official salary or rank
and no great good or evil;
thousands and millions of such people are the same.
Their success or failure, long life or early death,
follows the order or chaos of the world
and years of harvest or famine.
They come and go within the large and small kalpas
and are beyond counting.
But if someone has even a modest future
or is a small man of wealth,
the upper realm has a recorded destiny.
Those with virtue rise,
and those with evil fall.
Furthermore, the most virtuous and most wicked among the populace
are the product of Heaven’s special energy,
and their names must be entered into the Ledgers of Good and Evil.
Moreover, for a rebel leader,
the length of his life
relates to the whole world on a large scale
and to a whole region on a small scale;
how could the Heavenly Court not have a record?
Let us set aside the idle talk.
It turns out Wáng Zé was originally a reincarnation of the Lustful Mara King from the Asura realm,
who appears in the world every five hundred years,
either as a man or a woman,
demonic, lustful, and fond of killing,
arising in response to the demonic fate of the human world.
If he encounters a weak and unprincipled ruler,
he throws the universe into chaos.
If he runs into a wise sovereign of a well-governed age,
the demon cannot show its power.
Because Emperor Zhēnzōng forged the Heavenly Book,
posed as gods and spoke of ghosts,
and brewed religious ceremonies,
the demonic energy became heavy and deep,
which is why Wáng Zé was born,
meeting with this demonic fate.
Fortunately, the Chìjiǎo Dàxiān is governing the world,
and the Wénqǔ and Wǔqǔ stars are all assisting,
so no great harm will come of it.
In a previous kalpa, Empress Wǔ Zétiān’s fortune and longevity were far too excessive.
In this kalpa, although reincarnated in a male body,
everything is reduced.
He was destined to hold the royal throne for thirteen years
and would end upon meeting the Star of Heavenly Longevity
at the age of forty.
Who is that Star of Heavenly Longevity?
It is the Pacification Commissioner Wén Yànbó.
In the Táng Dynasty, his surname was Zhāng and his name was Jiǎnzhī.
He possessed literary and martial talents throughout his life,
yet at nearly eighty years of age,
he had not found his opportunity.
Fortunately, Dí Rénjié, the Duke of Liáng, recommended him as Prime Minister;
he led the Feather Forest Army to exterminate the Wǔ clan
and re-established the Lǐ family.
Later, because Emperor Zhōngzōng was not wise,
he was unjustly demoted and died.
The Emperor on High pitied him
and matched him to the position of the Star of Heavenly Longevity,
to enjoy wealth and long life throughout his future lives.
In the Five Dynasties, he was Prince Féng Yìngwáng,
and today he is Wén Yànbó.
In both cases, he reached the highest ministerial rank
and lived to be nearly a hundred.
Back then, the chaos of Zétiān
was settled by him;
today, the chaos of Wáng Zé
will still be his achievement.
This is destined by Heaven's numbers
and is not by chance.
It is said Wáng Zé was allotted thirteen years of kingship;
as of now, over five years have passed,
so half should still remain.
Because within those five years he has killed a hundred thousand living souls
and forcibly seized many married women,
causing the death of one chaste woman,
his transgressions are too heavy.
The Bureau of Good and Evil decided to count two of Wáng Zé’s years as one.
Within only three months from now,
he shall suffer execution under the law of the state
to serve as a warning to the masses.
Lord Star Lǐ and the various bureaus of the Heavenly Administration reported back to the Jade Emperor.
The Jade Emperor said:
"The sentencing of Wáng Zé is most appropriate.
However, as for that group of sorcerers,
I fear Wén Yànbó cannot manage them alone."
Lord Star Lǐ reported:
"Sorcery has always been easy to break,
but this involves the secret volumes of the Heavenly Book,
with seventy-two transformations without end.
Since it was stolen from the Báiyuán Shén’s Báiyún Cave,
I am willing to receive Your Majesty's decree
to place the responsibility on the Báiyuán Shén to subdue the demonic faction,
to atone for the sin of allowing the magic to leak."
The Jade Emperor approved the request.
At once, Lord Star Lǐ received the Jade Decree,
exited the Heavenly Gate,
parted the clouds,
and descended toward the incense smoke of a white jade brazier.
It is said that Yuán Gōng was in his cave cultivating his reality and nurturing his nature
when he suddenly saw Tàibái Lǎo Jīnxīng descending.
Startled,
he hurriedly knelt to receive him
and asked,
"For what reason has the Xīngjūn descended to this mortal cave?
I know not what your decree is."
Lǐ Xīngjūn supported him up with both hands
and said,
"I have submitted a memorial before Shàngdì
to give you a great achievement to perform."
Yuán Gōng said,
"How could a humble official like me perform any great achievement?"
Lǐ Xīngjūn then recounted the matters of Bèizhōu, saying,
"That group of demon-people who practice illusions and evil arts
all obtained them from the walls of the Báiyún Dòng.
Yùdì intended to hold you accountable for lax supervision.
It was this old man who submitted a memorial
asking that you suppress the demons
to atone for your guilt."
Yuán Gōng was so panicked he was at a loss,
and said,
"This minor god only has a crude knowledge of sword arts
and has never had the power to subdue demons or sweep away devils.
I fear I would fail in such a great task."
Lǐ Xīngjūn said,
"I will show you a way;
unless you go and plead with Jiǔtiān Xuánnǚ Niángniáng,
then there will be a solution."
Yuán Gōng kowtowed to thank him for the instruction
and after seeing off the Jīnxīng,
he lit the incense of faith from his master's sect,
bowed toward the void,
and called out "Master Jiǔtiān Xuánnǚ Niángniáng" three times.
Suddenly, banners and streamers gleamed brilliantly,
and ritual plumes fluttered in abundance.
The Niángniáng’s holy carriage halted in mid-air.
It turns out the Niángniáng is the ancestor of the Dàofǎ of the Nine Heavens,
and all her disciples are given incense of faith;
should there be an emergency,
when the incense is lit,
she immediately comes to rescue and protect.
Yuán Gōng then kowtowed to the Niángniáng
and recounted the Imperial Decree brought by Lǐ Chánggēng once over,
begging for his Master's holy power to resolve the matter!
The Niángniáng smiled and said,
"So that is how it is.
Wén Zhāotǎo has shown me kindness in the past,
and it is right that I should help him succeed.
However, this matter was started by Dànzǐ Héshang,
and we need him to put in effort.
Currently, he has built a hermitage on Zǐjīn Shān in Dàmíng Fǔ;
I will now go there with you.
You shall lead him to see me."
Having said this,
she rose upon a cloud.
Yuán Gōng followed the cloud carriage
straight to the high peak of Zǐjīn Shān.
This Zǐjīn Shān was where the Jade Maiden of antiquity cultivated reality.
The entire mountain was made of emerald rocks,
without a single pinch of soil.
Dàn Shī loved its beauty,
and since leaving Gānquán Sì,
he had built a hermitage on this mountain to live.
Indeed:
On the ancient mountain, immortals left their traces,
In the secluded hermitage, rocks are his neighbors.
A sound of heavenly pipes from the horizon
does not stir the dust of the mortal world.
Dàn Shī was relaxing in front of the hermitage
when he looked up and suddenly saw an old man,
recognizing him as the one who had previously guided him to the Báiyún Dòng.
He hurriedly greeted him, saying,
"In the past, I received much guidance from you, Old Gentleman,
but had no way to kowtow in thanks.
Fortunately, we meet again today;
please come to my small hermitage to converse."
The old man said,
"I am none other than
the Báiyuán Shén.
I was ordered by Yùdì to guard the stone walls of the Heavenly Books in Báiyún Dòng,
and I did not dare to transmit them lightly.
Years ago, because I saw you, my Master, pleading three times
and making a sincere oath,
I guided you to the cave to copy the methods.
Who would have known that the old fox spirit would rely on you to achieve her transformations,
and then go to support Wáng Zé in rebelling and declaring himself king,
killing a hundred thousand people.
Now the demonic aura rises to the heavens,
and Yùdì has discovered the reason the methods were stolen.
He intends to punish both you and me together;
heavenly punishment is hard to escape.
What can be done about it?"
Dànzǐ Héshang was, after all, an honest person;
he was already panicked
and said,
"May I ask, Old Gentleman,
is there any rescue now?"
The old man said,
"I have invited the holy carriage of Jiǔtiān Xuánnǚ Niángniáng here.
If you, my Master, go with me to plead with her,
this matter can be resolved."
The monk's worry turned to joy,
and he cupped his hands, saying,
"I rely entirely on your introduction, Old Gentleman!"
The two of them then ascended the high peak.
Dàn Shī saw the Niángniáng
and hurriedly bowed down to state his case:
"Although this poor monk was graced with a karmic connection to the dharma
and obtained the Heavenly Book from the left wall of Báiyún Dòng,
I have never deceived Heaven or betrayed my oath,
nor have I caused trouble or harmed the people.
Now, hearing that Heaven is enraged,
I hope the Niángniáng will grant me rescue!"
The Niángniáng then ordered Yuán Gōng to help him up
and said to him,
"On the right wall in Báiyún Dòng is the Tiāngāng Zhèngfǎ,
and on the left wall is the Dìshà Xiéfǎ.
Now the demon fox relies on this evil method
to cause trouble and harm the people.
Tracing back where this method came from,
how can you be without guilt?
Currently, Wén Zhāotǎo's great army is on a punitive expedition;
if you can assist the orthodox and eliminate the evil,
using your merit to cover your guilt,
this would be a most perfect blessing."
Dànzǐ Héshang said,
"My skills and theirs
are only equal;
how can I defeat them?"
The Niángniáng said,
"I shall transmit the Tiāngāng method for breaking evil to you.
His evil methods will then naturally be unable to be applied.
Although this is so,
that fox spirit is an old demon of many years,
and furthermore, she has infinite transformations of the heterodox path;
she cannot be captured in a hurry.
You must request the Zhàoyāojìng from the Heavenly Court
to reveal her original form
before the matter can be ended."
Dànzǐ Héshang immediately took Jiǔtiān Xuánnǚ Niángniáng as his master
and she transmitted the Tiāngāng method for breaking evil to him.
The Niángniáng instructed,
"Previously in Bèizhōu,
did you live inside or outside the city?"
The monk said,
"Your disciple saw that Wáng Zé was not benevolent,
so I settled in Gānquán Sì outside the city
and never entered the city."
The Niángniáng said,
"Go now and stay in Gānquán Sì again.
I will personally direct Wén Zhāotǎo to meet you,
in order to complete the matter of the Sānsuì."
Dànzǐ Héshang did not know what the Sānsuì meant,
nor did he dare to ask.
Receiving the dharma decree,
he bid farewell and left the mountain,
heading again toward Bèizhōu.
On the way, he thought,
"When I lived in Gānquán Sì before,
all the monks in the temple
knew my name and title;
who among them does not say I am of the demon-people's party?
If I go back now,
I will have no face."
He thought again and said,
"I have a plan.
In the temple, there was an old monk
surnamed Zhūgé and named Suìzhì.
He went out on a pilgrimage to the mountains
and has not returned for fifteen years.
There has been no news of him at all,
and the monks suspect he is already dead,
so they set up a spirit tablet for him.
I once saw his portrait hanging there
and also know he should be seventy-one years old.
Why not change into his appearance,
which would make it easy to stay there?"
Inevitably, he once again used the Huànxíng Fǎ from the seventy-two transformations of the Dìshà.
Reciting a mantra,
he wiped his face
and transformed into the old monk Zhūgé.
Just as he entered Gānquán Sì,
the monks received him;
recognizing him as their temple's master,
they were both surprised and joyful.
They quietly removed the spirit tablet,
and everyone, great and small, came to exchange greetings
and ask about his well-being.
Dànzǐ Héshang answered them accordingly,
watching with grand satisfaction as they swept the rooms and prepared the bed,
and served tea and meals with respect.
He accepted their calling him Master and Grand Master
without any concern.
Reader, keep this part of the story in mind:
Dànzǐ Héshang remained in Gānquán Sì living as the old monk Zhūgé Suìzhì.
Furthermore, Jiǔtiān Xuánnǚ Niángniáng led the Báiyuán Shén to the Heavenly Court to see Yùdì and apologize.
She then requested the Zhàoyāojìng and went with Yuán Gōng to the region of Héběi.
Living in the clouds and sleeping in the mist,
they waited specifically for the time to arrive.
Pacifying demons and settling disorder.
The story splits into two paths.
To return to the city of Bèizhōu, seeing the government army had attacked for three consecutive days,
with cloud ladders,
artillery stones,
sky bridges,
and fire arrows pressing close below the walls.
Although the city had not been breached,
everyone was in a state of extreme panic.
Táo Bìxiǎn discussed with several trusted subordinates that on the day the city fell,
their lives would be hard to save,
so they planned to seek redemption at the South Gate.
They wrote a secret letter and tied it to an arrowhead,
waiting for the next day when the government army attacked urgently
to find an opening and shoot it out.
Unexpectedly, on the fourth day, Commissioner Wén withdrew the troops to camp,
so they could not shoot it.
One of the conspiring soldiers thought the government army had retreated
and wanted to claim merit before Wáng Zé,
so he stole the secret letter and informed on them.
Wáng Zé was furious
and immediately took Táo Bìxiǎn and the other conspirators,
bound them together on the city wall,
and beheaded them for public display.
The soldier who informed
was rewarded with the post of Qiānhù.
Later people have a poem saying:
Following the king or the rebel, both come to naught;
vacillating to steal a life, yet failing to live.
How can it compare to Rú Gāng dying for his principles?
Under the walls of Gānlíng, both showed their loyalty.
There is another poem specifically about the soldier,
who first conspired when things were urgent,
but informed when the troops withdrew;
he was truly a base person.
The poem says:
Offering the gate to save their lives was the original plot;
with the troops gone, he turned to flatter the rebel.
Worldly friendships based on power are all like this;
in how many people's hearts can one find no worry?
Wáng Zé saw that people's hearts had changed
and became even more anxious.
He invited Zuǒ Chù and his wife Hú Yǒng'ér to the drill ground
to discuss the matter together.
Hú Yǒng'ér said:
"Great King!
Do not worry for now.
I have a plan
that will make Commissioner Wén die an unnatural death outside the city.
When his hundred thousand troops
lose their commander,
they will disperse without a fight.
Wouldn't that be good?"
Wáng Zé said:
"Virtuous Queen, what wonderful magic do you have
to arrange his death,
disperse his hundred thousand troops,
and lift the siege of our Bèizhōu?"
Yǒng'ér whispered into Zuǒ Chù's ear:
"If we do this and that, would it be good?"
Zuǒ Chù clapped his hands and laughed loudly:
"If we want the government army to disperse,
there is no better plan than this!"
He then ordered his subordinates to the mill to fetch a large millstone.
Before long,
about ten people were seen
carrying a large millstone into the hall.
Hú Yǒng'ér walked down into the hall,
wrote a talisman on the millstone with a cinnabar brush,
held a sword in her right hand
and a bowl of water in her left.
She chanted incantations under her breath,
took a mouthful of water,
sprayed it onto the millstone,
and shouted:
"Swiftly!"
The millstone was seen spinning left and right on the ground,
then suddenly it rose up into the air,
like a kite blown by the wind,
and flew directly out of the city.
Wáng Zé and the others saw this
and all cheered.
They thought:
"Even if this large millstone just grazes someone,
it will take off a thick layer of skin.
If it hits directly,
it will be no small matter.
Not to mention the nearly eighty-year-old Wén Pacification Commissioner;
even if it were a strong youth,
even if ten were lined up there,
they would surely all be turned into meat patties.
This time it will surely be settled!"
Truly, using demonic magic in haste,
waiting foolishly for good news.
We will leave that aside.
Now, Pacification Commissioner Wén had just ascended his platform and invited Vice-Commissioner Cáo Wěi,
Superintendent Wáng Xìn,
and Vanguard Sūn Fǔ to the tent to discuss strategies for attacking the city.
Suddenly a violent wind arose,
and a millstone fell from the sky,
dropping straight toward the crown of Commissioner Wén's head.
With a world-shaking crash,
everyone was so terrified their faces turned the color of earth,
thinking the commissioner had been crushed to death.
However, while Commissioner Wén was sitting in his chair,
he was suddenly grabbed around the waist and pulled aside by someone,
five or seven steps away from the chair.
The millstone came down,
missing Commissioner Wén,
but smashing the chair to pieces
and creating a pit one or two feet deep in the ground.
When the generals saw that Commissioner Wén was unharmed,
they were all overjoyed.
Commissioner Wén was greatly startled;
he took another chair and sat down.
He asked:
"Who was the one who just grabbed me?"
Before he finished speaking,
a man appeared before him and bowed.
He was tall and large in stature,
with an ugly appearance.
When the others looked at him,
none recognized him.
He was not a personal attendant,
nor a soldier of the camp.
Commissioner Wén asked:
"Who are you,
who came to save my life?
Please tell me in detail,
and I shall reward you greatly."
The man said:
"I am not a man of the army.
Today Wáng Zé of Bèizhōu used magic to send a millstone to crush Your Excellency,
so I came specifically to save your life
to repay the kindness of a meal and the virtue of your assistance in the past."
Hearing this, Commissioner Wén was overjoyed
and said:
"I thank you for coming to save me,
but I do not know where I, Wén Yànbó, bestowed such kindness.
Might I ask your name?"
When the man spoke his name,
truly it is not found in the hundred schools of fiction,
and such an event never occurred in the Twenty-One Histories.
It is just as it is said:
The divine and holy have spirits to support the upright;
demonic evil has no art to harm a high official.
What name, after all, did he speak?
Please listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
A thousand pieces of gold for a single meal is truly real;
even ghosts and gods repay their private debts.
Witness the matter of the Multi-Eyed Silver Basin;
secret virtue should never be doubted.
It is said that if Recruiter Wén Zhāotǎo were not a man of great fortune of his generation,
he would have nearly been crushed to death by a millstone.
Fortunately, that man saved his life.
When asked for his name,
the man said:
"I fear that if I speak it, your lordship might forget it.
Please lend me a silver basin, brush, and inkstone."
His subordinates brought a silver basin, brush, and inkstone and arranged them on the table.
The man said:
"I beg you to dismiss your attendants."
Recruiter Wén Zhāotǎo shouted for his attendants to withdraw.
After the man had picked up the brush and finished writing,
he turned the silver basin upside down on the ground
and strode out of the tent.
Recruiter Wén Zhāotǎo immediately sent people to pursue him,
but he had already vanished.
Recruiter Wén Zhāotǎo said:
"How strange indeed!"
When he ordered someone to lift the silver basin to look,
written in the middle were the three large characters 'Duōmù Shén',
and none among the crowd understood their meaning.
Recruiter Wén Zhāotǎo pondered for a long while
before finally being able to remember.
It turned out that in his youth, before Recruiter Wén Zhāotǎo had passed the imperial examinations,
he had once prayed for a dream in the temple of Jiǔtiān Xuánnǚ Niángniang.
In the dream, he saw the Goddess bestow ten characters upon him,
which said: "A famous Grand Councilor in the human world,
the Old Man Star in the heavens."
From then on, Yànbó entreated a master painter
to paint a sacred image of the Goddess,
which he mounted as a scroll to worship.
On the first day of every month, he would personally unfurl it,
burning incense and praying.
Another day, while on a journey, he stayed at a post station.
The station master told him:
"There are ghosts and demons here;
those who stay in this room
are often harmed."
At that time, Wén Yànbó did not believe these words,
so he lit bright lamps and candles,
set out wine in the station room, and drank alone.
When the night reached the third watch,
a sudden gust of wild wind arose.
Where the wind passed, a man with disheveled hair appeared before the table and kowtowed,
calling Yànbó 'your lordship'
and begging for food and wine.
Wén Yànbó asked:
"Are you human or a ghost?
Tell the truth, and I shall grant you your fill of wine."
The man said:
"Has your lordship not heard that under the command of Jiǔtiān Xuánnǚ Niángniang, there are Shùnfēng'ěr
and Qiānlǐyǎn, the two gods?
I am indeed Qiānlǐyǎn.
The Goddess assigned me to keep watch over a matter,
but because I was greedy for wine and got drunk, I neglected my duty,
provoking the wrath of Xuánnǚ Niángniang.
I was banished to this place to endure hunger for three months.
The term of my punishment is not yet over,
but seeing your lordship today, a person of high status,
I have come specifically to beseech you."
Wén Yànbó said:
"How do you know that I am a person of high status?"
The man said:
"Wherever a person of great status arrives,
the local deities must ahead of time drive away wild ghosts, demons, and their ilk for him.
That is how I know.
I am a subordinate official of the Goddess,
which is why I was permitted to stay here."
Wén Yànbó said:
"Since you have been punished here,
how do you dare to harm the residents?"
The man said:
"Because I was born with an ugly face,
and at the time of my punishment,
the Goddess's divine decree ordered a divine blade to pierce my face,
piercing it until it had many eyes,
making it even more fierce and strange.
When people see me begging for food,
they die of fright;
this is also their ill fate,
not my crime."
Wén Yànbó said:
"Show me your face."
The man said:
"I fear it would frighten your lordship."
Wén Yànbó insisted on seeing him.
The man parted his hair,
and on his green face, there were eight fierce eyes blinking and flickering,
gleaming and terrifying.
Upon seeing this, Wén Yànbó
was also struck with horror.
He then gave him as much wine and food as he could consume.
Wén Yànbó asked again:
"I usually worship the sacred image of Xuánnǚ Niángniang.
How about I pray and ask for mercy on your behalf tomorrow morning?"
The man said:
"If I could obtain a single word from your lordship,
my guilt would be absolved.
Should your lordship encounter trouble in the future,
I shall surely come to save you."
Having finished speaking, he vanished.
The next day,
Wén Yànbó prepared incense and candles and prayed before the divine scroll,
asking for leniency in the punishment of Qiānlǐyǎn.
That night, he dreamed again of the man coming to thank him, saying:
"I have received your lordship's kindness,
and the term of my punishment has been canceled.
Your lordship's fortune and longevity are extraordinary;
remember that we shall meet again in the future with a change of eyes."
From then on, Wén Yànbó held great ambitions.
Later, he achieved glory by passing the imperial examinations,
becoming a general abroad and a grand councilor at court.
He believed even more in the spiritual power of Xuánnǚ Niángniang,
performing rituals on the first day of every month,
remaining respectful without fail until old age.
Even when in the army,
he never interrupted this practice.
Because at that time in the post station he had seen someone with disheveled hair and a dirty face,
with four pairs of fierce eyes on his face.
Today, although the person was still ugly,
his clothes and cap were neat and orderly,
and he had only a single pair of bright eyes,
which was why Recruiter Wén Zhāotǎo could not recall him for a moment.
Seeing the three characters 'Duōmù Shén',
and recalling the words about 'meeting again with a change of eyes',
he finally realized that this person was indeed the god Qiānlǐyǎn under the Goddess's command.
Recruiter Wén Zhāotǎo told these events to the gathered generals,
and the generals all cupped their hands in congratulation,
while their hearts were all filled with awe.
When they all went to look at the silver basin,
they saw six small characters written on the side, saying:
"Encounter the three Suìs,
the demons shall retreat."
Recruiter Wén Zhāotǎo examined them carefully,
and when he asked the crowd,
none understood their meaning.
Cáo Wěi said:
"The Commander's fortune is as high as the heavens,
and the spirits protect him.
As I, Cáo, see it,
these rebels can be suppressed within days."
Recruiter Wén Zhāotǎo asked:
"How do you see this?"
Cáo Wěi said:
"The god's name is Duōmù,
and he had eight fierce eyes,
which is the meaning of the character 'Bèi'.
Meeting today with a change of eyes,
the eight eyes have all vanished,
which is a sign of the impending destruction of Bèizhōu.
Because the Commander respectfully serves Xuánnǚ Niángniang,
she sent the god to foretell this omen.
Although 'three Suìs' is not yet clear,
there will surely be a confirmation later.
We should just proceed with advancing the troops."
Recruiter Wén Zhāotǎo said:
"The great disaster mentioned by the Heroic Woman Zhào Lièfù in the dream
can be considered fulfilled by this.
Since there was an order to rest the troops for three days,
it will not be too late to advance the troops once the period is over.
Let all of you go and think carefully on the meaning of 'three Suìs'."
The generals gave their assent and withdrew,
each returning to their own camp to ponder,
of which no more need be said.
It is said that the band of sorcerers in Bèizhōu,
hoping fully for the success of the grinding stone,
set out wine to celebrate,
while sending men to scout for news in the imperial army's camp to report back.
A scout arrived to report, saying:
"Wén Zhāotǎo's army looks stern,
the ranks are orderly,
and they remain untroubled."
Wáng Zé spoke to the others:
"If they had lost their commander over there,
even if they were orderly,
they would have no heart for battle.
Today there was no activity in Wén Yànbó's ranks;
I wonder if the grinding stone harmed him or not?"
Zuǒ Chù said:
"This school's magic is unerring,
and no one can undo it;
he must surely have been crushed to death."
Wáng Zé said:
"If we wish to know the truth,
we can send someone to deliver a challenge.
Dispatch a reliable soldier
to go straight before Wén Zhāotǎo's tent to deliver it."
When Wén Zhāotǎo heard that someone had come to deliver a challenge,
he summoned him to the tent.
Attendants received the letter and placed it on the table;
Wén Zhāotǎo opened and read it,
and immediately understood Wáng Zé's intent,
thinking to himself:
"He only thinks he used sorcery to crush me with a grinding stone.
Little does he know I am safe and sound;
seeing no movement here,
he uses this challenge as a pretext
to scout the reality."
Thereupon, Wén Zhāotǎo endorsed the response for a battle the next day in the messenger's presence and sent him back.
Wáng Zé looked at the endorsed reply
and asked the messenger:
"Did you go inside Wén Zhāotǎo's tent?"
The messenger said:
"Reporting to the Great King!
Wén Zhāotǎo had no suspicion or hesitation;
he called me straight to the tent,
personally wrote the reply,
and sent me back."
Hearing that Wén Zhāotǎo was unharmed, Wáng Zé
was anxious and panicked;
that very night, he invited Zuǒ Chù to his residence to discuss a strategy against the enemy with Hú Yǒng'ér.
When Zuǒ Chù and Hú Yǒng'ér heard that the grinding stone had failed to kill Wén Zhāotǎo,
they were also somewhat flustered.
While they were hesitating,
it was suddenly reported that Shèng Gūgu had arrived.
Everyone hurried to welcome her to the seat of honor.
Wáng Zé told her about Wén Zhāotǎo using blood cylinders to break the spell,
and the matter of the grinding stone until the current scheduled battle.
Shèng Gūgu said to Zuǒ Chù:
"Why not use the White Horse Army-Confusing Ritual?"
Zuǒ Chù said:
"We have used magic twice;
both were of the highest power,
yet both were broken by him.
I fear that if we perform it without effect,
we will instead lose men and horses,
so I have been hesitating."
Shèng Gūgu said:
"My school's magic
has ten thousand transformations.
But it must not be tested lightly;
how could there be a reason for it to fail when tried?
It is only because those who perform the ritual
are greedy for wine and lust;
their seven emotions and six desires dissipate their spirit,
so their visualization is unstable
and their gathering of Qi is imprecise.
Their own strength cannot match the magic;
since their spiritual energy is thin,
it is naturally easy to break.
For example, when blowing a feather into the air,
it may fall after five or six feet,
or fall after one or two feet;
this is all because the spirit and energy are either sufficient or insufficient.
Tomorrow on the battlefield,
watch my performance
to see if they can break it or not!"
Zuǒ Chù and Yǒng'ér lowered their heads in silence.
Wáng Zé said:
"We rely entirely on Shèngmǔ Niángniáng's divine power."
The plan was then settled.
At dawn the next day,
Wáng Zé mustered ten thousand troops,
opened the city gates wide,
lowered the drawbridge,
and formed his ranks for a long time
as the two armies faced off.
Wén Zhāotǎo brought the pump-users as before,
along with the blood of pigs and sheep,
and sent someone to call Wáng Zé to talk.
No one emerged from Wáng Zé's ranks.
Meanwhile, Zuǒ Quéshī, naked and barefoot,
wearing no armor,
led Zhāng Qí,
Wú Wàng, and their group,
accompanying Shèng Gūgu
to watch her perform the magic.
Shèng Gūgu, with disheveled hair and a sword in hand,
led a white horse
and performed magic within the ranks while clattering her teeth,
stepping the patterns of Kuígāng,
and muttering incantations,
shouting:
"Swiftly!"
She pierced the white horse's head with the sword tip,
drawing blood,
took a mouthful of the bloody water,
went to the front of the ranks, and sprayed it.
Before she sprayed, the sky was clear and the sun was bright;
once she sprayed, dark clouds and fierce rain appeared,
thunderbolts crashed,
and sand flew while stones rolled.
