The wind blew so hard it became pitch black;
those facing each other could not see one another,
and one could not see one's own hand.
The blood-cylinder team and the archers
did not know East from West;
in the darkness, how could they use their skills?
The soldiers were struck randomly by sand and stones;
everyone lost their courage,
all were terrified,
discarding armor and throwing down spears,
each seeking a way to survive.
Wén Zhāotǎo bumped left
and right in the chaotic army,
losing his sense of direction,
nearly falling from his horse.
Suddenly, another whirlwind rose before his horse;
where the wind went, it blew open a path of light
as pale as a cold moon.
Wén Zhāotǎo took advantage of this light
to flee the formation and escape;
looking back,
not a single person followed him.
Riding his horse alone,
he was extremely panicked and distressed.
It was just like:
A phoenix landing on a desolate slope,
losing all the beautiful feathers on its body;
A dragon dwelling in shallow water,
losing the bright pearl beneath its chin.
Shǔ Wáng's spring regret, weeping blood;
Sòng Yù's sorrow and resentment of green.
Lǚ Qián losing the blade at his waist;
Léi Huàn losing the sword in its case;
A lonely traveler's lamp going out at night;
A broken boat tossed by wind while the rain returns.
That day, while Regional Pacification Commissioner Wén Zhāotǎo was traveling,
he saw only mountain forests and trees ahead,
not knowing what place it was.
Reining his horse around a mountain spur,
the weather gradually cleared up,
and he saw a banner pole.
He also heard the sound of a bell ringing,
and when he stopped his horse to look, it was a monastery.
Commissioner Wén said:
"Having come to this, I have no choice;
I must go into the monastery to find someone to ask for the way back to the camp,
and then decide what to do."
Arriving before the monastery, he dismounted,
entered the monastery,
and saw a traveling monk.
Commissioner Wén told the monk he wanted to see the Abbot.
The monk said:
"Might the old general's surname be Wén?"
Commissioner Wén said:
"How could you know my surname is Wén?"
The monk said:
"My master said
that a general surnamed Wén would arrive here today,
and instructed me to wait and welcome him."
Though Commissioner Wén said nothing,
he thought to himself:
"His master knew in advance that I would arrive here;
he must be no ordinary person."
He then said to the monk:
"I truly wish to see your master."
The monk led the horse
and walked ahead to guide him.
The old monk was already waiting at the door of the abbot’s quarters to welcome him,
hurriedly inviting him in and exchanging greetings,
and they sat down in the positions of guest and host.
The Abbot said:
"The general must be hungry and thirsty."
He quickly called his disciples and ordered the kitchen to prepare a vegetarian meal,
and had the horse led to the back of the courtyard to be fed grass.
First, he asked the monk to bring tea for him to drink.
After the tea,
the Abbot asked:
"Old general!
Are you the one who once entered the Central Secretariat as Chancellor,
and is now leading a hundred thousand troops
to suppress Wáng Zé, the Regional Pacification Commissioner Wén?"
Commissioner Wén said:
"How does my master know this?"
The Abbot said:
"Last night, the Qiélán deity informed me in a dream,
so I know it.
I have heard your name for a long time;
today the monastery is most fortunate
to have the Commissioner arrive here.
Why are there no attendants with you?"
Commissioner Wén said:
"This morning, while facing the rebels in battle,
I unexpectedly suffered a great defeat
and fled here alone on horseback to escape the disaster."
Upon hearing this, the Abbot
was greatly shocked and said:
"Not to mention the Commissioner's great talent,
even with a hundred thousand troops,
it should not be difficult to handle.
Bèizhōu is but a small, low-lying place;
how many men and horses can they have?
How could you lose to them?"
Commissioner Wén said:
"If it were a matter of standard battle array,
they certainly could not triumph over me.
But now, Wáng Zé and his band of rebels
all know demonic arts.
Whenever we engage in battle,
they release from within their ranks spirit heads and ghostly faces,
as well as fierce beasts and monsters.
When the army and horses see them,
they all flee in terror.
Deputy Commissioner Cáo Wěi offered a strategy,
using the blood of pigs and sheep,
horse urine,
and garlic-filled syringes to win one battle against them,
and the rebel troops did not dare leave the city for several days.
A few days ago, I held court in the tent with the generals to discuss the strategy for attacking the city,
but unexpectedly, the sorcerer used an evil spell
and caused a millstone to fall from the sky to crush me.
Fortunately, the Duōmù deity saved my life.
Early this morning, while facing the rebel troops in battle,
I was caught off guard when from Wáng Zé's ranks
a sinister wind arose;
suddenly the sky grew dim and the earth turned dark,
with violent thunder and sudden rain,
flying sand and rolling stones,
which battered our battle formation into chaos.
I lost my way alone and ended up here.
I beg my master to guide me on the way back,
and I shall reward you handsomely upon returning to camp."
After the Abbot finished listening,
he left his seat, clapped his hands, and said in great anger:
"The present age is the era of Yáo and Shùn,
the Emperor is sagely and the ministers are virtuous,
yet such sorcerers dare to disturb the court!
I ask the Commissioner not to worry;
allow this old monk to exert effort for the Commissioner,
to break their evil spells
and wipe out the rebel party."
Hearing these words, Commissioner Wén was overjoyed and said:
"I venture to ask, what is my master's esteemed name?"
The Abbot said:
"This old monk has the compound surname Zhūgě and the name Suìzhì."
Upon hearing this, Commissioner Wén said joyfully:
"The Duōmù deity once wrote six characters, saying:
'Encounter the Three Suì,
and the demons will retreat.'
We have pondered over it day and night
but completely failed to understand its meaning.
Today, Heaven has allowed me to meet my master;
if my master is willing to go and defeat Bèizhōu,
I shall memorialize the court,
and the official rewards for your merit will not be small."
The Abbot said:
"This old monk is a person of the Empty Gate;
how could I covet wealth, status, or rewards?
However, in today's peaceful world,
we cannot tolerate such sorcerers.
This old monk shall offer his humble service
to assist the Commissioner in suppressing the demons and
rebels.
Tonight, the Commissioner may stay in the monastery for one night,
and at the fifth watch tomorrow morning, we shall go together to the main camp."
The Commissioner removed his armor,
ate his evening vegetarian meal,
and talked with the Abbot for half the night.
He slept until the fifth watch,
got up and finished washing,
and ate some food.
The Abbot called the monk:
"Lead out a horse from the monastery;
I will go with the Commissioner to defeat the rebels."
The monks all called out to their Grand-Master and Master,
saying:
"You have been away for fifteen years
and have just returned home;
it hasn't even been a few days.
On normal days, you only doze off;
when did you ever know anything about fighting and killing?
Yet you are following this old general;
this makes no sense at all."
The Abbot chuckled and said:
"You need not stop me;
I have my own way to defeat the rebels,
to perform a service for the court,
and also bring glory to the monastery.
When the matter is finished, I shall return to the monastery
to be with you all."
The monks had no choice but to prepare the horse.
Commissioner Wén and the Abbot both mounted their horses,
and with three monks carrying lit torches, they left the monastery,
and traveled until they arrived before the camp.
When the generals and soldiers saw Commissioner Wén,
they were beyond joy,
welcoming him to the central army.
Commissioner Cáo and others all came to inquire, saying:
"The Commander-in-Chief did not return for the night;
all the generals were worried and at a loss,
not knowing where you had gone after the battle array collapsed.
Why have you returned with this old master?"
Commissioner Wén said:
"Yesterday, I was caught in a sinister wind produced by Wáng Zé's evil spells,
which blew me off course and made me lose my way.
I arrived at a monastery
and by chance met this holy monk,
who says he can break the evil spells.
I think this exactly corresponds to the words of the Duōmù deity."
He then whispered into Commissioner Cáo's ear:
"This monk is named Zhūgě Suìzhì."
Commissioner Cáo was overjoyed,
dismissed his attendants,
and asked the Abbot:
"What divine arts does my master possess
to be able to break demonic evils?"
Zhūgě Suìzhì said:
"This old monk has traveled for fifteen years
and once met an extraordinary person who transmitted the Wǔléi Tiānxīn Zhèngfǎ.
Whenever I encounter Jīngāng Chán or any sort of heterodox evil arts,
when I see them
and recite the true incantations,
I can immediately turn the evil back to the correct path.
If the Commissioner does not believe me,
tomorrow on the battlefield,
you shall see for yourself."
That day, Commissioner Wén kept the Abbot and the monk in the central army
and immediately drafted a challenge to battle,
ordering a soldier to deliver it to Bèizhōu,
setting the date for battle the next day.
Meanwhile, he selected ten thousand fresh troops from the old camp at Fùjiātuǎn
to replenish the losses in the central army
and to replace the wounded soldiers,
sending them back to the rear camp to rest and recover.
Now it is said that Wáng Zé saw [the challenge],
wrote a reply to the battle challenge,
and sent the soldiers back.
He then discussed with the various sorcerers, saying:
"In the battle the other day,
they were slaughtered by me and fled in a great defeat.
Today they still dare to come and press for battle;
we must ask Shèngmǔ Niángniáng to use the method from the other day once more,
to kill our way straight to the border
and ensure that not one of their hundred thousand troops remains."
To cut the story short,
both sides organized their respective troops
and simply waited for the next day's combat.
The following day,
Wáng Zé led his troops out of Bèizhōu city and formed a battle array.
The two armies faced each other,
with banners and drums in sight of one another.
From within the shadow of the gate banners,
the sorcerers were seen once more surrounding Shènggūgū, who had disheveled hair and held a sword.
She led a white horse in front,
chanting incantations.
She pierced the white horse with the tip of her sword,
took a mouthful of blood and water and sprayed it out.
Immediately, upon Wáng Zé’s formation,
a fierce wind suddenly rose,
bringing sand, stones, rain, and hail,
approaching the front of Wén Zhāotǎo's formation.
Zhūgě Suìzhì saw this from within the army;
he shook his bell and vajra-pestle,
chanted true words,
and pointed with the bell and pestle.
Strangely enough,
that gust of fierce wind, sand, stones, rain, and hail
turned around and beat down upon Wáng Zé’s own formation.
Wáng Zé had just cried out, "Ai-ya!"
when he saw that the group of sorcerers had all vanished.
Knowing the wind was unfavorable,
he hurriedly signaled his troops to turn back.
Wén Zhāotǎo pointed with the tip of his whip,
and the entire army, large and small, charged forward together to slaughter them.
The rebel soldiers fell and horses collapsed;
more than half were lost.
Those who were driven into the city moat and died
were beyond counting.
Wáng Zé hurriedly gathered the few remaining defeated troops
and fled into Bèizhōu,
pulled up the drawbridge,
closed the city gates,
and maintained a tight defense without coming out.
Meanwhile, Wén Zhāotǎo's army reached the foot of the city walls,
cutting off heads and ears
and seizing gongs, drums, and banners.
Wén Zhāotǎo ordered the gongs sounded to withdraw the troops
and set up camp not far from Bèizhōu city.
Wén Zhāotǎo invited Zhūgě Suìzhì to the seat of honor
and bowed, saying:
"This victory was all due to your power, Master.
If it continues like this,
the rebel troops will be broken in no time."
Zhūgě Suìzhì said:
"This old monk uses the orthodox to defeat the heterodox;
everywhere I go, I am successful.
As long as this old monk is in the army,
why fear Wáng Zé and his lot of sorcerers!"
Hearing this, Wén Zhāotǎo was very pleased and said:
"Wáng Zé lost a battle today
and will only defend the city even more tightly.
Issue orders for the soldiers to attack the city with combined strength."
One could see a stream of bluish-black vapor in Bèizhōu
shrouding the top of the city walls.
Within it, sometimes ten thousand balls of fierce fire were seen,
and sometimes a surge of floodwaters appeared,
with all sorts of ghosts and monsters arrayed in countless ways.
Wén Zhāotǎo ordered his three-route army to encircle Bèizhōu city,
surrounding it like an iron bucket,
beating drums and shouting,
simply waiting for the city's troops to emerge.
Here, Zhūgě Suìzhì used the orthodox to defeat the heterodox,
taking the opportunity to charge in.
Unexpectedly, Wáng Zé relied on sorcery to defend to the death
and simply would not come out.
Wén Zhāotǎo had no choice but to order the soldiers to set up camp away from Bèizhōu city,
sounding bells and calling out signals as before,
and passing arrows to announce the night watches.
He discussed with Cáo Zhāotǎo, saying:
"You and I lead a hundred thousand troops,
costing the imperial court much wealth and grain every day.
It has been nearly two months since we arrived,
yet we still cannot break Bèizhōu.
What should be done?"
Cáo Zhāotǎo said:
"Commander, please put your mind at ease
and allow Cáo Wěi to think further of a good plan."
That day, Cáo Zhāotǎo took his leave of Wén Zhāotǎo
and returned to his own camp.
Wén Zhāotǎo was worried in his tent,
unaware that the night had grown deep.
One could see:
The Milky Way was bright,
the jade water-clock dripped slowly.
A slanting moon pierced the camp, reflecting a cold light,
a cool breeze penetrated the tent, blowing the night air.
The honking of wild geese was loud and clear,
startling the dreaming soul of the lonely scholar.
The chirping of crickets was desolate,
making the solitary lady's feelings bitter.
The war drums in the camp—
before the first watch ended, the second watch was struck.
Distant pounding on the cold laundry block—
as a hundred strokes finished, a thousand more began.
Between the painted eaves,
the tinkling of wind-chimes
shattered the sentiments of men and women.
Upon the banners,
flickering green lanterns
shone specifically on the long sighs of the soldiers.
The hearts of the sorcerous rebels were like frightened birds,
while the spirit of the loyal heroes was like a rainbow.
That night, Wén Zhāotǎo was in his tent,
tossing and turning, unable to sleep.
Around the third watch,
hearing that it was quiet outside the camp,
Wén Zhāotǎo got up and left his quarters.
At that moment, the third watch was being struck,
and he saw a soldier striking a wooden clapper to change the watch,
softly singing a little tune.
Because of this very tune,
it was destined that
the humble watchman
would join in the campaign against the rebels,
and the commander wielding the battle-axe
would early on decide
the strategy to pacify the demons.
Truly it is:
An army's value lies in its quality, not its numbers;
a general's value lies in his strategy, not his bravery.
After all, what tune was he singing,
and what events did it trigger?
Please listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
In a small study during the long summer, an incense burner glows,
the window and desk are cool where bamboo and trees meet.
Waking from a midday nap with nothing else to do,
I listen to people clap their hands and tell the tale of pacifying demons.
It is said that Wén Zhāotǎo could not sleep at the third watch,
so he got up and left his quarters
and patrolled quietly.
He only heard the sound of singing.
He went forward to steal a look
and saw it was a watchman soldier
who was keeping time with his clapper as he sang a tune.
He sang:
I loathe that sorcerer’s recklessness and audacity,
for he does not fear the laws of the Cháotíng.
Since you seized this city of Bèizhōu,
who knows how many millions of lives of soldiers and civilians have been destroyed.
Just for the sake of you alone,
you have harmed our army of one hundred thousand,
forcing us to leave our homes, take up spears, and don armor,
suffering such peril and distress.
Furthermore, we soldiers who patrol the watch,
blocking the wind,
braving the dew,
walking back and forth all night long,
pacing to and fro,
shouting the passwords and ringing the bell.
Working so hard and bitterly like this,
when has anyone ever come to say a single word of pity?
Thinking of the future,
it is only the unfair Yánjūn.
Born in the same way,
raised in the same way,
why was I specifically assigned to be a soldier?
If it were a time of achieving merit,
a great general would be credited with great merit,
a minor general with minor merit,
but when has it ever been assigned to me, a lowly soldier?
Only the spears and blades on the battlefield,
and the lashings and beatings in the camp,
are within our duty as soldiers,
things we must endure and accept.
It was wrong to become a lowly soldier;
even if you have the wisdom of Zhāng Liáng
or the talent of Hán Xìn,
who would take notice?
Where would one go to seek a career?
It is laughable, those two, Wén Zhāotǎo and Cáo Zhāotǎo,
those two famous Zhāotǎo;
up until now, how many have they recruited,
and how many have they suppressed?
Watching with wide eyes this city no bigger than a palm,
where they practice sorcery and play the demon,
when will peace ever be attained?
How bitter!
We lowly soldiers
actually have a few ideas,
but I only regret not being in a position of power;
it is hard to offer loyalty,
and hard to fulfill one’s ambitions.
How bitter!
If only there were a Xiāo Hé who would build an altar to appoint a general,
with this heart of loyalty and gall of righteousness of mine,
I would be willing to serve the Cháotíng!
Wén Zhāotǎo heard this clearly,
so he returned to his tent
and called a confidant to his side, saying:
“Quietly go and call that soldier who was striking the watch to come in;
I have words to say.”
In a moment, he was summoned
and came directly before the bed.
Wén Zhāotǎo asked:
“The one who just said he has the wisdom of Zhāng Liáng
and the talent of Hán Xìn,
was that you?”
The soldier knelt and kowtowed, saying:
“Your humble servant was just talking nonsense,
I did not expect the Zhāotǎo to hear it;
your humble servant deserves to die!”
Wén Zhāotǎo said:
“Do not be alarmed.
Currently, we have no strategy to attack the city,
and this is exactly the time to use people.
Those ‘three ideas’ of yours,
what are they?
If they are worth hearing,
then what would be the difficulty
in me building an altar to appoint you?”
The soldier said:
“It is not that your humble servant is boasting,
but your humble servant can cut off the head of Wáng Zé
and present it to the Zhāotǎo.”
Wén Zhāotǎo hurriedly helped him up with his own hands
and asked:
“What strategy do you have
that makes it so convenient?”
The soldier said:
“I will not hide it from the Zhāotǎo:
your humble servant is from the same hometown as Wáng Zé,
and we attended school in the same hall from childhood,
having sworn brotherhood.”
It turned out that the soldier was indeed a native of Bèizhōu
and was very close friends with Wáng Zé.
Because he followed a paternal uncle to Dōngjīng to be a merchant,
he lost his capital.
After his uncle died,
he stayed in Dōngjīng
and was registered in the military rolls.
Wén Zhāotǎo asked:
“What is your surname and given name?”
The soldier said:
“Your humble servant’s surname is Mǎ and his name is Suì.”
When Wén Zhāotǎo heard this,
he secretly rejoiced, saying:
“I think this man must correspond to the words of the deity Duōmù Shén.
If this fellow goes,
he will certainly be able to settle the matter.”
Wén Zhāotǎo said:
“Tell me then, how will you use your plan?”
Mǎ Suì walked straight to Wén Zhāotǎo’s side,
and whispered into his ear:
“Your humble servant will go like this,
and act in this manner,
and I will certainly behead Wáng Zé.”
After hearing this, Wén Zhāotǎo was greatly pleased and said:
“If the day comes that the task is successful,
I will certainly recommend you with all my might,
and ensure your advancement is not small.
You must not leak this to anyone.”
Mǎ Suì gave his word,
quietly left the tent,
and went to hand over his watch and rest.
At dawn the next day,
Wén Zhāotǎo ascended his command bench.
All the officers arrived at the tent and gave their salutations,
then stood on both sides.
Wén Zhāotǎo finished issuing military orders
and told his attendants to call the soldier who struck the third watch last night.
Before long, the attendants inquired and found it was Mǎ Suì,
and summoned him to kneel before the tent.
Wén Zhāotǎo asked:
“Are you the one who struck the third watch last night and sang resentful lyrics?”
Mǎ Suì said:
“I beg the Zhāotǎo!
Your humble servant was afraid of nodding off and missing the watch,
so I sang a little tune for diversion;
I truly did not sing any ‘resentful lyrics’.”
Wén Zhāotǎo said in a great rage:
“You said you left your home,
braved wind and dew,
had a share in the lashings
but no share in the merit—
are these not resentful lyrics?
This fellow fabricates slanderous words
and demoralizes the army;
he should be beheaded immediately.”
He shouted for the executioners to drag him out of the camp gate, behead him, and report back.
Mǎ Suì said:
“I beg the Zhāotǎo!
Forgive your humble servant’s crime;
your humble servant is willing to go and persuade Wáng Zé to surrender.”
Wén Zhāotǎo ordered him to be brought back for now
and asked:
“You fellow are talking nonsense;
what ability do you have to persuade Wáng Zé to surrender?”
Mǎ Suì said:
“Your humble servant once had a passing acquaintance with Wáng Zé.
Today the rebel troops have suffered successive defeats
and are trapped within a single city,
their situation being critical.
If your humble servant uses words to explain it to him,
I will surely make him surrender without a fight.”
Wén Zhāotǎo said:
“I will now write a secret letter for you.
If you can deliver this letter
and induce Wáng Zé to come and surrender,
your merit will certainly be recorded and heavily rewarded.
If not,
your death still awaits you.”
Wén Zhāotǎo then wrote the letter,
sealed it up,
and handed it to Mǎ Suì.
Mǎ Suì hurriedly left the tent
and went straight to the walls of Bèizhōu city,
calling out loudly across the moat:
“People on the wall!
I have a major secret matter to report to your Great King;
open the city gate and let me enter the city!”
Hearing this, the soldiers guarding the city
reported to the gate officer,
who opened the city gate,
used a small boat to cross the river,
and ferried Mǎ Suì to the shore.
Naturally, they searched him thoroughly,
and he carried not even an inch of iron.
Seeing the letter from Wén Zhāotǎo,
the people thought it was a challenge to battle
and escorted him to see Wáng Zé.
Wáng Zé recognized Mǎ Suì as a fellow villager and brother,
and said:
"I have not seen you for a long time.
So it turns out you were in Wén Yànbó's army.
What business brings you to see me today?"
Mǎ Suì said:
"I report to the Great King!
I, Mǎ Suì, am untalented
and lost my way among the ranks of the army;
originally I did not dare to come see the Great King.
However, the other night,
it was Mǎ Suì's turn to patrol during the third watch.
Fearing I would fall asleep,
I improperly sang a little tune.
Pacification Commissioner Wén said I was disturbing the army's morale
and wanted to execute me.
Fortunately, I spoke up quickly
and reported:
'I have the ability to persuade the Great King to surrender.'
Pacification Commissioner Wén believed this
and wrote a letter with his own hand,
sending me to deliver it.
I was lucky to escape
and have come specifically to submit to the Great King.
I know all the strengths and weaknesses within Pacification Commissioner Wén's army.
I hope the Great King will take me in as a runner under your command,
and I shall repay you like a dog or a horse."
He then handed Pacification Commissioner Wén's letter to Wáng Zé.
Wáng Zé saw that the letter contained much boastful talk
and immediately tore it to pieces.
He then told Mǎ Suì to change his clothes
and invited him to sit together in a private room.
Mǎ Suì said:
Since I have received the Great King's kindness in taking me in,
to hold your whip and follow your stirrup would be enough;
how could I dare sit like this?"
Wáng Zé said:
"I and you are fellow villagers,
and have been like brothers since childhood;
it is different from other people."
Mǎ Suì had no choice but to sit down.
Wáng Zé ordered wine to be prepared.
While inviting Mǎ Suì to drink,
he asked about the strengths and weaknesses of Pacification Commissioner Wén's army.
Mǎ Suì said:
"Pacification Commissioner Wén has only fifty thousand troops,
though he falsely claims to have one hundred thousand.
A few days ago he lost several battles
and lost over ten thousand men.
Furthermore, in Míng Gǎo's camp at Fùjiātuǎn,
there are ten thousand old, weak, and wounded people;
now the actual number is less than thirty thousand.
Yesterday, when they counted the grain and fodder,
I heard it said that it could only last for ten-odd days.
If the Great King defends carefully now,
in only a few days,
Pacification Commissioner Wén's army
will retreat of its own accord without a fight."
Wáng Zé was extremely happy to hear what Mǎ Suì said.
That day they drank straight until evening.
Wáng Zé said to Mǎ Suì:
"I remember when we were young in our hometown,
we composed couplets and recited poetry in the schoolroom.
Ever since I took a liking to spears and staves,
I have not practiced literature or ink.
Today, meeting an old friend,
we should each compose a poem
to express our inner thoughts."
Mǎ Suì said:
"I have been foolish and dull since childhood
and could not keep up with the Great King's heels then,
much less today.
Please recite first, Great King;
I shall only clumsily imitate you."
Wáng Zé ordered the four treasures of the study to be brought
and, while drunk, wrote out four lines:
Shedding military gear to change into imperial robes,
Displaying heroic prowess among six thousand men.
On the day when the enemy is crushed and success achieved,
Would I dare be stingy with honors for an old friend?
Wáng Zé said:
"Because I distributed the money and rice intended for six thousand soldiers,
the Prefect took offense,
and thus I began my undertaking.
The fourth line expresses that I have not forgotten the past."
Mǎ Suì said:
"The Great King's fine work is most wonderful;
how could I dare to harmonize with it?"
Wáng Zé said:
"I precisely wish to see you harmonize
to judge the rise or fall of your learning!"
Following the previous rhyme, Mǎ Suì also wrote four lines:
True friendship is rarely seen since the tale of the silk robe,
How fortunate to meet a hero supported by Heaven today.
I wish to follow the generals to assist your mandate,
How would I dare speak of deeds or look toward banners of honor?
Wáng Zé looked at it
and laughed loudly, saying:
"Your intention is most beautiful,
and not only the literary style!"
The two drank until completely drunk and then parted.
The next day,
Mǎ Suì came to give thanks,
and Wáng Zé appointed him to the post of Personal Army Commandery Envoy,
keeping him in the rebel government office
to keep watch at night together with Zhāng Qí,
frequently inviting him to converse.
Mǎ Suì wanted to kill Wáng Zé,
but could not find the opportunity to strike.
Suddenly one night,
while sitting and drinking wine with Zhāng Qí,
they each spoke their minds.
When they reached a point of complete abandon in their talk,
Mǎ Suì said:
"I hear that among the Great King's subordinates,
everyone possesses Daoist arts.
I wonder what supernatural powers you have, elder brother?"
Zhāng Qí then told him all about the origins and magical uses of the Water and Fire Gourd.
Mǎ Suì saw that he was drunk
and insisted on asking to see it.
Zhāng Qí lifted his clothes,
and on the undershirt next to his skin,
there was a soft silk cord tied,
and on the cord hung a tiny gourd.
He held it up for Mǎ Suì to see
but did not untie it.
Mǎ Suì took note of it.
That night he feigned being drunk
and stayed overnight with Zhāng Qí.
Mǎ Suì had a plan;
in the middle of the night, he feigned getting up to relieve himself
and called out, "Brother Zhāng!"
Zhāng Qí was sound asleep from the wine.
Mǎ Suì wanted to untie the magical object at his waist,
but saw it was tied very tightly.
Fearing he would wake him,
he took out the foul blood and garlic juice he carried in a leather pouch on his person,
gently removed the plug of the gourd,
dripped a few drops of the foul liquid inside,
and plugged it back as before.
Rising at dawn,
Zhāng Qí was completely unaware.
Truly it is:
A joyful matter becomes a joyless one;
An unwitting person meets a calculating one.
It is not further discussed.
Furthermore, Commander Wén Zhāotǎo saw that Mǎ Suì had been gone for a long time
without any news,
so he issued an order
for the various generals to lead the troops to attack the city from all four sides.
Sūn Fǔ attacked the West Gate,
Dǒng Zhōng attacked the East Gate,
Liǔ Chūnshēng attacked the South Gate,
and Liú Yànwēi attacked the North Gate.
Each approached the city,
beating drums and shouting to provoke battle.
Wáng Zé hastily invited everyone to deliberate.
Only Quēzi happened to be drunk
and could not be awakened;
the rest all arrived and went up the city wall to patrol.
Meanwhile, a messenger was sent to report to Shèng Gūgu,
and Hú Yǒng'ér was informed.
Wáng Zé summoned Mǎ Suì and asked,
"You said Wén Zhāotǎo's army lacks provisions;
for what reason have they come to attack the city again?"
Mǎ Suì said,
"He has only managed to secure a few days' worth of supplies;
why would he not combine his strength to attack!
He only assumes that Your Majesty has lost a battle
and will certainly not dare to send troops to face the enemy.
If we strike when they least expect it,
we will surely defeat them.
Once one branch of his army is crushed,
the others will lose their footing
and must all retreat."
Mǎ Suì's intention
was merely to lure away the group of sorcerers from Wáng Zé's side
so that he could take advantage of the situation.
Wáng Zé did not understand his intent
and nodded, saying,
"Who dares to go and charge the enemy lines?"
Zhāng Qí relied on his Water and Fire Calabash;
since only he had been successful the last time,
he stepped forward and replied,
"Sūn Fǔ is a general who was defeated by my hand.
I have seen through his methods,
and I am willing to lead a troop out of the West Gate to face the enemy."
Having spoken,
he galloped down from the wall.
Wáng Zé said,
"It would be better to have another person to support him."
He looked at Wú Wàng.
Wú Wàng had been frightened before
and was originally unwilling to go,
but out of necessity,
he had to accept the task
and departed resentfully.
Wáng Zé leaned against a hanging bench,
gripping the wooden railing,
and watched the battle from atop the West Gate wall.
Now, Vanguard Sūn Fǔ
was leading the masses to attack the city
when he suddenly saw the city gate open
and a troop of soldiers come flying out.
Sūn Fǔ hurriedly pulled back his soldiers,
held his spear, and sat on his horse,
waiting for the fight.
Zhāng Qí held no weapon
but carried the calabash in his hand.
Estimating the government troops were close,
he recited the Divine Fire Incantation,
removed the stopper from the calabash,
and shouted,
"Swift!"
Yet no light of fire emerged.
He then recited the Holy Water Incantation
and repeatedly shouted,
"Swift!
Swift!"
He shook the calabash several times like a fortune-telling tube,
but not even a single drop came out.
Peering into the mouth of the calabash,
he only smelled a stench of blood and garlic.
Realizing the magic was broken,
he turned his horse and fled.
Sūn Fǔ galloped in pursuit.
It turned out that Wáng Zé and Hú Yǒng'ér had become husband and wife,
and he had only learned two spells:
one was the Body-freezing Magic,
and the other was the Invisibility Spell.
When the Body-freezing Magic was performed,
no matter if there were thousands of men and horses
chasing as if flying,
it could instantly freeze both their feet
so they could not move;
they would only be released after two hours.
Wáng Zé, from atop the wall, saw Zhāng Qí's defeat
and the rear army pursuing,
and was just about to recite the Body-freezing Incantation.
Mǎ Suì, standing by his side, thought,
"If I do not strike now,
when should I wait for?
But on both the left and right sides,
all were holding knives, axes, and weapons."
Mǎ Suì wanted to seize a knife to kill Wáng Zé,
but feared being noticed.
He clenched his fists tight.
It was slower in the telling
than in the doing;
before Wáng Zé could finish his incantation,
Mǎ Suì struck with a fierce punch
that hit him in the mouth,
knocking out his two front teeth,
splitting his lip,
and sending him falling onto the gate tower.
Mǎ Suì then tried to seize a knife from those on the left and right to strike,
but a trusted rebel general by Wáng Zé's side
named Shí Qìng
had already drawn a knife from his waist.
With a lift and fall of the blade,
he chopped off one of Mǎ Suì's arms.
Everyone rushed forward together,
captured Mǎ Suì,
and rescued Wáng Zé.
Wáng Zé was furious
and ordered his attendants to behead him and report back.
Mǎ Suì cursed loudly,
"Because I had no knife in hand,
I could not cut off the head of this demonic rebel
to rid the people of this harm.
After I die, I will surely become a vengeful ghost to kill you!"
The crowd pushed Mǎ Suì away to be beheaded.
Later generations have a poem in praise:
"The calabash's water and fire have already come to naught,
and now the sorcerer suffers the omen of broken teeth.
One can only laugh at the famous swordsman Jīng Qīng;
of what use was his circling the pillar after Zǔ Lóng?"
Meanwhile, Zhāng Qí reached the edge of the drawbridge.
The soldiers were scrambling for their lives
and had already trampled the drawbridge until it broke.
Sūn Fǔ pursued from behind.
Zhāng Qí rode around the moat
and came upon a muddy patch;
his horse's front legs sank,
and Sūn Fǔ caught up and struck with his spear,
thrusting him off his horse.
He fell into the moat and drowned.
How pitiable that Zhāng Qí, who sold meat for a living,
did not keep to his place
and today became a ghost in the water.
Sūn Fǔ ordered the soldiers to use grappling hooks to drag up the corpse,
cut off the head,
and went to the central command tent to present his achievement.
Wú Wàng used the broken bridge as an excuse
and did not come to help at all,
leading his troops back.
Furthermore, because Wáng Zé's lip had been split open by Mǎ Suì's punch,
he could not make a sound.
Just then, Shèng Gūgu and Hú Yǒng'ér both arrived;
seeing Wáng Zé in such a state
and having lost Zhāng Qí,
they deeply resented the matter of Mǎ Suì.
They hurried to have men carry Wáng Zé in a sedan chair to the rebel palace,
and meanwhile called for physicians to treat him.
Zuǒ Chù woke up from his wine
and, knowing of this matter,
also came to inquire after his health.
Hú Yǒng'ér grumbled that Quēzi's drinking had ruined things.
Quēzi smiled and said,
"My own lips aren't split;
why should I be forbidden from drinking?"
Hú Yǒng'ér said,
"Stop making jokes for now.
The siege is urgent,
so we must consider a long-term plan;
only when one or two of their primary generals are beheaded
will they be willing to retreat."
Shènggūgū said:
"Since he has someone who can break our magic,
there is no other plan
except to perform the Wūlóng Zhǎnjiàng method.
This method is extremely difficult to break,
but the Rúyì Bǎocè states:
'This is a most evil technique;
it must never be used lightly,
for using it will surely bring hidden calamities.'
Now there is nothing else to be done.
Originally, this method used the essence of the five metals,
placed beneath the Liùjiǎ altar,
refined for seven times seven, totaling forty-nine days,
to cast a ghost-head blade
named the Shéndāo,
which can whistle and leap by itself.
Use a stone casket to contain it
and hide it at the bottom of the water;
when metal and water harmonize,
only then will it not leap away.
If one encounters a moment of extreme danger,
take a pure black male dog,
write three Zhǎnjiàng talismans in cinnabar,
along with the names of the persons to be slain,
and burn them together.
Recite the Zhǎnjiàng incantation three times,
inhale a mouthful of western metal-qì,
visualize the scene of the heads falling to the ground,
and with great force, strike the dog's head off with the Shéndāo.
Then the heads of those whose names were burned
will fall simultaneously.
If the military register is burned,
even if there are ten million people,
all their heads will fall.
This is why it is called a most evil technique."
When Shènggūgū and the other two were refining the method in the beginning,
because this method was so formidable,
they only cast one Shéndāo
and hid it in the pond atop Tiānzhù Shān.
Shènggūgū intended to go and fetch it to strike off the heads of Wén and
Cáo, the two Zhāotǎo,
as well as the heads of various famous generals.
Zuǒ Chù and Hú Yǒng'ér were both delighted and said:
"It must be so
to ensure there are no worries."
Shènggūgū flew away.
Zuǒ Chù went with Wú Wàng to patrol the city and enforce the bans.
Hú Yǒng'ér also returned to the false palace to seek pleasure.
Wáng Zé was distressed by his pain,
unable to eat or drink,
and had no way to distract himself.
Usually, he most liked a musician who played the role of a fùjìng,
called Lǐ Yúgēng,
who played the pípá well,
sang fine songs,
was skilled at storytelling,
and making jokes and jests.
Wáng Zé called him to relieve his boredom.
That day, Lǐ Yúgēng came before Wáng Zé
but neither played
nor sang;
he kept his mouth shut and did not make a sound.
Wáng Zé asked:
"Lǐ Yúgēng!
Why do you not speak?
What trouble do you have in your heart?"
Lǐ Yúgēng said:
"If Your Majesty is troubled,
how could I, a lowly person, not be troubled?
I and Your Majesty are both doing things in secret.
What Your Majesty relies on
are only a few people who raise demons and cause trouble.
Now Dànzǐ Guóshī has gone,
Chancellor Zhāng Luán has gone into hiding,
General Bǔ Jí has fled,
Military Advisor Zuǒ Chù has lost,
Rèn Qiān has been captured,
Zhāng Qí is dead,
and Shènggūgū has found an excuse to hide.
Today we are in a besieged city,
and the troops outside the city are increasing more and more,
exerting all their strength to attack.
If they do not succeed on an even day, they will on an odd day;
in the end, you will be captured by them.
Now it is too late for regret."
Wáng Zé said:
"What do you mean?"
Lǐ Yúgēng said:
"It is better to accept the offer of surrender as soon as possible,
turning calamity into fortune."
Wáng Zé was greatly enraged and said:
"How intolerable that this fellow does not serve me
but instead uses words to offend me!"
He shouted for his attendants to seize him.
His subordinates captured Lǐ Yúgēng.
Wáng Zé ordered:
"Bind his hands and feet,
hang him on the end of a catapult and fire him out from the city wall
until he is smashed into a pulp of bone and meat."
The men bound Lǐ Yúgēng,
hung him on the end of the catapult,
and pulled the frame.
With a loud bang from the catapult,
Lǐ Yúgēng was fired out of the city.
Truly:
Among friends, a thousand cups of wine are too few;
when talk is disagreeable, even half a sentence is too much.
As for what happened to Lǐ Yúgēng's life,
please listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
The instruments of state must never be usurped;
who can find peace after claiming the throne and title?
On that day Lù Gōng captured Wáng Zé,
leaving him as an example for all wicked and evil ones to see.
To continue, Wáng Zé was angry that Lǐ Yúgēng's blunt words had offended him,
hung him on the end of a catapult,
and fired him out of the city.
It was truly strange;
neither too early nor too late,
he happened to fall into the river beside the city moat.
The soldiers besieging the city
saw a person fired out by a catapult from the city wall;
they went immediately to see,
and using grappling hooks, pulled him onto the bank.
He was still alive.
They then untied the ropes
and escorted him to the tent of Wén Zhāotǎo.
Wén Zhāotǎo asked:
"What kind of man are you?
What is your surname and name?
For what reason were you fired out of the city?"
Lǐ Yúgēng said:
"I report to the Zhāotǎo!
I am a musician from Bèizhōu,
named Lǐ Yúgēng.
For a moment, I unwisely advised Wáng Zé to surrender to the Zhāotǎo.
Wáng Zé was greatly enraged
and used me as a catapult projectile to fire me out of the city,
wanting to smash me into a pulp of bone and meat.
Fortunately, by the grace of Heaven, I did not die,
and I have come to see the Zhāotǎo."
Wén Zhāotǎo said:
"You are a musician;
how did you advise Wáng Zé?"
Lǐ Yúgēng said:
"Wáng Zé had two of his front teeth knocked out by a punch from Mǎ Suì,
his lips were split,
he could not recite incantations,
and he called me to relieve his boredom.
Seizing upon his agitated state of mind,
I advised him to surrender.
Otherwise,
he would surely be captured by the Zhāotǎo in a matter of days.
Who would have thought he would never realize it
but instead blame me?"
When Wén Zhāotǎo heard this,
he was overjoyed
and said:
"Though you are but a musician,
you understand when to advance and when to retreat."
He ordered his attendants to reward him with wine and food.
Lǐ Yúgēng ate his meal,
and Wén Zhāotǎo asked again:
"Since you are a musician,
you must have been in Bèizhōu for a long time
and certainly know the internal conditions of the city?"
Lǐ Yúgēng said:
"I report to the Zhāotǎo!
The rebel leader Wáng Zé had his lips split open
and cannot chant incantations,
so he is already useless.
Previously, there were the National Preceptor Dànzi Héshang,
Chancellor Zhāng Luán,
and Great General Bǔ Jí,
who all possessed real talent;
however, seeing that Wáng Zé was not benevolent,
they all left one after another.
Now only the Lame Strategist called Zuǒ Chù remains,
who is skilled in using sorcery.
There is also Wáng Zé's wife, Hú Yǒng'ér,
who can also stir up demons and perform magic.
Hú Yǒng'ér's mother is called Shèng Gūgū,
and she is even more formidable.
Wáng Zé relies entirely on these few sorcerers;
the others are mostly not worth mentioning.
Recently, after the government troops broke their sorcery
and defeated them in several battles,
they have all become anxious.
Shèng Gūgū has now gone to Tiānzhù Shān to fetch some sort of Divine Blade,
but I fear it is merely a plan to escape."
Wén Zhāotǎo asked:
"How many troops and how much food remain in the city?"
Lǐ Yúgēng said:
"What they rely on are bean-men and paper-horses;
as for the soldiers,
there were originally no more than ten thousand,
and after successive losses, more than half are gone.
Now they are filled in by commoners,
who are all a motley crew
and unfamiliar with battle formations.
Money and grain in the treasury were originally scarce,
but it was all gathered by Zuǒ Chù and the other sorcerers through magic for their expenses,
so they are never in short supply."
Wén Zhāotǎo asked again:
"How many people are in the city,
and what are the lanes,
waterways,
and government offices
like?"
Lǐ Yúgēng described them all one by one.
Wén Zhāotǎo said:
"Heaven has sent this man to leak their secrets;
Wáng Zé can now be beheaded."
While Wén Zhāotǎo was speaking,
an officer stepped out from below the tent
and said:
"I report to the Zhāotǎo!
I can capture Wáng Zé alive and bring him to the Zhāotǎo."
Seeing this man come forward, Wén Zhāotǎo
was very pleased and said:
"This exactly matches the words of the Duōmù Shén:
'When the Sān Suì meet,
Bèizhōu can be broken.'"
It turned out that this officer's surname was Lǐ and his name was Suì.
Previously, Zhūgé Suìzhì had broken the magic
and won a battle.
Later, Mǎ Suì split Wáng Zé's lips,
making him unable to chant incantations
or perform sorcery.
Now meeting Lǐ Suì,
there are exactly Sān Suì.
For this reason, Wén Zhāotǎo was delighted.
Wén Zhāotǎo asked Lǐ Suì:
"What plan do you have to capture Wáng Zé?"
Lǐ Suì said:
"I currently command five hundred sappers.
Now that Lǐ Yúgēng has revealed the internal conditions of the city,
the lanes and alleys in the city,
and all the various locations,
as well as the dimensions on the map,
allow me to question him carefully once more for the details,
and measure the distance on the ground against the map.
I only need to lead the five hundred sappers
to dig a tunnel at the north of the city
to enter directly into Bèizhōu City,
reach the front of Wáng Zé's tent,
seize the whole group of sorcerers,
and then open the city gates to let the main army in;
why should this not be possible?"
Wén Zhāotǎo was greatly pleased,
rewarded Lǐ Yúgēng
and Lǐ Suì each with a set of clothes,
and immediately appointed Lǐ Yúgēng as a personal guard before the tent,
instructing Lǐ Yúgēng to explain in detail the offices, grounds, and lanes of the city.
He then ordered the camp-building official to survey,
draw a map,
and give it to Lǐ Suì.
Lǐ Suì examined it,
calculated the distances and conditions,
the widths and directions,
and reported to Wén Zhāotǎo:
"This matter must be kept secret,
and it cannot be done in an instant.
I hope the Zhāotǎo will prepare the troops;
as soon as the way is cleared,
it will be easy to provide support.
I must take Lǐ Yúgēng to serve as a guide."
Wén Zhāotǎo said:
"You must be careful and diligent;
if you capture Wáng Zé
and recover Bèizhōu,
when I report this to the Imperial Court,
your merit will not be small."
He then summoned the five hundred sappers
and rewarded them all.
Just as Lǐ Suì was about to set off,
Zhūgé Suìzhì stepped forward and said:
"I report to the Zhāotǎo!
Even if General Lǐ digs a tunnel to enter the city,
I fear he may not be able to capture Wáng Zé."
Wén Zhāotǎo asked:
"How does my Master know this?"
Zhūgé Suìzhì said:
"Those around Wáng Zé in Bèizhōu City
are all a group of sorcerers.
When General Lǐ enters through the tunnel,
if they become aware
and perform their sorcery,
not only will he be unable to capture Wáng Zé,
but General Lǐ will instead be harmed by them."
Wén Zhāotǎo said:
"If that is so,
when can we ever destroy this rebel?"
Zhūgé Suìzhì said:
"There is no need for the Zhāotǎo to worry;
I, this old monk, shall go along,
using the orthodox to break the heterodox,
ensuring they cannot perform their sorcery,
and then they can all be captured."
Wén Zhāotǎo said with great joy:
"If my Master is willing to go,
the great matter is settled!"
Zhūgé Suìzhì first took his leave and left the tent
to go and see Jiǔtiān Xuánnǚ Niángniáng,
informed her of the matter,
and asked for her assistance from the void,
so that Wáng Zé would certainly be captured this time.
Xuánnǚ Niángniáng already knew that Wáng Zé's time was up
and told him to proceed without worry.
On this side, Lǐ Suì received his orders
and instructed the five hundred sappers
to prepare the blood of pigs and sheep,
horse urine, garlic, and such.
He then looked at the map with Lǐ Yúgēng;
seeing that only the ground north of the city had a wide moat and shallow water,
he calculated the terrain
and, with Zhūgé Suìzhì, commanded the sappers
to bore a tunnel and break into Bèizhōu.
There is a poem to prove it:
Quelling the demons
is a matter of great difficulty,
yet happily today there is a hole to crawl through.
Even if their heaven-deceiving sorcery is fierce,
we shall ensure they lose their peace on this very spot.
The story splits into two branches.
To continue, Shèng Gūgū arrived at the summit of Tiānzhù Shān,
retrieved a divine blade from within a stone chest, and returned.
Qiānlǐyǎn had already seen this
and reported it to Xuánnǚ Niángniáng.
Niángniáng transformed into the appearance of a young maiden
and intercepted her midway, asking,
"Where does Grandmother come from?
I hope you will stay a moment so I may seek your instruction."
Shèng Gūgū said,
"I have some official business
and cannot stay for conversation."
The maiden said,
"What official business does Grandmother have?"
Shèng Gūgū said,
"My children are in dire straits;
I must go to save them."
The maiden said,
"What skills do you have to save them?"
Shèng Gūgū said,
"I have a rough knowledge of Daoist arts."
The maiden said,
"What I love most are Daoist arts;
fortunately, you can teach me one or two."
Shèng Gūgū said,
"Which school of Daoist arts does the young lady prefer?"
The maiden said,
"What I like is the method of the Tiāngāng Sānshíliù Transformations.
I have a slight understanding of the skills,
but have not yet mastered them."
Shèng Gūgū was secretly startled and thought,
"What she has learned is even superior to mine."
Then she said,
"What I know are the Qīshí'èr Dìshà Transformations."
The maiden said,
"This Dìshà method is a heterodox path;
there is no benefit in learning it."
She asked again,
"What blade is that Grandmother is holding in her hands?"
Shèng Gūgū said,
"This is a divine blade."
There is a poem as proof:
Refined from the essence of gold, it is called the divine blade;
Relying on this, one can make gods and ghosts howl.
Constantly it cries and constantly it leaps;
Beheading generals at leisure requires no labor.
The maiden said,
"How does this blade cry and leap?
I beg to see a demonstration."
Shèng Gūgū slapped the scabbard three times with her hand;
only a great roar was heard,
as wretched as the mournful wail of a wronged ghost,
as fierce as the shouting of a violent god.
With a crashing sound,
it suddenly leapt into the air,
ten feet high,
and in an instant fell back into the scabbard.
The maiden said,
"I also have divine swords;
I will show them to Grandmother."
From her sleeve, she took out a lead pellet,
spun it twice in her palm, and threw it.
It rose about twenty feet high
and transformed into a precious sword white as snow and frost,
radiating light in all directions.
It descended like a long rainbow
straight to the ground,
then leapt up again,
falling into her palm,
turning back into a pellet.
The maiden said,
"My sword can fly a thousand lǐ,
decapitate a person's head,
and fly back on its own.
Furthermore, it can expand and contract,
with infinite transformations.
Is it not far superior to Grandmother's blade?"
Shèng Gūgū thought to herself,
"If I could obtain this sword,
what difficulty would there be in taking the head of Zhāotǎo Wén!"
So she said,
"I wish to exchange my divine blade with the young lady for the divine sword;
I wonder if you are willing?"
The maiden said,
"I shall follow your command."
The maiden received the ghost-head blade in her hand,
pulled it out to take a look,
and secretly chanted the Demon-Subduing Incantation,
withdrawing its divine radiance.
The blade could no longer cry out or leap.
The maiden said,
"Your divine blade's
divine spirit is already damaged;
it is completely useless,
and I will not exchange for it."
Shèng Gūgū said,
"How can this be!"
She took back the divine blade
and slapped the scabbard on the left and right,
but it did not move at all.
Shèng Gūgū said,
"This divine blade also submits to the virtuous;
seeing that the divine sword's power is superior,
it is ashamed and dares not show its head."
Shèng Gūgū then had an evil thought;
she cast aside the divine blade,
grabbed the divine sword, and ran.
The maiden said,
"If Grandmother wants to exchange, then let us exchange,
but there is still a secret formula
that I will teach you as well."
Shèng Gūgū did not believe her
and said secretly to herself,
"I will try it myself first."
She threw the pellet into the air.
Meanwhile, the maiden held another pellet in her palm.
That pellet in the air
descended like a long rainbow,
bounced off the ground,
and went directly into the maiden's palm.
It turned out that the two pellets
were exactly the male and female swords.
Since the female was kept,
the male one naturally came to join it.
Shèng Gūgū did not notice this;
she only thought she had thrown it to the ground.
When she looked,
it was gone.
Looking up,
even the maiden was gone.
Shèng Gūgū did not get the divine sword
and lost the divine blade as well;
she felt utterly helpless.
She rose to the clouds to look around,
trying to find that maiden.
She saw ahead a white-bearded old man
sitting on a mountain crag,
playing with two lead pellets in his hands.
Shèng Gūgū went to the front of the mountain
and bowed to the old man, saying,
"Old sir!
What is that you are playing with in your hands?"
The old man said,
"These are divine swords."
There is a poem as proof:
The male and female swords combine yīn and yáng;
They use no sharp edge, only their radiance.
Flying back and forth at will,
A thousand armies and ten thousand horses cannot withstand them.
Shèng Gūgū said:
“These are clearly two pellets;
how are they used?”
The old man said:
“I shall perform with them once for you to see.”
He then tossed the two pellets up;
in an instant,
they leaped to the left
and leaped to the right
like two golden snakes,
twining and circling,
never leaving the old woman’s side.
Coming and going,
they burst forth with ten thousand rays of cold light,
freezing and piercing to the bone.
In one's ears, it was like hearing the sound of a thousand knives and ten thousand blades stabbing,
terrifying the old woman so much that she trembled.
Forming the Weapon-evading Seal
and reciting the Weapon-evading Incantation,
she stood firmly in the Kuí Gāng position.
Seeing that he could not harm the old woman, the old man
withdrew his sword arts
and called out secretly:
“Master, Jiǔtiān Xuánnǚ Niángniang!”
Suddenly, the Maiden appeared before him again.
When Shèng Gūgū saw this, she was furious.
She shook herself and transformed
into the holy image of Pǔxián Púsà,
riding a white elephant,
descending through the void to trample the Maiden.
The Maiden pulled the Treasure Mirror for Reflecting Demons from the Heavenly Court out of her brocade pouch
and shot a beam of golden light toward her.
That white elephant made of cut paper
fell from the sky.
Shèng Gūgū tumbled down,
covering her head with her sleeves
and closing her eyes tightly,
only kowtowing and begging for mercy.
It turns out that the spirits of all things
are concentrated within the two pupils;
no matter how many thousands of transformations one undergoes,
the pupils do not change.
When this Heavenly Mirror shines upon the pupils,
the original form is revealed.
Shèng Gūgū had practiced for many years
and had reached the status of a Heavenly Fox.
She had long heard of the Heavenly Mirror’s power,
and seeing the Maiden take out the seamless brocade pouch woven on the loom of Tiānsūn,
she knew it was that dharma treasure.
Fearing that her true form would be revealed,
she kept her eyes tightly shut
and allowed herself to be bound without resistance.
Xuánnǚ Niángniang took back the Treasure Mirror
and ordered Yuán Gōng to escort the old fox spirit to the Heavenly Court
to atone for the sin of leaking the dharma.
Yuán Gōng entered the Heavenly Gate,
and just as he knelt below the Língxiāo Hall
to memorialize the matter,
there were already 108,000 heavenly foxes in the Heavenly Palace serving as attendants
who all came to the hall to kowtow,
all pleading for mercy and admitting guilt on behalf of Shèng Gūgū.
When Shèng Gūgū heard the voices of the heavenly foxes,
she finally dared to open her eyes.
Seeing the Yù Dì,
she collapsed into a gasping heap
and pleaded incessantly.
Yù Dì issued a decree,
granting that she should not die,
but temporarily sending her to the Heavenly Prison
until the day the demon race was entirely suppressed,
to be dealt with when Xuánnǚ Niángniang arrives.
The heavenly foxes all dispersed,
and Yuán Gōng descended from the Heavenly Gate
to follow Xuánnǚ Niángniang.
The story splits into two paths;
it is said that the city of Bèizhōu had been besieged by Wén Zhǎotǎo for more than three months.
Initially, the provisions in the city
were all brought from various places by Zuǒ Chù’s magic.
Now that Xuánnǚ Niángniang had cast the Net of Heaven and Earth,
all demonic talismans and incantations
could no longer be performed.
The Liù Dīng,
Liù Jiǎ,
Chénghuáng,
and Tǔdì deities all came to follow the Niángniang’s dharma decree
and were no longer driven by the demons.
The provisions were exhausted,
so they had to seize the belongings of the common people in the city to use.
The suffering of the people at that time
goes without saying.
Zuǒ Chù and
Hú Yǒng'ér relied on their myriad transformations
so that they themselves would not suffer,
enjoying themselves for the time being,
specifically waiting for Shèng Gūgū to bring the divine blade
to see how things would turn out.
While the old fox spirit was already sitting in the Heavenly Prison,
how could they know it here?
Relying foolishly on this one plan,
they were completely unconcerned.
Furthermore, Lǐ Suì, Zhūgě Suìzhì,
and Lǐ Yúgēng led five hundred sappers
and dug for a long time
until they reached a place
roughly to the left side of Wáng Zé’s puppet palace.
Lǐ Suì ordered the sappers to dig out from here.
The sappers broke through
and asked Lǐ Yúgēng:
“Where is this?”
When Lǐ Yúgēng looked,
it was indeed the back hall of the puppet palace.
It was then around the fourth watch.
Lǐ Yúgēng led the way in front;
Lǐ Suì and the others gave a shout
and rushed into the bedroom where Wáng Zé was recovering from illness.
It is said that Wáng Zé, because his toothache had not healed,
was sleeping in bed
with his eyes closed.
He saw the virtuous woman Zhào Wúxiá leading thousands of ghosts coming to demand his life.
Wáng Zé was sleepless that night,
feeling afraid in his heart,
so he ordered many candles to be lit
and had his concubines form a "flesh screen" surrounding him.
He was also feeling irritable
and would not allow them to speak,
quietly guarding like a living corpse.
Suddenly, he heard a great shout,
and soldiers swarmed in.
The concubines were terrified and scattered first,
leaving only Wáng Zé lying alone in bed.
Because his lip was split
and his two front teeth had fallen out,
he could not chant incantations.
He had only learned a binding spell
and an invisibility spell, but neither could be relied upon.
Lǐ Suì stepped forward
and ordered the soldiers to take a hemp rope
and bind him like a hog-tied horse.
They then broke into Hú Yǒng'ér’s puppet palace,
only to see a vast expanse of water
with no path or gate.
Everyone was panicked.
Zhūgě Suìzhì shook his bell and vajra
and recited the Divine Incantation for Breaking Evil;
instantly, the water disappeared.
Lǐ Suì heard a "clang" sound from a kick at his feet,
and picked it up;
it turned out to be a silver hairpin.
This was Hú Yǒng'ér’s demonic magic.
It is said that Hú Yǒng'ér was currently enjoying herself in bed with the Little Prince Wáng Jùn,
performing the acts of clouds and rain.
When the soldiers suddenly broke in,
Hú Yǒng'ér did not know the severity of the situation;
she had just pulled on a small garment
and had not even gotten out of bed
when the soldiers, regardless of anything,
threw the blood of pigs and sheep,
horse urine,
and garlic
all over the bed.
Zhūgě Suìzhì recited the incantation again,
leaving Hú Yǒng'ér with no way to use her tricks,
and she was bound together with Wáng Jùn.
Lǐ Suì had the soldiers surround Wáng Zé,
Hú Yǒng'ér,
and Wáng Jùn with their blades.
The soldiers then set fire to the puppet palace.
Because Zhūgě Suìzhì had used his arts,
the people outside were completely unaware.
Wú Wàng saw the fire rise
and thought it was an accidental fire.
Leading the palace guards
with hooks and buckets, he came to extinguish it.
He ran straight into Lǐ Yúgēng,
who pointed him out to Lǐ Suì.
He and his confidant Shí Qìng and others were all captured and bound.
Regardless of whether they knew demon magic or not,
anyone captured
had the blood of pigs and sheep,
horse urine, and garlic poured over their heads.
Wén Zhǎotǎo’s grand army was outside,
ready to support.
Seeing the fire rise in the city,
he knew the sapper army had begun their operation within
and attacked with combined force.
Some also entered the city through the tunnels.
The troops struck down the city guards
and threw open the gates of Bèizhōu City,
lowering the drawbridge.
Wén Zhǎotǎo entered the city immediately
and sat in the side hall of the puppet palace.
While he ordered the fire to be extinguished,
Lǐ Suì brought Wáng Zé,
Hú Yǒng'ér, and their group before him.
Wén Zhǎotǎo ordered them to be put into prisoner carts,
along with the rebel criminal Rèn Qiān who had been captured earlier at the Old Stockade,
to be held pending trial.
He ordered the vanguard Sūn Fǔ to keep a close watch.
To continue, Zhūgě Suìzhì led the various soldiers and generals to surround the Military Advisor's mansion,
intending to capture Zuǒ Chù.
They searched as far as the central hall,
and a soldier shouted:
"He is here!"
As the troops rushed in to look,
they clearly saw the cripple leaning against the wall,
but in the blink of an eye,
he stepped into the wall.
The soldiers pushed the wall down all at once,
but there was no trace of him.
While they were searching beneath the wall,
a messenger arrived from Steward Wáng Xìn to report:
"Someone saw Zuǒ Chù enter a milling house;
we specially invite Master Zhūgě to go and capture him."
It turned out that Zuǒ Chù was determined to flee,
but unfortunately, a "heavenly net" had been densely laid out,
and he could not escape.
He happened to hide in the milling house
but was spotted by someone.
Zhūgě Suìzhì immediately went with the others straight to the milling house.
Steward Wáng Xìn personally led the troops there
and ordered the soldiers to surround the front and back doors
before entering to search and capture.
The household was startled
and asked:
"What has happened at my house
to cause such a commotion?"
The crowd replied:
"The demon Zuǒ Chù has entered your house;
if you are sensible, let him out
to avoid being implicated."
The homeowner said:
"I beg you, General!
No one has come in to hide in my house."
Wáng Xìn ordered the soldiers to search the house minutely.
Zhūgě Suìzhì entered the milling room and looked around;
pointing at a pestle head,
he asked the homeowner:
"Is this an object of your house or not?"
The homeowner looked
and said:
"My house never had this extra pestle head."
Zhūgě Suìzhì said:
"This is exactly Zuǒ Chù;
his two pupils are clearly on the pestle head.
If not for this old monk,
no one would recognize him.
Quickly bring filth to pour on it."
Before he had finished speaking,
the pestle head had already vanished.
They searched again,
but there was no trace.
Suddenly, several consecutive claps of thunder were heard in the clear blue sky,
sounding like mountains crumbling and the earth splitting.
The soldiers raised a shout.
When Wáng Xìn went personally to look,
it was a lame male fox
struck dead on the ground.
It turned out that Zuǒ Chù had transformed into the pestle head,
hoping to deceive the crowd,
but he was seen through by the monk;
he then vanished again,
intending to take the form of Zhūgě Suìzhì
to harm Pacification Commissioner Wén.
However, Xuánnǚ Niángniáng had suspended the Demon-Reflecting Treasure Mirror in the sky,
reflecting and breaking his original form,
making it impossible for him to transform.
She then ordered the Thunder Department to strike him dead instantly,
thereby fulfilling the oath made at the stone wall of the Báiyuán Shén.
Pity Zuǒ Chù, who had been a lame demon with magic for many years,
only to become a spiritless, lonely ghost in a single day.
Truly:
Though one may use infinite schemes to reach the heavens,
it is hard to avoid eternal calamity in Fèngdū.
That is besides the point.
To continue, Zhūgě Suìzhì looked at the dead fox,
recognized it as Zuǒ Chù,
and knowing it was the divine power of Xuánnǚ Niángniáng,
he was overcome with joy.
He ordered the soldiers to carry it to the gate of the pseudo-mansion.
After Pacification Commissioner Wén and the generals had inspected it,
Wén Zhāotǎo said with great joy:
"If my Master had not used the righteous to break the evil,
how could the demon faction be pacified?"
Zhūgě Suìzhì whispered into Pacification Commissioner Wén's ear:
"This is because the Imperial Court follows the Way,
removing the treacherous and employing the virtuous,
which has moved the Heavenly Court.
Jiǔtiān Xuánnǚ Niángniáng assisted from the sky;
it is not the merit of this old monk."
While they were speaking,
a messenger from Vanguard Sūn Fǔ arrived to report,
and only then did they know that the demon criminal Hú Yǒng'ér had also just been struck dead by heavenly thunder.
It further proved that creating trouble and harming the people
cannot escape heavenly execution;
it was no empty oath.
When Pacification Commissioner Wén saw that both demon leaders were dead,
he finally felt at ease.
He immediately posted notices to pacify the people:
all soldiers in Bèizhōu
who did not know demon magic were considered coerced followers
and were all exempt from investigation.
Wáng Zé
and Zuǒ Chù had abducted beautiful women from the populace;
those with husbands were returned to their original husbands,
and those without husbands were left to their parents to take back and choose matches for.
As for the wealthy households
who were plundered and harmed by the rebels,
the remaining military rations
were distributed by household
to support the poor.
The whole city cheered and filled the roads.
Pacification Commissioner Wén held a celebratory banquet in the mansion hall
and invited Míng Gǎo to the feast.
The large and small armies camped outside the city
and all received rewards.
Meanwhile, a memorial was submitted to the Imperial Court,
detailing the order of merits,
and stating that the captured demon rebels would either be sent to the capital Jīng
or dealt with in this prefecture,
specifically awaiting the Imperial Decree for a final decision.
On the register of merits,
Zhūgě Suìzhì was first.
Zhūgě Suìzhì said:
"This old monk is one who has left the world;
what use is it to record merit?
I beg you to distribute it among the names of the hardworking officers and soldiers.
Just return my original horse
so I may go to Gānquán Sì to answer to my disciples;
to fulfill this old monk's word,
my wish will be complete."
Pacification Commissioner Wén repeatedly urged him to stay, but he would not comply.
He was offered gold and silk,
but took nothing.
Taking three young attendants,
he bid farewell to the generals
and rode out of the city.
Pacification Commissioner Wén secretly sent someone to follow and find out his whereabouts.
Now, in Gānquán Sì, there was an old monk named Zhūgě Suìzhì
who had been away for fifteen years
and had just happened to return during these few days.
The various disciples and grandsons thought he had returned from the war
and asked him about Pacification Commissioner Wén's affairs,
of which he knew nothing at all.
The monks were also unable to decide on the matter.
On this day,
they saw three attendants from afar
leading a horse back.
Sitting on the horse
was another Zhūgě Suìzhì,
who was no different from the one in the temple.
The monks were greatly shocked
and discussed:
"We need not waste our breath;
let us simply invite the old monk inside to come out
and let the two of them distinguish the true from the false themselves."
The elder from outside dismounted
and walked straight into the Buddha Hall.
When the elder from inside came out and saw him,
he cursed:
"What monster is impersonating the appearance of this old monk?"
He was about to explode with anger,
while the monks stood on both sides watching coldly.
When the elder from outside heard the word "false,"
he hurried to wave his hand and said:
"Old Bodhisattva, do not speak;
this poor monk has already attained enlightenment
and will return clarity to you."
He took brush and ink and wrote a gatha on the sutra table:
"The false 'you' is fundamentally not real;
the true 'I' is also false.
Cast aside the false 'you' and 'me,'
and there naturally are the true father and mother.
Ah!
Fortunately, you are willing to be 'real' today;
laugh at me for ten years of playing in vain."
He wrote another four lines:
"Thunder roared under the walls of Bèizhōu;
somersaults were flipped in Báiyún Dòng.
All dharmas are empty, I now return;
Dànzǐ shall no longer make a fool of himself."
Having finished writing, he threw down the brush,
sat down cross-legged,
closed his eyes, and passed away.
When the monks went forward to look,
his appearance had already changed.
They saw thick eyebrows and a prominent nose,
a broad mouth and a square jaw;
it was clearly the look of Dànzi Héshàng.
Only then did they know that Dànzi Héshàng was a holy monk,
and each was endlessly amazed.
Now, the messenger sent by Commissioner Wén to investigate his whereabouts
learned of this matter
and hurriedly returned to report it.
Commissioner Wén was greatly shocked,
and immediately, along with Commissioner Cáo
and Wáng Xìn, the three on horseback led their personal soldiers
and came in person to Gānquán Sì.
While the monks were just about to discuss the funeral arrangements,
they heard it said:
“Commissioner Wén has arrived.”
This frightened them into a fluster,
and even the old monk Zhūgě Suìzhì came out to welcome them;
upon seeing Commissioner Wén,
they all knelt down together.
Commissioner Wén was still caught between doubt and belief,
so he hurriedly supported them
and said:
“Why does my master perform such a ritual?”
The monks reported:
“This is the abbot of this temple,
who previously followed the Commissioner;
it was actually Master Dàn assuming his form.
Now he has passed away while sitting in the Buddha hall
and has returned to his original form.”
Commissioner Wén then finally believed it.
The monks led him into the Buddha hall,
and Commissioner Wén looked at the holy body,
seeing his awe-inspiring appearance,
as solemn as if he were alive.
He said to Commissioner Cáo:
“Bāo Dàizhì once said this monk was formidable
and told me to be carefully on guard.
Now he has instead helped me succeed;
thus I know this monk is no ordinary person.”
The monks presented the two gāthās to Commissioner Wén,
who read them and praised them endlessly.
Together with the generals, they all took up incense and bowed.
After the bowing was finished,
he ordered that highly skilled craftsmen be sought out
to lacquer his flesh body
and build a shrine to worship him.
He also took a thousand taels of silver from the army funds
to serve as the monks' expenses for maintaining the incense and shrine.
To this day, the true body of Dànzi Héshàng is still in Gānquán Sì,
serving as the temple’s Qiélán Shàngrén,
called the Dànzi Púsà,
or sometimes called the Dàntóu Púsà,
and the incense offerings have never ceased.
Later people had a poem inscribed on the wall of Gānquán Sì which said:
Three times the book was stolen, all were false;
one day the falsehood is broken and it becomes true.
If one breaks through from the midst of success,
then one is the person who progresses from the top of the pole.
Commissioner Wén drafted another memorial
to present to the Imperial Court,
specifically reporting the miracles of Jiǔtiān Xuánnǚ Niángniáng and Dànzi Héshàng.
It is said that the Bureau of Military Affairs presented both memorials for the Emperor's inspection;
the Rénzōng Emperor's dragon countenance was greatly pleased,
and an imperial edict was immediately sent down to Bèizhōu:
The sorcerer rebel Wáng Zé is to be taken to the prefecture’s marketplace
to be hacked and sliced to pieces.
The follower rebels Rèn Qiān,
Wú Wàng,
Wáng Jùn,
Shí Qìng, and the others are all to be decapitated.
Although Hú Yǒng'ér has already received Heaven's punishment,
she shall still be beheaded;
after all the heads have been transmitted to the capital to inform the ancestral temple,
they shall be sent to various prefectures, departments, and counties as a public warning;
the fox corpse of Zuǒ Chù shall be burned to ash and scattered to the winds.
The common people of Bèizhōu suffered under Wáng Zé's tyranny;
a certain amount of army provisions is permitted to be distributed to each household
to support the poor.
The illegal fake palace built by Wáng Zé
shall be immediately converted into a temple for Jiǔtiān Xuánnǚ Niángniáng,
bestowed with the title Shèngyòu.
The prefecture’s administrative office
shall be built on another selected site.
Dànzi Héshàng abandoned the heterodox and returned to the orthodox;
in pacifying the sorcerers
he has merit,
and is posthumously granted the title of Hùguó Chánshī.
Mǎ Suì
and Rú Gāng,
whose loyalty and integrity are commendable,
shall both receive generous posthumous titles and benefits for their heirs.
The heroic woman Zhào Wúxiá
is permitted to have a memorial archway of chastity and heroism erected.
The post of Bèizhōu Prefect has been vacant for a long time;
Wén Yànbó is ordered to select and recommend a replacement from nearby officials based on talent.
For the officials of various prefectures and counties in Héběi,
many of whom were first coerced by the rebels
but later returned to the orthodox path,
their cases must be distinguished by gravity
and dealt with accordingly.
Those with merit in the expedition,
both primary and secondary generals and officers,
shall all wait until the day they return to court
to be promoted and rewarded based on merit.
Commissioner Wén and the various officials received the imperial edict
and carried it out one by one.
Early the next morning,
the group of sorcerers was brought out from prison with their crime-stating boards written;
the prisoner carts were opened,
and they were pushed onto wooden donkeys.
Commissioner Wén signed the warrant for slow-slicing
and decapitation,
and they were pushed out to the marketplace.
Wáng Zé, Rèn Qiān,
Wú Wàng, and the others all had tears in their eyes,
looking at each other in dismay,
unable to make a sound.
The spectators in Bèizhōu
were crowded shoulder to shoulder.
Some were cursing and spitting,
and some were sighing.
One saw only:
Two sounds of a broken drum,
one strike of a shattered gong.
The black banners
fluttered like clouds.
The willow-leaf spears
crisscrossed like snow.
The crime boards were posted high;
people say, after this departure, when will they return?
White paper flowers were inserted in pairs;
everyone says this time it is hard to live again.
The "long rest" meal
is hard to swallow in the throat.
The "eternal farewell" wine,
how can it be gulped down?
The execution supervisor on his tall horse
is more formidable than a living Yánluó.
The executioners in the forest of knives and swords
are like life-chasing ghosts.
Please look at those being slow-sliced today;
they are all people who stirred up sorcery and rebellion.
The executioners' murderous aura all arose,
and it was exactly the third quarter of the hour of Wǔ.
Wáng Zé and the others were escorted to the crossroads;
after the crimes were read,
they were all executed by slow-slicing according to the law.
It is a pity that Wáng Zé had rebelled for exactly five years and six months
before receiving the ultimate punishment today,
ending the lineage of the Great House of Wáng.
At that time, he was the fifth child born,
with five "Fú" characters tattooed on his back,
and his childhood name was Wǔfú'ér;
this was the prophecy of the five years.
The execution supervisor was sitting inside the reed mat enclosure,
watching the executioners perform the punishment.
He saw a person in the crowd
supporting an old woman and squeezing through;
kneeling before the table,
they laid out eight ingots of gold and silver
and wailed loudly.
When asked the reason,
that person was indeed Guān Yí,
the old woman was his mother,
and his wife was the Heroic Woman Zhào.
Because she refused Wáng Zé's forced marriage,
she had hanged herself and died.
The mother and son had fled to Dōngjīng;
today, hearing that Wáng Zé had been captured
and the imperial edict was being carried out in Bèizhōu,
the mother and son returned to their hometown.
This gold and silver was Wáng Zé's betrothal gift;
they were willing to hand it over to the officials for distribution,
hoping to buy a few pieces of Wáng Zé's flesh to offer in sacrifice to the deceased wife.
The execution supervisor did not dare act on his own
and reported it to Commissioner Wén.
Commissioner Wén ordered the executioners
to give Wáng Zé's heart and liver to Guān Yí and his mother,
and as for the gold and silver, he let them use it for the expenses of building a shrine for the heroic woman.
He also appointed Guān Yí as a Xiùcai in the prefectural school.
Later, Guān Yí studied and passed the imperial examinations,
and never took a primary wife for the rest of his life.
People said a righteous husband and a chaste wife came from the same household;
this is a later story.
On that day, Pacification Commissioner Wén Zhāotǎo had the various criminals beheaded,
and sent word to the capital Jīngshī for their disposal.
The local officials
settled the pacification of the soldiers and civilians.
They renovated the traveling palace of Xuánnǚ Niángniáng,
and sculpted several divine statues to be enshrined within,
summoning practicing Daoists to manage the incense and offerings.
Wén Zhāotǎo also held a Jiào ritual in the temple for seven days and seven nights,
to release the souls of the fallen generals and soldiers,
as well as the unjustly killed souls of Bèizhōu.
After the matters were concluded,
an auspicious day was chosen to lead the army back to the capital.
Truly it was:
Brimming with joy,
whips strike the golden stirrups with a ring;
beaming with smiles,
the people sing songs of victory upon their return.
Throughout the march, the army maintained strict discipline,
and not even a hair's breadth of the people's property was disturbed.
When the common people heard that Wén Zhāotǎo was already eighty years old,
and that today,
having suppressed the demons and quelled the rebellion,
he had achieved great merit,
everyone vied to be first,
each fearing to be left behind,
all coming to gaze upon the countenance of Wén Zhāotǎo.
Fearing that the crowds would crush the people, Wén Zhāotǎo
only rode his horse every day,
instead of taking a covered sedan chair,
allowing everyone to see him.
Everyone who watched cheered,
all saying:
"In the past, Grand Duke Lǚ Shàng met Wén Wáng at eighty
and raised an army to destroy Zhòu;
since then, there has been no second such man.
Today, Wén Zhāotǎo is of such spirit and elegant demeanor;
is it not because the Imperial Court possesses the Way
that such a god of fortune was born to govern the world?
We commoners are all truly blessed."
To cut the story short,
in no time they arrived at Dōngjīng for an audience with the Emperor.
Emperor Rénzōng expressed his gratitude,
and Wén Yànbó remained as the Chief Grand Councilor,
enfeoffed as the Duke of Lù Guó.
Because Bāo Zhěng had recommended the right person,
he was appointed as the Second Grand Councilor,
with the title of Tóng Píngzhāngshì.
Cáo Wěi was appointed to the post of Shūmìshǐ.
Those below Wáng Xìn and the rest
were each promoted in rank.
Lǐ Yúgēng was promoted to the position of Tǒngzhì.
Liú Yànwēi was promoted to the General Manager of Héběi.
Not long after,
Dí Qīng had already suppressed Nóng Zhìgāo in Yōngzhōu,
and sent officials to announce the victory.
Fàn Zhòngyān's prestige awed Xīxià;
Zhào Yuánhào was afraid
and sent someone to submit a letter of surrender,
paying tribute every year.
Truly it is:
When the court possesses the Way, the people are at peace and happy;
when the four seas are without concern, the nation is in great peace.
Let this matter not be mentioned further.
Now to speak of Jiǔtiān Xuánnǚ Niángniáng, who, after eliminating the demonic chaos in Bèizhōu,
returned with Yuán Gōng to report to the Heavenly Court.
Yùdì rewarded the merit of Bái Yuán Shén,
pardoned his previous crimes,
restored his title of Báiyún Dòngjūn,
and he remained in the Xiūwényuàn in charge of the secret books of the Nine Heavens.
Monk Dànzǐ had already attained the fruit of a Bodhisattva;
that goes without saying.
Although the old female fox spirit had many heavenly foxes interceding for her,
her sins were not small;
she was punished by being sent to Báiyún Dòng to guard the Heavenly Books for Bái Yuán Shén.
When Shèng Gūgu heard this,
although she had lost a pair of children,
she was pleased to have been released from the Heavenly Prison,
and to have been assigned to such a good place;
she was overjoyed beyond measure,
thinking to herself:
"When I go there,
I will be free to read the Heavenly Books to my heart's content,
and even the Tiāngāng transformations
will be within my reach."
Just as she reached the stone walls of Báiyún Dòng,
there was a sudden thunderous roar,
and the mountain peak where the White Jade Incense Burner was placed collapsed,
perfectly sealing the cave entrance.
The Mist Curtain and the White Jade Incense Burner were taken back to heaven,
and from then on, no one ever reached Báiyún Dòng again.
This was Yùdì's intention to prevent future troubles.
Emperor Rénzōng was wise and possessed the Way;
he was able to employ the virtuous and talented,
bringing peace to the people and the nation;
Heaven granted him a long reign.
Later, having occupied the throne for forty-three years,
there was one inexplicable thing in his life:
he was unwilling to formally appoint a Crown Prince.
The officials submitted many memorials regarding this matter,
but he simply would not grant his consent.
Suddenly one day,
he summoned the Hanlin Academician Wáng Guī to draft an edict,
establishing Zōngshí as the Imperial Son.
That night,
Rénzōng went to the Fúníng Diàn to bathe;
having sat down,
he took off both his shoes,
and suddenly passed away.
This was a foreknowledge of the time of his life and death.
Throughout the palace, celestial music was heard echoing clearly,
and a rare fragrance was rich in the air,
as he returned to his position as the Chìjiǎo Dàxiān.
A poem says:
A cup of clear tea, a stick of incense,
at leisure, I ponder the past in detail.
All manner of fates are hard to escape,
but one's spirit can remain in command.
Whether an Emperor is dim or wise distinguishes order from chaos,
while whether hearts are wicked or upright determines calamity or blessing.
If one can act with extraordinary virtue and remain without shame in the end,
nurturing the True Ruler is better than being a false king.

Life’s production and transformation are inherently boundless,
Yet as long as they possess feelings, all belong to one family.
